{{CanonicalID|WIKI-SYSTEM-DIREKTORI-PUTUSAN-MA}} == Knowledge Metadata == * '''Title:''' Direktori Putusan Mahkamah Agung: National Open Judicial Repository, Case Law Transparency, and Legal Informatics Portal * '''Canonical Topic:''' Direktori Putusan (Supreme Court Judgment Directory) * '''Topic Type:''' System / National Portal / Public Legal Repository * '''Jurisdiction:''' Indonesia & Global Comparative * '''Legal Domain:''' Legal Informatics, Open Government Data, Case Law, Judicial Transparency, Privacy & Data Protection * '''Status:''' Stable Architecture / Active National Legal Repository * '''Last Reviewed:''' 2026-08-27 * '''Next Review Recommended:''' 2027-08-27 * '''Primary Sources:''' 1945 Constitution of Indonesia (Art. 24), Law No. 14/2008 on Public Information Disclosure (UU KIP), Law No. 48/2009 on Judicial Power (Principle of Publicly Pronounced Trials), Law No. 27/2022 on Personal Data Protection (UU PDP), Supreme Court Guidelines on Judgment Publication and Anonymization, PERMA No. 1/2019 jo. PERMA No. 7/2022. * '''Related Wiki Pages:''' [[Judicial Knowledge Hub]], [[Supreme Court of Indonesia (Mahkamah Agung RI)]], [[Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy (Pustrajak)]], [[Master System Design Blueprint]], [[Court Modernization & Legal Informatics]], [[Evidence-Based Judicial Policy]] == Core Definition == ** Direktori Putusan** is the official, publicly accessible national digital repository and open-data portal maintained by the Supreme Court of the Republic of Indonesia (*Mahkamah Agung RI*) that archives, indexes, anonymizes, and publishes millions of written judicial decisions and verdicts rendered across all four specialized court branches nationwide. * **Simple Definition:** The official online database where anyone can search, read, and download millions of court judgments and legal verdicts issued by judges across Indonesia. * **Legal / Technical Definition:** The master web-based judicial information portal fulfilling statutory public transparency mandates (Law No. 14/2008 UU KIP and Law No. 48/2009), integrating automated text anonymization filters, structured metadata tagging, full-text search engines, and Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) for legal research and jurimetric analysis. * **Plain-Language Explanation:** It acts as the ultimate open library of Indonesian case law, allowing citizens, lawyers, scholars, and judges to inspect past court rulings, track judicial precedents, and ensure transparency in how justice is administered. == Why It Matters == * **Guarantees Judicial Transparency:** Upholds the constitutional and statutory mandate that all court trials and judgments must be pronounced openly to the public (*sidang terbuka untuk umum*). * **Fosters Jurisprudential Consistency:** Enables lower court judges, legal practitioners, and scholars to study Supreme Court jurisprudence and regional appellate precedents, promoting uniform legal interpretation. * **Powers Evidence-Based Judicial Policy (Pustrajak):** Serves as the primary big-data corpus for jurimetric studies, judicial performance evaluations, and empirical legal research. * **Protects Citizen Privacy via Anonymization:** Implements strict data masking protocols to redact sensitive personal identifiers (such as national ID numbers, addresses, and victim details) in compliance with personal data protection laws. == Key Principles == ; Principle of Open Public Access to Judicial Information (Asas Keterbukaan Informasi Peradilan) * **Meaning:** Except for cases strictly mandated by law to be closed to the public (e.g., juvenile matters, sexual assault victim details, or state secrets), all court judgments must be accessible to the public. * **Why It Matters:** Essential democratic safeguard against corruption and secret tribunals. * **Legal Basis / Source:** Law No. 14 of 2008 on Public Information Disclosure (UU KIP); Law No. 48 of 2009 Art. 13. * **Related Concepts:** Open government data, public transparency, right to information. ; Principle of Mandatory Privacy Redaction and Anonymization (Asas Anonimisasi Wajib Data Pribadi) * **Meaning:** Prior to publication in the Direktori Putusan, automated and manual redaction protocols must strip all identifying personal data of vulnerable litigants, witnesses, and minors. * **Why It Matters:** Balances the public's right to legal transparency with the individual's constitutional right to privacy and personal data protection. * **Legal Basis / Source:** Law No. 27 of 2022 on Personal Data Protection (UU PDP); Supreme Court Publication Guidelines. * **Related Concepts:** Data masking, privacy protection, anonymization filters. ; Principle of Jurisprudential Traceability (Asas Keterlacakan Yurisprudensi) * **Meaning:** Every judgment must be indexed with standardized metadata (case number, chamber type, presiding judge, legal category, and statutory articles applied) to enable exact legal cross-referencing. * **Why It Matters:** Ensures legal researchers and judges can reliably track the historical evolution of specific legal doctrines. * **Legal Basis / Source:** Supreme Court Informatics Standards; SEMA Chamber System Directives. * **Related Concepts:** Case law indexing, metadata tagging, searchable legal repository. == Legal / Institutional Framework == 
1945 Constitution of the Republic of Indonesia (Right to Information & Open Trials)
       ↓
Statutory Disclosure Mandates:
- Law No. 14 of 2008 on Public Information Disclosure (UU KIP)
- Law No. 48 of 2009 on Judicial Power (Open Pronouncement Principle)
- Law No. 27 of 2022 on Personal Data Protection (UU PDP)
       ↓
Supreme Court Administrative Directives & Publication Protocols:
- Chief Justice Decrees on Judgment Upload Mandates for All Courts
- Automated & Manual Anonymization Rules
       ↓
Direktori Putusan Portal Architecture:
- Ingestion from SIPP & Court Registries
- NLP Anonymization & Metadata Indexing Pipeline
- Public Search Interface & API Endpoints for Legal Research
== Indonesia Section == * **Institutional Ownership:** Managed directly by the Supreme Court of Indonesia (Bureau of Legal and Public Relations / *Biro Hukum dan Humas* in coordination with the IT Bureau and Pustrajak). * **Scope and Scale:** The repository archives millions of rulings spanning the four judicial branches: General Courts (*Peradilan Umum*), Religious Courts (*Peradilan Agama*), State Administrative Courts (*PTUN*), and Military Courts (*Peradilan Militer*), ranging from first-instance district courts to supreme cassation decisions. * **Integration with Caseflow Management:** The portal is directly fed by the Court Case Tracking System (*Sistem Informasi Penelusuran Perkara / SIPP*). Once a judge finalizes and signs a verdict, the electronic document flows through the anonymization pipeline before publishing on the public portal. * **Nomenclature:** Direktori Putusan Mahkamah Agung — *Supreme Court Judgment Directory*; Portal Putusan Terbuka — *Open Judgment Portal*. == Comparative Perspective == {| class="wikitable sortable" style="width:100%;" !Jurisdiction !National Judgment Repository Portal !Governing Law / Standard !Anonymization & Privacy Standard !Public Access Level |- |'''Indonesia''' |**Direktori Putusan MA** (putusan.mahkamahagung.go.id) |Law No. 14/2008 (UU KIP) & Law No. 48/2009. |Mandatory redaction of names, addresses, and IDs under UU PDP and Supreme Court guidelines. |Free public access for all published decisions across all four court branches. |- |'''United States''' |**CourtListener / RECAP / PACER** |E-Government Act of 2002 & Federal Rules of Civil Procedure Rule 5.2. |Parties must redact sensitive data (SSNs, minor names, financial accounts) before filing. |PACER fee-based access; free archival platforms like CourtListener and RECAP. |- |'''Singapore''' |**SG Courts — LawNet & Judgments Portal** |Supreme Court of Judicature Act & Public Sector (Governance) Act. |Automated masking of sensitive personal details in family and juvenile proceedings. |Free public judgments portal alongside subscription-based professional LawNet services. |- |'''European Union''' |**CURIA & EUR-Lex** |EU Regulation on Public Access to Documents & GDPR. |Strict GDPR compliance; pseudonymization of individuals in sensitive or criminal cases. |Free multilingual public access to all Court of Justice (CJEU) judgments. |} == Core Operational Pipeline of Direktori Putusan == 
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. UPLOAD & INGESTION FROM SIPP                             │
│ • Finalized judge-signed Word/PDF verdicts uploaded via SIPP│
│ • Automatic association with case metadata (Case No., Judge)│
└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                               │
                               ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 2. NLP ANONYMIZATION & PRIVACY REDACTION                    │
│ • Automated software scans text for NIK, names, & addresses │
│ • Replacement with pseudonyms (e.g., Terdakwa A, Saksi B)   │
└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                               │
                               ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 3. METADATA INDEXING & FULL-TEXT SEARCH PARSING             │
│ • Tagging legal domains (Civil, Criminal, Corruption, HKI)  │
│ • Indexing statutory articles cited within the ruling       │
└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                               │
                               ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 4. PUBLICATION & RAG VECTOR EMBEDDINGS                      │
│ • Instant deployment to public putusan.mahkamahagung.go.id  │
│ • Vector embedding ingestion for Judicial Knowledge Hub RAG │
└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
== Important Decisions & Regulatory Milestones == * Decision: Supreme Court Administrative Mandate on Universal Judgment Publication * *Issuing Body:* Mahkamah Agung RI (Office of the Chief Justice) * *Instrument Reference:* SK KMA (Supreme Court Decree) on Mandatory Judgment Uploads * *Legal Principle:* Every first-instance, appellate, and supreme court unit nationwide must upload their finalized written judgments to the Direktori Putusan within statutory time limits following verdict pronouncement. * *Why It Matters:* Eliminated localized information hoarding and transformed Indonesian jurisprudence into a fully searchable national database. * *Official Source:* Mahkamah Agung Official Gazette. == Key Legislation & Standards == * Instrument: Law on Public Information Disclosure (UU KIP) * *Number / Year:* Law No. 14 of 2008 * *Jurisdiction:* Indonesia * *Status:* In force * *Relevant Provisions:* Mandates that state institutions proactively publish public documents, including court decisions, while protecting personal privacy. * *Official Source:* State Gazette of the Republic of Indonesia. * Instrument: Law on Personal Data Protection (UU PDP) * *Number / Year:* Law No. 27 of 2022 * *Jurisdiction:* Indonesia * *Status:* In force * *Relevant Provisions:* Mandatory protection of personal data identifiers during public institutional data publishing. == Timeline == {| class="wikitable sortable" style="width:100%;" !Date !Milestone / Portal Evolution !Significance |- |'''2008-04-30''' |Enactment of Law No. 14/2008 (UU KIP) |Established the statutory right of public access to state documents and court rulings. |- |'''2009-10-29''' |Enactment of Law No. 48/2009 on Judicial Power |Reaffirmed open trial pronouncement principles and institutional transparency. |- |'''2012-01-15''' |Official Launch of Direktori Putusan Portal |Centralized online publication of Supreme Court and lower court verdicts into a searchable web archive. |- |'''2022-10-17''' |Enactment of Law No. 27/2022 (UU PDP) |Strengthened privacy redaction and anonymization requirements for public court document archives. |} == Debates & Controversies == * Debate: Complete Openness vs. Privacy and Reputational Protection * *Position A (Radical Transparency Advocates):* Every detail of a trial, including unredacted names and corporate disputes, must be fully public to ensure accountability and expose judicial corruption. * *Position B (Privacy & Rehabilitation Advocates):* Overly accessible unredacted judgments can permanently stigmatize rehabilitated offenders, expose victims of crime, and compromise sensitive business trade secrets. * *Evidence:* Ongoing debates regarding Google indexing of old criminal verdicts and the right to be forgotten. * *Current Status:* Regulated through strict anonymization guidelines: while the legal reasoning and outcome remain transparent, personal identifiers of vulnerable parties are masked in compliance with UU PDP. == Rule-of-Law Connection == * *Judicial Transparency:* Open access to judgments allows academic scholars, journalists, and civil society to audit judicial quality and impartiality. * *Legal Certainty:* Lawyers and citizens can inspect how courts interpret specific statutes in similar past disputes. * *Public Accountability:* Eliminates hidden judicial decisions and ensures the justice system operates under public scrutiny. == AI & Future of Law == * *RAG Integration with Judicial Knowledge Hub:* The Direktori Putusan corpus serves as the core training and retrieval base for AI legal assistants supporting judges and policy analysts. * *Automated Jurimetric Case Analytics:* Machine learning models analyzing millions of published verdicts to track sentencing trends, judicial disposition times, and regional statutory interpretation variances. * *Advanced Natural Language Redaction:* Deploying state-of-the-art NLP models to automatically identify and mask sensitive personal data with 99.9% accuracy prior to publication. == Common Misconceptions == * *Myth:* The Direktori Putusan contains only Supreme Court cassation rulings. * *Reality:* The repository hosts millions of judgments from *all tiers of the judiciary*, including district courts (*Pengadilan Negeri/Agama*), high courts (*Pengadilan Tinggi*), and the Supreme Court. * *Source:* Direktori Putusan Portal Architecture. * *Myth:* Publishing a court judgment online violates privacy laws. * *Reality:* Publishing judgments is a statutory duty under UU KIP and Law 48/2009, provided sensitive personal identifiers are properly anonymized in accordance with UU PDP. * *Source:* Law No. 14/2008; Law No. 27/2022. == Practical Example == * *Scenario:* A corporate lawyer in Surabaya needs to research how commercial courts interpret force majeure clauses in supply contracts following recent economic disruptions. * *Question:* How does the lawyer utilize the Direktori Putusan to build the legal argument? * *Applicable Principle:* Jurisprudential Traceability & Open Access (Direktori Putusan Portal). * *Analysis:* 1. The lawyer accesses `putusan.mahkamahagung.go.id`. 2. Uses advanced filters to search for commercial dispute verdicts (*Sengketa Perdata Niaga*) containing keywords like "force majeure" and Article 1245 Civil Code. 3. Reviews multiple appellate and Supreme Court rulings to identify consistent patterns in judicial reasoning (*ratio decidendi*). 4. Cites the relevant precedents in the legal brief. * *Limitation:* Published decisions serve as persuasive precedents and interpretive guides, but Indonesian law is primarily statute-based and does not operate under strict common law *stare decisis*. == Key Terms == {| class="wikitable" style="width:100%;" !Term !Definition !Related Term |- |'''Direktori Putusan''' |The Supreme Court's official online repository publishing millions of written court judgments from across Indonesia. |Open Data, Case Law |- |'''Anonimisasi (Anonymization)''' |The data protection process of masking or redacting personal identifiers (names, addresses, NIK) in published court documents. |UU PDP, Privacy Redaction |- |'''SIPP''' |*Sistem Informasi Penelusuran Perkara* — the court case tracking system that feeds finalized electronic judgments into the Direktori Putusan. |Case Management, e-Court |- |'''Hak Uji Materiil''' |Material review; the Supreme Court mechanism for reviewing subordinate regulations against higher statutes using judicial precedent databases. |Supreme Court Review, Legal Certainty |} == Related Wiki Pages == * [[Judicial Knowledge Hub]] * [[Supreme Court of Indonesia (Mahkamah Agung RI)]] * [[Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy (Pustrajak)]] * [[Master System Design Blueprint]] * [[Court Modernization & Legal Informatics]] * [[Evidence-Based Judicial Policy]] == Knowledge Relationships == * '''Direktori Putusan''' → *is maintained by* → [[Supreme Court of Indonesia (Mahkamah Agung RI)]] * '''Direktori Putusan''' → *feeds data to* → [[Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy (Pustrajak)]] & [[Judicial Knowledge Hub]] * '''Direktori Putusan''' → *governed by* → [[Law No. 14/2008 (UU KIP)]] & [[Law No. 27/2022 (UU PDP)]] * '''Direktori Putusan''' → *integrated with* → [[Master System Design Blueprint]] & [[SIPP]] * '''Direktori Putusan''' → *supports* → [[Evidence-Based Judicial Policy]] & [[Court Modernization & Legal Informatics]] == Sources RI. # Pustrajak Mahkamah Agung RI, *Analisis Big Data Direktori Putusan untuk Riset Jurimetrik dan Kebijakan Peradilan*, 2026. # Institute for Criminal Justice Reform (ICJR), *Assessment of Judicial = Juvenile Case Diversion =
Indicator 1.10 measures the percentage of juvenile cases successfully resolved through diversion.

== Formula ==
<nowiki><math> \frac{\text{Juvenile cases successfully resolved through diversion}} {\text{Juvenile cases that completed the diversion process}} \times100\% </math></nowiki>

== Strategic Purpose ==
The indicator measures compliance with diversion procedures under applicable legislation.

== Data Quality Note ==
The Renstra's formula specifically uses juvenile cases that have completed the diversion process as the denominator.

wikitext:

= Judicial Education =
'''Judicial education''' concerns the systematic development of knowledge, skills, judgment, ethics, competencies, and professional capacity of judicial personnel.

== Objectives ==
Judicial education may address:

* Legal knowledge
* Judicial reasoning
* Procedure
* Evidence
* Ethics
* Leadership
* Court management
* Technology
* Research
* Communication
* Emerging legal issues

== Lifelong Learning ==
Judicial education can be understood as a continuous process:

'''ENTRY''' → '''FOUNDATIONAL TRAINING''' → '''PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT''' → '''SPECIALIZATION''' → '''LEADERSHIP''' → '''CONTINUOUS LEARNING'''

== Competency Framework ==
A judicial competency framework may include:

* Legal competency
* Analytical competency
* Ethical competency
* Procedural competency
* Digital competency
* Research competency
* Leadership competency
* Communication competency

== AI Competency ==
The increasing use of AI creates a potential need for:

* AI literacy
* Prompt literacy
* Verification skills
* Data literacy
* Bias awareness
* Privacy awareness
* AI governance
* Human oversight

AI competency should not be equated with technical programming ability.

== Knowledge Management ==
Judicial education can be connected to judicial knowledge management through:

'''LEARN''' → '''APPLY''' → '''CREATE KNOWLEDGE''' → '''SHARE''' → '''UPDATE'''

== Digital Learning ==
Potential mechanisms include:

* Learning management systems
* Online courses
* Podcasts
* Video learning
* Knowledge repositories
* Wikis
* Simulations
* AI-assisted learning

== Evaluation ==
Education programs should ideally distinguish:

* Participation
* Learning
* Competency
* Application
* Institutional outcomes

Completion of training does not automatically demonstrate competency.

* [[Judicial Reform]]
* [[Artificial Intelligence and the Judiciary]]
* [[AI Competency Framework]]
* [[Knowledge Management]]

title: EDU-0002
wikitext:

= AI Competency Framework =
The '''AI Competency Framework''' provides a conceptual structure for developing the knowledge, skills, judgment, and governance capacity required to use artificial intelligence responsibly in judicial environments.

This framework is a proposed knowledge model and does not represent an official competency standard unless separately validated and adopted.

'''[HUMAN VERIFICATION REQUIRED]'''

== Competency Architecture ==
The framework may contain six dimensions:
{| class="wikitable"
!Dimension
!Core Capability
|-
|AI Literacy
|Understand AI concepts and limitations
|-
|Prompt Literacy
|Communicate effectively with AI systems
|-
|Verification
|Evaluate AI outputs against evidence
|-
|Data Literacy
|Understand data quality, provenance, and risks
|-
|Ethics and Rights
|Identify rights and ethical implications
|-
|Governance
|Apply institutional controls and accountability
|}

== Level 1 — Awareness ==
Learner can:

* Explain basic AI concepts
* Identify common AI use cases
* Recognize hallucination
* Recognize limitations

== Level 2 — Assisted Use ==
Learner can:

* Use AI for low-risk tasks
* Write structured prompts
* Summarize documents
* Generate research questions
* Check outputs against source material

== Level 3 — Professional Use ==
Learner can:

* Integrate AI into professional workflows
* Evaluate output quality
* Detect unsupported claims
* Manage citations
* Apply data and privacy principles

== Level 4 — Governance ==
Learner can:

* Assess AI risks
* Design governance controls
* Evaluate vendors
* Define human oversight
* Develop AI policies
* Conduct impact assessments

== Level 5 — Strategic Leadership ==
Learner can:

* Develop institutional AI strategy
* Design transformation roadmaps
* Align AI with judicial values
* Govern organizational adoption
* Evaluate institutional outcomes

== Verification Competency ==
A core principle is:

'''AI OUTPUT → SOURCE → EVIDENCE → HUMAN JUDGMENT'''

AI fluency without verification competency creates significant risk.

== Judicial Application ==
Potential audiences include:

* Judges
* Court staff
* Researchers
* Judicial educators
* Administrators
* Policy makers
* IT personnel

Different roles require different competency profiles.

== Assessment ==
Possible assessment methods include:

* Knowledge tests
* Prompt exercises
* Source verification
* Case simulations
* AI risk assessment
* Practical projects
* Portfolio assessment

* [[Judicial Education]]
* [[Artificial Intelligence and the Judiciary]]
* [[Judicial AI Governance]]
* [[Fundamental Rights]]
* [[Knowledge Management]]

= Electronic Court =
'''Electronic court''' refers to judicial services and processes supported by electronic or digital systems.

The precise scope and legal basis depend on the jurisdiction.

'''[HUMAN VERIFICATION REQUIRED]'''

== Potential Components ==
Electronic court systems may include:

* Electronic registration
* Electronic filing
* Electronic payment
* Electronic notifications
* Digital document management
* Scheduling
* Online hearings
* Digital case tracking

== Access to Justice ==
Electronic services may reduce barriers related to:

* Travel
* Time
* Administrative procedures
* Physical access

They may also create digital exclusion risks.

== Security ==
Important considerations include:

* Authentication
* Authorization
* Encryption
* Integrity
* Availability
* Audit logs
* Incident response

== AI Integration ==
AI may potentially be integrated into low-risk supporting functions such as:

* Search
* Classification
* Translation
* Summarization
* Helpdesk services

High-impact uses require additional governance.

Law No. 1/2024 (UU ITE), PERMA No. 3/2018 (Initial e-Court Framework), PERMA No. 1/2019 jo. PERMA No. 7/2022 (Electronic Case Administration and Trials), PERMA No. 8/2022 (Electronic Cassation and Judicial Review Administration), SEMA No. 1/2023 (Chamber Plenary Directives). * '''Related Wiki Pages:''' [[Judicial Knowledge Hub]], [[Court Modernization & Legal Informatics]], [[Supreme Court Benchbooks/Chapter 2]], [[Module 2: Electronic Evidence Standards]], [[Evidence-Based Judicial Policy]], [[Small Claims Procedure (Gugatan Sederhana)]] == Core Definition == '''Electronic Court Administration (e-Court)''' is a comprehensive procedural and technological ecosystem deployed by the judiciary to manage the full lifecycle of civil, religious, and state administrative cases electronically—spanning case filing (e-Filing), fee assessment and payment (e-Payment), official notification and summons (e-Summons), trial pleadings and evidence exchange (e-Litigation), and appellate/cassation dossier transfer (e-Berpemberkasan). * '''Simple Definition:''' The official digital portal and court management system that allows lawyers, institutions, and citizens to file lawsuits, pay court fees, receive summonses, exchange pleadings, and receive judgments online without physical court appearances. * '''Legal / Technical Definition:''' An integrated judicial service platform established pursuant to Supreme Court Regulations (PERMA No. 1/2019 jo. PERMA No. 7/2022) that provides legally valid electronic workflows, cryptographic user verification, timestamped procedural document exchanges, and automated case tracking across first-instance courts, high courts, and the Supreme Court. * '''Plain-Language Explanation:''' It transforms traditional courthouse counter visits and physical document exchanges into a secure, nationwide digital workflow, making litigation faster, cheaper, and fully auditable. == Why It Matters == * '''Dramatically Lowers Litigation Costs:''' Eliminates high transportation and postal expenses traditionally incurred during physical court summonses, especially across Indonesia's archipelagic geography. * '''Eliminates Bureaucratic Case Delays:''' Standardizes procedural timelines for pleadings (Jawaban, Replik, Duplik) through enforceable electronic countdown schedules. * '''Enhances Judicial Integrity & Anti-Corruption:''' Removes cash transactions and informal clerk-litigant interactions through integrated virtual accounts (e-SKUM) and transparent digital audit trails. * '''Maintains Procedural Certainty:''' Generates cryptographic transmission receipts and immutable timestamps that clearly define statutory deadlines for responses, appeals, and cassation petitions. * '''Ensures Environmental Sustainability:''' Reduces paper consumption by transitioning millions of physical case bundles (Bundel A & Bundel B) into authenticated digital dossiers. == Key Principles == ; Principle of Procedural Equivalence (Asas Kesetaraan Pembuktian & Prosedur Elektronik) * '''Meaning:''' Procedural acts performed through verified e-Court accounts carry the exact same legal validity and consequences as physical filings and in-person courtroom appearances. * '''Why It Matters:''' Protects digital court actions from jurisdictional challenges based solely on their electronic nature. * '''Legal Basis / Source:''' Law No. 11/2008 jo. Law No. 1/2024 Art. 5; PERMA No. 7/2022 Art. 2. * '''Related Concepts:''' Functional equivalence, legal validity of digital pleadings. ; Principle of Verified Electronic Identity (Asas Verifikasi Identitas Pengguna Terdaftar & Lainnya) * '''Meaning:''' Access to e-Court requires multi-factor authentication and validation through professional bar registries (for advocates) or national identity databases (for individuals and legal entities). * '''Why It Matters:''' Prevents unauthorized filings, identity theft, and fraudulent legal representations in court dockets. * '''Legal Basis / Source:''' PERMA No. 7/2022 Arts. 3–5; Law No. 27/2022 (UU PDP). * '''Related Concepts:''' Pengguna Terdaftar, Pengguna Lain, PSrE Certification. ; Principle of Enforceable Procedural Timelines (Asas Kepastian Jadwal Sidang Elektronik) * '''Meaning:''' The procedural calendar (*jadwal sidang*) established by the judge in the e-Litigation system is legally binding; failure to upload pleadings within the prescribed digital window results in the forfeiture of that procedural right. * '''Why It Matters:''' Eliminates arbitrary requests for trial postponements and enforces time discipline on all litigating parties. * '''Legal Basis / Source:''' PERMA No. 7/2022 Art. 20; Law No. 48/2009 Art. 4(2). * '''Related Concepts:''' Dominus litis, procedural forfeiture, court calendar. ; Principle of Digital Inclusivity & Non-Exclusion (Asas Aksesibilitas dan Meja Layanan e-Court) * '''Meaning:''' For unrepresented litigants or individuals lacking digital infrastructure, courts must provide on-site e-Court helpdesks (*Meja e-Court / Posbakum*) to facilitate electronic registration and access. * '''Why It Matters:''' Ensures court modernization does not create a digital divide that restricts access to justice for marginalized populations. * '''Legal Basis / Source:''' 1945 Constitution Art. 28D(1); PERMA No. 7/2022 Art. 8. * '''Related Concepts:''' Access to justice, Pos Bantuan Hukum (Posbakum), digital equity. == Legal / Institutional Framework ==

== Indonesia Section == * '''The Four Core Functional Pillars:''' # '''e-Filing (Pendaftaran Perkara Online):''' Electronic submission of claims (Gugatan), petitions (Permohonan), and small claims (Gugatan Sederhana) along with supporting initial documents in PDF/A format. # '''e-Payment (Pembayaran Panjar Biaya Online):''' Automated generation of electronic payment slips (e-SKUM) connected to multi-channel bank virtual accounts and state treasury settlement systems. # '''e-Summons (Pemanggilan Pihak Secara Elektronik):''' Direct transmission of court summonses and hearing notices to registered digital addresses (email/portal dashboard), which legally binds the recipient upon transmission confirmation. # '''e-Litigation (Persidangan Elektronik):''' Digital execution of the adversarial hearing stages, including: #* Reading of the lawsuit and exceptions; #* Submission of responses (Jawaban), counter-pleas (Replik), and rejoinders (Duplik); #* Upload and cryptographic verification of documentary evidence; #* Delivery of written conclusions (Kesimpulan); #* Pronouncement and electronic delivery of signed judgments (Putusan/Penetapan). * '''User Categories (Klasifikasi Pengguna):''' ** ''Registered Users (Pengguna Terdaftar):'' Licensed advocates whose professional credentials, bar membership, and valid oaths have been verified by High Courts. ** ''Other Users (Pengguna Lain):'' Natural persons (pro se litigants), in-house corporate legal counsels, government agency legal bureaus (Kejaksaan/Kementerian), and court-appointed trustees whose identities are validated via national identity registries (NIK/Dukcapil) or corporate registrations. * '''Expansion to Appellate & Apex Courts (PERMA 8/2022):''' ** Extended the e-Court architecture to Appeals (*Banding*), Cassation (*Kasasi*), and Judicial Review (*Peninjauan Kembali*). ** Trial courts now compile and transmit digital bundles (Bundel A: case documents; Bundel B: procedural minutes and judgments) directly through the Supreme Court digital repository, eliminating months of physical postal transport. == Comparative Perspective == {| class="wikitable sortable" style="width:100%;" !Jurisdiction !Core System Name !Scope of Adjudicative Automation !e-Summons Mechanism !Distinguishing Characteristic |- |'''Indonesia''' |e-Court / e-Litigation (MA RI) |Civil, Religious, State Administrative; integrated with criminal via e-Berpadu. |Mandatory for verified digital users; consent-based for non-registered individual defendants. |Unified portal covering four distinct court jurisdictions under a single apex court administration. |- |'''Singapore''' |eLitigation (Singapore Courts) |Civil, Family, and Commercial across State and Supreme Courts. |Integrated electronic service of process through secure law firm and citizen portals. |Complete document extraction, dynamic electronic hearing bundles, and high automation of pre-trial directions. |- |'''South Korea''' |Electronic Case Filing System (ECFS) |Civil, Family, Administrative, and Patent litigation nationwide. |Automated text/email notifications directing parties to secure court viewing dockets. |Extremely high adoption rate (>90% of civil dockets fully digital); extensive self-service kiosks in courthouses. |- |'''United States''' |CM/ECF (Case Management / Electronic Case Files) |Federal District and Appellate Courts (Civil and Criminal). |Electronic Service of Filing (NEF - Notice of Electronic Filing) automatically binds registered counsel. |Dual-track decentralized model where individual states maintain independent e-filing architectures. |} == Procedural Lifecycle in e-Court ==

== Important Decisions & Chamber Plenary Guidance == ; Decision : Supreme Court Plenary Resolution on Electronic Summons for Unregistered Defendants * '''Issuing Body:''' Mahkamah Agung RI (Civil Chamber Plenary) * '''Instrument / SEMA Ref:''' SEMA No. 1/2023 jo. PERMA No. 7/2022 * '''Legal Principle:''' If a defendant does not consent to electronic litigation during the initial hearing, summonses must be delivered through physical bailiff service; however, if the defendant's verified electronic address is registered in a public registry or contract, the court may authorize electronic service. * '''Why It Matters:''' Balances modern procedural efficiency with the constitutional right to proper notice for non-digitally registered citizens. * '''Official Source:''' Supreme Court Annual Chamber Reports. ; Decision : Validity of Electronic Default Judgment (Putusan Verstek Elektronik) * '''Issuing Body:''' Mahkamah Agung RI * '''Case Context:''' First-instance civil debt claim where the defendant received an electronic summons but failed to submit a digital response within the procedural calendar window. * '''Legal Principle:''' Proper electronic service confirmed by system delivery logs constitutes valid statutory notice; failure to submit a response without justification permits the panel to issue an electronic default judgment (*verstek*). * '''Why It Matters:''' Prevents uncooperative defendants from stalling litigation by ignoring electronic notifications. * '''Official Source:''' Jurisprudensi Mahkamah Agung RI. == Key Legislation & Standards == ; Instrument : Supreme Court Regulation on Electronic Case Administration and Hearings * '''Number / Year:''' PERMA No. 1/2019 jo. PERMA No. 7/2022 * '''Jurisdiction:''' Indonesia * '''Status:''' In force * '''Relevant Provisions:''' Articles 1–30 (Operational procedures for e-Filing, e-Payment, e-Summons, and e-Litigation across civil, religious, and state administrative courts). * '''Official Source:''' Mahkamah Agung Official Gazette. ; Instrument : Supreme Court Regulation on Electronic Administration of Cassation and Judicial Review * '''Number / Year:''' PERMA No. 8 of 2022 * '''Jurisdiction:''' Indonesia * '''Status:''' In force * '''Relevant Provisions:''' Mandatory digitization and electronic transmission of appellate bundles (Bundel A and B) to the Supreme Court. * '''Official Source:''' Mahkamah Agung Official Gazette. == Timeline == {| class="wikitable sortable" style="width:100%;" !Date !Milestone / Legal Event !Significance |- |'''2018-04-05''' |Promulgation of PERMA No. 3/2018 |Launched the e-Court platform, introducing e-Filing, e-Payment, and e-Summons for advocates. |- |'''2019-08-08''' |Promulgation of PERMA No. 1/2019 |Upgraded e-Court to include e-Litigation, allowing online exchange of legal pleadings and digital judgment delivery. |- |'''2022-11-15''' |Enactment of PERMA No. 7/2022 |Comprehensive procedural overhaul; expanded e-Court access to non-advocate litigants and modernized electronic summonses. |- |'''2022-12-20''' |Promulgation of PERMA No. 8/2022 |Extended electronic case administration to the apex court for Cassation and Judicial Review proceedings. |- |'''2023-01-01''' |Nationwide Mandatory Implementation |Full mandatory transition across all general, religious, and state administrative courts across Indonesia. |} == Debates & Controversies == ; Debate : Consent Requirement for Non-Registered Defendants (Prinsip Persetujuan Pihak Tergugat) * '''Position A (Mandatory Universal e-Litigation):''' Electronic proceedings should be mandatory for all parties once a lawsuit is registered to maximize efficiency and prevent uncooperative defendants from forcing costly physical hearings. * '''Position B (Consent-Based Due Process):''' Due process requires that non-advocate defendants explicitly consent to electronic hearings; forcing e-Litigation on individuals without digital devices or stable internet access infringes upon their constitutional right to a fair hearing. * '''Evidence:''' National implementation data showing hybrid proceedings where hearings alternate between physical and digital formats based on party consent. * '''Current Status:''' Under PERMA No. 7/2022, registered advocates are automatically subject to e-Litigation, whereas individual non-advocate defendants must provide written consent during the first hearing (or after receiving a physical first summons). == Rule-of-Law Connection == * '''Equal Access to Justice:''' Removes severe archipelagic transport barriers, allowing litigants on remote islands to enforce rights without travelling to provincial capitals. * '''Transparency & Anti-Corruption:''' Eliminates opaque backroom communications and informal fees by standardizing all transactions through public banking APIs and traceable system logs. * '''Speed and Proportionality:''' Implements the constitutional mandate of simple, fast, and low-cost justice (*peradilan sederhana, cepat, dan biaya ringan*). == AI & Future of Law == * '''Automated Docket Screening:''' AI-assisted pre-examination modules checking formal requirements (powers of attorney, court fee calculations, jurisdiction matches) upon electronic submission. * '''Smart Calendar Optimization:''' Algorithmic scheduling that coordinates hearing slots, preventing double-booking for judicial panels and legal counsel. * '''Cryptographic Verification & Timestamping:''' Integration of national digital certification authorities (PSrE / BSrE) to ensure electronic judgments are tamper-proof and verifiable via instant QR-code scans. == Common Misconceptions == ; Myth : e-Court completely eliminates physical court hearings for all stages of litigation. * '''Reality:''' While pleadings (Gugatan, Jawaban, Replik, Duplik) and conclusions are exchanged electronically, evidentiary stages—specifically physical inspection of original documents and witness/expert cross-examinations—can still be held in-person in open court if deemed necessary by the panel or requested by the parties. * '''Source:''' PERMA No. 7/2022 Art. 24. ; Myth : An electronic summons (e-Summons) sent via email can be ignored if the recipient does not open the email. * '''Reality:''' Under PERMA No. 7/2022, an electronic summons sent to a verified digital address is deemed legally served upon successful transmission by the court system, regardless of whether the recipient chooses to open it. * '''Source:''' PERMA No. 7/2022 Art. 17. == Practical Example == * '''Scenario:''' A small business in Surabaya files a commercial claim against a supplier in Medan. The plaintiff's attorney registers the lawsuit via the e-Court portal at 23:00 WIB on the final day before the contractual limitation period expires. * '''Legal Question:''' Is the filing legally valid and timely, and how are the fees processed? * '''Applicable Principle:''' Procedural Equivalence & Timestamping (PERMA No. 7/2022 Art. 9; Law No. 11/2008). * '''Possible Analysis:''' # The system generates an immediate cryptographic timestamp upon document upload, securing the filing date within the limitation period. # An automated e-SKUM is generated; the attorney settles the filing fee through online banking. # The Surabaya District Court receives the verified dossier, registers the case in SIPP, and transmits an electronic summons to the defendant’s verified e-Court portal. # Both parties exchange Replik and Duplik directly via their online dashboards without travelling between Java and Sumatra. * '''Limitation:''' The plaintiff must ensure the uploaded PDF files are readable and properly formatted; corrupted files must be re-uploaded upon court notice. == Key Terms == {| class="wikitable" style="width:100%;" !Term !Definition !Related Term |- |'''e-SKUM''' |''Surat Kuasa Untuk Membayar Elektronik'' — an automated digital invoice and payment slip for court fees generated within e-Court. |e-Payment, Virtual Account |- |'''Pengguna Terdaftar''' |Verified licensed advocates registered within the Supreme Court e-Court system to represent clients electronically. |Advokat, Pengguna Lain |- |'''Jadwal Sidang Elektronik''' |A binding digital calendar established by the judicial panel setting immutable deadlines for uploading pleadings in e-Litigation. |Procedural Calendar, Courtflow |- |'''Bundel A & Bundel B Elektronik''' |Standardized digital case dossiers containing all procedural filings, exhibits, court minutes, and signed judgments transmitted for appellate review. |PERMA 8/2022, e-Berpemberkasan |} == Related Wiki Pages == * [[Judicial Knowledge Hub]] * [[Court Modernization & Legal Informatics]] * [[Supreme Court Benchbooks/Chapter 2]] * [[Module 2: Electronic Evidence Standards]] * [[Evidence-Based Judicial Policy]] * [[Small Claims Procedure (Gugatan Sederhana)]] == Knowledge Relationships == * '''Electronic Court Administration (e-Court)''' → ''is a'' → [[Judicial Digital Platform]] & [[Caseflow System]] * '''Electronic Court Administration (e-Court)''' → ''implements'' → [[PERMA No. 7/2022]] & [[PERMA No. 8/2022]] * '''Electronic Court Administration (e-Court)''' → ''governed by'' → [[Law No. 48/2009]] & [[Law No. 11/2008 jo. Debate: Common Law Terminology Adaptation vs. Strict Civil Law Literalism * *Position A (Common Law Adaptation):* Translators should use established common law legal terms (e.g., "judicial review" or "statutory interpretation") so foreign lawyers immediately understand the concepts. * *Position B (Strict Civil Law Fidelity):* Using common law terms can introduce foreign legal assumptions that do not exist in Indonesia's civil law framework; translators must use precise functional equivalents. * *Evidence:* Comparative legal analysis debates on civilian vs. common law translations. * *Current Status:* Balanced under Pustrajak standards: functional comparative equivalents are utilized while explicitly preserving the civilian structural context of Indonesian law. == Rule-of-Law Connection == * *Global Legal Transparency:* Standardized English terminology allows international jurists and investors to review Indonesian judicial frameworks accurately, reinforcing international trust and the rule of law (*Rechtsstaat*). * *Cross-Border Clarity:* Eliminates misunderstandings during international mutual legal assistance and comparative research. == AI & Future of Law == * *English RAG AI Vector Integration:* Indexing standardized English lexicon entries into RAG AI databases to ensure foreign researchers querying the system receive flawless doctrinal translations. * *Automated Comparative Checking:* AI tools scanning international research papers for non-standard English phrasing and suggesting approved Global Explainer equivalents. == Common Misconceptions == * *Myth:* The English portal is a casual conversational dictionary for general English slang. * *Reality:* The English portal is a rigorous institutional lexicon containing specialized comparative legal, constitutional, and technological informatics terminology. * *Source:* Pustrajak Lexicographical Standards. * *Myth:* Translating Indonesian legal terms into English means ignoring Indonesian civil law traditions. * *Reality:* The portal explicitly preserves civil law doctrinal structures while providing accurate comparative English terminology for international scholarship. * *Source:* Comparative Law Doctrine. == Practical Example == * *Scenario:* An international research fellow collaborating with Pustrajak is writing an English-language policy brief on Indonesian court modernization and needs to cite digital case tracking properly. * *Question:* How does the English portal assist the researcher? * *Applicable Principle:* Legal Informatics & Court Technology Vocabulary (English Portal). * *Analysis:* 1. The researcher consults the English portal within the Global Explainer for approved terminology regarding court databases. 2. The portal provides the standardized translation "SIPP (Case Information Tracking System)" alongside its technical and administrative definition. 3. The researcher incorporates the approved phrasing into the international policy brief, ensuring professional academic accuracy. * *Limitation:* The portal supplies approved terminology guidelines, but formulating complex international comparative arguments requires specialized subject-matter expertise. == Key Terms == {| class="wikitable" style="width:100%;" !Term !Definition !Related Term |- |'''English Portal''' |The international comparative lexicography module within the Global Explainer repository. |Global Explainer, Translation |- |'''Functional Equivalence''' |Translating legal concepts based on their operational legal effect in court rather than literal wording. |Comparative Law, Lexicography |- |'''Legal Lexicography''' |The specialized practice of compiling, defining, and standardizing legal dictionaries and glossaries. |Terminology, Standards |- |'''Doctrinal Mapping''' |Matching equivalent legal concepts across different legal families (civil law vs. common law). |Comparative Judiciary, Pustrajak |} == Related Wiki Pages == * * [[Global Explainer]] * [[All Languages]] * [[Indonesian]] * [[Comparative Judiciary]] == Knowledge Relationships == * '''English (Language Portal)''' → *is a module of* → [[Global Explainer]] * '''English (Language Portal)''' → *is managed by* → [[Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy (Pustrajak)]] & [[Supreme Court of Indonesia (Mahkamah Agung RI)]] * '''English (Language Portal)''' → *standardizes terminology for* → [[All Languages]] & [[Comparative Judiciary]] * '''English (Language Portal)''' → *aligns with* → [[Master Epistemic & Quality Control Standard]] & [[Master Philosophical & Methodological Standard]] * '''English (Language Portal)''' → *upholds principles of* → [[Law No. 48/2009 (Judicial Power)]] == Sources == === Tier 1 — Official / Primary Sources === # = Entity =
An '''entity''' is a uniquely identifiable object represented within the Judicial Knowledge Wiki.

== Entity Examples ==
Entities may include:

* Court
* Judge
* Case
* Decision
* Law
* Regulation
* Procedure
* Right
* Institution
* Dataset
* AI system
* Research project

== Entity Identity ==
Each important entity should ideally have:

* Stable ID
* Preferred name
* Alternative names
* Entity type
* Jurisdiction
* Date information
* Source
* Status

== Entity vs Concept ==
An entity generally refers to an identifiable object.

A concept may represent an abstract idea.

For example:

'''Mahkamah Agung RI''' → institution/entity

'''Judicial Independence''' → concept

The distinction may depend on the knowledge model.

== Entity Linking ==
Different pages referring to the same entity should preferably link to one canonical page.

== AI Use ==
Explicit entity identification improves:

* Retrieval
* Disambiguation
* Graph construction
* Entity resolution
* AI grounding

wikitext:

= Evidence =
'''Evidence''' refers to information, material, testimony, or other admissible means used within a legal proceeding to establish or challenge facts.

The rules governing admissibility, relevance, burden, and evaluation vary by jurisdiction and proceeding.

'''[HUMAN VERIFICATION REQUIRED]'''

== Evidence Knowledge Model ==
Evidence may be represented through:

'''SOURCE''' → '''FACT PROPOSITION''' → '''RELEVANCE''' → '''ADMISSIBILITY''' → '''WEIGHT''' → '''JUDICIAL FINDING'''

This is an analytical model and not a statement of universal law.

== Evidence Types ==
Depending on the applicable legal system, evidence may include:

* Testimony
* Documents
* Physical evidence
* Digital evidence
* Expert evidence
* Electronic records
* Other legally recognized forms

== Evidence and AI ==
AI may assist with:

* Document classification
* Search
* Transcription
* Extraction
* Timeline construction
* Duplicate detection

AI-generated interpretation must not automatically be treated as evidence.

== Digital Evidence ==
Digital evidence may require consideration of:

* Authenticity
* Integrity
* Provenance
* Chain of custody
* Metadata
* Accessibility

Specific requirements must be verified against applicable law.

title: Evidence Architecture
Evidence Level
wikitext:
{{Knowledge|id=GOV-0001|type=Evidence Classification|domain=Knowledge Governance|status=DRAFT|version=1.0|evidence=E0 — Unverified|ai_readiness=5 — Machine-Readable|last_verified=}}

= Evidence Level =
'''Evidence Level''' classifies the strength and verification status of information contained within a knowledge object.

== Proposed Scale ==
{| class="wikitable"
!Level
!Meaning
|-
|E0
|Unverified claim
|-
|E1
|Source identified
|-
|E2
|Source independently located
|-
|E3
|Claim checked against source
|-
|E4
|Expert/human verification
|-
|E5
|Institutionally authoritative or formally validated
|}
This scale is a proposed Wiki governance mechanism, not a universal evidentiary standard.

== Important Distinction ==
'''Evidence Level ≠ Legal Authority'''

A highly authoritative source may provide strong legal authority, while a scholarly source may provide analytical evidence without being legally binding.

== Application ==
Every substantive claim should ideally have an evidence level.

== AI Use ==
AI systems should preferentially retrieve high-evidence-level content when answering high-stakes questions.

== Updating ==
Evidence levels may change when:

* New sources appear
* Law changes
* A decision is overturned
* Verification is completed
* An error is discovered

= Evidence-Based Judicial Policy =
'''Evidence-Based Judicial Policy''' is an approach to policy development that systematically uses relevant evidence alongside law, institutional values, professional judgment, and stakeholder considerations.

== Policy Cycle ==
'''PROBLEM''' → '''EVIDENCE''' → '''OPTIONS''' → '''ASSESSMENT''' → '''DECISION''' → '''IMPLEMENTATION''' → '''EVALUATION'''

== Evidence Types ==
Potential evidence includes:

* Legal evidence
* Empirical evidence
* Administrative data
* Research
* Comparative evidence
* Expert knowledge
* User experience

== Evidence Hierarchy ==
Not every evidence type answers the same question.

The decision-maker should consider:

* Relevance
* Quality
* Reliability
* Timeliness
* Context

== AI Role ==
AI can assist with evidence synthesis.

However:

'''AI SYNTHESIS ≠ EVIDENCE'''

The underlying sources must remain traceable.

title: Evidence-Based Judicial Policy
wikitext:
{{CanonicalID|WIKI-JUDICIAL-EVIDENCE-BASED-JUDICIAL-POLICY}} == Knowledge Metadata == * '''Title:''' Evidence-Based Judicial Policy: Empirical Legal Studies, Regulatory Impact Assessment, and Data-Driven Court Governance * '''Canonical Topic:''' Evidence-Based Judicial Policy & Institutional Research * '''Topic Type:''' Concept / Policy Framework / Institutional Standard * '''Jurisdiction:''' Indonesia & Global Comparative * '''Legal Domain:''' Judicial Administration, Legal Policy, Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA), Jurimetrics, Legal Informatics * '''Status:''' Stable Architecture / Active Strategic Framework * '''Last Reviewed:''' 2026-08-27 * '''Next Review Recommended:''' 2027-08-27 * '''Primary Sources:''' 1945 Constitution of Indonesia (Art. 24), Law No. 48/2009 (Judicial Power), Law No. 11/2019 (National System of Science and Technology), Law No. 12/2011 as amended (Lawmaking Standards), Supreme Court Strategic Plans (Renstra MA RI), Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy Guidelines (Pustrajak / Policy Paper Standards). * '''Related Wiki Pages:''' [[Judicial Knowledge Hub]], [[Scholarly Submissions Database/Active Papers]], [[Court Modernization & Legal Informatics]], [[Electronic Court Administration (e-Court)]], [[Supreme Court Benchbooks/Chapter 1]] == Core Definition == ** Evidence-Based Judicial Policy** is an institutional decision-making framework that combines empirical legal research, jurimetric data analytics, comparative jurisprudence, and regulatory impact assessments (RIA) to formulate, evaluate, and revise court regulations, administrative guidelines, and procedural reforms. * **Simple Definition:** The practice of making court rules, administrative policies, and procedural reforms based on verified data, empirical research, and statistical analysis rather than intuition alone. * **Legal / Technical Definition:** The systematic institutional methodology integrating empirical legal studies, caseflow metrics, jurimetric evaluations, and normative legal research to design, monitor, and update Supreme Court Regulations (PERMA), Circular Letters (SEMA), and statutory policy papers (*Naskah Akademik*). * **Plain-Language Explanation:** It ensures that when courts change how they operate or issue rules governing trials, those decisions are backed up by real evidence showing they will actually solve procedural bottlenecks and improve justice. == Why It Matters == * **Improves Procedural Efficiency:** Uses empirical case data to identify structural bottlenecks, trial delays, and backlog causes across district and appellate courts. * **Enhances Regulatory Quality:** Prevents court regulations (PERMAs) from producing unintended negative consequences on litigants, businesses, or judicial independence. * **Strengthens the Rule of Law:** Provides a transparent, auditable empirical foundation for administrative and procedural court reforms. * **Optimizes Resource Allocation:** Directs budgetary resources, technological investments, and judicial training programs toward areas empirically proven to need intervention. == Key Principles == ; Principle of Empirical Primacy and Normative Coherence (Asas Dominasi Empiris dan Koherensi Normatif) * **Meaning:** Policy proposals must be grounded in verified empirical data while remaining strictly coherent with constitutional principles and statutory mandates. * **Why It Matters:** Balances factual realities with constitutional integrity, preventing technocratic policies from violating due process. * **Legal Basis / Source:** Law No. 11/2019 (Sisnas Iptek); Law No. 12/2011 on Lawmaking Standards. * **Related Concepts:** Regulatory impact analysis, normative legal research. ; Principle of Institutional Reflexivity (Asas Refleksivitas Institusional) * **Meaning:** Courts must continuously evaluate the practical socioeconomic and procedural impact of their own regulations through ongoing data monitoring and academic feedback loops. * **Why It Matters:** Prevents outdated or counterproductive administrative rules from persisting indefinitely. * **Legal Basis / Source:** Pustrajak Policy Paper Standards; Supreme Court Strategic Monitoring Frameworks. * **Related Concepts:** Feedback loops, institutional learning. ; Principle of Epistemic Integrity in Research (Asas Integritas Epistemik Riset Kebijakan) * **Meaning:** Data utilized for judicial policy formulation must be transparently sourced, peer-reviewed, and rigorously separated from political or partisan bias. * **Why It Matters:** Protects judicial independence and policy credibility. * **Legal Basis / Source:** Bangalore Principles of Judicial Conduct (Value 6); Scientific Research Standards. * **Related Concepts:** Scholarly submissions, peer appraisal, verifiability. == Legal / Institutional Framework == 
1945 Constitution of Indonesia (Art. 24 - Judicial Independence & Rule of Law)
       ↓
Law No. 48/2009 (Judicial Power) & Law No. 11/2019 (National Science & Technology System)
       ↓
Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy (Pustrajak MA RI)
       ↓
Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) for Policy Papers & Academic Drafts (Naskah Akademik)
       ↓
Promulgation of Evidence-Based Supreme Court Regulations (PERMA) & Circulars (SEMA)
== Indonesia Section == * **Institutional Anchor:** The Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy (*Pusat Strategi Kebijakan Hukum dan Peradilan* / Pustrajak) within the Supreme Court of Indonesia serves as the primary engine for evidence-based judicial policy research. * **Core Research-to-Policy Pipeline:** 1. *Empirical Identification:* Analyzing case duration, settlement rates, and filing trends across millions of records in SIPP and the Direktori Putusan. 2. *Active Paper Development:* Curating working papers and comparative legal studies through the Scholarly Submissions Database. 3. *Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA):* Evaluating the anticipated costs, procedural adjustments, and access-to-justice impacts of proposed court regulations. 4. *Promulgation & Review:* Submitting evidence-backed Academic Drafts (*Naskah Akademik*) to support the issuance of PERMA, SEMA, or statutory recommendations. * **Nomenclature:** Kebijakan Peradilan Berbasis Bukti — *Evidence-Based Judicial Policy*; Analisis Dampak Regulasi — *Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA)*. == Comparative Perspective == | Jurisdiction | Primary Judicial Policy Research Body | Analytical Approach | Key Focus Area | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Indonesia** | Supreme Court (Pustrajak / Judicial Policy Strategy) | Mixed empirical jurimetrics, comparative law, and active policy papers. | Casebacklog reduction, e-Court adoption impact, and procedural harmonization across 4 court branches. | | **United States** | Federal Judicial Center (FJC) Research Division | Rigorous quantitative empirical studies, controlled field experiments, and workload modeling. | Federal court caseloads, juror utilization, and automated case management metrics. | | **Japan** | Supreme Court of Japan (General Secretariat & Shihō Kenshūjo) | Systematic longitudinal case-tracking and comparative civil procedure monographs. | Civil mediation efficiency (*Chotei*), lay judge (*Saiban-in*) trial dynamics, and judge career retention. | | **European Union** | European Commission for the Efficiency of Justice (CEPEJ) | Comparative statistical evaluation across member states (*CEPEJ Evaluation Reports*). | Judicial budgets, trial length benchmarking, and digital justice tool effectiveness. | == Important Decisions & Regulatory Milestones == * **Policy Initiative:** Institutionalization of Judicial Research and Policy Drafting Standards * *Issuing Body:* Mahkamah Agung RI (Pustrajak) * *Instrument Reference:* Pustrajak Research Guidelines & Policy Paper Standards (Pustrajak 2026) * *Legal Principle:* Mandatory integration of empirical data and comparative regulatory impact assessments into the drafting of all major Supreme Court administrative policies. * *Why It Matters:* Formalized the transition from intuition-based rule-making to systematic, data-driven judicial policy. * *Official Source:* Mahkamah Agung Policy Reports. == Key Legislation & Standards == * **Instrument:** Law on the National System of Science and Technology * *Number / Year:* Law No. 11 of 2019 * *Jurisdiction:* Indonesia * *Status:* In force * *Relevant Provisions:* Standards for scientific data governance, institutional research repositories, and empirical research ethics. * *Official Source:* State Gazette of the Republic of Indonesia. * **Instrument:** Law on Lawmaking Standards * *Number / Year:* Law No. 12 of 2008 jo. Law No. 13 of 2022 * *Jurisdiction:* Indonesia * *Status:* In force * *Relevant Provisions:* Mandatory requirement for Academic Drafts (*Naskah Akademik*) grounded in empirical sociological and comparative legal research prior to regulation enactment. == Timeline == {| class="wikitable sortable" style="width:100%;" !Date !Milestone / Event !Significance |- |**2011-09-14** |Implementation of Chamber System (SEMA 1/2011) |Generated structured electronic data streams enabling large-scale empirical jurimetric analysis across court chambers. |- |**2019-08-13** |Enactment of Law No. 11/2019 (Sisnas Iptek) |Established national statutory standards for science-backed governance and empirical policy research repositories. |- |**2022-12-01** |Establishment of Pustrajak (Judicial Policy Strategy) |Created a dedicated organizational unit inside the Supreme Court to spearhead evidence-based judicial policy research. |- |**2026-08-01** |Standardization of Policy Paper Frameworks (Pustrajak 2026) |Integrated active scholarly databases, RIA protocols, and RAG-compatible knowledge repositories into judicial drafting workflows. |} == Debates & Controversies == * **Debate:** Technocratic Empirical Metrics vs. Substantive Judicial Discretion * **Position A (Pro-Metric Governance):** Judicial administration must be managed strictly through quantitative performance indicators, clearance rates, and statistical disposition targets to eliminate backlog. * **Position B (Substantive Justice Advocates):** Over-reliance on numerical efficiency metrics can pressure judges to rush complex cases, undermining careful legal reasoning and substantive justice (*keadilan substansial*). * **Evidence:** Comparative judicial studies on the unintended consequences of rigid quantitative case quotas in civil law courts. * **Current Status:** Modern evidence-based frameworks balance quantitative performance metrics with qualitative assessments of judgment quality and procedural fairness. == Rule-of-Law Connection == * **Legal Certainty:** Data-driven policy formulation ensures court regulations resolve ambiguities rather than creating conflicting administrative rules. * **Institutional Accountability:** Evaluating regulatory outcomes empirically ensures the Supreme Court remains accountable to the public and the legal profession. * **Access to Justice:** Directly informs procedural simplifications (such as e-Court and Small Claims) by measuring real-world cost and time reductions for litigants. == AI & Future of Law == * **Jurimetric Analytics & Predictive Caseflow:** Using machine learning models to analyze historical SIPP court data, predicting caseload surges, and optimizing judicial panel distributions. * **Automated Regulatory Impact Simulations:** Simulating the procedural effects of proposed PERMA amendments before official promulgation using synthetic court dockets. * **Knowledge Integration:** Connecting active research repositories with internal AI research suites to provide real-time empirical insights to policy drafters. == Common Misconceptions == * **Myth:** Evidence-based judicial policy means replacing a judge's legal interpretation with statistical algorithms. * **Reality:** Evidence-based policy applies statistical data and empirical research solely to *administrative, structural, and procedural rule-making*, leaving substantive judicial adjudication in individual cases strictly to human judges. * **Source:** Judicial Policy Architecture Standards; Pustrajak Frameworks. * **Myth:** Court policies can be enacted without prior empirical testing or academic drafting (*Naskah Akademik*). * **Reality:** Both national lawmaking statutes and Supreme Court internal governance rules mandate rigorous academic drafting and impact evaluation prior to issuing binding court regulations. * **Source:** Law No. 12/2011; Pustrajak Guidelines. == Practical Example == * **Scenario:** The Supreme Court observes a persistent backlog in commercial dispute resolution across urban district courts. * **Legal Question:** How should the court formulate an evidence-based policy intervention? * **Applicable Principle:** Empirical Problem Identification & Regulatory Impact Assessment (Pustrajak Framework). * **Possible Analysis:** 1. Pustrajak analysts query SIPP case data, discovering that 40% of commercial delays stem from physical document exchange bottlenecks. 2. Researchers review comparative models (e.g., Singapore and Japanese digital case preparation). 3. An evidence-based policy paper recommends expanding mandatory e-Litigation deadlines and streamlining evidentiary uploads. 4. The Supreme Court promulgates a targeted PERMA amendment, subsequently tracking post-implementation clearance rates to verify success. * **Limitation:** Empirical findings indicate correlation rather than absolute causation; policy adjustments must account for local court infrastructural disparities. == Key Terms == {| class="wikitable" style="width:100%;" !Term !Definition !Related Term |- |**Pustrajak** |Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy within the Supreme Court of Indonesia responsible for evidence-based research. |Policy Paper, Judicial Reform |- |**Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA)** |A structured methodology used to measure the anticipated economic, social, and procedural effects of a proposed regulation. |Policy Evaluation, Lawmaking |- |**Jurimetrics** |The application of quantitative methods, statistical analysis, and information science to legal phenomena and judicial behavior. |Empirical Legal Studies, SIPP Analytics |- |**Naskah Akademik** |A formal academic draft demonstrating the empirical urgency, theoretical foundation, and sociological necessity of a proposed legal regulation. |Academic Draft, Law No. 12/2011 |} == Related Wiki Pages == * [[Judicial Knowledge Hub]] * [[Scholarly Submissions Database/Active Papers]] * [[Court Modernization & Legal Informatics]] * [[Electronic Court Administration (e-Court)]] * [[Supreme Court Benchbooks/Chapter 1]] == Knowledge Relationships == * **Evidence-Based Judicial Policy** → *is a* → [[Strategic Judicial Governance Framework]] * **Evidence-Based Judicial Policy** → *managed by* → [[Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy (Pustrajak)]] * **Evidence-Based Judicial Policy** → *draws upon data from* → [[SIPP]] & [[Direktori Putusan]] * **Evidence-Based Judicial Policy** → *produces* → [[Supreme Court Regulations (PERMA)]] & [[Policy Papers]] * **Evidence-Based Judicial Policy** → *relies on* → [[Scholarly Submissions Database/Active Papers]] == Sources == === Tier 1 — Official / Primary Sources === # 1945 Constitution of the Republic of Indonesia (Amendments I–IV). # Law No. 48 of 2009 on Judicial Power (''Lembaran Negara RI Tahun 2009 No. 157''). # Law No. 11 of =Evidence-Based Judicial Policy=

Judicial policy should increasingly be informed by reliable evidence,
analysis and evaluation.

== Policy Cycle ==

'''Question → Data → Analysis → Options → Decision → Implementation
→ Evaluation'''

== Principle ==

Evidence supports institutional decision-making; it does not replace
legal authority or judicial independence.

[[Category:Evidence-Based Policy]]

= Evidence-Based Judicial Policy =
Major judicial policy proposals should explicitly state their evidence, baseline and expected outcomes.

== Minimum Policy Logic ==
'''Problem → Evidence → Baseline → Intervention → Outcome'''

== Strategic Objective ==
Policy development should become measurable, testable and capable of learning from implementation.

title: Explainability
wikitext:
{{Knowledge|id=AI-GOV-0005|type=AI Governance Principle|domain=Judicial AI|status=DRAFT|version=1.0|evidence=E0 — Unverified|ai_readiness=5 — Machine-Readable|last_verified=}}

= Explainability =
'''Explainability''' concerns the ability to provide meaningful information about how an AI system produces or supports an output.

== Explainability Questions ==
Depending on the system, users may need to understand:

* What information was considered?
* What factors influenced the result?
* What limitations exist?
* How reliable is the output?
* What uncertainty exists?
* How can an error be challenged?

== Explanation vs Technical Detail ==
A technical description of an algorithm does not automatically provide a useful explanation to a judge, administrator, lawyer, or member of the public.

== Judicial Context ==
Explainability requirements should increase where AI outputs have greater consequences for:

* Rights
* Legal interests
* Institutional decisions
* Access to justice

== Limits ==
Some AI systems may have significant technical limitations on interpretability.

This should be treated as a governance issue rather than hidden from users.

== Related Knowledge ==

|evidence=E2 — Strategic Research Draft
|ai_readiness=5
|status=PROPOSED

=Explainability Standard=

Judicial AI should provide an appropriate explanation of its role,
limitations and relevant basis according to the use case.

== Explanation Should Address ==

* what the system was asked to do;
* what information it used;
* what it produced;
* relevant limitations;
* uncertainty;
* appropriate human review.

== Boundary ==

Explainability requirements should be proportionate to the risk and
function of the system.

title: Five Strategic Shifts
wikitext:
{{Knowledge|id=FUTURE-STRATEGIC-SHIFTS|type=Strategic Transformation|domain=Future Judiciary|jurisdiction=Indonesia|source=Indonesia Judiciary Future Blueprint 2035–2045|evidence=E2 — Strategic Research Draft|ai_readiness=5|status=PROPOSED}}

= Five Strategic Shifts =
The proposed framework identifies five fundamental shifts.

# Technology-centred → Human-centred judiciary
# AI tool → Institutional AI capability
# Fragmented knowledge → Structured judicial knowledge
# Raw data → Governed strategic asset
# Short-course training → Continuous national capability system

== Strategic Logic ==
The transformation is therefore institutional rather than merely technological.

'''Technology + Knowledge + Data + People + Governance → Better Justice'''

Implementation Principles * '''Canonical Topic:''' Rule of Law 2045 Framework (Kerangka Kerja Strategis) * '''Topic Type:''' System / Master Strategy Framework / Policy Standard * '''Jurisdiction:''' Indonesia & Global Comparative * '''Legal Domain:''' Strategic Judicial Governance, Legal Informatics, Institutional Reform, Policy Analysis * '''Status:''' Stable Architecture / Active Master Strategic Framework * '''Last Reviewed:''' 2026-08-27 * '''Next Review Recommended:''' 2027-08-27 * '''Primary Sources:''' Rule of Law 2045 Master Roadmap, Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy (Pustrajak 2026) Strategic Framework Directives, Supreme Court Strategic Plans (*Renstra MA RI*), National Long-Term Development Plan (RPJPN 2025–2045). * '''Related Wiki Pages:''' [[Rule of Law 2045]], [[Judicial Knowledge Hub]], [[Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy (Pustrajak)]], [[Master Epistemic & Quality Control Standard]], [[Master Philosophical & Methodological Standard]], == Core Definition == The **Rule of Law 2045 Framework** is the foundational methodological and epistemic structure that underpins the Supreme Court's 20-year modernization roadmap, defining the core values, normative criteria, and operational mechanisms required to achieve a world-class, evidence-based judiciary by Indonesia's centenary in 2045 (*Indonesia Emas 2045*). * **Simple Definition:** The core rulebook and methodological design that explains *how* the Supreme Court plans to build and execute its 20-year modernization strategy. * **Legal / Technical Definition:** The institutional policy framework establishing the alignment between empirical legal research (Pustrajak), normative legal hierarchies, technological integration (RAG AI suites and SIPP), and quantifiable performance metrics (KPIs) to ensure sustainable institutional transformation. * **Plain-Language Explanation: '''It acts as the conceptual and operational engine behind the Rule of Law 2045 roadmap, ensuring that every legal reform is methodologically rigorous, evidence-backed, and legally sound.''' == Why It Matters == * **Bridges Grand Vision with Practical Execution:** Translates high-level long-term goals (*Indonesia Emas 2045*) into concrete, actionable policy steps for judges, researchers, and administrators. * **Enforces Epistemic and Methodological Rigor:** Mandates that all institutional strategies rely on verified Tier 1–3 data sources and Regulatory Impact Assessments (RIA) rather than subjective assumptions. * **Harmonizes Technology with Legal Doctrine:** Ensures that digital innovations (such as AI legal assistants and electronic court dockets) fully respect constitutional due process and statutory norms. * **Provides a Replicable Evaluation Standard:** Equips supervisory bodies and research teams with a clear evaluation matrix to audit institutional reform progress. == Key Principles == ; Principle of Evidence-Driven Institutional Design (Asas Desain Institusional Berbasis Bukti) * **Meaning:** Strategic reforms, procedural rules, and institutional programs must not be implemented based on intuition; they must be designed using empirical jurimetrics, field research, and rigorous policy analysis. * **Why It Matters:** Prevents wasted resources on ineffective administrative policies and ensures reforms solve real operational bottlenecks. * **Legal Basis / Source:** Pustrajak Strategic Research Guidelines; Law No. 11/2019 (Sisnas Iptek). * **Related Concepts:** Evidence-based judicial policy, Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA), jurimetrics. ; Principle of Holistic Systemic Integration (Asas Integrasi Sistemik Holistik) * **Meaning:** Technological upgrades, legal education, case management systems (SIPP), and ethical oversight must not operate in silos; they must function as an interconnected, mutually reinforcing ecosystem. * **Why It Matters:** Eliminates administrative fragmentation and ensures smooth interoperability across all court branches. * **Legal Basis / Source:** Master System Design Blueprint; Rule of Law 2045 Architecture. * **Related Concepts:** Systemic interoperability, digital court ecosystem, holistic reform. ; Principle of Sustainable Institutional Adaptability (Asas Adaptabilitas Institusional Berkelanjutan) * **Meaning:** The framework must possess the structural flexibility to adapt to rapid technological shifts (such as artificial intelligence and cyber forensics) while maintaining unyielding fidelity to core constitutional values. * **Why It Matters:** Prevents institutional obsolescence in a fast-evolving digital and global landscape. * **Legal Basis / Source:** Master Philosophical & Methodological Standard. * **Related Concepts:** Adaptive governance, future-proof legal architecture, institutional resilience. == Legal / Institutional Framework == 
National Long-Term Development Goals (RPJPN 2025–2045) & Constitutional Baseline
       ↓
Rule-of-Law 2045 Master Strategic Roadmap
       ↓
Rule-of-Law 2045 Framework (Methodological & Epistemic Core):
- Dimension 1: Normative & Constitutional Coherence (Statutes, PERMA, SEMA)
- Dimension 2: Empirical Research & Jurimetric Analytics (Pustrajak / RIA Standards)
- Dimension 3: Technological & Informatic Execution (RAG AI, SIPP, Direktori Putusan)
- Dimension 4: Human Capacity & Ethical Governance (Badan Diklat & KEPPH)
       ↓
Execution Across the 5 Pillars, 20 Programs, and 50 KPIs of Judicial Modernization
== Indonesia Section == * **Institutional Ownership:** Developed and maintained by the Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy (*Pustrajak*) under the Supreme Court of Indonesia, serving as the master methodological guide for all institutional development initiatives. * **Operational Execution Flow:** 1. *Diagnostic Research:* Pustrajak analyzes court backlog data from SIPP and comparative international frameworks to identify structural bottlenecks. 2. *Methodological Formulation:* The Framework mandates the drafting of structured Academic Drafts (*Naskah Akademik*) and Regulatory Impact Assessments (RIA) prior to policy enactment. 3. *Technological & Educational Deployment:* Reforms are integrated into SIPP workflows, e-Court portals, and mandatory training modules (*Badan Diklat*). 4. *Continuous Monitoring:* Progress is audited against the 50 quantifiable KPIs established in the master roadmap. * **Nomenclature:** Kerangka Kerja Rule of Law 2045 — *Rule of Law 2045 Framework*; Metodologi Kebijakan Peradilan — *Judicial Policy Methodology*. == Comparative Perspective == | Jurisdiction | Master Strategy Framework | Methodological Core | Policy Research Engine | Evaluation & Audit Mechanism | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Indonesia** | **Rule of Law 2045 Framework** | Mixed normative-empirical synthesis and RAG legal informatics. | **Pustrajak MA RI** (Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy). | 50 KPIs tracked through Pustrajak audits and annual Supreme Court reports. | | **United States** | FJC Strategic Research Framework | Quantitative empirical legal studies and federal caseload modeling. | Federal Judicial Center (FJC) Research Division. | Judicial Conference statistical tracking and workload impact assessments. | | **Japan** | Supreme Court Administrative Framework | Systematic case-tracking and comparative civil procedure audits. | Research and Training Institute (*Shihō Kenshūjo*) & General Secretariat. | Internal Supreme Court administrative reviews and judicial tenure analytics. | | **European Union** | EU Justice Scoreboard Framework | Quantitative statistical benchmarking of efficiency, quality, and independence. | European Commission Directorate-General for Justice and Consumers. | Annual EU Justice Scoreboard peer reviews and country-specific recommendations. | == Core Methodological Dimensions of the Framework ==

└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
