'''Global Environmental Regulatory Trends – Fall 2025 Update''' is a global environmental regulatory update webinar and publication hosted by [[Eversheds Sutherland]] on September 29, 2025, as part of its Global Sustainability & ESG series [1–5].

== Summary ==
This initiative focused on major developments in environmental regulatory compliance requirements affecting businesses operating across international jurisdictions [1–5]. The webinar examined how evolving environmental rules reshape corporate sustainability frameworks and legal ESG obligations [1–5].

== Legal Basis & Disclaimer ==

* '''Formal Legal Basis''': Not found in the available sources [1–5].
* '''Disclaimer Notice''': Materials presented during the event and published on the platform are provided strictly for general informational purposes and do not constitute formal legal advice [1–5].

== Background ==
The global environmental regulatory landscape is evolving rapidly, demanding continuous updates to corporate governance and compliance programs [1–5]. Multinational corporations face growing challenges in aligning cross-border operations with increasingly stringent ESG standards [1–5].

== Objectives ==

# Provide insights into the latest international environmental regulatory trends [1–5].
# Assist commercial organizations in evaluating the impact of new rules on sustainability and ESG compliance [1–5].
# Encourage proactive compliance with emerging global environmental standards [1–5].

== Key Provisions & Themes ==

* '''Cross-Border Scope''': Addresses environmental regulatory compliance obligations across multiple international jurisdictions [1–5].
* '''ESG Integration''': Emphasizes incorporating Environmental, Social, and Governance criteria into core corporate compliance strategies [1–5].
* '''Non-Consultative Notice''': Explicitly clarifies that the information delivered does not replace specialized legal counsel [1–5].

== Implementation & Leadership ==

* '''Primary Contacts''': Led by R. Todd Silliman (Partner, Atlanta, US), Annamária Tóthová (Partner, Bratislava, Slovakia), and Claire Gregory (Partner, UK) [1–5].

== Policy Issues & Analysis ==

* '''Cross-Jurisdictional Complexity''': Challenges faced by international enterprises in harmonizing divergent regional environmental compliance standards [1–5].
* '''ESG Risk Mitigation''': The necessity of rapid internal adjustments to meet regulatory ESG demands and mitigate legal or reputational exposure [1–5].

Act)''': الإطار القانوني للاتحاد الأوروبي الساري بالكامل منذ 12 سبتمبر 2025 لتنظيم مشاركة بيانات المنتجات المتصلة والخدمات السحابية [[قانون البيانات]]. * '''إرشادات الامتثال التنفيذي من إيفرشيدس == * '''Background & Policy Problem''': ** '''FACT''': The previous English land registration regime relied on the Land Registration Act 1925 (LRA 1925) for nearly 80 years, exhibiting procedural deficiencies and a lack of support for digital legal frameworks. ** '''FACT''': Core problems under the legacy regime included complex title deed verification for unregistered land (requiring title history tracing back at least 15 years), high risk of hidden third-party interests, and substantial legal fees for conveyancing. * '''Policy Objectives''': ** '''FACT''': Achieve comprehensive land registration in England and Wales (aiming for 100% registered land by 2030). ** '''FACT''': Accelerate modernization and transition to paperless electronic conveyancing (e-conveyancing). ** '''FACT''': Ensure legal certainty, transparency, and a state-backed title guarantee. * '''Key Provisions & Reforms''': ** '''FACT''': '''Three Core Registration Principles''': Mirror Principle (register accurately reflects legal state), Curtain Principle (register hides behind-the-scenes trust details), and Insurance Principle (state guarantees accuracy and compensates errors). ** '''FACT''': '''Compulsory Registration Triggers''': Transfers of freehold, creation of leaseholds over 7 years, and first legal mortgages mandatorily trigger initial registration under Section 4. ** '''FACT''': '''Restriction of Overriding Interests''': Narrows overriding interests binding buyers without registration under Schedules 1 and 3 (e.g., leases <= 7 years, actual occupation). ** '''FACT''': '''Adverse Possession Reform''': Reconciles adverse possession for registered land under Schedule 6; squatters after 10 years must apply to the registrar, allowing registered owners notice to object. ** '''FACT''': '''e-Conveyancing Framework''': Sections 91–95 and Schedule 5 establish a network-based electronic land transaction system. * '''Dispute Resolution''': ** '''FACT''': Land registration disputes were reassigned to the specialized First-tier Tribunal (Property Chamber). == Internal Wiki Links == * '''People''': [[Flora Tri Melfanny Buulolo]] *(Unverified)*, [[Cecep == Dasar Hukum ==

* '''Undang-Undang Induk''' : 出入国管理及び難民認定法（Act No. 319 of 1951）
* '''Undang-Undang Perubahan''' : 平成16年法律第73号（Act No. 73 of 2004）
* '''Regulasi Terkait''' : 特殊開錠用具の所持の禁止等に関する法律（Act No. 65 of 2003）

== Latar Belakang ==
'''FACT''': Kebijakan ini dilatarbelakangi oleh keputusan Rapat Kabinet Penanggulangan Kejahatan (Desember 2003) mengenai "Rencana Aksi Mewujudkan Masyarakat yang Tahan Terhadap Kejahatan", yang menargetkan pengurangan separuh jumlah warga asing yang tinggal ilegal (sekitar 250.000 orang) dalam jangka waktu 5 tahun, serta kebutuhan memperbarui sistem pengakuan pengungsi agar lebih adil, transparan, dan efisien.

== Tujuan ==

# Memperketat penegakan hukum terhadap pendatang dan pemukim ilegal.
# Mendorong kepulangan sukarela bagi pelanggar izin tinggal melalui prosedur yang disederhanakan.
# Menghapus penyalahgunaan status tinggal sah yang diperoleh melalui pemalsuan atau penipuan.
# Menyediakan perlindungan hukum yang lebih adil dan cepat bagi pemohon status pengungsi.

== Ruang Lingkup ==
Kebijakan ini berlaku nasional di seluruh wilayah hukum Jepang, mencakup kontrol perbatasan, pemeriksaan status tinggal, penanganan kejahatan imigrasi, serta peninjauan permohonan suaka.

== Ketentuan Utama ==

# '''Peningkatan Sanksi Denda & Masa Larangan Masuk（罰金の引上げ等）'''
#* Denda maksimum overstay ilegal dinaikkan dari 300.000 yen menjadi 3.000.000 yen.
#* Masa larangan masuk kembali bagi orang yang dideportasi berulang dinaikkan dari 5 tahun menjadi 10 tahun.
# '''Sistem Perintah Pemulangan（出国命令制度）'''
#* Memberikan pengecualian dari prinsip penahanan total untuk pelanggar overstay yang melapor secara sukarela.
#* Masa larangan masuk kembali dikurangi dari 5 tahun menjadi hanya 1 tahun.
# '''Sistem Pencabutan Status Tinggal（在留資格取消制度）'''
#* Memungkinkan pencabutan status tinggal yang diperoleh dengan penipuan dokumen atau tidak menjalankan aktivitas sesuai status tinggal selama lebih dari 3 bulan tanpa alasan sah.
# '''Pembaruan Prosedur Pengungsi（難民認定制度の見直し）'''
#* Pembentukan Sistem Izin Tinggal Sementara（仮滞在許可制度）.
#* Pengakuan status tinggal bagi yang dinilai sebagai pengungsi.
#* Pembentukan 難民審査参与員（Refugee Examination Counselors） dalam proses banding.
#* Penghapusan aturan 60 hari（60日ルールの撤廃）untuk mengajukan permohonan pengungsi.

== Implementasi ==
'''FACT''': Ketentuan penanggulangan pemukim ilegal diberlakukan pada 2 Desember 2004. Ketentuan pengakuan pengungsi diberlakukan dalam jangka waktu satu tahun sejak pengundangan. Peninjauan penolakan masuk bagi penderita gangguan jiwa diberlakukan mulai 2 Agustus 2004.

== Permasalahan Kebijakan ==

* Penumpukan tunggakan permohonan suaka dan potensi penyalahgunaan permohonan suaka semata-mata untuk bekerja.
* Penanganan HAM dalam pusat penahanan imigrasi dan efisiensi prosedur deportasi bagi pelanggar yang menolak dipulangkan.

== Reformasi / Perubahan ==

* Reformasi menggabungkan tindakan tegas terhadap kejahatan imigrasi berat dengan insentif kelonggaran (mis. penurunan masa deportasi dari 5 tahun menjadi 1 tahun) bagi yang kooperatif dan melapor sukarela.

title: JPW-MANUAL-001
wikitext:
'''Chambers Practice Manual of the International Criminal Court''' (Eighth Edition, October 2024) is the official judicial policy document containing consolidated operational guidelines and procedural deadlines for ICC Judges [1, 2–11].

== Summary ==
This Manual establishes operational standards for pre-trial proceedings, trial preparation, judgment delivery deadlines, victim participation schemes, confidential evidence redaction protocols, as well as guidelines for judgment drafting and the registration of dissenting or separate opinions [1, 12–136, 137–211].

== Legal Basis ==

* [[Rome Statute]]: Articles 15, 58, 60, 61, 64, 67, 74, 76, 82, 83, 89, 91, 101.
* [[Rules of Procedure and Evidence]]: Rules 68, 76, 77, 81, 85, 89, 118, 121, 122, 129, 130, 132, 141, 155.
* [[Regulations of the Court]]: Regulations 24, 34, 42, 53.

== Background ==
First published in September 2015, the Manual has undergone periodic updates, culminating in the Eighth Edition adopted on 21 October 2024 following the judicial retreat. It is designed to address procedural delays and ensure consistency in judicial practices across Chambers.

== Objectives ==

* Accelerate international criminal justice proceedings (expeditiousness).
* Establish strict deadlines for key decisions.
* Standardize judgment drafting and the management of confidential documents/witnesses.

== Key Provisions ==

* **Pre-Trial Deadlines**: Article 15 investigation authorization within a maximum of 120 days; confirmation of charges decision within 60 days; pre-confirmation responses within 5 days.
* **Trial Deadlines**: Article 74 written judgment within 10 months of the end of closing statements; Article 76 sentencing decision within 4 months of conviction.
* **Appeals Deadlines**: Appeals judgment on conviction/reparation within 10 months; Article 82 interlocutory appeals within 4 months [77–79].
* **Victim Participation**: A-B-C categorization scheme administered by the Registry [83–88].
* **Evidence Redaction**: Coding systems categories A.1–A.8 (Rule 81(2)) and B.1–B.5 (Rule 81(4)) [89–100].
* **Judgment Drafting**: Establishment of dedicated drafting sub-teams and the adoption of Structure Option 1 or 2 [146, 194–201].

== Implementation ==
Mandatorily applied by all Judges across the Pre-Trial, Trial, and Appeals Divisions in coordination with the Registry and the OTP [12–211].

== Policy Issues ==

* Restriction on deadline extensions, permitted only under exceptional circumstances.
* Risk management regarding the leakage of witness identities during investigations and inter-party contacts.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* **[[International Criminal Court]]**: Publishing institution.
* **[[Pre-Trial Chamber]]**: Implementer of pre-trial guidelines.
* **[[Trial Chamber]]**: Implementer of trial and judgment drafting guidelines.
* **[[Appeals Chamber]]**: Implementer of appellate deadline guidelines.
* **[[Cecep Mustafa]]**: '''Not found in the available sources.''' [1–211]
* **[[Ferdi Raditya Akbar]]**: '''Not found in the available sources.''' [1–211]

* [[International Criminal Court]]

title: JPW-MEDIA-001
wikitext:
'''Wawancara Nieuwsuur tentang Kerangka Hukum Biofuel dan Risiko Kecurangan (2025)''' (''Nieuwsuur Interview on Biofuel Legal Framework and Fraud Risk'') adalah wawancara media dan publikasi analisis kebijakan hukum yang ditayangkan oleh program berita Belanda ''Nieuwsuur'' pada 16 Juli 2025.

== Ringkasan ==
Wawancara ini menghadirkan peneliti dari Amsterdam Center for Criminal Justice (ACCJ), Merle Kooijman, yang diwawancarai oleh jurnalis Marijn Duintjer Tebbens. Liputan ini mengkritisi kerangka hukum energi terbarukan dan menyoroti betapa mudahnya praktik kecurangan (*fraude*) terjadi di sektor biobrandstof (*biofuel*).

== Dasar Hukum ==

* **Kerangka Hukum Energi Terbarukan**: Regulasi yang mengatur standar produksi, verifikasi, dan keberlanjutan biobrandstof di Belanda dan kawasan Eropa.

== Latar Belakang ==
Penggunaan biobrandstof dipromosikan sebagai solusi energi terbarukan. Namun, muncul kekhawatiran serius mengenai keabsahan klaim ramah lingkungan akibat ditemukannya celah regulasi yang dimanfaatkan untuk kecurangan.

== Tujuan ==

* Menganalisis kerangka hukum energi terbarukan dan biobrandstof.
* Menjelaskan mekanisme dan kemudahan terjadinya kecurangan dalam industri biobrandstof kepada publik.

== Ketentuan Utama ==

* **Kerentanan Regulasi Biofuel**: Penjelasan mengenai celah dalam hukum energi terbarukan yang mempermudah praktik kecurangan.
* **Dampak Kecurangan**: Praktik kecurangan menyebabkan ketidakpastian total mengenai tingkat keberlanjutan riil biobrandstof yang beredar.

== Implementasi ==
Ditayangkan dalam siaran program ''Nieuwsuur'' (episode 5138) di NPO Start serta dipublikasikan dalam bentuk artikel berita online di situs NOS pada 16 Juli 2025.

== Permasalahan Kebijakan ==

* Lemahnya pengawasan dan verifikasi hukum terhadap rantai pasok biobrandstof.
* Tingginya risiko manipulasi data keberlanjutan oleh pelaku industri.

== Hubungan dengan Entity Lain ==

'''The Italian Legal Imaginary and Journal Policy Framework''' refers to the editorial, epistemological, and comparative policy structure developed by ''The Italian Law Journal'' (ItALJ) to critically analyze, unpack, and disseminate the Italian legal tradition within global legal discourse.<ref>Crea, C. (2025). "The Italian Legal Imaginary – Inside, Outside, or Upside Down? Learning From the History of a Journal." ''The Italian Law Journal'', 11(1), 1–28.</ref>

== Lead ==
Founded in 2014 by [[Camilla Crea]] and a group of Italian civil and comparative law scholars, ''The Italian Law Journal'' is an open-access, peer-reviewed e-journal using English as a lingua franca.<ref>Crea (2025), pp. 1, 4, 31.</ref> Grounded in the post-WWII constitutionalization of private law under the [[Constitution of Italy|1947 Italian Constitution]] and the rise of comparative legal studies, the framework seeks to move Italian legal thought beyond classic formalism and national insularity.<ref>Crea (2025), pp. 4, 10, 16–17.</ref>

== Summary ==
The framework addresses two major epistemological turns in Italian legal history:

# '''National constitutionalization of private law''': infusing the [[Italian Civil Code|1942 Civil Code]] with constitutional values — human dignity, personalism, substantive equality (Art. 3(2)), and solidarity — shifting private law's focus from purely economic concerns toward the person.<ref>Crea (2025), pp. 10–12.</ref>
# '''Rise of comparative legal studies''': breaking the isolation of domestic law through methodologies including [[Gino Gorla]]'s case method, [[Mauro Cappelletti]]'s functionalism, and [[Rodolfo Sacco]]'s theory of legal formants and cryptotypes.<ref>Crea (2025), pp. 16–22.</ref>

== Legal basis ==
The policy framework operates at the intersection of:

* '''[[Constitution of Italy|Italian Constitution (1947)]]''': Articles 2 (inviolable rights), 3 (formal and substantive equality), and 42 (social function of property).<ref>Italian Constitution, Arts. 2, 3, 42; Crea (2025), pp. 10–14.</ref>
* '''Civil Code of 1942''': reinterpreted through constitutionally oriented reading and general clauses (good faith, social utility, unjust harm).<ref>Italian Civil Code (1942); Crea (2025), pp. 10–12.</ref>
* '''Ministerial decrees of 1999 and 2005''': establishing comparative law as an autonomous, mandatory course in Italian law school curricula.<ref>Decreto Ministeriale, 23 December 1999; Decreto Ministeriale, 25 November 2005; Crea (2025), p. 24.</ref>

== Background ==
Italian legal scholarship was historically constrained by a perception of rigid positivism and dogmatism, described by [[John Henry Merryman]] as the "Italian Style."<ref>Merryman, J.H. (1965–1966). "The Italian Style" (I, II, III). ''Stanford Law Review''; Crea (2025), pp. 7, 10, 16.</ref> Earlier domestic benchmarks — Alessandro Pizzorusso's ''Italian Studies in Law'' (1992) and Giacinto della Cananea's ''Italian Journal of Public Law'' (2009) — preceded ItALJ's focus on private law as a tool of social engineering.<ref>Crea (2025), pp. 4–6.</ref>

== Objectives ==
* Make the Italian legal tradition visible and accessible to the international community in English.<ref>Crea (2025), pp. 4, 8, 25.</ref>
* Foster bidirectional, critical dialogue rather than uncritical repetition of settled narratives.<ref>Crea (2025), pp. 8, 25.</ref>
* Promote interdisciplinary openness linking private law with history, economics, sociology, and philosophy.<ref>Crea (2025), pp. 9, 25.</ref>

== Scope ==
Applies to international legal scholarship, private law reform, comparative jurisprudence, legal education, and judicial interpretation across continental Europe, the Americas, and other global legal systems.<ref>Crea (2025), pp. 1, 8, 16–25.</ref>

== Key concepts ==
* '''Theory of legal formants''': dissecting legal systems into statutory, judicial, and doctrinal "formants," alongside unexpressed "cryptotypes."<ref>Sacco, R. (1991); Crea (2025), pp. 20–22.</ref>
* '''Indirect ''Drittwirkung'' ''': applying constitutional fundamental rights to horizontal relationships between private parties.<ref>Crea (2025), p. 12.</ref>
* '''Alternative use of law''': applying constitutional interpretation to advance social justice and protect disadvantaged parties.<ref>Crea (2025), pp. 13–15.</ref>

== Implementation ==
Published biannually under the auspices of Università degli Studi del Sannio and sponsored by the [[Harvard Italian Law Association]] (HILA), the Società Italiana degli Studiosi del Diritto Civile (SISDIC), the Società Italiana per la Ricerca nel Diritto Comparato (SIRD), and the National Italian American Bar Association (NIABA).<ref>Crea (2025), pp. 1, 7.</ref>

== Policy problems ==
* '''Linguistic periphery''': esoteric Italian legal terminology and outdated, hard-to-access English translations of the Italian Civil Code.<ref>Crea (2025), pp. 26–27.</ref>
* '''Disciplinary silos''': persistent academic fragmentation between public, private, and comparative law departments.<ref>Crea (2025), p. 26.</ref>

== Reform proposals ==
Scholars advocate translating primary Italian judicial decisions into English and expanding trans-systemic legal education programs.<ref>Crea (2025), pp. 24, 26–27.</ref>

== Related entities ==
* '''[[Camilla Crea]]''': Author and Co-Editor-in-Chief.<ref>Crea (2025), pp. 1, 27.</ref>
* '''[[Harvard Italian Law Association]]''': Sponsoring organization.<ref>Crea (2025), p. 7.</ref>

== 3. POLICY ANALYSIS ==
* '''Background''': Traditional Public-Private Partnership (PPP) models established in the 1990s primarily governed bilateral, profit-oriented relationships between public authorities and market operators for infrastructure delivery. Modern urban challenges—including climate disruption, social inequality, and rapid technological transition—demonstrate the limitations of purely commercial PPPs, prompting a shift toward inclusive urban co-governance models.
* '''Problem''': Conventional market procurement and standard PPPs frequently fail to address localized poverty, urban decay, socio-spatial polarization, and climate adaptation because they prioritize pure financial returns over public value, equity, and civic participation.
* '''Legal/Policy Gap''': Public procurement frameworks (such as traditional EU tendering rules) emphasize price competition and market efficiency, creating procedural barriers that exclude non-profit community groups, civil society actors, and scientific institutions from co-designing public services or managing urban assets.
* '''Objectives''': Establish legal, financial, institutional, and digital instruments that enable multi-stakeholder governance (Public-Private-Science-Social-Community Partnerships or 5Ps), operationalize the "quintessential quintuple helix" governance model, and secure equitable sharing of economic and social benefits among urban residents.
* '''Scope''': Encompasses local municipal administration, urban commons regeneration, innovation procurement (e.g., Pre-Commercial Procurement and Public Procurement of Innovative Solutions), social enterprise incubation, and urban climate transition projects across European cities.
* '''Implementation''': Executed through local administrative regulations (e.g., Turin's Regulation for Governing Urban Commons, Reggio Emilia's Climate Democracy Regulation); Pacts of Collaboration (*patti di collaborazione*); social partnerships (*baratto amministrativo*) under Art. 190 of Legislative Decree n. 50/2016; co-design arrangements under Art. 55 of Legislative Decree n. 117/2017; and EU-funded experimental programs such as Urban Innovative Actions (UIA).
* '''Evidence''': Empirical evaluation of 13 lighthouse city case studies funded by the EU Urban Innovative Actions initiative—including Co-City Turin (Italy), B-MINCOME Barcelona (Spain), USE-IT! Birmingham (UK), FED Gothenburg (Sweden), TAST'in FIVES Lille (France), 5Bridges Nantes (France), Vienna CoRE (Austria), Curing the Limbo Athens (Greece), URBAN SOIL 4 FOOD Maribor (Slovenia), CALICO Brussels (Belgium), E-Co-Housing Budapest (Hungary), Home Silk Road Lyon (France), and Yes We Rent Mataró (Spain).
* '''Impact''': Legal recognition of urban commoning; creation of district-based social enterprises and community land trusts; tax credits/exemptions for residents maintaining public spaces under horizontal subsidiarity; and establishing active civic roles in delivering public services.
* '''Reform''': Enact explicit statutory recognition of USDIPs in procurement codes; establish "Urban Commons Project Finance" / Social Finance mechanisms to share risk; deploy City Science Offices (CSOs) and Urban Co-Labs as innovation procurement brokers; and codify non-competitive collaborative dialogue procedures for social and environmental co-governance.
* '''Unresolved Issues''':
** Financial self-sustainability of community-managed urban projects once initial EU or municipal seed grants expire.
** Legal risk aversion among municipal civil servants reluctant to depart from traditional competitive tendering procedures.
** Ensuring genuine representativeness and avoiding the instrumentalization or exploitation of vulnerable or low-income residents in uncompensated social partnership schemes.

'''Urban Sustainable Development and Innovation Partnerships''' (USDIPs) refers to a legal category, administrative policy framework, and multi-stakeholder co-governance instrument designed to enable collaborative delivery of urban technological, ecological, and social innovations.<ref>Iaione, C. (2023). Urban Sustainable Development and Innovation Partnerships. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', pp. 521–605.</ref>

=== Lead ===
Conceived as an evolution beyond traditional bilateral [[Public-Private Partnership|Public-Private Partnerships]] (PPPs), USDIPs establish formal "quintuple helix" or Public-Private-Science-Social-Community Partnerships (5Ps).<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 525, 528, 535, 543.</ref> Legal analysis led by [[Christian Iaione]] of [[Luiss Guido Carli University]] demonstrates how municipal authorities can leverage horizontal subsidiarity under [[Article 118(4) of the Italian Constitution]], statutory mechanisms in the [[Italian Public Contracts Code]] (Legislative Decree n. 50/2016), and the [[Italian Third Sector Code]] (Legislative Decree n. 117/2017) to engage urban residents, social enterprises, and scientific institutions as equal co-governors of urban commons.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 525–528, 531–533.</ref>

=== Summary ===
The USDIP model shifts urban governance from a Schumpeterian market-driven framework toward mission-oriented, citizen-centric co-production.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 525–526, 550.</ref> Rather than relying exclusively on competitive commercial concessions, USDIPs operationalize non-competitive, solidarity-based legal vehicles—such as Pacts of Collaboration (*patti di collaborazione*), administrative barter (*baratto amministrativo*), social partnerships, and Community Land Trusts—to manage public infrastructure and local services.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 527, 531, 192, 213.</ref>

=== Legal Basis ===
The administrative legal architecture rests upon national statutory acts and European directives:
* '''[[Constitution of Italy]]''': Article 118, paragraph 4, establishing the constitutional principle of horizontal subsidiarity.<ref>Italian Constitution, Art. 118(4); Iaione (2023), p. 531.</ref>
* '''[[Legislative Decree n. 50/2016]] (Public Contracts Code)''': Article 189 (horizontal subsidiarity interventions), Article 190 (social partnerships / administrative barter), and Article 36 (direct awards below thresholds).<ref>Legislative Decree n. 50/2016, Arts. 36, 189, 190; Iaione (2023), pp. 531–532.</ref>
* '''[[Legislative Decree n. 117/2017]] (Third Sector Code)''': Articles 55 and 71, authorizing public-social co-design (*co-progettazione*) and concession of public cultural heritage to non-profit entities.<ref>Legislative Decree n. 117/2017, Arts. 55, 71; Iaione (2023), p. 531.</ref>
* '''[[Directive 2014/24/EU]]''': Recognizing innovation partnerships, social innovation, and public-public cooperation.<ref>Directive 2014/24/EU; Iaione (2023), pp. 536–537.</ref>
* '''[[International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights]]''': Article 15, establishing the human right to science and citizen participation in scientific progress.<ref>ICESCR, Art. 15; Iaione (2023), pp. 546–548.</ref>

=== Background ===
Over three decades of empirical evidence reveal the limitations of conventional PPPs in resolving urban poverty, climate adaptation, and spatial polarization.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 528–530.</ref> In response to the post-2008 economic crisis and climate challenges, European municipalities (pioneered by cities such as Bologna, Turin, Barcelona, and Reggio Emilia) developed local regulations for urban commons.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 527, 542, 556–557, 560.</ref>

=== Objectives ===
* Transition public administration from a top-down regulator to an "Enabling State" that facilitates civic co-governance.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 526, 545, 569.</ref>
* Democratize innovation procurement by incorporating end-users and community groups into service design.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 535–538, 591.</ref>
* Ensure an equitable distribution of social and economic benefits generated by urban assets.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 526, 541, 605.</ref>

=== Scope ===
Applies to local municipal governments, public infrastructure development, urban renewal, social enterprise incubation, circular economy initiatives, and district-level energy transitions across EU Member States.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 523–524, 550, 566–568.</ref>

=== Key Provisions & Policy Tools ===
The framework defines four operational tools necessary to implement USDIPs:
# '''Regulatory Procurement Tool''': Adapting innovation procurement rules (PPI/PCP) and establishing non-competitive "collaborative dialogue" procedures via Pacts of Collaboration.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 524, 536, 593, 596.</ref>
# '''Financial Tool''': Deploying "Urban Commons Project Finance" and Social Finance instruments (e.g., Social Impact Bonds) to share operational risks.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 524, 596–598, 604.</ref>
# '''Institutional & Learning Tool''': Establishing Collaboratories (Co-Labs), Living Labs, and City Science Offices (CSOs) to act as urban innovation brokers.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 524, 555–557, 598–601.</ref>
# '''Digital Tool''': Implementing cooperatively owned platforms, e-procurement systems, and civic participation forums.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 525, 601–602.</ref>

=== Implementation ===
Operationalized through local municipal enactments, such as Turin's Regulation for Governing Urban Commons (tested in the UIA Co-City Turin project) and Reggio Emilia's Regulation on Climate Democracy and Justice.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 527, 549, 560–561.</ref> Adjudicated by the Italian Court of Auditors (*Corte dei Conti*), which qualified social partnerships as non-market expressions of horizontal subsidiarity exempt from competitive EU concession rules.<ref>Corte dei Conti, Sez. autonomie, n. 16/2017; Iaione (2023), pp. 531–532.</ref>

=== Policy Problems ===
* '''Risk Aversion''': Inertia among public officials accustomed to standard profit-oriented procurement.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 589, 593, 599.</ref>
* '''Representativeness Deficits''': Risk that unorganized community groups may lack technical expertise or fail to represent marginalized residents.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 533, 537.</ref>
* '''Financial Sustainability''': Maintaining long-term operations once initial public grants or EU trial subsidies expire.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 556, 576, 604.</ref>

=== Reform ===
Scholars advocate explicit legislative codification of USDIPs within national procurement codes, formalizing the role of Innovation Public Procurement Brokers (IPPB) and establishing dedicated Urban Commons Project Finance vehicles.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 558, 591, 596, 603–605.</ref>

=== Related Entities ===
* '''[[Christian Iaione]]''': Author and lead legal scholar on USDIPs.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 521, 525.</ref>
* '''[[Luiss Guido Carli University]]''': Primary academic research institution.<ref>Iaione (2023), p. 521.</ref>
* '''[[Urban Innovative Actions]]''': EU funding initiative for lighthouse case studies.<ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 523, 558–560.</ref>
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 521–605.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>Iaione (2023), pp. 521–605.</ref>

== 3. POLICY ANALYSIS ==
* '''Background''': Rapid global advances in FinTech, crowdfunding, and initial coin offerings (ICOs) provided alternative financing mechanisms to lower transaction costs and expand capital access. Following Presidential instructions and the Strategy for the Development of the Information Society, Russia developed a comprehensive legal model for digital assets.
* '''Problem''': Unregulated digital asset offerings created severe shadow economy risks, lack of investor protection against fraud or hacking, and inability of state authorities (Ministry of Finance, Bank of Russia) to monitor financial flows or prevent money laundering.
* '''Legal/Policy Gap''': Traditional Russian civil law lacked statutory definitions for virtual property and digital tokens. Furthermore, Russian statutory terminology ("digital rights", "DFA", "utility digital rights") diverged from standard international classifications (Security Tokens, Utility Tokens, Payment Tokens/Cryptocurrencies).
* '''Objectives''': Establish a clear legal environment for the digital economy, enable civil transactions and fundraising via digital technologies, protect investors, and bring token issuance under formal regulatory supervision.
* '''Scope''': Governs investment platform operators, DFA information system operators, exchange operators, natural person investors, and issuing entities within Russian jurisdiction, including mandatory conflict-of-laws rules for cross-border transactions involving Russian residents.
* '''Implementation''': Enacted via Federal Law No. 259-FZ on Investment Platforms (2 August 2019), Federal Law No. 259-FZ on DFA (31 July 2020), and Civil Code Amendments (Articles 128, 141.1; effective 1 October 2019). Oversight is managed by the Bank of Russia via official registers.
* '''Evidence''': Empirical statutory analysis, comparative review of EU market regulations (Prospectus Directive/Regulation, MiFID II, MAR, EU Digital Finance Package), and conflict-of-laws analysis under Russian private international law and EU Rome I Regulation.
* '''Impact''': Legally recognized "digital rights" as property objects in Russian civil law. Introduced statutory caps on retail investments (600,000 rubles/year cap for non-qualified natural persons across platforms) and strict registration requirements for operators.
* '''Reform''': Legal scholars recommend aligning national digital asset terminology with global standards, establishing explicit statutory consumer protection rules, creating dedicated regional legislation for federal subjects, and forming an international comity of national regulators to set uniform global ICO standards.
* '''Unresolved Issues''':
** Excessive national isolationism resulting from restricting operator status exclusively to Russian legal entities.
** Potential reduction in foreign investment due to unfamiliar legal terminology.
** Lack of direct enforcement authority by the Bank of Russia over unlicensed offshore crypto entities.
** Jurisdictional friction under international conflict-of-laws rules when classifying utility tokens.

'''The Russian Legal Framework for Initial Coin Offerings and Digital Assets''' is a statutory policy model in the [[Russian Federation]] governing initial coin offerings (ICOs), digital rights (*tsifrovye prava*), digital financial assets (DFA), and investment platforms.<ref>Kasatkina, M. (2021). Legal Regulation of Initial Coin Offerings in Russia. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 13(1), 637–665.</ref>

=== Lead ===
Adopted through a series of legislative reforms between 2019 and 2020, the framework establishes a "synthetic" regulatory model combining new federal statutes with targeted amendments to existing civil legislation.<ref>Kasatkina (2021), pp. 642–643.</ref> Legal analysis by scholar [[Marina Kasatkina]] highlights that while Russia established one of the world's most detailed legal structures for digital assets, its unique terminology ("digital rights" and "digital financial assets") diverges from international crypto-market standards.<ref>Kasatkina (2021), pp. 637, 646, 659.</ref>

=== Summary ===
The regulatory framework rests upon two primary federal statutes and core Civil Code revisions:
# '''Civil Code Amendments (Arts. 128, 141.1)''': Effective 1 October 2019, recognizing "digital rights" as a distinct category of property rights under civil law.<ref>Civil Code RF, Arts. 128, 141.1; Kasatkina (2021), p. 646.</ref>
# '''Federal Law No. 259-FZ of 2 August 2019 (Law on Investment Platforms)''': Regulating crowdfunding and the issuance of "utility digital rights."<ref>Federal Law No. 259-FZ (2019); Kasatkina (2021), pp. 642, 650.</ref>
# '''Federal Law No. 259-FZ of 31 July 2020 (Law on DFA)''': Regulating "digital financial assets," digital currency, and exchange operators.<ref>Federal Law No. 259-FZ (2020); Kasatkina (2021), pp. 642, 655–656.</ref>

=== Legal Basis ===
* '''[[Civil Code of the Russian Federation]]''': Article 128 classifies digital rights as objects of civil rights under "other property"; Article 141.1 defines their exercise and transfer within designated information systems.<ref>Civil Code RF, Arts. 128, 141.1.</ref>
* '''Law on Investment Platforms (No. 259-FZ/2019)''': Governs contracts concluded via online investment platforms and defines utility digital rights.<ref>Federal Law No. 259-FZ (2019), Art. 8.</ref>
* '''Law on Digital Financial Assets (No. 259-FZ/2020)''': Defines DFAs as digital rights encompassing monetary claims, equity security rights, and non-public JSC shares issued via distributed ledgers.<ref>Federal Law No. 259-FZ (2020), Art. 1(2).</ref>

=== Background ===
To prevent the expansion of shadow markets and protect investors from fraudulent schemes, the Russian President and Government issued directives in 2017 and 2019 ordering the creation of a legal framework for the digital economy.<ref>Kasatkina (2021), pp. 643–644.</ref>

=== Objectives ===
* Provide legal certainty for fundraising and civil transactions using digital technologies.<ref>Kasatkina (2021), p. 643.</ref>
* Protect retail investors from unmitigated financial losses.<ref>Kasatkina (2021), pp. 643, 653.</ref>
* Bring digital asset turnover under the supervision of state financial authorities.<ref>Kasatkina (2021), p. 643.</ref>

=== Scope ===
Applies to all digital rights issued, accounted for, or circulated within Russian jurisdiction, as well as cross-border transactions involving Russian resident investors or entities.<ref>Kasatkina (2021), pp. 659–661.</ref>

=== Key Provisions ===
* '''Digital Rights Definition''': Property rights existing digitally in an information system meeting statutory criteria.<ref>Kasatkina (2021), pp. 646, 649.</ref>
* '''Retail Investment Cap''': Non-qualified natural persons are limited to investing a total of 600,000 rubles per calendar year across all investment platforms.<ref>Law on Investment Platforms; Kasatkina (2021), p. 653.</ref>
* '''Issuer Limit''': Entities attracting investments through utility digital rights cannot exceed 1 billion rubles per calendar year (excluding public JSCs).<ref>Law on Investment Platforms; Kasatkina (2021), p. 653.</ref>
* '''Mandatory Operator Inclusion''': Only Russian legal entities included in official Bank of Russia registers may operate investment platforms or DFA exchanges.<ref>Kasatkina (2021), pp. 652, 657, 659.</ref>

=== Implementation ===
Supervised by the [[Bank of Russia]] (*Central Bank of Russia*), which maintains the registry of investment platform operators and DFA exchange operators.<ref>Kasatkina (2021), pp. 652, 657–658.</ref>

=== Policy Problems ===
* '''Terminology Disconnect''': Replacing international concepts (Security/Utility Tokens) with "DFA" and "Utility Digital Rights" creates confusion for foreign investors.<ref>Kasatkina (2021), p. 659.</ref>
* '''National Isolationism''': Restricting operator status to Russian legal entities limits foreign ICO project participation.<ref>Kasatkina (2021), p. 659.</ref>
* '''Consumer Protection Gap''': Lack of specific statutory dispute resolution rights for retail consumers compared to professional market participants.<ref>Kasatkina (2021), pp. 644, 664.</ref>

=== Reform ===
Scholars advocate harmonizing Russian terminology with global standards and forming an international regulatory comity to establish uniform global ICO guidelines.<ref>Kasatkina (2021), p. 665.</ref>

== Summary ==
'''José Pedro Pérez-Llorca''' (1940–2019) (Stable ID: '''JPW-PERSON-000662''') was a prominent Spanish jurist, diplomat, *Letrado de las Cortes*, member of parliament (*diputado*), minister during the Spanish Transition (*años de la Transición*), founding attorney of law firm Pérez-Llorca, and one of the seven drafters (*ponentes*) who authored the Spanish Constitution of 1978 (*Constitución Española de 1978*). Recognized for his lifelong commitment to democracy, deep expertise in legal history and the Cádiz Constitution of 1812, and dedication to political consensus (*espíritu de la concordia*). His life and political testament were honored in the debut issue of *Revista Jurídica Pérez-Llorca* (March 2019) by former Ombudsman Soledad Becerril (*Defensora del Pueblo* 2012–2017).

The constitutional framework and legal precedents tied to Pérez-Llorca's legacy include:

* '''Article 20 of the Spanish Constitution of 1978''': Guarantees freedom of expression (*libertad de expresión*), forming the foundation for open academic debate and legal publishing in Spain.
* '''Articles 138 & 139 of the Spanish Constitution of 1978''': Articulates Pérez-Llorca's political testament, mandating inter-territorial economic balance (Art. 138) and strictly forbidding Statutes of Autonomy (*estatutos de autonomía*) from creating economic or social privileges (Art. 139).
* '''Historical Precedent''': The Cádiz Constitution of 1812 (*Constitución de Cádiz de 1812*), serving as an enduring historical symbol of universal liberty and individual rights.

'''José Pedro Pérez-Llorca''' (1940–2019) (ID Estable: '''JPW-PERSON-000662''') fue un relevante jurista español, diplomático, *Letrado de las Cortes*, diputado, ministro durante la Transición española (*años de la Transición*), abogado fundador del bufete Pérez-Llorca y uno de los siete ponentes (*ponentes*) que redactaron la Constitución Española de 1978 (*Constitución Española de 1978*). El marco constitucional y los precedentes legales vinculados a su legado comprenden:

* '''Artículo 20 de la Constitución Española de 1978''': Garantiza la libertad de expresión (*libertad de expresión*), constituyendo el pilar para el debate académico y la publicación jurídica.
* '''Artículos 138 y 139 de la Constitución Española de 1978''': Expresan el testamento político de Pérez-Llorca, exigiendo el equilibrio económico interterritorial (Art. 138) y prohibiendo que los Estatutos de Autonomía (*estatutos de autonomía*) establezcan privilegios económicos o sociales (Art. 139).
* '''Precedente Histórico''': La Constitución de Cádiz de 1812 (*Constitución de Cádiz de 1812*), símbolo histórico del constitucionalismo liberal.

== Antecedentes ==
En marzo de 2019, tras su fallecimiento, la *Revista Jurídica Pérez-Llorca* publicó un escrito de homenaje redactado por Soledad Becerril analizando la contribución de Pérez-Llorca a la consolidación de la democracia constitucional y las instituciones del Estado.

== Objetivos ==
1. Conmemorar el legado jurídico y el espíritu de consenso (*espíritu de concordia*) de la Ponencia Constitucional de 1978. 2. Promover el debate jurídico y la libertad de expresión académica al amparo del Artículo 20 de la CE. 3. Reafirmar el principio de igualdad territorial frente a pretensiones de privilegios estatutarios (Arts. 138 y 139 CE). 4. Reconocer su labor en la diplomacia, la defensa nacional y la presidencia del Patronato del Museo Nacional del Prado.

== Alcance ==
La trayectoria de Pérez-Llorca abarcó múltiples ámbitos de la vida pública española: 1. ''Redacción Constitucional (*Ponencia Constitucional*)'': Participación directa como uno de los siete padres de la Constitución. 2. ''Diplomacia y Gobierno'': Servicio público como Ministro de Asuntos Exteriores y diputado durante la Transición. 3. ''Ejercicio Profesional y Cultura'': Socio fundador de Pérez-Llorca y Presidente del Patronato del Museo Nacional del Prado.

== Disposiciones y Principios Clave ==

* '''Prohibición de Privilegios Estatutarios (Art. 139 CE)''': Los Estatutos de Autonomía no pueden consagrar ventajas ni privilegios económicos entre Comunidades Autónomas.
* '''Principio de Concordia''': El diseño de las normas fundamentales debe apoyarse en el diálogo y el pacto entre distintas fuerzas políticas.

== Implementación ==
Consolidado en el ordenamiento constitucional español, la yurisprudencia del Tribunal Constitucional y la práctica profesional del bufete Pérez-Llorca.

== Problemas de Política Pública ==

* Riesgos de fragmentación territorial y peticiones de privilegios económicos estatutarios.
* Mantenimiento del consenso constitucional frente a la polarización política contemporánea.

== Reforma ==

* Aplicación rigurosa del equilibrio económico interterritorial (Art. 138 CE).
* Garantía de la libertad de expresión y debate jurídico (Art. 20 CE).

== Relación con otras Entidades ==

* '''Coautor de''': Constitución Española de 1978.
* '''Fundador de''': Bufete Pérez-Llorca y *Revista Jurídica Pérez-Llorca*.
* '''Afiliado a''': Cortes Generales, Gobierno de España y Museo Nacional del Prado.
* '''Homenaje escrito por''': Soledad Becerril (Defensora del Pueblo 2012–2017).

== 3. POLICY ANALYSIS ==
* '''Background''': Proclaimed at the Nice European Council on 7 December 2000, the Charter gained binding primary legal status equal to the Treaties upon the entry into force of the Lisbon Treaty in December 2009 via Article 6(1) TEU. Prior to the Charter becoming binding, fundamental rights in the EU were protected mainly as unwritten general principles derived from CJEU case law and constitutional traditions common to Member States.
* '''Problem''': The Charter lacks explicit statutory canons of interpretation within its text, sharing this silence with EU primary Treaties and secondary legislation. The CJEU generally refrains from explicitly codifying its interpretative methods to avoid being restricted by rigid schemes.
* '''Legal/Policy Gap''': Ambiguity surrounding how traditional interpretative criteria—textual, systemic/comparative, teleological (effet utile), and subjective—apply to a sui generis legal instrument incorporated into primary law by reference rather than negotiated line-by-line in an intergovernmental conference.
* '''Objectives''': Maintain coherence across the EU legal order, ensure the practical effectiveness (effet utile) of fundamental rights, provide dynamic adaptability for living legal instruments, and prevent restrictions on individual protection.
* '''Scope''': Applies to the CJEU and national courts whenever EU institutions adopt secondary acts or when Member States act within the scope of EU law pursuant to Article 51(1) CFREU.
* '''Implementation''': Enforced through preliminary references under Article 267 TFEU, applying Article 52 CFREU guidelines (para 2 for Treaty conditions, para 3 for ECHR alignment, para 4 for common constitutional traditions) and official Charter Explanations.
* '''Evidence''': Case-law analysis of key rulings including AMS (Case C-176/12), Bauer (Joined Cases C-569/16 & C-570/16), Garlsson Real Estate (Case C-537/16), Di Puma e Zecca (Joined Cases C-596/16 & C-597/16), Max-Planck (Case C-684/16), CCOO (Case C-55/18), Vernaza Ayovi (Case C-96/17), and Kossowski (Case C-486/14).
* '''Impact''': Established direct horizontal effect for self-executing provisions like Article 31(2) paid annual leave in Bauer, while denying direct horizontal effect to broad conditional principles like Article 27 worker information in AMS.
* '''Reform''': Shifted CJEU practice from ad hoc reliance on general principles toward a text-grounded yet flexible interpretative model that uses international instruments (such as ILO conventions and ECHR case law) to expand worker safety and non-discrimination protections.
* '''Unresolved Issues''':
** Managing friction between dynamic fundamental rights expansion and the principle of attributed competences under EU Treaties.
** The difficulty of subjective interpretation due to the Charter being drafted by an inter-institutional Convention rather than negotiated in an intergovernmental conference.
** Ensuring consistent application of the distinction between directly effective "rights" and non-self-executing "principles" across horizontal private litigation.

'''Judicial Interpretation Framework for EU Fundamental Rights''' refers to the hermeneutic rules, principles, and judicial methods applied by the [[Court of Justice of the European Union]] (CJEU) when interpreting the [[Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union]] (CFREU).<ref>D’Agnone, G. (2021). On the Criteria Used for the Interpretation of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union: Some Short Remarks After Twenty Years From Its Proclamation. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 13(2), 619–636.</ref>

=== Lead ===
Since the entry into force of the Lisbon Treaty in 2009, the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union holds primary legal value equal to the EU Treaties under [[Article 6(1) TEU]].<ref>D’Agnone (2021), p. 620.</ref> Research by legal scholars, including [[Giulia D'Agnone]] of the [[University of Campania "Luigi Vanvitelli"]], analyzes how the CJEU navigates the absence of explicit statutory interpretive canons by applying textual, systemic/comparative, and teleological (''effet utile'') methods.<ref>D’Agnone (2021), pp. 619–622.</ref> This framework balances legal certainty with dynamic protection for fundamental rights as living legal instruments.<ref>D’Agnone (2021), p. 635.</ref>

=== Summary ===
The CJEU generally avoids binding itself to a rigid, predetermined scheme of interpretation.<ref>D’Agnone (2021), p. 620.</ref> Because the Charter is a ''sui generis'' instrument incorporated by reference rather than negotiated line-by-line in an intergovernmental conference, the Court uses dynamic techniques to ensure rights remain effective in practice.<ref>D’Agnone (2021), pp. 621, 634–635.</ref>

=== Legal Basis ===
The interpretative framework operates under:
* '''[[Article 6(1) TEU]]''': Attributing binding Treaty-level legal value to the Charter.<ref>TEU, Art. 6(1).</ref>
* '''[[Article 52 CFREU]]''': Defining scope and interpretation, including alignment with the [[European Convention on Human Rights]] (para 3) and constitutional traditions common to Member States (para 4).<ref>CFREU, Art. 52.</ref>
* '''[[Article 53 CFREU]]''': Establishing minimum levels of protection.<ref>CFREU, Art. 53.</ref>
* '''[[Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties]] (1969)''': Codifying standard international rules of treaty interpretation.<ref>Vienna Convention (1969), Arts. 31-33.</ref>

=== Background ===
Prior to 2009, fundamental rights were protected in the EU primarily as unwritten general principles derived from CJEU case-law and common constitutional traditions.<ref>D’Agnone (2021), pp. 625, 635.</ref> Proclaimed at Nice in 2000, the Charter provided a written catalogue, leading to an increasing reliance on codified textual provisions alongside established systemic principles.<ref>D’Agnone (2021), pp. 620, 624.</ref>

=== Objectives ===
* Ensure the practical effectiveness (''effet utile'') of individual rights guaranteed by EU law.<ref>D’Agnone (2021), p. 629.</ref>
* Maintain coherence across the EU legal order and national legal systems.<ref>D’Agnone (2021), p. 625.</ref>
* Provide dynamic adaptability to evolving social and economic conditions.<ref>D’Agnone (2021), p. 635.</ref>

=== Scope ===
Applies to all EU institutions adopting secondary legislation and to EU Member States whenever they implement or act within the scope of EU law pursuant to [[Article 51(1) CFREU]].<ref>D’Agnone (2021), p. 621.</ref>

=== Key Provisions & Canons ===
# '''Textual Interpretation''': Evaluates specific wording (e.g., distinguishing self-executing rights under Article 31(2) in ''Bauer'' from non-self-executing principles under Article 27 in ''AMS'').<ref>D’Agnone (2021), pp. 622–624.</ref>
# '''Systemic & Comparative Interpretation''': Contextualizes Charter articles using international instruments, such as [[ILO]] conventions and ECHR case-law.<ref>D’Agnone (2021), pp. 625–628.</ref>
# '''Teleological Interpretation (''Effet Utile'')''': Focuses on achieving the core objective of the provision (e.g., requiring mandatory working time recording systems in ''CCOO'').<ref>D’Agnone (2021), pp. 629–631.</ref>
# '''Subjective Interpretation''': References historical intentions of drafters, though largely set aside in post-Lisbon CJEU jurisprudence due to the Charter's unique drafting process.<ref>D’Agnone (2021), pp. 633–635.</ref>

=== Implementation ===
Enforced through preliminary reference rulings under Article 267 TFEU, establishing binding precedent for national courts across all Member States.<ref>D’Agnone (2021), pp. 620–625.</ref>

=== Policy Problems ===
* '''Textual Vagueness''': Abstract formulations in Title IV (Solidarity) require secondary legislation to clarify justiciability.<ref>D’Agnone (2021), p. 624.</ref>
* '''Horizontal Direct Effect Uncertainty''': Borderline distinctions between "rights" that create private obligations and "principles" that require legislative implementation.<ref>D’Agnone (2021), pp. 622–624, 633.</ref>

=== Reform ===
Scholars emphasize maintaining interpretive flexibility to preserve the Charter as a living legal instrument without overstepping the principle of attributed competences under EU Treaties.<ref>D’Agnone (2021), p. 635.</ref>

=== Related Entities ===
* '''[[Giulia D'Agnone]]''': Author and legal scholar at University of Campania "Luigi Vanvitelli".<ref>D’Agnone (2021), p. 619.</ref>
* '''[[Court of Justice of the European Union]]''': Primary judicial authority.<ref>D’Agnone (2021), p. 619.</ref>

= The Transformative Private Law Research Framework =

== Lead ==
The framework was formulated by [[Marija Bartl]], Professor of Transnational Private Law at the [[University of Amsterdam]] and Principal Investigator of the [[European Research Council]]-funded N-EXTLAW project. It challenges the complicity of traditional private law modules — contract, property, corporate, and financial law — in the current global poly-crisis.<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 413–414.</ref> By deploying three distinct research strategies — historical variance, comparative research and varieties of capitalisms, and diverse economies — the framework seeks to renew private legal imagination and to provide legal infrastructure for non-extractive economic models.<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 413, 415, 419, 422.</ref>

== Summary ==
The framework critiques current European Union legislative initiatives for falling prey to "neoliberal naturalism" — the assumption that market transparency and profit maximisation are the sole drivers of prosperity.<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 414–415.</ref> Instead, it demonstrates that alternative economic practices, such as cooperatives, social enterprises, and care economies, already exist and account for a significant share of European GDP.<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 419–421.</ref>

== Background ==
Private law institutions — contract, property, corporate, insolvency, and financial law — form the core infrastructure of modern economies. Standard private law modules have, however, been used to generate capital and concentrate wealth while externalising environmental and social costs, contributing directly to a contemporary poly-crisis marked by climate emergency, wealth inequality, democratic backsliding, and technological surveillance.<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 413–414.</ref> Scholarly interventions, notably Katharina Pistor's ''The Code of Capital'', show how leading law firms deploy private law modules to generate wealth for capital holders while socialising environmental and democratic costs.<ref>Bartl (2023), p. 414.</ref> In response, transformative private law seeks to reorient the deep legal infrastructure of the economy toward sustainable, non-extractive futures.<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 413–414.</ref>

== Policy Problem ==
Contemporary law and policy remain captive to '''neoliberal naturalism''' — the uncritical belief that high-profit extractive capitalism is the sole engine of human prosperity, and that market transparency and profit-seeking incentives alone drive innovation.<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 415, 423.</ref> Recent EU legislative initiatives, including sustainability reporting, corporate due diligence, and ecodesign regulation, tinker at the edges of the market without altering foundational private law assumptions such as privity of contract, property as absolute dominion, limited liability, and shareholder primacy.<ref>Bartl (2023), p. 414.</ref>

== Legal Basis ==
The framework evaluates and interacts with several key EU legal instruments:
* '''[[Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive]] (CSRD)''' — the EU framework for mandatory corporate sustainability disclosure.<ref>Bartl (2023), p. 414.</ref>
* '''[[Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive]] (CSDDD Proposal)''' — imposing environmental and human-rights due-diligence obligations across global supply chains.<ref>Bartl (2023), p. 414.</ref>
* '''[[Proposal for Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation]]''' — expanding product sustainability requirements across the EU single market.<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 414–415.</ref>
* '''[[Net Zero Industry Act Proposal]]''' — an EU industrial framework for clean-technology manufacturing.<ref>Bartl (2023), p. 421.</ref>

== Objectives ==
* Decentre neoliberal naturalism and the myth of profit-seeking human nature in private law doctrine.<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 415, 422.</ref>
* Institutionalise non-extractive economic practices built on care, solidarity, and the collective interest.<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 420–422.</ref>
* Reform law-school curricula to include social-economy structures alongside traditional profit-maximising corporations.<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 420–421.</ref>

== Scope ==
The framework applies to European Union private-law policy, national corporate legislation, contract theory, property-law reform, and comparative legal pedagogy across European law faculties.<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 414, 417, 420.</ref>

== Key Provisions and Research Strategies ==
# '''Historical Variance''' — historicising limited liability, freedom of contract, and property as absolute dominion, to demonstrate that corporate power is a contingent political choice rather than a natural state.<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 416–417.</ref>
# '''Comparative Research and Varieties of Capitalisms''' — using comparative law to challenge the notion that Anglo-American "shareholder primacy" is the inevitable end point of corporate law history.<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 417–419.</ref>
# '''Diverse Economies and the Social Economy''' — mapping and supporting entities in which social or environmental purpose takes precedence over profit, surpluses are reinvested, and governance is democratic (e.g., cooperatives, social enterprises, fair-trade organisations, care cooperatives).<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 419–421.</ref>

== Implementation ==
The framework is carried out through academic research under ERC Grant Agreement No. 852990 (the N-EXTLAW project, ''Mainstreaming Law as a Vehicle of Social Change''), with findings published in ''[[The Italian Law Journal]]''.<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 413, 415.</ref>

== Evidence ==
Empirical studies cited in support of the framework indicate that the social economy accounts for roughly 10% of GDP in countries such as Italy, that SMEs contribute around 50% of EU GDP, and that social-economy structures showed greater economic resilience during the 2008 financial crisis in Southern Europe.<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 419–421.</ref>

== Impact ==
The framework offers a theoretical and institutional blueprint for a transformative private law capable of supporting realistic socio-ecological alternatives, redirecting corporate purpose toward the common good, and legitimising non-extractive business models.

== Reform Proposals ==
* Establishing a dedicated EU industrial policy for the social economy.
* Linking executive compensation to non-financial, sustainability-related performance metrics.
* Reforming corporate law to remove limited-liability shields for systemic environmental harm.
* Embedding diverse-economy models into standard law-school curricula.
* Expanding consumer repair rights.<ref>Bartl (2023), pp. 421–422.</ref>

== Unresolved Issues ==
# Persistent EU legislative reluctance to move beyond communications and action plans toward binding structural private-law statutes for the social economy.
# The risk that traditional private-law doctrines — such as legal certainty and legitimate expectations — will be invoked to block socio-ecological reform.
# Reconciling profit-capping or surplus-reinvestment requirements with traditional capital-market expectations.

* '''[[University of Amsterdam]]''' (Stable ID: JPW-INST-001) — Host academic institution.<ref>Bartl (2023), p. 413.</ref>

'''Strategic Plan of the International Criminal Court for 2023-2025''' is the ICC's official strategic policy document for the 2023–2025 period, setting out 10 strategic goals across 3 pillars, supported by 27 measurable Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and, for the first time, aligning the four principal components of the Court (the Court/Presidency, the OTP, the Registry, and the TFV) within a single strategic cycle.

== Summary ==
The document harmonizes four internal strategic plans — the Court as a whole, the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP), the Registry, and the Trust Fund for Victims (TFV) — into one coordinated cycle. The plan is anchored by 10 strategic goals across 3 pillars, complemented by 27 KPIs for objective measurement of results.

== Legal Basis ==

* [[Rome Statute]]: particularly the complementarity principle and Article 93(10) on information-sharing with national authorities.
* Mandate of the [[Assembly of States Parties]] (ASP).
* Recommendations of the [[Independent Expert Review]] (IER), 2020.
* The [[One-Court Principle]] coordination framework, through the [[Coordination Council]].

== Background ==
The plan continues and expands on the achievements of the 2019–2021 Strategic Plan (extended through 2022). It responds to a sharp increase in judicial workload, the growing complexity of global conflicts, historical liquidity crises, and the need for internal governance reform following the Independent Expert Review. For the first time in the Court's history, it aligns four concurrent strategic plans in a single cycle and integrates 384 recommendations from the IER's Final Report of 30 September 2020.

== Objectives ==

* Provide a responsive, flexible, and resilient operational framework.
* Accelerate the expeditiousness of proceedings without compromising fairness or the highest legal standards.
* Integrate victims' rights, gender perspectives, and the handling of sexual and gender-based crimes (SGBC) and crimes against children (CAC).
* Strengthen international cooperation, complementarity, and resource-management efficiency.

== Key Provisions ==
The plan sets out 10 strategic goals across 3 pillars:

* '''Pillar 1: Judicial and Prosecutorial Performance'''
** '''Goal 1''': Improve the speed and efficiency of core judicial activities.
** '''Goal 2''': Develop the Court's approach to victims and reparations.
** '''Goal 3''': Mainstream gender perspectives across all areas of work.
* '''Pillar 2: Cooperation and Complementarity'''
** '''Goal 4''': Strengthen political support and operational cooperation modalities.
** '''Goal 5''': Advance complementarity and close gaps in impunity.
* '''Pillar 3: Organizational Performance'''
** '''Goal 6''': Strengthen professionalism, dedication, and integrity.
** '''Goal 7''': Ensure a safe, secure work environment focused on staff wellbeing.
** '''Goal 8''': Achieve fair geographical representation and gender balance (GRGB).
** '''Goal 9''': Manage resources effectively, transparently, and sustainably (environmentally responsible).
** '''Goal 10''': Develop and implement a completion strategy for situations under investigation.

== Implementation ==
Implementation is anchored in the One-Court principle and monitored via the Court-wide Values Project (launched 13 July 2022), advisory case-handling deadlines in the 5th edition of the Chambers' Practice Manual, expanded field presence, adoption of SGBC and CAC investigation policies, appointment of an Ombuds for informal dispute resolution, alignment with the 2023 annual budget, and regular risk monitoring by the Risk Management Committee (RMC).

== Evidence ==
The framework is monitored through 27 quantitative and qualitative KPIs developed via inter-organ consultation. Key indicators include:

* '''Judicial Timeframes (KPI 1.1)''': Targets for investigation authorization (120 days), first appearance (48–96 hours), confirmation-of-charges decisions (60 days), Article 74 judgments (10 months), and appeal judgments (10 months).
* '''Hearing Cancellation Rate (KPI 1.2)''': Baseline of 42.2%, with a target for significant reduction.
* '''Geographical and Gender Representation (KPI 8.1–8.3)''': Target to reduce the number of non-represented/under-represented States Parties (baseline 25/54, target 24/53) and ensure at least 50% of senior staff recruitment (P-4 and above) are women.
* '''Budget Compliance (KPI 9.1)''': Baseline budget execution rate of 97.4%, with a target of 100%.

title: JPW-PLAN-002
wikitext:
'''Office of the Prosecutor Strategic Plan 2023-2025''' is the first comprehensive official strategy document issued during the tenure of Prosecutor Karim A.A. Khan KC, setting out the framework, vision, values, and 10 strategic goals of the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) of the International Criminal Court for the 2023–2025 period.

== Summary ==
The plan is designed to make the OTP more dynamic, efficient, technology-driven, field-centric, and victim-centred, aligning its priorities with the concurrent ICC and Registry strategic plans and integrating recommendations from the Independent Expert Review (IER), including R14, R71, R87, R270, and R278.

== Legal Basis ==

* [[Rome Statute]]: The complementarity principle and Article 93(10) on mutual legal assistance.
* Mandate of the [[Assembly of States Parties]] (ASP).
* Recommendations of the [[Independent Expert Review]] (IER), 2020.

== Background ==
The plan was developed based on an assessment of OTP performance over 2019–2021/2022 by the Independent Oversight Mechanism (IOM), together with internal consultations and workplace-culture panels. It is aligned with the concurrent ICC and Registry strategic plans.

== Objectives ==

* Accelerate and improve the quality of investigations and prosecutions at trial.
* Strengthen national authorities' capacity to combat impunity through a renewed complementarity approach.
* Establish the OTP as a global technology leader in digital evidence processing and AI.
* Bring justice closer to affected communities and deepen partnerships with civil society.
* Improve the working environment, gender diversity, and geographical staff representation.

== Key Provisions ==
The plan establishes 10 Strategic Goals:

* '''Goal 1''': Deliver results in the courtroom.
* '''Goal 2''': Enhance efforts by national authorities to fight impunity.
* '''Goal 3''': Make the Office a global technology leader.
* '''Goal 4''': Bring justice closer to communities and deepen engagement with civil society.
* '''Goal 5''': A renewed policy framework for the Office.
* '''Goal 6''': Ensure effective investigations and prosecutions of SGBC and CAC.
* '''Goal 7''': Increase the field presence of the Office of the Prosecutor.
* '''Goal 8''': Increase efficiency of work and ensure proper resourcing and staffing.
* '''Goal 9''': Strengthen global support for the work of the Office.
* '''Goal 10''': Improve the working environment and ensure a respectful working culture.

== Implementation ==
Implementation is monitored via 20 Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) in Annex 1, annual performance reporting, and an independent evaluation by the IOM at the end of the 2024/2025 cycle. Execution involves integrated planning (situation, investigation, cooperation, outreach, and complementarity plans), digital case-management systems, an updated Operations Manual (2023), internal/external evidence reviews, an AI/machine-learning-based cloud e-discovery platform, expanded field staffing, active participation in Joint Investigation Teams (JITs), and the Court-wide Values Project.

== Evidence ==
Key indicators from the 20-KPI framework (Annex 1) include:

* '''Applications for Warrants of Arrest (KPI 1)''': Target of at least 10 applications per year.
* '''Response to Article 93(10) RFAs (KPI 3)''': Target initial substantive response within 2 months.
* '''Civil Society Engagement (KPI 7)''': Annual outreach program plus 2 thematic roundtable discussions with NGOs per year.
* '''SGBC & CAC Training (KPI 12)''': Target 100% of relevant staff and team members certified in SGBC/CAC training.
* '''Senior Management Gender Balance (KPI 20)''': Baseline of 72% male : 28% female (2021), with a target of 60% male : 40% female by 2023.

== Policy Issues ==

* Processing large-scale digital evidence requiring significant technology investment.
* Handling sensitive cases such as sexual and gender-based crimes (SGBC) and crimes against children (CAC), requiring a trauma-informed approach.
* The need to address internal workplace-culture issues and increase the share of women in leadership at the P-4 level and above.

== Reform / Future Directions ==
Adoption of a forensic rotation model, use of a dedicated Financial Investigations Unit, a shift from an HQ-centric to a field-centric presence model, application of a trauma-informed approach, and close cooperation with the IOM for periodic strategic evaluation in 2024/2025.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''[[Office of the Prosecutor]]''': Principal implementing organ.
* '''[[International Criminal Court]]''': Parent institution.
* '''[[Registry (ICC)]]''': Partner organ providing administrative and technical services.
* '''[[Karim A.A. Khan KC]]''': ICC Prosecutor, sworn in 16 June 2021, who led development of this strategic plan.
* '''[[Eurojust]]''': Joint Investigation Team (JIT) partner, notably for the situation in Ukraine (with 7 countries) and cooperation on crimes against migrants and refugees in Libya.
* '''[[EU Genocide Network]]''': Partner organization.
* '''[[Independent Oversight Mechanism]]''' (IOM): Body conducting independent evaluation of OTP performance.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''
* '''[[Ferdi Raditya Akbar]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''

title: JPW-PLAN-003
wikitext:
'''Registry Strategic Plan 2023-2025''' is the official strategic policy document of the Registry of the International Criminal Court for the 2023–2025 period, setting out 2 strategic goals, 10 priority objectives, and 31 Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) to support judicial efficiency and organizational governance across the Court.

== Summary ==
The plan is fully synchronized with the concurrent strategic plans of the Court as a whole, the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP), and the Trust Fund for Victims (TFV), aiming to create Court-wide performance synergy. It builds on the achievements of the 2019–2021 Registry Strategic Plan (extended through 2022 as a transition year) and integrates recommendations from the September 2020 Independent Expert Review (IER) Final Report and the December 2021 Independent Oversight Mechanism (IOM) evaluation.

== Legal Basis ==

* [[Rome Statute]] mandate and decisions of the [[Assembly of States Parties]] (ASP).
* [[Financial Rules and Regulations]] (FRR).
* Recommendations of the [[Independent Expert Review]] (IER) Final Report, September 2020.
* Evaluation report of the [[Independent Oversight Mechanism]] (IOM), December 2021.

== Background ==
A substantial increase in judicial workload and new investigations opened by the OTP required extensive operational, technical, administrative, and security support. The Registry also had to manage post-COVID-19 recovery, mitigate the effects of external sanctions such as U.S. Executive Order 13928 (June 2020), address gender imbalance at senior management levels, and confront geographical staff representation gaps, with 79 States Parties classified as non-represented or under-represented by the end of 2021.

== Objectives ==

* '''Strategic Goal 1''': A more efficient Registry delivering more effective services across all areas, reflecting a culture of continuous improvement.
* '''Strategic Goal 2''': A more engaged Registry workforce, through the promotion of organizational culture and values, and improved geographical representation and gender balance (GRGB).

== Key Provisions ==
The plan sets out 10 Priority Objectives:

* '''1.1''': Effectiveness of management, judicial, and external operational services.
* '''1.2''': Efficient management of resources and budget.
* '''1.3''': Application of continuous-improvement principles.
* '''1.4''': Strengthened State cooperation environment and public awareness.
* '''1.5''': Effective support for victims and witnesses.
* '''1.6''': Strengthened structure for defence teams and victims' legal representation.
* '''2.1''': Improved geographical representation and gender balance (GRGB), diversity, and inclusion.
* '''2.2''': Staff capacity development and application of the ICC Leadership Framework.
* '''2.3''': Flexible workforce framework and talent acquisition.
* '''2.4''': Strengthened staff engagement, wellbeing, and accountability mechanisms.

== Implementation ==
Implementation follows a cascade model, with modernization of the Judicial Workflow Platform (JWP) and migration of data to Microsoft Cloud, automation via an ERP system (SAP S/4 HANA), recruitment of an Ombuds position, development of administrative guidance on discrimination and harassment, rollout of the Court-wide Values Project, and integration of the ICC Leadership Framework. Progress is monitored quarterly by the Registry Management Team (RMT) via a digital Registry Dashboard and Activity Tracker.

== Evidence ==
Selected KPIs from Annex 1's 31-indicator framework:

* '''Budget Execution Rate (KPI 4)''': Baseline 98.8% (2021), target 99% (2023).
* '''Competitive Procurement Tenders (KPI 5)''': Baseline 64%, target 65%.

== Policy Issues ==

* Long processing times for permanent relocation of protected witnesses/victims, requiring intensive coordination with States Parties.
* A high number of States Parties remaining non-represented or under-represented among staff.
* The need to mitigate liquidity crises and arrears in state financial contributions.

== Reform / Future Directions ==
Full implementation of IER recommendations across 2023–2025; adoption of a tenure policy; creation of a National Professional Officer (NPO) category; conduct of a Secondary Trauma Survey; and implementation of a Sustainability Plan to reduce the Court building's carbon footprint through ATES systems, LED lighting, and a paperless-organization model.

categorized as copyright infringement [[Infringement Risk]]. * '''Jurisdictional Challenges''': Enforcing IP law against generative AI systems is hindered by differences in legal standards across countries [[Jurisdictional Challenges]]. * '''Global Regulatory Compliance Obligation''': AI providers and users are advised to strengthen internal governance and monitor continually evolving global AI regulation [[Regulatory Compliance]]. == Implementation == * '''Official Release Date''': Published by Eversheds Sutherland on 9 October 2025 and accessible through the [[Apple]] and [[Spotify]] Fort (شريكة في أتلانتا، الولايات المتحدة)، وCaroline Lyannaz (شريكة في باريس، فرنسا)، وDavid Wilkinson (شريك في المملكة المتحدة) [1–4]. * تشمل القضايا الرئيسية التي تُناقش: مخاطر حقوق النشر لمزوّدي الذكاء الاصطناعي ومستخدميه، وتحليل ما إذا كان تدريب نماذج الذكاء الاصطناعي على محتوى الغير يُشكّل انتهاكاً لحقوق النشر، واتجاهات التقاضي التي تُشكّل قانون الذكاء الاصطناعي والملكية الفكرية، وتحديات الاختصاص القضائي في الإنفاذ، وأثر اللوائح العالمية على الامتثال في مجال الملكية الفكرية [1–4]. * تُوزَّع الحلقة عالمياً عبر الموقع الرسمي لشركة Eversheds Sutherland وكذلك عبر منصتَي البث Apple وSpotify [1–3]. * المادة المنشورة مقدَّمة من Eversheds Sutherland لأغراض المعلومات العامة فقط ولا تُعد استشارة قانونية محددة [1–3]. * لم يُعثر على الكيانَين Cecep Mustafa وRosianna Maretha Hasibuan في وثائق المصدر المتاحة [1–6]. '''التفسير (INTERPRETATION)''' * يدفع عدم اليقين القانوني بشأن مشروعية استخدام البيانات المحمية بحقوق النشر لتدريب الذكاء الاصطناعي إلى ضرورة مواءمة اللوائح العالمية والاستعداد للتخفيف من مخاطر الامتثال لدى مطوّري الذكاء الاصطناعي ومستخدميه [1–4]. '''الاستنتاج (INFERENCE)''' * يواجه مزوّدو تقنية الذكاء الاصطناعي ومستخدموها العاملون عبر الولايات القضائية مخاطر تقاضٍ كبيرة وغرامات عدم امتثال إذا لم يعتمدوا بشكل استباقي عمليات تدقيق امتثال حقوق النشر لبيانات التدريب الخاصة بهم [1–4]. ---- == خريطة المعرفة (Knowledge Graph Mapping) == [Nasser Ali Khasawneh / Ann G.
