title: JPW-POLICY-000009
wikitext: {{Infobox Judicial Policy | name = Indian Dispute Resolution and Judicial System Framework | original_name = Dispute Resolution Process in India (IDE Asian Law Series No. 16) | stable_id = JPW-POLICY-000009 | jurisdiction = Republic of India | issuing_authority = Indian Law Institute (ILI) and Institute of Developing Economies (IDE-JETRO) | date_established = 2002-03-01 | legal_basis = Constitution of India; Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996; Consumer Protection Act 1986; Industrial Disputes Act 1947; Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 | status = Active / Judicial Policy Benchmark | related_entities = Supreme Court of India, High Courts of India, Indian Law Institute, NALSA, CPCB, NCDRC, IDE-JETRO }} The '''Indian Dispute Resolution and Judicial System Framework''' (Stable ID: JPW-POLICY-000009) is a national judicial policy and research framework evaluating the unitary court hierarchy, case pendency, specialized tribunals, and alternative dispute resolution (ADR) mechanisms in the Republic of India. Documented under IDE Asian Law Series No. 16 by Professor (Ms) S. K. Verma and Professor S. C. Srivastava of the Indian Law Institute, the policy examines statutory Lok Adalats, Fast Track Courts, Gram Panchayats, commercial arbitration under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, consumer dispute redressal agencies, labor adjudication, and environmental litigation. Note: Named entities ''Cecep Mustafa'' and ''Reihan Abdan Syakur'' are ''Not found in the available sources''. == Summary == The framework addresses the severe case pendency affecting Indian courts (exceeding 20.3 million cases in subordinate courts and 3.55 million in High Courts in late 2001). It outlines seven core structural pillars: (1) Unitary Judiciary, maintaining a single integrated court hierarchy under the Supreme Court and 21 High Courts; (2) Fast Track Courts, deploying 1,734 centrally funded ad-hoc courts under the 11th Finance Commission to clear sessions cases; (3) Statutory Lok Adalats, institutionalizing conciliatory people's courts under the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 that settled 13–15 million cases; (4) Grass-Roots Justice, establishing 3-tier Panchayati Raj institutions under the 73rd Constitutional Amendment with 33% female reservation; (5) Commercial Arbitration & Conciliation, modernizing domestic and international arbitration under the UNCITRAL-based 1996 Act; (6) Consumer Dispute Redressal, creating 3-tier summary fora under the Consumer Protection Act 1986; and (7) Environmental Public Interest Litigation (PIL), enforcing constitutional rights to a clean environment. == Legal Basis == Authority and execution derive from constitutional provisions and statutory enactments: * '''Constitutional Basis:''' Constitution of India (1950, Arts. 32, 39-A, 48A, 51(d), 51A(g), 130, 136, 145, 215, 226, 235, 243–243O, 246(4), 252, 323B, 348). * '''Arbitration & Legal Services Statutes:''' Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996; Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987. * '''Specialized Adjudication Statutes:''' Consumer Protection Act, 1986; Industrial Disputes Act, 1947; Family Courts Act, 1984. * '''Environmental Statutes:''' Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 & Cess Act, 1977; Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981; Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991; National Environment Appellate Authority Act, 1997. * '''Procedural Codes & Amendments:''' Code of Civil Procedure, 1908; Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973; Constitution (73rd Amendment) Act, 1992. == Background & Policy Problems == === Background === Post-independence economic expansion and rising rights consciousness flooded India's adversarial court system with unprecedented litigation. By 2001, civil and criminal case pendency reached over 20 million subordinate court cases and 3.55 million High Court cases, prompting comprehensive judicial and ADR reforms. === Policy Problems === * Colossal Case Pendency & Backlog: Over 20.32 million cases pending in subordinate courts and 3.55 million in High Courts. * Excessive Trial Delays: Average civil lawsuit disposition times range between 5 to 15 years due to summons service delays, interlocutory applications, and trial adjournments. * Judge Shortages & Vacancies: High vacancy rates (~15.14% of 13,140 sanctioned judicial posts vacant in 2001). * Low Conviction Rates: IPC conviction rate hovered around 39.02%, overcrowding jails with 180,000 undertrial prisoners. * Demoralization of Trial Judges: Higher appellate judges frequently issuing intemperate or derogatory remarks against trial judges. == Objectives == 1. Reduce court pendency through Fast Track Courts and procedural law amendments. 2. Expand accessible, low-cost ADR via statutory Lok Adalats, Permanent Lok Adalats, and conciliation. 3. Guarantee legal aid and class-action representation (PIL) for poor and disadvantaged citizens. 4. Empower rural self-government (Panchayati Raj) with mandatory representation for women, SC, and ST populations. 5. Provide summary, court-fee-free redressal for consumer complaints within a 90-day target. 6. Enforce absolute liability and polluter-pays doctrines in environmental protection. == Scope & Implementation == === Scope === Applies across all Federal, State, and Union Territory judicial structures, specialized tribunals, arbitration bodies, consumer fora, labor courts, and environmental agencies in the Republic of India. === Key Provisions === * '''Fast Track Court Scheme:''' Setting up 1,734 ad-hoc courts in districts to dispose of 2+ year old sessions cases and undertrial detentions. * '''Lok Adalat Finality:''' Binding civil-decree status for compromise awards made by Lok Adalats without statutory right of appeal (Sec. 19–21 Legal Services Authorities Act). * '''Panchayati Raj Empowerment:''' Mandatory 5-year terms, direct elections, and 33% female reservation in Gram Panchayats (Art. 243B–243D). * '''Summary Consumer Adjudication:''' 3-tier quasi-judicial fora empowered to order repair, replacement, refund, or compensation without mandatory lawyer representation. * '''Citizens' Environmental Prosecutions:''' 60-day notice requirement for private citizens to prosecute non-complying industrial polluters before magistrates. === Implementation === * '''Pendency Reduction:''' Supreme Court pendency reduced from 104,936 cases in 1991 to 21,716 in 2001. * '''Lok Adalat Settlements:''' Over 108,000 Lok Adalats held, resolving 13.45 million cases and disbursing Rs. 32.7 billion in MACT claims. * '''Consumer Fora Disposals:''' 1.41 million cases filed in District Forums with an 82.8% disposal rate. == Policy Problems == * Subordinate Court Congestion: Over 20 million pending trial court cases and 3.55 million High Court cases. * Judicial Vacancies: 15.14% vacancy rate across total judge posts in 2001. * Relitigation of Arbitration Awards: Repeated appeals in High Courts delaying award execution for 10–20 years. == Reform == * Proposed enactment of the Legal Services Authorities (Amendment) Bill 2002 for Permanent Lok Adalats. * Implementation of court computerization, e-filing, and prison-court video linkages. == Related Key Figures & Institutions == === Key Figures === * '''Prof. (Ms) S. K. Verma:''' Director, Indian Law Institute (ILI); Project Director and principal contributor. * '''Prof. S. C. Srivastava:''' Research Professor, Indian Law Institute; author of chapters on labor and court systems. * '''Ms. Geeta Obrai:''' Research Assistant at the Indian Law Institute; contributor. * '''M. C. Mehta:''' Renowned environmental advocate who obtained landmark Supreme Court decisions (Taj Trapezium, Ganga pollution, Oleum gas leak, CNG conversion). * '''Justice K. T. Thomas:''' Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of India; author of ''Braj Kishore Thakur v. Union of India'' protecting trial judges against intemperate remarks. * '''Justice B. N. Kirpal:''' Associate Justice (later Chief Justice) of the Supreme Court of India; author of opinions in ''R.C. Sood v. High Court of Rajasthan''. * '''Justice A. S. Anand:''' Former Chief Justice of India who presided over benches enforcing clean fuel (CNG) conversion. === Key Institutions === * [[Indian Law Institute]] (ILI) * [[Supreme Court of India]] * National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission ([[NCDRC]]) * Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) * [[Institute of Developing Economies]] (IDE-JETRO) == Knowledge Graph & Entity Relationships == {| class="wikitable" |- ! title: JPW-POLICY-000010
wikitext: {{Infobox Judicial Policy | name = Malaysian Dispute Resolution and Judicial System Framework | original_name = Dispute Resolution Process in Malaysia (IDE Asian Law Series No. 17) | stable_id = JPW-POLICY-000010 | jurisdiction = Malaysia | issuing_authority = Faculty of Law, University of Malaya and Institute of Developing Economies (IDE-JETRO) | date_established = 2002-03-01 | legal_basis = Federal Constitution of Malaysia; Consumer Protection Act 1999; Industrial Relations Act 1967; Employment Act 1955; Environmental Quality Act 1974 | status = Active / Judicial Policy Benchmark | related_entities = Federal Court of Malaysia, Court of Appeal, High Court of Malaya, High Court of Sabah & Sarawak, Tribunal for Consumer Claims, Industrial Court, SOCSO, Department of Environment, IDE-JETRO }} The '''Malaysian Dispute Resolution and Judicial System Framework''' (Stable ID: JPW-POLICY-000010) is a national judicial policy and research framework evaluating the common law judicial hierarchy, trial backlogs, case-management rules, specialized dispute settlement tribunals, and statutory environmental enforcement in Malaysia. Documented under IDE Asian Law Series No. 17 by Associate Professor Sharifah Suhana Syed Ahmad and Associate Professor Mary George of the Faculty of Law, University of Malaya, the policy analyzes court backlogs, High Court Order 34 case management, the Tribunal for Consumer Claims, the Industrial Court, SOCSO social security schemes, and environmental litigation under the Environmental Quality Act 1974. Note: Named entities ''Cecep Mustafa'' and ''Reihan Abdan Syakur'' are ''Not found in the available sources''. == Summary == The framework addresses the severe civil and criminal case backlogs affecting Malaysian courts in the late 1990s and 2000. It outlines six core structural pillars: (1) Common Law Judicial Hierarchy, maintaining a court structure topped by the Federal Court, Court of Appeal, and two High Courts (Malaya, Sabah & Sarawak); (2) Pre-Trial Case Management, introducing High Court Order 34 in September 2000 to streamline trials and limit witness lists; (3) Consumer Redressal, creating the Tribunal for Consumer Claims under the Consumer Protection Act 1999 for claims up to RM10,000 without lawyer representation; (4) Labour & Industrial Adjudication, combining Labour Court wage inquiries under the Employment Act 1955 with compulsory Industrial Court arbitration under the Industrial Relations Act 1967; (5) Social Security Protection, administering employment injury and invalidity benefits through SOCSO and the Social Security Appellate Board; and (6) Environmental Enforcement, executing strict statutory liability for water, air, and open burning pollution under the Environmental Quality Act 1974. == Legal Basis == Authority and execution derive from constitutional provisions and statutory enactments: * '''Constitutional Basis:''' Federal Constitution of Malaysia (Arts. 4(1), 73–77, 95B(1), 145(3), Ninth Schedule Lists I, II, III, IIIA). * '''Consumer & Commercial Statutes:''' Consumer Protection Act 1999 (Act 599); Sale of Goods Act 1957; Contracts Act 1950 & Hire Purchase Act 1967. * '''Labour & Employment Statutes:''' Industrial Relations Act 1967 (Act 177, Revised 1976); Employment Act 1955 (Act 265, Revised 1981); Employees' Social Security Act 1969 (Act 4); Trade Unions Act 1959. * '''Environmental Statutes:''' Environmental Quality Act 1974 (Act 127, as amended by Act A636, Act A953, Act A1030, Act A1102). * '''Procedural Codes & Rules:''' Rules of the High Court (Order 34). == Background & Policy Problems == === Background === Economic growth and expanded education in Malaysia generated a surge in trading, commercial, labor, and environmental disputes during the late 20th century. Court registries became overwhelmed with active files, trial postponements, and delayed written judgments, driving reforms to computerize court files, introduce pre-trial case management, and establish specialized non-court tribunals. === Policy Problems === * Severe Court Backlogs: Massive pendency across all levels of the court hierarchy (e.g., 159,163 civil and 338,218 criminal cases pending in Magistrates' Courts; 84,329 civil cases in Sessions Courts; 54,235 civil cases in High Courts as of December 2000). * Judicial Overwork & Delayed Judgments: Trial judges hearing chamber matters and trials all day, leaving minimal time to draft written judgments. * Inaccessibility for Small Claims: High litigation costs, technical civil procedure rules, and advocate fees preventing ordinary consumers from enforcing minor claims. * Industrial Unrest: Trade disputes threatening national economic productivity, requiring mandatory arbitration mechanisms. * Environmental Hazards: Atmospheric pollution, industrial effluent, open burning, and constitutional friction between federal environmental rules and state land/water rights. == Objectives == 1. Clear trial court backlogs through High Court Order 34 pre-trial conferences and file computerization. 2. Provide summary, low-cost consumer dispute resolution up to RM10,000 within a 60-day target. 3. Guarantee industrial stability via compulsory labor arbitration and prohibition of strikes during proceedings. 4. Provide comprehensive social security injury coverage for workers through SOCSO. 5. Combat environmental pollution, hazardous waste dumping, and illegal open burning. == Scope & Implementation == === Scope === Applies across all Superior Courts (Federal Court, Court of Appeal, High Courts), Subordinate Courts (Sessions Courts, Magistrates' Courts), consumer tribunals, labor courts, SOCSO boards, and environmental enforcement divisions in Malaysia. === Key Provisions === * '''Pre-Trial Case Management (Order 34):''' Mandatory pre-trial conference requiring document exchange, witness limits, and show-cause notices for non-compliance. * '''Consumer Claims Jurisdiction:''' Summary hearings for claims up to RM10,000 for an RM5 fee, prohibiting advocate representation. * '''Labour Court Inquiries:''' Director General of Labour empowered under Sec. 69 Employment Act 1955 to issue binding cash payment orders with 8% interest. * '''Compulsory Labour Arbitration:''' Ministerial discretion to refer trade disputes and dismissals to the Industrial Court, making awards binding and prohibiting strikes. * '''Open Burning Ban (Sec. 29A/29AA EQA):''' Strict prohibition on open burning carrying fines up to RM500,000 or 5 years imprisonment, shifting burden of proof to landowners. === Implementation === * '''Pre-Trial Case Management Execution:''' Implementation of High Court Order 34 conferences across civil registries. * '''Consumer Tribunal Operations:''' Settling 1,025 claims in 2001 through hearings and conciliation. * '''Industrial Dispute Adjudication:''' Industrial Court hearing 664 cases in 1998 and 701 in 2000. * '''Environmental Prosecutions:''' Prosecuting 158 premises in 2000 and issuing 1,645 compound notices totaling RM2.56 million. == Policy Problems == * Trial Backlogs & Overworked Judges: High Courts and Sessions Courts burdened by heavy dockets and delayed written judgments. * Public EIA Non-Disclosure: Lack of statutory duty under Section 34A EQA to distribute EIA reports to the public without explicit request and fee payment. * Legalism in Labour Adjudication: Federal Court decisions (''Syarikat Kenderaan Melayu Kelantan'', ''Ramachandran'') subjecting Industrial Court awards to extensive civil court judicial review. == Reform == * Proposed expansion of court-annexed ADR to civil family, motor accident, and property claims. * Adoption of ISO 9002 standardized procedures for reviewing detailed EIA reports by DOE. == Related Key Figures & Institutions == === Key Figures === * '''Sharifah Suhana Syed Ahmad:''' Associate Professor, Faculty of Law, University of Malaya; co-author. * '''Mary George:''' Associate Professor, Faculty of Law, University of Malaya; co-author. * '''Puan Noor Azian Shaari:''' President of the Tribunal for Consumer Claims in Malaysia. * '''Dato' Seri Abdullah bin Hj Ahmad Badawi:''' Deputy Prime Minister of Malaysia (in 2000). * '''YB Datuk Law Hieng Ding:''' Minister of Science, Technology and the Environment. * '''Gopal Sri Ram JCA:''' Judge of the Court of Appeal of Malaysia who delivered landmark judgments in administrative law and environmental appeals (''Kajing Tubek case''). * '''Ahmad Fairuz JCA & Mokhtar Sidin JCA:''' Judges of the Court of Appeal of Malaysia sitting on the ''Kajing Tubek'' appeal bench. * '''Gani Patail:''' Senior Federal Counsel representing the Director General of Environmental Quality and Government of Malaysia. * '''Datuk Fong:''' State Attorney General of the State of Sarawak. * '''Gurdial Singh Nijar:''' Counsel representing native respondents in the ''Kajing Tubek Bakun Dam'' litigation. === Key title: JPW-POLICY-000011
wikitext: {{Infobox Judicial Policy | name = Philippine Dispute Resolution and Judicial System Framework | original_name = Dispute Resolution Mechanism in the Philippines (IDE Asian Law Series No. 18) | stable_id = JPW-POLICY-000011 | jurisdiction = Republic of the Philippines | issuing_authority = College of Law, University of the Philippines and Institute of Developing Economies (IDE-JETRO) | date_established = 2002-03-01 | legal_basis = 1987 Philippine Constitution; Consumer Act (R.A. 7394); Labor Code (P.D. 442); Local Government Code (R.A. 7160); IPRA (R.A. 8371) | status = Active / Judicial Policy Benchmark | related_entities = Supreme Court of the Philippines, Court of Appeals, PHILJA, PMC, NLRC, NCMB, DTI-BTRCP, DARAB, CIAC, NCIP, IDE-JETRO }} The '''Philippine Dispute Resolution and Judicial System Framework''' (Stable ID: JPW-POLICY-000011) is a national judicial policy and research framework evaluating the 4-tiered court hierarchy, court congestion, Supreme Court judicial reform programs, court-referred mediation, Katarungang Pambarangay, and specialized dispute resolution mechanisms in the Republic of the Philippines. Documented under IDE Asian Law Series No. 18 by legal scholars from the University of the Philippines College of Law (Profs. Concepcion Lim-Jardeleza, Rowena E.V. Daroy-Morales, Elizabeth Aguiling-Pangalangan, Domingo P. Disini, Jr., and Dante B. Gatmaytan), the policy examines court docket declogging (''The Davide Watch''), Philippine Mediation Center (PMC) court-annexed mediation, consumer protection arbitration, dual labor adjudication, and environmental/indigenous dispute resolution. Note: Named entities ''Cecep Mustafa'' and ''Reihan Abdan Syakur'' are ''Not found in the available sources''. == Summary == The framework addresses the severe court docket congestion affecting Philippine courts (exceeding 824,000 pending cases in December 2000). It outlines six core structural pillars: (1) Four-Tiered Judicial Hierarchy, comprising First Level Trial Courts (MeTC, MTC, MTCC, MCTC), Second Level Courts (RTC, Shari'a District Courts), Court of Appeals / Sandiganbayan / CTA, and the Supreme Court; (2) Court-Referred Mediation, creating the Philippine Mediation Center (PMC) under PHILJA via Supreme Court A.O. 21-2001 to mandate 30-day mediation for civil cases, estate settlements, and summary procedure; (3) Katarungang Pambarangay, institutionalizing community-based conciliation through Lupong Tagapamayapa in over 40,000 barangays with an 87% settlement rate; (4) Administrative Consumer Protection, deploying Consumer Arbitration Officers across DTI, DOH, and DA linked via CONSUMERNET; (5) Dual Labour Dispute Settlement, balancing constitutional preference for collective bargaining and voluntary arbitration with compulsory NLRC arbitration in national interest industries; and (6) Environmental & Indigenous Resource Dispute Resolution, integrating social acceptability into Environmental Impact Assessments and upholding customary law under the Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act (IPRA). == Legal Basis == Authority and execution derive from constitutional provisions and statutory enactments: * '''Constitutional Basis:''' 1987 Constitution of the Philippines (Art. VIII, Sec. 1; Art. II, Secs. 9, 16, 23, 24; Art. XIII, Sec. 3; Art. XVI, Secs. 9, 11). * '''Arbitration & Local Governance Statutes:''' Arbitration Law of 1953 (R.A. 876); Local Government Code of 1991 (R.A. 7160 - Katarungang Pambarangay, Secs. 399–422); P.D. 1508 (1978). * '''Consumer & Commercial Statutes:''' Consumer Act of the Philippines (R.A. 7394); Electronic Commerce Act (R.A. 8792); Securities Regulation Code (R.A. 8799); Intellectual Property Code (R.A. 8293). * '''Labour Statutes:''' Labor Code of the Philippines (P.D. 442, as amended); Migrant Workers and Overseas Filipinos Act (R.A. 8042); Productivity Incentives Act (R.A. 6971). * '''Environmental, Resource & Injunction Statutes:''' Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act of 1997 (R.A. 8371); Philippine Clean Air Act of 1999 (R.A. 8749); Philippine Mining Act of 1995 (R.A. 7942); R.A. 8975 (2000), P.D. 605 (1974), and P.D. 1818 (1981) (Anti-Injunction Laws). * '''Procedural Codes & Rules:''' 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure (Rule 18, Rule 70, Rule 43, Rule 65); Supreme Court A.O. No. 21-2001; Rules on Electronic Evidence; Rule on Examination of a Child Witness. == Background & Policy Problems == === Background === Colonial Western litigation systems altered traditional conversational dispute resolution in the Philippines into adversarial court battles. Expanding trade, industrialization, and population growth created severe court docket congestion, prompting Supreme Court Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide, Jr. to launch ''The Davide Watch'' and the ''Action Plan for Judicial Reform'' to promote out-of-court ADR and court-annexed mediation. === Policy Problems === * Perennial Court Congestion: As of December 2000, 824,821 cases were pending across Philippine courts (including 266,395 in RTCs, 191,290 in MeTCs, 159,451 in MTCCs, and 117,095 in MTCs). * Protracted Adjudication & Appeals: Technical rigidity, automatic death penalty/life imprisonment appeals, bouncing check collection cases (B.P. 22), lawyer delaying tactics, and judicial vacancies stalling final disposition. * Consumer Power Imbalance: Individual buyers facing institutional sellers with vastly superior financial and legal resources, while administrative protection agencies lack authority to award consequential damages. * Low Unionization & Reliance on Compulsory Labor Arbitration: Only 15% of the workforce unionized, forcing the majority of workers to rely on compulsory labor arbitration rather than voluntary bargaining. * Natural Resource Conflicts & Injunction Restrictions: Natural resource access conflicts (mining, forestry, fishing) paired with statutory prohibitions against lower court temporary restraining orders (TROs) on public infrastructure projects. == Objectives == 1. Clear clogged court dockets and dispose of existing case backlogs through Supreme Court reform programs (''The Davide Watch''). 2. Institutionalize court-referred and court-annexed mediation nationwide via the Philippine Mediation Center (PMC) under PHILJA. 3. Preserve community harmony through mandatory local conciliation (Katarungang Pambarangay). 4. Protect consumers against trade malpractices, deceptive sales, and hazardous products under the Consumer Act (R.A. 7394). 5. Foster industrial peace by balancing voluntary collective bargaining/arbitration with compulsory labor arbitration in national interest industries. 6. Guarantee indigenous ancestral domain ownership and customary conflict resolution under IPRA (R.A. 8371). == Scope & Implementation == === Scope === Applies across all regular courts, special courts, constitutional bodies, administrative quasi-judicial agencies, barangay councils, and ADR institutions in the Republic of the Philippines. === Key Provisions === * '''Court-Referred Mediation Referral:''' Mandatory pre-trial order referring civil cases, estate settlements, B.P. 22 civil aspects, and summary procedure cases to PMC units. * '''Katarungang Pambarangay Condition Precedent:''' Mandatory Lupon/Pangkat conciliation for same-city residents prior to judicial filing, with awards becoming final court decrees after 10 days. * '''Consumer Welfare Desks & Arbitration:''' Original jurisdiction of Consumer Arbitration Officers over product safety, mislabeling, and deceptive sales under R.A. 7394. * '''Compulsory Labour Jurisdiction:''' Original jurisdiction of NLRC Labor Arbiters over termination, unfair labor practices, money claims exceeding P5,000, and overseas migrant worker claims (R.A. 8042). * '''IPRA Primacy of Customary Law:''' Mandatory application of customary laws and council of elders certification prior to NCIP or court adjudication of ancestral domain disputes (Sec. 15 / 59 R.A. 8371). === Implementation === * '''PMC Nationwide Rollout:''' Establishing PMC units in courthouses following pilot testing success (85% agreement rate) in four Metro Manila cities. * '''Katarungang Pambarangay Disposals:''' Processing 147,341 annual cases with an 87% settlement rate. * '''DTI Consumer Complaint Resolution:''' Resolving 11,177 cases in 1999 (92% resolution rate). * '''NLRC & NCMB Operations:''' NLRC disposing of 28,599 labor cases in 2000; NCMB settling 80%+ of preventive mediation cases. == Policy Problems == * Severe Lack of ADR Data Monitoring: Systematic failure across government agencies to track settlement durability, cost savings, or post-award compliance. * Lack of Consequential Damage Authority in Consumer ADR: Consumer Arbitration Officers restricted to product repair, replacement, or refund without authority to award consequential damages. * Statutory Anti-Injunction Restrictions: Laws prohibiting lower courts from issuing TROs against infrastructure and natural resource projects. == Reform == * Proposed creation of specialized Small Claims Courts to handle small money claims. * Mandatory inclusion of ADR in law school curricula and MCLE accreditation. == Related Key Figures & Institutions == === Key Figures === * '''Prof. Concepcion Lim-Jardeleza:''' Law Education Specialist at the Institute of Judicial Administration, UP Law Center; title: JPW-POLICY-000012
wikitext: {{Infobox Judicial Policy | name = Thai Alternative Dispute Resolution and Court-Annexed Mediation Framework | original_name = Alternative Dispute Resolution in Thailand (IDE Asian Law Series No. 19) | stable_id = JPW-POLICY-000012 | jurisdiction = Kingdom of Thailand | issuing_authority = Central Intellectual Property and International Trade Court (CIPITC) and IDE-JETRO | date_established = 2002-03-01 | legal_basis = 1997 Constitution of Thailand; Civil Procedure Code (Sec. 20, 20 bis); Arbitration Act B.E. 2530; Court of Justice Mediation Regulations B.E. 2544 | status = Active / Judicial Policy Benchmark | related_entities = Supreme Court of Thailand, CIPITC, Central Labour Court, Thai Arbitration Institute, OCPB, CDRAC, IDE-JETRO }} The '''Thai Alternative Dispute Resolution and Court-Annexed Mediation Framework''' (Stable ID: JPW-POLICY-000012) is a national statutory, judicial, and out-of-court dispute resolution policy framework evaluating court-annexed mediation, commercial arbitration, specialized court procedures, consumer protection, financial debt restructuring, and environmental dispute resolution in the Kingdom of Thailand. Documented under IDE Asian Law Series No. 19 by a judicial working party comprising Senior Justice Prasobsook Boondech, Judge Vichai Ariyanuntaka, Judge Jagkrit Jenjesda, Judge Pinyo Sangphu, Judge Pongratana Cruecrin, and Chief Prosecutor Dr. Chatchom Akapin in collaboration with IDE-JETRO, the policy outlines structural measures for court docket declogging, 2.5% court fee refund incentives, 45-day NPL financial mediation, tripartite labor adjudication, and OCPB consumer litigation. Note: Named entities ''Cecep Mustafa'' and ''Reihan Abdan Syakur'' are ''Not found in the available sources''. == Summary == The framework addresses the trial court backlogs generated by the 1997 Asian economic crisis and the strict 2- to 3-judge trial quorum mandated by Section 236 of the 1997 Constitution. It outlines six core structural pillars: (1) Court-Annexed Mediation, empowering judges under Civil Procedure Code Sections 20 and 20 bis to conduct closed-door conciliation, caucus without attorneys present, and refund up to 2.5% in court fees (up to 200,000 baht) upon early settlement; (2) Financial NPL Restructuring, establishing the Court of Justice Regulation Pertaining to Mediation of Financial Dispute B.E. 2544 (2001) alongside CDRAC/Bank of Thailand frameworks for a 45-day mediation target; (3) Commercial Arbitration, administering domestic and international arbitration via the Thai Arbitration Institute (TAI) under the UNCITRAL-aligned Arbitration Act B.E. 2530; (4) Specialized IP & International Trade Adjudication, deploying 3-judge panels (2 career, 1 lay associate judge), Anton Piller orders, continuous trials, and direct leap-frog Supreme Court appeals under CIPITC Act B.E. 2539; (5) Tripartite Labour Adjudication, combining 3-party judicial panels with free, informal, and compulsory court mediation under the Central Labour Court; and (6) Consumer & Environmental Redress, deploying OCPB administrative enforcement and court representation alongside community-based compromise mechanisms. == Legal Basis == Authority and execution derive from constitutional provisions and statutory enactments: * '''Constitutional Charter:''' Constitution of the Kingdom of Thailand B.E. 2540 (1997, Secs. 236, 271, 276). * '''Procedural Codes & Arbitration Acts:''' Civil Procedure Code (Secs. 19, 20, 20 bis, 193, 210–222); Arbitration Act B.E. 2530 (1987). * '''Court Regulations:''' Court of Justice Regulation Pertaining to Mediation of Financial Dispute B.E. 2544 (2001); Court of Justice Regulation Pertaining to Mediation B.E. 2544 (2001); Practice Guidance Concerning Conciliation (1996); Civil Court Regulation on Mediation B.E. 2537 (1994). * '''Specialized & Administrative Statutes:''' Act Establishing the Intellectual Property and International Trade Court B.E. 2539 (1996); Act on Establishment of Labour Courts B.E. 2522 (1979); Labour Relations Act B.E. 2518 (1975); Labour Protection Act B.E. 2541 (1998); Consumer Protection Act B.E. 2522 (1979, as amended B.E. 2541); Enhancement and Conservation of National Environmental Quality Act B.E. 2535 (1992). == Background & Policy Problems == === Background === Following the 1997 economic crisis and the expansion of international commercial transactions, Thai court registries faced an unprecedented influx of civil and NPL lawsuits, accumulating over 216,000 pending cases in 2001. To avoid trial paralysis under 1997 constitutional quorum mandates, the Court of Justice, after separating from the Ministry of Justice, established court-annexed mediation divisions and standardized national mediation regulations. === Policy Problems === * Excessive Trial Delays & Backlogs: Standard adversary procedures delaying civil lawsuits for 5 to 10 years. * Mandated Quorum Pressures: Section 236 of the 1997 Constitution requiring full 2- or 3-judge quorums sitting across all hearings, threatening docket paralysis. * Disadvantage of Individual Consumers: Financial and technical imbalances preventing consumers from suing large firms in formal litigation. * Escalation of Labor Disputes: Post-war industrialization multiplying labor court filings and threatening industrial harmony. * Complex Proof in Environmental Claims: Strict civil tort causation rules preventing victims of environmental pollution from proving toxic liability. == Objectives == 1. Eliminate trial court backlogs through court-annexed mediation and pre-trial conciliation. 2. Resolve NPL financial disputes through structured 45-day mediation schedules. 3. Provide specialized, fast-track adjudication for IP and international trade disputes via CIPITC. 4. Ensure speedy, cost-free labor adjudication using tripartite quorums and mandatory court mediation. 5. Protect consumers against false advertising, deceptive labels, and hazardous goods via OCPB. 6. Promote "win-win" out-of-court settlements aligned with Thai cultural preferences for compromise. == Scope & Implementation == === Scope === Applies across all Courts of First Instance (Civil Court, Kwaeng/Municipal Courts, Provincial Courts), specialized courts (CIPITC, Central Labour Court), TAI arbitration, OCPB, CDRAC, and administrative agencies in Thailand. === Key Provisions === * '''Closed-Door Mediation & Caucusing (Sec. 20 bis CPC):''' Judicial authority to conduct mediation behind closed doors, caucus with individual parties without counsel present, and appoint expert conciliator panels. * '''Financial Mediation Timeframe:''' Mandatory 45-day mediation target (extendible twice by 15 days) for court-referred financial disputes. * '''CIPITC Special Procedures:''' 3-judge quorums, Anton Piller search orders, video-conferencing, un-translated English documents by consent, and direct Supreme Court appeals. * '''Tripartite Labour Bench:''' Requirement for equal representation of career judges, employer associate judges, and employee associate judges on Labour Court quorums, exempt from court fees. * '''OCPB Court Enforcement:''' Authority of consumer protection officers to sue business operators on behalf of consumers exempt from court fees. === Implementation === * '''National Court Mediation Execution:''' Courts of First Instance across Thailand mediated 33,376 cases in 2001. * '''Labour Court Compromise Volume:''' Resolving 55.7% of all Central Labour Court cases in 1998 through mediated compromise or withdrawal. * '''TAI Commercial Arbitration Expansion:''' Handling 64 cases worth 38.4 billion baht in 2000. * '''OCPB Complaint Handling:''' Processing 7,946 complaints in 1999 and litigating 108 court cases in 2000. == Policy Problems == * Stalling Tactics by Litigants: Unscrupulous lawyers entering mediation solely to delay trial execution. * Heavy Burden of Proof in Environmental Tort Claims: Citizens struggling to establish causal links between industrial toxic emissions and health impairments. * Execution Deficit in Arbitration Awards: Arbitrators lacking direct enforcement authority, requiring court judgment decrees. == Reform == * Establishing national registries of qualified expert conciliators. * Setting strict statutory time limits on conciliation proceedings. * Creating tripartite conciliation quorums (judge, expert, law professor/lawyer). == Related Key Figures & Institutions == === Key Figures === * '''Justice Prasobsook Boondech:''' Senior Justice of the Supreme Court of Thailand; former Chief Justice of CIPITC; Honorary Advisor. * '''Judge Vichai Ariyanuntaka:''' Judge of CIPITC; former Director of the Arbitration Office; co-author. * '''Judge Jagkrit Jenjesda:''' Judge of CIPITC; former Director of Judicial Training Institute; co-author. * '''Judge Pinyo Sangphu:''' Chief Judge of North Bangkok Kwaeng Court; co-author. * '''Judge Pongratana Cruecrin:''' Judge of the Central Labour Court; Secretary of the Central Labour Court; co-author. * '''Chief Prosecutor Dr. Chatchom Akapin:''' Chief Prosecutor for Civil Rights Protection and Legal Aid, Nonthaburi State Attorney Office; co-author. * '''General Prem Tinsulanonda:''' Former Prime Minister of Thailand who countersigned the Arbitration Act B.E. 2530 (1987). * '''Khunying Chodchoy Soponpanich:''' President of the Thai Environmental and Community Development Association. === Key Institutions === * [[Central Intellectual Property and International Trade Court]] (CIPITC) * [[Thai Arbitration Institute]] (TAI) * [[Office of Consumer Protection Board (Thailand)]] (OCPB) * Central Labour Court of Thailand * Supreme Court of Thailand * [[Institute of Developing Economies]] (IDE-JETRO) == Knowledge Graph & Entity title: JPW-POLICY-000014
wikitext: {{Infobox Judicial Policy | name = Vietnamese Alternative Dispute Resolution and Judicial System Framework | original_name = Alternative Dispute Resolution in Vietnam (IDE Asian Law Series No. 20) | stable_id = JPW-POLICY-000014 | jurisdiction = Socialist Republic of Vietnam | issuing_authority = Institute of State and Law and Institute of Developing Economies (IDE-JETRO) | date_established = 2002-03-01 | legal_basis = 1992 Constitution of Vietnam; Law on Organization of People's Courts; 1994 Economic Case Ordinance; 1994 Labour Code; 1993 Environment Protection Law | status = Active / Judicial Policy Benchmark | related_entities = Supreme People's Court of Vietnam, VIAC, VCCI, Decree 116/CP Centres, Ministry of Justice, MOSTE, MOLISA, IDE-JETRO }} The '''Vietnamese Alternative Dispute Resolution and Judicial System Framework''' (Stable ID: JPW-POLICY-000014) is a national statutory, judicial, and out-of-court dispute resolution policy framework evaluating the 3-tiered court hierarchy, judge appointment mechanisms, non-governmental arbitration, procedural conciliation, consumer protection, labor dispute adjudication, and environmental dispute resolution in the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. Documented under IDE Asian Law Series No. 20 by a research team from the Institute of State and Law led by Prof. Dr. Dao Tri Uc in collaboration with IDE-JETRO, the policy analyzes court reforms, the dual-track arbitration system (VIAC vs. Decree 116/CP centres), mandatory labor conciliation, and environmental damage compensation models. Note: Named entities ''Cecep Mustafa'' and ''Reihan Abdan Syakur'' are ''Not found in the available sources''. == Summary == The framework examines judicial and ADR reforms following Vietnam's transition to a market-oriented economy under ''Doi Moi''. It outlines six core structural pillars: (1) Three-Tiered Judicial Structure, comprising District People's Courts, Provincial People's Courts, and the Supreme People's Court, featuring specialized Economic, Labour, and Administrative Chambers; (2) Judicial Professionalization, introducing 5-year judge appointment terms and establishing the Judicial Training School; (3) Non-Governmental Commercial Arbitration, creating a dual arbitration framework under VIAC (Prime Minister Decision 204/114-TTg) and provincial economic arbitration centres (Government Decree 116/CP); (4) Labour Dispute Adjudication, establishing mandatory 7-day grass-root labor conciliation and 61 Provincial Labour Arbitration Councils under the 1994 Labour Code; (5) Consumer Protection Mechanisms, enforcing six statutory consumer rights through multi-agency state administration; and (6) Environmental Dispute Resolution, executing non-contractual strict liability and administrative-executive mediation via MOSTE inspectorates. == Legal Basis == Authority and execution derive from constitutional provisions and statutory enactments: * '''Constitutional Charter:''' 1992 Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam (Arts. 12, 23, 26, 29, 35, 59–62, 68, 73–74, 127). * '''Judicial & Procedural Codes:''' 1992 Law on Organization of People's Courts (as amended 1993, 1995); 1994 Ordinance on Procedures for Settlement of Economic Cases; 1995 Civil Code of Vietnam (Arts. 7, 11, 268, 628); Ordinance on Procedures for Resolution of Administrative Cases (1996, as amended 1998). * '''Arbitration & International Decrees:''' Government Decree No. 116/CP dated 5 September 1994; Prime Minister Decision No. 204-TTg (1993) & Decision No. 114-TTg (1996); Ordinance on Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Decisions (1995) & 1958 New York Convention (Presidential Decision No. 453/QD-CTN). * '''Labour & Environmental Statutes:''' 1994 Labour Code of Vietnam (Arts. 157, 163–173); 1993 Law on Protection of the Environment (Arts. 7, 29, 30, 52) & Decree No. 175-CP; Law on Complaint and Denunciation (1998). == Background & Policy Problems == === Background === Economic liberalization under ''Doi Moi'' created diverse business ownership types and complex commercial relationships. To resolve mounting economic disputes and replace the administrative State Economic Arbitration system, the National Assembly created Economic, Labour, and Administrative Courts in 1994 and authorized non-governmental arbitration centres. === Policy Problems === * Judge Qualification Gaps: Severe shortage of judges with formal university law degrees, particularly at the district court level where many held only short-course training qualifications. * Inconsistent Arbitration Frameworks: Conflict and regulatory duplication between Decision 204/114-TTg (VIAC) and Decree 116/CP provincial economic arbitration centres. * Unlawful Labour Strikes: Widespread spontaneous strikes occurring without trade union conciliation due to missing grass-root conciliation councils in private/FDI firms. * Short Economic Limitation Window: A rigid 6-month statutory limitation period for filing economic court actions under Article 31 of the 1994 Ordinance that prematurely foreclosed private negotiations. * Environmental Compensation Deficit: Local communities facing immense scientific difficulties in proving non-contractual causation, with mediated settlements recovering only 20% to 30% of actual damage. == Objectives == 1. Modernize state judicial administration and establish specialized court chambers. 2. Expand non-governmental arbitration and court-annexed conciliation. 3. Guarantee basic consumer safety, quality, and compensation rights. 4. Provide fast, zero-cost grass-root conciliation for workplace labor disputes. 5. Enforce non-contractual strict liability for environmental pollution. == Scope & Implementation == === Scope === Applies across all regular courts, specialized chambers, arbitration bodies, labor councils, consumer agencies, and environmental inspectorates in Vietnam. === Key Provisions === * '''Specialized Court Jurisdiction:''' Economic Court jurisdiction over business disputes, share purchases, and company dissolution. * '''Dual-Track Arbitration Structure:''' Independent operation of VIAC under VCCI and Decree 116/CP provincial economic arbitration centres. * '''Mandatory Grass-Root Labour Conciliation:''' Requirement for a 7-day conciliation process before filing court lawsuits. * '''MOSTE Environmental Mediation Model:''' Executive mediation led by environmental inspectorates to evaluate damage and determine compensation. === Implementation === * '''Judicial Output:''' Vietnamese courts tried 165,048 cases in 2000 (86.05% trial disposal rate). * '''Court Conciliation Ratio:''' Achieving 44%–54% settlement rates in civil/economic disputes. * '''Environmental Compensation Impact:''' Settling 51 major environmental compensation cases across 30 provinces via MOSTE mediation. == Policy Problems == * Judge Qualification Gaps: High proportion of district judges lacking regular university law degrees. * Dual Regulatory Frameworks in Arbitration: Friction between Decision 204/114-TTg and Decree 116/CP. * Unlawful Labour Strikes: Widespread strikes occurring without trade union conciliation in private/FDI firms. == Reform == * Establishing a dedicated Judges Training Academy. * Enacting a unified national Arbitration Law. * Extending the economic lawsuit limitation period beyond 6 months. == Related Key Figures & Institutions == === Key Figures === * '''Prof. Dr. Dao Tri Uc:''' Director of the Institute of State and Law; Research Team Leader. * '''Dr. Tran Dinh Hao:''' Researcher at the Institute of State and Law; co-author. * '''Dr. Pham Huu Nghi:''' Researcher at the Institute of State and Law; co-author. * '''Nguyen Duc Minh, LL.M.:''' Researcher at the Institute of State and Law; co-author. * '''Ha Hung Cuong:''' Legal scholar and official at the Ministry of Justice. === Key Institutions === * [[Institute of State and Law]] * [[Vietnam International Arbitration Centre]] (VIAC) * [[Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry]] (VCCI) * Provincial Economic Arbitration Centres * Supreme People's Court of Vietnam * Ministry of Science, Technology and Environment (MOSTE) * Ministry of Labour, War Invalids and Social Affairs (MOLISA) * [[Institute of Developing Economies]] (IDE-JETRO) == Knowledge Graph & Entity Relationships == {| class="wikitable" |- ! title: JPW-POLICY-000015
wikitext: {{Infobox Judicial Policy | name = Indonesian Dispute Resolution and Judicial System Framework | original_name = Dispute Resolution Process in Indonesia (IDE Asian Law Series No. 21) | stable_id = JPW-POLICY-000015 | jurisdiction = Republic of Indonesia | issuing_authority = Faculty of Law, University of Indonesia and Institute of Developing Economies (IDE-JETRO) | date_established = 2003-03-01 | legal_basis = 1945 Constitution of Indonesia; Judicial Power Act (Act 14/1970 & 35/1999); Arbitration and ADR Act (Act 30/1999); Consumer Protection Act (Act 8/1999); Environmental Management Act (Act 23/1997) | status = Active / Judicial Policy Benchmark | related_entities = Supreme Court of Indonesia, Central Jakarta District Court, Commercial Court, BANI, BAMUI, BAPMI, BPSK, KPPU, P4D/P4P, YLKI, WALHI, IDE-JETRO }} The '''Indonesian Dispute Resolution and Judicial System Framework''' (Stable ID: JPW-POLICY-000015) is a national statutory, judicial, and alternative dispute resolution (ADR) policy framework evaluating court jurisdictions, judge appointments, commercial arbitration, labor dispute settlement, consumer protection, and environmental litigation in the Republic of Indonesia. Documented under IDE Asian Law Series No. 21 by Prof. Hikmahanto Juwana of the Faculty of Law, University of Indonesia in collaboration with IDE-JETRO, the policy analyzes the "One-Roof" judicial reform (Act No. 35 of 1999), commercial arbitration under Act No. 30 of 1999, Consumer Dispute Settlement Boards (BPSK), labor dispute committees (P4D/P4P), and NGO legal standing in environmental suits. Note: Named entities ''Cecep Mustafa'' and ''Reihan Abdan Syakur'' are ''Not found in the available sources''. == Summary == The framework examines judicial and ADR mechanisms during Indonesia's ''Reformasi'' transition following the end of the Soeharto administration. It outlines six core structural pillars: (1) Four-Jurisdiction Judicial Hierarchy, comprising General, Religious, Military, and Administrative Tribunals topped by a single Supreme Court (*Mahkamah Agung*); (2) One-Roof Judicial Independence, transferring organizational, administrative, and financial management of courts from executive departments to the Supreme Court under Act No. 35 of 1999; (3) Commercial Arbitration and ADR, establishing statutory rules for consultation, negotiation, mediation, conciliation, expert assessment, and arbitration under Act No. 30 of 1999; (4) Consumer Dispute Resolution, creating regency-level BPSK boards under Act No. 8 of 1999; (5) Tripartite Labour Adjudication, operating Regional and Central Labor Dispute Settlement Committees (P4D/P4P) under Act No. 22 of 1957; and (6) Environmental Tort Litigation, enforcing strict tort liability, class actions, and NGO legal standing (*WALHI v. PT Inti Indorayon Utama*) under Act No. 23 of 1997. == Legal Basis == Authority and execution derive from constitutional provisions and statutory enactments: * '''Constitutional Charter:''' 1945 Constitution of the Republic of Indonesia (Transitional Provisions Art. II; Art. 5(1), Art. 20(1)). * '''Judicial Power & Court Acts:''' Judicial Power Act (Act No. 19 of 1964; Act No. 14 of 1970; as amended by Act No. 35 of 1999); Supreme Court Act (Act No. 14 of 1985); General Tribunal Act (Act No. 2 of 1986); Bankruptcy Act of 1998 (Act No. 4 of 1998); Human Rights Court Act (Act No. 26 of 2000); Tax Court Act (Act No. 14 of 2002). * '''Arbitration & Commercial Statutes:''' Arbitration and Alternative Dispute Resolution Act (Act No. 30 of 1999); Antimonopoly Act (Act No. 5 of 1999); Presidential Decree No. 34 of 1981 (1958 New York Convention). * '''Consumer, Labour & Environmental Statutes:''' Consumer Protection Act (Act No. 8 of 1999); Labor Dispute Act of 1957 (Act No. 22 of 1957); Termination of Employment Act of 1964 (Act No. 12 of 1964); Environmental Management Act of 1997 (Act No. 23 of 1997). * '''Colonial Procedural Codes:''' HIR (*Het Herziene Indonesisch Reglement*); RBg (*Rechtsreglement voor De Buitengewesten*); Rv (*Reglement op de Rechtsvordering*). == Background & Policy Problems == === Background === Following independence, Indonesia retained Dutch colonial court structures and procedural codes. During the New Order, executive departments controlled judicial administration. The post-1998 *Reformasi* era triggered comprehensive legal reforms to establish judicial independence, clear severe Supreme Court backlogs, and provide out-of-court commercial arbitration. === Policy Problems === * Perennial Court Congestion & Backlogs: Unrestricted appeal rights accumulating thousands of pending cases at the Supreme Court (e.g., 23,915 total cases in 1999/2000). * Protracted Civil Litigation: Civil lawsuits taking an average of 8 to 9 years to reach an enforceable judgment. * Systemic Corruption & Distrust: Widespread bribery leading citizens to rely on extra-judicial debt collectors. * Lack of ADR Finality: Statutory provisions allowing parties to unilaterally declare out-of-court settlements "unsuccessful" and litigate afresh in court. * Foreign Award Enforcement Bottlenecks: Local courts frequently delaying or denying enforcement of foreign arbitral awards despite New York Convention accession. == Objectives == 1. Guarantee judicial independence by consolidating court administration under the Supreme Court. 2. Declog court dockets through pre-trial court-administered mediation (S.C. Circular Letter 1/2002). 3. Provide statutory recognition and enforcement for commercial arbitration and ADR (Act 30/1999). 4. Establish accessible consumer dispute resolution via BPSK boards. 5. Adjudicate labor disputes through bipartite negotiations and LDSC committees. 6. Authorize class actions and NGO standing in environmental protection. == Scope & Implementation == === Scope === Applies across all courts of first instance, appellate courts, the Supreme Court, specialized commercial/tax/human rights courts, arbitration centers (BANI, BAMUI, BAPMI), BPSK boards, and labor committees in Indonesia. === Key Provisions === * '''One-Roof Judicial Consolidation:''' Full transfer of lower court administration, personnel, and finances to the Supreme Court by 2004. * '''Statutory Commercial ADR (Act 30/1999):''' 14-day consultation/mediation targets, 30-day registration of settlement agreements at District Courts, and exclusive Central Jakarta District Court exequatur jurisdiction. * '''Consumer Board Jurisdiction:''' BPSK authority to conciliate, mediate, or arbitrate consumer disputes and issue binding awards within 21 working days. * '''Environmental NGO Standing:''' Statutory right of environmental NGOs to file lawsuits to demand environmental restoration. === Implementation === * '''Supreme Court Output:''' Handled 23,915 total cases in 1999/2000, deciding 14,208 cases. * '''Foreign Arbitral Award Enforcement:''' Central Jakarta District Court granted 9 out of 29 foreign award enforcement applications between 1990 and 2002. * '''Consumer Complaints:''' YLKI processed 798 complaints in greater Jakarta during the first half of 2000. == Policy Problems == * Severe Supreme Court Backlogs: Unrestricted cassation rights accumulating thousands of carryover cases. * Lack of ADR Finality: Statutory provisions allowing parties to unilaterally declare out-of-court settlements "unsuccessful" and litigate in court. * Systemic Corruption & Loss of Public Trust: Widespread bribery leading to extra-judicial debt collection by gangsters. == Reform == * Appointment of non-career justices to the Supreme Court. * One-Roof administrative consolidation. * Enactment of the Industrial Relations Dispute Settlement Bill (PPHI). * Supreme Court Regulation No. 1 of 2002 on Class Action Procedures. == Related Key Figures & Institutions == === Key Figures === * '''Prof. Hikmahanto Juwana:''' Professor of Law, Faculty of Law, University of Indonesia; author. * '''Chief Justice Bagir Manan:''' Former Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Indonesia who issued Circular Letter No. 1 of 2002. * '''President Bachrudin Jusuf Habibie:''' Signed Act No. 30 of 1999 concerning Arbitration and ADR into law. * '''Minister Muladi:''' Minister of State for the State Secretariat who enacted Act No. 30 of 1999. * '''Henry P. Panggabean:''' Former Supreme Court Justice and legal scholar. * '''Trimoelja D. Soerjadi:''' Prominent Indonesian lawyer and anti-corruption legal researcher. * '''Prof. Sudargo Gautama:''' Law Professor and practicing legal scholar. * '''Prof. Mochtar Kusumaatmadja:''' Prominent Indonesian legal scholar. * '''Mas Achmad Santosa:''' Legal scholar and environmental mediation pioneer. === Key Institutions === * [[Faculty of Law, University of Indonesia]] * [[Supreme Court of Indonesia]] (*Mahkamah Agung*) * District Court of Central Jakarta * [[Indonesian National Board of Arbitration]] (BANI) * Indonesian Muamalat Board of Arbitration (BAMUI) * Indonesian Capital Market Arbitration (BAPMI) * Consumer Dispute Settlement Board (BPSK) * Central Labor Dispute Settlement Committee (P4P) * [[Institute of Developing Economies]] (IDE-JETRO) == Knowledge Graph & Entity Relationships == {| class="wikitable" |- ! title: JPW-POLICY-000016
wikitext: {{Infobox Judicial Policy | name = Chinese Labour Dispute Settlement and Policy Framework | original_name = Labour Disputes Settlement System in China: Past and Perspective (IDE Asian Law Series No. 22) | stable_id = JPW-POLICY-000016 | jurisdiction = People's Republic of China | issuing_authority = Ministry of Labour and Social Security (PRC), China University of Politics and Law, and IDE-JETRO | date_established = 2003-03-01 | legal_basis = Labour Law of the PRC (1994); Regulations on Settlement of Labour Disputes in Enterprises (1993); SPC Legal Interpretation 2001 No. 14 | status = Active / Judicial Policy Benchmark | related_entities = Ministry of Labour and Social Security, Labour Dispute Arbitration Committees, Supreme People's Court, ACFTU, CEC, IDE-JETRO }} The '''Chinese Labour Dispute Settlement and Policy Framework''' (Stable ID: JPW-POLICY-000016) is a national statutory, administrative, and judicial policy framework evaluating the evolution, structure, procedures, social security integration, and reform of the labour dispute resolution system in the People's Republic of China. Documented under IDE Asian Law Series No. 22 by Wang Zhenqi (Ministry of Labour and Social Security), Prof. Wang Changshuo, and Assoc. Prof. Zheng Shangyuan (China University of Politics and Law) in collaboration with IDE-JETRO, the policy analyzes the "one-track, three-stage" dispute process (enterprise mediation, mandatory labour arbitration, and court litigation), social insurance pooling, Supreme People's Court Legal Interpretation 2001 No. 14, and proposed double-track reforms. Note: Named entities ''Cecep Mustafa'' and ''Reihan Abdan Syakur'' are ''Not found in the available sources''. == Summary == The framework examines the restoration and modernization of China's labour dispute resolution machinery following the 1994 Labour Law and market reforms. It outlines six core structural pillars: (1) One-Track, Three-Stage Adjudication, requiring parties to proceed from Enterprise Mediation to mandatory Labour Dispute Arbitration Committees (LDAC) before accessing two-instance court litigation; (2) Social Insurance Legal System, integrating social pooling with individual accounts across pension, unemployment, medical, work injury, and maternity insurance; (3) Tripartite Arbitration Structure, composing LDACs with equal representation from labour administrative departments, trade unions, and enterprise associations; (4) Procedural Burden-Shifting, applying Supreme People's Court Legal Interpretation 2001 No. 14 to shift the burden of proof onto employers for termination/dismissal claims; (5) Collective Dispute Tripartism, operating joint coordination mechanisms between MOLSS, ACFTU, and CEC to manage strikes and mass incidents; and (6) Trade Union Legal Aid, delivering free legal representation to impoverished workers in arbitration and court suits. == Legal Basis == Authority and execution derive from constitutional, statutory, and judicial enactments: * '''Statutory Legislation:''' Labour Law of the People's Republic of China (adopted 5 July 1994, effective 1 January 1995); Legislation Law of the PRC (Art. 8); Civil Procedure Law of the PRC. * '''Administrative Regulations:''' Regulations on Settlement of Labour Disputes in Enterprises (State Council, 1993); Provisional Regulations on Settlement of Labour Disputes in State-run Enterprises (1987); Provisional Regulations on Collection of Social Insurance Contributions (1999); Regulations on Unemployment Insurance (1999); Regulations on Minimum Living Standard Security for Urban Residents (1999). * '''Judicial Interpretations & Ministerial Rules:''' Interpretations on Some Questions on Application of Laws and Regulations in Handling Labour Disputes (Supreme People's Court Legal Interpretation 2001 No. 14); Rule on Organisational Structure and Working Procedure of Enterprise Labour Dispute Mediation Committee (1993); Rules on Working Procedure of LDAC (1993); Methods on Settlement of Social Insurance-related Administrative Disputes (2001). == Background & Policy Problems == === Background === Following the 1949 founding of the PRC, early labour dispute rules were established in 1950 but suspended in 1957. For 30 years under the planned economy, disputes were handled as administrative complaints without judicial recourse. Market reforms and state enterprise restructuring in the 1980s and 1990s triggered a surge in employment conflicts, prompting the State Council and National People's Congress to enact the 1993 Regulations and 1994 Labour Law. === Policy Problems === * Protracted Procedural Chain: The mandatory "one-track, three-stage" chain (Enterprise Mediation → Mandatory Arbitration → First-Instance Court → Second-Instance Court) often takes over a year to reach a final judgment. * Overly Restrictive Statute of Limitations: Article 82 of the Labour Law imposed a strict 60-day filing limit starting from the date of dispute occurrence, causing many workers to forfeit their rights during negotiations. * Non-Final Arbitration Awards: LDAC decisions lack finality, operating with heavy administrative influence while routinely leading to de novo court litigation upon appeal. * Surge in Mass Collective Disputes: Rapid enterprise restructuring caused a sharp rise in collective disputes, particularly within state-owned enterprises undergoing conversion. * Reliance on Enterprise Mediation: Enterprise mediation committees are financially and organizationally dependent on employer management, compromising their structural neutrality. == Objectives == 1. Protect the legitimate rights of workers and employing units under market economy conditions. 2. Pool social insurance risks across urban enterprises and employees. 3. Provide accessible mediation and arbitration for individual and collective labour disputes. 4. Prevent and resolve mass incidents through tripartite coordination. 5. Guarantee legal aid for impoverished workers in labour litigation. == Scope & Implementation == === Scope === Applies across all urban enterprises, state-owned entities, foreign-funded firms, private businesses, individual entrepreneurs, trade unions, LDACs, and People's Courts in China. === Key Provisions === * '''Mandatory Statute of Limitations (Art. 82 Labour Law):''' Requirement to file arbitration petitions within 60 days of dispute occurrence. * '''Burden of Proof Reversal (SPC Interpretation 2001 No. 14):''' Employer duty to adduce evidence in dismissal, demotion, and wage reduction claims. * '''Tripartite Arbitration Bench:''' Mandatory 3-member arbitration tribunal representing MOLSS, ACFTU, and CEC. * '''Thirty-Day Notice & Compensation (Art. 26 Labour Law):''' Requirement for 30 days' written notice and financial compensation for contract revocation due to changed objective circumstances. === Implementation === * '''Arbitration Disposals:''' LDACs accepted 154,621 cases in 2001, settling 92% of disputes. * '''Enterprise Mediation Impact:''' Enterprise Mediation Committees resolved 1.32 million disputes by June 2002. * '''Judicial Case Volume:''' People's Courts tried 360,000 labour cases between 1997 and 2001. * '''Social Security Coverage:''' Pension pooling covering 142 million residents and medical insurance covering 83 million employees by 2001/2002. == Policy Problems == * Protracted Procedural Chain: One-track, three-stage process taking over a year to reach final judgment. * Overly Short Statute of Limitations: 60-day filing window causing forfeiture of rights during negotiations. * Non-Final Arbitration Awards: Arbitration decisions lack finality, encouraging repetitive court litigation. == Reform == * Enacting a double-track system allowing voluntary choice between arbitration and litigation. * Drafting a standalone Labour Dispute Settlement Law and Labour Contract Law. * Granting conditional legal binding force to mediation agreements. * Unifying arbitrator accreditation under the national judicial examination. == Related Key Figures & Institutions == === Key Figures === * '''Wang Zhenqi:''' Official at the Ministry of Labour and Social Security, People's Republic of China; co-author. * '''Prof. Wang Changshuo:''' Professor at the School of Continuing Education, China University of Politics and title: JPW-POLICY-000017
wikitext: {{Infobox Judicial Policy | name = IDE Asian Law Research and Legal Information Framework | original_name = Doing Legal Research in Asian Countries (IDE Asian Law Series No. 23) | stable_id = JPW-POLICY-000017 | jurisdiction = International / Asian Regional (China, India, Malaysia, Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam) | issuing_authority = Institute of Developing Economies (IDE-JETRO, Japan) | date_established = 2003-03-01 | legal_basis = Constitutions & Statutory Enactments of China, India, Malaysia, Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam | status = Active / Comparative Legal Research Benchmark | related_entities = IDE-JETRO, CASS Institute of Law, Indian Law Institute, UP Law Complex, CIPITC, Institute of State and Law }} The '''IDE Asian Law Research and Legal Information Framework''' (Stable ID: JPW-POLICY-000017) is a multi-jurisdictional legal research, judicial documentation, and legal education policy framework evaluating primary statutory/case law sources, official gazettes, digital databases, court hierarchies, and research methodologies across six Asian nations (China, India, Malaysia, Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam). Published under IDE Asian Law Series No. 23 by IDE-JETRO in collaboration with leading legal scholars (including Prof. Xin Chunying, Dr. S.K. Verma, Mercy Selvaratnam, Prof. Antonio M. Santos, Judge Vichai Ariyanuntaka, and Prof. Dr. Dao Tri Uc), the policy outlines legislative publication structures, digital legal research tools (CALR), judicial training institutions, and comparative legal systems analysis. Note: Named entities ''Cecep Mustafa'' and ''Reihan Abdan Syakur'' are ''Not found in the available sources''. == Summary == The framework synthesizes three years of comparative research conducted by IDE-JETRO domestic research committees on law, economic development, and judicial reform in Asia. It covers six national legal research guides: (1) China, evaluating NPC legislation, State Council regulations, Ministry Gazettes, CASS law compilations, and digital databases (*Chinalawinfo*, *Law-Star*); (2) India, analyzing constitutional grundnorms, Parliament/State statutes, law reporting (*AIR*, *SCC*, *SCR*), *SCC Online*, and *JUDIS*; (3) Malaysia, mapping Straits Settlements, FMS, Unfederated States, Federal Gazettes, *Laws of Malaysia* (Acts 1–615), *Mallal's Digest*, and *LawNet*; (4) Philippines, details on 1987 Constitution, Republic Acts, Presidential Decrees, ONAR administrative register, *SCRA*, and CD Asia *Lex Libris*; (5) Thailand, examining Prince Rapee's 1897 Law School, civil codification, bar examinations, Judicial Training Institute, and university LL.B./LL.M. curricula; and (6) Vietnam, documenting *Cong Bao*, *Hong Duc* and *Gia Long* codes, 1992 Constitution, ONAR-equivalent CDS/ISIS systems, village regulations (*Huong uoc*), and the Institute of State and Law library. == Legal Basis == Authority and execution derive from constitutional charters and procedural statutes across six jurisdictions: * '''People's Republic of China:''' 1982 Constitution of the PRC; Legislation Law of the PRC (Arts. 52, 71). * '''Republic of India:''' Constitution of India (1950, Arts. 141, 245–253, 372); Code of Civil Procedure (1999/2002). * '''Malaysia:''' Federal Constitution of Malaysia (1957/1963, Art. 4(1), Ninth Schedule); Revision of Laws Act 1968 (Act 1); Interpretation Act 1948/1967 (Act 388). * '''Republic of the Philippines:''' 1987 Constitution of the Philippines (Art. VIII); Administrative Code of 1987 (Exec. Order 292); Judiciary Reorganization Act of 1980. * '''Kingdom of Thailand:''' Constitution of the Kingdom of Thailand; Civil and Criminal Codes; Judicial Service Act B.E. 2543 (2000); Advocate Act B.E. 2528. * '''Socialist Republic of Vietnam:''' 1992 Constitution of Vietnam; Law on Organization of People's Courts; 1995 Civil Code; Commercial Law 1997. == Background & Policy Problems == === Background === Market liberalization and booming intra-Asian investment in the late 1990s highlighted severe legal information deficits among Asian scholars, practitioners, and judiciaries. IDE-JETRO established comparative committees to systematically map primary legal materials, gazette structures, and judicial training systems. === Policy Problems === * Heterogeneity & Complexity of Legal Traditions: Comparative legal analysis complicated across civil law, common law, mixed systems, and socialist law. * Accessibility Bottlenecks: Official legal gazettes historically restricted to paper formats or internal government distribution without robust indices. * Severe Court Backlogs: Massive docket congestion delaying resolution across trial and appellate courts in major Asian jurisdictions. * Lack of Standardized Citators: Inconsistent legal citation standards and absence of automated case treatment tools in Southeast Asia. == Objectives == 1. Provide standard research guides for primary legislative and judicial sources in Asia. 2. Standardize legal citations and document retrieval methods. 3. Promote computer-assisted legal research (CALR) and official online legal databases. 4. Comparative analysis of court hierarchies and ADR mechanisms. 5. Support legal education and judicial training reform. == Scope & Implementation == === Scope === Applies across legal libraries, universities, judicial academies, court registries, and bar associations in China, India, Malaysia, Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam. === Key Provisions === * '''Official Gazette Mandates:''' Statutory requirement for publication of laws in standard gazettes (*State Council Gazette*, *Gazette of India*, *Federal Gazette*, *Official Gazette*, *Cong Bao*). * '''Administrative Rule Registries:''' Requirement to deposit agency regulations in centralized registers (e.g., ONAR at UP Law Center). * '''Judicial Training Frameworks:''' Mandatory pre-service and in-service training for judges (e.g., Thai Judicial Training Institute 1-year course). * '''Village Customary Law Integration:''' Preservation of customary rules (e.g., *Adat* in Malaysia, *Barangay* in Philippines, *Huong uoc* in Vietnam) alongside formal statutory codes. === Implementation === * '''Digital Legal Publishing:''' Widespread adoption of CD-ROM and online databases (*Chinalawinfo*, *SCC Online*, *LawNet*, *Lex Libris*, *vietlaw.gov.vn*). * '''Judicial Output & Education:''' Operationalizing judicial academies and expanding law faculties across state and private universities. == Policy Problems == * Publication and Accessibility Barriers: Incomplete public access to trial court judgments in civil/socialist law jurisdictions. * Lack of Standardized Citators: Absence of shepardized case treatment tools in Southeast Asia. * Judicial Backlogs: Severe case delays in India, Thailand, and the Philippines. == Reform == * Integrating open-access national electronic legal databases. * Adopting neutral electronic citation formats for judicial opinions. * Strengthening specialized judicial training academies. == Related Key Figures & Institutions == === Key Figures === * '''Prof. Xin Chunying:''' Deputy Director, Institute of Law, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS); co-author. * '''Ding Ke:''' Librarian, Institute of Law, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS); co-author. * '''Dr. S.K. Verma:''' Director, Indian Law Institute (ILI); author. * '''Mercy Selvaratnam:''' Barrister-at-Law, Advocate & Solicitor, Chartered Librarian; co-author. * '''Hulwana Mohd Labib:''' Librarian, Lee Hishammuddin Law Firm; co-author. * '''Prof. Antonio M. wikitext: {{Infobox Judicial Policy | name = Taiwanese Constitutional Development and Human Rights Framework | original_name = Development of Constitutional Law and Human Rights in Taiwan Facing the New Century (IDE Asian Law Series No. 24) | stable_id = JPW-POLICY-000018 | jurisdiction = Taiwan / Republic of China | issuing_authority = NTU Law School, Academia Sinica, and Institute of Developing Economies (IDE-JETRO) | date_established = 2003-03-01 | legal_basis = 1947 ROC Constitution; Constitutional Additional Articles (1991–2000); Grand Justices Adjudication Law | status = Active / Judicial Policy Benchmark | related_entities = Judicial Yuan, Council of Grand Justices, Legislative Yuan, Executive Yuan, Presidential Human Rights Advisory Group, IDE-JETRO }} The '''Taiwanese Constitutional Development and Human Rights Framework''' (Stable ID: JPW-POLICY-000018) is a national constitutional law, judicial review, democratization, and human rights policy framework evaluating the six constitutional revisions (1991–2000), semi-presidential governance, Grand Justice constitutional review, and millennium human rights policies in Taiwan. Documented under IDE Asian Law Series No. 24 by Assoc. Prof. Jau-Yuan Hwang (NTU), Dr. Fort Fu-Te Liao (Academia Sinica), and Assistant Prof. Wen-Chen Chang (NTU) in collaboration with IDE-JETRO, the policy outlines electoral legitimization, the dual-executive system, landmark Grand Justice interpretations (Nos. 261, 325, 387, 499), the National Human Rights Commission bill, and the domestication of the International Bill of Rights. Note: Named entities ''Cecep Mustafa'' and ''Reihan Abdan Syakur'' are ''Not found in the available sources''. == Summary == The framework analyzes Taiwan's constitutional transformation from post-WWII martial law rule to a consolidated democracy. It outlines six core structural pillars: (1) Six Constitutional Revisions (1991–2000), terminating emergency martial provisions, introducing 100% direct legislative and presidential elections, and reducing the National Assembly to an ad hoc body; (2) Semi-Presidential Governance, establishing a dual-executive system where the President appoints the Premier without legislative confirmation, balanced by legislative no-confidence and conditional dissolution powers; (3) Constitutional Judicial Review, empowering the Council of Grand Justices to enforce abstract/concrete review, non-delegation, due process, and judicial deadlines; (4) Landmark Judicial Jurisprudence, terminating lifetime parliamentarians (Interpretation No. 261) and voiding unconstitutional self-term extensions (Interpretation No. 499); (5) National Human Rights Infrastructure, establishing the Presidential Human Rights Advisory Group and Executive Yuan Human Rights Committee to draft National Action Plans and create the National Human Rights Museum; and (6) International Treaty Domestication, enacting domestic statutory incorporation for the ICCPR and ICESCR alongside the Human Rights Basic Law bill. == Legal Basis == Authority and execution derive from constitutional charters, amendments, and procedural statutes: * '''Constitutional Charters & Amendments:''' 1947 Constitution of the Republic of China; Six Sets of Constitutional Additional Articles (1991, 1992, 1994, 1997, 1999, 2000). * '''Emergency & Security Statutes:''' Temporary Provisions Effective During the Period of National Mobilization for the Suppressing of the Communist Rebellion (1948, repealed 1991); Emergency Martial Law Decree (May 1949 – July 1987); National Security Law (1987, as amended 1992). * '''Judicial & Organic Laws:''' Law on Adjudication of Cases by the Council of Grand Justices (1958, as amended 1993); Organic Law of the Judicial Yuan; Presidential and Vice Presidential Election and Recall Law (1995); Local Autonomy Act. * '''Human Rights & Gender Statutes:''' Domestic Violence Prevention Law (1999); Law of Equal Employment between Two Sexes (2002); Aborigine Status Act, Aborigine Education Act & Aborigine Employment Rights Protection Act. == Background & Policy Problems == === Background === Following 50 years of Japanese colonial rule and post-1945 ROC administration, Taiwan was subjected to 38 years of martial law and political suppression under the White Terror era. Democratic protests led to the 1987 lifting of martial law, the 1991 termination of the MSCR, and judicial mandates ordering competitive elections. === Policy Problems === * Executive-Legislative Gridlock: Minority President facing hostile legislative majorities without discretionary dissolution powers. * UN Treaty Deposit Obstruction: Diplomatic blocking of formal UN treaty deposits by Beijing. * Stalled Human Rights Bills: Legislative delays on the National Human Rights Commission Act. * Retention of Capital Punishment: Mandatory death penalty sentences across special criminal statutes obstructing complete human rights compliance. == Objectives == 1. Consolidate constitutional democracy through full direct elections. 2. Enforce checks and balances through active Grand Justice judicial review. 3. Establish an independent National Human Rights Commission. 4. Incorporate the ICCPR and ICESCR into domestic law. 5. Promote human rights education, historical archives, and victim compensation. == Scope & Implementation == === Scope === Applies across all central government Yuans, courts, local governments, educational institutions, civil service academies, and human rights bodies in Taiwan. === Key Provisions === * '''Direct Presidential Election (1994 Amendment):''' Requirement for direct popular election of the President and Vice President by plurality vote. * '''Semi-Presidential Appointment (1997 Amendment):''' Presidential authority to appoint the Premier without legislative consent, subject to legislative no-confidence votes. * '''Super-Majority Relaxation (1993 Grand Justice Law):''' Reducing decision quorums to two-thirds for constitutional interpretations. * '''Burden of Proof Non-Delegation:''' Mandatory statutory specificity for administrative restrictions on fundamental rights (Interpretation No. 313). === Implementation === * '''Grand Justice Output:''' Invalidating unconstitutional laws/regulations in 98+ cases across the 5th and 6th Councils. * '''Victim Compensation:''' Awarding NT$117.8 million+ in compensation to White Terror victims. * '''Civil Service Training:''' Training 6,000+ civil servants annually in human rights and gender equality. == Policy Problems == * Executive-Legislative Gridlock: Minority President facing hostile legislative majorities without discretionary dissolution powers. * UN Treaty Deposit Obstruction: Diplomatic blocking of formal UN treaty deposits by Beijing. * Stalled Human Rights Bills: Legislative delays on the National Human Rights Commission Act. == Reform == * Unifying the Judicial Yuan court structure. * Passing the Human Rights Basic Law. * Completing the National Human Rights Action Plan. * Replacing mandatory death penalties with discretionary sentences. == Related Key Figures & Institutions == === Key Figures === * '''Assoc. Prof. Jau-Yuan Hwang:''' Associate Professor of Law, National Taiwan University Law School; lead author. * '''Dr. Fort Fu-Te Liao:''' Assistant Research Fellow, Academia Sinica; co-author. * '''Assistant Prof. Wen-Chen Chang:''' Assistant Professor, National Taiwan University; co-author. * '''President Chen Shui-bian:''' President of Taiwan (elected March 2000); initiated millennium human rights policies. * '''Former President Lee Teng-hui:''' Former President of Taiwan (1988–2000); presided over democratic transition. * '''Dr. Sun Yat-sen:''' Founding father of the ROC whose Five-Power theory shaped the 1947 Constitution. * '''Vice President Hsiu-lien Annette Lu:''' Vice President of Taiwan; convener of the Presidential Human Rights Advisory Group. === Key Institutions === * [[National Taiwan University Law School]] * [[Academia Sinica]] (Institute of European and American Studies) * [[Council of Grand Justices]] (Judicial Yuan) * Presidential Human Rights Advisory Group * Executive Yuan Human Rights Protection and Promotion Committee * [[Institute of Developing Economies]] (IDE-JETRO) == Knowledge Graph & Entity Relationships == {| class="wikitable" |- !
