== Summary ==
'''Virtual Desktop for Digital Immediation (EVID)''' (''Escritorio Virtual de Inmediación Digital'') (Stable ID: '''JPW-PROJECT-002160''') is a public service cloud platform and blockchain-based digital system developed by the Spanish Ministry of the Presidency, Justice, and Parliamentary Relations. Registered under project ID PSTW-2160, EVID modernizes judicial administration by supporting remote court hearings and secure, transparent, and inclusive digital document management. EVID eliminates geographic distances, lowers travel costs for citizens and law enforcement personnel, and ensures evidential integrity through a decentralized, tamper-proof ledger.

== Legal Basis ==

* '''Formal Statutory Basis''': Not found in the available sources. (The document indicates that integrating EVID into the existing legal framework represented a key challenge, though no specific statute number is cited).

== Background ==
Prior to EVID, the Spanish judicial system suffered operational inefficiencies driven by mandatory physical appearances at court headquarters. This required extensive travel for out-of-province citizens, created document submission delays, and caused temporary closures of Civil Guard barracks when officers traveled to ratify police reports.

== Objectives ==
1. Enhance judicial efficiency and accessibility across all regions of Spain. 2. Facilitate remote court hearings with evidential guarantees equivalent to in-person trials. 3. Enforce non-repudiation, non-manipulation, and non-impersonation standards via blockchain. 4. Provide inclusive access for remote residents and individuals with special needs or disabilities.

== Scope ==
The project encompasses four core operational pillars:

* ''Remote Trial Proceedings'': Conducting interactive digital hearings for judges, lawyers, law enforcement officers, and citizens.
* ''Blockchain Infrastructure'': Permanently logging document transactions and participant verifications on a decentralized ledger.
* ''Pseudonymized Identification'': Protecting law enforcement officers' privacy via pseudonymized identities during remote testimony.
* ''Deployment Options'': Flexible hosting across public cloud, private SaaS, or on-premises environments.

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Reliable Audit Trail''': All document submissions and modifications are permanently logged on an immutable ledger.
* '''Inclusivity Protocols''': Inclusion of accessibility devices enabling individuals with disabilities to participate fully in proceedings.
* '''Official Management''': Fully administered by the Spanish Ministry of the Presidency, Justice, and Parliamentary Relations.

== Implementation ==
Implementation was achieved through a public-private GovTech partnership with Councilbox (software/blockchain), Telefónica (ICT/telecom), and Kawaru Consulting. Deployment followed a phased approach using focus groups, stakeholder workshops in May 2024, and training sessions for legal practitioners.

== Policy Problems ==

* Adapting legal practitioners' established workflows from traditional to digital processes.
* Managing regional technological infrastructure disparities across Spain.
* Safeguarding sensitive data privacy during remote trial participation.

== Reform ==

* Plans to expand EVID across additional judicial sectors in Spain.
* System integration and coordination with Autonomous Communities holding delegated judicial powers.
* Potential international replication of the platform architecture by foreign judicial bodies.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''Issued by''': Spanish Ministry of the Presidency, Justice, and Parliamentary Relations.
* '''Developed with''': Councilbox, Telefónica, and Kawaru Consulting.
* '''Applies to''': Judges, Lawyers, Law Enforcement Personnel (Civil Guard), and Spanish Citizens.

* [[Blockchain in Public Sector]]

title: JPW-PROJECT-VIDI2024
wikitext:
'''Marieke de Hoon Vidi research project on the new role of prosecutors in international criminal law''' is a five-year research project led by Mr. dr. A.M. (Marieke) de Hoon at the Faculty of Law of the University of Amsterdam (UvA), funded by a Vidi grant from the Dutch Research Council (NWO). It examines how prosecutors in the Netherlands, Germany, Sweden, France and Ukraine handle the abundance of digital and video material on international crimes and turn it into admissible evidence. The project was announced by the UvA on 12 November 2024.<ref name="uva">Universiteit van Amsterdam, "Oorlogsmisdaden gefilmd, maar waarom wordt er niet vervolgd?", UvA Nieuws, published 12 November 2024.</ref>

'''Vidi-onderzoeksproject van Marieke de Hoon over de nieuwe rol van de aanklager in het internationaal strafrecht''' is een vijfjarig onderzoeksproject onder leiding van mr. dr. A.M. (Marieke) de Hoon aan de Faculteit der Rechtsgeleerdheid van de Universiteit van Amsterdam (UvA), gefinancierd met een Vidi-beurs van de Nederlandse Organisatie voor Wetenschappelijk Onderzoek (NWO). Het onderzoekt hoe aanklagers in Nederland, Duitsland, Zweden, Frankrijk en Oekraïne omgaan met de overvloed aan digitaal en videomateriaal over internationale misdrijven en dit omzetten in toelaatbaar bewijs. Het project werd op 12 november 2024 door de UvA aangekondigd.<ref name="uva" />

== Also known as / Ook bekend als ==

* Vidi-onderzoek Marieke de Hoon
* Oorlogsmisdaden gefilmd UvA
* Riset Peran Jaksa dalam Penuntutan Kejahatan Internasional

== Summary / Samenvatting ==
'''EN:''' The project focuses on information overload caused by smartphones and social media, and on its effect on prosecutors handling international crimes at national level.<ref name="uva" />

'''NL:''' Het project richt zich op de informatie-overload door smartphones en sociale media en op de gevolgen daarvan voor aanklagers die internationale misdrijven op nationaal niveau vervolgen.<ref name="uva" />

== Background / Achtergrond ==
'''EN:''' Because of smartphones and social media, almost anyone can film war crimes, which produces very large amounts of material for investigators. Even so, prosecution faces obstacles. Short videos usually show that an event took place, but not who the perpetrator was or what their intent was. In addition, perpetrators are often protected by their home states, such as Syria or Russia.<ref name="uva" />

'''NL:''' Door smartphones en sociale media kan bijna iedereen oorlogsmisdaden filmen, wat zeer grote hoeveelheden materiaal voor onderzoekers oplevert. Toch stuit vervolging op obstakels. Korte video's laten meestal zien dat een gebeurtenis plaatsvond, maar niet wie de dader was of wat diens opzet was. Daarnaast worden daders vaak beschermd door hun land van herkomst, zoals Syrië of Rusland.<ref name="uva" />

== Objectives / Doelstellingen ==

* '''EN:''' To analyse the constraints faced by prosecutors in five countries. / '''NL:''' De beperkingen analyseren waarmee aanklagers in vijf landen te maken hebben.<ref name="uva" />
* '''EN:''' To study interaction with NGOs and victims. / '''NL:''' De interactie met ngo's en slachtoffers onderzoeken.<ref name="uva" />
* '''EN:''' To formulate a theory supporting prosecutorial discretion and to develop new evidentiary standards for international criminal law. / '''NL:''' Een theorie ter ondersteuning van vervolgingsdiscretie formuleren en nieuwe bewijsstandaarden voor het internationaal strafrecht ontwikkelen.<ref name="uva" />

|Background / Achtergrond

|Volgens de bron. Geen fysieke rechtsmacht over beschermde daders in Syrië of Rusland, mogelijke bias in ngo-data (bijvoorbeeld weinig data over seksueel geweld) en de noodzaak dat aanklagers extern onderzoek zoals de MH17-berichtgeving van Bellingcat opnieuw verifiëren voordat rechters het accepteren.<ref name="uva" />

'''Horizon Scanner – Financial Crime''' is a global regulatory horizon-scanning report and intelligence publication released by [[Eversheds Sutherland]] on August 14, 2025 [1–4]. The report synthesizes legal, policy, and enforcement developments surrounding financial crime across the United Kingdom, European Union, and United States over a two-year forward-looking horizon [1–4].

== Executive Summary ==
The publication provides a comprehensive risk-navigation framework for international business organizations and financial institutions to anticipate shifts in the global financial crime regulatory landscape [1–4]. It details upcoming corporate criminal enforcement, anti-money laundering (AML) reforms, sanctions compliance priorities, and legal frameworks governing digital assets and stablecoins [1–4].

== Legal Basis & Legal Disclaimer ==

* '''Formal Legal Basis''': Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 (ECCTA) (UK), Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) (US), GENIUS Act (US), alongside regulatory enforcement guidance issued by the FCA, NCA, FinCEN, DOJ, and OFAC [1–4].
* '''Informational Disclaimer''': The content presented in the report is provided strictly for general informational purposes and does not constitute formal legal advice [1–4].

== Background ==
Escalating regulatory scrutiny regarding money laundering, corporate fraud, terrorism financing, and digital currency exploitation demands that commercial entities maintain deep operational awareness of legal reforms across multiple jurisdictions [1–4]. This report is designed to assist market participants in identifying legal exposure and upgrading internal compliance frameworks [1–4].

== Objectives ==

# Provide a consolidated overview of financial crime regulatory developments across the UK, EU, and US over the next two years [1–4].
# Outline the operational implications of the new corporate offense of "failure to prevent fraud" under the UK ECCTA [1–4].
# Detail US statutory changes, including the GENIUS Act regulating stablecoins and extended AML compliance timelines for investment advisers under the Bank Secrecy Act [1–4].
# Clarify beneficial ownership reporting requirements mandated by FinCEN for non-US entities registered to conduct business in the United States [1–4].

== Key Provisions & Recommendations ==

* '''UK Corporate Offense (ECCTA)''': The new corporate criminal offense of "failure to prevent fraud" under the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 officially takes effect on September 1, 2025 [1–4].
* '''UK Economic Crime Priorities''': In July 2025, the National Crime Agency (NCA) and Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) published joint economic crime priorities aligned with the 2025 National Risk Assessment on money laundering and terrorist financing [1–4].
* '''FCA PEP Guidance''': The FCA issued updated guidance regarding Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs) for anti-money laundering compliance [1–4].
* '''US GENIUS Act''': Enactment of the GENIUS Act by President Trump, establishing the first comprehensive federal regulatory framework governing stablecoins [1–4].
* '''US Investment Adviser AML Program''': The effective date requiring investment advisers to implement formal AML programs under the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) has been extended to January 2028 [1–4].
* '''US FinCEN Beneficial Ownership Reporting''': Mandatory beneficial ownership information reporting rules apply to non-US companies registered to operate in the United States [1–4].

'''International FundsNet Country Updates – August 2025''' is a global financial and investment regulatory thought leadership publication released by [[Eversheds Sutherland]] on September 2, 2025 (August 2025 edition) [1–6]. The report summarizes recent legal, policy, and regulatory changes across international jurisdictions that impact investment managers, fund operators, and institutional investors [1–6].

== Executive Summary ==
The publication provides a global regulatory horizon-scanning framework to assist asset managers in anticipating legal shifts across multiple jurisdictions [1–6]. Key updates cover regulatory burden reductions in Croatia, account transfer and liquidity rule updates in Canada, expanded alternative asset access for 401(k) plans in the United States, and tax treatment clarifications under Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTA) in Cambodia [1–6].

== Legal Basis & Legal Disclaimer ==

* '''Formal Legal Basis''': Not found in available sources (The document is compiled from various national regulatory updates) [1–6].
* '''Informational Disclaimer''': The content presented in the publication is provided strictly for general informational purposes and does not constitute formal legal advice [1–6].

== Background ==
Rapidly evolving international financial market regulations require investment managers to continuously monitor legal developments across multiple jurisdictions [1–6]. This publication serves as a structured intelligence brief to help market participants maintain cross-border regulatory compliance and optimize fund operational strategies [1–6].

== Objectives ==

# Deliver a concise global summary of regulatory developments affecting investment managers [1–6].
# Detail proposed regulatory burden reductions for AIF and UCITS managers in Croatia [1–6].
# Outline modernized account transfer rules and fund liquidity relief measures implemented in Canada [1–6].
# Explain expanded alternative asset investment access for US 401(k) plan participants [1–6].
# Clarify Cambodian DTA tax treatments regarding share premiums and capital gains [1–6].

== Key Provisions & Recommendations ==

* '''Croatia (HANFA)''': The Croatian Financial Services Supervisory Agency (HANFA) proposed major reforms to reduce regulatory burdens on Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) and UCITS managers [1–6].
* '''Canada (CIRO, AMF, CSA)''': The Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization (CIRO) and Autorité des marchés financiers (AMF) modernized account transfer rules, while the Canadian Securities Administrators (CSA) provided targeted liquidity relief for investment funds [1–6].
* '''United States''': A Presidential Executive Order aims to democratize access to alternative asset classes for 401(k) retirement plan investors [1–6].
* '''Cambodia''': Clarified tax treatment of share premiums and capital gains under Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTA) [1–6].

== Implementation & Deployment ==

* '''Publication Release''': Officially published globally on September 2, 2025 [1–6].
* '''Lead Practice Team''': Led by Eversheds Sutherland UK legal practitioners Lindi Rudman (Legal Director) and Michaela Arter (Partner) [1–6].

== Policy & Operational Challenges ==

* '''Cross-Border Regulatory Friction''': Investment managers face increasing compliance complexity when harmonizing global fund operations with localized country rules [1–6].

Operating under Article 15.b of the Statute of the Council of Europe, the recommendation establishes a European framework to safeguard, support, and develop quality youth work across member States. It defines youth work as a social practice rooted in non-formal and informal learning by, with, and for young people; recommends establishing a competency-based training framework for paid and volunteer youth workers; calls for setting up an ad hoc high-level taskforce to elaborate a mid-term strategy; promotes the Council of Europe Youth Work Portfolio and Quality Label for Youth Centres; and mandates a 5-year implementation review by the Committee of Ministers.

== 4. POLICY ANALYSIS ==

* '''Background''': [FACT] Adopted at the 1287th meeting of the Ministers' Deputies on 31 May 2017, Recommendation CM/Rec(2017)4 builds upon decades of Council of Europe standards in democratic citizenship, human rights education, and youth policy. It draws directly from the 2015 2nd European Youth Work Convention ("Making a world of difference") to establish a unified European agenda for quality youth work.
* '''Policy Problem''': [FACT]
** '''Socio-Economic Disruption & Youth Vulnerability''': Young people face complex transitions to adulthood exacerbated by high youth unemployment, poverty, social exclusion, discrimination, and the lingering impacts of economic crises.
** '''Risk of a 'Lost Generation'''': Inadequate support risks creating a "lost generation" of disillusioned, disengaged youth, undermining European stability, democratic values, and social cohesion.
** '''Emerging Societal Threats''': Increased vulnerability to violent extremism, radicalization, unmanaged migration pressures, and democratic deficits.
** '''Inconsistent Youth Worker Training & Validation''': Lack of coherent, recognized competency frameworks for paid and volunteer youth workers across member States.
* '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] The absence of standardized, cross-border recognition and competency-based validation frameworks for youth workers, alongside uneven funding and legislation for non-formal/informal youth work across local, regional, and national levels.
* '''Policy Objectives''': [FACT] Safeguard and proactively support quality youth work within local, regional, and national youth policies; establish a flexible competency-based framework for youth worker education and training; set up an ad hoc high-level taskforce for a mid-term strategy; foster national/European research on youth work impact; promote the Council of Europe Youth Work Portfolio and Quality Label for Youth Centres; and ensure full translation, dissemination, and 5-year review.
* '''Policy Implementation''': [FACT]
** '''National Action''': Member States are urged to provide sustainable structures, resources, and legislation for youth work; facilitate cross-sectoral collaboration (with health, employment, social care, criminal justice, and formal education); and protect the autonomy of youth NGOs.
** '''Education & Competency Frameworks''': Develop core competence sets for youth workers; establish validation, certification, and documentation pathways for informal learning; and align with broader European non-formal learning agendas.
** '''European Co-governance''': Taskforce creation to carry out mapping exercises of vocational/higher education training, stimulate cross-sector co-operation, and strengthen links between formal education, research, and public/private sectors.
* '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] Youth work enhances critical thinking, digital/information literacy, leadership, intercultural understanding, democratic citizenship, and resilience against negative influences/extremism. Investing in quality youth work protects civil society and prevents long-term economic and democratic costs.
* '''Reform & Evaluation''': [FACT] Member States and the Committee of Ministers are instructed to examine the implementation of Recommendation CM/Rec(2017)4 five years after its adoption (scheduled for 2022).

== Summary ==
'''Recommendation CM/Rec(2017)4 of the Committee of Ministers to member States on youth work''' (Stable ID: '''JPW-REG-000144''') is an official international policy instrument adopted on 31 May 2017 by the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe at the 1287th meeting of the Ministers' Deputies. Enacted pursuant to Article 15.b of the Statute of the Council of Europe, the recommendation establishes a comprehensive European framework to protect, sustain, and advance quality youth work across member States. It conceptualizes youth work as a value-driven social practice founded on non-formal and informal education; urges member States to develop national competency and validation frameworks for paid and volunteer youth workers; directs the creation of an ad hoc high-level taskforce to formulate a European mid-term strategy; promotes the Council of Europe Youth Work Portfolio and Quality Label for Youth Centres; and stipulates a mandatory 5-year review of national implementation.

== Legal Basis ==
The recommendation derives its mandate from foundational Council of Europe treaties and international conventions:

* '''Statute of the Council of Europe''': Article 15.b of the Statute of the Council of Europe.
* '''Human Rights & Social Charters''': European Convention on Human Rights (1950, ETS No. 5); European Social Charter (1961, ETS No. 35, revised 1996, ETS No. 163); and the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child.
* '''Related Statutory Instruments''': Resolution CM/Res(2008)23; Recommendations Rec(2003)8, Rec(2004)13, Rec(2006)1, CM/Rec(2007)13, CM/Rec(2010)7, CM/Rec(2010)8, CM/Rec(2012)2, CM/Rec(2012)13, CM/Rec(2015)3, CM/Rec(2016)7; Declaration of the 3rd Summit of Heads of State and Government (Warsaw, 2005); and the Declaration of the 2nd European Youth Work Convention (2015).

== Background ==
Young people across Europe face structural challenges during their transition to independent adulthood, including high youth unemployment, poverty, marginalization, and social inequality. Without targeted non-formal support, societies risk giving rise to a "lost generation" characterized by civic disengagement and alienation from democratic values.

== Objectives ==
1. Encourage member States to actively support and integrate quality youth work within local, regional, and national policy frameworks. 2. Formulate flexible, competency-based education and training systems for professional and volunteer youth workers. 3. Establish an ad hoc high-level taskforce tasked with creating a European mid-term strategy for youth work. 4. Support cross-European research into the socio-economic impacts of non-formal youth learning. 5. Expand the implementation of the Council of Europe Youth Work Portfolio and Quality Label for Youth Centres.

== Scope ==
The policy covers all areas of non-formal and informal youth practice across member States: 1. ''Youth Work Scope'': Out-of-school activities (social, cultural, educational, political, or environmental) conducted by, with, and for young people based on voluntary participation. 2. ''Competency & Validation'': Recognition, certification, and documentation of skills acquired through non-formal learning environments. 3. ''Inter-Sectoral Collaboration'': Coordinated strategies uniting youth work with formal education, employment services, health, sport, social work, and criminal justice systems. 4. ''NGO Autonomy'': Safeguarding the legal and operational independence of youth non-governmental organizations.

== Key Provisions & Principles ==

* '''Voluntary Participation & Universal Access''': Youth work must remain participant-centered, inclusive, and accessible to all young people without discrimination.
* '''Ad Hoc High-Level Taskforce''': Mandated to map national training methodologies and support capacity-building efforts across member States.
* '''Five-Year Implementation Review''': Instructs the Committee of Ministers to conduct a systematic evaluation of national implementation five years after adoption (2022).

== Implementation ==
Implemented through member State governments, national youth ministries, local and regional authorities, the European Youth Centres (Strasbourg and Budapest), the European Youth Foundation, and the joint Partnership between the European Union and the Council of Europe in the field of youth.

== Policy Problems ==

* Fragmented legal recognition and variable financial support for non-formal youth work across jurisdictions.
* Lack of standardized certification and qualification pathways for youth workers.
* Vulnerability of marginalized youth to social exclusion, democratic alienation, and radicalization.

== Reform ==

* Creation of European-wide recognition tools for non-formal and informal learning.
* Strengthening structural linkages between formal education systems, academic research, and youth policy development.

== Relationship with Other Entities ==

* '''Issued by''': Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe.
* '''Based on''': Statute of the Council of Europe, ECHR, European Social Charter.
* '''Supported by''': European Youth Centres, European Youth Foundation, EU-CoE Youth Partnership.

== See Also ==

* [[European Convention on Human Rights]]
* [[European Social Charter]]
* [[Non-Formal Learning and Youth Work]]

== References ==

* Council of Europe, Committee of Ministers. (2017). *Recommendation CM/Rec(2017)4 of the Committee of Ministers to member States on youth work*. Adopted on 31 May 2017 at the 1287th meeting of the Ministers' Deputies.

== 1. IDENTIDAD DE LA ENTIDAD ==

== 4. ANÁLISIS DE POLÍTICA PÚBLICA ==

* '''Antecedentes''': [HECHO] Adoptada en la 1287.ª reunión de los Delegados de los Ministros el 31 de mayo de 2017, la Recomendación CM/Rec(2017)4 se basa en décadas de estándares del Consejo de Europa sobre ciudadanía democrática, educación en derechos humanos y políticas de juventud. Se inspira directamente en la 2.ª Convención Europea de Trabajo con Jóvenes de 2015 ("Making a world of difference") para fijar una agenda europea unificada en materia de juventud.
* '''Problema de Política Pública''': [HECHO]
** '''Disfunción Socioeconómica y Vulnerabilidad Juvenil''': Los jóvenes se enfrentan a transiciones complejas hacia la vida adulta, agravadas por el desempleo juvenil, la pobreza, la exclusión social, la discriminación y los efectos persistentes de las crisis económicas.
** '''Riesgo de una "Generación Perdida"''': La falta de apoyo adecuado corre el riesgo de crear una "generación perdida" de jóvenes desencantados, minando la estabilidad europea, los valores democráticos y la cohesión social.
** '''Amenazas Sociales Emergentes''': Mayor vulnerabilidad frente al extremismo violento, la radicalización, las presiones migratorias y el déficit democrático.
** '''Desigualdad en la Formación de Trabajadores con Jóvenes''': Inexistencia de marcos de competencia homogéneos para el personal asalariado y voluntario en los Estados miembros.
* '''Vacío Legal/de Política Pública''': [HECHO] Ausencia de un marco estandarizado a nivel transfronterizo para el reconocimiento y validación de competencias de los trabajadores con jóvenes, junto con una financiación y legislación desiguales para el aprendizaje no formal e informal a escala local, regional y nacional.
* '''Objetivos de Política Pública''': [HECHO] Salvaguardar y apoyar activamente un trabajo con jóvenes de calidad dentro de las políticas de juventud locales, regionales y nacionales; establecer un marco flexible basado en competencias para la educación y formación de trabajadores con jóvenes; constituir un grupo de trabajo *ad hoc* de alto nivel para diseñar una estrategia a medio plazo; impulsar la investigación nacional/europea sobre el impacto del trabajo con jóvenes; promover el Portafolio de Trabajo con Jóvenes del Consejo de Europa y la Etiqueta de Calidad para Centros de Juventud; y garantizar su traducción, difusión y revisión quinquenal.
* '''Implementación de Política Pública''': [HECHO]

** '''Cogobernanza Europea''': Creación de un grupo de trabajo para realizar estudios de mapeo de la formación profesional/superior, estimular la cooperación intersectorial y fortalecer los vínculos entre la educación formal, la investigación y los sectores público y privado.

Invertir en un trabajo de calidad con jóvenes protege a la sociedad civil y evita costes económicos y democráticos a largo plazo.

== Resumen ==
'''Recomendación CM/Rec(2017)4 del Comité de Ministros a los Estados miembros sobre el trabajo con jóvenes''' (ID Estable: '''JPW-REG-000144''') es un instrumento oficial de política internacional adoptado el 31 de mayo de 2017 por el Comité de Ministros del Consejo de Europa durante la 1287.ª reunión de los Delegados de los Ministros. Dictada en virtud del artículo 15.b del Estatuto del Consejo de Europa, la recomendación establece un marco europeo integral para proteger, sostener y promover un trabajo con jóvenes de calidad en todos los Estados miembros. Concibe el trabajo con jóvenes (*youth work*) como una práctica social basada en la educación no formal e informal; insta a los Estados miembros a desarrollar marcos de competencias y validación para el personal asalariado y voluntario; ordena la creación de un grupo de trabajo *ad hoc* de alto nivel para elaborar una estrategia europea a medio plazo; promueve el Portafolio de Trabajo con Jóvenes del Consejo de Europa y la Etiqueta de Calidad para Centros de Juventud; y exige un análisis periódico de su aplicación transcurridos cinco años.

== Base Legal ==
La recomendación fundamenta su mandato en tratados constitutivos del Consejo de Europa y convenios internacionales:

* '''Estatuto del Consejo de Europa''': Artículo 15.b del Estatuto del Consejo de Europa.
* '''Derechos Humanos y Cartas Sociales''': Convenio Europeo de Derechos Humanos (1950, STE n.º 5); Carta Social Europea (1961, STE n.º 35, revisada en 1996, STE n.º 163); y la Convención de las Naciones Unidas sobre los Derechos del Niño.
* '''Instrumentos Normativos Relacionados''': Resolución CM/Res(2008)23; Recomendaciones Rec(2003)8, Rec(2004)13, Rec(2006)1, CM/Rec(2007)13, CM/Rec(2010)7, CM/Rec(2010)8, CM/Rec(2012)2, CM/Rec(2012)13, CM/Rec(2015)3, CM/Rec(2016)7; Declaración de la 3.ª Cumbre de Jefes de Estado y de Gobierno (Varsovia, 2005); y la Declaración de la 2.ª Convención Europea de Trabajo con Jóvenes (2015).

== Antecedentes ==
Los jóvenes europeos se enfrentan a obstáculos estructurales en su transición hacia la vida adulta independiente, entre los que destacan las altas tasas de desempleo juvenil, la pobreza, la marginalidad y la desigualdad social. Sin el apoyo de programas de educación no formal, las sociedades corren el riesgo de consolidar una "generación perdida", ajena a la participación ciudadana y desvinculada de los valores democráticos.

== Objetivos ==
1. Impulsar a los Estados miembros a apoyar e integrar activamente el trabajo con jóvenes en sus políticas locales, regionales y nacionales. 2. Diseñar sistemas flexibles de educación y formación basados en competencias para trabajadores con jóvenes, ya sean profesionales o voluntarios. 3. Constituir un grupo de trabajo *ad hoc* de alto nivel encargado de redactar una estrategia europea a medio plazo. 4. Fomentar la investigación interjurisdiccional sobre los impactos socioeconómicos del aprendizaje no formal. 5. Difundir el uso del Portafolio de Trabajo con Jóvenes del Consejo de Europa y la Etiqueta de Calidad para Centros de Juventud.

== Alcance ==
El texto abarca los ámbitos de la práctica no formal e informal con la juventud en los Estados miembros: 1. ''Ámbito del Trabajo con Jóvenes'': Actividades extraescolares (sociales, culturales, educativas, políticas o ambientales) realizadas por, con y para jóvenes sobre la base de la participación voluntaria. 2. ''Competencias y Validación'': Reconocimiento, certificación y documentación de capacidades adquiridas en entornos de aprendizaje no formal. 3. ''Colaboración Intersectorial'': Estrategias coordinadas entre el sector de la juventud, la educación formal, los servicios de empleo, sanidad, deportes, bienestar social y sistemas de justicia. 4. ''Autonomía de las ONG'': Salvaguardia de la independencia jurídica y operativa de las organizaciones no gubernamentales de juventud.

== Disposiciones y Principios Clave ==

* '''Participación Voluntaria y Acceso Universal''': El trabajo con jóvenes debe centrarse en la persona joven, ser inclusivo y garantizar el acceso sin discriminación.
* '''Grupo de Trabajo *Ad Hoc* de Alto Nivel''': Encargado de cartografiar los modelos formativos nacionales y apoyar la creación de capacidades en los Estados miembros.
* '''Evaluación Quinquenal''': Ordena al Comité de Ministros realizar una evaluación sistemática del grado de aplicación de la recomendación tras cinco años de su adopción (2022).

== Implementación ==
Se ejecuta a través de los gobiernos de los Estados miembros, ministerios de juventud, autoridades locales y regionales, los Centros Europeos de la Juventud (Estrasburgo y Budapest), la Fundación Europea de la Juventud y la Asociación mixta entre la Unión Europea y el Consejo de Europa en materia de juventud.

== Problemas de Política Pública ==

* Reconocimiento legal fragmentado y financiación desigual del trabajo no formal entre jurisdicciones.
* Carencia de itinerarios homogéneos de cualificación y certificación para los trabajadores con jóvenes.
* Vulnerabilidad de los jóvenes marginados ante la exclusión social, el alejamiento democrático y el extremismo.

== Reforma ==

* Creación de herramientas europeas de reconocimiento del aprendizaje no formal e informal.
* Fortalecimiento de las conexiones entre el sistema educativo formal, la investigación académica y la formulación de políticas públicas de juventud.

== Relación con otras Entidades ==

* '''Emitida por''': Comité de Ministros del Consejo de Europa.
* '''Basada en''': Estatuto del Consejo de Europa, CEDH, Carta Social Europea.
* '''Con el apoyo de''': Centros Europeos de la Juventud, Fundación Europea de la Juventud, Asociación UE-Consejo de Europa en Juventud.

== 1. ENTITY IDENTITY ==

* '''Stable ID''': JPW-REG-000166
* '''Canonical Name''': Opinion CDL-AD(2025)038 on the Election of Judicial Members of the General Council of the Judiciary of Spain (Venice Commission, 2025)
* '''Official Name''': Opinion on the Manner of Election of the Judicial Members of the General Council of the Judiciary (Spain) (Opinion No. 1248/2025, CDL-AD(2025)038)
* '''Entity Type''': Official International Legal & Policy Advisory Opinion / Council of Europe Venice Commission Instrument
* '''Aliases''': Venice Commission Opinion CDL-AD(2025)038, Opinion No. 1248/2025, Venice Commission CGPJ/GCJ Reform Opinion (2025), Dictamen de la Comisión de Venecia sobre la elección del CGPJ
* '''Definition''': [FACT] An official international legal advisory opinion adopted by the European Commission for Democracy through Law (Venice Commission of the Council of Europe) at its 144th Plenary Session (Venice, 9–10 October 2025). Requested on 21 April 2025 by Ms Isabel Perelló Doménech, President of the Spanish General Council of the Judiciary (*Consejo General del Poder Judicial - CGPJ / GCJ*) and President of the Supreme Court, pursuant to the Additional Provision of Organic Law No. 3/2024 of 2 August 2024. The opinion evaluates two alternative reform options prepared by the CGPJ for electing its 12 judicial members against European standards of judicial independence and peer election (Committee of Ministers Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)12, CCJE Opinion No. 24, ECHR and CJEU jurisprudence). The Venice Commission concludes that Option 1 (direct peer election by judges) aligns with European peer election standards provided safeguards are incorporated against internal politicisation via judicial associations, whereas Option 2 (pre-election shortlist by judges followed by parliamentary election) fails to comply because final political election by Parliament frustrates peer election and exacerbates politicisation risks.
* '''Jurisdiction''': Spain / Council of Europe Member States
* '''Issuing Authority / Publisher''': European Commission for Democracy through Law of the Council of Europe (*Venice Commission / Comisión de Venecia*)
* '''Legal Basis''': Statute of the Council of Europe; Additional Provision of Spanish Organic Law 3/2024 of 2 August 2024; Spanish Constitution of 1978 (Art. 122); Spanish Organic Law 6/1985 on the Judiciary (LOPJ Arts. 560, 561, 567, 574, 578); Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)12 of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe; Consultative Council of European Judges (CCJE) Opinion No. 24 (2021).
* '''Date''': Adopted 9–10 October 2025 (144th Plenary Session in Venice); Published 13 October 2025.
* '''Status''': Official / Adopted Advisory Opinion
* '''Related Institutions/Regulations/Policies/People''':
** '''Institutions''': General Council of the Judiciary of Spain (*Consejo General del Poder Judicial - CGPJ / GCJ*), Venice Commission (*Comisión de Venecia*), Supreme Court of Spain (*Tribunal Supremo*), Ministry of the Presidency, Justice and Relations with Parliament, Congress of Deputies (*Congreso de los Diputados*), Senate of Spain (*Senado*), European Union Commission, GRECO, Consultative Council of European Judges (CCJE), Professional Association of Magistrates (*Asociación Profesional de la Magistratura - APM*), Francisco de Vitoria Association of Judges (*Asociación de Jueces Francisco de Vitoria - AJFV*), Judges for Democracy (*Juezas y Jueces para la Democracia - JJpD*), Independent Judicial Forum (*Foro Judicial Independiente - FJI*).
** '''Regulations/Policies''': Spanish Constitution of 1978 (Art. 122), Organic Law 1/1980 on the CGPJ, Organic Law 6/1985 on the Judiciary (LOPJ), Organic Law 2/2001, Organic Law 3/2024, Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)12, CCJE Opinion No. 24 (2021), CGPJ Reform Proposal (CDL-REF(2025)038).
** '''Associated People''': Ms Isabel Perelló Doménech (President of CGPJ/Supreme Court); Rapporteurs: Ms Marta Cartabia (Member, Italy), Ms Regina Kiener (Member, Switzerland), Mr François Séners (Substitute member, France); Ms Simona Granata-Menghini (Secretary of the Commission); Mr Taras Pashuk (Secretariat); Mr José María Fernández Seijo (CGPJ); Ms Camino Vidal Fueyo (Director General of Constitutional Affairs); Mr Joaquín Martínez Salmerón (President of Justice Committee, Congress); Mr Pedro Rollán Ojeda (President of Senate); Cecep Mustafa (JPW-PERSON-000001) [FACT: Not found in sources]; Johana Crishele Ohoira (JPW-PERSON-000002) [FACT: Not found in sources].

== 4. POLICY ANALYSIS ==

* '''Background''': [FACT] Under Article 122 of the 1978 Spanish Constitution, the General Council of the Judiciary (*Consejo General del Poder Judicial - CGPJ*) is the governing body of Spain's judiciary, comprising 21 members (the President of the Supreme Court plus 20 members: 12 judges/magistrates and 8 legal experts/jurists) serving a 5-year term. Under Organic Law 1/1980, the 12 judicial members were elected directly by their judicial peers. In 1985, Organic Law 6/1985 transferred the election of all 12 judicial members to Parliament (Congress and Senate electing 6 each by 3/5 majority). Although upheld as constitutional by Constitutional Court Ruling 108/1986, the Court explicitly warned against the risk of partisan politicisation. In 2018, the CGPJ's mandate expired and entered a 5.5-year parliamentary deadlock ad interim. Following international pressure from the EU Commission and GRECO, an agreement was reached on 25 June 2024 to renew the Council and enact Organic Law 3/2024 (2 August 2024). The law's Additional Provision required the CGPJ to submit within 6 months a report examining European judicial council election systems and a reform proposal adopted by a 3/5 majority. On 5 February 2025, the CGPJ adopted a report submitting two alternative reform options (Option 1 and Option 2). On 21 April 2025, CGPJ President Isabel Perelló Doménech requested an official opinion from the Venice Commission.
* '''Policy Problem''': [FACT]
** '''Risk of Partisan Deadlock & External Politicisation''': Parliamentary election of judicial members by 3/5 majority resulted in repeated multi-year political deadlocks (2018–2024), eroding public trust and generating concerns from the EU Commission, GRECO, and UN Human Rights Rapporteurs.
** '''Risk of Internal Politicisation''': Direct peer election solely among judges (Option 1) carries the risk of internal politicisation via powerful judicial associations (APM 45.2%, AJFV 29.9%, JJpD 14%, FJI 11%, representing 58% of active judges), which could act as proxies for political parties and disadvantage the 42% of non-associated judges.
** '''Incompatibility of Dual-Phase Parliamentary Selection (Option 2)''': Option 2 combines judicial pre-election with final election by Parliament. The Venice Commission finds that giving Parliament the final choice frustrates the peer election standard, duplicates political alignment risks, grants Parliament unguided discretion without objective criteria or reasons, and lacks an anti-deadlock mechanism.
* '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] The gap between international standards requiring that at least half of a judicial council's members be judges elected directly by their peers without political intervention (CM/Rec(2010)12, CCJE Opinion No. 24), and Spain's 40-year statutory practice of parliamentary election under LOPJ Article 567.
* '''Policy Objectives''': [FACT] Align Spain's judicial election model with European peer election standards; eliminate political influence and partisan quota distribution; safeguard judicial independence; ensure fair representation of all court tiers (Supreme Court, senior judges, lower courts); and maintain pluralism and diversity (gender, region, specialisation).
* '''Policy Implementation (Venice Commission Evaluation of the 2 Options)''': [FACT]
** '''Option 1 (Direct Peer Election)''':
*** ''Mechanism'': Judicial candidates are endorsed by 25 judges or a judicial association; members are directly elected by all active judges.
*** ''Evaluation'': '''COMPLIES IN PRINCIPLE''' with European peer election standards.
*** ''Required Safeguards'': To prevent internal politicisation via judicial associations, the Commission recommends: (1) substantially reducing or abolishing the 25-endorsement threshold and introducing an open call for independent candidates; (2) replacing the alternate system with by-elections for early vacancies; (3) reviewing/capping the maximum number of votes per voter (e.g., 8 votes) to prevent majoritarian domination by associations; and (4) guaranteeing equal campaign access, information, and transparent financing.
** '''Option 2 (Pre-Election Shortlist + Parliamentary Election)''':
*** ''Mechanism'': Candidates endorsed by 30 judges or an association; judicial pre-election creates a shortlist (3x vacancies); final election held by Parliament by 3/5 majority.
*** ''Evaluation'': '''NON-COMPLIANT WITH EUROPEAN STANDARDS'''. Final parliamentary election frustrates peer election, duplicates political influences, grants unguided discretion to political parties, and lacks an automatic anti-deadlock mechanism (e.g., automatic appointment of top-ranked shortlisted candidates if Parliament fails to vote within a set timeframe).
* '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] Cites European consensus standards (CM/Rec(2010)12 para 27; CCJE Opinion No. 24; ENCJ Compendium); CJEU ruling *A.K. and Others* (C-585/18); ECtHR landmark rulings *Reczkowicz v. Poland* (App. 43447/19), *Grzęda v. Poland* (App. 43572/18), and *Denisov v. Ukraine*.
* '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] Recommendation to entrench the peer election method in the Spanish Constitution if future constitutional reform occurs; review the 25-year seniority threshold for senior judge quotas in Option 1; strengthen technical support for the Supreme Court Electoral Committee; and provide clear judicial remedies for electoral disputes.

== Summary ==
'''Opinion CDL-AD(2025)038 on the Election of Judicial Members of the General Council of the Judiciary of Spain''' (Stable ID: '''JPW-REG-000166''') is an official international legal advisory opinion adopted by the European Commission for Democracy through Law (Venice Commission of the Council of Europe) at its 144th Plenary Session in Venice (9–10 October 2025). Requested on 21 April 2025 by Ms Isabel Perelló Doménech (President of the CGPJ and the Spanish Supreme Court) pursuant to the Additional Provision of Organic Law 3/2024, the opinion evaluates two alternative reform options prepared by the CGPJ for electing its 12 judicial members against European standards of judicial independence and peer election. The Venice Commission concluded that '''Option 1''' (direct peer election by judges) complies in principle with European peer election standards provided safeguards are incorporated against internal politicisation via judicial associations, whereas '''Option 2''' (pre-election shortlist by judges followed by parliamentary election) fails to comply because final political election by Parliament frustrates peer election and exacerbates politicisation risks.

== Legal Basis ==
The international and national statutory frameworks analyzed in this Opinion derive from Council of Europe instruments and Spanish constitutional law:

* '''International & Council of Europe Instruments''': Statute of the Council of Europe; Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)12 of the Committee of Ministers (para 27); Consultative Council of European Judges (CCJE) Opinion No. 24 (2021); and jurisprudence of the CJEU (*A.K. and Others*, C-585/18) and ECtHR (*Reczkowicz v. Poland*, *Grzęda v. Poland*, *Denisov v. Ukraine*).
* '''Spanish Domestic Legislation''': Article 122 of the Spanish Constitution of 1978; Organic Law 6/1985 on the Judiciary (LOPJ Arts. 560, 561, 567, 574, 578); Organic Law 1/1980 on the CGPJ; and the Additional Provision of Organic Law 3/2024 of 2 August 2024.

== Background ==
Under Article 122 of the 1978 Spanish Constitution, the General Council of the Judiciary (*CGPJ*) is the governing body of the judiciary, comprising 21 members (the President of the Supreme Court plus 20 members: 12 judges/magistrates and 8 jurists). Since the 1985 LOPJ reform, Parliament elected all 12 judicial members by a 3/5 majority. This system led to repeated multi-year political deadlocks, including a 5.5-year impasse between 2018 and 2024. Following a political agreement in June 2024 and the enactment of Organic Law 3/2024, the CGPJ submitted a report detailing Options 1 and 2 in February 2025, leading to President Isabel Perelló Doménech requesting this official Venice Commission opinion.

== Objectives ==
1. Ensure the judicial election model for the CGPJ aligns with European peer election standards without political interference. 2. Eliminate multi-year partisan deadlocks and external political quota distributions. 3. Prevent internal politicisation driven by dominant judicial associations (*APM, AJFV, JJpD, FJI*). 4. Guarantee fair representation across all court tiers, gender balance, and regional diversity.

== Scope ==
The Venice Commission conducted a detailed comparative analysis of the two proposed reform models: 1. ''Option 1 (Direct Peer Election)'':

* '''Evaluation''': '''COMPLIES IN PRINCIPLE''' with European standards.
* '''Recommended Safeguards''': Substantially reduce/abolish the 25-endorsement threshold for independent candidates; replace alternates with by-elections; cap/review maximum votes per voter to prevent association bloc-voting; and establish clear rules for campaign equality and transparent financing.

2. ''Option 2 (Pre-Election Shortlist + Parliamentary Election)'':

* '''Evaluation''': '''NON-COMPLIANT WITH EUROPEAN STANDARDS'''. Final election by Parliament frustrates peer election, duplicates political alignment risks, grants unguided discretion to political parties, and lacks an automatic anti-deadlock mechanism.

== Key Provisions & Principles ==

* '''Peer Election Standard (CM/Rec(2010)12)''': At least half of the members of judicial councils must be judges elected directly by their peers without executive or parliamentary selection.
* '''Automatic Anti-Deadlock Mechanism''': If a parliamentary vote is retained, candidates shortlisted by judges should be automatically appointed if Parliament fails to vote within a set timeframe.

== Implementation ==
Directed to the Spanish Parliament (*Cortes Generales*), the Government of Spain, the General Council of the Judiciary (*CGPJ*), and the Supreme Court of Spain.

== Policy Problems ==

* Extended multi-year institutional deadlocks eroding public trust in judicial independence.
* Potential domination of judicial elections by political proxies or entrenched judicial associations, marginalizing the 42% of non-associated judges.

== Reform ==

* Adoption of Option 1 accompanied by the four recommended safeguards against internal politicisation.
* Constitutional entrenchment of the peer election method in future constitutional revisions.

== 4. ANÁLISIS DE POLÍTICA PÚBLICA ==

* '''Antecedentes''': [HECHO] Según el artículo 122 de la Constitución Española de 1978, el Consejo General del Poder Judicial (*CGPJ*) es el órgano de gobierno del poder judicial, integrado por 21 miembros (el Presidente del Tribunal Supremo más 20 vocales: 12 jueces/magistrados y 8 juristas de reconocida competencia) por un mandato de 5 años. Bajo la Ley Orgánica 1/1980, los 12 vocales judiciales eran elegidos directamente por sus compañeros de profesión. En 1985, la Ley Orgánica 6/1985 atribuyó la elección de los 20 vocales al Parlamento (Congreso y Senado eligiendo 6 judiciales cada uno por mayoría de 3/5). Aunque avalado por la STC 108/1986, el Tribunal Constitucional advirtió expresamente del riesgo de partidización. En 2018, el mandato del CGPJ caducó, iniciando un bloqueo parlamentario en funciones de 5,5 años (2018–2024). Tras la mediación de la Comisión Europea y el acuerdo de 25 de junio de 2024, se aprobó la Ley Orgánica 3/2024, cuya Disposición Adicional encargó al CGPJ redactar una propuesta de reforma. El 5 de febrero de 2025, el CGPJ aprobó un informe con dos opciones alternativas (Opción 1 y Opción 2), y el 21 de abril de 2025 la Presidenta Isabel Perelló Doménech solicitó formalmente el dictamen de la Comisión de Venecia.
* '''Problema de Política Pública''': [HECHO]
** '''Riesgo de Bloqueo Partidista y Politización Externa''': La elección parlamentaria por mayoría reforzada de 3/5 provocó bloqueos institucionales prolongados (2018–2024), deteriorando la confianza pública y motivando advertencias de la Comisión Europea, el GRECO y la ONU.
** '''Riesgo de Politización Interna''': La elección directa entre jueces (Opción 1) conlleva el riesgo de politización interna a través de las asociaciones judiciales (APM 45,2%, AJFV 29,9%, JJpD 14%, FJI 11%, que representan al 58% de los jueces activos), las cuales podrían actuar como apoderadas de partidos políticos en perjuicio del 42% de jueces no asociados.
** '''Incompatibilidad de la Selección Parlamentaria en Dos Fases (Opción 2)''': La Opción 2 combina una preselección judicial con una elección final parlamentaria. La Comisión de Venecia concluye que otorgar la decisión final al Parlamento desvirtúa el estándar de elección entre iguales, duplica los riesgos de alineación política, otorga discrecionalidad no guiada a los partidos y carece de un mecanismo antibloqueo.
* '''Vacío Legal/de Política Pública''': [HECHO] La contradicción entre los estándares internacionales que exigen que al menos la mitad de los miembros del Consejo Judicial sean jueces elegidos directamente por sus iguales sin interferencia política (CM/Rec(2010)12, Dictamen n.º 24 del CCJE), y la práctica legal española de 40 años de elección parlamentaria bajo el artículo 567 de la LOPJ.
* '''Objetivos de Política Pública''': [HECHO] Alinear el sistema de elección del CGPJ con los estándares europeos de *peer election*; eliminar las cuotas partidistas; salvaguardar la independencia judicial; garantizar una representación equitativa de todas las categorías judiciales; y preservar el pluralismo (género, territorio y especialización).
* '''Implementación de Política Pública (Evaluación de las 2 Opciones)''': [HECHO]
** '''Opción 1 (Elección Directa por Jueces)''':
*** ''Mecanismo'': Candidaturas avaladas por 25 jueces o una asociación judicial; elección directa por todos los jueces activos.
*** ''Evaluación'': '''CUMPLE EN PRINCIPIO''' con los estándares europeos.
*** ''Garantías Requeridas'': Para evitar la politización asociativa, se recomienda: (1) reducir sustancialmente o abolir el requisito de 25 avales e introducir convocatorias abiertas para independientes; (2) sustituir el sistema de suplentes por elecciones parciales (*by-elections*); (3) limitar/revisar el número máximo de votos por elector (ej. máximo 8 votos) para impedir el mayoritarismo asociativo; y (4) fijar reglas de igualdad en la campaña y transparencia en la financiación.
** '''Opción 2 (Preselección Judicial + Elección Parlamentaria)''':
*** ''Mecanismo'': Candidaturas avaladas por 30 jueces o una asociación; preselección judicial que genera una lista corta (3 candidatos por plaza); elección final por el Parlamento por mayoría de 3/5.
*** ''Evaluación'': '''NO CUMPLE CON LOS ESTÁNDARES EUROPEOS'''. La decisión final parlamentaria anula el carácter de *peer election*, duplica las presiones políticas, otorga discrecionalidad sin criterios objetivos y carece de mecanismo antibloqueo automático (ej. nombramiento automático de los más votados por los jueces si el Parlamento no vota en un plazo determinado).
* '''Evidencia e Impacto''': [HECHO] Fundamentado en consensos europeos (CM/Rec(2010)12 párr. 27; Dictamen n.º 24 del CCJE); jurisprudencia del TJUE (*A.K. y otros*, C-585/18); y del TEDH (*Reczkowicz c. Polonia*, *Grzęda c. Polonia*, *Denisov c. Ucrania*).
* '''Reformas y Cuestiones Pendientes''': [HECHO] Recomendación de blindar el método de elección corporativa en la Constitución Española en una futura reforma constitucional; revisar la exigencia de 25 años de antigüedad para la cuota de magistrados en la Opción 1; reforzar el soporte técnico de la Junta Electoral de la Ilustre Sala de Gobierno del Tribunal Supremo; y regular recursos judiciales claros ante disputas electorales.

== Resumen ==
'''Dictamen CDL-AD(2025)038 sobre la Elección de los Vocales Judiciales del Consejo General del Poder Judicial de España''' (ID Estable: '''JPW-REG-000166''') es un dictamen consultivo jurídico internacional oficial adoptado por la Comisión de Venecia del Consejo de Europa en su 144.ª Sesión Plenaria en Venecia (9-10 de octubre de 2025). Solicitado el 21 de abril de 2025 por D.ª Isabel Perelló Doménech (Presidenta del CGPJ y del Tribunal Supremo) en virtud de la Ley Orgánica 3/2024, el dictamen evalúa las dos opciones de reforma redactadas por el CGPJ para la elección de sus 12 vocales judiciales. La Comisión de Venecia concluyó que la '''Opción 1''' (elección directa por los propios jueces) cumple en principio con los estándares europeos de *peer election*, siempre que se introduzcan garantías frente a la politización asociativa interna; mientras que la '''Opción 2''' (preselección por jueces y elección final parlamentaria) incumple las exigencias europeas al mantener la decisión final en el ámbito político.

== Base Legal ==
El marco jurídico internacional y nacional examinado procede de instrumentos del Consejo de Europa y del derecho constitucional español:

* '''Derecho Internacional y Consejo de Europa''': Estatuto del Consejo de Europa; Recomendación CM/Rec(2010)12 del Comité de Ministros (párr. 27); Dictamen n.º 24 del Consejo Consultivo de Jueces Europeos (CCJE); y jurisprudencia del TJUE (*A.K. y otros*, C-585/18) y del TEDH (*Reczkowicz c. Polonia*, *Grzęda c. Polonia*, *Denisov c. Ucrania*).
* '''Legislación Española''': Artículo 122 de la Constitución Española de 1978; Ley Orgánica 6/1985 del Poder Judicial (LOPJ Arts. 560, 561, 567, 574, 578); Ley Orgánica 1/1980 del CGPJ; y la Disposición Adicional de la Ley Orgánica 3/2024, de 2 de agosto.

== Antecedentes ==
Conforme al artículo 122 de la Constitución de 1978, el CGPJ es el órgano de gobierno del poder judicial, compuesto por 21 miembros (el Presidente del Tribunal Supremo y 20 vocales: 12 judiciales y 8 juristas). Desde la reforma de la LOPJ de 1985, el Parlamento elegía a los 12 vocales judiciales por mayoría de 3/5. Este modelo originó reiterados bloqueos institucionales, destacando el periodo sin renovación entre 2018 y 2024. Tras el acuerdo político de junio de 2024 y la Ley Orgánica 3/2024, el CGPJ aprobó su informe de alternativas en febrero de 2025, solicitando la Presidenta Isabel Perelló Doménech el dictamen oficial a la Comisión de Venecia.

== Objetivos ==
1. Garantizar que el sistema de elección de los vocales judiciales del CGPJ se adecue a los estándares europeos de *peer election* sin interferencias políticas. 2. Desbloquear de forma permanente el sistema de nombramientos eliminando la lógica de cuotas partidistas. 3. Prevenir la politización interna derivada del monopolio de las asociaciones judiciales (*APM, AJFV, JJpD, FJI*). 4. Asegurar una representación plural por categorías judiciales, equilibrio de género y cohesión territorial.

== Alcance ==
El dictamen realiza un análisis comparativo de las dos propuestas de reforma: 1. ''Opción 1 (Elección Directa Corporativa)'':

* '''Evaluación''': '''CUMPLE EN PRINCIPIO''' con los estándares europeos.
* '''Garantías Recomendadas''': Reducir/abolir el requisito de 25 avales; sustituir suplentes por elecciones parciales; limitar el número máximo de votos por elector para evitar bloques mayoritarios; y regular la equidad de las campañas y la transparencia presupuestaria.

2. ''Opción 2 (Preselección Judicial + Elección Parlamentaria)'':

* '''Evaluación''': '''INCUMPLE LOS ESTÁNDARES EUROPEOS'''. La decisión final parlamentaria desvirtúa el estándar de elección por pares, duplica las presiones políticas, otorga discrecionalidad no guiada al Parlamento y carece de un mecanismo antibloqueo automático.

== Disposiciones y Principios Clave ==

* '''Principio de Elección entre Iguales (CM/Rec(2010)12)''': Al menos la mitad de los miembros de los consejos judiciales deben ser jueces elegidos directamente por sus pares.
* '''Mecanismo Antibloqueo Automático''': En caso de mantenerse la intervención parlamentaria, los candidatos de la lista corta judicial deberían quedar nombrados automáticamente si las Cortes no votan en un plazo fijado.

== Implementación ==
Dirigido a las Cortes Generales de España, al Gobierno de España, al Consejo General del Poder Judicial (*CGPJ*) y al Tribunal Supremo.

== Problemas de Política Pública ==

* Bloqueos institucionales recurrentes que debilitan la independencia y credibilidad de la justicia.
* Riesgo de sustituir la politización parlamentaria externa por una politización corporativa interna dominada por asociaciones partidistas.

== Reforma ==

* Adopción de la Opción 1 incorporando las cuatro garantías recomendadas por la Comisión de Venecia.
* Constitucionalización del método de elección corporativa en caso de una futura reforma de la Constitución.

== Relación con otras Entidades ==

* '''Emisor''': Comisión de Venecia del Consejo de Europa.
* '''Solicitado por''': D.ª Isabel Perelló Doménech (Presidenta del CGPJ y del Tribunal Supremo).
* '''Analiza''': Ley Orgánica 3/2024, LOPJ 6/1985, Artículo 122 de la Constitución Española y Recomendación CM/Rec(2010)12.

== 4. POLICY ANALYSIS ==

* '''Background''': [FACT] On 14 March 2020, the Spanish Council of Ministers approved Royal Decree 463/2020 declaring a national state of alarm due to COVID-19. Court proceedings were suspended, generating severe operational backlogs across all judicial jurisdictions. To address this crisis, the Government issued emergency Royal Decree-Law 16/2020 (28 April 2020). During its subsequent parliamentary processing as a bill, Congress and Senate enacted **Ley 3/2020, de 18 de septiembre**, which repealed RDL 16/2020 and established refined procedural, technological, organizational, bankruptcy, and corporate measures. Santabaya González and Riofrío Casajoana (Pérez-Llorca) published a comprehensive monograph evaluating Ley 3/2020.
* '''Policy Problem''': [FACT]
** '''Severe Judicial Backlog & Surge in Litigation''': The pandemic forced court suspensions while triggering mass litigation regarding mortgages, residential/commercial leases, labor disputes, and insolvencies.
** '''Threat of Mass Involuntary Liquidation of Viable Firms''': Applying general insolvency rules (mandatory bankruptcy filing within 2 months of insolvency, TRLC Arts. 2 & 5) and corporate dissolution triggers (net equity below 50% of capital due to losses, LSC Art. 363.1.e) threatened to liquidate viable businesses experiencing temporary liquidity shocks.
** '''Health Risks in Physical Court Hearings''': Traditional in-person hearings presented severe infection risks for judicial staff, lawyers, and litigants.
** '''Inflexible Pre-Pandemic Bankruptcy Agreements''': Debtors in approved bankruptcy agreements (*convenio de acreedores*) or refinancing agreements (*acuerdos de refinanciación*) could not meet payment schedules, risking immediate breach claims (*declaración de incumplimiento*) and forced liquidation.
* '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] The pre-pandemic statutory framework (TRLC, LSC, LEC, CC) contained no force majeure mechanisms to freeze mandatory bankruptcy filings, suspend loss-based dissolution, or adjust existing refinancing agreements without triggering immediate liquidation.
* '''Policy Objectives''': [FACT] Ensure court health safety; streamline judicial processing of COVID-19 disputes; incentivize fresh corporate financing; preserve business continuity; suspend forced corporate dissolutions; and prevent insolvency court collapse.
* '''Policy Implementation & Statutory Mechanics''': [FACT]
** '''1. Chapter I: Procedural Measures & Preferential Processing (Arts. 1–2)''':
*** Preferential court processing until 31 December 2020 for: (i) claims against lenders for mortgage moratoria on primary residences and business properties; (ii) lease claims regarding statutory moratoria or mandatory contract extensions; and (iii) natural person bankruptcy proceedings.
** '''2. Chapter III: Organizational & Technological Measures (Arts. 14–19 & Add. Prov. 5, Fin. Prov. 4)''':
*** ''Remote Judicial Acts'': Until 20 June 2021, trials, hearings, declarations, and court deliberations are held preferentially via electronic/telematic means if technical facilities exist.
*** ''Courtroom Access & Robe Dispensation'': Restricted courtroom access; public broadcasting of hearings permitted; dispensation from wearing robes (*togas*) until 20 June 2021.
*** ''Public Service & Cita Previa'': Court attention delivered via videoconference, phone, or email; mandatory advance appointment (*cita previa*) for the public (excluding lawyers, procurators, and social graduates).
*** ''COVID-19 Courts & 100 New Units'': Transformation or advance activation of pending judicial bodies into exclusive COVID-19 courts; creation of at least 100 new judicial units over 3 years (1/3 in year 1).
*** ''Tablón Edictal Judicial Único'': Additional Final Provision 4 creates a single electronic judicial notice board managed by AEBOE, replacing all traditional bulletin/newspaper edict publications from 1 June 2021.
*** ''Shift Schedules'': Morning and afternoon work shifts for court personnel.
** '''3. Contract Law Reform Mandate (Add. Prov. 7)''':
*** Enjoins the Government to submit a study within 3 months on incorporating the *cláusula rebus sic stantibus* into contract law (Civil Code) to modulate contractual risks during extraordinary crises.
** '''4. Chapter II: Bankruptcy & Corporate Measures (Arts. 3–13 & Addenda)''':
*** ''Modification of Approved Agreements (Art. 3)'': Debtors can present proposals to modify existing approved bankruptcy agreements (*convenio de acreedores*) until 14 March 2021 (extended by RDL 34/2020), accompanied by a viability plan, payment plan, and unpaid credit list.
*** ''Suspension of Creditor Breach Claims (Art. 3.10)'': Creditor claims for agreement breach received up to 31 October 2020 (and extended dates under RDL 34/2020) are stayed for 3 months, giving debtors priority to file modification proposals.
*** ''Suspension of Duty to Request Liquidation (Art. 4)'': Suspends until 14 March 2021 the debtor's duty to request liquidation when unable to meet agreement payments, provided a modification proposal is submitted.
*** ''Refinancing Agreements (Art. 5)'': Debtors can modify existing refinancing agreements or reach new ones until 14 March 2021, even if 1 year has not elapsed since prior court approval (overriding TRLC Art. 617). Creditor breach claims stayed to allow 3-month negotiation periods.
*** ''Insolvency Filing Moratorium (Art. 6)'': Suspends the insolvent debtor's duty to file for bankruptcy (*concurso voluntario*) until 31 December 2020 (extended to 14 March 2021 by RDL 34/2020). Involuntary bankruptcy applications (*concurso necesario*) filed by creditors from 14 March 2020 to 31 December 2020 are stayed, giving priority to voluntary filings. Debtors communicating negotiations before 31 December 2020 receive a 6-month extension from communication date to file.
*** ''Fresh Financing & Related Party Claims (Arts. 4.3 & 7)'': In agreements approved/modified within 2 years from 14 March 2020, fresh cash loans (including from specially related persons) are classified as claims against the estate (*créditos contra la masa*) upon liquidation. In bankruptcies declared up to 14 March 2022, financing and subrogated claims provided by specially related persons are upgraded from subordinated to ordinary claims (*créditos ordinarios*).
*** ''Streamlining Insolvency Proceedings (Arts. 8–12)'': Preferential processing for labor incidents, asset/unit production sales, refinancing approvals, and asset reintegration until 14 March 2021. Optional oral hearings for inventory/creditor list challenges until 14 March 2022. Preferential use of electronic auctions for asset sales.
*** ''Suspension of Loss-Based Dissolution Trigger (Art. 13)'': Losses incurred in fiscal year 2020 are excluded when calculating whether net equity is reduced below 50% of share capital under LSC Art. 363.1.e. If 2021 losses still result in net equity below 50%, administrators must convene a general meeting within 2 months of fiscal year-end.
* '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] Evaluates Ley 3/2020 statute; RDL 16/2020; RDL 34/2020; TRLC (RDL 1/2020); LSC (RDL 1/2010); and Pérez-Llorca legal analysis by Santabaya González & Riofrío Casajoana.
* '''Evaluation & Reform''': [FACT] Concludes that Ley 3/2020 provides necessary, well-directed emergency relief, but cautions that moratoria and procedural tweaks will prove insufficient without substantial budgetary investment in court personnel, new judicial units, and accelerated electronic infrastructure. Recommends: (1) accelerating the operational deployment of the 100 new judicial units; (2) advancing the electronic launch of the *Tablón Edictal Judicial Único*; and (3) enacting a statutory reform in the Civil Code codifying the *rebus sic stantibus* doctrine.

== Summary ==
'''Law 3/2020 of 18 September on procedural and organisational measures to tackle COVID-19 in the field of the Administration of Justice''' (*Ley 3/2020, de 18 de septiembre, de medidas procesales y organizativas para hacer frente a la COVID-19 en el ámbito de la Administración de Justicia*) (Stable ID: '''JPW-REG-000375''') is an emergency national statute enacted by the Cortes Generales and published in the Official State Gazette (BOE) on 19 September 2020 (entering into force on 20 September 2020). Originating from the parliamentary processing of Royal Decree-Law 16/2020 (RDL 16/2020), which it repealed and replaced, Ley 3/2020 established an extraordinary statutory framework covering procedural, organizational, technological, bankruptcy, and corporate measures to adapt the Spanish judicial system to the COVID-19 pandemic, prevent court backlog, and protect viable companies from automatic insolvency or loss-based dissolution.

== Legal Basis ==
The emergency precedents and statutory codes modified include:
* '''Emergency Precedents & Royal Decree-Laws''': Royal Decree 463/2020 declaring the national state of alarm; Royal Decree-Law 8/2020; Royal Decree-Law 11/2020; Royal Decree-Law 15/2020; Royal Decree-Law 16/2020 (repealed and replaced by Ley 3/2020); Royal Decree-Law 34/2020 (extending moratorium periods).
* '''General Codes & Corporate Statutes''': Recast Text of the Insolvency Law (*TRLC*, Royal Legislative Decree 1/2020); Recast Text of the Capital Companies Act (*LSC*, Royal Legislative Decree 1/2010, Arts. 363.1.e, 365); Civil Procedure Rules (*LEC*); Civil Code (*CC*).

== Background ==
Following the declaration of the state of alarm on 14 March 2020 (Royal Decree 463/2020), judicial deadlines across Spain were suspended, generating severe backlogs. To prevent a collapse of insolvency courts and protect solvent companies facing temporary COVID-19 liquidity shocks from automatic liquidation, the Spanish Parliament enacted Ley 3/2020, substituting the temporary regime of RDL 16/2020 with refined statutory measures. Juan Ignacio Santabaya González and María José Riofrío Casajoana (Pérez-Llorca) authored a comprehensive monograph evaluating the statutory mechanics and economic impact of Ley 3/2020.

== Objectives ==
1. Streamline judicial processing and resolve court backlogs triggered by pandemic suspensions.
2. Ensure health safety during judicial proceedings through telematic trials and digital court communication.
3. Suspend mandatory insolvency filings (*moratoria concursal*) to prevent premature liquidation of viable firms.
4. Freeze corporate dissolution triggers linked to pandemic losses under Article 363.1.e of the Capital Companies Act (LSC).
5. Incentivize fresh corporate financing (*fresh cash*) by upgrading debt priority upon restructuring or liquidation.
6. Centralize and digitize judicial edict publishing via the Single Judicial Edict Board (*Tablón Edictal Judicial Único*).

== Scope ==
Ley 3/2020 is structured into three primary chapters, along with additional and final provisions:
1. ''Procedural Measures (Chapter I)'': Preferential processing until 31 December 2020 for mortgage moratoria, lease disputes, and individual bankruptcies.
2. ''Organizational & Technological Measures (Chapter III)'': Remote telematic trials until 20 June 2021, robe dispensation, advance appointment systems (*cita previa*), creation of 100 new judicial units, and the Single Judicial Edict Board.
3. ''Insolvency & Corporate Measures (Chapter II)'': Moratorium on bankruptcy filings (*concurso voluntario/necesario*), suspension of loss-based dissolution (LSC Art. 363.1.e), renegotiation of bankruptcy agreements (*convenio*) and refinancing plans, and fresh financing priority upgrades.

== Key Provisions & Principles ==
* '''Insolvency Filing Moratorium (Art. 6)''': Suspended insolvent debtors' statutory duty to file for bankruptcy (*concurso voluntario*) until 31 December 2020 (extended to 14 March 2021 by RDL 34/2020), while staying all creditor-filed involuntary bankruptcy petitions (*concurso necesario*).
* '''Suspension of Loss-Based Dissolution Trigger (Art. 13)''': Fiscal year 2020 losses were excluded when determining whether corporate net equity dropped below 50% of share capital for the mandatory cause of dissolution under LSC Art. 363.1.e.
* '''Single Judicial Edict Board (Add. Fin. Prov. 4)''': Established a centralized electronic judicial notice board managed by AEBOE starting 1 June 2021, replacing traditional bulletin board edicts.

== Implementation ==
Applied by Commercial Courts (*Juzgados de lo Mercantil*), Courts of First Instance (*Juzgados de Primera Instancia*), Ministry of Justice, Public Prosecutor's Office (*Fiscalía*), AEBOE, and corporate boards of directors.

== Policy Problems ==
* Risk of insolvency moratoria delaying necessary corporate restructurings, leading to "zombie company" accumulation.
* Implementation delays regarding the operational launch of the Single Judicial Edict Board and the deployment of 100 new judicial units.
* Budgetary constraints in regional justice administrations slowing down telematic court infrastructure rollouts.

== Reform ==
* Enjoining the Government (Additional Provision 7) to submit a statutory study within 3 months regarding the codification of the *rebus sic stantibus* contract doctrine in the Civil Code.
* Mandatory budgetary deployment for new judicial units and electronic court management systems.

== Relationship with Other Entities ==
* '''Issued by''': Cortes Generales / Jefatura del Estado.
* '''Replaces''': Royal Decree-Law 16/2020 (RDL 16/2020).
* '''Amends/Overrides''': Recast Text of the Insolvency Law (TRLC) and Capital Companies Act (LSC Art. 363.1.e).
* '''Amended by''': Royal Decree-Law 34/2020 (RDL 34/2020).
* '''Analyzed by''': Juan Ignacio Santabaya González & María José Riofrío Casajoana (Pérez-Llorca).

== 4. ANÁLISIS DE POLÍTICA PÚBLICA ==

* '''Antecedentes''': El 14 de marzo de 2020, el Consejo de Ministros aprobó el Real Decreto 463/2020 declarando el estado de alarma por la COVID-19. La paralización de los plazos procesales generó un atasco judicial en todas las jurisdicciones. Para responder a la crisis, el Gobierno dictó el Real Decreto-ley 16/2020. Tras su tramitación parlamentaria como proyecto de ley, las Cortes aprobaron la **Ley 3/2020, de 18 de septiembre**, derogando el RDL 16/2020 e introduciendo medidas refinadas procesales, organizativas, tecnológicas, concursales y societarias. Santabaya González y Riofrío Casajoana (Pérez-Llorca) publicaron una monografía evaluando la norma.
* '''Problema de Política Pública''':
** '''Grave Colapso Judicial y Aumento de Litigiosidad''': La paralización procesal acumuló asuntos pendientes y desencadenó pleitos sobre hipotecas, arrendamientos, despidos y solicitudes de concurso de acreedores.
** '''Riesgo de Liquidación Masiva de Empresas Viables''': La aplicación estricta de las normas de insolvencia (obligación de solicitar concurso en 2 meses) y disolución (pérdidas que dejen el patrimonio neto por debajo del 50% del capital) amenazaba con liquidar empresas viables con iliquidez temporal.
** '''Riesgo Sanitario en Vistas Presenciales''': Los juicios presenciales tradicionales suponían un grave riesgo de contagio para personal judicial, abogados y litigantes.
** '''Inflexibilidad de los Convenios Concursales Previos''': Los deudores con convenios o acuerdos de refinanciación aprobados no podían cumplir los calendarios de pago, arriesgando la declaración de incumplimiento y la liquidación forzosa.
* '''Vacío Legal/de Política Pública''': El marco legal pre-pandémico (TRLC, LSC, LEC, CC) carecía de mecanismos de fuerza mayor para congelar la solicitud de concurso obligatorio, suspender la causa de disolución por pérdidas o modificar los acuerdos de refinanciación sin causar la resolución inmediata.
* '''Objetivos de Política Pública''': Garantizar la seguridad sanitaria en los juzgados; agilizar la tramitación de pleitos COVID-19; incentivar la financiación fresca (*fresh cash*); preservar el tejido empresarial; suspender disoluciones forzosas; y evitar el colapso de los juzgados de lo mercantil.
* '''Implementación de Política Pública y Mecánica Normativa''':
** '''1. Capítulo I: Medidas Procesales y Tramitación Preferente (Arts. 1–2)''':
*** Tramitación preferente hasta el 31 de diciembre de 2020 para: (i) moratoriums hipotecarios en vivienda habitual y inmuebles de actividad económica; (ii) moratorias de arrendamiento; y (iii) concursos de personas naturales.
** '''2. Capítulo III: Medidas Organizativas y Tecnológicas (Arts. 14–19 y Disp. Adic. 5ª, Disp. Final 4ª)''':
*** ''Actos Judiciales Telemáticos'': Hasta el 20 de junio de 2021, juicios, vistas y declaraciones se celebraron preferentemente por vía telemática si había medios técnicos.
*** ''Acceso a Salas y Dispensa de Togas'': Limitación de aforo en salas; emisión pública de vistas; dispensa del uso de togas hasta el 20 de junio de 2021.
*** ''Atención al Público y Cita Previa'': Atención por videoconferencia, teléfono o correo; cita previa obligatoria para el público (excepto abogados, procuradores y graduados sociales).
*** ''Juzgados COVID-19 y 100 Nuevas Unidades'': Conversión o puesta en marcha anticipada de órganos judiciales como juzgados exclusivos COVID-19; creación de al menos 100 unidades judiciales en 3 años.
*** ''Tablón Edictal Judicial Único'': La Disposición Final 4ª creó un tablón edictal electrónico único gestionado por el BOE desde el 1 de junio de 2021, sustituyendo los edictos en tablones de anuncios y periódicos.
*** ''Jornadas de Trabajo en Turnos'': Establecimiento de turnos de mañana y tarde para el personal judicial.
** '''3. Mandato de Reforma del Derecho de Contratos (Disp. Adic. 7ª)''':
*** Encargó al Gobierno presentar un estudio en 3 meses para incorporar la cláusula *rebus sic stantibus* en el Código Civil para modular el riesgo contractual en crisis extraordinarias.
** '''4. Capítulo II: Medidas Concursales y Societarias (Arts. 3–13 y Adiciones)''':
*** ''Modificación de Convenios Aprobados (Art. 3)'': Los deudores pudieron presentar propuestas de modificación de convenios concursales hasta el 14 de marzo de 2021, con plan de viabilidad y calendario de pagos.
*** ''Suspensión de Solicitudes de Incumplimiento (Art. 3.10)'': Las solicitudes de incumplimiento presentadas por acreedores se paralizaron 3 meses para dar prioridad a la propuesta de modificación del deudor.
*** ''Suspensión del Deber de Solicitar Liquidación (Art. 4)'': Se suspendió hasta el 14 de marzo de 2021 el deber del deudor de solicitar la liquidación cuando no pudiera cumplir los pagos, si presentaba una modificación.
*** ''Acuerdos de Refinanciación (Art. 5)'': Se autorizó modificar acuerdos de refinanciación aprobados o firmar nuevos hasta el 14 de marzo de 2021 aunque no hubiera transcurrido 1 año desde el anterior (modificando el Art. 617 TRLC).
*** ''Moratoria Concursal (Art. 6)'': Suspensión del deber de solicitar el concurso voluntario hasta el 31 de diciembre de 2020 (prorrogado al 14 de marzo de 2021 por el RDL 34/2020). Las solicitudes de concurso necesario de acreedores quedaron congeladas, dando prioridad a las voluntarias.
*** ''Financiación Fresca y Personas Vinculadas (Arts. 4.3 y 7)'': En convenios modificados dentro de los 2 años desde el 14 de marzo de 2020, los préstamos de dinero fresco se clasificaron como créditos contra la masa. En concursos declarados hasta el 14 de marzo de 2022, la financiación de personas especialmente relacionadas se elevó de crédito subordinado a crédito ordinario.
*** ''Agilización Procesal Concursal (Arts. 8–12)'': Tramitación preferente para incidentes laborales, venta de unidades productivas, homologación de refinanciaciones y reintegración de masa hasta el 14 de marzo de 2021. Vistas orales optativas para impugnaciones de inventario e informe hasta el 14 de marzo de 2022.
*** ''Suspensión de la Causa de Disolución por Pérdidas (Art. 13)'': Las pérdidas del ejercicio 2020 no se computaron para determinar si el patrimonio neto quedó reducido a menos de la mitad del capital social a efectos de la disolución (Art. 363.1.e LSC).
* '''Evidencia e Impacto''': Evalúa la Ley 3/2020; el RDL 16/2020; el RDL 34/2020; el TRLC (RDL 1/2020); la LSC (RDL 1/2010); y el análisis doctrinario de Santabaya González y Riofrío Casajoana.
* '''Evaluación y Propuestas de Reforma''': Concluye que la Ley 3/2020 proporciona un alivio oportuno, pero advierte que las moratorias procesales serán insuficientes sin inversión presupuestaria en personal, nuevas plazas judiciales y digitalización. Recomienda: (1) acelerar el despliegue de las 100 nuevas unidades judiciales; (2) poner en marcha el *Tablón Edictal Judicial Único*; y (3) tramitar la reforma del Código Civil para codificar la regla *rebus sic stantibus*.
