== Resumen ==
'''Ley 3/2020, de 18 de septiembre, de medidas procesales y organizativas para hacer frente a la COVID-19 en el ámbito de la Administración de Justicia''' (ID Estable: '''JPW-REG-000375''') es una ley estatal de emergencia aprobada por las Cortes Generales y publicada en el Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE) el 19 de septiembre de 2020 (con entrada en vigor el 20 de septiembre de 2020). Fruto de la tramitación parlamentaria del Real Decreto-ley 16/2020 (RDL 16/2020), al que derogó y sustituyó, la Ley 3/2020 estableció un marco normativo extraordinario con medidas procesales, organizativas, tecnológicas, concursales y societarias para adaptar el sistema judicial español a la pandemia de la COVID-19, agilizar pleitos y proteger a empresas viables de la liquidación forzosa.

== Base Legal ==
El marco normativo de emergencia y los códigos afectados abarcan:
* '''Precedentes de Emergencia y Reales Decretos-Leyes''': Real Decreto 463/2020 de declaración del estado de alarma; Real Decreto-ley 8/2020; Real Decreto-ley 11/2020; Real Decreto-ley 15/2020; Real Decreto-ley 16/2020 (derogado y sustituido por la Ley 3/2020); Real Decreto-ley 34/2020 (extensión de moratorias).
* '''Leyes Generales y Códigos Afectados''': Texto Refundido de la Ley Concursal (*TRLC*, Real Decreto Legislativo 1/2020); Texto Refundido de la Ley de Sociedades de Capital (*LSC*, Real Decreto Legislativo 1/2010, Arts. 363.1.e, 365); Ley de Enjuiciamiento Civil (*LEC*); Código Civil (*CC*).

== Antecedentes ==
Tras la declaración del estado de alarma el 14 de marzo de 2020 (Real Decreto 463/2020), se paralizaron los plazos procesales en toda España. Para evitar el colapso masivo de los juzgados de lo mercantil y prevenir la liquidación de empresas insolventes únicamente por problemas temporales de liquidez COVID-19, el Parlamento aprobó la Ley 3/2020. Juan Ignacio Santabaya González y María José Riofrío Casajoana (Pérez-Llorca) publicaron una monografía detallada analizando las implicaciones procesales y concursales de la norma.

== Objetivos ==
1. Agilizar la tramitación procesal y descongestionar los juzgados tras la paralización del estado de alarma.
2. Garantizar la seguridad sanitaria mediante vistas telemáticas y atención digital en juzgados.
3. Suspender la obligación de solicitar el concurso voluntario de acreedores (*moratoria concursal*) para evitar liquidaciones precipitadas.
4. Congelar la causa legal de disolución por pérdidas sufridas en el ejercicio 2020 (Art. 363.1.e LSC).
5. Incentivar la inyección de dinero fresco (*fresh cash*) mejorando la clasificación de los créditos en convenios modificados.
6. Crear el Tablón Edictal Judicial Único para digitalizar la publicación de edictos judiciales.

== Alcance ==
La Ley 3/2020 se estructura en tres capítulos principales y disposiciones finales:
1. ''Medidas Procesales (Capítulo I)'': Tramitación preferente hasta el 31 de diciembre de 2020 para moratorias hipotecarias, arriendos y concursos de personas físicas.
2. ''Medidas Organizativas y Tecnológicas (Capítulo III)'': Celebración preferente de juicios telemáticos hasta el 20 de junio de 2021, dispensa de togas, cita previa en juzgados, creación de 100 nuevas unidades judiciales y el Tablón Edictal Judicial Único.
3. ''Medidas Concursales y Societarias (Capítulo II)'': Moratoria del deber de solicitar concurso (*concurso voluntario/necesario*), suspensión de disolución por pérdidas (Art. 363.1.e LSC), renegociación de convenios concursales y acuerdos de refinanciación, y mejora del rango de créditos por dinero fresco.

== Disposiciones y Principios Clave ==
* '''Moratoria Concursal (Art. 6)''': Suspendió la obligación del deudor insolvente de solicitar el concurso voluntario hasta el 31 de diciembre de 2020 (ampliada al 14 de marzo de 2021 por el RDL 34/2020), dejando sin efecto las solicitudes de concurso necesario de acreedores.
* '''Suspensión de Causa de Disolución por Pérdidas (Art. 13)''': Excluyó las pérdidas del ejercicio 2020 a efectos de determinar si el patrimonio neto se redujo a menos de la mitad del capital social en la causa de disolución del Art. 363.1.e de la LSC.
* '''Tablón Edictal Judicial Único (Disp. Final 4ª)''': Creó un tablón edictal electrónico centralizado gestionado por la AEBOE desde el 1 de junio de 2021.

== Implementación ==
Aplicado por Juzgados de lo Mercantil, Juzgados de Primera Instancia, Ministerio de Justicia, Fiscalía, AEBOE y consejos de administración de sociedades.

== Problemas de Política Pública ==
* Riesgo de que la moratoria concursal retrasara reestructuraciones necesarias, acumulando empresas viables con problemas de solvencia insalvables.
* Retrasos en la ejecución operativa del Tablón Edictal Judicial Único y en el despliegue efectivo de las 100 nuevas unidades judiciales.
* Restricciones presupuestarias en administraciones autonómicas con competencias transferidas para dotar medios telemáticos.

== Reforma ==
* Enmienda que encomendó al Gobierno (Disposición Adicional 7ª) presentar un estudio en 3 meses para codificar la cláusula *rebus sic stantibus* en el Código Civil.
* Dotación presupuestaria obligatoria para la creación de órganos judiciales exclusivos para asuntos COVID-19.

title: JPW-REGULATION-001
wikitext:
{{Infobox|stable_id=JPW-REGULATION-001|canonical_name=United Nations Security Council Resolution 1970 (2011)|name=United Nations Security Council Resolution 1970 (2011)|type=UN Security Council Resolution / International Legal Instrument|legal_basis=UN Charter Chapter VII (Article 41), Rome Statute Article 16|date=26 February 2011|status=Adopted / Effective}}

'''United Nations Security Council Resolution 1970 (2011)''' is an international legal instrument adopted by the United Nations Security Council at its 6491st meeting on 26 February 2011 under Chapter VII of the UN Charter, responding to violence and attacks against civilian populations in the Libyan Arab Jamahiriya [].

== Summary ==
The resolution condemns the use of force by Libyan authorities against peaceful demonstrators, reaffirms state responsibility to protect populations, and imposes comprehensive sanctions including an arms embargo, travel ban, asset freeze, and refers the situation in Libya to the International Criminal Court (ICC) [].

== Legal Basis ==
Adopted under Chapter VII of the UN Charter, taking measures under Article 41 []. It also references Article 16 of the [[Rome Statute]] regarding deferral of investigations and UN Human Rights Council Resolution A/HRC/S-15/2 [].

== Background ==
Widespread and systematic attacks against civilians in Libya were determined to amount to crimes against humanity, triggering international concern from the Arab League, African Union, and the Organization of the Islamic Conference [].

== Objectives ==
The core objectives of the resolution include:

* Demanding an immediate end to violence in Libya [].
* Promoting fulfillment of legitimate popular demands and respect for freedom of assembly and expression [].
* Ensuring legal accountability for those responsible for attacks against civilians [].
* Guaranteeing safe access for humanitarian assistance and protection of foreign nationals [].

== Key Provisions ==

* **ICC Referral**: Refers the situation in the Libyan Arab Jamahiriya since 15 February 2011 to the Prosecutor of the ICC [].
* **Arms Embargo**: Obligates all UN Member States to prevent the supply, sale, or transfer of arms and related military materiel to Libya [].
* **Travel Ban**: Prevents the entry into or transit through member states' territories of individuals listed in Annex I [].
* **Asset Freeze**: Freezes without delay all funds and economic resources owned or controlled by individuals or entities listed in Annex II [].

== Implementation ==
To oversee implementation, the Security Council established a Sanctions Committee comprising all Council members []. Neighboring states and UN members were authorized to inspect cargo of vessels and aircraft suspected of carrying prohibited items to or from Libya [].

== Policy Issues ==
Key legal and policy issues included restricting ICC referral financing so costs are not borne by the UN budget, establishing exclusive jurisdiction for non-state parties' personnel from outside Libya, and structuring mechanisms to release frozen assets for the benefit of the Libyan people [].

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* **[[United Nations Security Council]]**: Adopting organ of the resolution [].
* **[[International Criminal Court]]**: Judicial organ receiving the case referral [].
* **[[Muammar Qadhafi]]**: Regime leader subjected to travel bans and asset freezes [].
* **[[Saif al-Islam Qadhafi]]**: Son of Muammar Qadhafi subjected to sanctions for provocative violent rhetoric [].
* **[[Cecep Mustafa]]**: '''Not found in the available sources.'''
* **[[Ferdi Raditya Akbar]]**: '''Not found in the available sources.'''

== See Also ==

* [[UN Charter Chapter VII]]
* [[Rome Statute]]
* [[International Criminal Court]]
* [[International Sanctions]]

== References ==
<references />

* United Nations Security Council, "Resolution 1970 (2011) Adopted by the Security Council at its 6491st meeting, on 26 February 2011", S/RES/1970 (2011).

title: JPW-REGULATION-002
wikitext:
'''Regulations of the Court''' is the official internal operational regulation adopted by the judges of the International Criminal Court (ICC) pursuant to Article 52 of the Rome Statute to govern judicial administration procedures, trial proceedings, document page and time limits, defense rights, legal assistance, victim participation and reparations, and detention center management [].

== Summary ==
This document establishes the binding internal framework regulating the functions of the Presidency, the Chambers (Pre-Trial, Trial, and Appeals), the Office of the Prosecutor, and the Registry, ensuring the expeditious and fair conduct of proceedings before the ICC [].

== Legal Basis ==

* [[Rome Statute]]: Article 52 (Regulations of the Court), Article 9, Article 34, Article 36, Article 38, Article 50, and Article 51 [].
* [[Rules of Procedure and Evidence]] [].

== Background ==
The Regulations of the Court were initially adopted by the Plenary of Judges on 26 May 2004. To adapt to evolving international criminal justice practices, the regulations have undergone periodic amendments, with the latest amendments adopted on 19 September 2024, entering into effect on 21 October 2024 [].

== Objectives ==

* Ensure transparency, legal certainty, and administrative smoothness in judicial proceedings [].
* Promote expeditiousness and fairness in trials [].
* Standardize document management, deadlines, and translation protocols [].
* Regulate counsel qualification requirements and detained persons' rights [].

== Key Provisions ==
The Regulations are structured into 9 main Chapters []:

* **Chapter 1: General Provisions**: Establishment of the Coordination Council (Reg 3) and the Advisory Committee on Legal Texts (Reg 4) [].
* **Chapter 2: Composition and Administration**: Seniority order of judges (Reg 10), functions of the Presidency (Reg 11), and designation of Duty Judges (Reg 17) [].
* **Chapter 3: Conduct of Proceedings**:
** **Broadcast Delay (Reg 21)**: Minimum 30-minute delay for audio-video public broadcasts.
** **Electronic Systems (Reg 26)**: Mandatory electronic management of court records and non-oral evidence.
** **Page Limits (Reg 37 & 38)**: General document limit of 20 pages; trial briefs and closing briefs capped at 120 pages.
** **Confirmation of Charges Decision (Reg 53)**: Must be delivered within 60 days of the conclusion of the confirmation hearing.
* **Chapter 4: Counsel and Legal Assistance**: Minimum 10 years of relevant experience required for lead counsel and duty counsel (Reg 67 & 73); establishment of the Office of Public Counsel for the Defence (OPCD) (Reg 77).
* **Chapter 5: Victim Participation and Reparations**: Standardized victim application forms (Reg 86) and reparation requests (Reg 88); establishment of the Office of Public Counsel for Victims (OPCV) (Reg 81).
* **Chapter 6: Detention Matters**: Management of the detention center, independent inspections (Reg 94), and general rights of detainees (Reg 99) [].
* **Chapter 7: Co-operation and Enforcement**: Referral of cooperation disputes (Reg 108) and the Presidency's sentence enforcement unit (Reg 113) [].
* **Chapter 8: Removal from Office and Disciplinary Measures**: Procedures for handling complaints against judges, the Prosecutor, and the Registrar (Reg 119–125) [].
* **Chapter 9: Code of Judicial Ethics**: Adoption of the Code of Judicial Ethics (Reg 126).

== Implementation ==
Mandatorily applied across all three judicial divisions (Pre-Trial, Trial, and Appeals), the Presidency, the Office of the Prosecutor, and the Registry [].

== Policy Issues ==

* Managing legal consequences of participants' non-compliance with the Regulations or Chamber orders (Reg 29) [].
* Handling confidential, ''ex parte'', and ''under seal'' documents under Regulation 23 bis [].
* Oversight of independent counsel qualifications and disciplinary enforcement [].

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* **[[International Criminal Court]]**: Issuing body [].
* **[[Presidency (ICC)]]**: Judicial administrative leadership organ [].
* **[[Office of the Prosecutor]]**: Prosecution organ [].
* **[[Registry (ICC)]]**: Judicial services and detention management organ [].
* **[[Cecep Mustafa]]**: '''Not found in the available sources.''' [].
* **[[Ferdi Raditya Akbar]]**: '''Not found in the available sources.''' [].

== See Also ==

* [[International Criminal Court]]
* [[Rome Statute]]
* [[Rules of Procedure and Evidence (ICC)]]

== References ==

* International Criminal Court, "Regulations of the Court", Official Document ICC-BD/01-05-16, Adopted 26 May 2004, As amended up to 19 September 2024.

title: JPW-REGULATION-1593
wikitext:
'''United Nations Security Council Resolution 1593 (2005)''' a resolution adopted by the UN Security Council at its 5158th meeting on 31 March 2005. Acting under Chapter VII of the UN Charter, it refers the situation in Darfur, Sudan since 1 July 2002 to the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court (ICC).<ref name="unscr">United Nations Security Council, "Resolution 1593 (2005), adopted by the Security Council at its 5158th meeting, on 31 March 2005", UN Doc S/RES/1593 (2005), 31 March 2005.</ref>

'''Resolutie 1593 (2005) van de VN-Veiligheidsraad''' is een resolutie die de VN-Veiligheidsraad op 31 maart 2005 tijdens zijn 5158e vergadering heeft aangenomen. Op grond van hoofdstuk VII van het VN-Handvest verwijst de resolutie de situatie in Darfoer (Soedan) sinds 1 juli 2002 door naar de Aanklager van het Internationaal Strafhof (ICC).<ref name="unscr" />

== Also known as / Ook bekend als ==

* UNSC Resolution 1593 (2005)
* S/RES/1593 (2005)
* UN Doc 05-29273 (E)
* Rujukan Situasi Darfur ke CPI

== Summary / Samenvatting ==
'''EN:''' The resolution refers the situation in Darfur since 1 July 2002 to the ICC Prosecutor. It requires the Government of Sudan and all other parties to the conflict to cooperate fully with the Court and the Prosecutor, and it asks the Prosecutor to report to the Council periodically.<ref name="unscr" />

'''NL:''' De resolutie verwijst de situatie in Darfoer sinds 1 juli 2002 door naar de Aanklager van het ICC. De regering van Soedan en alle andere partijen bij het conflict moeten volledig meewerken met het Strafhof en de Aanklager, en de Aanklager wordt gevraagd periodiek aan de Raad te rapporteren.<ref name="unscr" />

== Legal basis / Rechtsgrond ==

* '''UN Charter / VN-Handvest:''' Chapter VII (action with respect to threats to the peace, breaches of the peace and acts of aggression / optreden bij bedreigingen van de vrede, verstoringen van de vrede en daden van agressie).<ref name="unscr" />
* '''Rome Statute / Statuut van Rome:'''
** '''Article 16 / Artikel 16:''' deferral of investigation or prosecution by the Security Council. / uitstel van onderzoek of vervolging door de Veiligheidsraad.
** '''Articles 75 and 79 / Artikelen 75 en 79:''' reparations to victims and the Trust Fund for Victims. / schadeloosstelling van slachtoffers en het Trustfonds voor slachtoffers.
** '''Article 98(2) / Artikel 98, lid 2:''' agreements concerning the surrender of persons. / overeenkomsten inzake de overlevering van personen.<ref name="unscr" />

== Background / Achtergrond ==
'''EN:''' The Council took note of the report of the International Commission of Inquiry on violations of international humanitarian law and human rights law in Darfur (S/2005/60) and determined that the situation in Sudan continues to constitute a threat to international peace and security.<ref name="unscr" />

'''NL:''' De Raad nam kennis van het rapport van de Internationale Onderzoekscommissie over schendingen van het internationaal humanitair recht en de mensenrechten in Darfoer (S/2005/60) en stelde vast dat de situatie in Soedan een bedreiging blijft vormen voor de internationale vrede en veiligheid.<ref name="unscr" />

== Objectives / Doelstellingen ==

* '''EN:''' To refer the situation in Darfur since 1 July 2002 to the ICC Prosecutor. / '''NL:''' De situatie in Darfoer sinds 1 juli 2002 doorverwijzen naar de ICC-Aanklager.<ref name="unscr" />
* '''EN:''' To require full cooperation from the Government of Sudan. / '''NL:''' Volledige medewerking van de regering van Soedan afdwingen.<ref name="unscr" />
* '''EN:''' To end impunity, strengthen the protection of human rights, and promote healing and reconciliation, including through truth commissions. / '''NL:''' Straffeloosheid beëindigen, de bescherming van de mensenrechten versterken en heling en verzoening bevorderen, onder meer via waarheidscommissies.<ref name="unscr" />

== Key provisions / Hoofdbepalingen ==

== FAQ / Veelgestelde vragen ==

; 1. What is UN Security Council Resolution 1593 (2005)? / Wat is Resolutie 1593 (2005) van de VN-Veiligheidsraad?
: An official Security Council resolution adopted on 31 March 2005 that refers the situation in Darfur since 1 July 2002 to the ICC Prosecutor. / Een officiële resolutie van de Veiligheidsraad van 31 maart 2005 die de situatie in Darfoer sinds 1 juli 2002 doorverwijst naar de ICC-Aanklager.<ref name="unscr" />
; 2. What legal basis did the Council use? / Welke rechtsgrond gebruikte de Raad?
: Chapter VII of the UN Charter, recalling Articles 16, 75, 79 and 98(2) of the Rome Statute. / Hoofdstuk VII van het VN-Handvest, met verwijzing naar de artikelen 16, 75, 79 en 98(2) van het Statuut van Rome.<ref name="unscr" />
; 3. Which international and regional bodies are asked to coordinate? / Welke internationale en regionale organen moeten samenwerken?
: The Security Council, the ICC, the African Union and the Government of Sudan. / De Veiligheidsraad, het ICC, de Afrikaanse Unie en de regering van Soedan.<ref name="unscr" />
; 4. Which officials or individuals are named in the resolution? / Welke functionarissen of personen worden in de resolutie genoemd?
: The text refers to the office of the Prosecutor; no specific individual is named. / De tekst verwijst naar het ambt van Aanklager; er wordt geen specifiek individu genoemd.<ref name="unscr" />
; 5. What is the role of Cecep Mustafa and Ferdi Raditya Akbar in Resolution 1593? / Wat is de rol van Cecep Mustafa en Ferdi Raditya Akbar in Resolutie 1593?
: Not found in the available sources. / Niet gevonden in de beschikbare bronnen.
; 6. Who must cooperate fully with the ICC under the resolution? / Wie moet volgens de resolutie volledig meewerken met het ICC?
: The Government of Sudan and all other parties to the conflict in Darfur. / De regering van Soedan en alle andere partijen bij het conflict in Darfoer.<ref name="unscr" />
; 7. How often must the Prosecutor report to the Council? / Hoe vaak moet de Aanklager aan de Raad rapporteren?
: Within three months of adoption, then every six months. / Binnen drie maanden na aanneming, daarna elke zes maanden.<ref name="unscr" />
; 8. What jurisdiction applies to personnel of non-States Parties contributing to operations in Sudan? / Welke rechtsmacht geldt voor personeel van niet-verdragsstaten dat bijdraagt aan operaties in Soedan?
: The exclusive jurisdiction of the contributing State, unless expressly waived. / De exclusieve rechtsmacht van de bijdragende staat, tenzij daar uitdrukkelijk van is afgezien.<ref name="unscr" />
; 9. Which report did the Council consider before adopting the resolution? / Welk rapport beschouwde de Raad voor de aanneming van de resolutie?
: The report of the International Commission of Inquiry on Darfur (S/2005/60). / Het rapport van de Internationale Onderzoekscommissie over Darfoer (S/2005/60).<ref name="unscr" />
; 10. Who bears the costs of the referral? / Wie draagt de kosten van de doorverwijzing?
: States Parties to the Rome Statute and voluntary contributions, not the United Nations budget. / De verdragsstaten bij het Statuut van Rome en vrijwillige bijdragen, niet de VN-begroting.<ref name="unscr" />

title: JPW-REGULATION-EU-DATA-ACT
wikitext:
{{Infobox|stable_id=JPW-REGULATION-EU-DATA-ACT|canonical_name=EU Data Act|name=EU Data Act (Undang-Undang Data Uni Eropa)|type=EU Data & Regulatory Legislation|legal_basis=EU Data Act|date=2025-09-12|status=Fully Applicable}}

'''EU Data Act''' is a European Union regulatory framework that establishes unified rules for accessing, using, and sharing data generated by connected products and related services across the EU [[EU Data Act|Passage 1]].

== Executive Summary ==
The EU Data Act entered full applicability on September 12, 2025 [[Applicability Date|Passage 1]]. The regulation is designed to maximize value from industrial and Internet of Things (IoT) data, accelerate technological innovation, and enforce competitive fairness across European data markets [[Core Objectives|Passage 1, Passage 2]].

== Legal Basis ==

* '''EU Data Act''', fully applicable across all EU Member States as of September 12, 2025 [[EU Legal Basis|Passage 1]].
* '''Eversheds Sutherland Executive Compliance Guide''', released on September 22, 2025 [[Compliance Guide|Passage 4]].

== Background ==
The exponential increase in connected products and IoT ecosystems yields vast volumes of industrial data [[IoT Data|Passage 2]]. This legislative framework was enacted to remove barriers to data reuse and establish equitable rights for both personal and non-personal data processing within the EU single market [[EU Data Market|Passage 1, Passage 2]].

== Objectives ==

# Expand access to and economic utilization of industrial and IoT data [[Data Access|Passage 2]].
# Foster digital innovation and preserve fair market competition [[Market Fairness|Passage 1]].
# Protect commercial entities from unfair standard B2B contractual terms [[B2B Protection|Passage 3]].
# Enable seamless switching between cloud service providers and enhance cross-system interoperability [[Cloud Switching|Passage 3]].

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Data Scope:''' Encompasses both personal and non-personal data generated by connected devices and associated digital services [[IoT Scope|Passage 2]].
* '''B2B Data Sharing:''' Enforces rules requiring data holders to share data under fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory conditions [[B2B Transmission|Passage 3]].
* '''Cloud Provider Switching & Interoperability:''' Removes technical and legal barriers preventing users from migrating data and applications between competing cloud processing services [[Cloud Interoperability|Passage 3]].

== Implementation ==

* '''Full Enforcement:''' Mandatory compliance binding all EU Member States effective September 12, 2025 [[Enforcement Date|Passage 1]].
* '''Compliance Strategy:''' Guidance published by Eversheds Sutherland on September 22, 2025, to assist enterprise governance and contract reviews [[Eversheds Guidance|Passage 4]].

== Policy & Compliance Issues ==

* '''Unfair Contractual Clauses:''' Identifying contractual imbalance criteria and invalidating unilateral data access restrictions in B2B transactions [[Unfair Terms|Passage 3]].
* '''Technical Cloud Architecture:''' Upgrading cloud and IoT architecture standards to conform with statutory interoperability protocols [[Cloud Standards|Passage 3]].

title: JPW-REGULATION-EU-EWC-2025
wikitext:
{{Infobox|stable_id=JPW-REGULATION-EU-EWC-2025|canonical_name=EU European Works Council Directive (Revised)|name=New European Works Council Directive|type=Judicial / Employment Policy Directive|legal_basis=EU European Works Council Directive|date=2025-10-09|status=In Transposition Phase}}

'''EU European Works Council Directive (Revised)''' is a European Union regulatory framework agreed upon on October 9, 2025, to strengthen worker rights, enhance employer Information and Consultation (I&C) obligations, and enforce stricter non-compliance penalties for European Works Councils [[EWC Directive|Passage 7]].

== Executive Summary ==
The revised Directive ensures European Works Councils (EWCs) can be formed more easily, are better funded, and receive robust legal protections [[EWC Protection|Passage 7]]. Member States must transpose the regulations into national law by 2027, with full enforcement taking effect in 2028 [[EU Transposition|Passage 7]].

== Legal Basis ==

* '''EU European Works Council Directive''' (Agreed October 9, 2025) [[EU Law|Passage 7]].
* '''EU/EEA Member State Transposition Acts''', mandated for statutory enactment by 2027 [[National Transposition|Passage 7]].

== Background ==
Accelerated cross-border corporate restructurings, outsourcing, and redundancies necessitate worker consultation at earlier strategic phases [[I&C Background|Passage 7]]. Previous legislation contained legal loopholes regarding transnational scope definitions and EWC expense coverage [[Legal Loopholes|Passage 7]].

== Objectives ==

# Expand the scope of transnational information and consultation (I&C) [[Transnational Scope|Passage 7]].
# Eliminate exemption status for "legacy" EWCs created prior to the 1994 Directive [[Legacy EWC|Passage 7]].
# Ensure funding certainty for expert advisors, training, and legal representation [[EWC Expenses|Passage 7]].
# Increase gender balance across EWC delegations [[Gender Equality|Passage 7]].

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Coverage Thresholds:''' Applies to undertakings employing at least 1,000 workers in the EU/EEA and at least 150 workers in each of at least two Member States [[Corporate Scope|Passage 7]].
* '''Timely Consultation:''' Management must provide a reasoned written response to EWC opinions prior to finalizing executive decisions [[Reasoned Response|Passage 7]].
* '''Gender Targets:''' Parties must target a minimum of 40% representation of each gender in EWC membership [[Gender Targets|Passage 7]].
* '''Confidentiality Rules:''' Management withholding of confidential information requires objective justification based on Member State criteria [[Confidentiality|Passage 7]].

== Implementation ==

* '''Phasing Out Legacy EWCs:''' Exemptions for pre-1994 EWCs are abolished (by end-2027), triggering a 2-year window for renegotiating agreements [[Legacy Transition|Passage 7]].
* '''Plenary Meetings:''' Increases mandatory plenary sessions to two in-person meetings per year [[Plenary Sessions|Passage 7]].
* '''Enhanced Sanctions:''' Member States must establish effective financial penalties calculated relative to corporate annual turnover [[Financial Sanctions|Passage 7]].

== Policy & Compliance Issues ==

* '''Employer Cost Burden:''' Uncapped funding for expert assistance, legal defense, and mandatory training raises operational cost concerns [[Cost Burden|Passage 7]].
* '''National Variation:''' Potential divergence across EU Member States regarding confidentiality thresholds and sanction caps [[Sanction Disparities|Passage 7]].

title: JPW-REGULATION-EU-GPAI-2025

{{Infobox|stable_id=JPW-REGULATION-EU-GPAI-2025|canonical_name=EU General Purpose AI (GPAI) Model Guidelines|name=EU General Purpose AI Model Guidelines|type=EU AI & Regulatory Policy Guidance|legal_basis=EU AI Act|date=2025-08-02|status=In Force}}

'''EU General Purpose AI (GPAI) Model Guidelines''' are official implementation rules under the EU AI Act that clarify transparency, technical documentation, and data confidentiality obligations for general-purpose AI providers [[EU AI Act|Passage 1]].

== Executive Summary ==
Core compliance mandates under the EU AI Act for GPAI models became legally binding on August 2, 2025 [[Enforcement Date|Passage 1]]. These guidelines set clear definitions for operational scope, transparency standards, and enforcement mechanics applicable to both EU and non-EU providers selling or operating AI models within the European Union [[Scope|Passage 1, Passage 2]].

== Legal Basis ==

* '''EU Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act)''', specifically statutory provisions governing General Purpose AI models [[AI Act Legal Basis|Passage 1]].
* '''European Commission GPAI Guidelines''', published to establish enforcement procedures and compliance templates [[Commission Release|Passage 1]].
* '''GPAI Code of Practice''', released by the European Commission on July 10, 2025 [[Code of Practice|Passage 1]].

== Background ==
The rapid proliferation of foundation and general-purpose AI models created urgent demands for standardized regulatory governance across EU Member States [[Background Context|Passage 1]]. The European Commission enacted these practical guidelines to ensure developer compliance ahead of the August 2025 statutory deadline [[Regulatory Timeline|Passage 1]].

== Objectives ==

# Enforce complete transparency regarding datasets and sources used to train GPAI models [[Transparency Goal|Passage 1]].
# Maintain mandatory standards for technical documentation and corporate data confidentiality [[Documentation Mandates|Passage 1, Passage 2]].
# Define predictable legal enforcement mechanisms for AI products operating within the EU internal market [[Enforcement Scope|Passage 2]].

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Extraterritorial Reach:''' Mandates full compliance from both EU-based and non-EU AI developers if their models are deployed within the EU [[Extraterritorial Scope|Passage 2]].
* '''Training Data Summary Template:''' Obligates providers to submit structured disclosures detailing the content and sources used in model training [[Summary Template|Passage 1]].
* '''Transparency Obligations:''' Imposes mandatory technical records retention and data governance rules effective August 2, 2025 [[Core Requirements|Passage 1]].

== Implementation ==

* '''Code of Practice Release:''' Issued by the European Commission on July 10, 2025 [[Jul 10 Release|Passage 1]].
* '''Statutory Activation:''' Mandatory transparency and documentation obligations entered full effect on August 2, 2025 [[Aug 2 Applicability|Passage 1]].
* '''Executive Compliance Guidance:''' Eversheds Sutherland published an analysis guide on September 26, 2025, assisting enterprises with legal navigation [[Eversheds Guide|Passage 4]].

== Policy & Compliance Issues ==

* '''Cross-Border Compliance:''' Operational challenges related to auditing and enforcing compliance on foreign AI developers operating outside EU borders [[International Compliance|Passage 2]].
* '''Proprietary Balance:''' Harmonizing public training data transparency mandates with corporate trade secret protection [[Trade Secrets|Passage 1, Passage 5]].

== Entity Relationships & Knowledge Base Mapping ==

* [[European Union]] — Sovereign jurisdiction enacting the legal framework [[EU Authority|Passage 1]].

* [[Eversheds Sutherland]] — Legal firm issuing executive compliance guidance [[Legal Analysis|Passage 4]].

title: JPW-REGULATION-EU-PAYTRANS-2026
wikitext:
{{Infobox|stable_id=JPW-REGULATION-EU-PAYTRANS-2026|canonical_name=EU Pay Transparency Directive|name=EU Pay Transparency Directive|type=Judicial / Employment Policy Directive|legal_basis=Directive (EU) 2023/970|date=2026-06-07|status=In Transposition Phase}}

'''EU Pay Transparency Directive''' is a binding regulatory framework issued by the European Union that establishes mandatory compensation transparency standards, objective job evaluation mechanisms, and public gender pay gap disclosures for employers operating across EU Member States [[EU Pay Transparency Directive|Passage 7]].

== Executive Summary ==
The Directive defines minimum structural requirements across the European Union to enforce the constitutional principle of equal pay for work of equal value and eradicate gender-based wage discrimination [[Equal Pay Principles|Passage 7]]. Member States are bound to transpose the terms of the Directive into national law no later than June 7, 2026 [[Transposition Deadline|Passage 7]]. Formal gender pay gap reporting obligations commence in 2027 for commercial entities and public employers with 150 or more employees [[Pay Gap Reporting|Passage 7]].

== Legal Basis ==

* '''Directive (EU) 2023/970''' (EU Pay Transparency Directive), mandating full compliance and legislative adoption across all Member States by June 7, 2026 [[EU Law Framework|Passage 7]].
* '''National Implementing Legislation''', including draft bills, statutory amendments, and ministerial decrees progressing in Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Lithuania, Malta, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, and Sweden [[National Transposition Status|Passage 7]].

== Background ==
Structural opacity surrounding organizational salary brackets and career progression metrics has maintained systemic gender pay gaps across EU markets [[Gender Pay Disparities|Passage 7]]. The Directive establishes actionable legal rights for both job applicants and existing employees to access non-discriminatory compensation metrics [[Access to Pay Information|Passage 7]].

== Objectives ==

# Enforce pre-employment salary transparency for job applicants prior to interviews or contractual offers [[Applicant Transparency|Passage 7]].
# Guarantee employee access to objective, gender-neutral criteria used to determine pay levels and career progression [[Progression Criteria|Passage 7]].
# Provide workers with comparative wage data for job categories performing equal work or work of equal value [[Work of Equal Value|Passage 7]].
# Enforce periodic statutory reporting on gender pay gaps for medium and large-sized enterprises [[Statutory Reporting|Passage 7]].

== Key Requirements ==

* '''Universal Employer Applicability:''' Mandatory pre-employment wage disclosures and equal pay accessibility rules apply to every EU employer regardless of workforce size starting June 7, 2026 [[Day One Compliance|Passage 7]].
* '''Gender Pay Gap Reporting (2027):''' Organizations employing 150+ staff must submit their initial gender pay gap reports in 2027, based on financial and compensation data gathered between January 1, 2026, and December 31, 2026 [[2026 Data Tracking|Passage 7]].
* '''Lowered National Headcount Thresholds:''' Member States retain the right to enforce stricter headcount rules; for instance, Ireland reduced its reporting threshold to 50+ employees effective June 1, 2025 [[Irish Statutory Policy|Passage 7]].

== Member State Implementation Snapshot ==
Transposition measures across primary jurisdictions:

* '''Belgium:''' Regional decree enacted governing public sector transparency in the French Community [[Belgium Public Sector|Passage 7]].
* '''Finland:''' Ministerial working group issued draft implementation act on May 16, 2025, targeting statutory enactment by May 18, 2026 [[Finland Implementation|Passage 7]].
* '''France:''' Ministry of Labor launched multilateral consultations; updated Gender Equality Index rules confirmed on May 14, 2025 [[France Equal Index|Passage 7]].
* '''Germany & Greece:''' Inter-ministerial committees and expert advisory groups established to formulate draft labor code amendments [[German Transposition|Passage 7]].
* '''Ireland:''' Recruitment stage transparency bill progressing through the Seanad; corporate reporting threshold expanded to 50+ staff [[Ireland Reforms|Passage 7]].
* '''Lithuania & Malta:''' Enacted national statutory regulations governing recruitment salary range disclosures and data access rights in May and August 2025 [[Malta Statutory Order|Passage 7]].
* '''Netherlands:''' Legislative consultation concluded May 7, 2025; statutory entry into force scheduled for January 1, 2027, with inaugural reporting in 2027 [[Dutch Implementation Plan|Passage 7]].
* '''Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia, Sweden:''' Parliamentary bill drafts, social partner consultations, and official state commission inquiries ongoing [[EU Legislative Track|Passage 7]].

== Policy & Compliance Issues ==

* '''Local Statutory Variations:''' Jurisdictional divergence concerning definitions of "initial pay," maximum allowable width for advertised salary bands, and proactive versus reactive disclosure duties [[Local Variation Risks|Passage 7]].
* '''Data Privacy & Protection:''' Reconciling transparent wage disclosures with individual data privacy protections under GDPR regulations [[Remuneration Privacy|Passage 7]].

title: JPW-REGULATION-EU-PPWR-2025
wikitext:
{{Infobox|stable_id=JPW-REGULATION-EU-PPWR-2025|canonical_name=EU Packaging & Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR)|name=EU Packaging & Packaging Waste Regulation|type=EU Environmental & Packaging Regulation|legal_basis=EU Packaging & Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR)|date=2025-02-11|status=In Force}}

'''EU Packaging & Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR)''' is a European Union legal framework mandating sustainable packaging standards across all EU Member States [[PPWR|Passage 1]].

== Executive Summary ==
The EU Packaging & Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) officially entered into force on February 11, 2025 [[PPWR Enactment|Passage 1]]. The regulation targets the elimination of over-packaging and mandates that all packaging on the EU market must be fully recyclable or reusable by 2030 [[2030 Target|Passage 1, Passage 2]].

== Legal Basis ==

* '''EU Packaging & Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR)''', in force since February 11, 2025 [[PPWR Legal Basis|Passage 1]].
* '''Eversheds Sutherland Executive Compliance Guide''', published on September 22, 2025 [[Eversheds Guide|Passage 4]].

== Background ==
Escalating volumes of packaging waste in the EU internal market necessitated binding statutory intervention [[Environmental Background|Passage 1]]. The PPWR was enacted to curtail wasteful packaging habits and accelerate the transition toward a sustainable circular economy [[Circular Economy|Passage 1, Passage 2]].

== Objectives ==

# Reduce over-packaging and excessive material consumption across EU Member States [[Packaging Reduction|Passage 1]].
# Require 100% of commercial packaging to be recyclable or reusable by 2030 [[Recyclability Obligation|Passage 2]].
# Enforce corporate compliance and incentivize sustainable supply chain operations [[Management Accountability|Passage 3]].

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Sustainable Packaging Mandate:''' Establishes strict statutory requirements for resource-efficient packaging design [[Sustainability Standards|Passage 1]].
* '''2030 Recyclability Deadline:''' Requires all packaging formats to satisfy strict reusability or recyclability criteria by 2030 [[2030 Deadline|Passage 2]].
* '''Non-Compliance Sanctions:''' Failure to meet PPWR criteria risks immediate market access restrictions and heavy fines for corporations and executive management [[Penalty Provisions|Passage 3]].

== Implementation ==

* '''Territorial Applicability:''' Direct legal binding force across all EU Member States effective February 11, 2025 [[EU Scope|Passage 1]].
* '''Legal Navigation Support:''' Eversheds Sutherland released executive guidance on September 22, 2025, to aid commercial entities in adapting to compliance obligations [[Executive Guidance|Passage 4]].

== Policy & Compliance Issues ==

* '''Market Access Risk:''' Failure to adapt supply chains risks exclusion from doing business in EU markets [[Market Access Risk|Passage 3]].
* '''Executive Liability:''' Potential direct monetary fines and accountability measures targeting corporate management teams [[Executive Sanctions|Passage 3]].

title: JPW-REGULATION-GER-GEOBG-2025

{{Infobox|stable_id=JPW-REGULATION-GER-GEOBG-2025|canonical_name=Geothermal Energy Acceleration Act (Geothermie-Beschleunigungsgesetz)|name=German Geothermal Energy Acceleration Act|type=Energy & Climate Policy Legislation|legal_basis=Geothermie-Beschleunigungsgesetz (GeoBG), RED III (EU)|date=2025-08-06|status=Draft Law / Legislative Proposal}}

The '''Geothermal Energy Acceleration Act''' (German: ''Geothermie-Beschleunigungsgesetz'' – GeoBG) is a draft legislative proposal approved by the [[German Federal Cabinet]] on August 6, 2025, aimed at accelerating the transition toward a climate-neutral heat supply by streamlining approval processes for geothermal energy, heat pumps, and thermal storage [[GeoBG]].

== Overview ==
The legislation aims to eliminate regulatory and bureaucratic bottlenecks in geothermal energy deployment across Germany [[Heat Transition]]. GeoBG establishes statutory maximum approval deadlines, digitalizes permit processing, and legally categorizes geothermal infrastructure as an '''overriding public interest''' [[Public Interest]].

== Legal Basis ==

* '''Geothermie-Beschleunigungsgesetz (GeoBG)''': Drafted and submitted by the German Federal Cabinet on August 6, 2025 [[German Cabinet]].
* '''EU Renewable Energy Directive (RED III)''': Partially transposed into national German law via GeoBG [[RED III]].
* '''Statutory Amendments''': Amends the ''Water Resources Act'' (WHG), ''Federal Mining Act'' (BBergG), ''Environmental Impact Assessment Act'' (UVPG), and ''Code of Administrative Court Procedure'' (VwGO) [[German Mining Law]].

== Background ==
Geothermal and district heating projects in Germany previously experienced long development delays due to complex administrative procedures under mining and water regulations [[Bureaucratic Bottlenecks]]. GeoBG was created to overcome these obstacles and hit national climate neutrality targets.

== Key Objectives ==

# Accelerate planning and permitting procedures for geothermal energy and heat grid infrastructure [[Permit Acceleration]].
# Establish legally binding maximum deadlines for mining and water authority approvals [[Legal Timelines]].
# Facilitate subsurface exploration and streamlined access to seismic data [[Seismic Exploration]].
# Encourage recovery from heat sources such as river water, wastewater, and industrial waste heat [[Industrial Waste Heat]].

== Core Provisions ==

* '''Overriding Public Interest''': Legally grants geothermal developments prioritized status in administrative land-use balancing decisions [[Public Interest]].
* '''Landowner Tolerance Obligations''': Requires landowners to allow subsurface seismic testing, subject to property restoration and compensation for direct financial loss [[Land Use]].
* '''Heat Pipelines''': Aligns planning procedures for heat transfer pipelines with established fast-track rules for natural gas and hydrogen pipelines [[Heat Pipelines]].
* '''Year-Round Exploration''': Eases exploration permits in protected areas under strict conditions to prevent seasonal delays [[Exploration Permits]].

== Implementation & Timeline ==

* '''Cabinet Approval''': Adopted as part of a comprehensive federal energy package on August 6, 2025 [[Energy Package]].
* '''Legal Analysis''': Eversheds Sutherland published its legal analysis briefing on September 2, 2025 [[Eversheds Sutherland]].

title: JPW-REGULATION-GER-NETZENTGELT-2026
wikitext:
{{Infobox|stable_id=JPW-REGULATION-GER-NETZENTGELT-2026|canonical_name=German Network Access Fee Subsidy Bill 2026|name=German Network Access Fee Subsidy Bill 2026|type=Energy Regulation / Subsidy Legislation|legal_basis=Section 24c EnWG, Stromnetzentgeltverordnung|date=2026-09-15|status=Draft Bill / Pending Parliamentary Approval}}

The '''German Network Access Fee Subsidy Bill 2026''' (German: ''Entwurf eines Gesetzes zur Zuschussgewährung zur Dämpfung der Netzentgelte im Jahr 2026'') is a legislative proposal enacted by the [[Federal Government of Germany]] to cushion end-user electricity prices by providing a €6.5 billion subsidy for public transmission grid fees in 2026 [[Network Subsidy]].

== Overview ==
The Federal Government approved a draft bill allocating a direct €6.5 billion subsidy from the Climate and Transformation Fund (KTF) to Germany's four primary transmission system operators (TSOs) [[Climate and Transformation Fund]]. This measure directly targets transmission network fees, which form a substantial component of total retail electricity bills in Germany [[Electricity Subsidy]].

== Legal Basis ==

* '''Section 24c Energy Industry Act (EnWG)''': A new statutory provision inserted into the EnWG to establish the legal framework for TSOs to receive and account for the subsidy [[EnWG]].
* '''Electricity Network Access Fee Ordinance (Stromnetzentgeltverordnung)''': Framework governing non-discriminatory network access fee calculations [[Stromnetzentgeltverordnung]].
* '''Incentive Regulation Ordinance (Anreizregulierung)''': Regulatory revenue cap framework from which TSOs must deduct received subsidies [[Incentive Regulation]].

== Background ==
Persistently high energy costs in Germany continue to impact industrial competitiveness and consumer purchasing power [[German Energy Costs]]. The federal intervention subsidizes upstream transmission network fees to lower electricity bills across all consumer tiers [Energy Background].

== Key Objectives ==

# Lower end-user power prices by dampening transmission network access fees [[Tariff Reduction]].
# Distribute €6.5 billion in funding proportionally among the four national TSOs [[TSO Allocation]].
# Complement relief through electricity tax (''Stromsteuer'') reductions for manufacturing, agriculture, and forestry sectors [[Electricity Tax]].

== Core Provisions ==

* '''KTF Funding Allocation''': The €6.5 billion sum originates from the Climate and Transformation Fund (KTF) and is distributed based on each TSO's approved revenue cap [[KTF Funds]].
* '''Eligible Recipients''': The four recipient TSOs are 50Hertz, Amprion, TenneT, and TransnetBW [[German TSOs]].
* '''Fee Deduction Obligation''': TSOs and downstream distribution operators must deduct the subsidy from their revenue caps when calculating net fee schedules [[TSO Obligations]].
* '''October 15 Deadline''': TSOs remain legally obligated to determine and publish next year's network access fees by October 15 annually [[Publication Deadline]].

== Implementation & Oversight ==

* '''BNetzA Oversight''': The Federal Network Agency (''Bundesnetzagentur'') supervises compliance and proper accounting of the subsidy funds [[Bundesnetzagentur]].
* '''Consumer Pass-Through''': Electricity suppliers must pass along lowered network access fees to end consumers upon final parliamentary enactment [[Pass-Through]].

== Policy Considerations ==

* '''Tariff Relief Expectations''': The estimated reduction of 1.3 cents/kWh falls short of the government Coalition Agreement's broader target of 5 cents/kWh [[Coalition Targets]].
* '''Parliamentary Delays''': Industry groups express concern over potential delays in parliamentary adoption beyond the October 15 publication cut-off [[Parliamentary Risks]].
* '''Single-Year Limitation''': The policy applies exclusively to calendar year 2026, prompting calls for long-term structural relief such as an industrial power price cap (''Industriestrompreis'') [[Industriestrompreis]].

== Key Legal Contacts ==

* [[Dr. Arndt Scheffler]] (Counsel, Munich / Primary Contact)
* [[Dr. Martin Weitenberg]] (Partner, Düsseldorf / Primary Contact)

'''FS+ Country Updates – September 2025''' is the inaugural edition of a global regulatory update publication issued by [[Eversheds Sutherland]] to provide key insights into legal and regulatory changes affecting investment managers across multiple jurisdictions [1–6].

== Summary ==
This publication was previously released under the name ''International FundsNet Country Updates'' [1–6]. Each edition summarizes major regulatory shifts across global jurisdictions, including Ireland, Canada, Taiwan, and Mauritius [1–6].

== Legal Basis ==
The contents of this publication are provided for general information purposes only and do not constitute formal legal advice [1–6]. The legal basis for each update is derived from the respective local regulatory authorities:

* '''Ireland''': AIF Rulebook consultation issued by the Central Bank of Ireland [1–6].
* '''Canada''': New AML/CTF supervisory framework released by FINTRAC [1–6].
* '''Taiwan''': Securities firm rules and sustainability reporting updates issued by FSC and SITCA [1–6].
* '''Mauritius''': New ESG fund guidelines published by the FSC [1–6].

== Background ==
Investment managers face increasingly complex compliance challenges due to rapid regulatory shifts across international borders [1–6]. Eversheds Sutherland rebranded and structured this publication series to offer clearer, actionable regulatory intelligence for financial market participants [1–6].

== Objectives ==

# Provide a centralized summary of global regulatory developments for asset and investment managers [1–6].
# Outline updates to the QIAIF regime and UCITS regulations in Ireland [1–6].
# Inform market participants about new AML/CTF monitoring frameworks and penalty policies in Canada [1–6].
# Drive compliance with evolving ESG disclosure standards in Taiwan and Mauritius [1–6].

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Ireland''': The Central Bank of Ireland confirmed the publication of an AIF rulebook consultation in September 2025, focusing on enhancing the QIAIF regime and updating UCITS rules [1–6].
* '''Canada''': FINTRAC introduced a new AML/CTF oversight framework and penalty policy targeting mutual fund dealers [1–6].
* '''Taiwan''': FSC amended securities firm rules and sustainability reporting obligations; SITCA updated fund sales requirements and ESG disclosure guidelines [1–6].
* '''Mauritius''': FSC published new guidelines for ESG funds establishing explicit disclosure, reporting, and compliance standards [1–6].

== Implementation & Governance ==

* '''Publication Date''': Formally released as the inaugural FS+ edition in September/October 2025 [1–6].
* '''Editorial Contacts''': Oversight and primary contact roles are held by Lindi Rudman (Legal Director, UK) and Michaela Arter (Partner, UK) at Eversheds Sutherland [1–6].

== Policy Issues & Analysis ==

* '''ESG Disparities''': Significant variation remains in ESG disclosure thresholds between jurisdictions such as Taiwan and Mauritius [1–6].
* '''AML/CTF Enforcement''': Enhanced penalty structures under FINTRAC necessitate stricter internal compliance for global investment funds operating in Canada [1–6].

== Related Entities & Verification Status ==

* [[Eversheds Sutherland]]: Publisher and legal analysis provider [1–6].
* [[Central Bank of Ireland]]: Financial regulator for Ireland [1–6].
* [[FINTRAC Canada]]: Financial intelligence and oversight agency of Canada [1–6].
* [[Financial Services Commission (FSC) Taiwan]]: Regulatory body governing Taiwanese financial markets [1–6].

title: JPW-REGULATION-UK-CMA-TALENT-2025
wikitext:
{{Infobox|stable_id=JPW-REGULATION-UK-CMA-TALENT-2025|canonical_name=CMA Guidance on Competing for Talent|name=CMA Guidance on Competing for Talent|type=Competition & Labour Policy Guidance|legal_basis=UK Competition Law|date=2025-09-09|status=Active / Official Guidance Issued}}

'''CMA Guidance on Competing for Talent''' is official regulatory guidance issued by the [[Competition and Markets Authority]] (CMA) on September 9, 2025, regarding the application of competition law to employee recruitment and retention [[CMA Guidance|Passage 7]].

== Executive Summary ==
The guidance assists HR professionals, internal recruiters, and employers in understanding and complying with competition law within employment markets [[HR Compliance|Passage 7]]. It establishes that businesses competing to recruit or retain workers are competitors in the labor market subject to competition law, regardless of whether they compete for the same consumer client base [[Labor Competitors|Passage 7]].

== Legal Basis ==

* '''UK Competition Law''', which prohibits agreements or concerted practices that restrict or distort fair competition [[UK Competition Law|Passage 7]].
* '''CMA Labor Cartel Infringement Decision''' (March 2025), establishing that labor market restrictions are treated as hardcore cartel behavior [[CMA Decision 2025|Passage 7]].

== Background ==
Publication of this guidance follows intensified regulatory enforcement against anti-competitive labor behavior globally, particularly across the technology, media, and sports sectors [[Global Labor Markets|Passage 7]]. Many organizations were unaware that informal agreements regarding wages or hiring between employers constitute cartel infringements [[Cartel Risks|Passage 7]].

== Objectives ==

# Assist HR personnel and recruiters in avoiding competition law breaches [[Preventing Violations|Passage 7]].
# Safeguard labor mobility and workers' ability to negotiate fair remuneration [[Worker Mobility|Passage 7]].
# Identify and eliminate the three main types of labor cartels [[Cartel Types|Passage 7]].
# Foster a culture of competition compliance within corporate organizational structures [[Compliance Culture|Passage 7]].

== Key Provisions ==
The CMA defines three primary prohibited behaviors:

* '''No-Poaching Agreements:''' Agreements between businesses not to hire or recruit each other's employees [[No-Poaching|Passage 7]].
* '''Wage-Fixing Agreements:''' Agreements between employers to fix or cap wages, bonuses, or employment benefits [[Wage-Fixing|Passage 7]].
* '''Information Sharing & Benchmarking:''' Exchanging non-public, sensitive details on salaries, bonuses, and terms of employment [[Information Sharing|Passage 7]].

== Implementation ==
Employer compliance measures include:

* '''HR Training:''' Elevating HR departments into a frontline compliance role (*frontline compliance function*) [[HR Training|Passage 7]].
* '''Employment Audits:''' Reviewing hiring policies and recruitment workflows to ensure alignment with competition rules [[Employment Audit|Passage 7]].
* '''Regulatory Cooperation:''' Participating fully in CMA investigations to qualify for leniency or fine reductions where breaches occur [[CMA Leniency|Passage 7]].

== Policy & Compliance Issues ==

* '''Industry Communication Boundaries:''' Drawing clear lines between permissible economic trend discussions and prohibited wage data exchanges [[Market Trends|Passage 7]].
* '''Non-Solicitation vs. No-Poaching:''' Ensuring commercial non-solicitation clauses remain proportionate and limited in duration, scope, and geography so as not to be reclassified as unlawful no-poaching deals [[Commercial Clauses|Passage 7]].

== Entity Relationships & Knowledge Base Mapping ==

* [[Competition and Markets Authority]] — Regulatory body issuing the guidance [[CMA Regulator|Passage 7]].
* [[BT, IMG, ITV, BBC]] — Media entities penalized over £4 million for sharing freelance fee data [[Sports Broadcasting Case|Passage 7]].
* [[Eversheds Sutherland]] — Law firm providing legal analysis and HR compliance training [[Eversheds Sutherland|Passage 7]].
* [[Rosianna Maretha Hasibuan]] (JPW-PER-RMH002) — Preserved Person Entity Target in JPAIS Wiki; unlinked in source compliance text [[Person Entity JPAIS|Passage 1, Passage 7]].
* [[Cecep Mustafa]] (JPW-PER-CMU002) — Preserved Person Entity Target in JPAIS Wiki; unlinked in source compliance text [[Person Entity JPAIS|Passage 1, Passage 7]].

'''Product Regulation and Metrology Act 2025''' is a landmark United Kingdom statute enacted on July 21, 2025, granting the Secretary of State powers to make regulations to reduce or mitigate safety risks posed by products, including holding online marketplaces accountable for unsafe items sold through their platforms [1–55].

== Executive Summary ==
The Product Regulation and Metrology Bill received Royal Assent on July 21, 2025, officially becoming the '''Product Regulation and Metrology Act 2025''' (PRM Act) [1–55]. The legislation establishes a modern primary legal framework designed to enhance product safety enforcement and address the expanding complexities of global e-commerce and digital marketplace platforms [1–55].

== Legal Basis ==

* '''Product Regulation and Metrology Act 2025''': Enacted via Royal Assent on July 21, 2025 [1–55].
* '''Secondary Rulemaking Authority''': Grants delegated regulatory powers to the Secretary of State to introduce secondary legislation for evolving product risks [1–55].

== Background ==
The rapid growth of e-commerce and cross-border supply chains increased the exposure of UK consumers to unsafe third-party goods sold through online platforms [1–55]. Traditional product safety enforcement struggled to effectively regulate these non-traditional intermediaries, prompting the UK Government to establish an agile primary legal structure [1–55].

== Objectives ==

# Mitigate and reduce safety risks stemming from commercial products in the UK market [1–55].
# Hold online marketplace operators legally accountable for unsafe items distributed via their platforms [1–55].
# Ensure third-party sellers comply with product safety laws and provide accurate product information [1–55].
# Strengthen formal cooperation between digital platform operators and enforcement regulators [1–55].

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Secretary of State Powers''': Authority to issue secondary regulations addressing novel product safety hazards without needing primary statutory amendments [1–55].
* '''Online Marketplace Accountability''': Mandatory requirements for digital platforms to prevent unsafe listings, enforce seller compliance, and supply audit data to regulatory bodies [1–55].
* '''Express Product Exclusions''': Explicitly exempts specific regulated sectors from its scope, including:
** Food, plants, animal by-products, and products of animal origin [1–55].
** Aircraft and aircraft components [1–55].
** Military equipment [1–55].
** Medicines and medical devices [1–55].

== Implementation & Supply Chain Impact ==

* '''Secondary Regulation Rollout''': The UK Government announced its intention to use PRM Act powers to impose operational compliance duties on online marketplaces [1–55].
* '''Supply Chain Compliance''': Manufacturers, importers, distributors, and e-commerce platforms across global supply chains will face heightened regulatory scrutiny and due diligence requirements [1–55].

== Policy & Regulatory Challenges ==

* '''Cross-Border Enforcement''': Difficulties in reaching foreign third-party merchants operating on UK-accessible platforms [1–55].
* '''Regulatory Balance''': Calibrating compliance costs to avoid stifling e-commerce innovation while maintaining consumer protection standards [1–55].

== Related Entities & Verification Status ==

* [[UK Parliament]]: Enacting legislative body [1–55].
* [[Secretary of State (UK)]]: Designated executive official granted regulatory powers [1–55].
* [[Eversheds Sutherland]]: Publisher of the legal analysis in *Global Supply Chain Horizons – September 2025* [1–55].
* [[Cecep Mustafa]]: Verification Status — Not found in available sources [1–55].
* [[Rosianna Maretha Hasibuan]]: Verification Status — Not found in available sources [1–55].

title: JPW-REPORT-001

{{Infobox|stable_id=JPW-REPORT-001|canonical_name=2019 Report on Preliminary Examination Activities (ICC OTP)|name=Report on Preliminary Examination Activities (2019)|type=Official Institutional Report|legal_basis=Rome Statute (Articles 5, 12, 13, 14, 15, 53(1))|date=5 December 2019|status=Official / Published}}

'''2019 Report on Preliminary Examination Activities (ICC OTP)''' is the official annual report published by the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) of the International Criminal Court on 5 December 2019 [].

== Summary ==
This report summarizes the analysis and preliminary examination activities conducted by the OTP between 1 December 2018 and 30 November 2019 []. The document covers examinations of various international situations worldwide grouped according to analytical phases [].

== Legal Basis ==
The execution of preliminary examinations is grounded in Article 53(1) of the [[Rome Statute]], which stipulates that the Prosecutor must consider criteria of jurisdiction (temporal, territorial/personal, and subject-matter), admissibility (complementarity and gravity), and the interests of justice [].

== Background ==
The preliminary examination process can be triggered through three pathways: (i) information from individuals, groups, States, or NGOs via article 15 communications; (ii) referrals from States Parties or the UN Security Council; or (iii) declarations accepting jurisdiction under Article 12(3) of the Rome Statute [].

== Objectives ==
The primary objective of this report is to promote transparency in the preliminary examination process, provide rationale for decisions to proceed or not proceed with investigations, and encourage genuine national proceedings [].

== Key Provisions ==
The OTP applies a four-phase filtering process:

* **Phase 1**: Initial review of all incoming Article 15 communications [].
* **Phase 2**: Assessment of jurisdictional boundaries (territorial/personal) and subject-matter jurisdiction [].
* **Phase 3**: Assessment of admissibility, focusing on national complementarity and crime gravity [].
* **Phase 4**: Assessment of the interests of justice [].

== Implementation ==
During the reporting period, the OTP received 795 Article 15 communications []. Of those, 617 communications were manifestly outside the Court's jurisdiction, 112 were linked to ongoing situations under examination, 25 related to active investigations/prosecutions, and 41 required in-depth factual and legal analysis [].

== Policy Issues ==
Major challenges faced include the absence of investigative powers for the OTP during the preliminary examination stage, the compromising of evidence at domestic judicial levels in certain states, and the lack of a strict statutory time limit to complete examinations [].

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* **[[Office of the Prosecutor]]**: Publishing organ of the report [].
* **[[Fatou Bensouda]]**: ICC Prosecutor [].
* **[[Pre-Trial Chamber]]**: Judicial chamber reviewing OTP investigation requests [].

* **[[Ferdi Raditya Akbar]]**: '''Not found in the available sources.''' [1–386]

title: JPW-REPORT-002
wikitext:
{{Infobox|stable_id=JPW-REPORT-001|canonical_name=Report of the Court on Key Performance Indicators (2019)|official_name=Report of the Court on Key Performance Indicators (2019)|type=Official Institutional Report / Judicial Performance Policy Report|aliases=2019 ICC KPI Report|legal_basis=ICC-ASP/13/Res.5, Annex I, para. 7(b); ICC Strategic Plans 2019–2021; Rome Statute Arts. 74, 75, 76, 81|date=25 November 2019|status=Official / Published / Interim Report|jurisdiction=International Criminal Law / International Criminal Court (ICC)|institution=International Criminal Court (ICC) / Assembly of States Parties (ASP)}}

'''Report of the Court on Key Performance Indicators (2019)''' is an official interim evaluation document published by the International Criminal Court (ICC) on 25 November 2019.

== Summary ==
The report measures the Court's qualitative and quantitative achievements against the 2019–2021 Strategic Plan, adopted by the Presidency, the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP), and the Registry on 17 July 2019. Indicators are grouped into judicial/prosecutorial performance goals and organizational performance goals.

== Legal Basis ==

* Mandate of the Assembly of States Parties: Resolution [[ICC-ASP/13/Res.5]], Annex I, paragraph 7(b).
* [[ICC Strategic Plan 2019–2021]].
* [[Rome Statute]]: Article 74 (Trial Chamber decisions), Article 75 (Reparations), Article 76 (Sentencing), and Article 81 (Appeal).

== Background ==
Development of performance indicators began in 2014 at the ASP's request, to help States Parties strategically assess the ICC's performance. Following reports published in 2015, 2016, and 2017, no report was issued in 2018 due to leadership transitions and harmonization with the new strategic plan.

== Objectives ==

* Ensure judicial proceedings are expeditious, fair, and transparent.
* Measure the level of victim access and participation in proceedings.
* Assess management efficiency, budget execution, gender balance, geographical representation, and physical and IT security.

== Key Provisions ==
Judicial performance is measured across 7 phases:

* '''Phase 1''': Confirmation of Charges.
* '''Phase 2''': Trial Preparation.
* '''Phase 3''': Trial.
* '''Phase 4''': Chamber Deliberations.
* '''Phase 5''': Sentencing.
* '''Phase 6''': Reparations.
* '''Phase 7''': Final Appeal.

== Implementation ==
The Registry led Court-wide data collection. Data covers case activity from November 2017 through 30 September 2019.

== Policy Issues ==

* Indicators for Cooperation and Complementarity goals were not yet included in the 2019 report.
* Need to improve gender balance at senior levels (P-4 and above); at the D-1 level, only 11.11% were women, alongside uneven representation of States Parties.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

'''Digitalization of South Korea's Justice System: Enhancing Access and Efficiency''' is an official policy research and assessment report published by the [[World Bank Group]] (Law Reforms and Judicial Support Unit, Legal Vice Presidency), in partnership with South Korea's Ministry of Economy and Finance through the [[Korea-World Bank Partnership Facility]] (KWPF).<ref name="wb">World Bank Group. ''Digitalization of South Korea's Justice System: Enhancing Access and Efficiency''. Washington, DC: World Bank (2023/2024). Supported by the KWPF.</ref> It evaluates the digital transformation of South Korea's civil justice system ([[Electronic Case Filing System|E-Litigation/ECFS]]) and criminal justice system ([[KICS]]), assessing improvements to access to justice and efficiency in line with Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 16.3.

== Legal basis ==
South Korea's judicial digital transformation rests on:

* '''Constitution, Article 11''': the principle of equality before the law
* '''Constitution, Article 27''': the right to a fair and speedy trial by a qualified judge
* '''Act on the Use of Electronic Documents in Civil Litigations, etc. (2010)''': legal basis for civil E-Litigation
* '''Act on Promotion of the Digitalization of the Criminal Justice Process (2010)''': legal basis for KICS
* '''Act on Special Cases Concerning Remote Video Trials (1995, amended 2016/2021)'''
* '''Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA, 2011)'''
* '''Legal Aid Act (1987)'''

== Background ==
South Korea transformed its judicial system from paper-based to an integrated digital ecosystem, driven by a vision of national modernization, elimination of case backlogs, and alignment with SDG 16.3 on equal access to justice.<ref name="wb" /> Before digitalization, the courts faced case backlogs, high costs of handling physical documents, and inefficient inter-agency file transmission; the government leveraged national IT strength to build transparent, publicly accessible digital judicial infrastructure.

== Objectives ==

# Promote fast, transparent and affordable justice for all citizens.
# Increase automation of minor criminal cases (such as traffic violations and DUI) through Electronic Summary Proceedings, cutting average processing time from 47 to 25 days.
# Develop next-generation platforms, Smart Court 4.0 and Next-Gen KICS, using artificial intelligence and big-data analytics, targeted for 2024.

== Scope ==

* '''E-Litigation / ECFS:''' public portal, e-filing, e-case management, e-courtroom and remote work (Smart Work).
* '''KICS:''' federated server architecture, Electronic Summary Proceedings, the public criminal portal www.kics.go.kr.
* '''Virtual trials:''' remote hearings by interactive video and their security standards.
* '''Smart Court 4.0:''' application of AI, big data and intelligent case search.

== Policy problems ==

* '''Judicial cultural resistance.''' In the civil sector, early resistance came from judges' preference for in-person hearings and physical files.
* '''Multi-agency friction.''' In the criminal sector, merging data across police, prosecution, courts and the Ministry of Justice met resistance from concerns over eroding institutional autonomy and potential human-rights violations.
* '''Digital divide.''' Risk of excluding vulnerable groups (the elderly, people with disabilities, and those unfamiliar with technology) from E-Litigation services.

== Legal and policy gaps ==

* '''Cross-examination right.''' A 2021 Constitutional Court ruling (2018Hun-ba524) held that using video-recorded testimony of a child victim without guaranteeing the defendant's right to cross-examination violates the right to a fair trial.
* '''Need for a federated architecture.''' A centralized server model was rejected over cybersecurity risk and threats to institutional autonomy, leading Korea to adopt a federated server system instead.

Data protection: Korea's PIPA has been recognized as adequate by the European Commission (EU GDPR Adequacy Decision, 2021).

== Reform proposals ==

# '''Dual-pathway approach:''' keep a paper-based track and in-person court assistance for citizens facing technological limitations, to prevent access bottlenecks.
# '''Strengthen personal data protection,'''maintaining PIPA standards recognized as adequate under the EU GDPR.
# '''User-oriented AI adoption:''' deploy AI chatbots and intelligent case search to assist self-represented litigants without replacing judicial discretion.
# '''Roll out Smart Court 4.0 and Next-Gen KICS''' (2021–2024) and strengthen Mobile KICS for on-scene investigation.

== Frequently asked questions ==

; What is the report's title, publisher and focus?
: ''Digitalization of South Korea's Justice System: Enhancing Access and Efficiency'', published by the World Bank Group and KWPF, evaluating the modernization of civil (E-Litigation) and criminal (KICS) justice systems in Korea.
; What constitutional basis supports judicial digitalization in Korea?
: Article 11 (equality before the law) and Article 27 (the right to a speedy, fair trial by a qualified judge).
; Why did Korea choose a federated server architecture for KICS?
: To preserve the constitutional autonomy of each agency (police, prosecution, courts, Ministry of Justice) without concentrating control in a single centralized database vulnerable to hacking.
; How did Korea address judges' early resistance to E-Litigation?
: Through judicial autonomy, Supreme Court leadership, overseas training programs, grassroots initiatives by judges (such as self-built legal databases), and phased piloting starting at the Patent Court.
; What was the E-Litigation adoption rate in civil cases by 2020?
: 91% by the end of 2020.
; What was the effect of Electronic Summary Proceedings on DUI and traffic cases?
: It cut average processing time for minor criminal/DUI cases from 47 to 25 days.
; What did the Constitutional Court decide on 23 December 2021 about virtual trials?
: Ruling 2018Hun-ba524 held that using video recordings of a child victim without adequate cross-examination for the defendant violates the right to a fair trial.
; What is the name of Korea's next-generation e-court modernization project?
: Smart Court 4.0 (Next Generation Electronic Litigation System) and Next-Generation KICS.
; How does E-Litigation support judges through "Smart Work"?
: It lets judges securely access digital case files remotely through Smart Work Centers (SWC) located across major regions.
; What is the status of Cecep Mustafa and Qonita Mutmainah?
: They are kept as entities (JPW-PERSON-CECEP, JPW-PERSON-QONITA), but the source text does not mention them, so no role or authorship is attributed.

== 법적 근거 ==
대한민국 사법 디지털 전환의 근거는 다음과 같다.

* '''헌법 제11조''': 법 앞의 평등 원칙
* '''헌법 제27조''': 자격 있는 법관에 의한 신속·공정한 재판을 받을 권리
* '''민사소송 등에서의 전자문서 이용 등에 관한 법률(2010)''': 민사 전자소송의 법적 근거
* '''형사사법절차 전자화 촉진법(2010)''': KICS의 법적 근거
* '''영상재판에 관한 특례법(1995, 2016·2021 개정)'''
* '''개인정보 보호법(PIPA, 2011)'''
* '''법률구조법(1987)'''

== 배경 ==
대한민국은 국가 정보화 비전, 사건 적체 해소, 사법 접근의 평등을 규정한 SDG 16.3과의 부합을 동력으로 삼아 종이 기반 사법 체계를 통합 디지털 생태계로 전환하였다.<ref name="wb-ko" /> 디지털화 이전에는 사건 적체, 종이 문서 처리 비용, 기관 간 비효율적인 서류 전달이 문제였으며, 정부는 국가의 IT 강점을 활용하여 투명하고 어디서나 접근 가능한 디지털 사법 인프라를 구축하였다.

== 목적 ==

# 모든 국민에게 신속하고 투명하며 저렴한 재판을 제공한다.
# 전자약식절차를 통해 교통위반·음주운전 등 경미 형사사건의 자동화를 확대하여 평균 처리 기간을 47일에서 25일로 단축한다.
# 인공지능과 빅데이터 분석을 활용하는 차세대 플랫폼 스마트법원 4.0과 차세대 KICS를 2024년까지 개발한다.

== 범위 ==

* '''전자소송/ECFS''': 공공 포털, 전자접수, 전자사건관리, 전자법정, 원격근무(스마트워크).
* '''KICS''': 연합형 서버 구조, 전자약식절차, 형사 공공 포털 www.kics.go.kr.
* '''영상재판''': 대화형 화상 원격 심리와 그 보안 기준.
* '''스마트법원 4.0''': 인공지능, 빅데이터, 지능형 사건 검색의 적용.

== 정책 문제 ==

* '''사법 문화의 저항''': 민사 분야에서는 대면 심리와 종이 서류를 선호하는 법관들의 관행에서 초기 저항이 생겼다.
* '''다기관 마찰''': 형사 분야에서는 경찰·검찰·법원·법무부 간 데이터 통합이 기관 자율성 침해 우려와 인권 침해 가능성으로 저항에 부딪혔다.
* '''디지털 격차''': 노인, 장애인, 기술에 익숙하지 않은 국민이 전자소송 서비스에서 소외될 위험.

== 법제 공백 ==

* '''반대신문권''': 2021년 헌법재판소 결정(2018헌바524)은 피고인에게 반대신문 기회를 충분히 보장하지 않은 채 아동 피해자의 영상진술을 증거로 사용하는 것은 공정한 재판을 받을 권리를 침해한다고 판시하였다.
* '''연합형 구조의 필요성''': 중앙집중형 서버 모델은 사이버 보안 위험과 기관 자율성 침해 우려로 배제되어, 한국은 연합형 서버 체계를 채택하였다.

; 보고서의 제목, 발간 기관, 초점은?
: 『Digitalization of South Korea's Justice System: Enhancing Access and Efficiency』, 세계은행그룹과 KWPF가 발간하였으며 한국의 민사(전자소송)·형사(KICS) 사법 현대화를 평가한다.
; 사법 디지털화를 뒷받침하는 헌법적 근거는?
: 법 앞의 평등을 규정한 제11조와 자격 있는 법관에 의한 신속·공정한 재판을 받을 권리를 규정한 제27조이다.
; 한국이 KICS에 연합형 서버 구조를 채택한 이유는?
: 해킹에 취약한 단일 중앙 데이터베이스에 통제를 집중시키지 않으면서 경찰·검찰·법원·법무부 각 기관의 헌법적 자율성을 지키기 위해서이다.
; 전자소송 초기 법관의 저항에 어떻게 대응했는가?
: 사법 자율성, 대법원의 리더십, 해외 연수 프로그램, 법관들의 자발적 법률 데이터베이스 구축과 같은 풀뿌리 이니셔티브, 특허법원부터 시작한 단계적 시범 도입을 통해 대응하였다.
; 2020년까지 민사 전자소송 도입률은?
: 2020년 말 기준 91%이다.
; 전자약식절차가 음주운전·교통사건에 미친 영향은?
: 경미 형사·음주운전 사건의 평균 처리 기간을 47일에서 25일로 크게 단축하였다.
; 2021년 12월 23일 헌법재판소가 영상재판과 관련해 내린 결정은?
: 2018헌바524 결정은 피고인에게 충분한 반대신문 기회를 주지 않은 채 아동 피해자의 영상진술을 사용하는 것은 공정한 재판을 받을 권리를 침해한다고 보았다.
; 차세대 전자법원 현대화 사업의 이름은?
: 스마트법원 4.0(차세대 전자소송시스템)과 차세대 KICS이다.
; 전자소송은 "스마트워크"를 통해 법관 업무를 어떻게 지원하는가?
: 주요 지역에 배치된 스마트워크센터(SWC)를 통해 법관이 디지털 사건 기록에 안전하게 원격 접근할 수 있도록 한다.
; Cecep Mustafa와 Qonita Mutmainah의 지위는?
: 개체(JPW-PERSON-CECEP, JPW-PERSON-QONITA)로 유지하나 원문에 언급이 없어 역할이나 저술 관계는 귀속하지 않는다.

              "type": "paragraph",
              "text": "South Korea transformed its judicial system from paper-based to an integrated digital ecosystem, driven by a vision of national modernization, elimination of case backlogs, and alignment with SDG 16.3 on equal access to justice.<ref name=\"wb\"/> Before digitalization, the courts faced case backlogs, high costs of handling physical documents, and inefficient inter-agency file transmission; the government leveraged national IT strength to build transparent, publicly accessible digital judicial infrastructure."

                "Increase automation of minor criminal cases (such as traffic violations and DUI) through Electronic Summary Proceedings, cutting average processing time from 47 to 25 days.",
                "Develop next-generation platforms, Smart Court 4.0 and Next-Gen KICS, using artificial intelligence and big-data analytics, targeted for 2024."

                "'''Virtual trials:''' remote hearings by interactive video and their security standards.",
                "'''Smart Court 4.0:''' application of AI, big data and intelligent case search."

      "lead": "'''대한민국 사법 시스템의 디지털화: 접근성과 효율성 제고'''(영어: ''Digitalization of South Korea's Justice System: Enhancing Access and Efficiency'')는 [[세계은행그룹]](법무부문 산하 법제개혁·사법지원팀)이 한국 기획재정부와 [[한국-세계은행 파트너십기금]](KWPF)을 통해 공동 발간한 공식 정책 연구·평가 보고서이다.<ref name=\"wb-ko\"/> 대한민국 민사 사법(전자소송/ECFS)과 형사 사법(KICS)의 디지털 전환을 평가하여 지속가능발전목표(SDG) 16.3에 부합하는 사법 접근성과 효율성 제고를 다룬다.",

          "level": 2,

            {
              "type": "paragraph",
              "text": "대한민국은 국가 정보화 비전, 사건 적체 해소, 사법 접근의 평등을 규정한 SDG 16.3과의 부합을 동력으로 삼아 종이 기반 사법 체계를 통합 디지털 생태계로 전환하였다.<ref name=\"wb-ko\"/> 디지털화 이전에는 사건 적체, 종이 문서 처리 비용, 기관 간 비효율적인 서류 전달이 문제였으며, 정부는 국가의 IT 강점을 활용하여 투명하고 어디서나 접근 가능한 디지털 사법 인프라를 구축하였다."
            }
          ]
        },
        {
          "title": "목적",
          "level": 2,
          "blocks": [

              "type": "ordered_list",
              "items": [

                "인공지능과 빅데이터 분석을 활용하는 차세대 플랫폼 스마트법원 4.0과 차세대 KICS를 2024년까지 개발한다."

                "'''디지털 격차''': 노인, 장애인, 기술에 익숙하지 않은 국민이 전자소송 서비스에서 소외될 위험."
