title: JPW-REPORT-003
wikitext:
{{Infobox|stable_id=JPW-REPORT-002|canonical_name=Report on Preliminary Examination Activities (2020) (OTP-ICC)|official_name=Report on Preliminary Examination Activities (2020)|type=Official Institutional Report / Preliminary Examination Report|aliases=2020 OTP Preliminary Examination Report|legal_basis=Rome Statute, Article 15, Article 53(1); Rule 49, ICC Rules of Procedure and Evidence; Policy Paper on Preliminary Examinations (2013)|date=14 December 2020|status=Official / Published|jurisdiction=International Criminal Law / International Criminal Court (ICC)|institution=Office of the Prosecutor (OTP), International Criminal Court (ICC)}}

'''Report on Preliminary Examination Activities (2020)''' is the official annual report published by the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) of the International Criminal Court on 14 December 2020, summarizing analysis and preliminary-examination activity concerning situations of international crimes under the Rome Statute for the period 6 December 2019 to 11 December 2020.

== Summary ==
The report covers the completion of four preliminary examinations (Palestine, Iraq/UK, Nigeria, Ukraine), the opening of two new state referrals (Bolivia, Venezuela II), and ongoing assessment of several other situations, including Colombia, Guinea, the Philippines, and Venezuela I, all at Phase 3 (Admissibility).

== Legal Basis ==
Preliminary examinations are conducted under Article 53(1) of the [[Rome Statute]], which sets out the evaluation criteria of jurisdiction (temporal, territorial/personal, subject-matter), admissibility (complementarity and gravity), and the interests of justice.

== Background ==
A preliminary examination may be triggered through three principal channels: (i) Article 15 communications from individuals, groups, states, or NGOs; (ii) a referral from a State Party or the UN Security Council; or (iii) a declaration accepting jurisdiction under Article 12(3) of the Rome Statute.

== Objectives ==
The report's core aims are to promote transparency in the preliminary examination process, explain the reasoning behind decisions to proceed or not proceed toward investigation, and support positive complementarity by encouraging genuine national proceedings.

== Key Provisions ==
The OTP applies a four-phase filtering process:

* '''Phase 1''': Initial assessment of all Article 15 communications received.
* '''Phase 2''': Assessment of jurisdictional preconditions — territorial/personal and subject-matter jurisdiction.
* '''Phase 3''': Admissibility assessment, focused on national judicial complementarity and gravity of the crimes.
* '''Phase 4''': Assessment of the interests of justice.

== Implementation ==
During the reporting period, the OTP received 813 Article 15 communications. Of these, 612 were found manifestly outside the Court's jurisdiction, 104 related to situations already under examination, 71 related to ongoing investigations or prosecutions, and 26 required further analysis ("WFA communications").

== Policy Issues ==
Key challenges include the OTP's lack of investigative powers during the preliminary examination stage, operational constraints from the COVID-19 pandemic, the absence of any fixed timeline under the Rome Statute, and the need to address delays in domestic proceedings in certain states.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''[[Office of the Prosecutor (ICC)]]''': Organ that published the report.
* '''[[Fatou Bensouda]]''': ICC Prosecutor who leads the OTP and presented the annual preliminary examination report.
* '''[[James Stewart]]''': ICC Deputy Prosecutor who presented on complementarity and transitional justice in Colombia.
* '''[[Pre-Trial Chamber]]''': Chamber that reviews investigation requests and jurisdictional issues.
* '''[[Moussa Dadis Camara]]''': Former Head of State of Guinea and leader of the CNDD military junta, implicated by a panel of judges in the investigation into the events of 28 September 2009.
* '''[[Rodrigo Duterte]]''': President of the Philippines, who launched the "war on drugs" campaign that is the subject of an OTP preliminary examination.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''
* '''[[Ferdi Raditya Akbar]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''

== See Also ==

* [[Rome Statute]]
* [[International Criminal Court]]
* [[Complementarity in International Law]]

== References ==

* Office of the Prosecutor, International Criminal Court, "Report on Preliminary Examination Activities (2020)," 14 December 2020.

title: JPW-REPORT-004
wikitext:
{{Infobox|stable_id=JPW-REPORT-003|canonical_name=Report of the Court on Key Performance Indicators 2020 (Revised Version)|official_name=Report of the Court on Key Performance Indicators (Revised version, 11 December 2020)|type=Official Institutional Report / Judicial Performance Policy Report|aliases=2020 ICC KPI Report|legal_basis=ICC-ASP/13/Res.5, Annex I, para. 7(b); ICC Strategic Plans 2019–2021 (Presidency, OTP, Registry); Rome Statute Arts. 74, 75, 76, 81, 93|date=11 December 2020|status=Official / Published (Revised Version)|jurisdiction=International Criminal Law / International Criminal Court (ICC)|institution=International Criminal Court (ICC) / Assembly of States Parties (ASP)}}'''Report of the Court on Key Performance Indicators 2020 (Revised Version)''' is the official ICC report dated 11 December 2020, presenting qualitative and quantitative data measuring judicial and prosecutorial efficiency, international cooperation, complementarity, and organizational performance through 30 September 2020.

== Summary ==
The report measures the Court's achievements against the 2019–2021 Strategic Plan adopted by the three organs of the Court on 17 July 2019. For the first time, it incorporates indicators on Cooperation and Complementarity alongside the seven-phase judicial performance framework and organizational performance metrics.

== Legal Basis ==

* Mandate of the Assembly of States Parties: Resolution [[ICC-ASP/13/Res.5]], Annex I, paragraph 7(b).
* [[ICC Strategic Plan 2019–2021]] (Presidency, OTP, Registry), dated 17 July 2019.
* [[Rome Statute]]: Article 74 (Trial Judgment), Article 75 (Reparations), Article 76 (Sentencing), Article 81 (Appeal), and Article 93 (International Cooperation).
* [[Chambers' Practice Manual]] (4th Edition, November 2019).

== Background ==
Development of the KPI framework began at the ASP's request in 2014. Following reports published in 2015, 2016, 2017, and 2019 (the 2018 report having been retroactively merged into the 2019 report), the 2020 report refines the measurement framework by incorporating cooperation and complementarity indicators for the first time on a systematic basis.

== Objectives ==

* Ensure judicial proceedings are fair and expeditious.
* Measure the effectiveness of requests for assistance and cooperation (RFA/RFC).
* Measure the impact of OTP support in strengthening national investigative and prosecutorial capacity (complementarity).
* Measure organizational performance in budget execution, geographical representation, gender balance, and IT security.

== Key Provisions ==
Judicial performance is measured across 7 phases:

* '''Phase 1''': Confirmation of Charges.
* '''Phase 2''': Trial Preparation.
* '''Phase 3''': Trial.
* '''Phase 4''': Trial Deliberations.
* '''Phase 5''': Sentencing.
* '''Phase 6''': Reparations.
* '''Phase 7''': Final Appeals.

Judges also adopted decision deadlines in the 4th edition of the Chambers' Practice Manual (November 2019), including a 10-month deadline for Article 74 written judgments following the end of closing statements.

== Implementation ==
Data collection was led by the Registry, in coordination with the Presidency and the OTP. In 2020, the OTP sent 402 requests for assistance (RFAs), with 32.33% executed as of 15 September 2020 (average execution time 40.5 days), and 10 preliminary-examination requests for information (RFIs). On complementarity, the OTP received 34 RFAs from national authorities, responding substantively to 97% within less than three months (average 42 days). On IT security, the Court's systems repelled 40 million cyberattack attempts per month, with critical incident response time improving from 46 minutes (2019) to 29 minutes (2020). Staff performance appraisal completion reached 95–96%.

== Policy Issues ==

* 23 States Parties remain under-represented and 56 non-represented among Court staff as of 30 September 2020.
* Gender imbalance at the senior D-1 management level (only 11.11% women).
* Operational constraints from the COVID-19 pandemic and unilateral US sanctions.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''[[International Criminal Court]]''': Institution that published the report.
* '''[[Assembly of States Parties]]''': Oversight body that mandated the KPI framework.
* '''[[Registry (ICC)]]''': Organ coordinating KPI data collection.
* '''[[Study Group on Governance]]''': Working group consulted on KPI development.
* '''[[Thomas Lubanga Dyilo]]''': Convicted in Case ICC-01/04-01/06, released on 15 March 2020 after serving his full sentence; symbolic and collective reparations for victims remain ongoing.
* '''[[Germain Katanga]]''': Convicted in Case ICC-01/04-01/06; implementation of individual and collective reparations orders totaling USD 1,000,000 continues to be monitored by Trial Chamber II.
* '''[[Jean-Pierre Bemba Gombo]]''': Former accused whose compensation claim relating to his detention was rejected by Pre-Trial Chamber II on 18 May 2020.
* '''[[Bosco Ntaganda]]''': Convicted by Trial Chamber VI on 8 July 2019 of 5 crimes against humanity and 13 war crimes, and sentenced to 30 years' imprisonment on 7 November 2019.
* '''[[Dominic Ongwen]]''': Accused member of the Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), whose evidentiary phase concluded on 6 December 2019 and entered the judicial deliberation phase on 13 March 2020.
* '''[[Laurent Gbagbo]]''' and '''[[Charles Blé Goudé]]''': Acquitted defendants, currently in the appeals phase without detention at the ICC Detention Centre.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''
* '''[[Ferdi Raditya Akbar]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''

== See Also ==

* [[International Criminal Court]]
* [[Rome Statute]]
* [[Assembly of States Parties (ICC)]]

== References ==

* International Criminal Court, "Report of the Court on Key Performance Indicators" (Revised version), 11 December 2020.

title: JPW-REPORT-005
wikitext:
{{Infobox|stable_id=JPW-REPORT-004|canonical_name=2021 Report of the Court on Key Performance Indicators|official_name=2021 Report of the Court on Key Performance Indicators|type=Official Institutional Report / Judicial Performance Policy Report|aliases=2021 ICC KPI Report|legal_basis=ICC-ASP/13/Res.5; ICC Strategic Plans 2019–2021; Rome Statute Arts. 74, 75, 76, 81, 85, 93(10); Chambers' Practice Manual|date=2021 (full calendar-year reporting, January–December 2021)|status=Official / Published|jurisdiction=International Criminal Law / International Criminal Court (ICC)|institution=International Criminal Court (ICC) / Assembly of States Parties (ASP)}}'''2021 Report of the Court on Key Performance Indicators''' is the official ICC report presenting the evaluation of judicial, prosecutorial, international cooperation, complementarity, and organizational performance for the full 2021 calendar year.

== Summary ==
For the first time, the report presents a complete year of performance data (January–December 2021), covering the seven-phase judicial framework, judicial decision timeframes, international cooperation, complementarity, and organizational performance.

== Legal Basis ==

* Mandate of the Assembly of States Parties: Resolution [[ICC-ASP/13/Res.5]].
* [[ICC Strategic Plan 2019–2021]] (Presidency, OTP, Registry).
* [[Rome Statute]]: Articles 74, 75, 76, 81, 85, and 93(10).
* [[Chambers' Practice Manual]] (source of judicial decision-timeframe indicators).

== Background ==
Development of the KPI framework began at the ASP's request in 2014. Following reports published in 2015, 2016, 2017, 2019, and 2020, the 2021 report introduces methodological reforms based on Recommendation 146 of the Independent Expert Review (IER).

== Objectives ==

* Measure the efficiency, expeditiousness, and fairness of judicial proceedings.
* Assess compliance with judicial decision deadlines under the Chambers' Practice Manual.
* Measure the effectiveness of international cooperation and mutual legal assistance.
* Assess the impact of positive complementarity at the national level.

== Key Provisions ==
Judicial performance is measured across 7 phases:

* '''Phase 1''': Confirmation of Charges.
* '''Phase 2''': Trial Preparation.
* '''Phase 3''': Trial.
* '''Phase 4''': Trial Deliberations.
* '''Phase 5''': Sentencing.
* '''Phase 6''': Reparations.
* '''Phase 7''': Final Appeals.

== Implementation ==
The Registry led data collection in coordination with the Presidency and OTP. In 2021, the OTP sent 338 requests for assistance (RFAs) to 57 partners, with a 57.19% execution rate and average execution time of 58 days. On complementarity, the OTP received 24 incoming RFAs from national authorities under Article 93(10) of the Rome Statute, responding substantively to 100% within less than three months (average 34 days). Transcript and translation service workload rose approximately 400% year-on-year while maintaining a 100% delivery rate. The Court recorded 5,956 new registrations for victim participation/reparations and 1,354 new beneficiaries of collective reparations in the *Lubanga* case. IT security systems handled 40 million threat attempts per month, and staff performance-goal-setting compliance reached 96%.

== Policy Issues ==

* 25 States Parties remain under-represented and 54 non-represented among Court staff as of 2021.
* Gender imbalance persists at senior management levels (P-4 and above).
* COVID-19 travel restrictions continued to affect missions and field cooperation.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''[[International Criminal Court]]''': Institution that published the report.
* '''[[Assembly of States Parties]]''': Oversight body that mandated the KPI framework.
* '''[[Registry (ICC)]]''': Organ coordinating KPI data collection.
* '''[[Study Group on Governance]]''': Working group that approved the shift to full calendar-year reporting in October 2021.
* '''[[Karim A.A. Khan QC]]''': ICC Prosecutor who began his term in 2021 and led strategic complementarity initiatives, including closing the Colombia preliminary examination and signing a Memorandum of Understanding with Venezuela.
* '''[[Yoshimitsu Yamauchi]]''': Special Advisor on Mutual Legal Assistance, appointed by Prosecutor Karim A.A. Khan QC to strengthen judicial cooperation relationships.
* '''[[Thomas Lubanga Dyilo]]''': Convicted in Case ICC-01/04-01/06; Trial Chamber II monitors implementation of the symbolic and service-based collective reparations plan.
* '''[[Germain Katanga]]''': Convicted in Case ICC-01/04-01/06; Trial Chamber II oversees implementation of individual and collective reparations orders.
* '''[[Laurent Gbagbo]]''' and '''[[Charles Blé Goudé]]''': Defendants whose acquittal was confirmed by the Appeals Chamber on 31 March 2021.
* '''[[Bosco Ntaganda]]''': Convicted defendant whose conviction and sentence were confirmed by the Appeals Chamber on 30 March 2021.
* '''[[Dominic Ongwen]]''': Convicted of 61 crimes against humanity and war crimes in Northern Uganda, sentenced to 25 years' imprisonment on 6 May 2021.
* '''[[Ali Muhammad Ali Abd-Al-Rahman]]''' ("Ali Kushayb"): Defendant whose war crimes and crimes against humanity charges were confirmed by Pre-Trial Chamber II on 9 July 2021.
* '''[[Paul Gicheru]]''': Defendant whose charges of offences against the administration of justice were confirmed by Pre-Trial Chamber A on 15 July 2021.
* '''[[Mahamat Said Abdel Kani]]''': Defendant whose war crimes and crimes against humanity charges were confirmed by Pre-Trial Chamber II on 9 December 2021.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''
* '''[[Ferdi Raditya Akbar]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''

title: JPW-REPORT-006
wikitext:
{{Infobox|stable_id=JPW-REPORT-005|canonical_name=Situation in the Plurinational State of Bolivia: Final Report|official_name=Situation in the Plurinational State of Bolivia: Final Report (14 February 2022)|type=Official Final Judicial Policy Report / Preliminary Examination Final Report|aliases=OTP Final Report on Bolivia (2022), Situation in Bolivia Final Report|legal_basis=Rome Statute, Article 5, Article 7 (7(1)(a), 7(1)(k), 7(2)(a)), Article 14(1), Article 30, Article 53(1), Article 53(3)(a), Article 53(4); Rules 105, 107, 108 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence|date=14 February 2022|status=Official / Published / Preliminary Examination Closed|jurisdiction=International Criminal Law / Plurinational State of Bolivia / International Criminal Court (ICC)|institution=Office of the Prosecutor (OTP-ICC) / Pre-Trial Chamber III / Government of the Plurinational State of Bolivia}}'''Situation in the Plurinational State of Bolivia: Final Report''' is the official final report published by the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) of the International Criminal Court on 14 February 2022, formally concluding the closure of the preliminary examination into the situation in Bolivia after finding no reasonable basis to believe that crimes against humanity occurred during the August 2020 road blockades.

== Summary ==
The report presents an independent factual and legal analysis of the Bolivian government's referral concerning nationwide road blockades from 3 to 14 August 2020. The Prosecutor concluded that there was no reasonable basis to believe that crimes against humanity within the Court's jurisdiction had been committed, and the preliminary examination was formally closed.

== Legal Basis ==

* [[Rome Statute]]: Article 5 (Jurisdiction of the Court), Article 7(1)(a) (Murder), Article 7(1)(k) (Other Inhumane Acts), Article 7(2)(a) (Organizational Policy/Attack Element), Article 14(1) (State Party Referral), Article 30 (Mental Element), Article 53(1) (Reasonable Basis Standard), Article 53(3)(a) (Pre-Trial Chamber Review), and Article 53(4) (Reconsideration on New Facts).
* Bolivia ratified the Rome Statute on 27 June 2002 (jurisdiction effective from 1 September 2002).

== Background ==
Following the resignation of President [[Evo Morales]] in November 2019, Interim President [[Jeanine Áñez]] scheduled new elections. Repeated postponements of the election date due to the COVID-19 pandemic triggered nationwide road-blockade protests organized by the *Central Obrera Boliviana* (COB) and the *Pacto de Unidad* (PdU) in August 2020.

== Objectives ==

* Assess whether allegations of medical oxygen shortages caused by the road blockades meet the subject-matter jurisdiction threshold for crimes against humanity under Article 7 of the Rome Statute.
* Determine whether a legally sufficient basis exists to seek authorization to open a formal investigation under Article 53(1).

== Key Provisions ==

* '''No Structured Attack Policy''': The road blockades constituted a limited (12-day) form of political protest not designed to attack the civilian population.
* '''Safe-Passage Directives''': Protest leadership (COB and PdU) issued official directives permitting medical and oxygen convoys to pass.
* '''Mens Rea Analysis''': The murder qualification under Article 7(1)(a) was rejected because protesters were not found to have acted with direct intent (*dolus directus*) as required by Article 30 of the Rome Statute.

== Implementation ==
The government activated "Operation Salvando Vidas," using the Bolivian Air Force to transport 158 tonnes of medical oxygen. The OTP examined the referral together with 250 supporting annexes and cross-institutional data, including from OHCHR, the OAS, and the IACHR.

== Evidence ==

* Leadership of the main organizations (COB and PdU) repeatedly issued written and verbal instructions for participants to allow safe passage to ambulances and medical oxygen convoys.
* Medical vehicles and convoys successfully passed through various blockade points following on-site negotiation.
* The government's air corridor operation transported 158 tonnes of medical oxygen across 41 Bolivian Air Force flights.
* For nine deaths potentially linked to supply delays, no evidence was found that protesters acted with direct intent (*dolus directus*) to kill under Article 30; at most, awareness of risk (*dolus eventualis*) was found, which does not meet the threshold for murder under Article 7(1)(a).

== Policy Issues ==

* Assessing the threshold distinguishing incidental consequences of political protest from a structured attack under Article 7 of the Rome Statute.
* The OTP's lack of investigative powers at the preliminary examination stage.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''[[Office of the Prosecutor (ICC)]]''': Organ that published the report.
* '''[[Pre-Trial Chamber III]]''': Chamber assigned to the situation.
* '''[[Government of Bolivia]]''': Party that submitted the Article 14(1) referral.
* '''[[Central Obrera Boliviana]]''' (COB): Organization that led the road blockades.
* '''[[Pacto de Unidad]]''' (PdU): Alliance of social organizations supporting the protests.
* '''[[Jeanine Áñez Chávez]]''': Interim President of Bolivia who signed the accreditation letter and submitted the official referral to the ICC on 4 September 2020; later arrested on 12 March 2021 on charges of terrorism and sedition related to the November 2019 transfer of power.
* '''[[Evo Morales]]''': Former President of Bolivia and leader of the *Movimiento al Socialismo* (MAS) party, who resigned in November 2019 amid the disputed October 2019 election, and voiced support for the August 2020 protests.
* '''[[Luis Arce]]''': MAS presidential candidate who won Bolivia's presidential election on 18 October 2020 with 55% of the vote.
* '''[[Juan Carlos Huarachi]]''': Executive Secretary of the *Central Obrera Boliviana* (COB), who led the organization of the nationwide road blockades and signed instructions to secure medical supply routes.
* '''[[Leonardo Loza]]''': Leader of the *Pacto de Unidad* (PdU) and a coca-growers' federation, involved in organizing the blockades and signing their suspension.
* '''[[Fatou Bensouda]]''': ICC Prosecutor who received Bolivia's official referral on 4 September 2020 and announced the opening of the preliminary examination on 9 September 2020.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''
* '''[[Ferdi Raditya Akbar]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''

== See Also ==

* [[International Criminal Court]]
* [[Rome Statute]]
* [[Crimes Against Humanity]]

== References ==

* Office of the Prosecutor, International Criminal Court, "Situation in the Plurinational State of Bolivia: Final Report," 14 February 2022.

title: JPW-REPORT-007
wikitext:
'''Twenty-Third Report of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court to the United Nations Security Council on the Situation in Libya''' is the 23rd periodic report submitted by the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) of the International Criminal Court to the UN Security Council on 28 April 2022, pursuant to UNSC Resolution 1970 (2011), presenting a comprehensive review, updated strategy, and accountability roadmap for crimes committed in Libya.

== Summary ==
The report presents a comprehensive evaluation of investigative progress on crimes in Libya since the 2011 referral, alongside a new strategy focused on leveraging AI technology, strengthening complementarity with Libyan authorities, and setting concrete, time-bound targets.

== Legal Basis ==

* [[UN Security Council Resolution 1970 (2011)]], adopted under Chapter VII of the UN Charter.
* [[Rome Statute]]: Article 42(6) (Prosecutor Recusal), Article 68 (Protection of Victims and Witnesses), and Article 93(10) (Mutual Legal Assistance).

== Background ==
Since receiving the UNSC referral in 2011, the OTP has investigated international crimes in Libya. The 23rd report reviews eleven years of investigative progress and sets out a new roadmap to address ongoing security and political obstacles.

== Objectives ==

* Prioritize the UNSC referral through adequate resource and staff allocation.
* Increase direct engagement with victims, witnesses, and affected communities on the ground.
* Advance complementarity by supporting Libyan domestic law enforcement and cooperation with third states/Europol.
* Develop a structured completion strategy for the Libya situation.

== Key Provisions ==
The OTP's work is organized around four main lines of inquiry:

* '''2011 Crimes''': Investigation complete; focus now on executing outstanding arrest warrants.
* '''Detention Facilities''': Investigation of torture and sexual violence in official and secret detention facilities, supported by 3D crime-scene modeling.
* '''2014–2020 Military Operations''': Investigation of mass killings and enforced disappearances in Tarhuna and Tripoli.
* '''Crimes Against Migrants''': Investigation of human trafficking, extortion, and torture, in cooperation with the Joint Team.

== Implementation ==
The OTP is deploying a big-data evidence-processing platform using artificial intelligence and machine learning for automated transcription and translation of Arabic-language audio and video material, alongside cloud-based eDiscovery tools. The Office has collected approximately 50,000 items of potential evidence, added 300+ new items during the reporting period, conducted 6 field missions, and held 35+ meetings with international partners and NGOs.

== Policy Issues ==

* Political deadlock and security instability limiting investigators' physical access to crime scenes in Libya.
* Budgetary and staffing constraints within the OTP.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''[[Office of the Prosecutor (ICC)]]''': Organ that published the report.
* '''[[United Nations Security Council]]''': UN body that received the report.
* '''[[Europol]]''': Operational cooperation partner within the Joint Team, alongside the Netherlands, Italy, the United Kingdom, and Ireland.
* '''[[Muammar Mohammed Abu Minyar Gaddafi]]''': Former Libyan leader against whom an ICC arrest warrant was issued in connection with the 2011 violence; proceedings were terminated on 22 November 2011 following his death.
* '''[[Saif Al-Islam Gaddafi]]''': Defendant whose ICC arrest warrant remains unexecuted; his admissibility challenge was rejected by the Appeals Chamber on 5 April 2019.
* '''[[Abdullah Al-Senussi]]''': Former Libyan official whose ICC case was declared inadmissible by the Appeals Chamber on 24 July 2014, as it was being handled by Libya's domestic judicial process.
* '''[[Al-Tuhamy Mohamed Khaled]]''': Subject of an ICC arrest warrant reportedly deceased; the OTP is confirming the reported death before withdrawing the warrant.
* '''[[Mahmoud Al-Werfalli]]''': Subject of two ICC arrest warrants (2017 and 2018) relating to crimes by groups affiliated with the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF), reportedly deceased.
* '''[[Stephanie Williams]]''': Special Adviser to the UN Secretary-General for Libya, who coordinates with the OTP on accountability efforts.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''
* '''[[Ferdi Raditya Akbar]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''

== See Also ==

* [[International Criminal Court]]
* [[United Nations Security Council]]
* [[Rome Statute]]

== References ==

* Office of the Prosecutor, International Criminal Court, "Twenty-Third Report of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court to the United Nations Security Council pursuant to Resolution 1970 (2011)," 28 April 2022.

title: JPW-REPORT-008
wikitext:
'''Twenty-Fourth Report of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court to the United Nations Security Council on the Situation in Libya''' is the 24th periodic report submitted by the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) to the UN Security Council on 9 November 2022, pursuant to UNSC Resolution 1970 (2011), presenting progress on the accountability roadmap and updated strategy for Libya.

== Summary ==
The report records significant progress in implementing the Libya accountability roadmap, including sustained physical presence in the country for the first time since 2011, the collection of over 1,000 items of evidence, full participation in the Joint Team on crimes against migrants, and the arrest and extradition of key suspects located in Ethiopia.

== Legal Basis ==

* [[UN Security Council Resolution 1970 (2011)]], invoking Chapter VII of the UN Charter.
* [[Rome Statute]]: Article 42(6) (Prosecutor Self-Recusal), Article 56 (Preservation of Evidence by the Pre-Trial Chamber), and Article 68 (Protection and Welfare of Victims and Witnesses).

== Background ==
Since receiving the UNSC referral in 2011, the OTP has investigated serious crimes in Libya. The 24th report evaluates implementation of the updated four-principle strategy first presented in the April 2022 report.

== Objectives ==

* Prioritize resource allocation for investigation and prosecution of the Libya situation.
* Strengthen empowerment of victims, witnesses, and civil society organizations (NGOs).
* Advance direct complementarity dialogue with Libyan law enforcement authorities.
* Expand international cooperation with third states, Europol, and the Joint Team.

== Key Provisions ==
The four lines of inquiry include:

* '''2011 Violence''': Confirmation of death and termination of proceedings against suspect Al-Tuhamy Mohamed Khaled.
* '''Detention Facilities''': Investigation of killings, torture, and gender-based violence in official and secret detention facilities.
* '''2014–2020 Military Operations''': Investigation of extrajudicial killings in Tarhuna and Tripoli, and termination of proceedings against suspect Mahmoud Al-Werfalli.
* '''Crimes Against Migrants''': Investigation of human trafficking and torture in cooperation with the Joint Team.

== Implementation ==
The OTP maintained a sustained field presence, conducted 20+ missions to 6 countries, collected 1,000+ items of evidence, and leveraged Microsoft Azure infrastructure and AI tools for processing Arabic-language material. On 7 September 2022, the OTP formally became a full member of the Joint Team investigating crimes against migrants.

== Policy Issues ==

* Political and security deadlock in Libya continuing to affect investigators' access.
* Delays in fulfilling requests for assistance (RFAs) and visa issuance.
* Constrained Court operational budget in the final quarter of the year.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''[[Office of the Prosecutor (ICC)]]''': Organ that published the report.
* '''[[United Nations Security Council]]''': Recipient of the periodic report.
* '''[[Joint Team]]''': Joint investigative team comprising Europol and partner states investigating migrant-related crimes.

title: JPW-REPORT-009
wikitext:
'''2022 Report of the Court on Key Performance Indicators''' is the official ICC report presenting qualitative and quantitative evaluation data on judicial, prosecutorial, international cooperation, complementarity, and organizational governance performance for the full 2022 calendar year.

== Summary ==
The report was prepared pursuant to the ASP mandate (ICC-ASP/13/Res.5, 2014) and Recommendation 146 of the 2020 Independent Expert Review (IER). It measures performance across three main categories: judicial and prosecutorial performance, cooperation and complementarity, and organizational performance, under the 2019–2021 Strategic Plan (extended to 2022).

== Legal Basis ==

* Mandate of the Assembly of States Parties: Resolution [[ICC-ASP/13/Res.5]], Annex I, paragraph 7(b).
* [[ICC Strategic Plan 2019–2021]] (Presidency, OTP, Registry).
* [[Rome Statute]]: Articles 60(1), 61(9), 74, 76, 82, 85, and Part 9 (notably Articles 93(1)(k) and 93(10)).
* [[Chambers' Practice Manual]] and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence (Rule 68).

== Background ==
KPI development began at the ASP's request in 2014. Following periodic reports since 2015 and the 2020 IER recommendations (Recommendation 146), the 2022 report refines its data-visualization format to be more reader-friendly.

== Objectives ==

* Measure the efficiency, expeditiousness, and fairness of judicial proceedings.
* Clarify per-case judicial activity evaluation through structured data-visualization tools.
* Measure the effectiveness of requests for cooperation assistance (RFA) and participation in joint investigation teams (JITs).
* Assess organizational governance, IT security, and budgetary performance.

== Key Provisions ==
Judicial performance is measured across 7 phases:

* '''Phase 1''': Confirmation of Charges.
* '''Phase 2''': Trial Preparation.
* '''Phase 3''': Trial.
* '''Phase 4''': Trial Deliberations.
* '''Phase 5''': Sentencing.
* '''Phase 6''': Reparations.
* '''Phase 7''': Final Appeals.

Section B ("Judicial Activity by Key Phases") was redesigned to highlight 5–6 core performance data points per case using structured visual tools, addressing prior years' readability issues from dense single-page case data.

== Implementation ==
The Registry led data collection in coordination with the Presidency and OTP. In 2022, the OTP sent 422 RFAs to over 70 partners (a 24.85% increase over 2021) and processed 16 incoming RFAs from national authorities under Article 93(10), responding substantively to 100% within less than three months (average 37 days). Five active trials were in the evidence-presentation phase (*Al Hassan*, *Yekatom & Ngaïssona*, *Abd-Al-Rahman*, *Said*, *Gicheru*); Trial Chambers issued 1,023 judicial decisions, held 268 court sessions, and heard 125 witnesses in person. Original transcript production reached 37,376 pages (a 534% increase over 2020) at 100% delivery, with 3,638 interpreter-days of courtroom interpretation. The Victims Participation and Reparations Section (VPRS) received 6,539 new applications for participation/reparations, the highest volume from the Ukraine situation (1,686 applications). IT critical-incident response time was cut from 60 minutes (2021) to 12 minutes (2022), against 40 million monthly cyberattack attempts. There were 10,164 physical visits to public trial galleries, and staff performance-goal-setting compliance reached 96%.

== Policy Issues ==

* Difficulty obtaining sensitive, financial, or social-media information from certain states in fulfilling RFAs.
* Historical case backlog in the ICCPP witness protection program awaiting relocation support from States Parties.
* Need for closer coordination between the KPI report's publication schedule and other program/budget/HR performance reports.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''[[International Criminal Court]]''': Institution that published the report.
* '''[[Assembly of States Parties]]''': Oversight body that mandated the KPI framework.
* '''[[Registry (ICC)]]''': Organ coordinating data collection.
* '''[[Karim A.A. Khan QC]]''': ICC Prosecutor who led the OTP and pursued complementarity initiatives in the Central African Republic, Georgia, Libya, Colombia, Guinea, Venezuela, and Nigeria.
* '''[[Paul Gicheru]]''': Defendant in *The Prosecutor v. Paul Gicheru*; trial began 15 February 2022, evidence presentation closed 12 May 2022, and proceedings were terminated by Trial Chamber III on 14 October 2022 following confirmation of his death.
* '''[[Maxime Jeoffroy Eli Mokom Gawaka]]''': Defendant in *The Prosecutor v. Maxime Jeoffroy Eli Mokom Gawaka*, who made his first appearance on 22 March 2022; his case involved the disqualification of appointed counsel (Mr. Kaufman) due to a conflict of interest.
* '''[[Thomas Lubanga Dyilo]]''': Convicted in *The Prosecutor v. Thomas Lubanga Dyilo*; Trial Chamber II oversees implementation of the symbolic and service-based collective reparations plan.
* '''[[Germain Katanga]]''': Convicted in *The Prosecutor v. Germain Katanga*; Trial Chamber II monitors implementation of a USD 1,000,000 reparations order for 297 victims.
* '''[[Laurent Gbagbo]]''' and '''[[Charles Blé Goudé]]''': Defendants whose Article 85 compensation claim (Blé Goudé) was rejected on 10 February 2022, and whose request regarding publication of trial recordings (Gbagbo) was decided by Trial Chamber VII on 13 April 2022.
* '''[[Bosco Ntaganda]]''': Convicted defendant whose reparations order was partially vacated by the Appeals Chamber on 12 September 2022 and remanded to Trial Chamber II for a revised order.
* '''[[Ahmad Al Faqi Al Mahdi]]''': Convicted defendant; Trial Chamber VIII continued to oversee implementation of the reparations order throughout 2022.
* '''[[Dominic Ongwen]]''': Convicted defendant whose conviction and sentence were unanimously confirmed by the Appeals Chamber on 15 December 2022; reparations proceedings handled by Trial Chamber IX.
* '''[[Al Hassan Ag Abdoul Aziz Ag Mohamed Ag Mahmoud]]''': Defendant whose prosecution and defense evidence presentation concluded in 2022, with over 1,150 judicial decisions issued.
* '''[[Alfred Yekatom]]''' and '''[[Patrice-Edouard Ngaïssona]]''': Defendants whose prosecution evidence presentation continued throughout 2022, with over 750 decisions and testimony from 53 witnesses.

title: JPW-REPORT-010
wikitext:
'''Twenty-Sixth Report of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court to the United Nations Security Council on the Situation in Libya''' is the 26th periodic report submitted by the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) to the UN Security Council on 8 November 2023, pursuant to UNSC Resolution 1970 (2011), presenting progress on the updated investigative strategy, the near-conclusion of the 2014–2020 military operations line of inquiry, and a roadmap toward completion of OTP activities in Libya.

== Summary ==
This is the third periodic report since the launch of the updated strategy and roadmap in the April 2022 report (23rd Report). The report opens with condolences for the flooding disaster caused by Storm Daniel, which struck Derna in September 2023.

== Legal Basis ==

* [[UN Security Council Resolution 1970 (2011)]], invoking Chapter VII of the UN Charter.
* [[Rome Statute]]: Article 15 (Communication of Information) and Article 42(6) (Prosecutor Self-Recusal).

== Background ==
Since receiving the UNSC referral in 2011, the OTP has investigated international crimes in Libya. The 26th report is the third periodic update measuring progress against the benchmarks set in the April 2022 roadmap.

== Objectives ==

* Optimize allocation of regular-budget resources and seconded expert staff.
* Strengthen empowerment of victims, witnesses, and NGOs through evidence-documentation Guidelines training.
* Advance direct complementarity partnerships with Libyan law enforcement authorities.
* Expand cooperation with the Joint Team, Europol, and third states.

== Key Provisions ==
The four lines of inquiry include:

* '''2011 Violence''': Focused on executing the outstanding public arrest warrant against Saif Al-Islam Gaddafi.
* '''Detention Facilities''': Investigation of torture and violence in detention facilities, supported by clinical forensic medical capacity.
* '''2014–2020 Military Operations''': This line of inquiry is approaching completion.
* '''Crimes Against Migrants''': Investigation of human trafficking, enslavement, and extortion in cooperation with the Joint Team.

== Implementation ==
The OTP launched the OTPLink portal, migrated evidence to an AI/machine-learning-based cloud system (Project Harmony), and recruited 7 psychosocial support specialists. The Prosecutor, Karim A.A. Khan QC, voluntarily recused himself under Article 42(6) of the Rome Statute from lines of inquiry posing a potential conflict of interest arising from his prior role as defense counsel; Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan assumed full oversight of the affected lines of inquiry.

The Unified Libya Team conducted over 15 missions to three regions, collected over 4,000 items of evidence (audio, video, forensic materials, satellite imagery), conducted 20+ witness interviews, screened 30+ potential witnesses, and held training on evidence-documentation Guidelines together with the International Commission of Jurists.

== Evidence ==

* Collection of over 4,000 new items of evidence.
* Analysis of hundreds of witness statements in cooperation with the Joint Team.
* Use of forensic clinical medical capacity to assess torture-related injuries.
* Recording of over 12,000 migrants intercepted at sea and returned to Libya in 2023.
* More than 2,000 migrants reported dead or missing along the Central Mediterranean Route.

== Policy Issues ==

* Delays in visa issuance by local Libyan authorities for operational-level investigators.
* Regular-budget constraints affecting the OTP's capacity to analyze financial flows and proceeds of crime.
* Psychological risks and re-traumatization concerns for victims and witnesses.
* Humanitarian crisis following the Storm Daniel flooding disaster in Derna in September 2023.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''[[Office of the Prosecutor (ICC)]]''': Organ that published the report.
* '''[[United Nations Security Council]]''': Recipient of the periodic report.
* '''[[Joint Team]]''': Joint investigative team on crimes against migrants.
* '''[[OTPLink]]''': Digital platform for receiving new evidence and Article 15 communications.
* '''[[Karim A.A. Khan QC]]''': ICC Prosecutor who voluntarily recused himself under Article 42(6) from any line of inquiry posing a potential conflict of interest arising from his prior role as defense counsel.
* '''[[Nazhat Shameem Khan]]''': ICC Deputy Prosecutor who assumed full oversight responsibility for investigations in the lines of inquiry affected by the Prosecutor's recusal.
* '''[[Zeiad S. S. Daghim]]''': Ambassador of Libya to the Netherlands, who confirmed the Presidential Council's directive to expand judicial cooperation with the OTP, including technical visas and forensic support.
* '''[[Mohamed al-Menfi]]''': President of the Presidential Council of Libya, who instructed the Libyan Embassy in the Netherlands to provide full cooperation to the OTP.
* '''[[Saif Al-Islam Gaddafi]]''': Sole subject of an outstanding public arrest warrant related to crimes committed against protesters and opponents of the Gaddafi regime in 2011.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''
* '''[[Ferdi Raditya Akbar]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''

title: JPW-REPORT-011
wikitext:
'''Fortieth Report of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court to the United Nations Security Council pursuant to Resolution 1593 (2005)''' is the official periodic evaluation document submitted by the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) of the International Criminal Court on 27 January 2025.

== Summary ==
This report outlines key developments in the execution of the investigative strategy in Darfur for the reporting period spanning August 2024 to January 2025. Key achievements include the conclusion of the trial proceedings for Ali Muhammad Ali Abd-Al-Rahman ("Ali Kushayb"), the compilation of over 6,000 items of evidence regarding crimes committed since April 2023, and preparations for filing new arrest warrant applications.

== Legal Basis ==

* [[United Nations Security Council Resolution 1593 (2005)]] under Chapter VII of the UN Charter.
* [[Rome Statute]]: Article 42(6) (Self-Recusal of the Prosecutor), Article 53 (Initiation of Investigation), and Article 58 (Issuance of Arrest Warrants).

== Background ==
Since the UN Security Council referral in 2005, the OTP has prosecuted international crimes committed in Darfur. This fortieth report responds to a renewed wave of violence erupting in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) across West and North Darfur.

== Objectives ==

* Submit multiple new applications for arrest warrants concerning 2023 and ongoing crimes.
* Broaden complementarity cooperation with domestic authorities and the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan (FFM-Sudan).
* Secure the arrest and surrender of main fugitives (Omar Al Bashir, Abdel Raheem Hussein, and Ahmad Harun).

== Key Provisions ==

* **Investigation of 2023–Ongoing Crimes**: Investigations focus on killings, looting, attacks on internally displaced person (IDP) camps, and gender-based crimes in Al Geneina and El Fasher.
* **Trial of Ali Abd-Al-Rahman**: Trial proceedings concluded in December 2024 across 31 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity.
* **Main Fugitive Cases**: Evaluation of Ahmad Harun's whereabouts and the Government of Sudan's obligations under Resolution 1593.
* **Abdallah Banda Case**: Proceedings overseen by Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan following the Prosecutor's recusal.

== Implementation ==
The OTP conducted investigative missions to Chad (Adre refugee camp), gathered 6,000 digital evidence items and testimonies, utilized the OTPLink platform, and collaborated closely with the UK War Crimes Team.

== Policy Issues ==

* Failure of the RSF to execute requests for assistance.
* Budgetary constraints and an urgent need for Arabic-speaking seconded experts.
* Field security challenges and witness protection measures.

* **[[Office of the Prosecutor]]**: Issuing institution of the report.

title: JPW-REPORT-012
wikitext:
'''Final Report on the Implementation of the Court-wide Strategy on Gender Equality and Workplace Culture (2023–2025)''' is the official three-year comprehensive evaluation report issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC), reviewing the progress of its first court-wide strategy across 30 action components and 3 strategic pillars [1–5, 10–12, 24, 110–125].

== Summary ==
This report evaluates the execution of the GEWC Strategy 2023–2025. Key outcomes include the strengthening of disciplinary frameworks, an increase in female representation among senior management (P-5 and D-1 levels), the formalization of flexible working arrangements, and the adoption of core organizational values [4, 6–9, 110–120].

== Legal Basis ==

* [[Rome Statute]]: Article 112(4) regarding independent oversight mechanisms.
* [[Assembly of States Parties Resolutions]]: ICC-ASP/1/Res.10, ICC-ASP/8/Res.1, ICC-ASP/12/Res.6, ICC-ASP/19/Res.6, and ICC-ASP/22/Res.3.
* [[ICC Administrative Instructions]]: ICC/AI/2022/001, ICC/AI/2022/002, ICC/AI/2022/003, ICC/AI/2022/004, ICC/AI/2023/001, ICC/AI/2024/002, and ICC/AI/2024/003.
* [[Presidential Directives]]: ICC/PRESD/G/2024/001 (Protection Against Retaliation).

== Background ==
The GEWC Strategy was launched at the 21st session of the ASP in December 2022 to address recommendations from the 2020 Independent Expert Review (IER) and staff engagement surveys from 2018 and 2021 [10, 16–19].

== Objectives ==

* Pillar I: Building a safe and inclusive workplace culture and processes [2, 25–70].
* Pillar II: Fostering the integration of personal and professional life [2, 71–80].
* Pillar III: Advancing gender equality and career opportunities [2, 81–108].

== Key Provisions ==

* **Disciplinary & Anti-Harassment Framework**: Implementation of zero-tolerance policies and reporting channels via the Ombuds and the Independent Oversight Mechanism (IOM) [6, 25–36].
* **Work-Life Integration**: Introduction of Flexible Working Arrangements (ICC/AI/2022/004) and gender-neutral parental leave (ICC/AI/2024/003).
* **Gender Parity Achievements**: Overall female staff representation reached 52% in 2024. P-5 female representation rose to 46%, and D-1 reached 44%.
* **Core Values**: Establishment of core values—"Integrity, Fairness, Accountability, and Inclusion"—in January 2024.

== Implementation ==
Monitoring was conducted jointly by the Focal Point for Gender Equality (FPGE) and the Staff Wellbeing and Engagement Committee (SWEC). Mandatory training modules ("United to Respect" and "Gender Equality") were completed by 1,090 and 991 personnel respectively as of 24 June 2025.

== Policy Issues ==

* Continued fear of retaliation (65% of misconduct victims remain reluctant to report incidents).
* The need to bridge gender gaps at the P-4 professional level (37% female representation in 2024).

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* **[[International Criminal Court]]**: Implementing institution.
* **[[Assembly of States Parties]]**: Oversight body.
* **[[Independent Oversight Mechanism]]**: Formal investigative body.
* **[[Ombuds]]**: Informal counseling and conflict resolution service.

title: JPW-REPORT-013
wikitext:
'''Report on Cooperation Challenges Faced by the Court with Respect to Financial Investigations''' is the official report summarizing the findings and recommendations of a 2015 workshop and panel discussion organized by the International Criminal Court in cooperation with the Principality of Liechtenstein and the International Centre for Asset Recovery (ICAR, Basel Institute on Governance), with financial support from the European Commission, to evaluate challenges and formulate recommendations for improving international cooperation in financial investigations and the tracing, freezing, and confiscation of assets.

== Summary ==
The report was prepared following a workshop held on 26–27 October 2015 in The Hague, and a panel discussion held on the margins of the Assembly of States Parties (ASP) session on 19 November 2015. It examines the legal framework and operational obstacles in financial investigations and sets out strategic recommendations for both States Parties and the Court aimed at tracing and confiscating illicit assets to fund victim reparations and improve judicial efficiency.

== Legal Basis ==

* [[Rome Statute]]:
** '''Article 54''': Duties and powers of the Prosecutor in investigations.
** '''Article 57(3)(e)''': Power of the Pre-Trial Chamber to issue protective/asset-freezing orders.
** '''Article 75''': Reparations orders for victims.
** '''Articles 86 and 88''': States Parties' general obligation to cooperate and to adapt domestic law accordingly.
** '''Article 93(1)(k)''': Form of international cooperation in the identification, tracing, freezing, and seizure of assets.
* [[Rules of Procedure and Evidence]]: Rule 21(5), on assessment of a suspect's financial means (indigence) for legal aid.

== Background ==
Rome Statute crimes are often linked to transnational organized crime and financial crime. International conventions such as UNCAC and UNTOC underscore the growing importance of asset tracing in international law enforcement. Strengthening financial-investigation capacity became especially pressing as the ICC entered the first reparations phase in the *Lubanga* case.

== Objectives ==

* Strengthen criminal evidence through financial linkage evidence, reducing reliance on witness testimony.
* Secure suspects' assets to enable confiscation orders and victim reparations.
* Ensure transparency and prevent abuse of the Court's legal aid scheme.
* Cut off perpetrators' financial capacity to continue criminal activity ("going after the money").

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Role of the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP)''': Gathers evidence of criminal financial flows and identifies assets for potential confiscation under Articles 54 and 93(1)(k).
* '''Role of the Chambers and Registry''': Chambers issue asset-freezing orders (Article 57(3)(e)), while the Registry coordinates execution of RFAs with partner states via internal MoU with the OTP and assesses a suspect's financial means under RPE Rule 21(5).
* '''Cooperation Challenges''': The absence of its own police force makes the Court heavily dependent on States Parties' cooperation under Articles 86 and 88.

== Implementation ==
Recommendations fall into three categories:

* '''For States Parties''': Adapt domestic law; designate specific financial-investigation contact points; hold informal consultations before formal RFAs; and open domestic money-laundering investigations based on Court-provided information ("reversed request").
* '''For the Court''': Develop a financial cooperation guidance manual; publish Appeals Chamber jurisprudence; map domestic legal systems; and explore secure network access to financial databases.
* '''For the Court and States Parties Jointly''': Conduct joint training; leverage Financial Intelligence Units (FIUs); and partner with the Egmont Group, CARIN, UNODC, StAR, Interpol, and Justice Rapid Response.

== Evidence ==
Financial investigations are grounded in Articles 54, 57(3)(e), 75, and 93(1)(k) of the Rome Statute and RPE Rule 21(5). In practice, asset tracing was directly applied in the first reparations phase of the *Lubanga* case.

== Policy Issues ==

* A shortage of qualified financial investigators both within the ICC and among national authorities.
* Domestic legal obstacles in some states that lack civil or criminal procedures for executing ICC asset-freezing requests.
* The absence of explicit guidance on the "nexus" limits of assets that may be frozen.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''[[International Criminal Court]]''': Organizing institution.
* '''[[Office of the Prosecutor]]''': Organ conducting financial evidence investigations.
* '''[[Registry (ICC)]]''': Organ executing RFAs and assessing legal aid eligibility.
* '''[[Principality of Liechtenstein]]''': Co-organizing partner of the workshop.
* '''[[ICAR]]''' (International Centre for Asset Recovery, Basel Institute on Governance): Technical substance partner on asset tracing.
* '''[[European Commission]]''': Financial sponsor of the workshop.
* '''[[Egmont Group]]''', '''[[CARIN]]''', '''[[UNODC]]''', '''[[StAR]]''', '''[[Interpol]]''', '''[[Justice Rapid Response]]''': International law-enforcement and capacity-building network partners.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''
* '''[[Ferdi Raditya Akbar]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''

title: JPW-REPORT-014
wikitext:
'''Report on Preliminary Examination Activities (2019)''' is the official annual report published by the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) of the International Criminal Court on 5 December 2019, summarizing the OTP's analysis and preliminary-examination activity concerning situations of international crime worldwide during the period 1 December 2018 to 30 November 2019, applying the Article 53(1) standard of the Rome Statute.

== Summary ==
The report presents the OTP's independent evaluation of communications and situations potentially warranting investigation of international crimes during the reporting period. It explains the application of the four-phase filtering framework and reports on progress in preliminary examinations across multiple regions.

== Legal Basis ==

* [[Rome Statute]]:
** '''Article 53(1)''': Legal framework for determining a reasonable basis to open an investigation, based on jurisdiction, admissibility, and the interests of justice.
** '''Articles 12 and 13''': Jurisdictional preconditions and triggering mechanisms (state/UNSC referral, Article 12(3) declaration, proprio motu under Article 15).
** '''Article 17''': Admissibility assessment based on complementarity and gravity.
* [[Rules of Procedure and Evidence]]: Rules 48 and 49.

== Background ==
Preliminary examination is the OTP's principal filtering mechanism for distinguishing situations that meet Rome Statute criteria from those that do not, while also encouraging genuine national proceedings.

== Objectives ==

* Ensure transparency and public accountability for OTP decisions.
* Apply a holistic analysis through the four-phase framework.
* Contribute to ending impunity and preventing crime.

== Key Provisions ==
'''Four-Phase Filtering Process''':

* '''Phase 1''': Initial assessment of Article 15 communications.
* '''Phase 2''': Subject-matter jurisdiction assessment.
* '''Phase 3''': Admissibility assessment (complementarity and gravity).
* '''Phase 4''': Interests of justice assessment.

'''2019 Phase 1 Closure Decisions''':

* '''North Korea (Dual Nationality)''': Rejected the claim that North Korean nationals held South Korean nationality from birth for purposes of personal jurisdiction.
* '''North Korea (Overseas Labourers)''': Rejected the qualification of enslavement under Article 7(1)(c) for North Korean overseas laborers in States Parties.
* '''Philippines (South China Sea)''': Rejected territorial jurisdiction over the EEZ/continental shelf, which does not form part of the coastal state's "territory."
* '''Yemen (Mercenaries)''': Found no evidence of involvement by State Party nationals as mercenaries in war crimes.

'''Phase 2 Situation''': Venezuela (analysis of alleged crimes against humanity since 2017).

'''Phase 3 Situations''': Colombia, Guinea, Iraq/UK, Nigeria, Palestine, Philippines, and Ukraine.

'''Completed Situation / Investigation Authorized''': Bangladesh/Myanmar (authorized by Pre-Trial Chamber III on 14 November 2019).

== Implementation ==
The OTP reviewed 795 Article 15 communications, conducted field missions to Conakry, Abuja, Kyiv, and Cox's Bazar, and participated in appellate proceedings before the ICC.

== Evidence ==

* Received 795 Article 15 communications (617 manifestly outside jurisdiction, 112 related to ongoing preliminary examinations, 25 related to active investigations/prosecutions, and 41 requiring further Phase 1 analysis).
* Completed the Bangladesh/Myanmar preliminary examination, with PTC III authorizing investigation on 14 November 2019 into alleged forced deportation of the Rohingya people (an estimated 600,000 to 1 million victims).
* Determined that the EEZ is not "territory" under the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and the *Island of Palmas* case.
* Collected tens of thousands of items of evidence and witness interviews across multiple countries.

== Policy Issues ==

* Limits on the Court's territorial jurisdiction in EEZ/international waters.
* Assessing the genuineness of domestic investigations under the complementarity framework.
* Constraints on evidence collection in active armed-conflict zones.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''[[Office of the Prosecutor (ICC)]]''': Organ that prepared the report.
* '''[[International Criminal Court]]''': Parent institution.
* '''[[Pre-Trial Chamber III]]''': Chamber that authorized the Bangladesh/Myanmar investigation.
* '''[[Fatou Bensouda]]''': ICC Prosecutor who led the OTP in determining and conducting preliminary examinations.
* '''[[Rodrigo Duterte]]''': President of the Philippines (former Mayor of Davao City), focus of a preliminary examination into the "war on drugs" campaign.
* '''[[Nicolás Maduro]]''': President of Venezuela, focus of a preliminary examination into violence against demonstrators and the opposition.
* '''[[Juan Guaidó]]''': President of the National Assembly of Venezuela, who proclaimed himself Interim President of Venezuela in January 2019.
* '''[[Viktor Yanukovych]]''': Former President of Ukraine, removed by the Ukrainian Parliament in February 2014 following the Maidan events.
* '''[[Moussa Dadis Camara]]''': Former Head of State / leader of the CNDD military junta in Guinea, in connection with the 28 September 2009 stadium massacre in Conakry.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''
* '''[[Ferdi Raditya Akbar]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''

== See Also ==

== References ==

title: JPW-REPORT-015
wikitext:
'''Twenty-Second Report of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court to the United Nations Security Council on the Situation in Libya''' is the 22nd periodic report submitted by the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) to the UN Security Council on 23 November 2021, pursuant to UNSC Resolution 1970 (2011), covering investigative progress in Libya, the Prosecutor's voluntary recusal from the Saif Al-Islam Gaddafi case, and the Office's complementarity and international-cooperation strategy.

== Summary ==
This is the first report issued under Prosecutor Karim A.A. Khan QC, who took office on 16 June 2021. It covers the reporting period 18 May to 17 November 2021, including the Prosecutor's voluntary recusal in the Saif Al-Islam Gaddafi case, investigations into crimes in Tarhuna, crimes against migrants, and cooperation with an international Joint Team.

== Legal Basis ==

* [[UN Security Council Resolution 1970 (2011)]]: Referral of the Libya situation.
* [[Rome Statute]]:
** '''Article 42(6)''': Voluntary recusal of the Prosecutor due to a conflict of interest.
** '''Article 93(10)''': Legal assistance and cooperation with States Parties (positive complementarity).

== Background ==
Since the UNSC referral in 2011, the OTP has investigated international crimes in Libya. This 22nd report was prepared following Karim A.A. Khan QC's appointment as Prosecutor on 16 June 2021.

== Objectives ==

* Ensure transparency of proceedings and safeguard institutional integrity against conflicts of interest.
* Encourage genuine national investigations by the Government of National Unity (GNU).
* Investigate crimes against migrants and detainees in official and unofficial detention facilities.

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Voluntary Recusal of Karim A.A. Khan QC''': Recusal from the Saif Al-Islam Gaddafi case under Article 42(6), with functions delegated to the Deputy Prosecutor.
* '''Verification of Suspects' Deaths''': Ongoing verification of reported deaths of Mahmoud Mustafa Busayf Al-Werfalli and Al-Tuhamy Mohamed Khaled.
* '''Crimes in Tarhuna and Tripoli''': Investigation into the discovery of mass graves in Tarhuna, allegedly linked to forces affiliated with the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF).
* '''Crimes Against Migrants''': Joint Team cooperation (Europol, Italy, UK, Netherlands) leading to a Dutch arrest warrant issued in October 2021.

== Implementation ==
The OTP processed requests for assistance (RFAs), met with victims' groups and NGOs, and facilitated complementarity-based investigative coordination under Article 93(10).

== Evidence ==

* Credible reports of mass graves in Tarhuna.
* IOM data showing 22,045 migrants and refugees intercepted and returned to Libya as of 14 August 2021.
* The October 2021 report of the UN Independent Fact-Finding Mission on Libya, documenting systematic and widespread abuses at detention facilities.
* A national arrest warrant issued by the Netherlands in October 2021, resulting from Joint Team cooperation.

== Policy Issues ==

* The practice of granting amnesties for serious crimes, which the OTP found incompatible with international human rights law.
* Limited field/in situ investigative access due to Libya's security situation.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''[[Office of the Prosecutor (ICC)]]''': Organ that published the report.
* '''[[United Nations Security Council]]''': Recipient of the report.
* '''[[Karim A.A. Khan QC]]''': ICC Prosecutor who took office on 16 June 2021, prepared the 22nd report, and voluntarily recused himself under Article 42(6) from the Saif Al-Islam Gaddafi case.
* '''[[Saif Al-Islam Gaddafi]]''': Suspect in the Libya situation for whom Prosecutor Khan had previously served as defence counsel, prompting delegation of prosecutorial functions in his case to the Deputy Prosecutor.
* '''[[Mahmoud Mustafa Busayf Al-Werfalli]]''': ICC suspect in the Libya situation, reportedly deceased, with the death under verification by the OTP.
* '''[[Al-Tuhamy Mohamed Khaled]]''': ICC suspect in the Libya situation, reportedly deceased, with the death under verification by the OTP.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''
* '''[[Ferdi Raditya Akbar]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''

title: JPW-REPORT-016
wikitext:
'''Thirty-Sixth Report of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court to the United Nations Security Council on the Situation in Darfur''' is the 36th periodic report submitted by the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) to the UN Security Council on 25 January 2023, pursuant to UNSC Resolution 1593 (2005), covering investigative progress, developments in the trial of Ali Muhammad Ali Abd-Al-Rahman, the Government of Sudan's continued lack of cooperation, and the Office's case-completion strategy.

== Summary ==
The report evaluates implementation of the Darfur situation's investigative strategy and roadmap for the period August 2022 to January 2023. Key achievements include rapid progress in the trial of Ali Muhammad Ali Abd-Al-Rahman, while the principal obstacle remains the Government of Sudan's failure to honor its cooperation commitments.

== Legal Basis ==

* [[UN Security Council Resolution 1593 (2005)]]: Referral of the situation in Darfur, Sudan.
* [[Rome Statute]]: Article 42(6), on the Prosecutor's voluntary recusal.

== Background ==
Since the UNSC referral in 2005, the OTP has investigated international crimes in Darfur, dating to 1 July 2002. The 36th report follows the Prosecutor's visit to Sudan and to refugee camps in August 2022.

== Objectives ==

* Complete presentation of the Prosecution's case in the trial of Ali Abd-Al-Rahman.
* Secure fulfillment of the Government of Sudan's cooperation commitments.
* Expand evidence-sharing cooperation with third states and civil society organizations.

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Trial of Ali Abd-Al-Rahman''': The first trial arising from the UNSC referral, on 31 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity.
* '''Cases of Al Bashir, Hussein, and Harun''': The suspects remain in detention in Sudan without surrender to the ICC.
* '''Case of Abdallah Banda''': Oversight assumed by Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan following Karim A.A. Khan KC's recusal.
* '''Sudan's Non-Cooperation''': 34 requests for assistance (RFAs) remain unanswered by Sudanese authorities.

== Implementation ==
The OTP heard testimony from 50 witnesses over 78 trial days in the Ali Abd-Al-Rahman trial, developed Guidelines for Civil Society Organisations jointly with Eurojust, and added Arabic-speaking personnel to the Darfur Unified Team.

== Evidence ==

* Presentation of evidence on 31 charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity relating to attacks on Kodoom, Bindisi, Mukjar, and Deleig.
* Collection of third-state evidence meeting the January 2023 benchmark.
* Testimony from 50 trial witnesses across 267+ hours, including 31 written statements, 24 full written testimonies, and 9 witnesses via video link.
* 274 victims authorized to participate in the trial.

== Policy Issues ==

* Obstacles to establishing a field office in Khartoum and visa restrictions.
* Denial of physical access to public and government archival documents in Sudan.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''[[Office of the Prosecutor (ICC)]]''': Organ that published the report.
* '''[[United Nations Security Council]]''': Recipient of the report.
* '''[[Government of Sudan]]''': Party that failed to execute 34 requests for assistance and denied field-office access.
* '''[[Ali Muhammad Ali Abd-Al-Rahman]]''' ("Ali Kushayb"): Principal defendant, a senior Militia/Janjaweed leader, tried on 31 counts of crimes against humanity and war crimes at Wadi Salih and Mukjar, West Darfur.
* '''[[Omar Hassan Ahmad Al Bashir]]''': Former President of Sudan, suspected of war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide in Darfur between 2003 and 2008; his arrest warrant remains outstanding.
* '''[[Abdel Raheem Muhammad Hussein]]''': Former senior Sudanese official, suspected of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Darfur between 2003 and 2004; held in detention in Sudan without surrender to the ICC.
* '''[[Ahmad Muhammad Harun]]''' ("Ahmad Harun"): Former senior Sudanese official, suspected of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Darfur between 2003 and 2004; also not surrendered to the ICC.
* '''[[Abdallah Banda Abakaer Nourain]]''' ("Abdallah Banda"): Fugitive suspected of three war crimes relating to a 29 September 2007 attack on a peacekeeping mission in Darfur.
* '''[[Karim A.A. Khan KC]]''': ICC Prosecutor who voluntarily recused himself under Article 42(6) from the Abdallah Banda case due to his prior role as defence counsel.
* '''[[Nazhat Shameem Khan]]''': ICC Deputy Prosecutor who assumed full oversight of the Abdallah Banda case following the Prosecutor's recusal.
* '''[[Amal Clooney]]''': Special Adviser for the Darfur situation, who facilitated review and analysis of large volumes of evidence and supported operational cooperation.
* '''[[General Abdel Fattah Al-Burhan]]''': Leader of the Government of Sudan, who made a direct commitment to the Prosecutor regarding access to documents and witnesses, which has not yet been fulfilled.
* '''[[Eurojust]]''': Partner organization in developing the Guidelines for Civil Society Organisations.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''
* '''[[Ferdi Raditya Akbar]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.'''

== See Also ==

* [[International Criminal Court]]
* [[United Nations Security Council]]
* [[Rome Statute]]

== References ==

* Office of the Prosecutor, International Criminal Court, "Thirty-Sixth Report of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court to the United Nations Security Council pursuant to Resolution 1593 (2005)," 25 January 2023.

title: JPW-REPORT-017
wikitext: == ICC 25th Report to UNSC on Libya — Wiki Entry (English) == '''Twenty-Fifth Report of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court to the United Nations Security Council on the Situation in Libya''' is the 25th periodic report submitted by the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) to the UN Security Council in May 2023, pursuant to UNSC Resolution 1970 (2011), presenting progress on the updated strategy, the issuance of arrest warrants under seal, adoption of the Relativity AI platform, and enforcement action against crimes affecting migrants. == Summary == The report covers investigative progress in Libya from November 2022 to May 2023. Key developments include arrest warrants issued under seal by Pre-Trial Chamber I, completion of an Article 56 evidence-preservation procedure, adoption of the Relativity AI platform, and successful Joint Team operations against a migrant-trafficking network. == Legal Basis == * [[UN Security Council Resolution 1970 (2011)]]: Referral of the Libya situation. * [[Rome Statute]]: ** '''Article 42(6)''': Voluntary Prosecutor recusal due to potential conflict of interest. ** '''Article 56''': Procedure for preserving key witness evidence before Pre-Trial Chamber I. ** '''Article 15''': Receipt of communications from civil society. == Background == Since the 2011 UNSC referral, the OTP has investigated international crimes in Libya. This 25th report is the second evaluation following the launch of the updated strategy and roadmap in April 2022, built on four principles: prioritized resource allocation, victim/witness empowerment, renewed partnership with Libyan authorities, and proactive cooperation with third states and international organizations. == Objectives == * Accelerate arrest-warrant applications in priority lines of inquiry. * Establish an OTP Liaison Office in Tripoli. * Strengthen the use of artificial intelligence in evidence analysis. == Key Provisions == * '''Arrest Warrants Under Seal''': Pre-Trial Chamber I issued several arrest warrants under seal. * '''Article 56 Procedure''': Completion of the witness-evidence preservation process before Pre-Trial Chamber I. * '''Adoption of Relativity AI''': Use of AI for automated processing and translation of Arabic-language documents. * '''Enforcement Against Migrant Crimes''': Extradition of Tewelde Goitom to the Netherlands, and arrest of an Eritrean suspect in Sudan. == Implementation == The OTP conducted 20+ investigative missions, collected 500+ items of evidence, engaged Arabic-speaking psychosocial experts, and collaborated with the UN Independent Fact-Finding Mission on Libya and Eurojust. Ongoing crimes persist against local residents and migrants at detention facilities across Libya (killings, torture, rape, enforced disappearance); crimes from the 2014–2020 military operations (extrajudicial killings, landmines, bombing of residential areas); and systematic crimes against migrants (trafficking, extortion, enslavement). == Evidence == * Collection of 500 new items of evidence (video, audio, satellite imagery, forensic materials). * 45+ witness interviews. * Successful extradition and pro forma hearing of a migrant-crimes case in the Netherlands. * Investigation of crimes at detention facilities in Tarhuna, Benghazi, Derna, and Murzuq. == Policy Issues == * Budgetary constraints following the ASP's rejection of an additional budget request. * Domestic legal obstacles restricting the movement of civil society organizations in Libya. * Limited scope for arresting the outstanding public fugitive Saif Al-Islam Gaddafi. * Need for full Libyan authority permits for forensic missions. == Relationships with Other Entities == * '''[[Office of the Prosecutor (ICC)]]''': Organ that published the report. * '''[[United Nations Security Council]]''': Recipient of the report. * '''[[Pre-Trial Chamber I]]''': Chamber that issued the arrest warrants. * '''[[Karim A.A. Khan KC]]''': ICC Prosecutor who made his first official visit to Libya in November 2022, briefed the UNSC directly from Libya, and voluntarily recused himself under Article 42(6) from lines of inquiry posing a potential conflict of interest. * '''[[Nazhat Shameem Khan]]''': ICC Deputy Prosecutor who assumed full oversight of the Libya investigations affected by the Prosecutor's recusal. * '''[[Saif Al-Islam Gaddafi]]''': Suspect in the Libya situation with an outstanding public arrest warrant related to violence against protesters in 2011. * '''[[Khalifa Haftar]]''': Leader of the Libyan National Army (LNA) in eastern Libya, met by the Prosecutor in November 2022 to affirm command responsibility for crimes under the Rome Statute. * '''[[Tewelde Goitom]]''' (alias Amanuel Gebreyesus Negahs Walid): Principal suspect in a human-trafficking network, extradited from Ethiopia to the Netherlands in October 2022 as a result of Joint Team international cooperation. * '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.''' * '''[[Ferdi Raditya Akbar]]''': '''Not found in the available sources.''' == See Also == * [[International Criminal Court]] * [[United Nations Security Council]] * [[Rome Statute]] == References == * Office of the Prosecutor, International Criminal Court, "Twenty-Fifth Report of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court to the United Nations Security Council pursuant to Resolution 1970 (2011)," May 2023. ==== Knowledge Graph Table (English) ==== {| class="wikitable" !Stable ID !Entity Type !Relationship !Related Stable ID !Evidence |- |JPW-REPORT-015 |Work (Report) |SUBMITTED_TO |JPW-INST-008 |Twenty-Fifth Report of the Prosecutor of the ICC to the UNSC pursuant to Resolution 1970 (2011). |- |JPW-REPORT-015 |Work (Report) |PUBLISHED_BY |JPW-INST-001 |Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, May 2023. |- |JPW-PERSON-020 |Person (Karim A.A.
