POLICY ANALYSIS ==== '''Background''': [FACT] Developments in Spanish business and judicial law in 2020 were marked by shifting regulatory frameworks across several key pillars: the transition from a unified code to sectoral decodification of commercial law; the pursuit of efficient enforcement of international financial security interests; the modernization of directors' loyalty standards to prevent value extraction (''tunneling''); harmonization of international arbitration standards (''Kompetenz-Kompetenz''); a surge in digital copyright infringement via link-aggregation websites; the mandatory allocation of operational risk under EU public contract law; and the transformation of the banking landscape through open banking and strong customer authentication (PSD2). '''Policy Problem''': [FACT] # ''Codification'': The stalling of the draft Commercial Code, worked on for six years across seven Ministers of Justice without ever being enacted into law. # ''Real Security Interests'': The need for rapid, out-of-court enforcement of security interests, constrained by the prohibition on ''pacto comisorio'' under Article 1859 of the Civil Code. # ''Corporate Law'': Interpretive uncertainty around "flexible imperativeness" (''imperatividad flexible'') regarding the duty of loyalty and the limits of conflict-of-interest waivers (''dispensa'') in M&A. # ''Arbitration'': The risk of arbitration proceedings being paralyzed due to vaguely worded (''inciertas''), unenforceable (''inoperantes''), or jurisdictionally hybrid (''híbridas'') clauses. # ''Digital Copyright'': Legal uncertainty over classifying hyperlinks as acts of "public communication," and difficulties proving profit motive (''ánimo de lucro'') and effective knowledge (''conocimiento efectivo'') prior to the LO 1/2015 reform. # ''Public Concessions'': Ambiguity in defining "operational risk" (distinguishing demand risk from supply risk) and potential conflict with the principle of economic rebalancing (''reequilibrio económico''). # ''PSD2/SCA'': Technical obstacles in API adaptation and potential disruption to e-commerce transactions caused by dual-authentication requirements. '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] The absence of explicit regulation of the ''pacto marciano'' for all types of unregistered assets; gaps in secondary liability rules for third-party linking sites prior to LO 1/2015; and a lack of clarity in treating "risk of availability" within public-service concession supply risk. '''Objectives''': [FACT] Ensure legal certainty and credit cost efficiency; prevent extractive "tunneling" practices by controlling shareholders; uphold the principle of "useful effect" (''efecto útil'') and the validity of arbitration agreements; provide effective protection to copyright holders through dynamic blocking injunctions against ISPs; place concession contractors under conditions of genuine market risk; and protect digital financial transactions from fraud. '''Implementation''': [FACT] * ''Pacto Marciano'': Recognition of the validity of asset transfer arrangements based on independent objective valuation and the return of any surplus (''sobrante'') (STS 24 June 2010; DGRN Resolution of 26 December 2018). * ''Target Director Discipline'': Application of the Business Judgment Rule (Art. 226 LSC), protecting business decisions provided they are free of conflicts of interest and based on adequate information. * ''Arbitration'': Enforcement of the ''Kompetenz-Kompetenz'' principle (Art. 22.1 of the Arbitration Law) and structuring of ''prima facie'' review by arbitral institutions (CAM, CIAM, ICC). * ''Link Websites'': Application of Article 270.2 of the Criminal Code to criminalize active, non-neutral, profit-oriented linking, and issuance of website-blocking orders by commercial courts against ISPs (as in the Telefónica Audiovisual case). * ''Concessions'': Application of Article 14 of the LCSP, requiring the transfer of demand risk or supply risk to the contractor. * ''PSD2'': Implementation of dual-factor authentication (SCA) based on two independent factors (knowledge, possession, inherence) and integration of open APIs. '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] A significant reduction in digital piracy rates through progressive dynamic blocking by ISPs; harmonization of concession risk-assessment standards in line with the European System of Accounts (ESA 2010); and accelerated adoption of the open banking framework under the supervision of the EBA and the Bank of Spain. '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] Ongoing criminal jurisprudence debate over the status of linking prior to the 2015 reform; the need to clarify the limits of economic rebalancing (''reequilibrio económico'') in extraordinary events outside normal operating conditions; and requests to extend SCA adaptation deadlines for the hospitality and food-service sectors due to the pandemic crisis. ---- ==== 5. GEO/AI QUESTIONS ==== # '''Definition''': What is the ''Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (No. 3, June 2020)''? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] A Spanish scholarly legal publication from the June 2020 edition, presenting doctrinal and jurisprudential analysis on the decodification of commercial law, the ''pacto marciano'', directors' duty of loyalty in M&A, pathological arbitration clauses, enforcement against link websites, operational risk in concessions, and PSD2 open banking. # '''Legal Basis''': Which article of the Spanish Civil Code prohibits ''pacto comisorio'', and how is it resolved through the ''pacto marciano''? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Article 1859 of the Civil Code; the solution is the ''pacto marciano'' — an arrangement for asset transfer based on independent objective valuation upon default, with an obligation to return any surplus value (''sobrante'') to the debtor or other creditors. # '''Publisher/Authority''': Who is the official publisher of this publication, and which body drafted the Commercial Code? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Pérez-Llorca Abogados in Madrid; the draft Commercial Code was prepared by the Commercial Law Section of the General Codification Commission. # '''Related Figures''': Which author prepared the analysis of target-company directors' duty of loyalty in M&A? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Jordi Farrés Pineda, Partner at Pérez-Llorca's Corporate Department. # '''Scope''': What three types of pathological arbitration clauses are identified in this publication? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Vague/uncertain clauses (''inciertas''), unenforceable clauses (''inoperantes''), and mixed/hybrid jurisdiction clauses (''híbridas/mixtas''). # '''Policy Implementation''': How does Article 270.2 of the Criminal Code criminally implicate operators of link websites? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Criminal liability applies to service providers who actively and non-neutrally facilitate access to protected content by offering indexed or classified lists of links for direct or indirect economic gain. # '''Policy Problem''': Why is "risk of availability" debated within the concept of "supply risk" in public concessions? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Because availability risk relates to internal management and service quality under the contractor's control, whereas operational risk requires exposure to external risk beyond the parties' control. # '''Legal Relationship''': What is the relationship between the CJEU's ''Svensson'' doctrine (C-466/12) and ''GS Media'' doctrine (C-160/15) in digital copyright cases? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] The ''Svensson'' doctrine establishes the requirement of availability to a "new public"; the ''GS Media'' doctrine adds a subjective element, under which a profit-oriented linker is presumed (''iuris tantum'') to know the illegal nature of the linked content. # '''Reform''': How does Article 226 of the Capital Companies Law (LSC) regulate the Business Judgment Rule? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] A judge will not re-evaluate directors' strategic business decisions so long as those decisions were made independently (free of conflicts of interest), based on adequate information, and in compliance with the law and the company's bylaws. # '''Evidence/Case Study''': What dual-factor authentication (SCA) requirements apply under PSD2 and RTS (EU) 2018/389? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] The use of at least two independent factors from the categories of knowledge (something only the user knows), possession (something only the user has), and inherence (a user's biological/physical characteristic). ---- ==== 6. Com. P.|legal_basis=Spanish Constitution of 1978 (Article 20)|jurisdiction=Spain / European Union|publication_date=June 2020|status=Official (Legal Deposit: M-7551-2019)|key_topics=Pacto Marciano, Duty of Loyalty in M&A, Pathological Clauses, Art. 270 Criminal Code, Operational Risk (LCSP), Open Banking (PSD2)}} == Summary == '''Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (Issue No. 3, June 2020)''' is a major scholarly legal publication presenting an in-depth analysis of developments in Spanish and EU jurisprudence and judicial policy. This edition contains seven strategic doctrinal studies: an evaluation of the decodification of commercial law by the General Codification Commission; the legitimacy of the *pacto marciano* as an alternative means of enforcing real security interests; the application of directors' duty of loyalty and the Business Judgment Rule in target-company M&A; a guide to resolving pathological arbitration clauses; civil and criminal enforcement against copyright-infringing link websites; the classification of operational risk in public concession contracts (LCSP); and the implementation of open banking and strong customer authentication (SCA) under the PSD2 framework. == Legal Basis == The policy and regulatory analysis in this publication is grounded in the following legal framework: * '''Spanish Constitution (CE)''': Article 20 (academic freedom) and Article 1255 (freedom of contract). * '''Civil and Security Law''': Articles 1859 and 1884 of the Spanish Civil Code (prohibition on *pacto comisorio*), Royal Decree-Law 5/2005 (financial services), and the Cape Town Convention. * '''Corporate Law''': Capital Companies Law (LSC), particularly Articles 190, 204.1, 226, 228, 229, 230, 232, and 234. * '''Arbitration Law''': Law 60/2003 on Arbitration (Articles 9, 11, 22, and 41). * '''Intellectual Property & Criminal Law''': Intellectual Property Law (LPI, Articles 20, 138–141), Article 270.2 of the Criminal Code (as reformed by Organic Law 1/2015), and Law 34/2002 (LSSI, Articles 16 and 17). * '''Public Contract Law''': Law 9/2017 on Public Sector Contracts (LCSP, Article 14) and Directive 2014/23/EU. * '''Banking & Financial Services''': Royal Decree-Law 19/2018 (PSD2) and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389 (RTS on SCA & CSC). == Background == The Spanish financial and judicial markets underwent significant transformation in mid-2020. The shift from a single code to sectoral legislation, the high cost of enforcing traditional security interests, the potential for "tunneling" practices in M&A transactions, legal uncertainty over the dissemination of protected content via internet hyperlinks, and the obligation to harmonize public concession regulation and digital payment transactions across the EU all demanded solid, well-established judicial doctrine. == Objectives == 1. Advance passage of the draft Commercial Code to preserve market unity. 2. Facilitate fast and efficient enforcement of real security interests without violating the prohibition on *pacto comisorio*. 3. Prevent value-extraction practices ("tunneling") by controlling shareholders or affiliated directors. 4. Uphold the validity of arbitration agreements through the principles of "useful effect" and *Kompetenz-Kompetenz*. 5. Provide effective protection to copyright holders against illegal, commercially motivated linking. 6. Ensure the transfer of genuine economic risk (operational risk) to public concession winners. 7. Open up competition in banking (open banking) while tightening customer digital security. == Scope == The study covers seven main policy areas: 1. ''History & Codification'': Evaluation of the General Codification Commission's work and the phenomenon of decodification. 2. ''Security Law'': Validity of the *pacto marciano* and requirements for objective valuation of unregistered assets. 3. ''Corporate Law'': Flexibility of conflict-of-interest waivers, the duty of confidentiality, and comparative analysis of the Business Judgment Rule. 4. ''Arbitration Law'': Typology of pathological clauses (uncertain, unenforceable, hybrid) and jurisdictional correction mechanisms. 5. ''Digital Copyright'': CJEU doctrine (*Svensson*, *GS Media*), ISP liability, and the criminal offense under Article 270.2 of the Criminal Code. 6. ''Public Contracts'': The boundary between demand risk and supply risk, and conformity with economic rebalancing. 7. ''Financial Sector'': Integration of Third-Party Providers (AIS/PIS), API communication standards, and dual-factor authentication (SCA) exceptions. == Key Provisions == * '''Validity of the Pacto Marciano''': Enforcement of security interests through objective market valuation upon default, with return of any surplus (*sobrante*), is legally valid and does not constitute a prohibited *pacto comisorio*. * '''Business Judgment Rule (BJR)''': Directors' business decisions are presumed valid and not subject to judicial re-evaluation if they meet the requirements of independence, adequate information, and compliance with the LSC's procedures. * '''Kompetenz-Kompetenz''': The primary authority to assess the validity of an arbitration clause rests with the arbitral tribunal (Art. 22.1 of the Arbitration Law); national courts must decline jurisdiction (*declinatoria*). * '''Criminal Criteria for Linking''': Actively, profit-oriented linking of unauthorized content satisfies the "public communication" element of the criminal offense under Article 270.2 of the Criminal Code. * '''Core of Public Concessions''': A contract qualifies as a concession only if the contractor bears genuine economic operational risk, with no guaranteed full recovery of investment. * '''Dual-Factor SCA Principle''': Verification of remote payment transactions must use at least two independent elements (knowledge, possession, or inherence). == Implementation == Enforcement and policy implementation occur through Spanish Supreme Court jurisprudence, CJEU rulings, DGRN decisions, and oversight by the Bank of Spain and the EBA over financial institutions' SCA migration plans. == Policy Problems == * Obstacles to integrating the *pacto marciano* for registered goods due to rules on the discharge of secondary encumbrances (*purga de cargas*). * Potential misuse of actions seeking annulment (*Acciones Tendentes a la Anulación*), which could disrupt certainty in M&A transactions. * Divergent interpretation among criminal judges regarding the validity of criminal liability for linking prior to the 2015 reform. * A regulatory gap regarding the limits of "risk of availability" within concession supply risk. == Reform == * Enactment of Organic Law 1/2015, reforming Article 270 of the Criminal Code to criminalize link websites. * Transposition of Directive 2014/23/EU through Law 9/2017 on Public Sector Contracts. * Implementation of Royal Decree-Law 19/2018 to integrate PSD2 in Spain. == Relationships with Other Entities == * '''Complements''': The jurisprudential framework of the Spanish Supreme Court and the CJEU. * '''Applies To''': M&A transactions, public concession contracts, and electronic payment systems. * '''Replaces''': The traditional approach to concessions based solely on "public service" status. == See Also == * [[Pacto Marciano]] * [[Business Judgment Rule in Spain]] * [[Pathological Arbitration Clauses]] * [[Crimes Against Intellectual Property on the Internet]] * [[Operational Risk under the LCSP]] * [[Open Banking and PSD2]] == References ==

POLICY ANALYSIS ==== '''Background''': [FACT] The declaration of a state of emergency (''estado de alarma'') under Royal Decree 463/2020 to combat the COVID-19 pandemic caused a sudden halt in economic activity and strict restrictions on citizens' mobility in Spain. This emergency required rapid legislative reform to prevent total paralysis of corporate operations (''bloqueo societario''), mass bankruptcies, and drastic layoffs. '''Policy Problem''': [FACT] # ''Corporate Law'': Inability to hold in-person shareholder general meetings (''Junta General'') or board meetings due to gathering restrictions. # ''Labor Law'': Collapse of the labor market due to business operation shutdowns, and ambiguity regarding force-majeure-based layoff requirements. # ''Competition & State Aid'': Vulnerability of nationally strategic companies to bankruptcy without state liquidity or capital support. # ''Judiciary & Insolvency'': Mass case backlogs (''colapso judicial'') and the risk of mandatory company dissolution due to consecutive losses (''causa legal de disolución por pérdidas''). # ''Foreign Investment'': Risk of low-cost takeovers of valuable Spanish strategic companies by investors outside the European Union. '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] The pre-pandemic legal framework (such as the Capital Companies Law or the Insolvency Law) did not provide a flexible mechanism for automatic virtual meetings without specific statutory clauses, lacked an expedited ERTE furlough procedure, and had no foreign investment screening mechanism for critical non-defense sectors. '''Objectives''': [FACT] Enable business continuity through digital channels; maintain employment through social security contribution relief schemes; provide a mandatory moratorium on insolvency filings; streamline judicial processes through remote hearings; and protect the integrity of national and EU strategic assets. '''Implementation''': [FACT] * Enactment of RDL 8/2020, permitting board and shareholder general meetings (Junta General) to be held remotely (video/teleconference) and suspending the obligation to dissolve companies. * Implementation of the Force Majeure ERTE and ETOP ERTE schemes, with social security contribution relief (''exoneración de cuotas'') and a six-month employment protection commitment (''salvaguarda de empleo''). * Establishment of the €10 billion Solvency Support Fund for Strategic Companies, managed by SEPI. * Application of Law 3/2020 to restructure the judiciary through remote hearings, creation of the Single Judicial Notice Board (''Tablón Edictal Judicial Único''), and an insolvency moratorium until 31 December 2020. * Suspension of the foreign investment liberalization regime for non-EU investments exceeding 10% in critical sectors, under Article 7bis of Law 19/2003. '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] As of September 2020, approximately 880,000 workers were recorded as protected under ERTE schemes across Spain. Meanwhile, remote hearings and insolvency filings were kept under control despite the potential for a drastic surge. '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] Divergent judicial interpretations regarding the classification of pandemic-era layoffs (whether void/''nulo'' or unfair/''improcedente''); uncertainty over the starting point for computing the six-month employment protection commitment; and the need to adopt the ''rebus sic stantibus'' doctrine into the Spanish Civil Code for private contracts. ---- ==== 5. #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Suspension of the obligation to file for insolvency until 31 December 2020, prioritization of remote hearings, creation of the Single Judicial Notice Board, and exclusion of 2020 losses from company dissolution calculations. # '''Evidence/Case Study''': Which sectors were protected from foreign acquisitions exceeding 10% under Article 7bis of Law 19/2003? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Critical infrastructure, critical and dual-use technology, essential energy/food supply, sectors with access to sensitive information/personal data, and mass media. ---- ==== 6. MEDIAWIKI OUTPUT ==== {{Infobox Legal Policy Entity|name=Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (COVID-19 Special Edition, No. 4)|stable_id=JPW-WORK-000004|official_name=Revista Jurídica Pérez-Llorca, Edición Especial COVID-19, Número 4, Noviembre de 2020|entity_type=Academic Legal Publication / Emergency Analysis Collection|publisher=Pérez-Llorca Abogados, S.L.P. y Cía., S. Com. P.|legal_basis=Spanish Constitution of 1978 (Article 20)|jurisdiction=Spain / European Union|publication_date=November 2020|status=Official (Legal Deposit: M-7551-2019)|key_topics=ERTE, Remote Meetings, Law 3/2020, SEPI Fund, Art. 7bis of Law 19/2003, Fiscal Residency}} == Summary == '''Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (COVID-19 Special Edition, No. 4, November 2020)''' is a major scholarly legal publication presenting a comprehensive analysis of the emergency legal framework enacted in Spain to address the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. This edition covers six strategic areas of study: corporate law flexibilization, employment protection through ERTE furlough schemes and remote work, recapitalization of strategic state-owned enterprises through the SEPI Fund under the EU State Aid framework, judicial and insolvency-law adjustments under Law 3/2020, suspension of foreign investment liberalization in strategic sectors (Art. 7bis of Law 19/2003), and the impact of mobility restrictions on international taxation. == Legal Basis == The emergency legal measures analyzed in this publication are grounded in the following decrees and legislation: * '''Royal Decree 463/2020, of 14 March''': Declaration of the state of emergency (*estado de alarma*). * '''Royal Decree-Law 8/2020, of 17 March''': Extraordinary emergency measures to address economic and social impact. * '''Royal Decree-Law 16/2020 & Law 3/2020, of 18 September''': Procedural and organizational measures for the judiciary. * '''Royal Decree-Law 25/2020, of 3 July''': Establishment of the Solvency Support Fund for Strategic Companies (SEPI). * '''Law 19/2003 (Article 7bis)''': Oversight of foreign direct investment. * '''Royal Decree-Law 28/2020 & RDL 30/2020''': Regulation of remote work (*teletrabajo*) and extension of ERTE schemes. == Background == The imposition of movement restrictions and the sudden halt of business activity during the state of emergency threatened the continuity of Spanish businesses. Without rapid legislative intervention, thousands of previously healthy companies faced the risk of legal decision-making paralysis (*bloqueo societario*), automatic bankruptcy due to declining net worth, and mass layoffs. == Objectives == 1. Ensure companies could continue making valid decisions through remote channels. 2. Prevent labor market collapse by facilitating a temporary furlough scheme (ERTE) supported by contribution incentives. 3. Maintain the solvency of nationally strategic companies through state capital injections approved by the European Commission. 4. Avoid judicial paralysis and mass insolvency through moratoria on bankruptcy filings and virtual hearings. 5. Protect Spain's critical assets and technology from unfriendly foreign takeovers. == Scope == The analysis covers six pillars of emergency judicial policy: 1. ''Corporate Law'': Virtual meetings, financial reporting formulation, suspension of withdrawal rights, and exemption from dissolution due to 2020 losses. 2. ''Labor Law'': Force Majeure and ETOP ERTE procedures, contribution relief, six-month employment protection commitment, and remote work. 3. ''State Aid'': The EU Temporary Framework and the SEPI recapitalization mechanism. 4. ''Judiciary & Insolvency'': Law 3/2020, remote hearings, the Single Judicial Notice Board, and the insolvency moratorium. 5. ''Foreign Investment'': Suspension of automatic authorization for acquisitions exceeding 10% in critical sectors. 6. ''Taxation'': Implications of tax-treaty tie-breaker rules amid human mobility restrictions. == Key Provisions == * '''Remote Meetings''': General Assembly and board sessions could be held via video/teleconference without requiring bylaw amendments. * '''ERTE Flexibility''': Expedited ERTE procedure (5 days) with social security contribution relief of up to 100% and a six-month employment protection obligation. * '''SEPI Fund''': A €10 billion recapitalization fund for strategic non-financial companies facing pandemic-related difficulties. * '''Insolvency Moratorium''': Suspension of the obligation to file for insolvency until 31 December 2020, and disregard of 2020 losses in company dissolution calculations. * '''Investment Screening (Art. 7bis)''': Mandatory authorization requirement for foreign investment in infrastructure, technology, energy supply, sensitive data, and media sectors. == Implementation == Implementation was carried out intensively by relevant ministries, the judiciary, and independent bodies: * '''Employment''': ERTE oversight by the Labor Inspectorate (*Inspección de Trabajo*) to prevent fraud. * '''Judiciary''': Rollout of remote hearings based on Law 3/2020. * '''Government & State-Owned Enterprises''': Management of the SEPI Fund by a Governing Council under the Spanish Ministry of Finance. == Policy Problems == * Divergent judicial interpretation by labor courts (*Juzgados de lo Social*) regarding the validity of pandemic-era layoffs. * Uncertainty in computing the duration of the six-month employment protection commitment. * Slow response from Spanish tax authorities in adjusting fiscal residency criteria for foreign nationals stranded by travel restrictions. == Reform == * Enactment of Law 3/2020, replacing RDL 16/2020, to restructure judicial procedures. * Issuance of Royal Decree-Law 28/2020 as a permanent legal framework for remote work (*teletrabajo*). * Refinement of foreign investment rules through Royal Decree-Law 34/2020. == Relationships with Other Entities == * '''Replaces''': The judicial and insolvency hearing framework under RDL 16/2020. * '''Implements''': The European Commission's Temporary State Aid Framework. * '''Amends''': Article 7bis of Law 19/2003 on foreign capital movement. == See Also == * [[Exceptional ERTE Regime]] * [[Law 3/2020 on Judicial Administration]] * [[Solvency Support Fund for Strategic Companies]] * [[Foreign Investment Screening in Spain]] * [[Remote Work and Fiscal Residency]] == References ==

POLICY ANALYSIS ==== '''Background''': [FACT] The development of Spanish judicial policy has been marked by a shift away from rigid legal positivism (''iuspositivismo'') toward the supremacy of general principles of law such as ''good administration'', ''legitimate expectation'', and ''legal certainty''. This shift was driven by the reform of administrative cassation (Organic Law 7/2015), EU banking resolution dynamics (BRRD2/TLAC), renewable energy market reform (RDL 23/2020), and rulings by Superior Courts of Justice (TSJ) annulling arbitral awards. '''Policy Problem''': [FACT] # ''Tax Law'': Automatic tax enforcement by fiscal authorities without responding to suspension/appeal requests (''recurso de reposición''), effectively equating the public interest with tax collection interest (''interés recaudatorio''). # ''Arbitration'': Overly broad (''expansive'') use of the "public policy" ground by TSJ courts as a backdoor to re-examine the merits of a case (''fondo del asunto'') and annul arbitral awards. # ''Corporate Law'': Legal uncertainty regarding the precise moment a shareholder loses status (''condición de socio'') when exercising the right of withdrawal (''derecho de separación''). # ''Energy'': Market failure due to "price cannibalization" (''canibalización de precios'') in renewable projects lacking a long-term guaranteed price scheme. # ''Urban Planning'': Use of ''ius variandi'' discretion by local governments without objective justification of public interest. '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] The Capital Companies Law (LSC) lacks explicit provisions on the transitional shareholder status period pending payment; the boundaries of "public policy" under the Arbitration Law remain unclear; and the rigidity of the General Tax Law (LGT) text has produced enforcement-procedure anomalies. '''Objectives''': [FACT] Guarantee the protection of fundamental rights and legal certainty (''tutela judicial efectiva''); establish fixed long-term prices to attract private investment in the energy sector; limit judicial interference in arbitration to preserve party autonomy; and balance minority shareholder rights against creditor interests in insolvency. '''Implementation''': [FACT] * Enforcement of the ''good administration'' doctrine by the Spanish Supreme Court to annul procedurally defective fiscal administrative actions (STS 1558/2020, 586/2020, 1309/2020). * Strict jurisprudence from the Spanish Constitutional Court (STC 46/2020, STC of 15 February 2021) prohibiting TSJ courts from re-assessing the substance of arbitral awards. * Implementation of "pay-as-bid" renewable energy auctions under the REER scheme (RD 960/2020). * Application of the "reimbursement theory," establishing that shareholder status is lost only once share-price payment is completed (STS 15 January 2021). '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] Annulment of various unilateral tax-collection and property-registration actions by authorities; restoration of arbitral award effectiveness by the Constitutional Court, which overturned a Madrid TSJ ruling. '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] Proposed legislative reform of the LGT concerning notification procedures and home-entry searches (''entrada en domicilio''); the need for legislative regulation of the intermediate status of withdrawing shareholders; and ongoing tension between Spanish tax authorities and the Supreme Court. ---- ==== 5. #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Under the reimbursement theory, a shareholder exercising the right of withdrawal retains their corporate status and rights until the value of their shares is fully reimbursed by the company. # '''Reform''': What reforms were introduced in the renewable energy sector under RDL 23/2020 and RD 960/2020? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] The launch of the Renewable Energy Economic Regime (REER), using "pay-as-bid" auctions with fixed long-term prices to address "price cannibalization." # '''Evidence/Case Study''': Which Constitutional Court ruling reaffirmed strict limits on "public policy" in early 2021? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] The ruling of 15 February 2021 (Mazacruz Case) and ruling STC 46/2020. ---- ==== 6. This issue includes scholarly contributions critiquing the rigid application of legal positivism (*iuspositivismo*) in public administration and affirming the supremacy of general principles of law such as the doctrine of good administration (*buena administración*), protection of arbitral autonomy from judicial interference, and reform of the renewable energy market and EU banking solvency regime. == Legal Basis == This publication is grounded in the right to freedom of expression and scholarly opinion guaranteed under Article 20 of the Spanish Constitution of 1978. The legal framework analyzed within it includes: * '''Spanish Constitution (CE)''': Article 9.3 (prohibition of arbitrariness), Article 24 (right to effective judicial protection), and Article 103 (objective service to the general interest). * '''Tax & Administrative Law''': Law 58/2003 General Tax Law (LGT) and Law 39/2015 / Law 30/1992 on Common Administrative Procedure. * '''Arbitration Law''': Law 60/2003 on Arbitration and the Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards (New York, 1958). * '''Corporate Law''': Capital Companies Law (LSC, particularly Article 348 bis). * '''Energy & Urban Planning Law''': Royal Decree-Law 23/2020, Royal Decree 960/2020, Law 24/2013 on the Electricity Sector, and Madrid's Law 9/2001 on Land Use. == Background == Between 2020 and 2021, the Spanish judiciary experienced tension between mechanically applied legal positivism (*iuspositivismo*) by public authorities and the general principles of law reaffirmed by the Supreme Court (*Tribunal Supremo*) and the Constitutional Court (*Tribunal Constitucional*). This tension was evident in tax enforcement procedures, oversight of inspection-related home entries, the annulment of arbitral awards by the Madrid TSJ, and the determination of when shareholder membership rights lapse. == Objectives == 1. Strengthen legal certainty (*seguridad jurídica*) and transparency in administrative and judicial procedures. 2. Limit unilateral actions by public authorities that prioritize revenue collection (*interés recaudatorio*) over good-governance principles. 3. Prevent arbitrary annulment of arbitral awards by reaffirming strict limits on "public policy." 4. Provide price certainty for renewable energy investors through long-term auctions to meet PNIEC 2021–2030 targets. == Scope == The analysis covers seven main policy areas: 1. Ethics and Law in Pandemic-Era Decision-Making (Bioethics). 2. AT1 and T2 Capital Instruments in EU Banking Solvency. 3. Renewable Auction Scheme (REER). 4. General Principles of Law vs. Positivism in Tax Law. 5. Limits of *Ius Variandi* Discretion in Urban Planning Law. 6. Shareholder Withdrawal Rights and the Reimbursement Theory. 7. Public Policy Violations in Arbitration Review. == Key Provisions == * '''Good Administration Doctrine''': Fiscal authorities must respond to objection/suspension requests before issuing enforcement orders (*apremio*). Citizens' rights must not be made contingent on opaque internal procedures. * '''Public Policy Limits in Arbitration''': "Public policy" covers only fundamental constitutional rights and cannot be used by courts as grounds to re-examine the substance of a case. * '''Reimbursement Theory''': A shareholder exercising the right of withdrawal retains their corporate rights until the share value is fully reimbursed (*efectivo reembolso*). * '''Urban Planning *Ius Variandi*''': Discretionary changes to urban planning must be limited by objective evidence of general interest and adherence to factual realities on the ground. == Implementation == Implementation of this policy is reflected in rulings from the highest courts: * '''Tax''': STS 1558/2020, STS 586/2020, STS 1309/2020, STS 904/2020, STS 1231/2020, and STS 1371/2020. * '''Arbitration''': STC 46/2020 and the ruling of 15 February 2021 (Mazacruz Case), which annulled a Madrid TSJ decision. * '''Corporate''': STS 15 January 2021, STS 2 February 2021, STS 9 February 2021, and STS 24 February 2021. == Policy Problems == * Public authority practice of assuming implicit denial (*silencio negativo*) and proceeding directly to forced collection. * Tendency of TSJ courts to act as a second-instance appellate body over arbitral awards. * Accounting and insolvency registration uncertainty regarding claims of withdrawing shareholders. == Reform == * Reform of the LGT regarding notification rules and authorization for home/business entry searches (*entrada en domicilio*). * Adjustment of insolvency claim subordination rules under the Insolvency Law due to BRRD2. * Consolidation of constitutional doctrine binding on all Spanish TSJ courts in arbitration cases. == Relationships with Other Entities == * '''Corrects / Amends''': Rigid administrative practices that disregard Articles 9.3 and 103 of the Spanish Constitution. * '''Synchronized With''': EU Banking Regulation (BRRD2, CRR2, TLAC/MREL). * '''Opposed To''': Excessive jurisdictional intervention in arbitral awards. == See Also == * [[Doctrine of Good Administration]] * [[Judicial Review of Arbitration]] * [[Renewable Energy Economic Regime]] * [[Reimbursement Theory]] * [[Urban Planning Ius Variandi]] == References ==

POLICY ANALYSIS ==== '''Background''': [FACT] The Spanish pension system is founded on a pay-as-you-go structure (''sistema de reparto'') and the constitutional principle of intergenerational solidarity, which binds current active workers to current pensioners. Since the 2010s, concern has grown over the baby-boom generation reaching retirement age (beginning around 2027), declining birth rates, and rising life expectancy. This was compounded by austerity policies during 2008–2014 and the introduction of the ''Sustainability Factor'' (Law 23/2013), which fueled younger generations' doubts about the future viability of their pensions. '''Policy Problem''': [FACT] # ''Risk of Intergenerational Rupture'': A conflict-inducing narrative has emerged suggesting that older generations' pensions are funded by imposing excessive sacrifice on younger workers (a "win-lose narrative"). # ''Financial and Demographic Deficit'': Rising pension expenditure burden due to a surge in high-value pensions among the highly educated baby-boom generation. # ''Weaknesses of the Sustainability Factor'': The automatic pension-reduction mechanism based on life expectancy cut spending without regard for social adequacy (''sostenibilidad social'') or pensioners' standard of living. '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] The existence of contribution ceilings (''topes máximos de cotización'') limiting contributions from high salaries, without a solidarity contribution mechanism for income above the maximum threshold. Additionally, high-earning self-employed workers (''autónomos'') are exempted from the solidarity contribution scheme. '''Objectives''': [FACT] Restore younger generations' trust in the public pension system; strengthen social security system revenue to address the surge in baby-boom pension costs through 2050; and ensure a balance between contributivity (''contributividad'') and pension adequacy (''suficiencia económica'') in accordance with Articles 41 and 50 of the Spanish Constitution. '''Implementation''': [FACT] Through Royal Decree-Law 2/2023 and Component 30 of the PRTR: * ''Intergenerational Equity Mechanism (MEI)'': A finalized contribution rate of 0.80% in 2025 (0.67% employer, 0.13% employee), allocated entirely to the Reserve Fund. * ''Additional Solidarity Contribution (CAS)'': A graduated rate (5.5%, 6%, and 7% by 2045) applied to the portion of salary exceeding the maximum contribution ceiling. * ''Increase in Maximum Contribution Ceiling'': Raising the annual monthly maximum contribution ceiling based on CPI plus 1.2 percentage points per year from 2024 through 2050. '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] Projected to increase Social Security revenue by an additional 0.6% of GDP by 2030 and 0.9% of GDP by 2050. Bank of Spain simulations indicate a small potential impact on employment (a decrease of approximately 0.25% in filled positions if the rate were raised by a full percentage point over four years), offset by stronger social investment and pensioner consumption. '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] The absence of an explicit provision directly allocating Additional Solidarity Contribution proceeds to the Reserve Fund (though doctrinally recommended); the exemption of self-employed workers/company directors from CAS; and the need for periodic evaluation of the contribution burden's impact on employers. ---- ==== 5. MEDIAWIKI OUTPUT ==== {{Infobox Legal Policy Entity|name=The Principle of Intergenerational Solidarity in Social Security (Moreno Romero, 2025)|stable_id=JPW-WORK-000007|official_name=El principio de solidaridad intergeneracional en el ámbito de la Seguridad Social y su renovación como elemento básico de nuestro sistema de reparto|entity_type=Academic Legal Research / Policy Analysis|author=Francisca Moreno Romero|publisher=Universidad Complutense de Madrid (Revista de Trabajo y Seguridad Social, Vol. 34)|legal_basis=Spanish Constitution of 1978 (Arts. 41 & 50)|jurisdiction=Spain / European Union|publication_date=June 2025 (Received: 11 April 2025)|status=Official / Published (ISSN 2255-1824)|key_topics=Intergenerational Solidarity, MEI, Solidarity Contribution, Maximum Base, Pay-As-You-Go System}} == Summary == '''The Principle of Intergenerational Solidarity in Social Security and Its Renewal as a Core Element of Our Pay-As-You-Go System''' is a Spanish social security law study written by Prof. Dr. Francisca Moreno Romero of Universidad Complutense de Madrid (UCM). This scholarly work analyzes the constitutional principle of intergenerational solidarity as the core pillar of the pay-as-you-go system (*sistema de reparto*). The study evaluates Spanish pension law reforms from 2019–2023, particularly the replacement of the automatic pension-reduction mechanism (*Sustainability Factor*) with the Intergenerational Equity Mechanism (MEI), the introduction of the Additional Solidarity Contribution (CAS), and the gradual increase of the maximum contribution base (*base máxima de cotización*) through 2050. == Legal Basis == Spain's public Social Security system and the reforms analyzed are grounded in the following constitutional and statutory provisions: * '''Spanish Constitution (CE)''': Article 41 (public social security), Article 50 (adequacy of pensions for the elderly), Article 31 (fair allocation of public resources), and Articles 1.1, 9.2, 9.3, and 14. * '''Law 27/2011, of 1 August''': Reform and modernization of the social security system, raising the retirement age to 67. * '''Law 23/2013, of 23 December''': Establishment of the Sustainability Factor and the Revaluation Index. * '''Royal Legislative Decree 8/2015 (TRLGSS)''': Consolidated text of the General Social Security Law (particularly Articles 2, 19, 19 bis, 127.2 bis, Transitional Provision 38, and Transitional Provision 42). * '''Royal Decree-Law 2/2023, of 16 March''': Pension reform integrating Component 30 of the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan. * '''Royal Decree 322/2024, of 26 March''': Implementing provisions for the additional solidarity contribution. == Background == Spain's pension system relies on contributions from active workers to fund current pensioners' benefits. Demographic challenges have emerged alongside rising life expectancy, low birth rates, and the onset of baby-boom-generation retirement beginning in 2027. Austerity policies during the 2008–2014 crisis and the implementation of the automatic pension-reduction mechanism (Sustainability Factor) raised widespread concern among younger workers that they would not receive adequate pensions in the future. == Objectives == 1. Restore and strengthen younger workers' trust in the sustainability of the public pension system. 2. Increase Social Security system revenue to anticipate the peak in baby-boom-generation pension expenditure through 2050. 3. Maintain a balance between the principles of contributivity (*contributividad*) and pension adequacy (*suficiencia económica*) as mandated by Articles 41 and 50 of the Spanish Constitution. == Scope == The study covers analysis of three main contribution instruments: 1. The ''Intergenerational Equity Mechanism'' (MEI) as a replacement for the Sustainability Factor. 2. The ''Additional Solidarity Contribution'' (CAS) for income exceeding the maximum contribution ceiling. 3. The gradual increase of the maximum contribution ceiling (*base máxima de cotización*), adjusted by CPI + 1.2% per year. == Key Provisions == * '''Intergenerational Equity Mechanism (MEI)''': A finalized contribution rate of 0.80% in 2025 (0.67% employer, 0.13% employee), allocated directly to the Reserve Fund without possibility of reduction or deduction. * '''Additional Solidarity Contribution (CAS)''': A three-tier progressive contribution (5.5%, 6%, and 7%) on income above the maximum contribution ceiling, phased in gradually through 2045. * '''Increase in Maximum Contribution Ceiling''': Approved annually through the National Budget (PGE) from 2024 through 2050, using the pension revaluation formula plus 1.2 percentage points. == Implementation == Reform implementation proceeds continuously through coordination between the Spanish Government, the Toledo Pact Commission, and social partners. MEI contribution proceeds are allocated to strengthen the Social Security Reserve Fund to ensure long-term liquidity. == Policy Problems == * A narrative of intergenerational conflict positioning pensioners as winners and younger workers as the disadvantaged party (a "win-lose narrative"). * High-earning self-employed workers (*autónomos*) are not reached by the Additional Solidarity Contribution scheme. * Potential impact on employer labor costs, though economic simulations indicate minimal impact on employment levels. == Reform == * Repeal of the Sustainability Factor (Law 23/2013), judged to be purely a cost-cutting instrument that disregarded social adequacy. * Implementation of a new progressive contribution scheme through RDL 2/2023 and RD 322/2024. == Relationships with Other Entities == * '''Replaces''': The Sustainability Factor (Law 23/2013). * '''Implements''': Component 30 of the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan & Recommendation 11 of the Toledo Pact. * '''Interprets''': Articles 41 and 50 of the Spanish Constitution of 1978. == See Also == * [[Principle of Intergenerational Solidarity]] * [[Intergenerational Equity Mechanism]] * [[Additional Solidarity Contribution]] * [[Pay-As-You-Go System]] * [[Toledo Pact]] == References ==

ENTITY IDENTITY ==== * '''Stable ID''': JPW-WORK-000009 * '''Canonical Name''': Youth Employment Policies Facing the Transformation of Work: A Chronicle of Challenges and Contrasts (González Cobaleda, 2025) * '''Official Name''': ''Las políticas de empleo juvenil ante la transformación del trabajo: una crónica de desafíos y contrastes'' * '''Entity Type''': Academic Legal Research / Youth Employment Policy Analysis * '''Aliases''': ''Study on Youth Employment Policies in Spain (2025)'', ''González Cobaleda (2025) Youth Employment Study'' * '''Definition''': [FACT] A scholarly work and analysis of Spanish labor law written by Estefanía González Cobaleda, published in the ''Revista de Trabajo y Seguridad Social'' (Volume 34, June 2025). The study offers a critical evaluation of youth employment public policy within the framework of EU coordination (the European Youth Strategy 2019–2027 and Council Decision (EU) 2024/3134), the implementation of Law 3/2023 on Employment (particularly Articles 3(d), 8, 50, and 53), the Youth Guarantee Plus Plan 2021–2027, labor reform under RDL 32/2021 (restrictions on temporary contracts and the renewal of training contracts under Article 11 of the Workers' Statute), specific programs (TándEM, First Professional Experience, Investigo), and the pillar of public-private collaboration in the digital and ecological transition. * '''Jurisdiction''': Spain / European Union * '''Issuing Authority / Publisher''': Universidad de Málaga (UMA) / Revista de Trabajo y Seguridad Social (Volume 34, June 2025, ISSN 2255-1824) * '''Legal Basis''': Spanish Constitution of 1978 (Arts. 9, 35, 40); Law 3/2023, of 28 February, on Employment; Royal Legislative Decree 2/2015 (Workers' Statute — ET, Arts. 11, 15, 16); Royal Decree-Law 32/2021; Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU, Arts. 2.3, 5.2, 145–150, 165–166); Council Decision (EU) 2024/3134. * '''Date''': Received 4 March 2025; Published June 2025 * '''Status''': Official / Published (Peer-reviewed publication) * '''Related Institutions/Regulations/Policies/People''': ** ''Institutions'': Universidad de Málaga (UMA); Spanish Employment Agency; National Employment System; JUVUMA Institute; European Commission; Council of the European Union; SEPE (Spanish Public Employment Service); Eurostat; INE (Spanish National Statistics Institute). ** ''Regulations/Policies'': Law 3/2023 on Employment; Royal Decree-Law 32/2021; Youth Guarantee Plus Plan 2021–2027; Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan (Component 23); Council Decision (EU) 2024/3134; Spanish Strategy for Active Employment Support 2021–2024; Digital Spain 2025 Agenda. ** ''Related Individuals'': Estefanía González Cobaleda; Monereo Pérez, J.L.; Gómez Salado, M.Á.; Molina Navarrete, C.; Cristóbal Roncero, R.; Cruz Villalón, J.; Durán Bernardino, M.; Pérez del Prado, D.; Rodríguez Escanciano, S.; Rojo Torrecilla, E. ---- ==== 2. NAMED ENTITIES ==== * '''Estefanía González Cobaleda''' (JPW-PERSON-000038): [FACT] Permanent Lecturer (accredited to Full Professor level) in the Department of Labor Law and Social Security at Universidad de Málaga (UMA), and a researcher at the JUVUMA University Research Institute. Sole author of the legal study ''Youth Employment Policies Facing the Transformation of Work: A Chronicle of Challenges and Contrasts'' (2025). * '''J.L. Monereo Pérez''' (JPW-PERSON-000039): [FACT] Labor law scholar cited regarding the right to decent work under EU law and youth social guarantee systems. * '''M.Á. Gómez Salado''' (JPW-PERSON-000040): [FACT] Labor law scholar cited regarding the analysis of employment contract reform under RDL 32/2021 and the legislative conceptualization of youth. * '''C. No documented role or connection to this publication exists in the source material. * '''Johana Crishele Ohoira''': [FACT] '''Not found in the available sources.''' No documented role or connection to this publication exists in the source material. ---- ==== 3. KNOWLEDGE GRAPH ==== * [JPW-WORK-000009] authored by [JPW-PERSON-000038] Estefanía González Cobaleda * [JPW-WORK-000009] affiliated with [JPW-ORG-000003] Universidad de Málaga (UMA) * [JPW-POLICY-000024] Youth Employment Policies based on [JPW-REG-000028] Spanish Constitution (Arts. 9.2, 35.1, 40) * [JPW-POLICY-000024] Youth Employment Policies applies to [JPW-REG-000029] Law 3/2023, of 28 February, on Employment (Arts. 3, 50, 53) * [JPW-POLICY-000025] National Youth Guarantee System implements [JPW-POLICY-000026] Youth Guarantee Plus Plan 2021–2027 * [JPW-POLICY-000027] Reform of Training Contracts implements [JPW-REG-000030] Royal Decree-Law 32/2021 & Art. 11 of the Workers' Statute * [JPW-POLICY-000028] European Employment Coordination based on [JPW-REG-000031] TFEU (Arts. 145–150) & Council Decision (EU) 2024/3134 * [JPW-POLICY-000029] Public-Private Employment Collaboration implements [JPW-REG-000029] Law 3/2023 on Employment (Art. 8) & PRTR Component 23 ---- ==== 4. POLICY ANALYSIS ==== '''Background''': [FACT] Youth employment in Spain represents a long-standing structural challenge, further aggravated by the COVID-19 pandemic and the accelerating digital and ecological transformation of the labor market. Key obstacles include structural unemployment, early school leaving (13.7% in 2023 versus a 9.5% EU average), overqualification (''sobrecualificación''), and very high job turnover. '''Policy Problem''': [FACT] # ''Uncertainty over the Age Boundary of "Youth"'': A varying age range of 16 to 34 years appears across different policy analyses, even though Law 3/2023 restricts priority status to ages 16–29. # ''Precariousness and Involuntary Part-Time Work'': The rate of involuntary temporary contracts among youth up to age 24 reaches 44.2% (versus 15.8% in the Eurozone in 2023), while the rate of involuntary part-time work (''parcialidad involuntaria'') reaches 46.7% (versus 19.2% in the EU). # ''Digital and Sustainability Gap'': Digital-related employment in the EU grew by 57.8% over the past decade (seven times faster than overall employment growth of 7.9%), yet low-skilled youth face major barriers to accessing it. # ''Age Discrimination Above 30'': Restricting priority programs to ages 16–30 leaves youth aged 25–34 — who still earn 20% below the national average — without special protection, raising potential concerns under the constitutional equality principle (Art. 9 CE). '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] Law 3/2023 on Employment establishes a programmatic framework but does not include an explicit definition or judicially enforceable legal guarantee (''mecanismos concretos exigibles jurídicamente'') regarding the right to quality employment. Additionally, public employment services face capacity limitations in providing personalized support without private-sector collaboration. '''Objectives''': [FACT] Shift the legislative focus away from merely achieving "quantitative full employment" (''pleno empleo'') and toward fostering "decent, stable, and quality employment" (''empleo digno, estable y de calidad''), in line with Article 2.2 of the Employment Law and Articles 35 & 40 of the Spanish Constitution. '''Implementation''': [FACT] * ''RDL 32/2021 Labor Reform'': Elimination of project-based/service contracts (''obra y servicio'') and reorganization of training contracts (alternating training contracts and professional practice contracts under Art. 11 ET) to promote permanent contracts. * ''Youth Guarantee Plus Plan 2021–2027'': Development of personalized guidance oriented toward green and digital economic sectors. * ''Active Support Programs (Law 3/2023)'': Implementation of the TándEM Program (alternating training), the First Professional Experience Program (recruitment into public bodies), and the Investigo Program (research and data science) for youth aged 16–30. * ''Public-Private Cooperation Model'': Integration of the Spanish Employment Agency, regional (autonomous community) services, and private placement agencies, under Article 8 of the Employment Law and Component 23 of the PRTR. '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] A decline in youth unemployment from its pandemic peak, and an increase in the proportion of permanent contracts following RDL 32/2021 — though vulnerability remains significant among low-education youth and those over age 30. '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] The need to extend protection coverage beyond the 30-year age threshold, refine mechanisms for objectively evaluating the impact of active programs, and strengthen certainty around decent-work indicators across all productive sectors. ---- ==== 5. #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] The TándEM Program (alternating training), the First Professional Experience in Public Administrations Program, and the Investigo Program (research and digitalization/data science). # '''Policy Problem''': What percentage of involuntary part-time work and involuntary temporary employment among youth in Spain, compared with the EU average, was reported in 2023? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Involuntary temporary employment among youth up to age 24 reached 44.2% in Spain (versus 15.8% in the Eurozone), while involuntary part-time work reached 46.7% (versus 19.2% in the EU). # '''Legal Relationship''': What is the relationship between Component 23 of the Recovery Plan (PRTR) and the enactment of Law 3/2023 on Employment? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] PRTR Component 23 required modernization of active employment policy to reduce structural youth unemployment as a condition for Next Generation EU funding, forming the basis for the enactment of Law 3/2023. # '''Reform''': How did RDL 32/2021 restructure training contract types under Article 11 of the Workers' Statute (ET)? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] RDL 32/2021 replaced the old scheme with two modalities: alternating training contracts (''formación en alternancia'') and training contracts for professional practice (''práctica profesional''). # '''Evidence/Case Study''': According to official data, what was the growth rate of digital-sector employment in the European Union over the past decade? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Digital and artificial-intelligence-related jobs grew by 57.8% over the past decade, seven times faster than the EU's overall workforce growth of 7.9%. ---- ==== 6. MEDIAWIKI OUTPUT ==== {{Infobox Legal Policy Entity|name=Youth Employment Policies Facing the Transformation of Work (González Cobaleda, 2025)|stable_id=JPW-WORK-000009|official_name=Las políticas de empleo juvenil ante la transformación del trabajo: una crónica de desafíos y contrastes|entity_type=Academic Legal Research / Youth Employment Policy Analysis|author=Estefanía González Cobaleda|publisher=Universidad de Málaga (Revista de Trabajo y Seguridad Social, Vol. 34)|legal_basis=Spanish Constitution (Arts. 9, 35, 40) & Law 3/2023 on Employment|jurisdiction=Spain / European Union|publication_date=June 2025 (Received: 4 March 2025)|status=Official / Published (ISSN 2255-1824)|key_topics=Youth Employment, Law 3/2023, Youth Guarantee Plus, RDL 32/2021, Public-Private Collaboration, Digital and Ecological Transition}} == Summary == '''Youth Employment Policies Facing the Transformation of Work: A Chronicle of Challenges and Contrasts''' is a labor law study written by Prof. Dr. Estefanía González Cobaleda of Universidad de Málaga (UMA). This scholarly work provides an in-depth analysis of Spain's youth employment policy framework in the era of digital and ecological transformation. The study evaluates EU policy coordination (the European Youth Strategy 2019–2027 and Council Decision (EU) 2024/3134), the instruments of Law 3/2023 on Employment, the Youth Guarantee Plus Plan 2021–2027, the impact of RDL 32/2021 on restricting temporary contracts and renewing training contracts under Article 11 of the Workers' Statute, active support programs (TándEM, First Experience, Investigo), and the public-private collaboration model within Spain's National Employment System. == Legal Basis == The youth employment policies and normative reforms analyzed are grounded in the following national and European legal framework: * '''Spanish Constitution (CE)''': Article 9.2 (substantive equality), Article 35.1 (right to work and remuneration guarantees), and Article 40 (mandate for full employment and vocational training). * '''Law 3/2023, of 28 February, on Employment''': Article 3(d) (definition of priority groups), Article 8 (National Employment System), Article 50 (priority vulnerable populations), and Article 53 (specific provisions for youth). * '''Royal Legislative Decree 2/2015 (Workers' Statute — ET)''': Article 11 (alternating training and professional practice contracts), Article 15, and Article 16 (permanent and fixed-discontinuous contracts). * '''Royal Decree-Law 32/2021, of 28 December''': Labor reform for employment stabilization. * '''Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU)''': Articles 2.3, 5.2, 145–150 (Employment Title), and Articles 165–166 (Education and Youth). * '''Council Decision (EU) 2024/3134''': Employment policy guidelines for EU Member States. == Background == Spain's youth labor market has historically been marked by structural problems such as high unemployment, early school leaving (13.7% in 2023), excessive job turnover, and overqualification. This situation has grown more complex with the acceleration of automation, artificial intelligence, and the demands of ecological transition, which require new technical qualifications. == Objectives == 1. Shift legal priorities from mere quantitative employment absorption toward guaranteeing dignified, stable, and quality employment (*empleo digno, estable y de calidad*). 2. Strengthen the effectiveness of the National Employment System through restructuring of the Youth Guarantee Plus scheme 2021–2027. 3. Minimize the digital and ecological skills gap among low-educated youth through alternating training programs. 4. Foster public-private synergy between the Spanish Employment Agency and private entities to optimize job placement. == Scope == The study covers analysis across four main pillars: 1. ''Quantitative Characterization of Youth'': Analysis of Eurostat/INE data on unemployment, involuntary temporary contracts (44.2%), and involuntary part-time work (46.7%). 2. ''EU Coordination Framework'': The role of the Open Method of Coordination (OMC), the TFEU, and Council Decision (EU) 2024/3134. 3. ''National Legal Instruments'': Implementation of Law 3/2023 on Employment, training-contract reform under RDL 32/2021, and the TándEM/First Experience/Investigo programs. 4. ''Public-Private Cooperation'': Implementation of Article 8 of the Employment Law and Component 23 of the PRTR. == Key Provisions == * '''Redefinition of Employment Policy Objectives (Art. 2.2 of the Employment Law)''': The primary focus shifts toward employability development, job stability, and the right to decent work. * '''Priority Age Classification (Art. 50 of the Employment Law)''': Youth under 30, or participants in the Youth Guarantee, are explicitly classified as a priority attention group. * '''New Training Contract Model (Art. 11 ET)''': Establishment of two contract types — alternating training contracts and professional practice contracts — to limit precariousness. * '''Public-Private Partnership (Art. 8 of the Employment Law)''': Enforcement of coordination principles between the Spanish Employment Agency, regional services, and private placement agencies. == Implementation == Implementation occurs through execution of the Youth Guarantee Plus Plan 2021–2027, allocation of Next Generation EU funds via PRTR Component 23, and recruitment incentive programs in the research sector and public administration. == Policy Problems == * Exclusion of the 30–34 age segment from special priority schemes, despite this group still earning 20% below the national average. * Absence of an explicit, judicially enforceable legal guarantee (*exigibilidad jurídica*) within the programmatic sections of the Employment Law. * Risk of labor market segmentation between digitally skilled youth and low-educated youth. == Reform == * Enactment of Law 3/2023 on Employment, replacing Royal Legislative Decree 3/2015. * Labor reform under RDL 32/2021, eliminating project/service-based contracts (*obra y servicio*). * Adoption of Council Decision (EU) 2024/3134 to align annual employment guidelines. == Relationships with Other Entities == * '''Implements''': Component 23 of the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan (PRTR). * '''Applies To''': Articles 11, 15, and 16 of Royal Legislative Decree 2/2015 (Workers' Statute). * '''Regulates''': The National Youth Guarantee System & the Spanish Employment Agency. == See Also == * [[Employment Law]] * ENTITY IDENTITY ==== * '''Stable ID''': JPW-WORK-000010 * '''Canonical Name''': The Job Precariousness of Young Researchers: Regulatory, Doctrinal, and Jurisprudential Treatment of Predoctoral Research Trainees in Spain (Cabello Roldán, 2025) * '''Official Name''': ''La precariedad laboral de las personas jóvenes investigadoras: tratamiento normativo, doctrinal y jurisprudencial del personal investigador en formación en España'' * '''Entity Type''': Academic Legal Research / Research Personnel Policy Analysis * '''Aliases''': ''Study on the Predoctoral Contract and Research Precariousness in Spain'', ''Cabello Roldán (2025) Predoctoral Contract Study'' * '''Definition''': [FACT] A scholarly work and analysis of Spanish labor law written by Aída Cabello Roldán, published in the ''Revista de Trabajo y Seguridad Social'' (Volume 34, June 2025). The study comprehensively analyzes the level of job precariousness among young researchers in Spain, the evolution of predoctoral contract regulation (Law 14/2011 LCTI, Law 17/2022, Organic Law 2/2023 LOSU), the reform of the Statute of Predoctoral Research Trainees in Training (EPIPF, via Royal Decree 103/2019 and Royal Decree 1251/2024 of 10 December), remuneration and severance-pay rights (''indemnización por extinción''), teaching-load limitations, and the evolving jurisprudence of the Supreme Court and the Superior Courts of Justice. * '''Jurisdiction''': Spain / European Union * '''Issuing Authority / Publisher''': Universidad de Málaga (UMA) / Revista de Trabajo y Seguridad Social (Volume 34, June 2025, ISSN 2255-1824) * '''Legal Basis''': Law 14/2011, of 1 June, on Science, Technology and Innovation (LCTI, as amended by Law 17/2022); Royal Decree 103/2019, of 1 March (EPIPF, as reformed by Royal Decree 1251/2024, of 10 December); Royal Legislative Decree 2/2015 (Workers' Statute — ET, Arts. 11, 15, 49.1.c); Organic Law 2/2023, of 22 March (LOSU, Art. 9.7); Royal Decree-Law 1/2023, of 10 January; Royal Decree-Law 32/2021, of 28 December. * '''Date''': Received 13 February 2025; Published June 2025 * '''Status''': Official / Published (Peer-reviewed publication) * '''Related Institutions/Regulations/Policies/People''': ** ''Institutions'': Universidad de Málaga (UMA); University of the Basque Country; University of Galicia; University of Castilla y León; University of Madrid; Supreme Court (Labor Chamber); SEPE (Spanish Public Employment Service); Ministry of Labor and Social Economy. ** ''Regulations/Policies'': Law 14/2011 (LCTI); Law 17/2022; Royal Decree 103/2019 (EPIPF); Royal Decree 1251/2024; Organic Law 2/2023 (LOSU); Royal Decree-Law 1/2023; Royal Decree-Law 32/2021; Recommendation 2005/251/EC (European Charter for Researchers). ** ''Related Individuals'': Aída Cabello Roldán; J. Moreno Gené; Ó. Requena Montes; N. Serrano Argüello; L. Nogueira Ferreiro; Y. Cano Galán; J.L. Monereo Pérez; B.M. López Insua; H. Álvarez Cuesta. ---- ==== 2. NAMED ENTITIES ==== * '''Aída Cabello Roldán''' (JPW-PERSON-000046): [FACT] Predoctoral research contract holder in the Department of Labor Law and Social Security at Universidad de Málaga (UMA). Sole author of the legal study ''The Job Precariousness of Young Researchers: Regulatory, Doctrinal, and Jurisprudential Treatment of Predoctoral Research Trainees in Spain'' (2025). * '''J. Moreno Gené''' (JPW-PERSON-000047): [FACT] Labor law scholar extensively cited regarding the legal nature of the predoctoral contract, the EPIPF reform, and as a commentator on Supreme Court ruling STS 903/2020 concerning severance pay. * '''Cecep Mustafa''': [FACT] '''Not found in the available sources.''' KNOWLEDGE GRAPH ==== * [JPW-WORK-000010] authored by [JPW-PERSON-000046] Aída Cabello Roldán * [JPW-WORK-000010] affiliated with [JPW-ORG-000003] Universidad de Málaga (UMA) * [JPW-POLICY-000036] Legal Regime of the Predoctoral Contract based on [JPW-REG-000036] Law 14/2011 (LCTI Art. 21, as amended by Law 17/2022) * [JPW-POLICY-000036] Legal Regime of the Predoctoral Contract applies to [JPW-REG-000037] Royal Decree 103/2019 (EPIPF, as reformed by RD 1251/2024) * [JPW-POLICY-000037] Severance Pay upon Termination of the Predoctoral Contract implements [JPW-REG-000038] Law 17/2022 & Art. 49.1.c of the Workers' Statute * [JPW-POLICY-000037] Severance Pay upon Termination of the Predoctoral Contract based on [JPW-CASE-000001] STS 903/2020 of 13 October * [JPW-POLICY-000038] Postdoctoral Transition within the Predoctoral Contract implements [JPW-REG-000039] Royal Decree 1251/2024 (Art. 4.1) * [JPW-POLICY-000039] Integration of the Predoctoral Framework with the University System implements [JPW-REG-000040] Organic Law 2/2023 (LOSU, Art. 9.7) ---- ==== 4. POLICY ANALYSIS ==== '''Background''': [FACT] Young researchers in Spain face working conditions marked by structural job precariousness, including temporary contracts, inadequate pay, and significant career uncertainty. This negatively affects motivation and scientific output, and contributes to a "brain drain" toward countries with more stable conditions. '''Policy Problem''': [FACT] # ''Historically Unequal Legal Treatment'': The use of scholarship schemes lacking full employment rights (the "grant holder" status under RD 1326/2003), or the assimilation of the predoctoral contract into either the training-contract category (RD 63/2006 & Art. 11 ET) or the project/service contract category (Art. 15 ET), both of which eliminated social protection and severance guarantees. # ''Low Economic Remuneration'': The minimum salary percentage scheme (56% in years 1–2, 60% in year 3, and 75% in year 4) is considered disproportionate to the level of qualification and cost of living in university regions. # ''Excessive Teaching Load'': Predoctoral researchers being used to cover structural teaching needs beyond the maximum limit of 180 total hours (60 hours per year). # ''Disputes over Severance Rights'': Historical legal uncertainty over whether severance pay (''indemnización por extinción'') applies at the end of a predoctoral contract term. '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] The absence of explicit severance-pay rules in the 2011 LCTI and the 2019 EPIPF led to conflicting rulings among Superior Courts of Justice (TSJ of the Basque Country rejecting it versus TSJ of Galicia accepting it), ultimately requiring resolution by the Supreme Court (STS 903/2020) and legislative reform through Law 17/2022. Additionally, a postdoctoral transition period (''orientación postdoctoral'') was previously not accommodated within the predoctoral contract's duration scheme. '''Objectives''': [FACT] Reduce job precariousness among young researchers; strengthen legal certainty; align Spanish regulation with European standards (the European Charter for Researchers); guarantee severance pay of 12 days' salary per year worked; and facilitate the transition to the postdoctoral stage. '''Implementation''': [FACT] * ''Law 17/2022 on Science & RD 1251/2024'': Explicit recognition of the right to severance pay of 12 days per year worked, under Article 49.1.c of the Workers' Statute, for contracts that end. * ''Royal Decree 1251/2024 (EPIPF)'': Addition of a postdoctoral transition period of up to 12 months (provided the overall 4-year maximum duration is not exceeded), adjustment of the minimum salary reference to Group M3 of the AGE Single Collective Agreement, contract extension for reduced working hours due to family reconciliation, adjustment of the social security contribution bonus (€115/month, RDL 1/2023), and a mandatory anti-harassment/violence protocol. * ''Application of the LOSU (Organic Law 2/2023)'': Expansion of predoctoral contract allocation into the industrial sector via the "industrial-mention doctorate" (Art. 9.7 LOSU). '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] Recent jurisprudence (STSJ Castilla y León, 6 May 2024 & 30 September 2024; STSJ Madrid, 21 March 2024) confirmed the non-retroactivity of severance pay: the right applies only to contracts still active as of 7 September 2022, or those signed thereafter. '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] The lack of an automatic continuity guarantee into the postdoctoral stage, which contributes to fragile scientific careers; limited university budgets to absorb managed researchers; and insufficient oversight of maximum teaching-hour limits. ---- ==== 5. #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Recognition of a postdoctoral transition period (up to 12 months), integration with the LOSU (industrial doctorate), a Group M3 salary reference, severance pay upon contract termination, extension due to family reconciliation, a €115/month contribution bonus, and an anti-harassment protocol. # '''Policy Problem''': Why did conflicting jurisprudence arise among Superior Courts of Justice prior to the enactment of Law 17/2022? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Because the 2011 LCTI and the 2019 EPIPF did not contain explicit severance-pay rules, the TSJ of the Basque Country rejected severance pay (treating it as a special training contract), while the TSJ of Galicia accepted it (assimilating it to a project/service contract). # '''Legal Relationship''': What did the Supreme Court rule in STS 903/2020, of 13 October, regarding severance pay for predoctoral contracts? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] The Supreme Court ruled that the predoctoral contract was a training contract equivalent to a practical-training contract (Art. 11 ET), and that at the time, the legislature had not established a severance-pay right upon contract termination. # '''Reform''': How did Law 17/2022, of 5 September, resolve the debate over predoctoral researchers' severance-pay rights? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Law 17/2022 formally recognized the right to severance pay of 12 days' salary per year worked, under Article 49.1.c of the Workers' Statute, for predoctoral researchers. # '''Evidence/Case Study''': How was the non-retroactivity rule for severance pay applied under 2024 jurisprudence from the TSJ of Castilla y León and the TSJ of Madrid? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Severance pay applies only to contracts that were still active when Law 17/2022 took effect (7 September 2022), or those signed thereafter; contracts that ended before that date do not carry a right to severance pay. ---- ==== 6. MEDIAWIKI OUTPUT ==== {{Infobox Legal Policy Entity|name=The Job Precariousness of Young Researchers (Cabello Roldán, 2025)|stable_id=JPW-WORK-000010|official_name=La precariedad laboral de las personas jóvenes investigadoras: tratamiento normativo, doctrinal y jurisprudencial del personal investigador en formación en España|entity_type=Academic Legal Research / Policy Analysis|author=Aída Cabello Roldán|publisher=Universidad de Málaga (Revista de Trabajo y Seguridad Social, Vol. 34)|legal_basis=Law 14/2011 (LCTI, as amended by Law 17/2022) & RD 103/2019 (EPIPF, as reformed by RD 1251/2024)|jurisdiction=Spain / European Union|publication_date=June 2025 (Received: 13 February 2025)|status=Official / Published (ISSN 2255-1824)|key_topics=Predoctoral Contract, EPIPF, RD 1251/2024, Law 17/2022, Postdoctoral Transition, Severance Pay}} == Summary == '''The Job Precariousness of Young Researchers: Regulatory, Doctrinal, and Jurisprudential Treatment of Predoctoral Research Trainees in Spain''' is a labor law study written by Aída Cabello Roldán of Universidad de Málaga (UMA). This scholarly work provides an in-depth analysis of job precariousness among young researchers in Spain. The study evaluates the transformation of predoctoral contract regulation from a historical scholarship scheme into an independent employment relationship (Law 14/2011 LCTI, Law 17/2022, and Organic Law 2/2023 LOSU), the reform of the Statute of Predoctoral Research Trainees in Training (EPIPF, via Royal Decree 1251/2024), recognition of severance-pay rights (12 days per year), the postdoctoral transition period, and the evolving jurisprudence determining employment rights within the university sector. == Legal Basis == The regulations and legal reforms analyzed in this publication are grounded in the following Spanish and EU legal framework: * '''Law 14/2011, of 1 June, on Science, Technology and Innovation (LCTI)''': Article 21 (initial regulation of the predoctoral contract as an independent modality). * '''Law 17/2022, of 5 September''': Reform of the LCTI explicitly recognizing severance-pay rights upon contract termination. * '''Royal Decree 103/2019, of 1 March (EPIPF)''': The initial framework for the Statute of Predoctoral Research Trainees in Training. * '''Royal Decree 1251/2024, of 10 December''': Reform of the EPIPF refining remuneration rights, the postdoctoral transition period, and social protections. * '''Royal Legislative Decree 2/2015 (Workers' Statute — ET)''': Article 11 (training contracts), Article 15, and Article 49.1.c (severance pay for fixed-term contracts). * '''Organic Law 2/2023, of 22 March (LOSU)''': Article 9.7 (integration of industrial doctorates). * '''Recommendation 2005/251/EC''': The European Charter for Researchers and Code of Conduct for the Recruitment of Researchers. == Background == The scientific labor market for young researchers in Spain has historically been marked by high contractual uncertainty, salaries disproportionate to high qualifications, and a lack of career certainty following the doctorate. This has delayed financial independence and contributed to a "brain drain" phenomenon, with young talent moving abroad. == Objectives == 1. Strengthen legal certainty and employment protection for predoctoral researchers. 2. Clearly distinguish the predoctoral contract from scholarship schemes or ordinary training contracts. 3. Guarantee fair remuneration and a severance-pay right of 12 days per year worked. 4. Facilitate the transition to a postdoctoral career through a postdoctoral orientation period. 5. Limit teaching loads so as not to interfere with completion of the doctoral thesis. == Scope == The study covers in-depth analysis of four main pillars: 1. ''Indicators of Precariousness'': Youth unemployment rates, delayed labor-market entry, and barriers to emancipation. 2. ''Regulatory Evolution'': The transition from RD 1326/2003 (scholarship holder) through RD 63/2006 (training contract), the 2011 LCTI, Law 17/2022, to RD 1251/2024. 3. ''Provisions of RD 1251/2024'': Alignment with the LOSU, the postdoctoral transition period (12 months), the Group M3 salary reference, extension due to family reconciliation, and the €115/month contribution bonus. 4. ''Jurisprudential Analysis'': The severance-pay debate at the TSJ of the Basque Country, the TSJ of Galicia, STS 903/2020, and the enforcement of Law 17/2022's non-retroactivity by the TSJ of Castilla y León and the TSJ of Madrid. == Key Provisions == * '''Independent Nature of the Predoctoral Contract''': Configured as a special employment relationship with a maximum duration of 4 years, full-time. * '''Postdoctoral Transition Period''': RD 1251/2024 permits an extension of up to 12 months post-doctorate to prepare for career transition. * '''Teaching Limit''': Teaching duties capped at a maximum of 180 hours over the total contract period (maximum 60 hours/year). * '''Severance Pay (Indemnización)''': Set at 12 days' salary per year worked, under Article 49.1.c of the Workers' Statute, following Law 17/2022 and RD 1251/2024. * '''Principle of Severance-Pay Non-Retroactivity''': Severance pay applies only to contracts active as of 7 September 2022, or signed thereafter. == Implementation == Implementation is carried out by universities and public/private research centers, with social-court oversight and adjustment of internal university regulations based on the LOSU. == Policy Problems == * Still-limited schemes for absorbing postdoctoral talent into stable positions, contributing to ongoing career fragility. * Insufficient university operating budgets to support the consolidation of permanent positions. * Inadequate oversight of violations of maximum teaching-load limits at some faculties. == Reform == * Enactment of Law 17/2022, of 5 September (reform of the Science Law). * Enactment of Royal Decree 1251/2024, of 10 December (reform of the EPIPF). * Enactment of Organic Law 2/2023 (LOSU). == Relationships with Other Entities == * '''Implements''': Law 14/2011 (LCTI, as amended by Law 17/2022) & Organic Law 2/2023 (LOSU). * '''Applies To''': Predoctoral research trainees in training at universities and research institutions. * '''Replaces''': The former "training contract" / "project-or-service contract" scheme for young researchers. == See Also == * [[Statute of Predoctoral Research Trainees in Training]] * [[Law on Science, Technology and Innovation]] * [[Organic Law on the University System]] * [[Workers' Statute]] * [[European Charter for Researchers]] == References ==
