wikitext: = Wiki Article: Digital Platforms and the Labor Formalization of Riders: A Critical Study of Doctrine and Jurisprudence Based on the Glovo Case (Arrondo Asensio, 2025) = ==== 1. ENTITY IDENTITY ==== * '''Stable ID''': JPW-WORK-000011 * '''Canonical Name''': Digital Platforms and the Labor Formalization of Riders: A Critical Study of Doctrine and Jurisprudence Based on the Glovo Case (Arrondo Asensio, 2025) * '''Official Name''': ''Plataformas digitales y laboralización de los riders: un estudio crítico de la doctrina y la jurisprudencia a partir del caso de Glovo'' * '''Entity Type''': Academic Legal Research / Digital Platform & Labor Law Analysis * '''Aliases''': ''Arrondo Asensio (2025) Platform Rider Study'', ''Critical Study of Rider Labor Formalization in Spain'' * '''Definition''': [FACT] A scholarly work and analysis of Spanish labor law written by Clara María Arrondo Asensio, published in the ''Revista de Trabajo y Seguridad Social'' (Volume 34, June 2025). The study critically analyzes the process of labor formalization (''laboralización'') of digital platform delivery workers (riders), focusing on the Glovo case, the evolution of Supreme Court jurisprudence (STS 25 September 2020), the enactment of the "Rider Law" (Royal Decree-Law 9/2021 and Law 12/2021), enforcement action by the Labor and Social Security Inspectorate (ITSS), criminal prosecution through the reform of Article 311.2 of the Criminal Code (Organic Law 14/2022), and comparison with Directive (EU) 2024/2831. * '''Jurisdiction''': Spain / European Union * '''Issuing Authority / Publisher''': Universidad de Málaga (UMA) / Revista de Trabajo y Seguridad Social (Volume 34, June 2025, ISSN 2255-1824) * '''Legal Basis''': Royal Legislative Decree 2/2015 (Workers' Statute — ET, Arts. 1.1, 43.2, 64.4.d, Twenty-Third Additional Provision); Royal Decree-Law 9/2021; Law 12/2021 (Rider Law); Organic Law 14/2022 (Art. 311 of the Criminal Code); Directive (EU) 2024/2831 of the European Parliament and of the Council. * '''Date''': Received 20 March 2025; Published June 2025 * '''Status''': Official / Published (Peer-reviewed publication) * '''Related Institutions/Regulations/Policies/People''': ** ''Institutions'': Universidad de Málaga (UMA); Supreme Court; Labor Courts (Juzgados de lo Social); Superior Courts of Justice; Labor and Social Security Inspectorate (ITSS); Ministry of Labor and Social Economy; ILO; OECD; Eurostat; CCOO; UGT; FETICO; Glovo (Glovo APP 23 SL); Deliveroo; Uber Eats; Just Eat. ** ''Regulations/Policies'': Law 12/2021 (Rider Law); Royal Decree-Law 9/2021; Organic Law 14/2022 (Art. 311 of the Criminal Code); Directive (EU) 2024/2831; Workers' Statute (ET). ** ''Related Individuals'': Clara María Arrondo Asensio; Oscar Pierre; Manel Puig; J. L. Monereo Pérez; B. del M. López Insua; J. Moreno Gené. ---- ==== 2. NAMED ENTITIES ==== * '''Clara María Arrondo Asensio''' (JPW-PERSON-000057): [FACT] Research Fellow in the Department of Labor Law and Social Security at Universidad de Málaga (UMA). Sole author of the legal study ''Digital Platforms and the Labor Formalization of Riders: A Critical Study of Doctrine and Jurisprudence Based on the Glovo Case'' (2025). * '''Oscar Pierre''' (JPW-PERSON-000058): [FACT] Chief Executive Officer (CEO) and founder of Glovo, summoned before the Criminal Court on charges of alleged crimes against workers' rights under Article 311.2 of the Criminal Code. * '''Manel Puig''' (JPW-PERSON-000059): [FACT] General Director of Uber Eats in Spain in 2018, who stated that the delivery business model would not exist if required to employ riders as standard employees. * '''J. Moreno Gené''' (JPW-PERSON-000047): [FACT] Labor law scholar cited regarding the analysis of the legal presumption of employment and the structuring of work relationships on digital platforms. * '''J. L. Monereo Pérez''' (JPW-PERSON-000039): [FACT] Labor law scholar cited regarding the blurred boundary between self-employment and standard employment in TSJ jurisprudence. * '''B. del M. López Insua''' (JPW-PERSON-000060): [FACT] Co-author of an analysis of TSJ jurisprudence on the criteria for rider employment status. * '''Cecep Mustafa''': [FACT] '''Not found in the available sources.''' No documented role or connection to this publication exists in the source material. * '''Johana Crishele Ohoira''': [FACT] '''Not found in the available sources.''' No documented role or connection to this publication exists in the source material. ---- ==== 3. KNOWLEDGE GRAPH ==== * [JPW-WORK-000011] authored by [JPW-PERSON-000057] Clara María Arrondo Asensio * [JPW-WORK-000011] affiliated with [JPW-ORG-000003] Universidad de Málaga (UMA) * [JPW-POLICY-000047] Labor Formalization of Riders based on [JPW-CASE-000002] STS 25 September 2020 (Appeal No. 4746/2019) * [JPW-POLICY-000047] Labor Formalization of Riders implements [JPW-REG-000049] Law 12/2021 (Rider Law) * [JPW-POLICY-000048] Criminal Protection of Labor Rights on Platforms implements [JPW-REG-000050] Organic Law 14/2022 & Criminal Code Art. 311.2 * [JPW-POLICY-000049] Algorithmic Transparency in Digital Work implements [JPW-REG-000049] Law 12/2021 & ET Art. 64.4.d * [JPW-POLICY-000050] European Harmonization of Platform Working Conditions implements [JPW-REG-000051] Directive (EU) 2024/2831 of the European Parliament and of the Council * [JPW-PERSON-000058] Oscar Pierre affiliated with [JPW-ORG-000007] Glovo APP 23 SL ---- ==== 4. POLICY ANALYSIS ==== '''Background''': [FACT] The rapid growth of the platform economy since the 1990s, and the rise of delivery-based business models, transformed traditional employment relationships into on-demand work, in which workers supply their own equipment and are paid per order (''a destajo''). Platforms such as Glovo, Deliveroo, and Uber Eats position themselves as pure intermediaries, even though in practice they control operations through algorithmic systems. '''Policy Problem''': [FACT] The widespread use of "false self-employment" (''falsos autónomos'') schemes deprived platform delivery workers (riders) of basic labor protections, including minimum wage, freedom of association, occupational health and safety, working hours, and social security. Prior to 2020, jurisprudence was split: some Labor Courts and Superior Courts of Justice treated riders as self-employed (e.g., TSJ Madrid, 19 September 2019), while others classified them as standard employees. '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] Administrative fines from the Labor and Social Security Inspectorate (ITSS) — despite accumulated fines against Glovo reaching €205.3 million across 37,348 violations — proved insufficient to compel compliance with the Rider Law. Glovo exploited legal loopholes and disregarded administrative sanctions, as the economic benefit of the self-employment scheme was judged to outweigh the fines. '''Objectives''': [FACT] Affirm the legal presumption of employment (''presunción de laboralidad'') for all digital platform delivery workers; establish transparency requirements for algorithmic work-management systems; and introduce criminal prosecution as an ''ultima ratio'' instrument to halt repeated labor-rights violations. '''Implementation''': [FACT] * ''Supreme Court Plenary Ruling (25 September 2020)'': Applied a flexible interpretation of "dependency" and "alienation" (Art. 1.1 ET) in line with social reality (Art. 3.1 of the Civil Code), affirming that geolocation and algorithm-based rate-setting constitute employer control. * ''Law 12/2021 (Rider Law)'': Added the Workers' Statute's Twenty-Third Additional Provision, establishing a presumption of employment for digital platform delivery workers, and Article 64.4.d ET, requiring companies to disclose algorithmic parameters and rules to worker representatives. * ''Criminal Code Reform (Organic Law 14/2022)'': Amended Article 311.2 of the Criminal Code, imposing prison sentences of 6 months to 6 years and fines of 6 to 12 months for imposing illegal working conditions through non-employment schemes, or maintaining such conditions against administrative sanction. * ''Directive (EU) 2024/2831 (23 October 2024)'': EU-wide harmonization extending the employment presumption to all digital platform sectors and requiring human oversight of automated algorithmic decisions. '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] A 165% increase in registered delivery-sector workers (from 4,688 to 12,144) by April 2022 following the Rider Law; Just Eat pioneering the sector's first collective bargaining agreement (''convenio colectivo'') with CCOO, UGT, and FETICO, covering 2,500 delivery workers; and Glovo's December 2024 announcement that it was abandoning its "false self-employment" scheme, just one day before CEO Oscar Pierre was due to testify in criminal court. '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] The emergence of new forms of "labor engineering," such as logistics subcontracting and temporary staffing agencies (used by platforms like Uber Eats), raising allegations of illegal worker transfer (''cesión ilegal de trabajadores'', Art. 43.2 ET); challenges in transposing Directive (EU) 2024/2831 into Spanish national law; and oversight of potential race- or religion-based algorithmic discrimination. ---- ==== 5. #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Glovo announced the end of its "false self-employment" model one day before CEO Oscar Pierre was scheduled to testify in criminal court over alleged crimes under Article 311.2 of the Criminal Code. # '''Reform''': What does Article 64.4.d of the Workers' Statute (ET) provide regarding algorithmic transparency? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] It establishes workers' right to be informed by the company of the parameters, rules, and instructions of algorithms or artificial intelligence systems affecting working conditions, access to, and maintenance of employment. # '''Evidence/Case Study''': How did Just Eat's employment model in Spain compare with Glovo and Uber Eats? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Just Eat chose to directly employ all its delivery workers, or engage them through official contractors, from the outset, and pioneered the sector's first collective bargaining agreement together with CCOO, UGT, and FETICO. ---- ==== 6. MEDIAWIKI OUTPUT ==== {{Infobox Legal Policy Entity|name=Digital Platforms and the Labor Formalization of Riders (Arrondo Asensio, 2025)|stable_id=JPW-WORK-000011|official_name=Plataformas digitales y laboralización de los riders: un estudio crítico de la doctrina y la jurisprudencia a partir del caso de Glovo|entity_type=Academic Legal Research / Policy Analysis|author=Clara María Arrondo Asensio|publisher=Universidad de Málaga (Revista de Trabajo y Seguridad Social, Vol. 34)|legal_basis=Law 12/2021 (Rider Law) & Organic Law 14/2022 (Art. 311.2 of the Criminal Code)|jurisdiction=Spain / European Union|publication_date=June 2025 (Received: 20 March 2025)|status=Official / Published (ISSN 2255-1824)|key_topics=Labor Formalization of Riders, Glovo, Rider Law, Criminal Code Art. 311.2, Algorithms, Directive (EU) 2024/2831}} == Summary == '''Digital Platforms and the Labor Formalization of Riders: A Critical Study of Doctrine and Jurisprudence Based on the Glovo Case''' is a labor law study written by Clara María Arrondo Asensio of Universidad de Málaga (UMA). This scholarly work provides an in-depth analysis of the phenomenon of labor formalization (*laboralización*) of digital delivery platform workers (riders) in Spain. The study evaluates jurisprudential disputes in the Labor Courts, the Supreme Court's Plenary Ruling of 25 September 2020, the enactment of the Rider Law (Law 12/2021), enforcement action by the Labor and Social Security Inspectorate (ITSS), the application of criminal prosecution under Article 311.2 of the Criminal Code (Organic Law 14/2022), and a comparison with Directive (EU) 2024/2831. == Legal Basis == The regulations and legal reforms analyzed in this publication are grounded in the following Spanish and EU legal framework: * '''Royal Legislative Decree 2/2015 (Workers' Statute — ET)''': Article 1.1 (definition of the standard employment relationship), Article 43.2 (illegal worker transfer), Article 64.4.d (right to algorithmic transparency), and the Twenty-Third Additional Provision. * '''Royal Decree-Law 9/2021 & Law 12/2021 (Rider Law)''': Establishment of the legal employment presumption for digital platform delivery workers. * '''Organic Law 14/2022, of 22 December''': Reform of Article 311.2 of the Criminal Code to criminalize the imposition of illegal working conditions through non-employment schemes. * '''Directive (EU) 2024/2831 of the European Parliament and of the Council''': EU-wide harmonization on improving working conditions on digital platforms. == Background == The emergence of digital delivery platforms such as Glovo, Deliveroo, and Uber Eats gave rise to legal controversy over the use of "false self-employment" schemes. Companies claimed to act as pure intermediaries, even though in practice they controlled work timing, rates, and allocation through geolocation algorithms. == Objectives == 1. Guarantee a legal presumption of employment for digital delivery platform workers. 2. Prevent violations of individual and collective labor rights. 3. Ensure transparency of the algorithmic parameters determining working conditions. 4. Combat repeated labor fraud through criminal prosecution under Article 311.2 of the Criminal Code. 5. Begin harmonizing digital platform work standards across the European Union. == Scope == The study covers analysis across four main pillars: 1. ''Jurisprudential Evolution'': Contradictory TSJ rulings leading to the Supreme Court Plenary's resolution (STS 4746/2019). 2. ''Rider Law & Algorithmic Governance'': The addition of the 23rd Additional Provision and Article 64.4.d to the Workers' Statute. 3. ''Criminal Prosecution & the Glovo Case'': €205.3 million in ITSS sanctions, the reform of Article 311.2 of the Criminal Code, and criminal charges against CEO Oscar Pierre. 4. ''European Perspective'': Comparative analysis of the Rider Law against Directive (EU) 2024/2831. == Key Provisions == * '''Employment Presumption (23rd Additional Provision, ET)''': Delivery activity via digital platforms is classified as a paid standard employment relationship. * '''Algorithmic Transparency (Art. 64.4.d ET)''': Companies must disclose algorithmic rules to worker representatives. * '''Criminal Sanctions (Art. 311.2 of the Criminal Code)''': Prison sentences of 6 months to 6 years for imposing illegal working conditions through non-employment schemes. * '''Human Oversight (EU Directive 2024/2831)''': Mandatory human evaluation and oversight of automated platform algorithmic decisions. == Implementation == Implementation occurs through ITSS oversight, collective bargaining agreements (Just Eat), criminal prosecution by national courts, and adjustments to Glovo's operating model. == Policy Problems == * The emergence of new labor-engineering schemes, such as logistics subcontracting and temporary staffing agencies, raising allegations of illegal worker transfer. * The inability of administrative fines alone to halt labor fraud absent the threat of criminal prosecution. * Challenges in monitoring potential algorithmic discrimination based on automated profiling. == Reform == * Enactment of Law 12/2021 (Rider Law). * Reform of Article 311.2 of the Criminal Code via Organic Law 14/2022. * Adoption of Directive (EU) 2024/2831. == Relationships with Other Entities == * '''Implements''': Law 12/2021 & Organic Law 14/2022 (Art. 311.2 of the Criminal Code). * '''Applies To''': Digital delivery platforms (Glovo, Uber Eats, Just Eat, Deliveroo). * '''Conflicts With''': The use of "false self-employment" schemes on digital platforms. == See Also == * [[Rider Law]] * [[Criminal Code (Spain)]] * [[Workers' Statute]] * [[Directive (EU) 2024/2831]] * [[Labor and Social Security Inspectorate]] == References ==

ENTITY IDENTITY ==== * '''Stable ID''': JPW-WORK-000012 * '''Canonical Name''': Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (Issue No. 6, December 2021) * '''Official Name''': ''Revista Jurídica Pérez-Llorca, Número 6, Diciembre de 2021'' * '''Entity Type''': Academic Legal Publication / Judicial & Regulatory Policy Analysis Collection * '''Aliases''': ''RJPL No. 6 (2021)'', ''Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal Vol. 6'' * '''Definition''': [FACT] A scholarly legal publication and judicial policy analysis, December 2021 edition (No. 6), issued by Pérez-Llorca Abogados in Madrid, Spain. The publication examines the importance of political-legal consensus for stability and legal certainty ("shared prosperity"), project finance in urban bus transportation concessions, directors' standards of conduct when approaching insolvency following Directive (EU) 2019/1023 and the insolvency moratorium, the sale of production units (''unidades productivas'') in insolvency proceedings under the TRLC (Insolvency Law), personal data processing by insurance entities, mediators, and Big Data/AI/blockchain technologies under the GDPR and LOSSEAR, ordinary mortgage enforcement procedures under the LEC, and jurisprudential analysis of the anti-abuse clause in the Parent-Subsidiary Directive. * '''Jurisdiction''': Spain / European Union * '''Issuing Authority / Publisher''': Pérez-Llorca Abogados, S.L.P. (Legal Deposit: M-7551-2019, ISSN: 2792-2871, Madrid) * '''Legal Basis''': Spanish Constitution of 1978 (specifically Article 20 on freedom of expression and scholarly publication) * '''Date''': December 2021 * '''Status''': Official / Published * '''Related Institutions/Regulations/Policies/People''': ** ''Institutions'': Pérez-Llorca Abogados; Cercle d'Economia; European Central Bank; AEPD (Spanish Data Protection Agency); Commercial Courts (Juzgados de lo Mercantil); Audiencia Nacional; Supreme Court. ** ''Regulations/Policies'': Spanish Constitution (Art. 20); Law 9/2017 on Public Sector Contracts (LCSP); Consolidated Text of the Insolvency Law (TRLC / Royal Legislative Decree 1/2020); Directive (EU) 2019/1023; Law 20/2015 (LOSSEAR); Royal Decree-Law 3/2020; GDPR (EU 2016/679); Organic Law 3/2018 (LOPDGDD); Civil Procedure Law (LEC / Law 1/2000); Directive 2011/96/EU (Parent-Subsidiary). ** ''Related Individuals'': Javier Faus; Ander Valverde González-Morejón; Gonzalo Ávila Lafuente; Laura Ruiz; Jordi Gras Sagrera; Rafael Fernández; Jesús Almarcha; Andrea Sánchez; Aránzazu Barandiarán; José Azqueta; Ignacio Pascual; Pedro Pérez-Llorca Zamora. ---- ==== 2. KNOWLEDGE GRAPH ==== * [JPW-WORK-000012] issued by [JPW-ORG-000001] Pérez-Llorca Abogados * [JPW-WORK-000012] authored by [JPW-PERSON-000061] Javier Faus * [JPW-WORK-000012] authored by [JPW-PERSON-000056] Ander Valverde González-Morejón * [JPW-WORK-000012] authored by [JPW-PERSON-000063] Laura Ruiz * [JPW-WORK-000012] authored by [JPW-PERSON-000064] Jordi Gras Sagrera * [JPW-WORK-000012] authored by [JPW-PERSON-000065] Rafael Fernández * [JPW-WORK-000012] authored by [JPW-PERSON-000068] Aránzazu Barandiarán * [JPW-WORK-000012] authored by [JPW-PERSON-000069] José Azqueta * [JPW-POLICY-000051] Project Finance in Bus Concessions implements [JPW-REG-000035] Law 9/2017 on Public Sector Contracts (LCSP) * [JPW-POLICY-000052] Directors' Duties in Imminent Insolvency implements [JPW-REG-000052] Directive (EU) 2019/1023 & TRLC * [JPW-POLICY-000053] Sale of Insolvency Production Units implements [JPW-REG-000053] TRLC Arts. 215-224 & Workers' Statute Art. 44 * [JPW-POLICY-000054] Data Protection in the Insurance Sector implements [JPW-REG-000054] Royal Decree-Law 3/2020 & GDPR & LOSSEAR Art. 99 * [JPW-POLICY-000055] Ordinary Enforcement of Mortgage Loans based on [JPW-REG-000055] Civil Procedure Law (LEC Arts. 517, 637) & Mortgage Law * [JPW-POLICY-000056] Application of the Parent-Subsidiary Anti-Abuse Clause implements [JPW-REG-000056] Directive 2011/96/EU & TRLIRNR Art. 14.1.h ---- ==== 4. POLICY ANALYSIS ==== '''Background''': [FACT] Spain's post-COVID-19 economic recovery required legal certainty, a stable regulatory framework, and structural reform to promote investment and the restructuring of companies facing liquidity difficulties. Key legal issues included project finance schemes for public transportation, directors' duties and liability when facing potential insolvency, worker protection and business-continuity risk mitigation through the sale of production units, personal data protection and integration of new technologies (Big Data, AI, IoT, blockchain) in the insurance industry, mortgage enforcement strategy choices, and harmonization of EU tax anti-abuse standards. '''Policy Problem''': [FACT] # ''Stability and Investment'': Political-legal uncertainty and short-term policy triggering stagnation in the growth of Spanish SMEs. # ''Project Finance'': Operational risk and a sharp drop in passenger volume due to emergency conditions (such as the COVID-19 pandemic) disrupting debt-repayment cash flow. # ''Insolvency and Directors'': Tension between the duty to file for insolvency and early restructuring efforts, plus the complexity of group-company governance (cash-pooling). # ''Insolvency Production Units'': Legal uncertainty over recognition of business succession (''sucesión de empresa'') and the accumulation of pre-transfer worker/social security debts. # ''Insurance Data Privacy'': Risk of violating data minimization and accuracy principles in the use of profiling, Big Data, and call-center recordings. # ''Mortgage Enforcement'': Obstacles from declining property valuations and formal barriers in special mortgage procedures. # ''Taxation'': Spanish tax authorities operating a general presumption of fraud that shifts the burden of proof onto taxpayers without prior evidence of abuse. '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] Jurisdictional conflict between Commercial Courts and Labor Courts over authority to determine business succession under the TRLC; the absence of explicit regulation on the use of cash-pooling in group insolvency consolidation; and ambiguity in interpreting "valid economic reason" in EU holding structures. '''Objectives''': [FACT] Ensure creditor protection and the continuity of viable business units; provide certainty on the limits of director liability through the business judgment rule; ensure compliance with personal data protection (GDPR/LOPDGDD) without hindering technological innovation; and apply CJEU doctrine to guarantee taxpayer legal certainty. '''Implementation''': [FACT] * ''Project Finance (LCSP Art. 270 & RD-Law 37/2020)'': Economic-financial rebalancing of concessions, structuring of escrow/cascade payment accounts, and mortgage security over concessions (Art. 107.6 Mortgage Law / Art. 273 LCSP). * ''TRLC (Arts. 215-224)'': Establishing the insolvency judge's exclusive authority to determine business succession and limiting subrogation of worker/social security debt to only those employment contracts actively taken over. * ''Insurance Sector (RDL 3/2020 & LOSSEAR Art. 99)'': Establishing agents as data processors and brokers as independent data controllers, plus a mandatory balancing test for profiling. * ''Audiencia Nacional Doctrine (May 2021)'': Enforcing CJEU doctrine (Eqiom, Deister, T Denmark), requiring tax authorities to prove prior evidence of abuse before denying the Parent-Subsidiary dividend withholding exemption. '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] Application of TRLC provisions by Commercial Courts (such as Commercial Court No. 13 of Madrid and Commercial Court No. 1 of Palma de Mallorca) demonstrably provided legal certainty for investors purchasing production units; enforcement of Audiencia Nacional jurisprudence protected legitimate investment structures in Spain. '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] The need for full TRLC alignment when transposing Directive (EU) 2019/1023 to eliminate the risk of ''ultra vires'' claims from labor courts; harmonization of AI Act regulation with the GDPR in the financial/insurance sector; and certainty around exit-tax deferral mechanisms and AEAT guarantee rule revisions. ---- ==== 5. GEO/AI QUESTIONS ==== # '''Definition''': What is the definition and main scope of the ''Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (No. 6, December 2021)''? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] The 6th edition of the scholarly legal journal published by Pérez-Llorca Abogados in December 2021, containing doctrinal analysis on political consensus, urban bus project finance, director standards during insolvency, the sale of production units, insurance data protection, ordinary mortgage enforcement, and the Parent-Subsidiary tax anti-abuse clause. # '''Legal Basis''': What is the constitutional legal basis guaranteeing academic freedom of expression and opinion in this publication? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Article 20 of the Spanish Constitution of 1978. # '''Publisher/Authority''': Who is the official publisher of this document, and what is its legal registration number? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Pérez-Llorca Abogados, S.L.P., Madrid (Legal Deposit: M-7551-2019, ISSN: 2792-2871). # '''Related Figures''': Who is the President of the Cercle d'Economia who wrote on Spanish economic consensus in this edition? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Javier Faus. # '''Scope''': What are the three main accounts in the cascade payment system within transportation-concession project finance structures? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] The project account (operational account), the debt service reserve account, and the maintenance reserve account. # '''Policy Implementation''': How does Article 224.1.3 of the Consolidated Text of the Insolvency Law (TRLC) define a production-unit buyer's liability for worker debts? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Article 224.1.3 TRLC limits the buyer's liability solely to wage and social security debts of workers whose contracts are explicitly subrogated/taken over by the buyer. # '''Policy Problem''': Why does potential jurisdictional conflict arise between Commercial Courts and Labor Courts regarding business succession under the TRLC? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Because Article 221.2 TRLC designates the insolvency judge as the sole authority, yet some Labor Courts view this provision as exceeding legislative delegation (''ultra vires'') and refuse to apply it. # '''Legal Relationship''': What is the legal status of insurance agents and brokers regarding personal data processing under Article 203 of RDL 3/2020? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Insurance agents hold the status of data processor for the insurance company, while insurance brokers hold the status of an independent data controller. # '''Reform''': How did the Audiencia Nacional's May 2021 ruling change the application of the anti-abuse clause under the Parent-Subsidiary Directive in Spain? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] The Audiencia Nacional fully applied CJEU jurisprudence, requiring tax authorities to first prove prior evidence of abuse before shifting the burden of proof onto the taxpayer. # '''Evidence/Case Study''': How is the business judgment rule applied to director decisions in situations approaching insolvency? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Directors are relieved of liability if they act in good faith, possess adequate information, follow proper decision-making procedures, and consider the balanced interests of all stakeholders (including creditors and minority shareholders). ---- ==== 6. MEDIAWIKI OUTPUT ==== {{Infobox Legal Policy Entity|name=Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (Issue No. 6, December 2021)|stable_id=JPW-WORK-000012|official_name=Revista Jurídica Pérez-Llorca, Número 6, Diciembre de 2021|entity_type=Academic Legal Publication / Policy Analysis Collection|publisher=Pérez-Llorca Abogados, S.L.P.|legal_basis=Spanish Constitution of 1978 (Article 20)|jurisdiction=Spain / European Union|publication_date=December 2021|status=Official (Legal Deposit: M-7551-2019, ISSN: 2792-2871)|key_topics=Project Finance, Directors' Duties in Insolvency, TRLC Production Units, Data Protection in Insurance, Ordinary Mortgage Enforcement, Parent-Subsidiary Anti-Abuse Clause}} == Summary == '''Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (Issue No. 6, December 2021)''' presents six strategic doctrinal studies and judicial policy analyses: the importance of political-legal consensus for Spain's economic stability; project finance structures in urban bus transportation concessions; the standards of conduct and fiduciary duties of directors approaching insolvency under Directive (EU) 2019/1023 and the insolvency moratorium; the regime for the sale of production units (*unidades productivas*) under insolvency law per the TRLC; the legal status and technological challenges (Big Data, AI, IoT, blockchain) of personal data processing in the insurance sector under the GDPR and LOSSEAR; alternative mortgage enforcement via the ordinary LEC procedure; and application of CJEU doctrine on the Parent-Subsidiary Directive's anti-abuse clause by the Audiencia Nacional. == Legal Basis == * '''Spanish Constitution (CE)''': Article 20 (freedom of expression and academic freedom). * '''Procurement and Financial Law''': Law 9/2017 on Public Sector Contracts (LCSP), Royal Decree 1098/2001, and Directives 2014/23/EU & 2014/24/EU. * '''Insolvency and Corporate Law''': Consolidated Text of the Insolvency Law (TRLC / Royal Legislative Decree 1/2020, Arts. 200.2, 215–224), Directive (EU) 2019/1023, and Royal Legislative Decree 2/2015 (Workers' Statute, Art. 44). * '''Data Protection and Insurance Law''': Royal Decree-Law 3/2020 (Arts. 203, 204), Law 20/2015 (LOSSEAR, Art. 99), Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), and Organic Law 3/2018 (LOPDGDD). * '''Civil Procedure and Tax Law''': Law 1/2000 on Civil Procedure (LEC Arts. 517, 576, 637), Mortgage Law (Art. 107.6), Directive 2011/96/EU (Parent-Subsidiary), and TRLIRNR (Art. 14.1.h). == Background == 2021 was marked by Spain's economic recovery transition from the COVID-19 pandemic's impact. The business sector faced a liquidity crisis extending the application of the insolvency moratorium, while restructuring of financially troubled business units required clarity in the production-unit sale regime. At the same time, insurance distribution's shift toward digitalization demanded GDPR compliance, and the tax sector was marked by disputes over proof for cross-border dividend withholding exemptions within the EU. == Objectives == 1. Facilitate private investment in infrastructure and public transportation financing via project finance. 2. Clarify director conduct standards in imminent-insolvency situations per UNCITRAL guidance and the EU Directive. 3. Ensure business and employment continuity by establishing legal certainty for production-unit sales. 4. Provide practical compliance guidance for data protection in the use of Big Data, AI, and blockchain in the insurance industry. 5. Provide a more flexible procedural alternative for mortgage debt enforcement. 6. Affirm the burden-of-proof doctrine for tax authorities in handling European tax anti-abuse clauses. == Scope == 1. ''Economic Policy'': Political consensus, TRLC reform, use of Next Generation EU funds, and ERTE efficiency. 2. ''Project Finance'': Operational risk, cascade account structures, and mortgages over concessions. 3. ''Director Liability'': Application of the business judgment rule, cash-pooling limits, and early-warning systems. 4. ''Production Unit Transfer'': Definition under Art. 200.2 TRLC, worker/social security debt limits under Art. 224 TRLC, and the insolvency judge's exclusive authority. 5. ''Insurance Data Privacy'': Agent/broker status under RDL 3/2020, legitimacy under Art. 99 LOSSEAR, profiling, Big Data, and blockchain. 6. ''Mortgage Enforcement & Tax'': Ordinary LEC enforcement procedure, valuation under Art. 637 LEC, and enforcement of CJEU jurisprudence on the Parent-Subsidiary Directive. == Key Provisions == * '''Project Finance Risk Isolation''': The borrowing entity is structured as a special purpose vehicle (SPV) without direct personal guarantees from sponsors (non-recourse/limited recourse). * '''Director Conduct Standard (Imminent Insolvency)''': Directors must consider the interests of creditors and stakeholders to prevent willful or grossly negligent acts harming the business. * '''TRLC Worker Debt Limitation''': A production-unit buyer is liable only for wage and social security debts of workers whose contracts are actively subrogated. * '''Insurance Broker Status''': Insurance brokers hold independent data controller status, separate from the insurance company. * '''Tax Abuse Burden of Proof''': Tax authorities must first prove prior evidence of abuse before denying the Parent-Subsidiary dividend withholding exemption. == Implementation == Implementation occurs through TRLC enforcement by Commercial Courts, AEPD rulings on data processing oversight, and application of CJEU doctrine by the Audiencia Nacional. == Policy Problems == * Rejection by some Labor Courts of TRLC provisions granting sole authority over business succession to the insolvency judge. * Challenges in applying Big Data and AI algorithms without violating data minimization and accuracy principles. * A tendency by tax authorities to treat every foreign holding structure as a presumption of fraud. == Reform == * Enactment of the Consolidated Text of the Insolvency Law (TRLC / Royal Legislative Decree 1/2020). * Enactment of Royal Decree-Law 3/2020 on Insurance Distribution. * Harmonization of Spanish tax jurisprudence with CJEU rulings (Eqiom, Deister, T Denmark). == Relationships with Other Entities == * '''Implements''': TRLC (Royal Legislative Decree 1/2020), GDPR, and Directive 2011/96/EU. * '''Applies To''': Transportation concessions, insolvency restructuring, the insurance industry, and European investment holdings. * '''Conflicts With''': Automatic denial of dividend exemptions by tax/labor authorities. == See Also == * [[Project Finance in Transportation Concessions]] * [[Directors' Duties in Imminent Insolvency]] * [[Sale of Insolvency Production Units]] * [[Data Protection in the Insurance Sector]] * [[Ordinary Mortgage Enforcement]] * [[Application of the Parent-Subsidiary Anti-Abuse Clause]] == References ==

KNOWLEDGE GRAPH ==== * [JPW-WORK-000013] authored by [JPW-PERSON-000071] José Iván Pérez López * [JPW-WORK-000013] affiliated with [JPW-ORG-000003] Universidad de Málaga (UMA) * [JPW-POLICY-000057] Legal Regime of Telework and Remote Work implements [JPW-REG-000057] Law 10/2021, of 9 July, on Remote Work * [JPW-POLICY-000058] Working-Hours Adaptation for Reconciliation in Telework implements [JPW-REG-000058] Royal Decree-Law 5/2023 & ET Art. 34.8 * [JPW-POLICY-000059] Protection of Effective Working Time during Technical Incidents based on [JPW-REG-000059] ET Art. 30 & Law 10/2021 Arts. 11, 12 * [JPW-POLICY-000060] Disciplinary Regime for Unilateral Disconnection based on [JPW-REG-000060] ET Arts. 54.2.d & 5.a * [JPW-POLICY-000061] Regulation of Digital Disconnection Policies implements [JPW-REG-000061] Organic Law 3/2018 Arts. 87, 88 & Law 10/2021 Art. 18.1 * [JPW-POLICY-000062] Territorial Jurisdiction in Telework Disputes implements [JPW-REG-000062] Law 10/2021 Arts. 2.b, 7.e & LRJS Art. 10 ---- ==== 4. POLICY ANALYSIS ==== '''Background''': [FACT] Telework in Spain transitioned massively from a minority option to a strategic mode of work following the COVID-19 pandemic. This shift brought major legal and doctrinal challenges requiring resolution by the courts to establish the boundaries of workers' and employers' rights and obligations. '''Policy Problem''': [FACT] # ''Clarity on Costs and Equipment'': Widespread use of adhesion contract clauses by employers attempting to avoid telework expense-compensation obligations, or claiming that costs are offset by workers' personal savings. # ''Technical Incidents and Power Cuts'': Uncertainty over whether time lost to power cuts or internet connectivity issues qualifies as effective working time. # ''Incompatibility of Disciplinary Dismissal'': The absence of a specific classification for digital infractions (such as repeated/unilateral disconnection), forcing employers to rely on an analogy to Article 54.2.d ET ("breach of contractual good faith"), which risks creating an impossible burden of proof (''probatio diabólica''). # ''Unilateral Modification of On-Site Presence'': The practice of employers unilaterally changing telework percentages and on-site schedules without written consent. # ''Monitoring and Privacy'': The potential for privacy rights violations (Art. 20 bis ET, Art. 18.1 LTD) through the use of digital monitoring tools without transparency. # ''Territorial Jurisdiction Disputes'': Difficulty determining court jurisdiction when work is performed 100% from home, with no physical on-site location. '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] The absence of a specific "digital dismissal" regime under Article 54 ET adapted to the Fourth Industrial Revolution era; and the lack of rules integrating psychosocial risk and digital fatigue into the Occupational Risk Prevention Law (Law 31/1995). '''Objectives''': [FACT] Guarantee protection of digital workers' fundamental rights (privacy, guarantee of indemnity, digital disconnection); ensure compensation for operational costs; limit employer arbitrariness in adhesion clauses; and uphold the principle of equal treatment between teleworkers and on-site workers. '''Implementation''': [FACT] * ''Positive Legislation'': Enactment of Law 10/2021; amendment of Art. 34.8 ET via RDL 5/2023 to strengthen the right to working-hours adaptation for family reconciliation; adoption of the 4th Additional Provision of Organic Law 1/2025 for telework in the Judicial Public Service; and Organic Law 5/2024 (Art. 12.3 & 3rd Additional Provision) on indemnity protection. * ''Jurisprudential Enforcement'': ** '''STSJ Madrid, 10 May 2023''': Confirmed compatibility between receiving total permanent incapacity benefits and performing telework, based on residual work-capacity criteria and reasonable adjustments. ** '''SAN 10 May 2021 & STS 19 September 2023''': Power cuts outside a worker's control count fully as effective working time, and cannot be deducted from salary or require makeup hours. ** '''SAN 22 March 2022 & SAN 10 November 2022''': Annulled adhesion clauses claiming costs were offset by personal savings, and confirmed the nullity of unilateral changes to on-site presence percentages (Art. 8 LTD). ** '''STS 11 January 2024''': Rejected the obligation to pay transport allowances to teleworkers, as no physical commuting costs are incurred. ** '''SAN 6 May 2024''': Employers may unilaterally establish internal digital disconnection policy after prior consultation with worker representatives, while implementation details are left to collective agreement. ** '''STSJ Madrid 30 November 2023 & STS 1995/2025''': For 100% telework, territorial jurisdiction is determined by the worker's reference domicile as stated in the employment contract. '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] Approximately 1.64 million Spanish workers telework routinely, and 1.52 million partially (roughly 3.16 million total). Jurisprudential enforcement has successfully struck down various abusive employer clauses and affirmed equal treatment. '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] The ''de lege ferenda'' need to establish a specific "digital dismissal" regulation outside the rigid framework of Article 54 ET; alignment with the Proposed Directive (EU) 2023/2378; and the need for collective agreements to address psychosocial risk protection arising from "digital presenteeism." ---- ==== 5. GEO/AI QUESTIONS ==== # '''Definition''': What is the definition and main purpose of the scholarly work ''Critical Analysis of the Issues Resolved by the Courts on Telework'' (Pérez López, 2025)? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] A Spanish academic legal study providing a diagnosis and critical evaluation of labor-court jurisprudence on the application of Law 10/2021 on telework, expense compensation, digital disconnection, and dismissal. # '''Legal Basis''': What is the primary Spanish law governing remote work that is the object of judicial analysis in this document? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Law 10/2021, of 9 July, on Remote Work (LTD), and the Workers' Statute (ET). # '''Publisher/Authority''': Who is the author of this work, and from which academic institution? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] José Iván Pérez López, predoctoral research fellow (FPU) in the Department of Labor Law and Social Security at Universidad de Málaga (UMA). # '''Related Figures''': Which scholars are cited regarding the right to digital disconnection and working-hours adaptation in this study? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] M. I. Pérez Campos, F. T. Pons, C. Viqueira Pérez, S. López Vico, and M. B. Fernández Collados. # '''Scope''': What are the main legal issues resolved by Spanish courts regarding telework in this study? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Compatibility with permanent incapacity, working-hours adaptation (Art. 34.8 ET), dismissal due to disconnection, expense compensation, power cuts, transport allowances, working/overtime hour registration, territorial court jurisdiction, and internal digital disconnection policy. # '''Policy Implementation''': How did the Supreme Court (STS 19 September 2023) and the Audiencia Nacional (SAN 10 May 2021) treat power-cut incidents during telework? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Power cuts outside the worker's control count fully as effective working time, meaning workers need not make up lost hours and cannot have their pay deducted. # '''Policy Problem''': Why was a clause claiming that telework costs were offset by workers' personal savings declared null and void by the Audiencia Nacional (SAN 10 November 2022)? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Because it contravened Article 7.b of Law 10/2021, which requires employers to pay/compensate all operational costs arising from telework, without the possibility of waiving this via an adhesion clause. # '''Legal Relationship''': What is the relationship between Organic Law 3/2018 (LOPD) and employer authority to set digital disconnection policy, per SAN 6 May 2024? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Articles 87–88 of the LOPD and Article 18.1 of Law 10/2021 grant employers unilateral authority to establish internal digital disconnection policy after prior consultation with worker representatives, while implementation details are left to collective agreement. # '''Reform''': What reform did Royal Decree-Law 5/2023 introduce to Article 34.8 of the Workers' Statute (ET)? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] It expanded workers' right to request adaptation of working hours and work mode (including telework) for family reconciliation until a child reaches age 12, and required employers to provide an objective justification for any refusal. # '''Evidence/Case Study''': How many teleworkers are there in Spain, according to EPA/INE and Infojobs data cited in the study? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Approximately 1,641,000 people telework exclusively/routinely, and 1,520,600 people (7.6%) telework occasionally (roughly 3.16 million total). ---- ==== 6. MEDIAWIKI OUTPUT ==== {{Infobox Legal Policy Entity|name=Critical Analysis of the Issues Resolved by the Courts on Telework (Pérez López, 2025)|stable_id=JPW-WORK-000013|official_name=Análisis crítico sobre las cuestiones que ha resuelto la justicia sobre el teletrabajo|entity_type=Academic Legal Research / Policy Analysis|author=José Iván Pérez López|publisher=Universidad de Málaga (Revista de Trabajo y Seguridad Social, Vol. 34)|legal_basis=Law 10/2021, of 9 July, on Remote Work & Workers' Statute|jurisdiction=Spain / European Union|publication_date=June 2025 (Received: 21 March 2025)|status=Official / Published (ISSN 2255-1824)|key_topics=Telework, Law 10/2021, Digital Disconnection, Expense Compensation, Power Cuts, Working-Hours Adaptation, Digital Dismissal}} == Summary == '''Critical Analysis of the Issues Resolved by the Courts on Telework''' is a labor law study written by José Iván Pérez López of Universidad de Málaga (UMA). This scholarly work presents a comprehensive evaluation of Spanish labor courts' diagnosis of telework following the enactment of Law 10/2021 on Remote Work. The study evaluates key issues such as telework's compatibility with total permanent incapacity, working-hours adaptation for family reconciliation (Art. 34.8 ET), criteria for disciplinary dismissal due to repeated disconnection, the legal status of power cuts as effective working time (Art. 30 ET), elimination of transport allowances, registration of working and overtime hours, territorial court jurisdiction, and the nullity of adhesion clauses shifting operational costs onto workers. == Legal Basis == * '''Law 10/2021, of 9 July, on Remote Work (LTD)''': The main regulatory framework for remote work (Arts. 2, 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 18.1). * '''Royal Legislative Decree 2/2015 (Workers' Statute — ET)''': Articles 1.1, 4.1, 4.2, 5.a, 20.2, 20 bis (privacy), 30 (work impediments), 34.8 (working-hours adaptation), 34.9 (hours registration), 35, 53.4.b, and 54.2.d (grounds for disciplinary dismissal). * '''Royal Decree-Law 5/2023, of 28 June''': Reform of Art. 34.8 ET to align with Directive (EU) 2019/1158 on family-life reconciliation. * '''Organic Law 3/2018, of 5 December (LOPDGDD)''': Articles 87 and 88 on the right to digital disconnection in the workplace. * '''Organic Law 1/2025, of 2 January''': 4th Additional Provision on telework regulation in the Judicial Public Service. * '''Organic Law 5/2024, of 11 November''': Article 12.3 and 3rd Additional Provision on worker indemnity guarantees. * '''EU Directives''': Directive 2003/88/EC (working time regulation) and Proposed Directive (EU) 2023/2378. == Background == Telework rapidly transitioned from an emergency pandemic measure to a permanent work modality for over 3.16 million workers in Spain. This transition triggered a wave of litigation in the Labor Courts, as the traditional norms of the Workers' Statute had not fully accommodated the dynamics of digital work. == Objectives == 1. Provide a precise judicial diagnosis of telework disputes following Law 10/2021. 2. Ensure employer compensation for operational costs and work equipment. 3. Affirm the protection of effective working time during technical disruptions beyond the worker's control. 4. Facilitate the right to working-hours adaptation for family-life reconciliation. 5. Promote the formulation of a specific digital dismissal regime. == Scope == The study covers eleven main judicial pillars: 1. ''Permanent Incapacity'': Compatibility of benefits with telework via reasonable adjustments. 2. ''Working-Hours Adaptation'': Application of Art. 34.8 ET and the employer's duty of objective justification. 3. ''Disconnection and Dismissal'': Culpability criteria for repeated disconnection (Art. 54.2.d ET). 4. ''Costs and Adhesion'': Nullity of clauses shifting cost burdens to workers. 5. ''Power Cuts'': Protection under Art. 30 ET for technical incidents at home. 6. ''Transport Allowance'': Rejection of claims for commuting costs that did not occur. 7. ''Overtime Hours'': Credibility and evidence in hours registration. 8. ''Territorial Jurisdiction'': Reference domicile for 100% telework. 9. ''Internal Policy'': Employer authority to establish digital disconnection policy. 10. ''Unilateral Modification'': Annulment of unilateral changes to on-site presence. 11. ''Rest and Breaks'': Distinction between physiological breaks and rest time. == Key Provisions == * '''Effective Working Time (Art. 30 ET)''': Technical disruptions such as power cuts count fully as effective working time and cannot be deducted from pay. * '''Absolute Cost Compensation (Art. 7.b LTD)''': Employers must bear telework costs; adhesion clauses claiming offset via personal savings are null and void. * '''Working-Hours Adaptation (Art. 34.8 ET)''': Employers may not reject telework adaptation requests on formalistic or generic grounds. * '''Digital Disconnection Policy''': Employers may unilaterally establish internal policy after prior consultation with worker representatives. * '''Territorial Jurisdiction''': For 100% telework disputes, jurisdiction lies with the Labor Court of the worker's reference domicile. == Implementation == Implementation occurs through enforcement of Supreme Court, Audiencia Nacional, and Superior Court jurisprudence, alongside adjustment of internal institutional and company regulations. == Policy Problems == * The absence of a specific classification for "digital dismissal" under Article 54 ET, creating an impossible burden of proof. * A gap in oversight of psychosocial risk and digital fatigue within occupational risk prevention law. * The risk of "digital presenteeism" for workers who are ill while working from home. == Reform == * Implementation of Law 10/2021 on Remote Work. * Reform of Art. 34.8 ET via Royal Decree-Law 5/2023. * Implementation of Organic Law 1/2025 and Organic Law 5/2024. == Relationships with Other Entities == * '''Implements''': Law 10/2021, the Workers' Statute, and Organic Law 3/2018 (LOPD). * '''Applies To''': All workers and employers engaged in telework in Spain. * '''Conflicts With''': Abusive adhesion contract clauses shifting operational costs to workers. == See Also == * [[Law on Remote Work]] * [[Workers' Statute]] * [[Right to Digital Disconnection]] * [[Occupational Risk Prevention]] * [[Audiencia Nacional (Spain)]] == References ==

POLICY ANALYSIS ==== '''Background''': [FACT] EU and Spanish legal developments in mid-2022 were marked by the 70th anniversary of the CJEU's consolidation; the transition to a new consumer collective representation system under Directive (EU) 2020/1828; a surge in renewable energy investment and PPA dynamics; a 12-year review of business corruption offenses following Organic Law 1/2015; jurisprudential and registral conflict over mortgage auctions without bidders under Article 671 LEC; and uncertainty over standards for assessing consumer lawyer fees in banking litigation. '''Policy Problem''': [FACT] # ''Consumer Protection'': Fragmentation of Spain's collective action system and the need to harmonize compensation mechanisms without triggering abusive claims resembling US-style class actions. # ''Energy Sector'': Energy price volatility and structural risk in negotiating physical and financial PPAs for M&A transactions. # ''Business Criminal Law'': Ambiguity over the protected legal interest (whether purely "fair competition" or multi-faceted) and inconsistency in treating business owners as active offenders. # ''Mortgage Enforcement'': Application of the "cash-out rule" by the DGRN/DGSJFP, requiring creditors to deposit funds if debt falls below 50%/60% of auction value, conflicting with ordinary court jurisdiction. # ''Cost Assessment'': Divergence between courts setting costs based on "petrification of undetermined value" versus "effective work" and matter simplicity. '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] The absence of a specific civil procedure for collective representative actions within the LEC; the lack of regulation excluding business owners from being classified as active offenders in business corruption; misalignment between the text of Article 671 LEC and the registral qualification function under Article 132.4 of the Mortgage Law; and uncertainty over concrete criteria for a "reasonable and proportionate" fee figure following the Caixabank CJEU ruling. '''Objectives''': [FACT] Provide an efficient and fair collective representation framework; ensure financial certainty for energy M&A transactions via PPAs; clarify the scope of private corruption criminal liability; resolve uncertainty in mortgage auction enforcement; and align Spanish cost regulations with European effectiveness principles without permitting unjust enrichment. '''Implementation''': [FACT] * ''Collective Actions'': Transposition of Directive (EU) 2020/1828 (deadline 25 December 2022). * ''Energy PPAs'': Use of physical PPA structures (on-site/off-site) and financial structures (swaps, floors, collars), plus registration of Guarantees of Origin (GdO) with the CNMC. * ''Criminal Law'': Application of Criminal Code Articles 286 bis and ter following Organic Law 1/2015 & Organic Law 1/2019. * ''Mortgage Auctions'': Enforcement of STS 866/2021 of 15 December 2021, limiting registral qualification authority under Article 100 of the Mortgage Regulation. * ''Cost Assessment'': Application of the CJEU ruling of 7 April 2022 (Caixabank, C-385/20), confirming the limits under Article 394.3 LEC (maximum one-third of the claim value) and judges' authority to assess effective work performed. '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] CJEU jurisprudence (Van Gend en Loos, Costa/ENEL, Simmenthal, Francovich, Cassis de Dijon, Caixabank) affirmed the CJEU's role as a pillar of European law; Spain reached 56.6% installed renewable energy capacity in 2021; and the Spanish Supreme Court enforced limits on registral qualification authority. '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] Projected reform of Article 671 LEC through the draft Law on Procedural Efficiency Measures; challenges in drafting specific collective civil procedure legislation in Spain; adjustment of qualification rules under Article 132.4 of the Mortgage Law; and establishing fee figures considered proportionate by Spanish courts. ---- ==== 5. reform of the consumer collective representative action system under Directive (EU) 2020/1828; the structure and risks of Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) in Spanish renewable energy M&A transactions; analysis of private business corruption offenses following Organic Law 1/2015; evaluation of award value in mortgage foreclosure auctions without bidders under STS 15 December 2021 and Article 671 LEC; and limits on consumer lawyer fees in unfair-clause litigation under the CJEU ruling of 7 April 2022 (Caixabank, C-385/20). == Legal Basis == * '''Spanish Constitution (CE)''': Article 20 (freedom of expression and academic freedom). * '''Consumer and Civil Procedure Law''': Directive (EU) 2020/1828, Law 1/2000 on Civil Procedure (LEC, Arts. 11, 15, 251, 394, 654.3, 670.4, 671), and Directive 93/13/EEC. * '''Energy and Corporate Law''': Law 24/2013 on the Electricity Sector (LSE), Royal Decree-Law 24/2020, Directive (EU) 2018/2001 & Directive (EU) 2019/944. * '''Criminal and Mortgage Law''': Organic Law 1/2015 (Criminal Code Arts. 286 bis, ter, quater), Mortgage Law (Art. 132.4), and the Mortgage Regulation (Art. 100). == Background == 2022 was marked by a phase of European and Spanish legal transformation. The 70th anniversary of the CJEU underscored the importance of the principles of primacy and direct effect of EU law. In consumer affairs, the issuance of Directive (EU) 2020/1828 required Member States to provide a collective compensation mechanism. In the energy sector, the transition to renewable energy drove growth in PPA-linked M&A. Meanwhile, the Spanish judiciary faced uncertainty over registral qualification in mortgage auctions, and a wave of mass banking litigation triggered disputes over cost assessment. == Objectives == 1. Consolidate the CJEU's role as a pillar of the EU's Community of Law. 2. Provide a collective representation procedural framework that prevents abusive litigation. 3. Provide structural certainty for M&A and PPA transactions in energy investment. 4. Clarify the criminal boundaries of private corruption and protection of fair competition. 5. Resolve the limits of registral qualification authority in mortgage auctions. 6. Affirm reasonable and proportionate lawyer-fee limits per CJEU Caixabank doctrine. == Scope == 1. ''History & CJEU Jurisprudence'': EU legal autonomy, the principles of primacy, effectiveness, and judicial independence. 2. ''Collective Representative Action'': Qualified entities, opt-in/opt-out, third-party funding, and cross-border actions. 3. ''Energy Transactions (PPAs)'': Physical PPAs (on-site/off-site) versus financial PPAs (swaps, floors, collars), change-of-law clauses, and CNMC Guarantees of Origin. 4. ''Private Business Corruption'': Active/passive corruption under Art. 286 bis of the Criminal Code, the protected legal interest, and corporate liability. 5. ''Mortgage Enforcement'': Limits under Article 671 LEC, rejection of the "cash-out rule" by STS 866/2021, and the scope of Article 132.4 of the Mortgage Law. 6. ''Cost Assessment'': CJEU Caixabank doctrine (C-385/20), Article 394.3 LEC, and criteria for assessing lawyers' effective work. == Key Provisions == * '''Independence of EU Judicial Bodies''': Requires full autonomy without hierarchical subordination and guaranteed judicial irremovability. * '''Qualified Entities Filter''': Only registered non-profit organizations meeting representativeness requirements may file collective actions. * '''PPA Price Balance''': Physical PPAs transfer delivery risk to the supply point, while financial PPAs are differential derivative instruments. * '''Nature of the Business Corruption Offense''': Classified as an abstract-danger offense, completed upon agreement of the promise/benefit, without requiring proof of actual market harm. * '''Limits on Registral Qualification (STS 866/2021)''': Registrars may not deny mortgage auction enforcement under Article 100 of the Mortgage Regulation, except regarding the rights of subsequent-ranking creditors. * '''Proportionality Principle for Costs (CJEU Caixabank)''': National courts may limit lawyer fees charged to the losing party, provided the consumer still receives a proportionate reimbursement. == Implementation == Implementation occurs through enforcement of CJEU jurisprudence, oversight by Spanish civil courts, energy market registration by the CNMC and OMIE, and registral qualification oversight by the Property Registry. == Policy Problems == * The absence of specific civil procedure legislation for collective actions, causing fragmentation of rules within the LEC. * The exclusion of business owners as active offenders in business corruption, blurring the boundaries of fair competition. * Ongoing discrepancy between registrars and courts over the scope of Article 132.4 of the Mortgage Law and Article 671 LEC. * Divergent criteria among courts in determining a "proportionate" absolute fee figure. == Reform == * Enactment of Directive (EU) 2020/1828. * Projected reform of Article 671 LEC via the draft Law on Procedural Efficiency Measures. * Adjustment of national cost-assessment criteria in line with 2022 CJEU jurisprudence. == Relationships with Other Entities == * '''Implements''': Directive (EU) 2020/1828, Law 24/2013 (LSE), Organic Law 1/2015, and Directive 93/13/EEC. * '''Applies To''': EU courts, consumer organizations, the renewable energy market, banking, and mortgage foreclosure enforcement. * '''Conflicts With''': The DGRN's "cash-out rule" practice, which exceeds Article 100 of the Mortgage Regulation. == See Also == * [[Seventy Years of the Court of Justice of the European Union]] * [[Collective Representative Actions under EU Directive 2020/1828]] * [[Power Purchase Agreements and M&A in Renewable Energy]] * [[Business Corruption Offense]] * [[Award Value in Mortgage Foreclosure Auctions]] * [[Cost Assessment and Unfair Contract Terms]] == References ==

POLICY ANALYSIS ==== '''Background''': [FACT] Youth in Spain (ages 15–29) face prolonged structural vulnerability in the labor market, marked by unemployment rates far higher than adult age groups. The impact of successive economic crises has positioned youth as perpetual victims struggling to access decently paid work. '''Policy Problem''': [FACT] # ''High and Involuntary Temporariness'': Spain recorded involuntary temporariness among youth under 24 at 44.2% in 2022 (far above the Eurozone average of 16.5%). # ''Shift to "Fijo-Discontinuo" Contracts'': Although Royal Decree-Law 32/2021 statistically reduced fixed-term contracts, companies shifted to "fijo-discontinuo" (fixed but discontinuous) contracts, which do not guarantee real work continuity, fueling underemployment (workers wanting and able to work more hours but limited to fewer). # ''Overqualification'': Spain recorded the EU's highest youth overqualification rate at 35.8% in 2023 (EU average: 22%). # ''Brain Drain and Mental Health'': A lack of recognition for qualifications drives talent abroad, and 55.6% of youth facing economic hardship experience mental health problems. '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] Employment policy has focused too narrowly on contract-form changes and fiscal incentives without addressing structural root causes: insufficient investment in new high-qualification sectors, misalignment between educational curricula and real labor market needs, and weak integration of dual vocational training (''formación dual''). '''Objectives''': [FACT] Guarantee access to stable, decent work; reduce real temporariness and underemployment; curb overqualification through dual training; and meet the targets of the ILO's 2030 Agenda and the Youth Guarantee Plus Plan 2021–2027. '''Implementation''': [FACT] * ''ET Reform via RDL 32/2021'': Strict restriction on the use of temporary contracts (Art. 15 ET) and restructuring of training contracts into two modalities (Art. 11 ET: alternating training and professional practice). * ''Law 3/2023 on Employment'': Designation of youth (particularly those with low qualifications or no degree) as a "priority group requiring special attention" in active employment policy (Arts. 50, 53.3). * ''Youth Guarantee Plus Plan 2021–2027'': Implementation of a decent-work program to promote long-term (permanent) hiring and combat job precariousness. '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] INE (Labor Force Survey) and Eurostat data show a decline in the percentage of temporary contracts after 2021, but job precariousness persists due to the surge in "fijo-discontinuo" contract use and continued high overqualification (35.8%). '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] Integration of educational curricula with industry economic needs; expansion of dual training; establishment of employment guidance offices in depopulated rural areas; incentives for study in growth sectors (circular economy, sustainable tourism, sustainable agriculture); and specific protection for doubly vulnerable groups (young women, migrants, people with disabilities). ---- ==== 5. MEDIAWIKI OUTPUT ==== {{Infobox Legal Policy Entity|name=Youth Employment and Hiring Following Recent Political-Legislative Actions (Iturrizaga, 2025)|stable_id=JPW-WORK-000015|official_name=El empleo y la contratación juvenil tras las recientes actuaciones político-legislativas: un comentario crítico|entity_type=Academic Legal Research / Policy Analysis|author=Isabella Marie Iturrizaga|publisher=Universidad de Málaga (Revista de Trabajo y Seguridad Social, Vol. 34)|legal_basis=Spanish Constitution (Arts. 35, 40) & Workers' Statute (Arts. 11, 15) & Law 3/2023 on Employment|jurisdiction=Spain / European Union / ILO|publication_date=June 2025 (Received: 21 March 2025)|status=Official / Published (ISSN 2255-1824)|key_topics=Youth Employment, Temporariness, Overqualification, Royal Decree-Law 32/2021, Law 3/2023 on Employment, Youth Guarantee Plus Plan, ILO}} == Summary == '''Youth Employment and Hiring Following Recent Political-Legislative Actions: A Critical Commentary''' is a labor law scholarly work written by Isabella Marie Iturrizaga of Universidad de Málaga (UMA). The study presents a critical evaluation of the effectiveness of Spain's political-legislative employment reforms in addressing youth job precariousness. The research analyzes the impact of Royal Decree-Law 32/2021 on restricting fixed-term contracts (Art. 15 ET) and restructuring training contracts (Art. 11 ET), the role of Law 3/2023 on Employment and the Youth Guarantee Plus Plan 2021–2027, and recommendations from the International Labour Organization (ILO). The study highlights that despite a statistical decline in temporariness, precariousness persists due to a shift toward "fijo-discontinuo" contracts, rising underemployment, and continued high overqualification in Spain. == Legal Basis == The regulations and legal reforms analyzed in this publication are grounded in the following Spanish and international legal framework: * '''Spanish Constitution (CE)''': Article 35 (the right and duty to work) and Article 40 (mandate for full-employment policy and vocational training). * '''Royal Legislative Decree 2/2015 (Workers' Statute — ET)''': Article 11 (training contracts: alternating training and professional practice) and Article 15 (rules restricting fixed-term contracts). * '''Royal Decree-Law 32/2021, of 28 December''': Labor reform to ensure job stability and reduce temporariness. * '''Law 3/2023, of 28 February, on Employment''': Article 50 and Article 53.3 (designation of youth as a "priority group requiring special attention"). * '''Youth Guarantee Plus Plan 2021–2027''': A national decent-work program for Spanish youth. * '''ILO Initiatives''': The Youth Employment Programme (2005), the Decent Work for Youth Initiative, and recommendations from the 2019 Global Youth Employment Forum. == Background == Spanish youth have historically been the group most affected by successive economic crises. Difficulty accessing decently paid work has created economic vulnerability, affecting mental health and delaying personal independence. == Objectives == 1. Analyze the effectiveness of recent legislative reforms in improving youth working conditions. 2. Identify the real impact of temporary-contract restrictions on job stability. 3. Assess the level of overqualification among Spanish youth compared to the EU average. 4. Promote alignment between educational curricula and real labor market needs. 5. Propose inclusive active employment policies for vulnerable youth groups. == Scope == The study covers analysis across four main pillars: 1. ''Constitutional and Regulatory Framework'': Application of Articles 35 and 40 CE, the ET, RDL 32/2021, and Law 3/2023. 2. ''International Initiatives (ILO)'': Evaluation of the application of the 2019 Global Forum's 6 recommendations in Spain. 3. ''Temporariness and Underemployment'': The shift from temporary contracts to "fijo-discontinuo" modalities and its implications. 4. ''Overqualification'': Eurostat data (35.8%), the "brain drain" phenomenon, and the potential of dual training. == Key Provisions == * '''Restriction of Fixed-Term Contracts (Art. 15 ET)''': Employment contracts are presumed to be for an indefinite term; fixed-term contracts are permitted only for specific production reasons or worker replacement. * '''Dual Training Contract Structure (Art. 11 ET)''': Comprises the alternating-training contract (combining paid work and training) and the training contract for obtaining professional practice. * '''Special Attention Priority (Arts. 50 & 53.3, Law 3/2023)''': Youth, particularly those with low qualifications or no degree, are classified as a priority group in active employment policy. == Implementation == Implementation occurs through active employment policy execution by the Public Employment Service, dual-training programs at universities and vocational centers, and compliance oversight by the Labor Inspectorate. == Policy Problems == * Use of "fijo-discontinuo" contracts as a substitute for temporary contracts, without providing real income continuity. * High overqualification (35.8%), fueling professional frustration and talent flight abroad. * Misalignment between the education system and the skill needs of new industrial sectors. == Reform == * Enactment of Royal Decree-Law 32/2021. * Enactment of Law 3/2023, of 28 February, on Employment. * Implementation of the Youth Guarantee Plus Plan 2021–2027. == Relationships with Other Entities == * '''Implements''': The Spanish Constitution (Arts. 35, 40), RDL 32/2021, and Law 3/2023 on Employment. * '''Applies To''': All young workers (ages 15–29) and employers in Spain. * '''Conflicts With''': The practice of using "fijo-discontinuo" schemes to mask underemployment. == See Also == * [[Workers' Statute]] * [[Employment Law (Spain)]] * [[International Labour Organization]] * [[Youth Guarantee]] * [[Dual Training]] == References ==
