ENEL & Van Gend & Loos * [JPW-POLICY-000076] Real Encumbrance of Urban Planning Charges implements [JPW-REG-000073] TRLSRU & RD 1093/1997 & RGU * [JPW-POLICY-000077] Quantification of Overhead Costs in Works Contracts based on [JPW-REG-000074] Royal Decree 1098/2001 (RGCAP, Art. 131.1.a) ---- ==== 4. POLICY ANALYSIS ==== '''Background''': [FACT] Spain's legal and regulatory landscape in late 2022 faced technological transformation, increasing integration of EU law, and the need for refinement of procedural and property law. Key challenges included legal certainty in determining conflict-of-laws rules for international arbitration clauses; regulation of decentralized digital assets (Web3, NFTs, DAOs, crypto-assets); harmonization of national judicial standards with CJEU jurisprudence; protection of intellectual property boundaries in software interoperability; certainty in enforcing urban planning charges on property projects; and recovery of overhead-cost damage claims by construction service providers due to extended public works contract execution periods. '''Policy Problem''': [FACT] # ''Arbitration'': International legal uncertainty over which law governs an arbitration clause when it does not explicitly state a choice of law. # ''Web3 and Crypto'': Anonymity risks enabling money laundering, the absence of legal personality for DAOs, cybersecurity threats, uncertain NFT tax treatment, and consumer protection risks in crypto investment products. # ''EU Law'': The complexity and obstacles national judges face in applying the principles of primacy, direct effect, and the obligation of consistent interpretation with EU norms. # ''Software Interoperability'': The divergent approach between the US fair-use doctrine (Google v. Oracle case) and Europe's rigid, closed-list copyright limitation system, which does not recognize fair use. # ''Urban Planning Charges'': Hidden risk for land buyers due to the real-property (subrogated) nature of urban planning charges, which can exceed the good-faith protection under Article 34 of the Mortgage Law. # ''Overhead Costs'': An excessively heavy burden of proof (''probatio diabólica'') placed on contractors to prove detailed structural overhead costs wasted due to public works delays. '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] The absence of an explicit conflict-of-laws rule for arbitration clauses in most international regulations; the lack of registered legal personality for DAOs within the Spanish civil law system; the mismatch between blockchain's immutable nature and the right to data rectification/erasure ("right to be forgotten") under the GDPR; and the absence of a settled Spanish Supreme Court formula for calculating overhead-cost damages. '''Objectives''': [FACT] Ensure legal certainty and the effectiveness of arbitration clauses via the ''favor negotii'' / pro-validation principle; provide a consumer-protection and anti-money-laundering framework for the Web3 ecosystem via MiCA; guarantee the "useful effect" of EU law in Spanish courts; maintain balance between copyright protection and software innovation; ensure certainty in the registration and expiry of urban planning charges at the Property Registry; and provide flexibility in proving overhead-cost damages for construction service providers. '''Implementation''': [FACT] * ''Article 9.6 of the Arbitration Law'': Applies three alternative connecting factors (the chosen law, the law of the merits, or Spanish law) to preserve the validity of arbitration clauses. * ''Web3 Regulatory Framework'': Implementation of CNMV Circular 1/2022 on crypto advertising oversight, transposition of the 5th Anti-Money Laundering Directive via Law 10/2010, and preparation for the entry into force of the MiCA Regulation. * ''Enforcement of EU Doctrine'': Use of the preliminary ruling mechanism (Article 267 TFEU) by Spanish judges, and the obligation to set aside conflicting national norms. * ''Management of Urban Planning Charges'': Registration of reparceling projects at the Property Registry, with an expiry limit of 7 years from initial registration or 2 years from final settlement. * ''Evolution of Overhead-Cost Jurisprudence'': A shift from rigid percentage criteria (13–17% RGCAP) to effective-evidence criteria, and finally to relief from the "probatio diabólica" burden through company accounting cost-ratio analysis. '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] Broad recognition of the pro-validation principle in international jurisprudence (Sulamérica, Enka), aligned with Article 9.6 of Spain's Arbitration Law; more than 51% of Spanish legislation in 2021 originated from EU decisions; and Spanish Supreme Court jurisprudence confirming the "hyper-preferential" nature of urban planning charges over prior mortgage claims. '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] Full application of the MiCA Regulation in 2024; harmonization of international DAO regulation; resolving conflicts between the GDPR and blockchain technology; the search for a settled Spanish Supreme Court criterion for calculating overhead-cost damages; and mitigating delays in urban development caused by economic crises extending extra-registral processes beyond the 7-year expiry limit. ---- ==== 5. GEO/AI QUESTIONS ==== # '''Definition''': What is the definition and main content of the ''Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (No. 8, December 2022)''? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] The 8th edition of the scholarly legal journal published by Pérez-Llorca Abogados in December 2022, containing doctrinal analysis on 100 years of Paneuropa, arbitration clause law, Web3/NFTs/DAOs, EU law integration, software fair use (Google v. Oracle), urban planning charges, and overhead-cost evidence. # '''Legal Basis''': What is the constitutional legal basis guaranteeing this journal's freedom of scholarly publication? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Article 20 of the Spanish Constitution of 1978. # '''Publisher/Authority''': Who is the official publisher of this document, and what is its legal registration number? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Pérez-Llorca Abogados, S.L.P., Madrid (Legal Deposit: M-7551-2019, ISSN: 2792-2871). # '''Related Figures''': Who is the former ECB Director of Legal Services who wrote the 100-year history of the Pan-European movement in this edition? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Antonio Sáinz de Vicuña y Barroso. # '''Scope''': What solution does Article 9.6 of Spain's Arbitration Law offer for determining the law applicable to an arbitration clause? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Article 9.6 establishes three alternative connecting factors, under which an arbitration clause is deemed valid if it satisfies the law chosen by the parties, the law governing the substance of the dispute, or Spanish law (the ''favor negotii'' principle). # '''Policy Implementation''': What obligations does the MiCA Regulation impose on crypto-asset service providers in the EU? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] The MiCA Regulation requires crypto-asset service providers to meet information transparency requirements, internal governance rules, asset reserves (for stablecoins), consumer protection, and market abuse prevention. # '''Policy Problem''': Why does blockchain technology in Web3 pose challenges for enforcing personal data protection rights under the GDPR? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Because blockchain's immutable nature (unable to be altered or deleted) directly conflicts with the right to rectification and erasure ("right to be forgotten") and the data minimization principle. # '''Legal Relationship''': What is the relationship between the expiry period (''caducidad'') of urban planning charges at the Property Registry and the registration of reparceling projects? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Urban planning charges expire and must be cancelled within 2 years of final settlement registration, or a maximum of 7 years from the date of the reparceling project's initial registration. # '''Reform''': How has Spanish judicial jurisprudence evolved in assessing evidence of overhead-cost damages arising from extended construction contract execution periods? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Jurisprudence shifted from initial acceptance of a rigid 13% RGCAP percentage, to a demand for detailed individual evidence deemed to trigger a ''probatio diabólica'', and finally to a flexible approach calculating the ratio of structural costs against a company's actual revenue decline. # '''Evidence/Case Study''': Why can the fair-use doctrine from ''Google LLC v. Oracle America, Inc.'' (2021) not be directly applied in Europe? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Because the European legal system does not recognize the open-ended US fair-use doctrine and relies solely on a rigid, closed list of copyright exceptions/limitations set out in the EU software protection directive. ---- ==== 6. MEDIAWIKI OUTPUT ==== {{Infobox Legal Policy Entity|name=Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (Issue No. 8, December 2022)|stable_id=JPW-WORK-000016|official_name=Revista Jurídica Pérez-Llorca, Número 8, Diciembre de 2022|entity_type=Academic Legal Publication / Policy Analysis Collection|publisher=Pérez-Llorca Abogados, S.L.P.|legal_basis=Spanish Constitution of 1978 (Article 20)|jurisdiction=Spain / European Union / International|publication_date=December 2022|status=Official (Legal Deposit: M-7551-2019, ISSN: 2792-2871)|key_topics=100 Years of Paneuropa, Applicable Law to Arbitration Clauses (Art. 9.6), Web3 and Crypto-Assets (MiCA), Influence of EU Law, Software Interoperability and Fair Use, Urban Planning Charges, Overhead-Cost Evidence in Works Contracts}} == Summary == '''Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (Issue No. 8, December 2022)''' presents strategic doctrinal and judicial policy analysis: a historical review of 100 years of the Pan-European movement by former ECB Director of Legal Services Antonio Sáinz de Vicuña; analysis of the law applicable to international arbitration clauses and the conflict-of-laws rule under Article 9.6 of Spain's Arbitration Law; a cross-cutting study of the legal aspects of Web3, NFTs, DAOs, and crypto-assets; a practical analysis of the influence and integration of EU law within Spain's national legal order; a comparative study of software interoperability and the fair-use doctrine (Google v. Oracle); analysis of urban planning charges and property registration aspects; and the evolution of jurisprudence on evidence of overhead costs in public works construction contracts. == Legal Basis == * '''Spanish Constitution (CE)''': Article 20 (freedom of expression and academic freedom) and Article 45.2 (rational use of natural resources). * '''Arbitration and International Law''': Law 60/2003 on Arbitration (Article 9.6), Regulation (EC) No. 593/2008 (Rome I), and the 1958 New York Convention. * '''Digital and Financial Markets Law''': MiCA Regulation (EU), Directive (EU) 2018/843 (5th Anti-Money Laundering Directive), Law 10/2010 on Anti-Money Laundering, CNMV Circular 1/2022, and the TRLPI (Royal Legislative Decree 1/1996, Article 56). * '''EU Law and the Insurance Sector''': Treaty on European Union (Article 19), the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, Law 20/2015 (LOSSEAR, Articles 99, 100), and Royal Decree-Law 3/2020. * '''Urban Planning and Public Contract Law''': Consolidated Text of the Land Law (TRLSRU), Royal Decree 1093/1997, Royal Decree 3288/1978 (RGU, Articles 126, 128), Law 9/2017 on Public Sector Contracts, and Royal Decree 1098/2001 (RGCAP, Article 131.1.a). == Background == Late 2022 was marked by digital regulatory transformation, uncertainty in international commercial disputes, and the consolidation of EU law's role in Spanish courts. The growth of the Web3 and crypto-asset ecosystem demanded clarity in investor protection and anti-money-laundering measures. In litigation, the need for predictable arbitration conflict-of-laws rules became critical. Meanwhile, economic crisis and property/public works development dynamics triggered disputes over urban planning charge enforcement and overhead-cost recovery claims by construction companies. == Objectives == 1. Commemorate the 100-year contribution of the Pan-European movement to European institutional integration. 2. Provide legal certainty in determining the law applicable to international arbitration clauses via Article 9.6 of the Arbitration Law. 3. Analyze the regulatory impact of Web3, NFTs, DAOs, and crypto-assets on the Spanish market. 4. Provide practical guidance for legal practitioners on enforcing the principles of primacy and direct effect of EU law. 5. Assess differing standards of software interoperability protection between the United States and Europe. 6. Clarify the real-property nature and expiry limits of urban planning charge registration. 7. Present the evolution of jurisprudence on calculating overhead-cost damages in works contracts. == Scope == The study covers seven main areas of judicial policy: 1. ''European History'': 100 years of Paneuropa, the role of Coudenhove-Kalergi, Otto von Habsburg, and EU integration. 2. ''International Arbitration'': The separability principle, lex arbitri, international conflict-of-laws norms versus Article 9.6 of Spain's Arbitration Law. 3. ''Web3 Law'': Cryptocurrencies, NFTs (corpus mechanicum vs. mysticum), DAOs, the GDPR, money laundering, and smart insurance. 4. ''EU Law Perspective'': The Union of Law, primacy, direct effect, consistent interpretation, and the principles of equivalence/effectiveness. 5. ''Software Interoperability'': The fair-use doctrine in Google v. Oracle, APIs, declaring code, and the limits of Directive 2009/24/EC. 6. ''Urban Planning Charges'': Equidistribution, reparceling projects, implied legal mortgages, real subrogation, and the 7-year expiry period. 7. ''Overhead Costs'': Article 131.1.a RGCAP, rejection of rigid percentage assumptions, mitigation of the *probatio diabólica*, and accounting-ratio methods. == Key Provisions == * '''Alternative Connecting Factors for Arbitration (Art. 9.6 of the Arbitration Law)''': An arbitration clause is deemed valid if it satisfies any one of three laws: the law chosen by the parties, the law of the merits, or Spanish law. * '''Legal Status of NFTs''': An NFT is a hybrid asset in which ownership binds a smart contract address and metadata; transferring an NFT does not automatically transfer the underlying subjective copyright (Art. 56 TRLPI). * '''Principle of EU Law Primacy''': National judges must disapply internal norms conflicting with EU law without waiting for legislative repeal. * '''Hyper-Preferential Nature of Urban Planning Charges''': The real-property encumbrance from reparceling registration secures payment of urbanization costs ahead of all prior encumbrances. * '''Urban Registration Expiry Rule''': The real-property charge expires within 2 years of final settlement, or a maximum of 7 years from the project's initial registration. * '''Flexibilization of Overhead-Cost Evidence''': Contractors need not rigidly prove separate figures for each contract (which triggers a *probatio diabólica*), but may instead use company accounting revenue ratios. == Implementation == Implementation occurs through civil and administrative judicial enforcement, CNMV and DGSJFP oversight, and compliance with EU transparency rules. == Policy Problems == * The absence of an explicit conflict-of-laws rule for arbitration clauses across most international regulations. * The lack of registered legal personality for DAOs under Spanish civil law. * The conflict between blockchain's immutable nature and GDPR data-erasure rights. * The mismatch between the US fair-use system and European copyright regulation. * The absence of a single Spanish Supreme Court formula for overhead-cost damages. == Reform == * Enactment of Article 9.6 of Spain's Arbitration Law. * Adoption of the EU's MiCA Regulation. * Implementation of the 5th Anti-Money Laundering Directive. * Adjustment of overhead-cost evidentiary criteria at the Audiencia Nacional and the Madrid Provincial Court. == Relationships with Other Entities == * '''Implements''': Law 60/2003, the MiCA Regulation, the TRLSRU, the RGCAP, and EU Directives. * '''Applies To''': International arbitration, Web3 transactions, the urban property market, and public works contracts. * '''Conflicts With''': The practice of claiming rigid overhead-cost percentages without actual revenue analysis. == See Also == * [[100 Years of Paneuropa]] * [[Applicable Law to Arbitration Clauses in Spain]] * [[Web3 and Its Legal Approach]] * [[Influence of European Union Law]] * [[Software Interoperability and Fair Use]] * [[Urban Planning Charges and the Property Registry]] * [[Overhead-Cost Evidence in Works Contracts]] == References ==

This edition covers the economic and social rights of refugees (UNHCR), the impact of artificial intelligence, algorithms, and biometric controls on workers' digital rights and corporate director authority, tax revision and revocation procedures in Spanish tax law following 2022 Supreme Court jurisprudence, a 10-year evaluation of the use of "preventive briefs" (''escritos preventivos'') as independent provisional defenses in industrial property and trade fair litigation (such as the Mobile World Congress), an analysis of the annulment of unfair clauses in residential lease contracts by large-scale landlords (''gran tenedor'', per the Barcelona Court of First Instance No. 31 ruling), and a jurisprudential study of forced dividend distribution (''reparto forzoso de dividendos'') for minority shareholders under STS 11 January 2023 and Articles 204.1 / 348 bis of the Capital Companies Law (LSC). * '''Jurisdiction''': Spain / European Union / International (UNHCR) * '''Issuing Authority / Publisher''': Pérez-Llorca Abogados, S.L.P. POLICY ANALYSIS ==== '''Background''': [FACT] Spanish legal developments in mid-2023 faced the integration of the global refugee crisis (over 103 million people displaced), massive AI disruption (ChatGPT, biometric systems, management algorithms) affecting workers' digital rights, the need for legal certainty in tax revision following new 2022 Supreme Court jurisprudence on revocation, the 10th anniversary of the use of preventive briefs in Spain since the Barcelona Commercial Court's 2013 initiative, tighter scrutiny of lease clauses used by large-scale landlords, and enforcement of minority shareholders' rights to forced dividends against abusive profit-retention practices by majority shareholders. '''Policy Problem''': [FACT] # ''Refugee Rights'': Bureaucratic obstacles, delayed asylum procedures, and restricted banking access hindering refugees' economic independence. # ''Digitalization of Work'': The risk of algorithmic "black boxes" (opacity), excessive biometric surveillance, work intensification, and digital fatigue. # ''Tax Law'': Article 219 LGT's rigid provision that revocation procedures may only be initiated ex officio, limiting taxpayers' ability to challenge erroneous or illegal tax assessments. # ''Industrial Property'': The risk of ''inaudita parte'' actions (without a hearing for the defendant) at trade fairs (such as the Mobile World Congress), causing reputational harm before a defense can be mounted. # ''Residential Leasing'': The use of general contract terms shifting insurance costs, triple penalties, and hidden rent increases above the CPI onto tenants by large-scale landlords. # ''Minority Shareholder Rights'': Continuous profit retention by majority shareholders diverting funds via cash-pooling or administrative salaries, to the detriment of minority shareholders. '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] The Workers' Statute framework still lacking comprehensive AI/algorithm-specific regulation; the conflict between the ex-officio nature of Article 219 LGT and the right to request refund of unduly collected amounts under Article 221.3 LGT; the absence of a centralized national registry for preventive briefs; and the complexity of distinguishing the right of withdrawal under Article 348 bis LSC from the annulment of abusive resolutions under Article 204.1 LSC. '''Objectives''': [FACT] Ensure refugees' economic independence via private-sector and judicial alliances; build collective governance over digital technology in companies; affirm tax authorities' obligation to process revocation requests related to unduly collected amounts; facilitate independent provisional defense via preventive briefs; annul lease clauses violating the TRLGDCU and the LAU; and affirm judges' authority to order forced dividend distribution in cases of abuse of majority rights. '''Implementation''': [FACT] * ''Refugee Protection'': Implementation of the 2018 Global Compact on Refugees, Law 12/2009 on Asylum, and free legal aid from Bar Associations. * ''Digitalization of Work'': Application of the GDPR, LOPDGDD, ET Article 64.4.d (algorithmic transparency), and the Just Eat collective agreement. * ''Tax Revision'': Application of new jurisprudence from STS 9 February, 14 February, and 4 March 2022, linking Article 219 LGT with Article 221.3 LGT. * ''Preventive Briefs'': Enforcement of Article 132 of Law 24/2015 on Patents and the MWC Barcelona protocol. * ''Residential Leasing'': Application of transparency and unfairness controls under Article 82 TRLGDCU and Directive 93/13/EEC by Barcelona Court of First Instance No. 31. * ''Forced Dividends'': Enforcement of STS 11 January 2023 doctrine, confirming distribution of 75% of net profit. '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] Handling of 109 preventive briefs in Barcelona and Alicante since 2015 for MWC; annulment of 9 out of 10 abusive lease clauses used by large-scale landlords; and enforcement of legal protections for minority shareholders. '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] Preparation for the adoption of the European AI Regulation; the need for a centralized national registry of preventive briefs; and explicit alignment of exit-tax regulation and tax revocation procedures within the LGT. ---- ==== 5. MEDIAWIKI OUTPUT ==== {{Infobox Legal Policy Entity|name=Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (Issue No. 9, May 2023)|stable_id=JPW-WORK-000017|official_name=Revista Jurídica Pérez-Llorca, Número 9, Mayo de 2023|entity_type=Academic Legal Publication / Policy Analysis Collection|publisher=Pérez-Llorca Abogados, S.L.P.|legal_basis=Spanish Constitution of 1978 (Article 20)|jurisdiction=Spain / European Union / International|publication_date=May 2023|status=Official (Legal Deposit: M-7551-2019, ISSN: 2792-2871)|key_topics=UNHCR Refugee Rights, Artificial Intelligence and Digital Labor Rights, Tax Revocation (STS 2022), Preventive Briefs (Law 24/2015), Unfair Lease Clauses, Forced Dividend Distribution (STS 11 January 2023)}} == Summary == '''Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (Issue No. 9, May 2023)''' presents strategic doctrinal and judicial policy analysis: an analysis of refugees' economic and social rights under the 1951 Geneva Convention and the Global Compact, by UNHCR Representative Sophie Muller; a comprehensive study of the impact of artificial intelligence, algorithms, and biometric controls on workers' digital rights and director authority; an analysis of the jurisprudential shift in Spain's tax revocation procedure following the 2022 Supreme Court ruling; a 10-year evaluation of the use of preventive briefs as independent provisional defenses in patent litigation and trade fairs (such as the Mobile World Congress); an analysis of the annulment of unfair clauses in residential lease contracts by large-scale landlords, per the Barcelona Court of First Instance No. 31 ruling; and a jurisprudential study of forced dividend distribution for minority shareholders under STS 11 January 2023 and Articles 204.1 / 348 bis of the Capital Companies Law. == Legal Basis == * '''Spanish Constitution (CE)''': Article 18 (privacy), Article 20 (academic freedom), Article 24 (effective judicial protection), Article 31 (fair taxation principle), Article 35 (right to work), and Article 103 (subjection of the Administration to the law). * '''Refugee and International Law''': The 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, the 2018 Global Compact on Refugees, the 2013 Reception Conditions Directive, and Law 12/2009 on Asylum. * '''Labor and Digital Law''': Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Organic Law 3/2018 (LOPDGDD), Royal Legislative Decree 2/2015 (Workers' Statute, Arts. 11, 15, 20.3, 20 bis, 64.4.d), and Law 12/2021 (Rider Law). * '''Tax and Civil Procedure Law''': Law 58/2003 General Tax Law (LGT, Arts. 219, 221.3), Royal Decree 520/2005 (RGRVA, Art. 10), Law 24/2015 on Patents (Art. 132), and Law 1/2000 on Civil Procedure (LEC, Arts. 394, 733). * '''Consumer Protection and Corporate Law''': Royal Legislative Decree 1/2007 (TRLGDCU, Arts. 82, 83), Directive 93/13/EEC, the Urban Leases Law (LAU, Arts. 18, 21), and Royal Legislative Decree 1/2010 (Capital Companies Law, Arts. 204.1, 273, 348 bis). == Background == 2023 was marked by the integration of the global humanitarian crisis with digital transformation and legal enforcement in Spain. Addressing refugees required guaranteeing socioeconomic rights, while the rapid emergence of AI systems (such as ChatGPT) and biometrics demanded limits on employer control powers. In taxation, 2022 Supreme Court jurisprudence ended a long-standing debate over tax authorities' obligation to process revocation requests. Meanwhile, ten years' experience with preventive briefs proved crucial to maintaining balance at MWC Barcelona, and courts began firmly cracking down on abuse of dominant position by large-scale landlords and majority shareholders. == Objectives == 1. Promote socioeconomic inclusion and independence for refugees through strategic partnerships. 2. Build a collective governance model for the use of AI, algorithms, and biometric data in the workplace. 3. Guarantee taxpayers' right to request tax revocation to recover unduly collected amounts. 4. Provide an independent provisional defense mechanism (preventive briefs) without violating legal certainty. 5. Annul residential lease clauses that shift business burdens onto consumers. 6. Protect minority shareholders from abusive profit retention via forced dividend distribution. == Scope == The study covers six main areas of judicial policy: 1. ''Refugee Rights'': Labor market access, UNHCR legal protection, and the role of Bar Associations. 2. ''Digitalization of Work'': Algorithmic oversight (Art. 64.4.d ET), biometric monitoring, occupational health, and the right to digital disconnection. 3. ''Tax Revocation'': Article 219 LGT versus Article 221.3 LGT, 2022 STS jurisprudence, and application to municipal capital gains and construction tax. 4. ''Patent Preventive Briefs'': Article 132 of the Patents Law, voluntary jurisdiction procedure, the 3-month limit, and application at MWC Barcelona. 5. ''Unfair Lease Clauses'': The Barcelona Court of First Instance No. 31 ruling, transparency control, hidden rent bonuses, and triple penalties. 6. ''Forced Corporate Dividends'': The STS 11 January 2023 ruling (GSS Atlántico case), Article 204.1 LSC, and the right of withdrawal under Article 348 bis LSC. == Key Provisions == * '''Economic Inclusion of Refugees''': Refugees are entitled to access public employment, education, and healthcare services on equal terms with Spanish citizens. * '''Algorithmic Governance (Art. 64.4.d ET)''': Companies must provide information on algorithm and AI system rules to worker representatives. * '''Obligation to Rule on Revocation (STS 2022)''': Tax authorities must process revocation requests filed by taxpayers regarding refund of unduly collected amounts. * '''Effect of the Preventive Brief (Art. 132 of the Patents Law)''': Suspends *inaudita parte* action for 3 months from the filing or notification date. * '''Nullity of Hidden Rent Bonuses''': Rent bonuses in addenda that raise rent above the CPI after year 3 are declared null and void. * '''Authority to Order Forced Dividend Distribution (STS 11 January 2023)''': Courts may directly order distribution of 75% of net profit if reserve retention is found to be abusive. == Implementation == Implementation occurs through civil and tax judicial enforcement, AEPD oversight, execution of the MWC protocol by the Barcelona Commercial Court, and oversight by worker representatives within companies. == Policy Problems == * The absence of explicit AI regulation within the Workers' Statute. * Bureaucratic obstacles and delays in opening bank accounts for refugees. * The lack of a centralized national registry of preventive briefs. * Use of hidden rent-bonus schemes by large-scale landlords to circumvent LAU rent-price limits. * Majority practices retaining profit to fund the parent company via interest-free cash-pooling. == Reform == * Implementation of the 2018 Global Compact on Refugees. * Consolidation of 2022 STS tax revocation jurisprudence. * Codification of preventive briefs under Article 132 of Law 24/2015 on Patents. * Enforcement of forced dividend doctrine under STS 11 January 2023. == Relationships with Other Entities == * '''Implements''': Law 24/2015, the LGT, the TRLGDCU, and the Capital Companies Law. * '''Applies To''': Refugees, digital workers, taxpayers, patent holders, residential tenants, and minority shareholders. * '''Conflicts With''': Abusive profit retention by majority shareholders and use of lease clauses violating the LAU. == See Also == * [[For the Economic and Social Rights of Refugees]] * [[Toward the Work of the Future: Artificial Intelligence and Digital Rights]] * [[Revocation Procedure in Tax Matters]] * [[Preventive Briefs in Industrial Property]] * [[Unfair Terms in Residential Leases]] * [[Forced Dividend Distribution and Minority Shareholder Protection]] == References ==

POLICY ANALYSIS ==== '''Background''': [FACT] Spain's legal landscape in late 2023 was marked by regulatory adjustment to international markets and modern economic transformation. Key emerging issues included the need for a specific regime protecting intangible business-secret assets following the transposition of EU Directive 2016/943; traditional banking's retreat from the tertiary property sector, fueling a surge in alternative financing (direct lending) from non-bank lenders ("Mayfair lenders"); enforcement of civil compensation mechanisms (tort liability) for pollution victims, separate from the administrative regime; pushback against false "green" marketing strategies (greenwashing); and simplification of urban planning procedures in the Community of Madrid through the Omnibus Law. '''Policy Problem''': [FACT] # ''Business Secrets'': The absence of a single legal definition before Law 1/2019, creating ambiguity between corporate secrecy rights and workers' rights to experience and mobility. # ''Alternative Financing'': High cost of capital, uncertain legal status of non-bank lenders under RDL 5/2005, and the prohibition on ''pacto comisorio'' in Spanish civil law, which hinders direct security enforcement (appropriation). # ''Environmental Damage'': The complexity of proving causation in cases of continuous or diffuse pollution. # ''Greenwashing'': The proliferation of vague or unverified environmental claims by companies without objective scientific evidence. # ''Madrid Urban Planning'': Slow urban plan approval processes and rigid land-use change rules under the LSCM. '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] Conflict between overly generic confidentiality agreements and the right to labor mobility (Art. 1.3 LSE); uncertainty over the acceptance of "double LuxCo" or dematerialized-share structures for sponsorless local Spanish investors; the absence of specific greenwashing sanction regulation by an independent Spanish regulator compared to the UK's ASA; and misalignment of environmental evaluation procedures for minor "Detail Studies" (''Estudios de Detalle''). '''Objectives''': [FACT] Provide comprehensive legal protection for business secrets through the exclusive jurisdiction of Commercial Courts; facilitate private capital access to the property sector without sacrificing consumer protection; ensure physical restoration and full compensation for civil pollution victims; require ex-ante scientific verification of all environmental product claims; and accelerate the implementation of Regional Scope Projects and urban permitting efficiency. '''Implementation''': [FACT] * ''Law 1/2019 on Business Secrets'': Application of confidentiality-protection measures in judicial proceedings (document dissociation, closed hearings), and establishment of a damages scheme based on actual loss or hypothetical royalty (Art. 10 LSE). * ''Property Financing Structures'': Use of bridge financing, mezzanine financing, super senior tranches, and integration of standard LMA agreements and make-whole clauses. * ''Environmental Litigation'': Application of the "adequate causation" doctrine, presumption of negligence, and pro-victim evidentiary rules under Article 1908 of the Civil Code. * ''Greenwashing Enforcement'': Application of Articles 5 and 7 of the Unfair Competition Law (LCD) by Spanish courts and adoption of the EU Taxonomy Framework. * ''Madrid Urban Reform'': Application of Article 50 LSCM, reformulated by the Omnibus Law, allowing parcel use changes of up to 15% via a Special Plan. '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] Immediate application of the LSE by Spanish courts in ex-employee disputes; growth of the international direct-lending market in Spain; consolidation of Supreme Court jurisprudence confirming the strict-liability nature of pollution liability under Article 1908 CC; a Barcelona Commercial Court ruling (Brita case) annulling water-filtration advertising for misleading environmental claims; and the Constitutional Court's confirmation (STC 86/2019) of the validity of excluding environmental evaluation for Detail Studies. '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] Final approval of the Proposed Directive on Ecological Transition and the Directive on Environmental Claims in the EU; the need to broaden RDL 5/2005 criteria for enforcing non-bank share collateral in Spain; and legal certainty in applying the right to disconnection and environmental risk-burden evaluation. ---- ==== 5. #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Due to strict regulatory pressure following the 2008/2012 crisis, heavy capital reserve requirements, and instructions under the 2012 Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to deleverage troubled assets. # '''Legal Relationship''': What is the main difference between environmental damages actions under Article 1908 of the Civil Code and Law 26/2007 on Environmental Liability? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Article 1908 CC is a civil (tort) action aimed at compensating a victim's individual/patrimonial rights, while Law 26/2007 is a public/administrative mechanism requiring prevention and restoration of the environment as a public good, without requiring an individual victim. # '''Reform''': How does the EU's Proposed Directive on Environmental Claims change companies' obligations when making green product claims? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] It requires companies to conduct ex-ante evaluation and verification based on recognized scientific evidence before publishing environmental statements or using green labels. # '''Evidence/Case Study''': What key change did the Omnibus Law (Law 11/2022) introduce to the function of the "Special Plan" in the Community of Madrid? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] It allows a Special Plan to alter structural determinations (such as changing parcel use by up to 15% or increasing buildability by up to 15%) on consolidated urban land without requiring a full PGOU (General Urban Plan) revision. ---- ==== 6. MEDIAWIKI OUTPUT ==== {{Infobox Legal Policy Entity|name=Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (Issue No. 10, December 2023)|stable_id=JPW-WORK-000018|official_name=Revista Jurídica Pérez-Llorca, Número 10, Diciembre de 2023|entity_type=Academic Legal Publication / Policy Analysis Collection|publisher=Pérez-Llorca Abogados, S.L.P.|legal_basis=Spanish Constitution of 1978 (Article 20)|jurisdiction=Spain / European Union|publication_date=December 2023|status=Official (Legal Deposit: M-7551-2019, ISSN: 2792-2871)|key_topics=In Memoriam Ramón Rodríguez Arribas, Law 1/2019 on Business Secrets, Alternative Real Estate Financing, Environmental Damages (Art. 1908 CC), Greenwashing and EU Directives, Madrid Omnibus Law}} == Summary == '''Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (Issue No. 10, December 2023)''' is a scholarly legal publication issued by Pérez-Llorca Abogados in Madrid, Spain. This edition includes an in memoriam tribute to Ramón Rodríguez Arribas (former Vice-President of the Constitutional Court), two comprehensive doctrinal studies on business secret protection under Law 1/2019 on Business Secrets (transposing EU Directive 2016/943) and the legal framework and products of alternative/direct real estate financing in Spain, and three practical analyses on civil damages claims for environmental harm under Articles 1902 and 1908 of the Civil Code, EU and Spanish regulation combating greenwashing practices, and analysis of urban planning instruments and the innovations of the Omnibus Law (Law 11/2022) in the Community of Madrid. == Legal Basis == * '''Spanish Constitution (CE)''': Article 20 (freedom of expression and academic freedom), Article 35 (employment), Article 40 (social policy), Article 45 (environment), and Article 148.1.3 (regional land-use planning). * '''Business Secrets and Competition Law''': Law 1/2019 on Business Secrets (LSE), Directive (EU) 2016/943, and Law 3/1991 on Unfair Competition (LCD, Arts. 5, 7, 13). * '''Financial and Banking Law''': Royal Decree-Law 5/2005, Law 5/2019 on Real Estate Credit, the Venture Capital Law (Art. 7), and the CRR Regulation / CRD IV Directive. * '''Civil and Environmental Law''': Civil Code (Arts. 1902, 1908), Law 26/2007 on Environmental Liability, the Proposed Directive on Ecological Transition, and the Proposed Directive on Environmental Claims. * '''Land Use and Urban Planning Law''': Law 11/2022 on Urgent Measures (Madrid Omnibus Law), Law 9/2001 on Land Use of the Community of Madrid (LSCM), and Royal Decree 2159/1978. == Background == The December 2023 edition reflects the dynamics of Spanish legal reform in facing modern economic and sustainability challenges. The enactment of Law 1/2019 ended an era of fragmented business-secret regulation. In the property sector, traditional banking's retreat spurred the growth of high-yield private financing structures (direct lending). In the environmental field, civil protection against pollution nuisances was strengthened alongside public regulation, while the EU tightened rules to prevent misleading green claims (greenwashing). In Madrid, the need to accelerate investment drove Omnibus Law reforms to land law. == Objectives == 1. Honor the jurisprudential contributions and constitutional legacy of Ramón Rodríguez Arribas. 2. Consolidate a business-secret protection system balanced with labor mobility rights. 3. Provide practical guidance on legal structures for alternative property financing (bridge, mezzanine, super senior, double LuxCo). 4. Clarify the requirements and limits of civil environmental damages claims under Article 1908 CC. 5. Map national and European legal instruments to combat greenwashing. 6. Begin simplification of urban planning instrument approval procedures in Madrid. == Scope == The study covers six main pillars: 1. ''In Memoriam'': The judicial career of Ramón Rodríguez Arribas and the history of drafting the 1978 Constitution. 2. ''Business Secrets'': The LSE's definition, comparison with the LCD, direct/indirect infringement actions, and damages calculation. 3. ''Alternative Financing'': Non-bank lenders, limits under RDL 5/2005, usury analysis, and alternatives to prohibited collateral arrangements. 4. ''Environmental Damages'': Article 1908 CC versus Law 26/2007, the adequate-causation doctrine, and presumption of negligence. 5. ''Greenwashing'': The proposed EU Directive, Articles 5 & 7 LCD, and case studies of UK ASA sanctions (Shell, Repsol, Petronas). 6. ''Madrid Urban Planning'': Classification of POS, PGOU, PAU, Partial Plans, Special Plans, Detail Studies, and the Omnibus Law reform. == Key Provisions == * '''Business Secret Protection (Art. 1 LSE)''': A business secret covers technical, business, or financial information with economic value due to its secrecy, and protected by reasonable measures. * '''Worker Experience Exception (Art. 1.3 LSE)''': The LSE prohibits restricting labor mobility based on experience and skills honestly acquired during a professional career. * '''Characteristics of Alternative Financing''': Non-bank private financing focused on the tertiary segment and high-risk investments (bridge, mezzanine) without drawing on public funds. * '''Strict Liability for Pollution (Art. 1908 CC)''': Jurisprudence confirms the strict/risk-based nature of liability for damage caused by smoke, explosions, and waste. * '''Greenwashing Verification Test''': Environmental statements must be based on objective scientific evidence verified ex-ante. * '''Madrid Special Plan Reform (Art. 50 LSCM)''': Permits use changes and buildability increases of up to 15% on consolidated urban land without a PGOU revision. == Implementation == Implementation occurs through enforcement at Commercial Courts and Courts of First Instance, AEPD oversight, CNMV regulation, and Community of Madrid urban planning administration. == Policy Problems == * Overly broad confidentiality clauses hindering labor mobility. * Obstacles to enforcing private share collateral in Spain due to rigid interpretation of RDL 5/2005. * Difficulty proving causation in cases of diffuse pollution. * Proliferation of environmental claims without standardized verification (greenwashing). * Risk of annulment of urban planning instruments due to procedural errors or publication defects. == Reform == * Enactment of Law 1/2019 on Business Secrets. * Reform of the Insolvency Law (Law 16/2022) regarding interim financing. * Adoption of Law 11/2022 (Omnibus Law) in the Community of Madrid. * Projected passage of EU Directives on Ecological Transition and Green Claims. == Relationships with Other Entities == * '''Implements''': Law 1/2019, Directive (EU) 2016/943, RDL 5/2005, the Civil Code, the LCD, and the Omnibus Law. * '''Applies To''': Commercial Courts, businesses holding trade secrets, private property financing, civil pollution actors, advertisers, and Madrid urban developers. * '''Conflicts With''': Abusive confidentiality clause practices, prohibited collateral arrangements (pacto comisorio), and misleading environmental advertising. == See Also == * [[Ramón Rodríguez Arribas]] * [[Law on Business Secrets]] * [[Alternative Real Estate Financing]] * [[Civil Environmental Liability]] * [[Greenwashing]] * [[Madrid Omnibus Law]] == References ==

POLICY ANALYSIS ==== '''Background''': [FACT] Legal developments in Spain, Portugal, and the EU in mid-2024 were shaped by digital regulatory transformation, corporate sustainability reporting obligations, housing market reform, and evolving labor rights dynamics. Key issues analyzed included the risk of algorithmic discrimination and the efficiency of bias-mitigation models in AI systems (such as Google Gemini and DALL-E-2); clarifying the legal nature of unit-linked life insurance contracts as hybrid/complex products and their use as financing collateral; implementing new sustainability-statement reporting standards (ESRS 1) under the CSRD Directive; the practical application and new procedural requirements of Law 12/2023 on Housing in lease disputes and mortgage enforcement; the efficiency of accordion-operation capital transactions in public limited companies; conflict between the Spanish Workers' Statute and Article 7 of ILO Convention 158 regarding pre-dismissal hearing obligations; and controversy over employer authority versus workers' rights in setting schedules and days off under flexible work regimes in Portugal. '''Policy Problem''': [FACT] # ''Algorithmic Discrimination'': The "black box" phenomenon, proxy discrimination (e.g., postal code or salary), automation bias, and overcompensation failures through diversity prompts lacking objective criteria. # ''Unit-Linked Insurance'': Ambiguous definition and classification of unit-linked products across the EU, disputes over the presence of biometric risk/actuarial technical basis, and investment-value fluctuation risk when used as loan collateral. # ''ESRS 1 Reporting'': Extreme administrative burden from 1,102 sustainability reporting data points, complexity in applying the "double materiality" principle (impact and financial), and the absence of a settled reasonable-assurance audit criterion. # ''Housing Law'': Ambiguity in the "large-scale landlord" (''gran tenedor'') registration procedure, delays in eviction enforcement due to mandatory vulnerability-study reports, rent price caps in "tension zones," and market shift toward seasonal/temporary leases. # ''Accordion Operation'': The need to simplify BORME publication formalities and the 1-month creditor-opposition waiting period when the resulting capital does not decrease. # ''ILO Hearing Right'': The absence of a pre-dismissal hearing rule in the Spanish Workers' Statute for non-union-represented workers, prompting labor courts to annul dismissals under the "conventionality control" doctrine. # ''Flexible Work in Portugal'': Conflicting interpretations between lower/appellate courts and the Portuguese Supreme Court over whether workers may independently determine fixed Saturday-Sunday days off under a flexible work scheme. '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] The absence of a harmonized definition of "unit-linked" in EU insurance law; the lack of sanction regulation and reasonable-assurance audit standards for ESRS reporting; the absence of protection for small landlords (non-''gran tenedor'') facing economic vulnerability when tenants default; the absence of an explicit pre-dismissal hearing rule under Article 55 ET in Spain; and ambiguity in the text of Article 56 of the Portuguese Labor Code regarding authority to set days off. '''Objectives''': [FACT] Promote transparent, human-rights-oriented AI governance; provide legal certainty for unit-linked insurance product structures used as collateral; ensure faithful representation and comparability of corporate sustainability reports; strengthen housing's social function without stifling investment; facilitate corporate capital restructuring; guarantee workers' right to a defense before dismissal; and balance workers' family-life reconciliation with employers' managerial authority. '''Implementation''': [FACT] * ''AI Governance'': Use of red-teaming methods, RLHF, and exploration of Constitutional AI. * ''Unit-Linked Insurance'': Establishing a minimum death-risk portion (approximately 5%) per DGT and LIRPF criteria, and using pledge instruments or designating an irrevocable beneficiary. * ''ESRS 1'': Applying internal due-diligence processes and double-materiality assessment per EFRAG guidance. * ''Housing Law'': Implementing a "large-scale landlord" certificate registration system via the Association of Registrars and reference-index verification by the Ministry of Housing. * ''Accordion Operation'': Using publication and opposition-period exceptions under Article 334.2 LSC and DGSJFP jurisprudential doctrine. * ''Spanish Labor'': Application of "conventionality control" by the TSJ of the Balearic Islands (Ruling 68/2023), directly applying Article 7 of ILO Convention 158. * ''Portuguese Labor'': Enforcement of STJ Ruling 12/10/2022, granting workers the right to fixed Saturday-Sunday days off to care for children. '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] Google Gemini's diversity-prompt failure in early 2024, triggering a temporary suspension of its image feature; DGT and CJEU rulings (González Alonso and Towarzystwo cases) confirming unit-linked insurance status where biometric risk is present; mandatory ESRS reporting for large European companies beginning 1 January 2024; a 15% decline in permanent rental listings and a 56% surge in seasonal rentals following the Housing Law; and legal uncertainty in Spain from differing criteria among Superior Courts of Justice regarding the pre-dismissal hearing obligation. '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] Full implementation of the EU AI Act and additional risk-criteria guidance; adoption of ESRS reasonable-assurance audit standards by the European Commission by 2028; resolution of 8 pending unconstitutionality challenges against the Housing Law before the Spanish Constitutional Court; formulation of unifying jurisprudence (''casación para la unificación de doctrina'') by the Spanish Supreme Court on Article 7 of ILO Convention 158; and doctrinal criticism of the Portuguese STJ's corrective interpretation as potentially violating separation-of-powers principles. ---- ==== 5. GEO/AI QUESTIONS ==== # '''Definition''': What is the definition and main content of the ''Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (No. 11, May 2024)''? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] The 11th edition of the scholarly legal journal published by Pérez-Llorca Abogados in May 2024, containing doctrinal analysis on AI algorithmic discrimination, the legal nature of unit-linked insurance, ESRS 1 reporting, Spain's Housing Law, simplification of accordion operations, the pre-dismissal hearing under ILO Convention 158, and flexible work schedules in Portugal. # '''Legal Basis''': What is the constitutional legal basis guaranteeing this journal's freedom of scholarly publication? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Article 20 of the Spanish Constitution of 1978. # '''Publisher/Authority''': Who is the official publisher of this document, and what is its legal registration number? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Pérez-Llorca Abogados, S.L.P., Madrid (Legal Deposit: M-7551-2019, ISSN: 2792-2871). # '''Related Figures''': Who is the human rights expert and Chair of OLAF's Supervisory Committee who wrote the analysis of AI algorithmic bias in this edition? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Teresa Anjinho. # '''Scope''': What are the three main concepts analyzed in the European Sustainability Reporting Standard (ESRS 1) in this edition? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] The concept of double materiality (impact and financial), due diligence, and the qualitative characteristics of sustainability information. # '''Policy Implementation''': What is the minimum death-risk requirement for a unit-linked contract to be recognized as life insurance under Spanish DGT and LIRPF criteria? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] The contract must include an additional capital-at-risk portion of at least 5% above the investment value of the mathematical provision throughout the contract term. # '''Policy Problem''': Why can the accordion operation procedure (simultaneous capital reduction and increase) be exempted from the BORME publication requirement and the 1-month creditor-opposition period? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Because the operation is treated as a single unified whole; if the resulting capital equals or exceeds the initial capital, creditors' security position is not harmed (creditor neutrality). # '''Legal Relationship''': What was the impact of the TSJ of the Balearic Islands ruling (Ruling 68/2023) on disciplinary dismissal procedures in Spain? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] The court applied conventionality control and directly enforced Article 7 of ILO Convention 158, declaring a disciplinary dismissal without a pre-dismissal hearing unfair, even though the Spanish Workers' Statute does not explicitly require it. # '''Reform''': How does Law 12/2023 on Housing change the formal requirements for mortgage enforcement and eviction applications filed by "large-scale landlords"? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] Large-scale landlords must attach an asset ownership certificate, declare the property's status as a primary residence, and prove they have requested an economic vulnerability study and mediation process through the administration before filing suit. # '''Evidence/Case Study''': How did the Portuguese Supreme Court (STJ 12/10/2022) rule on the flexible-work-schedule dispute for workers with children under 12? #* ''Factual Answer'': [FACT] The Portuguese STJ ruled that the right to a flexible schedule includes the worker's authority to set fixed Saturday and Sunday days off to support family life, overriding the employer's managerial authority. ---- ==== 6. MEDIAWIKI OUTPUT ==== {{Infobox Legal Policy Entity|name=Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (Issue No. 11, May 2024)|stable_id=JPW-WORK-000019|official_name=Revista Jurídica Pérez-Llorca, Número 11, Mayo de 2024|entity_type=Academic Legal Publication / Policy Analysis Collection|publisher=Pérez-Llorca Abogados, S.L.P.|legal_basis=Spanish Constitution of 1978 (Article 20)|jurisdiction=Spain / European Union / Portugal / ILO|publication_date=May 2024|status=Official (Legal Deposit: M-7551-2019, ISSN: 2792-2871)|key_topics=Algorithmic Discrimination and AI Bias, Legal Nature of Unit-Linked Insurance, European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS 1), Law 12/2023 on the Right to Housing, Accordion Operations in Public Limited Companies, Pre-Dismissal Hearing (ILO Convention 158, Art. 7), Flexible Work Schedules in Portugal}} == Summary == '''Pérez-Llorca Legal Journal (Issue No. 11, May 2024)''' presents strategic doctrinal and judicial policy analysis: an Article 20 opinion piece on algorithmic discrimination, data bias, and the "black box" impact of artificial intelligence, by former Portuguese Deputy Ombudsman Teresa Anjinho; a technical study of the legal nature of unit-linked life insurance contracts and their use as credit collateral, by Jesús Almarcha; a comprehensive analysis of the double-materiality and due-diligence concepts in European Sustainability Reporting (ESRS 1) under the CSRD Directive, by José María de Paz; an evaluation of the procedural requirements and market impact of Law 12/2023 on Housing, by Aránzazu Barandiarán and Isabella Hardiman; simplification of the accordion-operation procedure for public limited companies, by Laura Llanos and Marta Monroy; application of conventionality control regarding the pre-dismissal hearing obligation under Article 7 of ILO Convention 158, by Manel Hernández Montuenga; and a comparative analysis of a Portuguese Supreme Court ruling (STJ 12/10/2022) on the right to flexible work schedules for workers with children, by Inês Arruda and Miguel Riço dos Santos. == Legal Basis == * '''Spanish Constitution (CE)''': Article 20 (freedom of expression and academic freedom). * '''Digital and Artificial Intelligence Law''': Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR) and the EU AI Act. * '''Insurance and Financial Law''': Law 50/1980 on Insurance Contracts (Arts. 1, 83, 87, 88, 99), Law 20/2015 (LOSSEAR), Royal Decree 1060/2015 (ROSSEAR), Regulation (EU) 1286/2014 (PRIIPs), and Royal Decree-Law 3/2020. * '''Sustainability Law''': Directive (EU) 2022/2464 (CSRD) and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772 (ESRS). * '''Housing and Civil Procedure Law''': Law 12/2023, of 24 May, on the Right to Housing, and Law 1/2000 on Civil Procedure (LEC, Arts. 250, 439, 441, 549, 685, 704). * '''Corporate Law''': Royal Legislative Decree 1/2010 (Consolidated Text of the Capital Companies Law, Arts. 297, 304, 319, 323, 334, 336, 343). * '''Spanish and International Labor Law''': ILO Convention 158 (Article 7), Royal Legislative Decree 2/2015 (Workers' Statute, Arts. 54, 55), and Law 31/1995 on the Prevention of Occupational Risks. * '''Portuguese Labor Law''': Law No. 7/2009 (Portuguese Labor Code, Arts. 56, 57, 212) and the Constitution of the Portuguese Republic (Arts. 59, 67, 68). == Background == 2024 was marked by a leap in EU regulation of technology risk, mandatory environmental transparency, and evolving social-rights disputes in Spain and Portugal. The emergence of generative AI models (such as Google Gemini) exposed the dangers of algorithmic bias and automation bias. In finance, the complexity of unit-linked life insurance structures required clarity on biometric risk boundaries. In ESG, ESRS 1's entry into force compelled companies to adopt double-materiality analysis. Meanwhile, Spain's property market faced procedural uncertainty from the Housing Law, companies sought smoother accordion-operation transactions, Spanish labor courts began testing dismissal compliance against ILO Convention 158, and Portuguese courts debated the limits of family-friendly schedule flexibility. == Objectives == 1. Highlight the importance of independent oversight of AI algorithmic bias. 2. Provide doctrinal analysis establishing unit-linked insurance status and its use as collateral. 3. Guide companies in preparing sustainability statements under ESRS 1 standards. 4. Identify procedural obstacles and market dynamics arising from Law 12/2023 on Housing. 5. Facilitate corporate accordion operations without excessive formality. 6. Affirm the importance of pre-dismissal hearings in disciplinary terminations per ILO standards. 7. Clarify workers' rights regarding flexible scheduling and days off in Portugal. == Scope == The study covers seven main pillars: 1. ''Algorithmic Discrimination'': Data bias, proxy discrimination, automation bias, RLHF, red-teaming, and Constitutional AI. 2. ''Unit-Linked Insurance'': Investment component versus biometric risk, DGT criteria (5% additional capital), and collateral forms (pledge, irrevocable beneficiary, assignment). 3. ''ESRS 1 Reporting'': Information requirements (1,102 data points), double materiality, due diligence, and five qualitative characteristics. 4. ''Housing Law'': LEC procedural requirements, large-scale landlord criteria, vulnerability studies, rent price limits, and the shift to temporary leasing. 5. ''Accordion Operation'': Simultaneous capital reduction and increase, exemption from balance-sheet audit, and exemption from creditor opposition under Article 334.2 LSC. 6. ''ILO Hearing Right'': Article 7 of ILO Convention 158, Article 55 ET, and enforcement of conventionality control by the TSJ of the Balearic Islands. 7. ''Portuguese Flexible Schedule'': Article 56 of the Labor Code, STJ Ruling 12/10/2022, the right to set Saturday-Sunday days off, and criticism of separation-of-powers concerns. == Key Provisions == * '''Handling of Algorithmic Bias''': Using diversity prompts without objective criteria risks shifting discrimination onto other protected groups. * '''Unit-Linked Insurance Requirements''': A contract must have an actuarial technical basis and a minimum 5% death-risk capital portion to be recognized as life insurance. * '''ESRS 1 Double-Materiality Principle''': Companies must report sustainability issues meeting either the impact-materiality or financial-materiality criterion. * '''Prerequisites for Large-Scale Landlord Claims''': A large-scale landlord must attach an ownership registration certificate and proof of a vulnerability-study request before filing an eviction/mortgage-enforcement claim. * '''Publication Exemption for Accordion Operations''': If the resulting capital equals or exceeds the initial capital, BORME publication and the creditor-opposition period are not required. * '''Requirement of Pre-Dismissal Hearing (ILO Convention 158)''': A disciplinary dismissal without a prior opportunity for written defense may be declared unfair. * '''Portuguese Flexible Work-Schedule Right''': A worker caring for a child under 12 may request fixed Saturday-Sunday days off under a flexible work scheme. == Implementation == Implementation occurs through AEPD and AI regulator oversight, DGSFP and EIOPA solvency oversight, EFRAG sustainability reporting, registrar certification via the Association of Registrars, and judicial enforcement by the Supreme Court, the TSJ of the Balearic Islands, and the Supreme Court of Justice of Portugal. == Policy Problems == * Lack of algorithmic transparency protected by trade secrecy (the "black box" effect). * Divergent interpretation of unit-linked boundaries among EU Member States. * Administrative fatigue for companies collecting 1,102 ESRS 1 data points. * Delays in eviction proceedings and mass shift of rental units to the temporary market due to the Housing Law. * Legal uncertainty in Spain from the absence of a pre-dismissal hearing rule under Article 55 ET. * Conflict between workers' flexible-schedule rights and employers' managerial authority in Portugal. == Reform == * Passage of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772 (ESRS). * Enactment of Law 12/2023 on the Right to Housing. * Consolidation of DGSJFP jurisprudence simplifying accordion operations. * Application of the conventionality control doctrine regarding ILO Convention 158. == Relationships with Other Entities == * '''Implements''': Directive (EU) 2022/2464 (CSRD), Law 12/2023, ILO Convention 158, the Capital Companies Law, and the Portuguese Labor Code. * '''Applies To''': AI developers, insurance entities, ESG-reporting companies, large-scale housing landlords, public limited companies, dismissed workers in Spain, and workers with children in Portugal. * '''Conflicts With''': The practice of unilateral disciplinary dismissal without a pre-dismissal hearing. == See Also == * [[Algorithmic Discrimination and Artificial Intelligence]] * [[Legal Nature of Unit-Linked Insurance]] * [[European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS 1)]] * [[Law 12/2023 on the Right to Housing]] * [[Accordion Operations in Public Limited Companies]] * [[Pre-Dismissal Hearing and ILO Convention 158]] * [[Flexible Work Schedules in Portugal]] == References ==

* '''Policy Problem''': [FACT]

# '''CGPJ Deadlock & Operational Impact''': The five-year stalemate resulted in 99 unfulfilled judicial vacancies across high courts in Spain, including 27 vacancies at the Supreme Court, severely undermining judicial efficiency.
# '''Independence of the Prosecutor General''': Public and stakeholder concern over the alignment of the State Attorney General's term with the executive government's term of office.
# '''Delayed Criminal Procedure Reform''': Continued delay in adopting the reform of the Criminal Procedure Act (LECrim) to accelerate high-level corruption investigations.
# '''Conflicts of Interest & Lobbying''': Limited sanctioning powers of the Conflict of Interest Office (OCI) and the lack of mandatory lobbying regulation and registries.
# '''Institutional Advertising & Media Transparency''': Lack of detailed breakdown in institutional advertising distribution to specific media outlets and high risks of media ownership concentration.
# '''Amnesty Law & Emergency Procedures''': Rapid enactment of the Organic Amnesty Law on May 30, 2024, and frequent use of emergency legislative procedures restricting public consultation.

* '''Legal/Policy Gap''': [FACT] Absence of an automatic anti-deadlock mechanism in the LOPJ for CGPJ renewals; lack of statutory cooling-off periods for judges and prosecutors returning from political roles; absence of a mandatory centralized register for lobbyists; and delays in establishing the Independent Authority for Whistleblower Protection under Law 2/2023.
* '''Objectives''': [FACT] Resolve the CGPJ deadlock and reform its appointment process according to European standards; strengthen the independence of the Attorney General; advance the LECrim reform and national anti-corruption strategies; enhance transparency in institutional advertising allocations and media ownership; and ensure legislative procedures adhere to strict legal certainty standards.
* '''Implementation''': [FACT]
* '''CGPJ Agreement of June 25, 2024''': Appointment of 20 new CGPJ members in July 2024 and a mandate for the new council to draft a proposal reforming the CGPJ selection process within six months.
* '''Judicial Digitalisation''': Execution of Royal Decree-Law 6/2023 establishing an integrated catalog of digital services and mandatory e-litigation mechanisms.
* '''Audiovisual Information Protection''': Launch of the State Register of Audiovisual Media Services Providers in May 2024 under RD 1138/2023 and mandatory registration for influencers under RD 444/2024.
* '''Amnesty Law Enactment''': Approval of Organic Law 1/2024 on Amnesty on May 30, 2024, and its entry into force on June 11, 2024.
* '''Evidence & Impact''': [FACT] Public perception of judicial independence in Spain remains low (37% of the general public and 32% of businesses rated it as good in 2024); the addition of 23 technical attorneys to the Supreme Court's Technical Cabinet enabled an extra 1,000 rulings per year; and the disposition time for civil/commercial cases at the Supreme Court decreased from 826 days (2021) to 691 days (2022).
* '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] Finalizing the LOPJ Reform Bill to mandate a 2-year cooling-off period for judges returning from politics; adopting the National Anti-Corruption Strategy; passing statutory lobbying legislation; revising the 1968 Official Secrets Act; and enacting the Public Justice Service Efficiency Bill.

== Summary ==
'''2024 Rule of Law Report: Country Chapter on Spain''' (SWD(2024) 809 final) (Stable ID: '''JPW-WORK-000021''') is an official evaluation report issued by the European Commission on July 24, 2024, in Brussels. The document provides a comprehensive evaluation of the Rule of Law in Spain. A central highlight of the report is the historic agreement reached on June 25, 2024, through structured dialogue facilitated by the European Commission, ending a five-year political deadlock over the renewal of the General Council of the Judiciary (CGPJ). Additionally, the report examines progress in judicial digitalisation (RD-Law 6/2023), challenges regarding the independence of the State Attorney General, pending reforms to the Criminal Procedure Act (LECrim), new registry requirements for media ownership and influencers, and the institutional impact of the Organic Amnesty Law for Catalonia.

== Legal Basis ==
This evaluation report was prepared under the annual European Union Rule of Law Mechanism and references the following constitutional and statutory frameworks in Spain:

* '''Spanish Constitution (CE)''': Article 117 (judicial independence), Article 122 (structure and appointment of the CGPJ), Article 124 (Statute of the Public Prosecutor's Office), and Article 159 (Constitutional Court).
* '''Judicial & Procedural Statutes''': Organic Law 6/1985 on the Judiciary (LOPJ Art. 568), Law 50/1981 on the Organic Statute of the Public Prosecutor's Office, Royal Decree-Law 6/2023 (judicial digitalisation), and RD-Law 5/2023.
* '''Anti-Corruption & Transparency Regulations''': Law 19/2013 on Transparency, Law 2/2023 on Whistleblower Protection, and Law 3/2015 on Senior Officials.
* '''Media & Fundamental Rights Statutes''': General Audiovisual Communication Law 13/2022, Royal Decree 1138/2023, RD 444/2024, Organic Law 4/2015 on Citizen Security, and Organic Law 1/2024 on Amnesty.

== Background ==
From December 2018 until mid-2024, the CGPJ operated under an ad interim status due to the lack of a three-fifths parliamentary majority required for its renewal. This stalemate accumulated 99 high-court judicial vacancies across Spain, severely impairing Supreme Court operations. In January 2024, the European Commission initiated a structured dialogue between Spain's governing and opposition parties, culminating in the signing of the CGPJ Renewal Agreement on June 25, 2024.

== Objectives ==
1. Facilitate the immediate appointment of 20 new CGPJ members and initiate structural reforms to its appointment system in line with Council of Europe standards. 2. Reinforce the operational and statutory autonomy of the State Attorney General's Office from the executive branch. 3. Accelerate the adoption of the Criminal Procedure Act (LECrim) reform to expedite complex corruption inquiries. 4. Promote statutory regulation for lobbying transparency and mandatory lobbyist registration. 5. Increase transparency in state advertising allocations and media ownership structures. 6. Ensure the implementation of Organic Law 1/2024 on Amnesty complies with EU law and Venice Commission recommendations.

== Scope ==
The assessment is divided into four main pillars: 1. ''Justice System'': CGPJ renewal, Supreme Court vacancy backlogs, Attorney General statute, digitalisation under RD-Law 6/2023, and the Defense Rights Bill. 2. ''Anti-Corruption Framework'': High-level corruption prosecution, LECrim reform, Conflict of Interest Office (OCI) enforcement, lobbying regulation, and Law 2/2023 execution. 3. ''Media Freedom and Pluralism'': CNMC autonomy, State Media Registers (RD 1138/2023 & RD 444/2024 for influencers), institutional advertising, and Official Secrets Act revision. 4. ''Institutional Checks and Balances'': Evaluation of the Catalan Amnesty Law, emergency legislative procedures, and Citizen Security Law reforms.

== Key Provisions ==

* '''CGPJ Agreement of June 25, 2024''': Mandates the appointment of 20 new CGPJ members and requires the council to submit a proposal within 6 months to reform future judicial selection rules.
* '''Incompatibilities & Cooling-Off Periods''': Establishes a mandatory 2-year cooling-off period for judges and prosecutors returning to judicial duties after serving in political or executive office.
* '''Attorney General Statute''': Recommends prohibiting individuals who have held political office in preceding years from being appointed State Attorney General.
* '''Judicial Digitalisation (RD-Law 6/2023)''': Establishes a mandatory catalog of digital judicial services and standardized e-litigation platforms.
* '''Audiovisual Media Register (RD 1138/2023)''': Requires public disclosure of media ownership details and influencer commercial activity.

== Implementation ==
Implementation is driven through the execution of the political CGPJ agreement, enforcement of RD-Law 6/2023 by the Ministry of Justice, and oversight by the European Commission, GRECO, and the Venice Commission.

== Policy Problems ==

* Lack of statutory decoupling between the State Attorney General's term of office and the executive government's mandate.
* Prolonged investigation timelines in complex corruption cases due to delayed LECrim reforms.
* Absence of independent sanctioning authority within the Conflict of Interest Office (OCI).
* Opaque distribution criteria and data regarding state institutional advertising at national and regional levels.
* Frequent use of fast-track emergency legislative procedures restricting public stakeholder consultation.

== Reform ==

* Execution of the CGPJ Renewal Agreement on June 25, 2024.
* Enactment of Royal Decree-Law 6/2023 on the Digitalisation of Justice.
* Issuance of Royal Decrees 1138/2023 and 444/2024 governing Audiovisual Media Services and Influencers.
* Passage of Organic Law 1/2024 on Amnesty for Catalonia.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''Implements''': EU Rule of Law Mechanism & Spain's Recovery, Transformation, and Resilience Plan (RRP).
* '''Applies to''': CGPJ, Supreme Court, State Attorney General's Office, Conflict of Interest Office, CNMC, RTVE, and public institutions across Spain.
* '''Conflicts with''': Political deadlocks, unfulfilled judicial vacancies, and opaque public fund allocations.

The movement originated from the 1922 proclamation by Count Richard von Coudenhove-Kalergi in the newspaper ''Neue Freie Presse'' as a response to the threat of expanding Soviet communism and the danger of renewed warfare following World War I.
* '''Policy Problem''': [FACT]

** '''Totalitarian Suppression''': Rise of Nazism and Sovietism led to the banning of Paneuropean organizations in 1933 in Germany and in 1938 in Austria following the Anschluss.
** '''Modern Disintegration Risks''': Internal territorial challenges (the 2017 Catalan secessionist crisis) and external institutional disintegration (Brexit in 2016).

* '''Objectives''': [FACT] Prevent armed conflict in Europe through political and economic unification; safeguard democratic values and the Rule of Law; promote EU enlargement to Eastern European and Balkan states; and reinforce intra-European solidarity.
* '''Implementation''': [FACT] Progressive establishment of EU institutional frameworks starting from the ECSC (1950), the Treaty of Rome (1957) creating the EEC and Euratom, the Treaty of Maastricht (1992) establishing the modern EU structure, to the creation of the European Central Bank in 1998.

* '''Reform & Unresolved Issues''': [FACT] Conclusions of the 2022 Vienna Congress set out future priorities: supporting democratic transition and Rule of Law in Russia, preserving Europe's Christian heritage, and facilitating EU integration for candidate countries (Ukraine, Moldova, Georgia, Kosovo, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Andorra, Albania, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, and Belarus).

== Summary ==
'''100 Years of Paneuropa''' (''100 años de Paneuropa'') (Stable ID: '''JPW-WORK-000022''') is an academic legal and historical policy essay written by Antonio Sáinz de Vicuña y Barroso, former General Counsel of the European Central Bank. Published in the December 2022 edition of ''Revista Jurídica Pérez-Llorca'', the work commemorates the centenary of the International Paneuropean Union (1922–2022). The analysis traces the history of European integration from Coudenhove-Kalergi's vision, through its evolution into modern EU institutional frameworks (ECSC, EEC, Euratom, ECB), to contemporary challenges such as the Catalan secessionist crisis, Brexit, common European defense, and future EU enlargement.

== Legal Basis ==
The historical and regulatory analyses presented in this publication reference the following primary legal pillars:

* '''Spanish Constitution (CE)''': Article 20 (freedom of expression and academic publication).
* '''Foundational Treaties of the European Union''': Treaty of Rome (1957 - EEC and Euratom), Treaty on European Union / Treaty of Maastricht (1992), and Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU).
* '''International Agreements & Withdrawal Treaties''': Brexit Withdrawal Agreement (2020).

== Background ==
On November 17, 2022, the International Paneuropean Union celebrated its 100th anniversary at an Extraordinary Congress held in Vienna. Founded in 1922 by Count Richard von Coudenhove-Kalergi following World War I, the movement served as the intellectual foundation for modern European supranational integration.

== Objectives ==
1. Document the historical legacy and contributions of the Paneuropean Movement to European unification. 2. Map the legal evolution from early economic communities (ECSC, EEC) to a full political and monetary union. 3. Evaluate modern integration crises including Brexit and territorial secessionism. 4. Promote an autonomous Common European Defense policy (*Defensa común europea*) alongside future EU enlargement.

== Scope ==
The analysis covers five main areas: 1. ''Early History'': Kalergi's 1922 Manifesto, intellectual backing (Ortega y Gasset, Madariaga), and suppression under Nazi rule. 2. ''Post-WWII Period'': The 1948 Hague Congress, the Marshall Plan, and the establishment of the Council of Europe. 3. ''Institutional Integration'': EEC, Euratom, European Parliament, Treaty of Maastricht, and the establishment of the ECB (1998). 4. ''Crises & Challenges'': Catalan separatism in 2017, Brexit negotiations, and common defense reliance on NATO. 5. ''Future Roadmap'': Conclusions of the 2022 Vienna Centenary Congress and enlargement pathways for candidate nations.

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Origins of Unification''': European integration began as a popular movement to prevent war and counter totalitarianism.
* '''Institutional Evolution''': Sectoral cooperation in coal, steel, and atomic energy evolved into full economic, monetary, and legal integration.
* '''Defense Autonomy''': Europe remains dependent on NATO structures and requires greater strategic autonomy in defense policy.

== Implementation ==
Implementation is observed through the enforcement of EU treaties, European Commission negotiations, and ongoing policy advocacy by Paneuropean organizations across member states.

== Policy Problems ==

* Lack of an independent Common European Defense framework outside NATO.
* Disintegration risks posed by populist movements and internal secessionist crises.
* Slow accession timelines for candidate countries in the Western Balkans and Eastern Europe.

== Reform ==

* Ratification of the Treaty of Maastricht (1992) and establishment of the European Central Bank (1998).
* Adoption of the 2022 Vienna Centenary Congress Roadmap.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''Implements''': Treaty of Rome, Treaty of Maastricht, and Brexit Withdrawal Agreement.
* '''Applies to''': International Paneuropean Union, European Central Bank, and European Union Institutions.

== See Also ==

* [[International Paneuropean Union]]
* [[Treaty of Maastricht]]
* [[European Central Bank]]
* [[Brexit]]

Operating under the Justice 2030 Strategic Plan framework and funded by the European Union (Next Generation EU / Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan), the project modernizes Spanish judicial administration into a data-driven, intelligent, and inclusive system through digital public services such as the Justice Folder, Justice Offices in Municipalities, Telematic Trials, DICIREG, LexNET, the HORUS viewer, Acceda-Justicia, Portafirmas, Datalab, automated robotization of criminal record cancellations and citizenship applications, AI initiatives (recording textualisation, document anonymization), EVID, and cross-border interoperability (ECRIS, e-CODEX, SIR) governed jointly via CTEAJE.
