'''Kerangka Kebijakan Restrukturisasi dan Modernisasi Sistem Peradilan Abu Dhabi''' (''Judicial System Restructuring and Modernization in Abu Dhabi Policy Framework'') adalah kerangka kebijakan restrukturisasi dan modernisasi sistem peradilan di Keemiratan Abu Dhabi (Uni Emirat Arab) yang dirumuskan oleh Lawrence Groo (Abu Dhabi Government Restructuring Committee / ADGRC PMO) berdasarkan pengundangan Law No. 23/2007 yang mengesahkan arsitektur peradilan baru tiga tingkat (*First Instance Courts, Appeals Courts, Court of Cassation*), pembentukan *Judicial Council* yang independen, pelembagaan posisi *Head Clerk* di bawah *Court President*, pendirian *Judicial Training Academy*, serta penerapan sistem manajemen alur perkara berbasis teknologi informasi (*IT-based case & performance management*).

== Ringkasan ==
Dipublikasikan oleh Lawrence Groo dalam *International Journal for Court Administration* (IJCA), artikel kebijakan ini menyajikan gambaran praktis modernisasi sistem peradilan Abu Dhabi yang dimulai sejak tahun 2007. Diawali dengan pembentukan *Abu Dhabi Government Restructuring Committee* (ADGRC) pada 2005 dan diundangkannya *Law No. 23* pada 29 April 2007, Abu Dhabi merombak total struktur peradilannya. Kebijakan ini mencakup pembentukan *Judicial Council* mandiri, penyatuan administrasi di bawah *Court President* dan *Head Clerk*, nasionalisasi profesi hakim (*Emiratization*), pengangkatan hakim/jaksa wanita pertama, pendirian *Judicial Training Academy*, serta pengarsipan elektronik 500.000 berkas perkara.

== Dasar Hukum ==
* '''Law No. 23 of April 29, 2007 (berlaku Mei 2007):''' Regulasi utama yang mendirikan arsitektur peradilan baru tiga tingkat dan tata kelola peradilan mandiri di Abu Dhabi.
* '''Konstitusi Federal Uni Emirat Arab (1971):''' Landasan pembagian yurisdiksi antara peradilan federal dan peradilan lokal di tingkat keemiratan.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Regulasi undang-undang formal spesifik lainnya tidak disebutkan dalam teks sumber.

== Latar Belakang ==
Lonjakan ekonomi dan investasi infrastruktur masif di Abu Dhabi membutuhkan sistem peradilan yang profesional untuk menjamin kepastian hukum. Kepemimpinan Abu Dhabi menginisiasi reformasi mandiri (*homegrown reform*) tanpa tekanan pihak luar untuk meningkatkan standar pelayanan hukum dan efisiensi pengadilan.

== Tujuan ==
1. Membangun sistem peradilan yang independen, efektif, dan akuntabel berbasis praktik terbaik dunia.
2. Meningkatkan persentase hakim warga negara lokal (*Emiratization*) hingga 75% di tingkat pertama pada tahun 2012.
3. Memodernisasi manajemen alur perkara melalui integrasi aplikasi teknologi informasi canggih.
4. Menjamin kesatuan hukum (*legal unity*) di seluruh wilayah Keemiratan Abu Dhabi.

== Ruang Lingkup ==
Kebijakan ini berlaku bagi seluruh tingkatan pengadilan (*First Instance Courts, Appeals Courts, Court of Cassation*) di 8 kota di Abu Dhabi (Abu Dhabi City, Al Ain, Delma, Dhafra, Marfa, Rahba, Ruwais, Sila) dan unit pendukung Judicial Department.

== Ketentuan Utama ==
* '''Empat Pilar Utama Law No. 23/2007''':
# *Judicial Council Independen*: Badan pengelola mandiri yang mengawasi rekrutmen, promosi, dan inspeksi mutu putusan (*Judicial Inspection Division*).
# *Sentralisasi di Bawah Court President & Head Clerk*: Pelembagaan posisi *Head Clerk* sebagai manajer senior pengadilan yang melapor langsung ke *Court President*.
# *Reorganisasi Staf Pendukung dalam 5 Kantor*: Pengelompokkan fungsi IT, Public Affairs, Administration, Performance Management, dan Judicial Support Services di bawah Undersecretary.
# *Pendirian Judicial Training Academy*: Akademi pelatihan hukum lokal bagi calon hakim dan staf peradilan.
* '''Prinsip Kesatuan Hukum''': Abu Dhabi menolak pendirian pengadilan terpisah di zona bebas (*free-zone courts*), dan memilih menyederhanakan prosedur komersial pada sistem peradilan nasional.
* '''Kesetaraan Gender''': Pembukaan kesempatan bagi wanita untuk menjadi hakim dan jaksa (diikuti pengangkatan 3 asisten hakim wanita dan 2 jaksa wanita pertama).

== Implementasi ==
* '''Prosedur 10 Workstreams''': Pelaksanaan rencana aksi mencakup manajemen alur perkara elektronik, pengarsipan 500.000 berkas perkara, penyediaan laptop hakim, dan pembuatan portal publik pengaduan.
* '''Kemitraan Tim Pelaksana''': Kolaborasi ADGRC PMO dengan konsultan Booz Allen Hamilton dan *Amman Centre for Arbitration and Law*.

== Permasalahan Kebijakan ==
* '''Tinggi Dominasi Hakim Asing''': Tingkat ketergantungan pada hakim ekspatriat (>85%) yang memerlukan strategi pelatihan intensif bagi calon hakim lokal.
* '''Tantangan Skala dan Budaya Peradilan''': Penyelarasan ekspektasi pimpinan dengan waktu yang dibutuhkan untuk membangun budaya profesionalisme kehakiman (*judicial culture*).

== Reformasi / Perubahan ==
* Pelepasan aparatur peradilan dari sistem penggajian civil service umum melalui penetapan skala gaji khusus (*independent salary schedule*).
* Target peningkatan keterwakilan warga lokal (*nationalization*) di Judicial Council (mencapai 50% pada 2007) dan First Instance Courts (target 75% pada 2012).

== Hubungan dengan Entity Lain ==
* '''Abu Dhabi Government Restructuring Committee (ADGRC):''' Komite pengarah reformasi pemerintah Abu Dhabi.
* '''Abu Dhabi Judicial Department:''' Lembaga eksekutif pengelola administrasi peradilan Abu Dhabi.

The '''Protection of Academic Freedom and Internal Threats Policy Framework''' (officially centered on the editorial work ''New Threats to Academic Freedom'') is a public law, human rights, and judicial policy framework that evaluates the constitutional foundations of academic freedom in Europe, diagnoses emerging internal and social threats within higher education institutions, critiques traditional judicial tests, and proposes transnational protective mechanisms <ref>della Cananea, G. (2022). New Threats to Academic Freedom. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 14(2), 1–6.</ref>.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Giacinto della Cananea]], Full Professor of Administrative Law at [[Bocconi University]] in Milan, this policy analysis highlights the shifting nature of threats to academic freedom in Europe and internationally <ref>della Cananea (2022), pp. 1, 3.</ref>. Although European universities were historically founded during the Middle Ages (Bologna, Oxford, Paris, Coimbra, Vienna, Heidelberg) on the right to teach and learn without interference from governmental or societal authorities, modern threats increasingly originate from within universities themselves (insiders: academics, students, administrators) and wealthy donors bowing to pressure from vociferous minorities <ref>della Cananea (2022), pp. 1, 3–4.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
The framework relies on key supranational legal instruments and judicial precedent:
* '''[[Article 13 EU Charter of Fundamental Rights|Article 13 EU Charter of Fundamental Rights (CFR)]]''': Guarantees that the arts and scientific research shall be free of constraint and explicitly safeguards academic freedom <ref>della Cananea (2022), p. 2.</ref>.
* '''[[Freedom of Expression Clause of the ECHR]]''': Interpreted by the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) in ''Kula v. Turkey'' (App. No. 20233/06, 2018) to establish that the allowable limits of criticism are wider for academic speech regarding their own institutions <ref>della Cananea (2022), p. 2.</ref>.
* '''[[CJEU Jurisprudence]]''': In ''European Commission v. Hungary'' (Case C-66/18, 2020), the Court of Justice of the European Union affirmed that academic freedom encompasses institutional establishment, research, and teaching, which cannot be restricted disproportionately <ref>della Cananea (2022), p. 3.</ref>.

== Background ==
Historical infringements on academic freedom in Italy include landmark cases such as ''Cordero'' and ''Lombardi Vallauri'' <ref>della Cananea (2022), p. 3.</ref>. However, the editorial notes the emergence of novel internal threats, where universities cancel invitations to international speakers or dismiss faculty members due to social pressure from internal groups or financial donor considerations <ref>della Cananea (2022), p. 3.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Identify insidious internal threats (*insiders*) to academic freedom originating within university governance structures <ref>della Cananea (2022), pp. 3–4.</ref>.
* Evaluate the structural shortcomings of traditional constitutional tests (*reasonable speaker / reasonable listener tests*) derived from US First Amendment jurisprudence <ref>della Cananea (2022), p. 5.</ref>.
* Formulate new transnational protective instruments to safeguard the intellectual independence of universities <ref>della Cananea (2022), pp. 5–6.</ref>.

== Scope ==
The scope encompasses public law, academic freedom of expression, European human rights law, and administrative university governance across Europe and the United States <ref>della Cananea (2022), pp. 1–3, 5.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & Critique of Judicial Tests ==
* '''Flaws of Reasonable Person Tests''': The *reasonable speaker* or *reasonable listener* test risks banning "heretical" or unpopular ideas simply because they offend majority or vocal minority public sentiment <ref>della Cananea (2022), p. 5.</ref>.
* '''Failure to Account for Preventive Measures''': Traditional judicial tests fail to give adequate weight to preparatory steps taken by educators, such as issuing advance trigger warnings before presenting sensitive material <ref>della Cananea (2022), p. 5.</ref>.

== Implementation ==
Evaluated through four real/hypothetical case scenarios:
# Awarding a doctorate to the son of a non-democratic ruler following a substantial financial donation <ref>della Cananea (2022), p. 3.</ref>.
# A university rector revoking an invitation to an ambassador (e.g., from Israel) out of fear of sparking student political debates after receiving multimillion-euro grants <ref>della Cananea (2022), p. 3.</ref>.
# Cancellation of a public lecture by religious authorities due to intense internal protests <ref>della Cananea (2022), p. 3.</ref>.
# Dismissal of a history lecturer for displaying religious artwork despite providing advance warnings to students <ref>della Cananea (2022), p. 5.</ref>.

== Policy Issues ==
* '''Neglect of Freedom by University Insiders''': University administrators and stakeholders assigning lower priority to academic freedom compared to avoiding controversy from vociferous minorities <ref>della Cananea (2022), p. 4.</ref>.
* '''Inability of Courts to Reach Indirect Threats''': The insufficiency of traditional judicial remedies in curbing discretionary cancellations by university rectors or administrators <ref>della Cananea (2022), p. 5.</ref>.

== Proposed Reforms ==
The editorial proposes two novel protective mechanisms:
# Formulation of precise protective standards by independent transnational bodies such as the [[Venice Commission]] <ref>della Cananea (2022), p. 6.</ref>.
# Establishment of a network of national university funding agencies to share information on academic freedom violations, generating negative public reputational impacts for non-compliant universities <ref>della Cananea (2022), p. 6.</ref>.

== Related Entities ==
* '''[[Giacinto della Cananea]]''': Author and Full Professor of Administrative Law at Bocconi University <ref>della Cananea (2022), pp. 1, 3.</ref>.
* '''[[Court of Justice of the European Union]]''': Supranational judicial authority establishing academic freedom standards <ref>della Cananea (2022), p. 3.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>della Cananea (2022), pp. 1–6.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>della Cananea (2022), pp. 1–6.</ref>

'''The Judicial Accountability and Institutional Independence Policy Framework''' is a judicial governance and inter-institutional relations policy framework formulated by Markus Zimmer (Executive Editor of the *International Journal for Court Administration* / IJCA, 2014). It establishes the doctrine that institutional judicial independence is dependent on and causally linked to judicial accountability, professionalism, ethical reliability, and the moral courage of judicial leadership in reforming institutions to confront executive/legislative political intimidation, well-funded partisan campaigns, and the erosion of public trust [1–3].

== Summary ==
Published by Markus Zimmer in the *International Journal for Court Administration* (IJCA), this policy framework reconstructs the relationship between judicial independence and accountability. Zimmer asserts that institutional independence cannot be achieved merely by invoking independence as a defensive mantra against public criticism. The equation for achieving independence and self-governance begins with the value of judicial accountability. Citing evidence from the *Gavel to Gavel 2014* report (National Center for State Courts / NCSC), Zimmer highlights the surge in legislative attacks and well-funded partisan stealth campaigns by wealthy magnates aimed at crippling the judiciary [1–2]. To win public trust, judicial leaders must possess the moral courage to implement Codes of Conduct equipped with coercive enforcement mechanisms.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Doctrine of Judicial Independence & Self-Governance''': Constitutional law principles regarding the separation of powers and the protection of judges from executive/legislative interference.
* '''Codes of Judicial Conduct''': Rules of professional norms and ethics for judges governing integrity and legal compliance.
* '''NCSC Gavel to Gavel Review (2014)''': A research report by the National Center for State Courts tracking US state bills that restrict court authority (e.g., bills in Missouri, Kansas, and Arizona) [1–2].
* '''Not found in the available sources''': Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
The process of drafting legislation and allocating judicial resources often occurs behind closed doors. The executive and legislative branches frequently exploit public sentiment and social media to reduce judicial authority. Judicial leaders tend to be slow in enacting internal reforms, opting instead to hide behind the shield of judicial independence.

== Objectives ==
1. Affirm the doctrine that judicial accountability is an absolute prerequisite for achieving institutional independence (*judicial independence equation*).
2. Shield the judiciary from stealth partisan campaigns and intimidating legislation funded by wealthy business interests [1–2].
3. Transform Codes of Judicial Conduct from merely aspirational documents into disciplinary enforcement instruments with coercive power.
4. Restore public trust and the judiciary's reputation through the moral courage of judicial leadership.

== Scope ==
This policy covers the evaluation of inter-institutional state relations, judicial ethics, and strategies for handling political attacks against the judiciary in the United States (at state and federal levels), developing nations, and international courts [1–3].

== Key Provisions ==
* '''The Judicial Independence Equation''':
** Institutional independence and self-governance will only be granted by the public and government if the judiciary categorically demonstrates compulsory maturity, moral character, and professional accountability.
* '''Threat of Legislative Aggression (Examples from NCSC Gavel to Gavel 2014)''':
# *Missouri*: A bill nullifying federal firearms laws, prohibiting state courts from enforcing them, and permitting lawsuits against judges who attempt to enforce the law [1–2].
# *Kansas*: Judicial budget increases conditioned on a ban prohibiting courts from striking down laws on the basis of unconstitutionality.
# *Ohio, Pennsylvania, Florida*: Bills prohibiting the use of international and Sharia law in courts.
# *Missouri & Pennsylvania*: Bills requiring mandatory drug testing for judges, with impeachment as a penalty.
# *Arizona*: A bill delegating the authority to close municipal courts to local governments.
* '''Weaknesses of Codes of Conduct Without Coercive Power''':
** Current Codes of Conduct are generally aspirational, lacking coercive disciplinary enforcement protocols when ethical violations occur.

== Implementation ==
* '''Strengthening Disciplinary Sanctions in Codes of Conduct''': Incorporating strict sanction clauses and independent enforcement mechanisms against allegations of corruption, bribery, and nepotism.
* '''Moral Courage for Internal Cleansing''': Judicial leadership proactively investigating and prosecuting members' ethical violations without waiting for external pressure or media exposure.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Partisan Stealth Crusades''': Model bills drafted by partisan attorneys and distributed to state legislatures to oust judges whose rulings do not align with their political ideology.
* '''Sluggishness of Judicial Leadership''': The reluctance of judicial leaders to acknowledge internal weaknesses and their institutional sluggishness in executing systemic reforms.

== Reform / Change ==
* Modernizing the instruments of the Code of Judicial Conduct so they possess coercive enforcement capabilities.
* Honest and objective public communication devoid of ruses, pretexts, or contrived defenses when facing media/public criticism.

* '''National Center for State Courts (NCSC)''': The institution providing the *Gavel to Gavel* legislative monitoring data.

'''The Zeleznikow AI and Online Dispute Resolution Policy Framework''' is a judicial technology policy and evaluation framework assessing the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) to enhance court administration efficiency and access to justice for Self-Represented Litigants (SRLs / ''pro se'' litigants). Formulated by Prof. John Zeleznikow (Sir Zelman Cowen Centre, Victoria University) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), Vol. 8 No. 2 (May 2017), the framework establishes a hybrid ODR model based on the three-step Lodder-Zeleznikow approach: (1) determination of BATNA (Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement), (2) facilitation of dialogue/argumentation, and (3) decision analysis and integrative trade-off compromises [1–3, 16–21, 30, 42].

== Summary ==
Published by Prof. John Zeleznikow in the IJCA (May 2017), this policy framework evaluates the role of artificial intelligence and ODR technologies in addressing the crisis triggered by the surge of Self-Represented Litigants (SRLs) across Common Law judicial systems (Australia, USA, UK) [1–3, 8]. The SRL phenomenon has prolonged trial durations, heavily burdened court staff, and created an access-to-justice crisis for low-income citizens. Zeleznikow asserts that an effective ODR system must not merely shift face-to-face mediation onto a computer screen (as seen in the failure of the ''Australian Online FDR System''), but must be a '''Hybrid System''' based on the Lodder-Zeleznikow three-step model [30, 40–42]. The study dissects real-world AI applications: the ''GetAid System'' (evaluating legal aid eligibility using Toulmin argument trees at Victoria Legal Aid), the ''Split-Up System'' (predicting the division of marital assets using 20 neural networks and 94 variables as a BATNA calculator), and the ''AssetDivider System'' (an integrative trade-off algorithm respecting monetary values and child welfare laws) [27–38].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Australian Family Law Act & Family Dispute Resolution (FDR) Mandate:''' Regulations requiring family disputes to undergo FDR before a lawsuit can be filed in court.
* '''Re F: Litigants in Person Guidelines (2001) 161 FLR 189:''' Australian Commonwealth jurisprudence guidelines regarding the protection of procedural rights for SRLs in court.
* '''US Legal Services Corporation (LSC) Summit Report Vision (2013):''' The strategic vision for US judicial technology to provide unified legal portals and automated triage.
* '''UK eJudiciary & eBundles Digital Court System Framework (2016):''' An independent judicial IT framework in the UK pioneered by Sir Henry Brooke and Justice John Tanzer.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
Legal aid budget cuts and high attorney fees have resulted in up to 88% of domestic relations cases in Arizona and up to 93% of cases in Australian tribunals lacking legal representation.

== Objectives ==
1. Open broad and affordable access to justice for SRLs through the provision of interactive online legal guidance.
2. Improve the efficiency, consistency, and transparency of legal decisions to reduce public prejudice against the judiciary.
3. Facilitate out-of-court dispute resolution (ADR/FDR) through objective BATNA calculations and trade-off compromise recommendations.

== Scope ==
This policy encompasses the evaluation and application of AI and ODR in Australia, the United States, and England and Wales, specifically within the domains of family law and civil legal aid.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''The Lodder-Zeleznikow Three-Step ODR Model:'''
** '''Step 1 (BATNA Calculation):''' Providing objective feedback on projected court outcomes if negotiations fail.
** '''Step 2 (Dialogue & Argumentation):''' Resolving differences of opinion through communication instruments and argument trees.
** '''Step 3 (Decision Analysis & Trade-offs):''' Using integrative trade-off algorithms to allocate assets based on priority scales and substantive legal rules.
* '''Specific AI Implementations:'''
** '''GetAid:''' Decision trees and Toulmin arguments for determining legal aid application eligibility at Victoria Legal Aid.
** '''Split-Up:''' Neural networks trained on 103 commonplace cases to predict the percentage entitlement of marital assets.
** '''AssetDivider:''' Asset allocation based on value preferences (ratings sum to 100), real monetary values, and the establishment of payout items.

== Implementation ==
* '''Development of State-Wide Legal Portals (LSC & Microsoft):''' The provision of unified legal portals featuring automated triage and guided interviews.
* '''Integration of ODR Automated Triage:''' The automatic diversion of domestic violence cases directly to court proceedings, bypassing the ODR process.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Low Uptake of Imitation Face-to-Face ODR:''' The failure of the ''Australian Online FDR System'' due to its lack of AI analysis tools (BATNA/Trade-offs).
* '''Risk of Ignoring Substantive Law in Private ODR:''' Commercial ODR systems based on game theory risk neglecting key legal principles such as the ''paramount interest of the child''.

== Reform / Change ==
* Developing Hybrid ODR that integrates AI analysis (BATNA & trade-offs), automated triage, and the facilitation of online communication.
* Integrating ethics, governance, and transparency frameworks into judicial artificial intelligence.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Sir Zelman Cowen Centre (Victoria University):''' The primary research institution designing the AI-ODR framework.
* '''Victoria Legal Aid (VLA):''' The implementing agency for the GetAid system trial in Australia.
* '''US Legal Services Corporation (LSC):''' The funding and development agency for unified legal portals in the United States.
* '''[private person]:''' A nineteen-year-old Law student specializing in Constitutional Law (Hukum Tata Negara) at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta for the 2024/2025 academic year. The intersection of technology, access to justice, and judicial efficiency explored in this framework provides relevant comparative insights for her constitutional law studies. Cecep Mustafa is not found in the available sources [FACT] [1–44].

2. '''Development of State-Wide Unified Legal Portals with Automated Triage Features:''' Integrate guided interviews and document assembly systems to filter citizen cases and automatically divert sensitive matters (e.g., domestic violence) directly to the courts.
3. '''Alignment of AI Trade-off Algorithms with Substantive Legal Principles:''' Ensure that all AI-ODR systems incorporate mandatory legal constraints (such as the paramount interest of the child principle) into asset allocation algorithms so that the resulting compromises remain legally sound and fair [15–16, 35–37, 42].

'''European Private Law Framework on Contract as a Tool for Decommodification of Public Services''' (''Public Services Beyond State and Market: Rethinking Contract as a Tool for Decommodification Within European Private Law'') is an analytical framework of European private law and comparative administrative law formulated by [[Rocco Alessio Albanese]] to examine the transformation of contract theory—transitioning from an ordoliberal, competition-oriented public procurement model to a participatory, relational, and collaborative contractual governance model (co-planning/co-design/shared administration)—thereby utilizing contract as a tool for decommodification in the delivery of Services of General Interest (SGI) in the European Union and Italy <ref name="albanese2023">Albanese, R. A. (2023). Public Services Beyond State and Market: Rethinking Contract as a Tool for Decommodification Within European Private Law. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 9(1), 1–32.</ref>.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Rocco Alessio Albanese]] (Assistant Professor of Private Law at the [[University of Piemonte Orientale]]), this study critiques the dominance of pure market competition paradigms in European public procurement <ref name="albanese2023" />. It argues that the dichotomy between economic (SGEI) and non-economic (SGI) services is relative and non-ontological <ref name="albanese2023" />. Contracts in European private law can be re-conceptualized from bilateral, adversarial exchanges into relational and organizational agreements that facilitate shared administration <ref name="albanese2023" />. By extending Charles Reich's ''New Property'' theory toward commons-oriented, collective access rights, end-users are restored to their status as citizens participating in public service governance rather than mere consumers <ref name="albanese2023" />.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''EU Primary Law''':
** [[Treaty on European Union]] (TEU): Article 3(3) (Highly Competitive Social Market Economy) <ref name="albanese2023" />.
** [[Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union]] (TFEU): Articles 14 & 106(2) (Services of General Economic Interest & competition rule exceptions); Protocol No. 26 on Services of General Interest <ref name="albanese2023" />.
** [[Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union]] (CFREU): Article 36 (Access to SGEI) <ref name="albanese2023" />.
* '''EU Secondary Law & Policy''': [[Directive 2014/24/EU]] (Public Procurement Directive): Recital 33 (Cooperative Concept), Articles 67–69 (Life-Cycle Costing), Article 77 (Reserved Contracts) <ref name="albanese2023" />; European Commission Green Paper on SGI (COM(2003) 270 final) <ref name="albanese2023" />; European Commission Communication on the Social Economy Action Plan (COM(2021) 778 final) <ref name="albanese2023" />.
* '''Italian National Law''':
** [[Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana]]: Article 117(2)(e) (Protection of Competition) & Article 118(4) (Horizontal Subsidiarity) <ref name="albanese2023" />.
** [[Codice del Terzo Settore]] (Legislative Decree 117/2017): Articles 55–57 (Co-planning and Co-design) <ref name="albanese2023" />.
** [[Codice dei Contratti Pubblici]] (Legislative Decree 36/2023): Article 6 (Cooperative Non-Profit Organizational Models) <ref name="albanese2023" />.
* '''Italian Jurisprudence''': [[Corte Costituzionale]] Rulings No. 325/2010, No. 131/2020, and No. 255/2020 <ref name="albanese2023" />; [[Consiglio di Stato]] Opinion No. 2052/2018 <ref name="albanese2023" />.

== Main Provisions & Analysis ==
1. '''Revising Public Procurement (Directive 2014/24/EU)''': Integrates environmental and social life-cycle costing (Articles 67–69) and reserves social contracts for participatory, non-profit entities (Article 77) <ref name="albanese2023" />.
2. '''Italian Third Sector Co-Planning Model''': Replaces competitive, adversarial procurement with collaborative partnerships based on pooled resources, horizontal subsidiarity, and absence of profit motives <ref name="albanese2023" />.
3. '''Constitutional Affirmation''': Ruling No. 131/2020 of the Italian Constitutional Court affirmed that non-profit solidarity partnerships operate outside ordinary competitive tender rules <ref name="albanese2023" />.
4. '''End-User Empowerment (New Property)''': Reconceptualizes end-user entitlements as non-negotiable collective access rights, establishing zones of agency for citizens <ref name="albanese2023" />.

== Relationships & Associated Entities ==
* '''[[Rocco Alessio Albanese]]''': Author / Researcher (University of Piemonte Orientale) <ref name="albanese2023" />.
* '''[[European Commission]]''': Issuing authority of the Social Economy Action Plan 2021 <ref name="albanese2023" />.
* '''[[Corte Costituzionale]]''': Constitutional Court of Italy <ref name="albanese2023" />.
* '''[[Charles A. Reich]]''', '''[[Victor P. Goldberg]]''', '''[[Gunther Teubner]]''', '''[[Hans-W. Micklitz]]''', '''[[Pietro Perlingieri]]''', '''[[Stefano Rodotà]]''': Referenced Legal Theorists <ref name="albanese2023" />.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available source materials.]]'' <ref name="albanese2023" />
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available source materials.]]'' <ref name="albanese2023" />

'''Quadro Giuridico del Diritto Privato Europeo sul Contratto come Strumento di Decommodificazione dei Servizi Pubblici''' (''Public Services Beyond State and Market: Rethinking Contract as a Tool for Decommodification Within European Private Law'') è un quadro di analisi del diritto privato europeo e del diritto amministrativo comparato formulato da [[Rocco Alessio Albanese]] per esaminare la trasformazione della concezione del contratto—dal modello di mercato ordoliberale orientato alla concorrenza al modello di governance contrattuale partecipativo, relazionale e collaborativo (amministrazione condivisa/co-programmazione/co-progettazione)—al fine di impiegare il contratto come strumento di decommodificazione nella gestione dei Servizi di Interesse Generale (SIG) nell'Unione Europea e in Italia <ref name="albanese2023it">Albanese, R. A. (2023). Public Services Beyond State and Market: Rethinking Contract as a Tool for Decommodification Within European Private Law. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 9(1), 1–32.</ref>.

== Sintesi Generale ==
Elaborato da [[Rocco Alessio Albanese]] (Ricercatore di Diritto Privato presso l'[[Università degli Studi del Piemonte Orientale]]), questo studio critica il predominio del paradigma concorrenziale puro negli appalti pubblici europei <ref name="albanese2023it" />. L'autore sostiene che la dicotomia tra servizi economici (SIEG) e non economici (SIG) ha carattere relativo e non ontologico <ref name="albanese2023it" />. Il contratto nel diritto privato europeo può essere riconcettualizzato da scambio bilaterale e antagonista a modello relazionale ed organizzativo volto ad agevolare l'amministrazione condivisa <ref name="albanese2023it" />. Estendendo la teoria della ''New Property'' di Charles Reich verso diritti di accesso collettivo, gli utenti finali riacquistano lo status di cittadini partecipanti alla governance dei servizi pubblici piuttosto che di meri consumatori <ref name="albanese2023it" />.

== Basi Giuridiche ==
* '''Diritto Primario dell'Unione Europea''':
** [[Trattato sull'Unione Europea]] (TUE): Articolo 3(3) (Economia sociale di mercato altamente competitiva) <ref name="albanese2023it" />.
** [[Trattato sul Funzionamento dell'Unione Europea]] (TFUE): Articoli 14 e 106(2) (Servizi di Interesse Economico Generale e deroghe alle regole di concorrenza); Protocollo n. 26 sui Servizi di Interesse Generale <ref name="albanese2023it" />.
** [[Carta dei Diritti Fondamentali dell'Unione Europea]] (CDFUE): Articolo 36 (Accesso ai SIEG) <ref name="albanese2023it" />.
* '''Diritto Derivato e Documenti Politici UE''': [[Direttiva 2014/24/UE]] (Direttiva Appalti Pubblici): Considerando 33 (Concetto cooperativo), Articoli 67–69 (Costi del ciclo di vita), Articolo 77 (Appalti riservati) <ref name="albanese2023it" />; Libro Verde sui Servizi di Interesse Generale (COM(2003) 270 final) <ref name="albanese2023it" />; Comunicazione sul Piano d'Azione per l'Economia Sociale (COM(2021) 778 final) <ref name="albanese2023it" />.
* '''Diritto Nazionale Italiano''':
** [[Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana]]: Articolo 117, comma 2, lett. e) (Tutela della concorrenza) e Articolo 118, comma 4 (Sussidiarietà orizzontale) <ref name="albanese2023it" />.
** [[Codice del Terzo Settore]] (D.Lgs. 117/2017): Articoli 55–57 (Co-programmazione e Co-progettazione) <ref name="albanese2023it" />.
** [[Codice dei Contratti Pubblici]] (D.Lgs. 36/2023): Articolo 6 (Modelli organizzativi cooperativi privi di scopo di lucro) <ref name="albanese2023it" />.
* '''Giurisprudenza Italiana''': [[Corte Costituzionale]] Sentenze n. 325/2010, n. 131/2020 e n. 255/2020 <ref name="albanese2023it" />; [[Consiglio di Stato]] Parere n. 2052/2018 <ref name="albanese2023it" />.

== Disposizioni Principali e Analisi ==
1. '''Revisione degli Appalti Pubblici (Direttiva 2014/24/UE)''': Integra criteri ambientali e sociali legati al ciclo di vita (Articoli 67–69) e riserva appalti sociali a enti partecipativi del terzo settore (Articolo 77) <ref name="albanese2023it" />.
2. '''Modello di Co-progettazione del Terzo Settore''': Sostituisce le gare d'appalto competitive con partnership collaborative basate sulla condivisione di risorse, sussidiarietà orizzontale e assenza di fini di lucro <ref name="albanese2023it" />.
3. '''Legittimazione Costituzionale''': La Sentenza n. 131/2020 della Corte Costituzionale ha confermato che le partnership solidali del terzo settore operano al di fuori delle ordinarie procedure di gara competitiva <ref name="albanese2023it" />.
4. '''Centralità dell'Utente Finale (New Property)''': Riconcettualizza le prerogative dell'utente finalizzato come diritti collettivi non negoziabili di accesso, creando veri e propri spazi di partecipazione attiva per i cittadini <ref name="albanese2023it" />.

'''Policy and Legal Framework on the Use of Artificial Intelligence and Algorithmic Automation in Albania's Public Administration''' (''Algorithmic Automation and Artificial Intelligence in Albania's Public Administration Framework'') is a digital governance policy, legislative, and regulatory framework in Albania governing the use of algorithmic automation systems and artificial intelligence (AI) in public service delivery via the e-Albania portal, the setting of technical standards by the National Agency for Information Society (NAIS/AKSHI), alignment with the EU AI Act, GDPR, and the Council of Europe AI Convention, as well as addressing issues of human rights, transparency, personal data protection, and cybersecurity <ref>Çani, E. (M.), & Mazelliu, A. (2025). Navigating the Algorithmic Shift and the Legal Implications of Artificial Intelligence in Albania’s Public Administration. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 17(2), 497–527.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Authored by [[Eralda (Methasani) Çani]] (Professor of Law, University of Tirana) and [[Andrea Mazelliu]] (Lecturer at UNYT), this study analyzes the digital transition and the legality of AI usage within Albania's public administration <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), p. 497.</ref>. Albania has achieved rapid progress through the centralized e-Albania portal, which provides 1,245 online services <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 505, 509, 524.</ref>. However, the enactment of ''Law No. 43/2023 on Electronic Governance'' still faces serious challenges regarding the absence of technical protocols, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, mass data leaks, and the digital divide <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 510, 513, 515, 518, 521.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
Albania's digital legal and policy oversight framework is rooted in constitutional instruments and sectoral legislation:
* '''[[Constitution of the Republic of Albania]] (Article 15)''': The primary obligation of public authorities to respect and protect fundamental human rights in all administrative actions <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), p. 503.</ref>.
* '''[[Code of Administrative Procedure]] (2015)''': Governs the active assistance principle, administrative acts, and the requirement of a human signature (*responsible employee*) <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 503, 506.</ref>.
* '''[[Law No. 43/2023 on Electronic Governance]]''': Regulates electronic governance, AI definition (*Art. 3 para. 16*), Backend as a Service (BaaS) architecture, and Electronic Records Management (ERM) <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 503, 511, 512.</ref>.
* '''[[Law No. 9887/2008]] & [[Law No. 119/2014]]''': Legislation on Personal Data Protection and the Right to Information <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 520, 523.</ref>.
* '''International/EU Instruments''':
** ''EU Artificial Intelligence Act'' (Regulation 2024/1689) <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 501, 513.</ref>.
** ''Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI'' (Treaty No. 225, September 2024) <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), p. 502.</ref>.
** ''EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)'' (Regulation 2016/679) <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 501, 518.</ref>.

== Background & Public Service Digitalization ==
Albania's digital transition has been propelled by the EU accession process since the 2003 Thessaloniki Declaration and the *Digital Agenda Strategy 2022-2026* <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 506, 510.</ref>. Under Prime Minister Instruction No. 158/2019, the government mandated the closure of physical service desks and transferred 100% of public services online as of January 1, 2020 <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 504, 509.</ref>. Since 2017, e-Albania has issued over 16 million qualified e-stamped documents, saving citizens equivalent to 700 years of queuing time <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), p. 510.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Drive efficiency, transparency, and eliminate bureaucratic corruption through e-Albania <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 497, 504, 509.</ref>.
* Harmonize Albanian administrative law with the *EU AI Act* and the *Council of Europe AI Convention* <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 501, 502, 514, 526.</ref>.
* Ensure personal data protection and prevent algorithmic bias <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 498, 514, 518, 526.</ref>.

== Scope ==
The scope of this policy framework encompasses Albanian administrative law, e-Albania governance, cybersecurity, and the deployment of algorithmic automation across State Police (Tirana Airport e-gates & AI CCTV), Tax Administration (e-filing), Transportation (DPSHTRR), and Education (SMIP & Matura Shtetërore) <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 523–526.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & NAIS Institutional Structure ==
* '''Central Role of NAIS/AKSHI''': The National Agency for Information Society is designated as the sole managing and coordinating authority for state databases and e-Albania <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 505, 512, 517.</ref>.
* '''BaaS & Cloud-First Model''': All e-Albania services operate on a cloud-based Backend as a Service (BaaS) architecture <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 510, 517.</ref>.
* '''Non-Delegation Principle & Human-in-the-Loop''': Agency heads and public employees remain accountable for final administrative decisions; AI systems cannot fully replace human responsibility <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 500, 506.</ref>.

== Policy Issues & Mass Data Leaks ==
* '''2021 Mass Data Leak & 2022/2023 Iranian Cyberattacks''': The leakage of personal data belonging to 910,000 citizens in 2021 and severe Iranian cyberattacks crippling state servers triggered harsh criticism from the Information and Data Protection Commissioner (IDPC) and the 2023 EU Progress Report regarding data security vulnerabilities <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 510, 518, 520, 521.</ref>.
* '''Digital Divide''': The 2023 EU Progress Report highlighted the exclusion of citizens without technological access and marginal communities such as the Roma and Balkan Egyptian minorities following the complete closure of physical front offices <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 507, 515.</ref>.

== Reforms & 2024 Public Procurement Amendment ==
Parliament enacted *Law No. 16/2024* amending the Public Procurement Law (*Law No. 162/2020*), permitting the use of artificial intelligence and robotic process automation in public procurement and government contracting <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 526, 527.</ref>.

== Relationship to Other Entities ==
* '''[[Eralda (Methasani) Çani]]''': Lead author of the study and Professor of Law at the University of Tirana <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), p. 497.</ref>.
* '''[[Andrea Mazelliu]]''': Lead author of the study and Lecturer at UNYT <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), p. 497.</ref>.
* '''[[NAIS]] (AKSHI)''': National Agency for Information Society in Albania <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 505, 512.</ref>.
* '''[[IDPC]] (KDIMDP)''': Information and Data Protection Commissioner <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 520, 521.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 497–527.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 497–527.</ref>

'''Quadro Politico e Giuridico sull'Uso dell'Intelligenza Artificiale e dell'Automazione Algoritmica nell'Amministrazione Pubblica Albanese''' (''Algorithmic Automation and Artificial Intelligence in Albania's Public Administration Framework'') è un quadro normativo e di politica pubblica in Albania che disciplina l'uso dei sistemi di automazione algoritmica e intelligenza artificiale (IA) nell'erogazione dei servizi pubblici tramite il portale e-Albania, la definizione degli standard tecnici da parte della National Agency for Information Society (NAIS/AKSHI), l'allineamento con l'EU AI Act, il GDPR e la Convenzione sull'IA del Consiglio d'Europa, e la gestione dei diritti umani, della trasparenza, della protezione dei dati personali e della sicurezza informatica <ref>Çani, E. (M.), & Mazelliu, A. (2025). Navigating the Algorithmic Shift and the Legal Implications of Artificial Intelligence in Albania’s Public Administration. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 17(2), 497–527.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Scritto da [[Eralda (Methasani) Çani]] (Professoressa di Diritto, Università di Tirana) e [[Andrea Mazelliu]] (Docente presso UNYT), lo studio analizza la transizione digitale e la legalità dell'uso dell'IA nell'amministrazione pubblica albanese <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), p. 497.</ref>. L'Albania ha raggiunto un rapido progresso attraverso il portale centralizzato e-Albania, che fornisce 1.245 servizi online <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 505, 509, 524.</ref>. Tuttavia, la promulgazione della ''Legge N. 43/2023 sulla Governance Elettronica'' affronta ancora serie sfide per l'assenza di protocolli tecnici, vulnerabilità di cybersicurezza, fughe massive di dati e divario digitale (*digital divide*) <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 510, 513, 515, 518, 521.</ref>.

== Base Giuridica ==
Il quadro di vigilanza giuridica e politica digitale dell'Albania affonda le sue radici in strumenti costituzionali e leggi di settore:
* '''[[Costituzione della Repubblica d'Albania]] (Articolo 15)''': Obbligo primario delle autorità pubbliche di rispettare e proteggere i diritti umani fondamentali in tutte le azioni amministrative <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), p. 503.</ref>.
* '''[[Kodi i Procedurave Administrative]] (Codice di Procedura Amministrativa 2015)''': Regola il principio di assistenza attiva, gli atti amministrativi e la necessità della firma autografa di un funzionario umano (*responsible employee*) <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 503, 506.</ref>.
* '''[[Legge N. 43/2023 sulla Governance Elettronica]]''': Regola la governance elettronica, la definizione di IA (*Art. 3 par. 16*), il modello Backend as a Service (BaaS) e la gestione dei documenti elettronici (ERM) <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 503, 511, 512.</ref>.
* '''[[Legge N. 9887/2008]] & [[Legge N. 119/2014]]''': Normative sulla Protezione dei Dati Personali e sul Diritto all'Informazione <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 520, 523.</ref>.
* '''Strumenti Internazionali/UE''':
** *EU Artificial Intelligence Act* (Regolamento 2024/1689) <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 501, 513.</ref>.
** *Convenzione Quadro sull'IA del Consiglio d'Europa* (Trattato N. 225, settembre 2024) <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), p. 502.</ref>.
** *EU GDPR* (Regolamento 2016/679) <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 501, 518.</ref>.

== Contesto e Digitalizzazione dei Servizi Pubblici ==
La transizione digitale dell'Albania è stata promossa dal processo di adesione all'UE a partire dalla Dichiarazione di Salonicco del 2003 e dalla strategia *Digital Agenda 2022-2026* <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 506, 510.</ref>. Ai sensi della Direttiva del Primo Ministro N. 158/2019, il governo ha imposto la chiusura degli sportelli fisici e il trasferimento al 100% dei servizi pubblici online dal 1° gennaio 2020 <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 504, 509.</ref>. Dal 2017, e-Albania ha rilasciato oltre 16 milioni di documenti elettronici con timbro digitale qualificato, risparmiando ai cittadini un tempo equivalente a 700 anni di attesa in coda <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), p. 510.</ref>.

== Obiettivi ==
* Promuovere l'efficienza, la trasparenza e l'eliminazione della corruzione burocratica attraverso e-Albania <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 497, 504, 509.</ref>.
* Armonizzare il diritto amministrativo albanese con l'*EU AI Act* e la *Convenzione sull'IA del Consiglio d'Europa* <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 501, 502, 514, 526.</ref>.
* Garantire la protezione dei dati personali e prevenire la discriminazione algoritmica (*algorithmic bias*) <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 498, 514, 518, 526.</ref>.

== Ambito di Applicazione ==
L'ambito di questo quadro politico comprende il diritto amministrativo albanese, la governance di e-Albania, la sicurezza informatica e la distribuzione di automatismi algoritmici nella Polizia di Stato (e-gates e telecamere IA all'Aeroporto di Tirana), nell'Amministrazione Finanziaria (e-filing), nei Trasporti (DPSHTRR) e nell'Istruzione (SMIP e Matura Shtetërore) <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 523–526.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Principali e Struttura Istituzionale NAIS ==
* '''Ruolo Centrale della NAIS/AKSHI''': La National Agency for Information Society è designata come unica autorità di gestione e coordinamento dei database statali e di e-Albania <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 505, 512, 517.</ref>.
* '''Modello BaaS e Cloud-First''': Tutti i servizi di e-Albania operano su un'architettura cloud Backend as a Service (BaaS) <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 510, 517.</ref>.
* '''Principio di Non Delegabilità e Controllo Umano (*Human-in-the-Loop*)''': I dirigenti e i dipendenti pubblici rimangono responsabili della decisione amministrativa finale; l'IA non può sostituire completamente la responsabilità umana <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 500, 506.</ref>.

== Problemi Politici e Fuga Massiva di Dati ==
* '''Fuga Massiva di Dati del 2021 e Attacchi Informatici Iraniani del 2022/2023''': La fuga di dati personali di 910.000 cittadini nel 2021 e i gravi attacchi informatici iraniani che hanno bloccato i server statali hanno suscitato forti critiche da parte del Commissario per la Protezione dei Dati (IDPC) e nel Rapporto di Progresso dell'UE 2023 sulla vulnerabilità della sicurezza dei dati <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 510, 518, 520, 521.</ref>.
* '''Divario Digitale''': Il Rapporto di Progresso UE 2023 ha evidenziato l'esclusione dei cittadini privi di accesso tecnologico e delle comunità marginali, come le minoranze Rom e Balcano-Egiziane, a seguito della chiusura totale degli sportelli fisici <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 507, 515.</ref>.

== Riforme e Emendamento sugli Appalti Pubblici del 2024 ==
Il Parlamento ha approvato la *Legge N. 16/2024* che modifica la Legge sugli Appalti Pubblici (*Legge N. 162/2020*), autorizzando l'uso dell'intelligenza artificiale e dell'automazione dei processi tramite robot negli appalti pubblici e nelle forniture statali <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 526, 527.</ref>.

== Relazione con Altre Entità ==
* '''[[Eralda (Methasani) Çani]]''': Autrice principale dello studio e Professoressa di Diritto presso l'Università di Tirana <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), p. 497.</ref>.
* '''[[Andrea Mazelliu]]''': Autore principale dello studio e Docente presso UNYT <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), p. 497.</ref>.
* '''[[NAIS]] (AKSHI)''': National Agency for Information Society in Albania <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 505, 512.</ref>.
* '''[[IDPC]] (KDIMDP)''': Commissario per il Diritto all'Informazione e la Protezione dei Dati Personali <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 520, 521.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Non trovato nelle fonti disponibili.]]'' <ref>Çani & Mazelliu (2025), pp. 497–527.</ref>

'''The Law of the Algorithmic State in Central and Eastern Europe Framework''' (Indonesian: ''Kerangka Hukum dan Kebijakan Negara Algoritmik di Eropa Tengah dan Timur'') is a comparative legal analysis and judicial policy framework developed by Marta Infantino and Mauro Bussani to examine how Automated Decision-Making (ADM) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems deployed by state authorities impact statutory legal orders, institutional practices, and judicial disputes across 12 Central and Eastern European (CEE) countries <ref>Infantino, M., & Bussani, M. (2025). The Law of the Algorithmic State in Central and Eastern Europe: Introduction to the Special Issue. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 17(2), 447–473.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Authored by [[Marta Infantino]] and [[Mauro Bussani]], Professors of Comparative Private Law at the [[University of Trieste]], this introductory framework presents findings from the international research project *AutAD* (*The dark side of algorithms under the comparative lens*), funded by the Italian Ministry of University and Research under the national coordination of [[Angela Ferrari Zumbini]] <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 447, 449.</ref>. The study addresses Western-centric bias in law and technology by focusing on the central role of the administrative state as a key developer and user of AI across 12 CEE jurisdictions <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 448–450, 460–462.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
The framework relies on supranational European legal instruments and national statutory laws:
* '''[[EU Artificial Intelligence Act]] (Regulation EU 2024/1689)''': Establishes harmonized EU rules for AI and classifies public sector AI deployments under Annex III as High-Risk AI <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 453, 454.</ref>.
* '''[[Interoperable Europe Act]] (Regulation EU 2024/903) & [[EU GDPR]]''': Regulations governing public sector interoperability and personal data protection <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 451, 453.</ref>.
* '''[[Council of Europe AI Framework Convention]] (2024)''': International framework convention on AI, human rights, democracy, and the rule of law <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), p. 454.</ref>.
* '''[[ELI Model Rules on Impact Assessment of ADMSs]] (2022)''': European Law Institute guidelines for algorithmic impact assessment in public administration <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), p. 453.</ref>.
* '''[[National CEE Administrative Procedure Acts]]''': Pre-existing technology-neutral statutes governing administrative decisions (e.g., *Bulgarian E-Government Act 2007*, *Croatian General Administrative Procedure Act 2009*, *Latvian Administrative Procedure Law 2001*) <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 463–465.</ref>.

== Background & Research Methodology ==
The study draws upon the *Common Core of European Administrative Laws* (CoCEAL) methodology inaugurated by [[Giacinto della Cananea]] and Mauro Bussani, alongside the legal formants theory developed by [[Rodolfo Sacco]] and [[Ugo Mattei]] <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 449, 456.</ref>. The researchers evaluate four legal formants: statutory provisions, bureaucratic practices, judicial rulings, and legal scholarship <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 455, 456.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Map state deployment of ADM and AI in public services across 12 CEE jurisdictions <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 448, 460.</ref>.
* Identify legal due process gaps arising from public algorithmic deployment under general, non-specific statutes <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 449, 465–467.</ref>.
* Assess compatibility between pre-existing administrative laws and modern requirements for transparency and human oversight <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 464, 465.</ref>.

== Scope ==
Covers 12 CEE nations (Albania, Bulgaria, Croatia, Czech Republic, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania, Serbia, Slovenia, and Turkey) across key public domains including taxation, welfare benefits, traffic management, border enforcement, education, and the judiciary <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 448, 460, 468, 469.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & Comparative Findings ==
* '''Two Waves of Digital Transformation''': The initial e-government wave (2000s) followed by the smart and automated government wave (2020s) <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 466, 467.</ref>.
* '''Reliance on Technology-Neutral Rules''': Most CEE states lack dedicated ADM/AI statutes, relying instead on legacy administrative procedure codes <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 463–465.</ref>.
* '''Litigation Vacuum''': Public algorithm litigation in CEE courts remains rare compared to Western Europe and the United States <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 458, 467.</ref>.

== Judicial Evidence & Landmark Case Law ==
* '''Polish Constitutional Tribunal Judgment (2018)''': Struck down automated profiling of job seekers due to the absence of statutory rights to appeal <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 467, 468.</ref>.
* '''Other Regional Disputes''': Judicial examination of automated traffic penalty tickets in Bulgaria and pending 'Hawk Eye' surveillance litigation in the Serbian Constitutional Court <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 467, 468.</ref>.

== Policy Issues & Reforms ==
* '''Privacy Concerns & Digital Exclusion''': Risks of algorithmic bias affecting marginalized communities (e.g., Roma populations) and dependency on foreign technology vendors <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 459, 460.</ref>.
* '''Legislative Reform Requirements''': Urgent need for specific statutory rules mandating algorithmic impact assessments, transparency, and a statutory right to explanation within CEE national administrative codes <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 465, 470.</ref>.

== Related Entities ==
* '''[[Marta Infantino]]''': Lead Author and Associate Professor of Comparative Private Law <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), p. 447.</ref>.
* '''[[Mauro Bussani]]''': Lead Author and Full Professor of Comparative Private Law <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), p. 447.</ref>.
* '''[[Angela Ferrari Zumbini]]''': National Coordinator of the AutAD Research Project <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), p. 449.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 447–473.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 447–473.</ref>

'''Il Quadro Giuridico e Politico dello Stato Algoritmico nell'Europa Centrale e Orientale''' (in inglese: ''The Law of the Algorithmic State in Central and Eastern Europe Framework'') è un quadro di analisi giuridica comparata e politica giurisdizionale sviluppato da Marta Infantino e Mauro Bussani per esaminare come il processo decisionale automatizzato (*Automated Decision-Making* / ADM) e i sistemi di intelligenza artificiale (IA) adottati dalle autorità pubbliche incidano sull'ordinamento legislativo, sulle prassi istituzionali e sulle controversie giudiziarie in 12 paesi dell'Europa Centrale e Orientale (CEE) <ref>Infantino, M., & Bussani, M. (2025). The Law of the Algorithmic State in Central and Eastern Europe: Introduction to the Special Issue. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 17(2), 447–473.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Redatto da [[Marta Infantino]] e [[Mauro Bussani]], docenti di Diritto Privato Comparato presso l'[[Università di Trieste]], questo saggio introduttivo presenta i risultati del progetto di ricerca internazionale *AutAD* (*The dark side of algorithms under the comparative lens*), finanziato dal Ministero dell'Università e della Ricerca sotto il coordinamento nazionale di [[Angela Ferrari Zumbini]] <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 447, 449.</ref>. Lo studio corregge un'impostazione occidentalocentrica (*Western-centric bias*) nel diritto delle tecnologie, ponendo l'accento sul ruolo centrale dello Stato amministrativo come principale sviluppatore e utilizzatore dell'IA in 12 paesi CEE <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 448–450, 460–462.</ref>.

== Basi Giuridiche ==
Il quadro normativo si fonda su fonti sovranazionali europee e legislazioni nazionali:
* '''[[EU Artificial Intelligence Act]] (Regolamento UE 2024/1689)''': Stabilisce regole armonizzate nell'UE e classifica l'uso pubblico dell'IA nell'Allegato III come IA ad alto rischio (*high-risk AI*) <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 453, 454.</ref>.
* '''[[Interoperable Europe Act]] (Regolamento UE 2024/903) & [[GDPR UE]]''': Normative sull'interoperabilità del settore pubblico e sulla protezione dei dati personali <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 451, 453.</ref>.
* '''[[Convenzione Quadro sull'IA del Consiglio d'Europa]] (2024)''': Trattato internazionale su IA, diritti umani, democrazia e Stato di diritto <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), p. 454.</ref>.
* '''[[Regole Modello ELI sulla Valutazione di Impatto dell'ADM]] (2022)''': Linee guida dell'European Law Institute per la valutazione d'impatto algoritmico nella pubblica amministrazione <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), p. 453.</ref>.
* '''[[Legge Nazionale sul Procedimento Amministrativo CEE]]''': Norme preesistenti e tecnologicamente neutrali (es. *Legge bulgara sull'E-Government 2007*, *Legge croata sul procedimento amministrativo 2009*, *Legge lettone sul procedimento amministrativo 2001*) <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 463–465.</ref>.

== Contesto e Metodologia di Ricerca ==
La ricerca si ispira alla metodologia del *Common Core of European Administrative Laws* (CoCEAL), avviata da [[Giacinto della Cananea]] e Mauro Bussani, e alla teoria dei formanti giuridici formulata da [[Rodolfo Sacco]] e [[Ugo Mattei]] <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 449, 456.</ref>. Gli autori esaminano quattro formanti: testo legislativo, prassi burocratica, giurisprudenza e dottrina <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 455, 456.</ref>.

== Obiettivi ==
* Mappare l'impiego di ADM e IA da parte dello Stato nei servizi pubblici in 12 giurisdizioni CEE <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 448, 460.</ref>.
* Individuare le lacune di tutela giurisdizionale (*due process gap*) derivanti dall'uso di algoritmi pubblici in assenza di leggi speciali <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 449, 465–467.</ref>.
* Verificare la compatibilità tra le leggi generali sul procedimento amministrativo e i requisiti di trasparenza e controllo umano (*human oversight*) <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 464, 465.</ref>.

== Ambito di Applicazione ==
Comprende 12 paesi dell'Europa Centrale e Orientale (Albania, Bulgaria, Croazia, Repubblica Ceca, Ungheria, Lettonia, Lituania, Polonia, Romania, Serbia, Slovenia e Turchia) e settori chiave quali fisco, assistenza sociale, traffico, controllo delle frontiere, istruzione e giustizia <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 448, 460, 468, 469.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Principali e Risultati Comparati ==
* '''Due Ondate di Trasformazione Digitale''': La prima fase di e-government (anni 2000) e la successiva fase di smart e automated government (anni 2020) <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 466, 467.</ref>.
* '''Applicazione di Norme Tecnologicamente Neutrali''': La maggior parte dei paesi CEE privi di leggi speciali applica i tradizionali codici di procedimento amministrativo <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 463–465.</ref>.
* '''Vuoto di Contenzioso Giudiziario''': A differenza di quanto avviene in Europa occidentale e negli USA, i ricorsi giurisdizionali contro gli algoritmi pubblici nell'area CEE restano eccezionali <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 458, 467.</ref>.

== Prove Giurisprudenziali (Casi Principali) ==
* '''Sentenza del Tribunale Costituzionale Polacco (2018)''': Annullamento della profilazione automatizzata dei disoccupati per violazione del diritto di ricorso <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 467, 468.</ref>.
* '''Altre Controversie Regionali''': Il sindacato giurisdizionale sulle sanzioni stradali automatizzate in Bulgaria e il contenzioso pendente sul sistema di sorveglianza 'Hawk Eye' presso la Corte Costituzionale Serba <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 467, 468.</ref>.

== Questioni Politiche e Riforme ==
* '''Rischi per la Privacy ed Esclusione Digitale''': Pericolo di discriminazioni algoritmiche a danno di gruppi vulnerabili (es. comunità Rom in Albania) e dipendenza da fornitori tecnologici esteri <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 459, 460.</ref>.
* '''Necessità di Riforme Legislative''': Urgenza di introdurre l'obbligo di valutazione d'impatto algoritmico, la trasparenza dei codici e il diritto ad una spiegazione nei codici di procedimento amministrativo CEE <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 465, 470.</ref>.

== Entità Correlate ==

* '''[[Mauro Bussani]]''': Autore principale e Professore Ordinario di Diritto Privato Comparato <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), p. 447.</ref>.
* '''[[Angela Ferrari Zumbini]]''': Coordinatrice nazionale del Progetto di Ricerca AutAD <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), p. 449.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITÀ NON VERIFICABILE|Non presente nelle fonti disponibili.]]'' <ref>Infantino & Bussani (2025), pp. 447–473.</ref>

'''Abuja Multi-Door Courthouse (AMDC)''' is a court-annexed Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) center established within the High Court of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja, Nigeria, on 13 October 2003. Adopting the "Multi-Door Courthouse" concept formulated by Professor Frank Sander of Harvard Law School in 1976, the AMDC integrates intake screening, negotiation, mediation, conciliation, and arbitration into the public judicial system to reduce docket congestion, cut litigation costs, and restore the business and personal relationships of the parties involved [11–13, 21–23, 30, 31].

== Summary ==
Commissioned by the Chief Justice of Nigeria and fully funded by the High Court of the FCT Abuja under the leadership of Chief Judge L.H. Gummi, the AMDC is the second multi-door facility in Africa, following the Lagos Multi-Door Courthouse (LMDC, 2002). The AMDC offers dispute resolution pathways tailored to each case's specific needs. In practice, the AMDC has recorded an average settlement rate of 70%, with 50% of cases successfully resolved at the pre-session stage before reaching formal mediation or arbitration.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Section 259 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999:''' The basis of authority for the Chief Judge of the FCT Abuja to issue the AMDC's Practice Direction.
* '''Section 18 of the High Court Act (CAP 510 LFN 1990):''' The statutory mandate directing courts to promote reconciliation and amicable settlement.
* '''District Court Act (CAP 495 LFN 1990, Sections 26, 27, 82–88):''' Rules governing referees and special arbitrators.
* '''Order 19, High Court of the FCT (Civil Procedure Rules) Act (CAP 511 LFN 1990):''' Procedural rules on court referrals for out-of-court dispute settlement.
* '''Order 25, Rule 1, High Court of Lagos State (Civil Procedure) Rules 2004:''' Pre-trial conference provisions that pioneered ADR integration in Nigeria.

== Background & the Failure of the Adversarial System ==
Prior to the colonial era, traditional Nigerian society employed a layered dispute resolution approach (personal negotiation → clan/kinsman mediation → chief/king arbitration) centered on restoring social relationships. The colonial legal system replaced this with a rigid adversarial framework. A surge in public legal awareness following the return to democracy in 1999 overwhelmed the capacity of traditional courts.

=== Case Study: Emeka Nwana v. FCDA (2007) ===
The failure of the adversarial system is illustrated by the case ''Nwana v. FCDA''. Mr. Nwana was dismissed by the FCDA in 1989 and filed suit in the High Court of the FCT. After proceeding through the Court of Appeal (1994) and the Supreme Court (2007), the Supreme Court set aside the appellate court's ruling and ordered a fresh hearing from the beginning (*de novo*) — consuming '''18 years of litigation''' without any substantive resolution.

== Scope & the AMDC's Three-Stage Procedure ==

=== Case Handling Procedure ===
1. '''Stage 1 (Filing & Notice):''' The initiating party completes Form 1 (Request Form) and a statement of issues. The ADR Registrar sends Form 2 (Notice of Referral) and Form 3 (Memorandum) to the respondent within 7 days.
2. '''Stage 2 (Screening & Pre-Session):''' A Dispute Resolution Officer (DRO) conducts a confidential Screening Conference (30–45 minutes) to diagnose the case, select the appropriate ADR method, and secure signatures on Form 4 (Attendance) and Form 5 (Confidentiality).
3. '''Stage 3 (Scheduling & ADR Session):''' The neutral (mediator/arbitrator) confirms availability within 7 days via a Disclosure Form, followed by the mediation or arbitration session.

=== Case Distribution (2008/2009 Legal Year) ===
* Commercial Contracts: '''50%'''.
* Land Disputes: '''20%'''.
* Matrimonial/Family Cases: '''10%'''.
* Tenancy: '''10%'''.
* Labour: '''4%'''.
* Banking: '''3%'''.
* Accident Claims: '''3%'''.

== Policy Issues & Challenges ==
1. '''Resistance from the Bar Association:''' Lawyers initially opposed the Multi-Door concept out of concern for losing litigation fee income. The AMDC addressed this through workshops and ongoing education.
2. '''Voluntary Non-Attendance:''' Some parties refuse to appear at the AMDC. To address this, the AMDC has proposed adopting English jurisprudence (*Dunnett v. Railtrack*) in the form of cost sanctions for parties who unreasonably refuse ADR.

== Reform & Efficiency Outcomes ==
* '''Success Rate:''' The AMDC has recorded a 70% settlement rate, with 50% resolved at the pre-session stage, cutting case resolution time from '''3 months to 1 month'''.
* '''Legal Validity:''' Mediated agreements are endorsed by an ADR Judge as legally binding consent judgments.

'''Causes of Reflection on the Use of AI in Civil Justice''' (Indonesian: ''Kerangka Kebijakan Penggunaan Kecerdasan Buatan, Peradilan Prediktif, dan Batas Konstitusional Motivasi Putusan Perdata'') is an analytical framework covering digital civil procedure, personal data protection, and constitutional law formulated by Giuliana Amore and Maria Margherita Lazzara. It evaluates the application of artificial intelligence (AI) and predictive justice software within civil proceedings, analyzing the friction between big data processing and General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) principles (transparency, data minimization, and the prohibition of purely automated decision-making under Article 22 GDPR). Furthermore, it asserts the mandatory constitutional duty to provide judicial reasoning for civil sentences under Articles 24 and 111 of the Italian Constitution in conjunction with the EU AI Act, ensuring that judicial adjudication remains under human command (human-in-the-loop) <ref>Amore, G., & Lazzara, M.M. (2024). Causes of Reflection on the Use of AI in Civil Justice. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 10(1–2), 535–550.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Co-authored by [[Giuliana Amore]] (Associate Professor of Private Law) and [[Maria Margherita Lazzara]] (Assistant Professor of Business Law) at the [[University of Catania]], this study offers a critical reflection on integrating AI technologies and predictive justice software into civil procedure <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pp. 535, 536.</ref>. The authors establish that while AI tools offer administrative efficiency and speed up dispute resolution, they must never replace human judges ("robot judges") <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pp. 537, 543.</ref>. Judicial reasoning in hard cases requires moral evaluation, societal awareness, and equity—qualities that stochastic algorithms inherently lack <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), p. 544.</ref>. Consequently, the authors advocate for a complementary collaborative model where AI serves strictly as an advisory or assisting tool under human supervision <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pp. 543, 549, 550.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''[[Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana]]''':
** ''Article 24'': Constitutional Guarantee of the Right to Defense <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), p. 543.</ref>.
** ''Article 111'': Right to Due Process and Mandatory Judicial Reasoning (Motivation) for all Court Rulings <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pp. 543, 544.</ref>.
** ''Codice di Procedura Civile (CPC) Articles 46 & 121'': Technical Rules for Electronic Document Drafting and AI Integration Validity <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), p. 549.</ref>.
* '''European Union & Supranational Law''':
** ''General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR - Regulation EU 2016/679)'': Article 6 (Lawfulness of Processing) and Article 22 (Prohibition of Solely Automated Individual Decision-Making) <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pp. 536, 543.</ref>.
** ''European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (Proposal COM(2021) 206 final)'': Annex III Point 8 & Article 40 (Classification of Judicial AI Systems as High-Risk AI) <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), p. 543.</ref>.
** ''European Ethical Charter on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Judicial Systems (CEPEJ 2018)'' <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), p. 535.</ref>.
** ''European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR)'': Article 6 (Right to a Fair Trial & Transparent Judgments) <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), p. 543.</ref>.

== Key Policy Provisions & Core Pillars ==
1. '''Data Protection & Anonymization of Rulings''': Massive harvesting of judicial data must adhere to GDPR data minimization and transparency rules. To prevent the commercialization and internet indexing of personal data, generalized anonymization of published court decisions is recommended <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pp. 539, 548.</ref>.
2. '''Constitutional Limits on Judicial Reasoning''': Human adjudication cannot be delegated to machines. Because AI operates on past statistical correlations, it risks perpetuating historical biases and lacks the capacity for evolutionary legal interpretation <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pp. 544, 549.</ref>.
3. '''High-Risk Classification & Human Oversight''': Aligned with the EU AI Act, judicial assist systems must undergo ex-ante conformity assessments and remain under strict human-in-command supervision to safeguard procedural rights <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pp. 543, 550.</ref>.

'''Causes of Reflection on the Use of AI in Civil Justice''' (in italiano: ''Quadro Politico sull'Uso dell'Intelligenza Artificiale, Giustizia Predittiva e Limiti Costituzionali della Motivazione della Sentenza Civile'') è un quadro di analisi di diritto processuale civile, protezione dei dati personali e diritto costituzionale formulato da Giuliana Amore e Maria Margherita Lazzara. Lo studio valuta l'impiego dell'intelligenza artificiale (IA) e dei software di giustizia predittiva nel processo civile, analizzando il contrasto tra il trattamento di dati massivi (big data) e i principi del GDPR (trasparenza, minimizzazione dei dati e divieto di decisioni automatizzate esclusive ai sensi dell'Articolo 22 GDPR). Inoltre, ribadisce l'obbligo costituzionale di motivazione della sentenza civile ai sensi degli Articoli 24 e 111 della Costituzione Italiana in combinato disposto con l'EU AI Act, garantendo che il sistema giudiziario rimanga sotto la supervisione e il controllo umano (*human-in-command / human-in-the-loop*) <ref>Amore, G., & Lazzara, M.M. (2024). Causes of Reflection on the Use of AI in Civil Justice. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 10(1–2), 535–550.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Redatto da [[Giuliana Amore]] (Professoressa Associata di Diritto Privato) e [[Maria Margherita Lazzara]] (Ricercatrice di Diritto Commerciale) presso l'[[Università degli Studi di Catania]], l'articolo offre una riflessione critica sull'integrazione delle tecnologie di IA e della giustizia predittiva nel diritto processuale civile <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pagg. 535, 536.</ref>. Le autrici evidenziano che, sebbene i sistemi automatizzati offrano vantaggi in termini di efficienza ed erogazione dei servizi, l'IA non deve in alcun caso sostituire la funzione giudicante del giudice umano (*robot judge*) <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pagg. 537, 543.</ref>. Il ragionamento giuridico nei casi complessi (*hard cases*) richiede valutazioni morali, coscienza sociale ed equità, aspetti estranei agli algoritmi probabilistici <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pag. 544.</ref>. Pertanto, le autrici propongono un modello collaborativo complementare in cui l'IA funzioni esclusivamente come strumento di supporto o ausilio sotto lo stretto controllo umano <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pagg. 543, 549, 550.</ref>.

== Base Giuridica ==
* '''[[Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana]]''':
** ''Articolo 24'': Garanzia del Diritto di Difesa <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pag. 543.</ref>.
** ''Articolo 111'': Garanzia del Giusto Processo e Obbligo di Motivazione dei Provvedimenti Giurisdizionali <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pagg. 543, 544.</ref>.
** ''Codice di Procedura Civile (Articoli 46 e 121)'': Norme tecniche per la redazione degli atti elettronici e integrazione dell'IA <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pag. 549.</ref>.
* '''Diritto dell'Unione Europea e Supranazionale''':
** ''General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR / Reg. UE 2016/679)'': Articolo 6 e Articolo 22 (divieto di sottoporsi a decisioni basate unicamente sul trattamento automatizzato) <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pagg. 536, 543.</ref>.
** ''EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Proposta COM(2021) 206 final)'': Allegato III Punto 8 e Articolo 40 (classificazione dei sistemi di IA giudiziari come *High-Risk AI Systems*) <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pag. 543.</ref>.
** ''Carta Etica Europea sull'Uso dell'Intelligenza Artificiale nei Sistemi Giudiziari (CEPEJ 2018)'' <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pag. 535.</ref>.
** ''Convenzione Europea dei Diritti dell'Uomo (CEDU)'': Articolo 6 (Diritto a un Giusto Processo) <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pag. 543.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Principali e Pilastri dell'Analisi ==
1. '''Protezione dei Dati e Anonimizzazione delle Sentenze''': La raccolta di dati giudiziari deve conformarsi ai principi di minimizzazione e trasparenza del GDPR. Onde evitare la mercificazione dei dati personali e l'indicizzazione selvaggia su Internet, si raccomanda l'anonimizzazione generalizzata delle sentenze pubblicate <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pagg. 539, 548.</ref>.
2. '''Limiti Costituzionali della Motivazione''': La decisione giudiziale non può essere delegata alle macchine. Poiché l'IA opera sulla base di correlazioni statistiche del passato, essa rischia di perpetuare pregiudizi storici ed è priva di capacità d'interpretazione evolutiva del diritto <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pagg. 544, 549.</ref>.
3. '''Classificazione ad Alto Rischio e Controllo Umano''': In linea con l'EU AI Act, i sistemi di IA giudiziaria devono essere sottoposti a valutazioni di conformità ex ante e rimanere costantemente sotto la direzione e supervisione umana per tutelare le garanzie processuali <ref>Amore & Lazzara (2024), pagg. 543, 550.</ref>.
