'''Policy Framework on Indigenous Sovereignty and Land/Energy Law in the Low-Carbon Transition: Analysis of the Osage Wind Judgement''' (official title: ''Indigenous Sovereignty in the Low-Carbon Transition: Reflections on the Osage Wind Judgement'') is a comparative legal analysis and legal pluralism policy framework formulated by Giuseppe Bellantuono and published in ''The Italian Law Journal'' (Vol. 10 Nos. 01-02/2024, pp. 451–468).<ref>Bellantuono, G. (2024). Indigenous Sovereignty in the Low-Carbon Transition: Reflections on the Osage Wind Judgement. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 10(1-2), 451–468.</ref> The work examines the legal dispute in ''Osage Wind'' in Oklahoma (US District Court N.D. Okla. 2023 / 10th Cir. 2017) between the Osage Minerals Council (OMC) and Osage Wind LLC / Enel Green Power North America;<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 451, 453, 454.</ref> analyzes the application of the Indian canon of interpretation;<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 451, 454, 455.</ref> evaluates contradictions within three-tiered sovereignty (Federal, State, and Tribal) following the US Supreme Court rulings in ''McGirt v. Oklahoma'' (2020) and ''Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta'' (2022);<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 451, 456, 458.</ref> dissects the split-estates land regime under the Osage Allotment Act of 1906;<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 452, 453.</ref> and assesses the integration of Indigenous knowledge systems within European Union climate policies (such as the Critical Raw Materials Act and Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive) and international frameworks.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 461, 465, 466, 467.</ref>

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Giuseppe Bellantuono]] (Professor of Comparative Law at the [[University of Trento]]), this study analyzes how Indigenous sovereignty and legal pluralism impact the speed and fairness of the low-carbon energy transition.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 451, 452.</ref> Taking as its central case study the US federal court judgment ordering the ejection and removal of Enel Green Power's multi-million-dollar wind farm built on Osage Nation land without a required mineral extraction lease,<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 451, 453, 454.</ref> the author explores the application of the Indian canon of statutory interpretation,<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 454, 455.</ref> jurisdictional tensions across federal, state, and tribal governments post-''McGirt'' and ''Castro-Huerta'',<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 456–458.</ref> and new European Union legislative acts including the ''Critical Raw Materials Act 2024'' and ''CSDDD 2024'' requiring Indigenous rights compliance in green projects.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 466, 467.</ref>

== Legal Basis ==
* '''United States Legislation & Case Law''':
** ''Osage Allotment Act of 1906 (34 Stat. 539)'': Separation of surface land ownership from subsurface mineral rights held in trust for the Osage Nation.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 452, 453.</ref>
** ''Federal Court Judgments'': ''United States & Osage Minerals Council v. Osage Wind et al.'' (N.D. Okla. 2023 / 871 F.3d 1078 (10th Cir. 2017)).<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 451, 454, 455.</ref>
** ''US Supreme Court Jurisprudence'': ''McGirt v. Oklahoma'', 140 S. Ct. 2452 (2020);<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 456.</ref> ''Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta'', 142 S. Ct. 2486 (2022);<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 458.</ref> ''Montana v. United States'', 450 U.S. 544 (1981);<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 456.</ref> ''Osage Nation v. Irby'', 597 F.3d 1117 (10th Cir. 2010).<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 453.</ref>
** ''US Federal Policies & Executive Actions'': Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (Direct Pay clean energy tax credits for tribal governments);<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 460.</ref> Tribal Energy Development Organization (TEDO 2018);<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 460.</ref> OSTP/CEQ Memoranda (2021/2022) & Executive Order 14096 (2023) on Indigenous Knowledge.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 461.</ref>
* '''European Union & International Law''':
** ''EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1252)'': Consultation obligations and impact mitigation for Indigenous communities.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 466.</ref>
** ''EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD / Directive (EU) 2024/1760)'': Mandatory human rights and Indigenous rights due diligence.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 467.</ref>
** ''UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) & IPCC 6th Assessment Report (2022)''.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 464, 465.</ref>

== Core Policy Analysis ==
1. '''Split Estates & Mining Qualification''': Excavation of limestone and rock for wind turbine foundations constitutes a "mining" operation under the Osage Allotment Act of 1906, requiring an explicit lease from the Osage Minerals Council (OMC).<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 452, 453, 454.</ref>
2. '''Application of the Indian Canon of Interpretation''': Statutory ambiguities involving tribal property rights must be broadly construed in favor of Indigenous sovereignty and tribal interests.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 454, 455, 457.</ref>
3. '''Transition from Asymmetric to Cooperative Legal Pluralism''': Achieving a fast and fair low-carbon transition requires moving away from developer disregard of tribal sovereignty toward co-stewardship, co-management, and recognition of Indigenous Knowledge Systems.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 461, 462, 467, 468.</ref>

== Related Entities ==
* '''[[Giuseppe Bellantuono]]''': Lead Author and Professor of Comparative Law at the [[University of Trento]].<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 451.</ref>
* '''[[Osage Nation]]''': Indigenous nation holding subsurface mineral rights in the Osage Wind dispute.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 452, 453.</ref>
* '''[[Enel]]''': Major energy developer behind Osage Wind LLC through Enel Green Power North America.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 453, 464.</ref>
* '''[[European Union]]''': Issuing authority of the Critical Raw Materials Act and CSDDD.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 466, 467.</ref>
* '''Cecep Mustafa''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]''<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 451–468.</ref>

Il '''Quadro Politico-Giuridico sulla Sovranità Indigena e Diritto Fondiario/Energetico nella Transizione Ecologica: Analisi della Sentenza Osage Wind''' (titolo originale: ''Indigenous Sovereignty in the Low-Carbon Transition: Reflections on the Osage Wind Judgement'') è un quadro di analisi giuridico-comparata e pluralismo giuridico formulato da Giuseppe Bellantuono e pubblicato in ''The Italian Law Journal'' (Vol. 10 Nos. 01-02/2024, pp. 451–468).<ref>Bellantuono, G. (2024). Indigenous Sovereignty in the Low-Carbon Transition: Reflections on the Osage Wind Judgement. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 10(1-2), 451–468.</ref> L'opera analizza la controversia giudiziaria ''Osage Wind'' in Oklahoma (US District Court N.D. Okla. 2023 / 10th Cir. 2017) tra l'Osage Minerals Council (OMC) e Osage Wind LLC / Enel Green Power North America;<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 451, 453, 454.</ref> analizza l'applicazione del canone di interpretazione indiano (''Indian canon of interpretation'');<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 451, 454, 455.</ref> valuta le contraddizioni della sovranità a tre livelli (Federale, Statale e Tribale) a seguito delle sentenze della Corte Suprema degli Stati Uniti ''McGirt v. Oklahoma'' (2020) e ''Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta'' (2022);<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 451, 456, 458.</ref> esamina il regime dei diritti di proprietà separati (''split estates'') ai sensi dell'Osage Allotment Act del 1906;<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 452, 453.</ref> ed esamina l'integrazione dei sistemi di conoscenza indigena (''Indigenous knowledge systems'') nelle politiche climatiche dell'Unione Europea (Critical Raw Materials Act e Direttiva CSDDD) e internazionali.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 461, 465, 466, 467.</ref>

== Sintesi ==
Redatto da [[Giuseppe Bellantuono]] (Professore Ordinario di Diritto Comparato presso l'[[Università di Trento]]), questo studio analizza l'impatto della sovranità indigena e del pluralismo giuridico sulla velocità e sull'equità della transizione energetica.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 451, 452.</ref> Utilizzando come caso di studio principale la sentenza della corte federale statunitense che ha ordinato la rimozione del parco eolico di Enel Green Power costruito sul territorio della Osage Nation senza la previa concessione mineraria,<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 451, 453, 454.</ref> l'autore approfondisce l'applicazione dell'''Indian canon of interpretation'',<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 454, 455.</ref> le tensioni giurisdizionali tra governi federali, statali e tribali post-''McGirt'' e ''Castro-Huerta'',<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 456–458.</ref> e i nuovi atti normativi dell'Unione Europea tra cui il ''Critical Raw Materials Act 2024'' e la Direttiva ''CSDDD 2024''.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 466, 467.</ref>

== Basi Giuridiche ==
* '''Legislazione e Giurisprudenza degli Stati Uniti''':
** ''Osage Allotment Act del 1906'': Regime di separazione dei diritti di superficie da quelli minerari sottostanti.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 452, 453.</ref>
** ''Sentenze delle Corti Federali Statunitensi'': ''United States & Osage Minerals Council v. Osage Wind et al.'' (N.D. Okla. 2023 / 10th Cir. 2017).<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 451, 454, 455.</ref>
** ''Giurisprudenza della Corte Suprema USA'': ''McGirt v. Oklahoma'' (2020);<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 456.</ref> ''Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta'' (2022);<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 458.</ref> ''Montana v. United States'' (1981);<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 456.</ref> ''Osage Nation v. Irby'' (2010).<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 453.</ref>
** ''Politiche Federali e Atti Esecutivi USA'': Inflation Reduction Act del 2022 (crediti d'imposta ''Direct Pay'' per i governi tribali);<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 460.</ref> Tribal Energy Development Organization (TEDO 2018);<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 460.</ref> Direttive OSTP/CEQ (2021/2022) ed Ordine Esecutivo 14096 (2023).<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 461.</ref>
* '''Unione Europea e Diritto Internazionale''':
** ''EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Regolamento (UE) 2024/1252)'': Obblighi di consultazione e mitigazione dell'impatto sulle comunità indigene.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 466.</ref>
** ''EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD / Direttiva (UE) 2024/1760)'': Obblighi di dovuta diligenza sui diritti umani e indigeni.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 467.</ref>
** ''Dichiarazione ONU sui Diritti dei Popoli Indigeni (UNDRIP) e VI Rapporto di Valutazione IPCC (2022)''.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 464, 465.</ref>

== Analisi Politico-Giuridica Fondamentale ==
1. '''Regime di Split Estates e Qualificazione dell'Attività Mineraria''': Lo scavo e l'estrazione di roccia calcarea per le fondamenta delle turbine eoliche rientra nella nozione di attività mineraria (''mining'') ai sensi dell'Osage Allotment Act del 1906, richiedendo la previa concessione da parte dell'Osage Minerals Council (OMC).<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 452, 453, 454.</ref>
2. '''Applicazione dell'Indian Canon of Interpretation''': Le ambiguità legislative in materia di diritti di proprietà tribali devono essere interpretate estensivamente a favore della sovranità e degli interessi indigeni.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 454, 455, 457.</ref>
3. '''Transizione dal Pluralismo Asimmetrico al Pluralismo Cooperativo''': La realizzazione di una transizione ecologica rapida ed equa richiede il passaggio dal disconoscimento della sovranità tribale a modelli di gestione condivisa (''co-management'') e al riconoscimento delle conoscenze ecologiche indigene.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 461, 462, 467, 468.</ref>

== Entità Correlate ==
* '''[[Giuseppe Bellantuono]]''': Autore principale e Professore Ordinario di Diritto Comparato presso l'[[Università di Trento]].<ref>Bellantuono (2024), p. 451.</ref>
* '''[[Osage Nation]]''': Nazione indigena titolare dei diritti minerari nella controversia Osage Wind.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 452, 453.</ref>
* '''[[Enel]]''': Gruppo energetico sviluppatore del progetto Osage Wind tramite Enel Green Power North America.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 453, 464.</ref>
* '''[[Unione Europea]]''': Autorità emittente del Critical Raw Materials Act e della Direttiva CSDDD.<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 466, 467.</ref>
* '''Cecep Mustafa''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Non presente nelle fonti disponibili.]]''<ref>Bellantuono (2024), pp. 451–468.</ref>

'''Legal Policy Framework for Sustainable Business Organizations''' (''Some Backdrops and Prospective Scenarios About the Emerging 'Law of Sustainable Business Organizations' '') is a comparative and interdisciplinary business law analysis framework formulated by Maurizio Bianchini in *The Italian Law Journal* (Vol. 10 Nos. 01-02/2024, pp. 297–343) <ref>Bianchini, M. (2024). Some Backdrops and Prospective Scenarios About the Emerging 'Law of Sustainable Business Organizations'. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 10(1-2), 297–343.</ref>. It maps the emergence of a new legal discipline titled *Law of Sustainable Business Organizations*, reconceptualizing the relationship between "sustainability" and the "corporation/company" <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 297, 298, 308.</ref>; analyzes the regulatory paradigm shift from voluntary Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR voluntary approach) to mandatory compliance (mandatory ESG regulatory approach) <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 297, 304, 305.</ref>; dissects the concept of "double materiality" and ESG risk management <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 327, 328.</ref>; evaluates the doctrine of the corporate entity as a cost-externalizing machine <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 298, 309, 316.</ref>; and details the integration of the organizational adequacy principle (''assetti organizzativi adeguati'') under Article 2086 of the Italian Civil Code with the ''Caremark'' director oversight doctrine from Delaware/US <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 329, 330, 331, 332, 335.</ref>.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Maurizio Bianchini]] (Associate Professor of Business Law at the University of Padova), this work provides a theoretical and pragmatic construction regarding the establishment of a new legal field: the *Law of Sustainable Business Organizations* <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 297, 298.</ref>. The author explains that the modern for-profit corporation has historically operated as a device for externalizing environmental and social costs to maximize short-term financial returns (short-termism) <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 298, 309, 316.</ref>. However, under the pressures of the global climate crisis, planetary boundaries, and the UN 2030 Agenda (17 SDGs), global business law is transitioning from voluntary CSR models toward mandatory hard law regimes anchored in double materiality <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 304, 305, 327.</ref>.

In Italy, this evolution is reinforced by the 2022 Constitutional Reform of Articles 9 and 41, alongside the statutory duty of directors under Article 2086(2) of the Civil Code to maintain adequate organizational structures (''assetti adeguati'') to detect risks and ensure business continuity <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 328, 330, 331, 332.</ref>. Internationally, this connects with Delaware’s ''Caremark'' oversight doctrine, EU CSRD and CSDDD directives, and the German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act (LkSG) <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 331, 333, 336.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Italian Constitutional & Civil Legislation''':
** ''Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana'': Articles 9 & 41 (2022 Sustainability Amendments) <ref>Bianchini (2024), p. 328.</ref>.
** ''Codice Civile Italiano'': Article 2082 (Entrepreneurial Economic Method), Article 2086(2) (Adequate Organizational Structures), Article 2247 (Profit Purpose), Articles 2381, 2403, 2475, 2392–2395 (Directors' Duties & Liabilities) <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 309, 310, 330, 331.</ref>.
** ''Codice della Crisi d'Impresa e dell'Insolvenza (D.Lgs. 14/2019)'': Article 3 <ref>Bianchini (2024), p. 332.</ref>.
** ''Special Italian Legislation'': Benefit Corporations / ''Società Benefit'' (Law 208/2015), Social Enterprise (D.Lgs. 112/2017), Third Sector Code (D.Lgs. 117/2017) <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 339, 340.</ref>.
* '''European Union Directives & Regulations''':
** ''Treaty on European Union (TEU)'': Articles 2 & 3 <ref>Bianchini (2024), p. 300.</ref>.
** ''Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD / Directive (EU) 2022/2464)'' & ''European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS)'' <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 327, 333.</ref>.
** ''Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD / Enacted May 2024)'' <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 307, 333, 336.</ref>.
** ''EU Taxonomy Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2020/852)'' & ''SFDR (Regulation (EU) 2019/2088)'' <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 332, 333.</ref>.
** ''General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR / Regulation (EU) 2016/679)'': Article 4(18) <ref>Bianchini (2024), p. 308.</ref>.
* '''International Guidelines & Jurisprudence''':
** ''UN 2030 Agenda (17 SDGs)'' & ''UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (Ruggie Principles 2011)'' <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 300, 306.</ref>.
** ''OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct (2023 Edition)'' <ref>Bianchini (2024), p. 306.</ref>.
** ''Delaware Jurisprudence'': ''In re Caremark'' (1996), ''Marchand v. Barnhill'' (2019), and ''In re McDonald's Corp.'' (2023) <ref>Bianchini (2024), p. 331.</ref>.
** ''Climate Litigation'': ''Shell Litigation'' (Netherlands/UK 2021–2023) <ref>Bianchini (2024), p. 335.</ref>.

== Core Pillars of Policy Analysis ==
# '''Double Materiality & Mandatory Transition''': ESG regulations mandate a two-way assessment: financial materiality (how ESG factors impact corporate financial value) and impact materiality (how corporate operations impact environmental and human rights systems) <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 304, 327, 328.</ref>.
# '''Integration of Organizational Adequacy and Duty to Monitor''': Directors are required to set up adequate organizational, administrative, and accounting frameworks (''assetti adeguati'') to monitor ESG risks across value chains. Failure of risk-monitoring systems removes protection under the Business Judgment Rule (BJR) <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 330, 331, 334, 335.</ref>.
# '''Compelling Legal Limits on Enterprise Freedom''': Sustainability is no longer a mere voluntary choice or corporate branding tool, but a compelling legal boundary established by statutes and constitutional norms, restricting pure profit maximization without publicizing the enterprise <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 309, 337, 338, 342.</ref>.

== Entity Relationships ==
* '''[[Maurizio Bianchini]]''': Author & Associate Professor at the University of Padova <ref>Bianchini (2024), p. 297.</ref>.
* '''[[European Union]]''': Enacting authority for CSRD, ESRS, Taxonomy, and CSDDD frameworks <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 307, 322, 333.</ref>.
* '''[[Delaware Court of Chancery]]''': Judicial originator of the Caremark duty to monitor doctrine <ref>Bianchini (2024), p. 331.</ref>.
* '''[[OECD]]''': Developer of the Multinational Enterprises Guidelines for Responsible Business Conduct <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 306, 325.</ref>.

Il '''Quadro di Politica Giuridica del Diritto delle Organizzazioni d'Impresa Sostenibili''' (''Some Backdrops and Prospective Scenarios About the Emerging 'Law of Sustainable Business Organizations' '') è un quadro analitico comparato e interdisciplinare di diritto commerciale formulato da Maurizio Bianchini in *The Italian Law Journal* (Vol. 10 Nos. 01-02/2024, pp. 297–343) <ref>Bianchini, M. (2024). Some Backdrops and Prospective Scenarios About the Emerging 'Law of Sustainable Business Organizations'. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 10(1-2), 297–343.</ref>. L'opera mappa la nascita della nuova disciplina intitolata *Law of Sustainable Business Organizations*, riconcettualizzando il rapporto tra "sostenibilità" e "società/impresa" <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 297, 298, 308.</ref>; analizza il passaggio dal regime di responsabilità sociale volontaria (CSR voluntary approach) alla conformità normativa obbligatoria (mandatory ESG regulatory approach) <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 297, 304, 305.</ref>; esamina il principio della "doppia materialità" (double materiality) e la gestione dei rischi ESG <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 327, 328.</ref>; valuta la dottrina della società commerciale come macchina di esternalizzazione dei costi sociali <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 298, 309, 316.</ref>; e delinea l'integrazione del principio degli adeguati assetti organizzativi in Italia (Art. 2086 c.c.) con la dottrina del dovere di controllo degli amministratori (*Caremark*) del Delaware/USA <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 329, 330, 331, 332, 335.</ref>.

== Sintesi Generale ==
Scritto da [[Maurizio Bianchini]] (Professore Associato di Diritto Commerciale presso l'Università degli Studi di Padova), questo studio fornisce una costruzione teorica e pragmatica sull'affermazione del nuovo ramo del diritto denominato *Law of Sustainable Business Organizations* <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 297, 298.</ref>. L'autore evidenzia come l'impresa lucrativa moderna sia stata storicamente concepita come uno strumento di esternalizzazione dei costi ambientali e sociali per perseguire profitti finanziari a breve termine (short-termism) <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 298, 309, 316.</ref>. Tuttavia, di fronte alla crisi climatica globale, ai limiti planetari e agli Obiettivi di Sviluppo Sostenibile dell'ONU (SDGs 2030), il diritto commerciale sta evolvendo da modelli CSR volontari verso un regime cogente basato sulla doppia materialità <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 304, 305, 327.</ref>.

In Italia, questo passaggio trova fondamento nella Riforma Costituzionale del 2022 (Artt. 9 e 41) e nell'obbligo codicistico per gli amministratori (Art. 2086, comma 2, c.c.) di istituire assetti organizzativi, amministrativi e contabili adeguati per rilevare tempestivamente i rischi e preservare la continuità aziendale <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 328, 330, 331, 332.</ref>. A livello internazionale, la disciplina si connette con la dottrina del dovere di monitoraggio *Caremark* negli Stati Uniti, le direttive UE CSRD e CSDDD, e la legge tedesca sulla due diligence nelle catene di fornitura (LkSG) <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 331, 333, 336.</ref>.

== Fonti Normative e Fondamenti Giuridici ==
* '''Legislazione Italiana (Costituzione e Codice Civile)''':
** ''Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana'': Articoli 9 e 41 (Riforma della Sostenibilità 2022) <ref>Bianchini (2024), p. 328.</ref>.
** ''Codice Civile Italiano'': Art. 2082 (Imprenditore), Art. 2086(2) (Assetti Organizzativi Adeguati), Art. 2247 (Scopo di Lucro), Artt. 2381, 2403, 2475, 2392–2395 (Responsabilità degli Amministratori) <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 309, 310, 330, 331.</ref>.
** ''Codice della Crisi d'Impresa e dell'Insolvenza (D.Lgs. 14/2019)'': Articolo 3 <ref>Bianchini (2024), p. 332.</ref>.
** ''Normativa Speciale'': Società Benefit (Legge 208/2015), Impresa Sociale (D.Lgs. 112/2017), Codice del Terzo Settore (D.Lgs. 117/2017) <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 339, 340.</ref>.
* '''Direttive e Regolamenti dell'Unione Europea''':
** ''Trattato sull'Unione Europea (TUE)'': Articoli 2 e 3 <ref>Bianchini (2024), p. 300.</ref>.
** ''Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD / Direttiva (UE) 2022/2464)'' e ''European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS)'' <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 327, 333.</ref>.
** ''Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD / Approvata nel Maggio 2024)'' <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 307, 333, 336.</ref>.
** ''Regolamento Tassonomia (Regolamento (UE) 2020/852)'' e ''SFDR (Regolamento (UE) 2019/2088)'' <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 332, 333.</ref>.
* '''Linee Guida Internazionali e Giurisprudenza''':
** ''Agenda ONU 2030 (17 SDGs)'' e ''Principi Guida delle Nazioni Unite su Imprese e Diritti Umani (Ruggie Principles 2011)'' <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 300, 306.</ref>.
** ''Linee Guida OCSE per le Imprese Multinazionali sulla Condotta D'Impresa Responsabile (Edizione 2023)'' <ref>Bianchini (2024), p. 306.</ref>.
** ''Giurisprudenza del Delaware'': ''In re Caremark'' (1996), ''Marchand v. Barnhill'' (2019), e ''In re McDonald's Corp.'' (2023) <ref>Bianchini (2024), p. 331.</ref>.
** ''Contenzioso Climatico'': ''Shell Litigation'' (Paesi Bassi/UK 2021–2023) <ref>Bianchini (2024), p. 335.</ref>.

== Pilastri Fondamentali dell'Analisi ==
# '''Doppia Materialità e Transizione Normativa''': La regolamentazione ESG impone una valutazione a due vie: la materialità finanziaria (impatto dei fattori ESG sul valore aziendale) e la materialità d'impatto (impatto dell'attività d'impresa sull'ambiente e sui diritti umani) <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 304, 327, 328.</ref>.
# '''Adeguati Assetti Organizzativi e Dovere di Controllo (Oversight Duty)''': Gli amministratori hanno l'obbligo di predisporre assetti organizzativi idonei a rilevare e gestire i rischi ESG lungo l'intera catena del valore. La mancanza di un sistema di monitoraggio adeguato esclude la protezione della Business Judgment Rule (BJR) <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 330, 331, 334, 335.</ref>.
# '''Limiti Legali alla Libertà d'Iniziative Economica''': La sostenibilità non costituisce più una mera scelta etica o promozionale, ma un limite giuridico vincolante imposto dalla Costituzione e dalle leggi, che perimetra l'esercizio dell'attività d'impresa senza snaturarne la natura privata <ref>Bianchini (2024), pp. 309, 337, 338, 342.</ref>.

{{Infobox
| stable_id = judicial-policy-boehmelt-populism-2022
| name = Populism and intra-party democracy
| type = Comparative Political Science Research Paper & Party Organization Analysis
| issuing_authority = Tobias Böhmelt, Lawrence Ezrow & Roni Lehrer / University of Essex & University of Mannheim / EJPR
| legal_basis = Not found in the available sources.
| date = November 2022
| status = Published / Active
}}

'''Populism and intra-party democracy''' is an empirical comparative political science and public policy research paper authored by Tobias Böhmelt (University of Essex), Lawrence Ezrow (University of Essex), and Roni Lehrer (University of Mannheim & Goethe University Frankfurt), published in the ''European Journal of Political Research'' (EJPR) in 2022.

== Summary ==
This study examines how populism relates to the internal organization of political parties, specifically intra-party democracy (IPD). Using data from the Populism and Political Parties Expert Survey (POPPA; Meijers & Zaslove, 2021), covering more than 200 political parties across 26 European countries (2017/2018), the study tests two competing theoretical approaches: the ideational perspective, which predicts that populist parties will be more internally democratic, and the leadership/organizational perspective, which predicts the opposite. The findings show that '''populist parties systematically have less democratic internal structures and tend to adopt personalized leadership styles''' [1, 9, 17–21].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This document is an academic political science research study and is not based on any specific statutory or judicial legislative instrument [1–55].

== Background ==
Populism has become a central topic in the media, academia, and policymaking across Europe. Political science literature is divided into two main views on populism: the ideational view, which defines populism as a thin-centered ideology built around anti-elitism and people-centrism, and the leadership view, which defines populism as a personalistic political-organizational strategy. Large-scale quantitative research was needed to test whether populism's ideological claims about "people-power" are actually reflected in parties' internal structures.

== Objectives ==
1. Test whether a party's populism score is positively or negatively associated with its level of intra-party democracy.
2. Test the effect of populism on personalized leadership.
3. Analyze whether the effect of populism on party organization differs between left-wing and right-wing parties.

== Scope ==
The research analyzes POPPA expert survey data (2017/2018) covering 229 to 236 political parties across 26 to 28 European countries represented in parliament.

== Key Provisions / Findings ==
* '''Decline in Intra-Party Democracy (IPD):''' The populism score has a statistically significant negative association with intra-party democracy (β = -0.43, p < 0.05) [17–19]. Moving from the lowest to the highest level of populism reduces the predicted IPD score from ~7 to ~2 on a 0–10 scale.
* '''Increase in Personalized Leadership:''' The populism score has a statistically significant positive association with personalized leadership (β = +0.38, p < 0.05) [21–25].
* '''Left-Wing vs. Right-Wing Comparison:''' The negative relationship between populism and intra-party democracy holds for both left-wing and right-wing parties (β = -0.33, p < 0.05 for left-wing parties). However, left-wing populist parties are generally somewhat more internally inclusive than right-wing populists, owing to a more inclusive view of society.
* '''Support for the Leadership Perspective:''' These findings directly confirm the predictions of the leadership perspective (Weyland 2001, 2021; Kenny 2019; Pappas 2016; Urbinati 2017) and reject the assumption that populist ideology automatically produces democratic party organization.

== Implementation ==
The methodology was implemented through hierarchical linear models with random intercepts for country and party family, controlling for median voter position (Eurobarometer). Replication data are sourced from the POPPA project (Meijers & Zaslove, 2021).

== Policy Issues ==
1. The contradiction between populist parties' public rhetoric celebrating "the voice of the people" and their authoritarian, centralized internal practices.
2. The risk of power concentration in charismatic leaders, which reduces internal party accountability.

== Reform / Implications ==
1. Incorporating indicators of internal party organizational structure into models of coalition formation, cabinet portfolio allocation, and party survival.
2. Recognizing that undemocratic organizational structures may be strategically adopted by populist parties to project an image of party unity to voters.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''University of Essex, University of Mannheim & Goethe University Frankfurt:''' Home institutions of the authors.
* '''European Consortium for Political Research (ECPR) & John Wiley & Sons Ltd.:''' Publisher of the EJPR journal.
* '''POPPA Project (Meijers & Zaslove, 2021):''' Provider of expert survey data.
* '''Cecep Mustafa:''' Not found in the available sources [1–55].
* '''[private person]:''' Not found in the available sources [1–55].

* [[European Consortium for Political Research]]

| type = Comparative Political Science Research Paper & Electoral Geography Analysis
| issuing_authority = Sophie Borwein et al. / University of British Columbia / EJPR
| legal_basis = Not found in the available sources.
| date = 2025
| status = Published / Active
}}

'''Urban–rural policy disagreement''' is an empirical comparative political science and public policy research paper authored by Sophie Borwein (University of British Columbia), Jack Lucas (University of Calgary), Tyler Romualdi, Zack Taylor, David A. Armstrong II, and Katharine McCoy (University of Western Ontario), published in the ''European Journal of Political Research'' (EJPR) in 2025.

== Summary ==
This study tests whether the sharpening urban–rural electoral divide since the 1990s is driven by widening disagreement over public policy preferences between urban and rural residents. Based on a synthesized dataset covering 456 unique policy issue questions (asked 973 times) drawn from 10 Canadian Election Study surveys (1993–2021), totaling N = 5.3 million individual-level responses, the study finds that although urban and rural residents hold genuinely large disagreements on cultural policy issues (such as gun control, immigration, and Indigenous affairs), '''the urban–rural policy issue divide has not widened at all over the past 30 years'''. Consequently, growing policy disagreement cannot explain the widening urban–rural electoral cleavage.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This document is an academic political science research study and is not based on any specific statutory or judicial legislative instrument [1–106].
* '''Canadian Federal Electoral District (FED) Boundaries:''' The study uses a latent district urbanity scale (Armstrong et al., 2022) based on indicators of population density, municipal size, economic diversity, social diversity, and dwelling type.

== Background ==
Since the 1990s, the electoral cleavage between urban and rural areas has re-emerged with growing intensity across North America and Europe. Political scientists frequently assume that this widening electoral gap is driven by diverging policy attitudes and preferences between urban and rural residents. However, earlier studies examined only specific issues at single points in time, without tracking longitudinal trends.

== Objectives ==
1. Test whether urban–rural policy disagreement is greater on cultural issues than on economic issues (Hypothesis 1).
2. Test the "progressive cities hypothesis" — whether urban voters consistently hold more progressive/left-leaning views than rural voters (Hypothesis 2).
3. Test whether the urban–rural policy preference divide has widened over recent decades (Hypothesis 3a vs. Hypothesis 3b).

== Scope ==
The research covers an analysis of 5.3 million responses from 10 Canadian national election surveys (1993–2021), spanning 20 policy topic domains (gun control, immigration, Indigenous affairs, health, social welfare, taxation, foreign trade, and the environment) [1, 5, 35, 37, 42–44].

== Key Provisions / Findings ==
* '''Cultural vs. Economic Issue Divide (Hypothesis 1 Supported):''' More than half (51%) of all policy issue questions show a statistically significant urban–rural divide. The largest divides occur on cultural policy issues (gun control, Indigenous affairs, immigration), while divides on economic and social-welfare issues are considerably smaller.
* '''Support for the Progressive Cities Hypothesis (Hypothesis 2 Supported):''' Urban residents hold progressive/left-leaning views on 75% of all questions and 90% of ideologically divided questions (the sole exception being free trade, due to strong support among highly educated urban workers) [1, 6, 25, 55–58].
* '''Static Nature of the Policy Divide (Hypothesis 3b Supported):''' Across 10 elections (1993–2021), '''the urban–rural policy disagreement gap did not widen at all'''. The estimated time-trend line remains consistently flat across all models (p = 0.84) [59–63, 80].
* '''Substantive Significance:''' The urban–rural policy preference divide proved larger than divides based on university education, gender, or union household membership.

== Implementation ==
The methodology was implemented through 973 separate Bayesian multilevel linear regression models, with dependent and independent variables rescaled to 0–1, along with topic and repeated-question fixed-effects analysis [47, 59–62, 76, 77, 79]. Replication code and data are published openly on Scholars Portal Dataverse at `https://doi.org/10.5683/SP3/YNZMH8`.

== Policy Issues ==
1. The mistaken assumption that geographic political polarization is caused by widening disagreement over public policy preferences.
2. The risk that political elites may exploit cultural issues to stoke place-based resentment for electoral gain.

== Reform / Implications ==
The study recommends that political science shift its focus away from policy issue divergence toward alternative, non-issue mechanisms:
1. '''Affective Place Polarization:''' Rising emotional animosity between urban and rural groups.
2. '''Partisan-Ideological Sorting:''' Urban and rural voters increasingly sorting into parties aligned with pre-existing ideological preferences, without any underlying shift in policy attitudes.
3. '''Strategic Elite Issue Activation:''' The strategic activation of prominent cultural flashpoint issues by political elites.

'''The Illinois Mental Health Courts Policy and Evaluation Framework''' is a specialized judicial (problem-solving/specialty court) policy framework and statewide comprehensive evaluation regarding Mental Health Courts (MHCs) in Illinois. Researched by Arthur J. Lurigio, Monte D. Staton, Shanti J. Raman, and Lorena Roque (2015) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), the framework is based on a 2010–2013 study of 9 operational MHCs (which expanded to 21 by 2014) funded by the ICJIA and the US Department of Justice (BJA). It integrates the principles of therapeutic jurisprudence, the CSG's 10 Essential Elements, cross-disciplinary team approaches, ACA/CountyCare enrollment, and a 4-year recidivism analysis to divert offenders with serious mental illness (PSMI) from prison into community clinical care [1–39].

== Summary ==
Published by Arthur J. Lurigio et al. in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this policy framework presents the first statewide examination of Mental Health Courts (MHCs) in Illinois. Reviewing the expansion from 9 operational MHCs in 2010 to 21 by 2014, the study confirms that the majority of MHCs in Illinois operate in accordance with the CSG's 10 Essential Elements [8, 10, 16–18]. Utilizing a non-adversarial hybrid team approach (comprising judges, prosecutors, public defenders, probation officers, and TASC), MHCs have successfully diverted PSMIs from incarceration [18–20]. A 4-year recidivism analysis of 210 participants demonstrated positive outcomes, with MHC 1 achieving a 70% survival rate free from re-arrest [30–31]. Lurigio et al. recommend the mass enrollment of participants into the ''Affordable Care Act (ACA) / CountyCare'' health insurance schemes to secure continuous funding for treatment [31–32].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''US Bureau of Justice Assistance (BJA) Mental Health Court Program Grant Authorizations:''' The foundation for federal funding and technical guidance for mental health courts.
* '''Council of State Governments (CSG) 10 Essential Elements of a Mental Health Court:''' The standard reference framework for the structure and operation of MHCs [8, 16–18, 21].
* '''Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA) / CountyCare Directives:''' Policies expanding public health insurance to finance the medical/psychiatric care of participants [31–32, 38].
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
The increasing population of people with serious mental illness (PSMI) in prisons spurred the innovation of Mental Health Courts. Based on therapeutic jurisprudence, MHCs aim to break the cycle of repeated incarceration through community medical intervention [2–3].

== Objectives ==
1. Divert offenders with serious mental illness (PSMI) from prison to community treatment facilities.
2. Reduce criminal recidivism rates while improving public safety and the clients' quality of life.
3. Build a flexible and coordinated non-adversarial judicial workgroup model [4, 18–20, 23].
4. Integrate participants into federal health insurance programs (ACA / CountyCare) [31–32].

== Scope ==
This policy encompasses the evaluation of all judicial circuits (23 circuits) in the State of Illinois, with a focus on 9 operational MHCs in urban counties.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Implementation of the CSG 10 Essential Elements:'''
** Requiring voluntary participation (informed consent), pre/post-adjudication referrals, and screening for clinical criteria (Axis I/II & co-occurring disorders) [17–18].
* '''Non-Adversarial Hybrid Team Approach:'''
** Hybrid collaboration between judges, prosecutors, public defenders, probation officers, and TASC (Treatment Alternatives for Safe Communities) case managers [18–20, 23].
* '''Graduated Sanctions and Incentives Scheme:'''
** The use of a ''fish bowl draw'' (e.g., movie tickets/vouchers) for positive behavior, alongside graduated sanctions (from community service to brief jail time) for rule violations.
* '''Application of Evidence-Based Practices (EBPs):'''
** Integration of modules such as Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), Motivational Interviewing, and Supportive Employment [27–28].

== Implementation ==
* '''Operational Growth (2004–2014):''' An increase in operational MHCs in Illinois from 2 programs in 2004 to 21 programs in 2014 [9–10, 14–15].
* '''Integration of ACA/CountyCare Enrollment:''' Active enrollment of MHC participants into health insurance schemes to ensure the continuity of therapy [31–32].

== Policy Problems ==

The '''Judges' Managerial Competencies and Judicial Performance Framework in Brazil''' is a competency-based judicial administration policy framework that evaluates the dual role of judges (adjudication and administration) and measures the influence of judges' managerial competencies on judicial efficiency and performance [2–5, 8–10].

== Summary ==
Published in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (2025) by Borba, Lunardi, and Guimaraes, this framework analyzes the influence of first-instance judges' managerial competencies on the performance of judicial units at the Court of Justice of the State of Minas Gerais (TJMG), Brazil. Using an integrative competency approach, a statistical study of 60 judges and 199 court clerks proved that the application of ''Outcomes-based Management'' and ''Judicial Process Management'' competencies by judges significantly reduces the court congestion rate [24–25, 42–43, 72, 75, 79].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Brazilian Federal Constitution 1988 (Article 99, Paragraph 1)''': Guarantees administrative and financial autonomy for State Courts of Justice.
* '''CNJ Resolution No. 240/2016 (National Council of Justice / CNJ)''': Regulates the implementation of competency-based management across all judicial branch units in Brazil.
* '''CNJ Resolution No. 219/2016''': Regulates the proportional allocation and distribution of personnel and commissioned positions in courts.
* '''Federal Law No. 11.416/2006''': The career law for civil servants of the Union's judicial branch.
* '''TJMG Resolution No. 819/2016''': Establishes the Matrix Management System and the formula for calculating the congestion rate.
* '''TJMG Resolution No. 953/2020''': Standards for the career development of judicial employees in Minas Gerais.

== Background ==
Under the influence of New Public Management, the Brazilian judiciary, which comprises 92 courts and 15,646 judicial units, is demanded to increase efficiency and accountability. First-instance judges bear a ''dual role'': acting as adjudicators while simultaneously serving as operational managers of judicial units overseeing staff, case workflows, and CNJ targets [5, 8–10, 33]. However, this managerial role frequently causes role conflict and role ambiguity due to a lack of structured managerial training [9, 26–27].

== Objectives ==
1. Identify the relevant managerial competency indicators for first-instance judges.
2. Analyze the differences in competency perceptions between judges (self-assessment) and court clerks [3, 39, 44–45].
3. Statistically prove the correlation between judges' managerial competencies and the backlog index and congestion rate [3, 68–70, 71–75].
4. Provide a policy reference for the CNJ and ENFAM in designing managerial training curricula for judges.

== Scope ==
Empirical research was conducted in 176 general jurisdiction courts under the Court of Justice of the State of Minas Gerais (TJMG)—the second-largest state court in Brazil. The sample included 60 judges and 199 court clerks [42–43].

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Integrative Competency Approach''': Combines the French tradition (the ability to mobilize internal/environmental resources) and the American tradition (knowledge, skills, and attitudes), assessed contextually [16, 21, 24–25, 77].
* '''Judges' Managerial Competency Factors (Judges' Perspective - 4 Factors, Variance 62.81%)''' [45–46]:
# ''Resolvability'': The ability to resolve cases quickly through conciliation agreements and accelerating public services.
# ''Outcomes-based Management'': Monitoring delegated tasks, setting targets, holding evaluation meetings, and coordinating with Prosecutors/Lawyers.
# ''Communication'': Encouraging team dialogue, providing feedback, and communicating targets.
# ''Judicial Process Management'': Making decisions directly during hearings and issuing written instructions for clerks.
* '''Judges' Managerial Competency Factors (Clerks' Perspective - 3 Factors, Variance 76.37%)''':
# ''Leadership and Team Management'': Encouraging transformational motivation, humanized leadership, and team unification [57–58].
# ''Judicial Process Management'': Supervising case workflows and eliminating procedural bottlenecks.
# ''Performance Monitoring'': Organizing regular meetings to monitor unit performance.

== Implementation ==
* '''Congestion Rate (CR) Formula''': Evaluated using the formula $CR = \frac{A}{B + A}$, where $A$ is the remaining active cases at year-end and $B$ represents the cases resolved/cleared within 12 months [68–69].
* '''Linear Regression Evidence''': Regression results proved that higher implementation of ''Outcomes-based Management'' by judges corresponds to a lower court congestion rate ($\beta = -0.46, p = 0.006$) [72–74, 79]. Similarly, the clerks' perception of ''Judicial Process Management'' significantly correlated with a reduction in the congestion rate ($\beta = -0.32, p = 0.010$).

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Resource Limitations & Recognition''': Judges complain about the lack of administrative staff and the absence of moral recognition (emotional payoff) from top-level court leadership [54–55, 80].
* '''Ignoring Targets & Senior Clerks''': Clerks reported instances where judges ignored planning meetings or sidelined the expertise of senior clerks.

== Reform / Change ==
* '''Drafting ENFAM/CNJ Training Curricula''': Incorporating modules on outcomes-based management, team leadership, and communication into the initial and ongoing training for judges.
* '''Development of Humanized Management''': Encouraging the CNJ to adopt evaluation indicators that encompass humanization, accessibility, and occupational health criteria (similar to Portugal's ''Programa Justiça Mais Próxima'').

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''National Council of Justice (CNJ)''': The Brazilian judicial oversight body that sets national performance targets.
* '''ENFAM & UnB''': The judicial education institution and the university where the researchers are affiliated.
* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]''': ''Not found in the available sources.'' [FACT] [1–103].

'''The Relationship Between Judicial Staff and Court Performance Policy & Econometric Framework''' is a judicial human resources governance policy and econometric performance evaluation model in Brazil. Formulated by Adalmir de Oliveira Gomes, Tomas de Aquino Guimaraes, and Luiz Akutsu (University of Brasilia) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), Vol. 8 No. 1 (October 2016), it analyzes the impact of the number of judges and legal/support staff (judicial assistants) on court productivity (resolved cases per judge/year). It also examines the moderating effect of staffing on the relationship between caseloads and productivity across 27 Brazilian State Courts from 2003 to 2012 [1–25].

== Summary ==
Published by Gomes, Guimaraes, and Akutsu in the IJCA (October 2016), this policy framework evaluates strategies for increasing judicial staff to overcome the crisis of surging caseloads in Brazil [1–3]. Analyzing 10-year panel data (2003–2012) from 27 Brazilian State Courts (''Justiça Estadual'') sourced from the National Council of Justice's (CNJ) ''Justiça em Números'' reports, the study tests four econometric hypotheses using Fixed Effects panel regression with Panel-Corrected Standard Errors (PCSE) [15, 18–20]. The research proves that hiring additional judicial assistants has a direct, positive impact on court productivity (H2 Confirmed), where adding 1 assistant per judge increases productivity by approximately 1%. Furthermore, the number of judicial assistants mitigates the intense pressure that high caseloads place on productivity (H4 Confirmed) [23–24]. Conversely, the proportional number of judges per capita was not proven to significantly impact productivity (H1 & H3 Rejected), effectively rejecting the "Exogenous Productivity of Judges Hypothesis" [21–24].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Federal Constitution of Brazil 1988 (Constituição da República Federativa do Brasil 1988):''' The constitutional foundation for the governance, authority, and structure of the Brazilian Judicial Branch.
* '''National Council of Justice Resolutions & National Goals (Resoluções do CNJ & Metas Nacionais):''' The regulatory framework for national judicial governance and case resolution targets.
* '''"Justiça em Números" Official Database (CNJ 2003–2012):''' The official empirical data source for the Brazilian judiciary.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
Between 2003 and 2012, the number of pending cases in Brazil surged by 57%, while the number of judges only increased by 20% and judicial assistants by 28%. Consequently, state courts faced the threat of severe congestion and operational collapse.

== Objectives ==
1. Analyze the direct impact of adding judges and judicial assistants on case resolution productivity (resolved cases per judge/year).
2. Examine the moderating role of judicial staff in the relationship between caseload and productivity.
3. Provide evidence-based econometric guidance for the CNJ and court managers regarding human resources budget allocation.

== Scope ==
This policy covers all 27 Brazilian State Courts (''Justiça Estadual''), encompassing 11,300 judges and 180,000 judicial assistants across 2,760 districts.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Positive Impact of Judicial Assistants (H2 Confirmed):'''
** Adding 1 assistant per judge increases court productivity by approximately 1% annually.
* '''Moderating Effect of Judicial Assistants (H4 Confirmed):'''
** The number of judicial assistants mitigates or weakens the extreme pressure of high workloads on court productivity.
* '''Rejection of the Exogenous Productivity Hypothesis (H1 & H3 Rejected):'''
** The proportion of judges per 100,000 inhabitants does not have a direct, statistically significant impact on increasing average court productivity.

== Implementation ==
* '''PCSE Panel Data Operationalization (2003–2012):''' The processing of 270 court-year observations to isolate heterogeneity effects among different courts.
* '''Optimization of Judicial-Administrative Division of Labor:''' The full transfer of administrative duties (scheduling, file management, communications) to judicial assistants.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Budgetary Constraints on Hiring Assistants:''' Adding 50% more judicial assistants (a massive financial investment) only yields a productivity increase of roughly 10%.
* '''Disproportionate Allocation of Judges:''' The deployment of judges to various districts does not consistently account for actual real-world caseload volumes.

== Reform / Change ==
* Relieving judges from non-judicial administrative tasks to allow them to focus 100% of their time on substantive adjudication.
* Formulating a caseload-based staffing model to allocate judges and assistants based on actual workload analyses.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''National Council of Justice (Conselho Nacional de Justiça / CNJ):''' The judicial governance body determining policies and providing official data.
* '''University of Brasilia (UnB):''' The home institution of the research team (Gomes, Guimaraes, Akutsu).
* '''[private person]:''' A Law student specializing in Constitutional Law (Hukum Tata Negara) at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta. === Deutsch (Schweizer Hochdeutsch) ===
'''Rahmenwerk zur Beziehung zwischen Justizpersonal und Gerichtsleistung in Brasilien'''
Dieser von Adalmir de Oliveira Gomes et al. im ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA, 2016) veröffentlichte Rahmen bewertet ökonometrisch die Auswirkungen von Justizpersonal auf die Produktivität brasilianischer Gerichte. Anhand von Paneldaten aus 27 Bundesstaatsgerichten (2003–2012) belegt die Studie, dass die Einstellung zusätzlicher juristischer Assistenten die Produktivität direkt und positiv beeinflusst (Hypothese 2 bestätigt) und den Druck hoher Fallzahlen mildert (Hypothese 4 bestätigt). === Français ===
'''Cadre de la relation entre le personnel judiciaire et la performance des tribunaux au Brésil'''
Publié par Adalmir de Oliveira Gomes et al. dans l' ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA, 2016), ce cadre évalue de manière économétrique l'impact du personnel sur la productivité des tribunaux brésiliens. À l'aide de données de panel portant sur 27 tribunaux d'État (2003-2012), l'étude prouve que l'embauche d'assistants judiciaires supplémentaires a un impact direct et positif sur la productivité (Hypothèse 2 confirmée) et atténue la pression des charges de travail élevées (Hypothèse 4 confirmée). Cependant, le nombre proportionnel de juges n'a montré aucun impact significatif, rejetant ainsi l'"Exogenous Productivity Hypothesis".

'''Administrative Law Framework for Digitalization and Public Service Delivery in Italy and the European Union''' (''Digitalization and Public Services: Critical Notes Concerning Emerging Ways of Administrating'') is an administrative legal analysis framework formulated by [[Vinicio Brigante]] to evaluate the transformation of telematic public service provision, massive data integration (Big Data), alignment with the Public Service Charter (''Carta dei Servizi'') principles, digital citizenship, and practical testing within the digital health (e-health) and smart mobility (smart mobility/Uber) sectors <ref name="brigante2021">Brigante, V. (2021). Digitalization and Public Services: Critical Notes Concerning Emerging Ways of Administrating. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 13(1), 203–274.</ref>.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Vinicio Brigante]] (Assistant Professor of Administrative Law at the [[Università degli Studi di Napoli “Federico II”]]), this study posits that the digitalization of public services must prioritize a user-centered service delivery model <ref name="brigante2021" />. Telematic service administration must adhere to the principles of the ''Carta dei Servizi'' (equality, impartiality, continuity) <ref name="brigante2021" />. Ultra-sensitive medical data confidentiality (electronic self-determination) must be fully protected under Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR) <ref name="brigante2021" />, while collaborative economy transport platforms such as Uber require clear national and EU competition regulatory frameworks <ref name="brigante2021" />.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''[[Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana]]''': Article 3 (Principle of Equality) <ref name="brigante2021" />; Article 32 (Right to Health) <ref name="brigante2021" />; Article 97 (Impartiality & Good Administration) <ref name="brigante2021" />.
* '''Italian Digital & Administrative Law''': [[Codice dell'Amministrazione Digitale]] (CAD / Legislative Decree 82/2005) Articles 1 & 7 <ref name="brigante2021" />; [[Legge 241/1990]] as amended by Legislative Decree 76/2020 (Legge 120/2020 - Decreto Semplificazioni) <ref name="brigante2021" />; DPCM 27 January 1994 & Legislative Decree 163/1995 (Public Service Charter Framework / ''Carta dei Servizi'') <ref name="brigante2021" />.
* '''EU Law & Jurisprudence''': Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR) Recitals 34, 35 & 52 <ref name="brigante2021" />; [[Corte Costituzionale]] Ruling No. 265/2016 <ref name="brigante2021" />; Court of Justice of the European Union ([[CJEU]]) Case C-434/15 (''Élite Taxi v. Uber'') <ref name="brigante2021" />; [[Garante per la Protezione dei Dati Personali]] Authorisation No. 8/2016 <ref name="brigante2021" />.

== Main Provisions & Analysis ==
1. '''Digital Public Service Charter (''Carta dei Servizi'')''': Ensures service continuity (24/7 access) and external impartiality, while highlighting the risk of shifting discrimination barriers to the point of access due to the digital divide <ref name="brigante2021" />.
2. '''E-Health & Medical Data Privacy''': Medical data processing must satisfy four core parameters established by the Italian Privacy Authority (''Garante Privacy''): purpose limitation, necessity, proportionality, and non-excessiveness, anchored by electronic self-determination <ref name="brigante2021" />.
3. '''Smart Mobility & Uber Jurisprudence''': Following rulings by the [[Corte Costituzionale]] (No. 265/2016) and the [[CJEU]] (Case C-434/15), platforms like Uber are classified as transport services subject to national and EU competition laws <ref name="brigante2021" />.
4. '''Administrative Reforms''': Stresses the need for a harmonized EU artificial intelligence regulatory framework and the discontinuation of "streamed digitalization decrees" lacking real capital investment <ref name="brigante2021" />.

== Relationships & Associated Entities ==
* '''[[Vinicio Brigante]]''': Primary Author / Researcher (University of Naples "Federico II") <ref name="brigante2021" />.
* '''[[Garante per la Protezione dei Dati Personali]]''': Italian Data Protection Authority regulating health data parameters <ref name="brigante2021" />.
* '''[[Agenzia per l'Italia Digitale]] (AgID)''': Related administrative body for digital implementation <ref name="brigante2021" />.
* '''[[Stefano Rodotà]]''', '''[[Sabino Cassese]]''', '''[[Franco Gaetano Scoca]]''', '''[[Marcello Clarich]]''': Referenced legal scholars <ref name="brigante2021" />.

'''Quadro Giuridico-Amministrativo della Digitalizzazione e dei Servizi Pubblici in Italia e nell'Unione Europea''' (''Digitalization and Public Services: Critical Notes Concerning Emerging Ways of Administrating'') è un quadro di analisi del diritto amministrativo formulato da [[Vinicio Brigante]] per valutare la trasformazione dell'erogazione dei servizi pubblici telematici, l'integrazione dei Big Data, la conformità ai principi della [[Carta dei Servizi]], la cittadinanza digitale e la verifica nei settori della sanità digitale (e-health) e della mobilità intelligente (smart mobility/Uber) <ref name="brigante2021it">Brigante, V. (2021). Digitalization and Public Services: Critical Notes Concerning Emerging Ways of Administrating. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 13(1), 203–274.</ref>.

== Sintesi Generale ==
Elaborato da [[Vinicio Brigante]] (Ricercatore/Professore Aggregato di Diritto Amministrativo presso l'[[Università degli Studi di Napoli “Federico II”]]), questo studio sostiene che la digitalizzazione della pubblica amministrazione debba privilegiare un modello di erogazione dei servizi incentrato sul cittadino (''user-centered service delivery'') <ref name="brigante2021it" />. L'erogazione dei servizi telematici deve rispettare i principi della Carta dei Servizi (uguaglianza, imparzialità, continuità) <ref name="brigante2021it" />. La riservatezza dei dati medici ultra-sensibili (autodeterminazione informatica) deve essere pienamente tutelata ai sensi del Regolamento (UE) 2016/679 (GDPR) <ref name="brigante2021it" />, mentre le piattaforme di trasporto della collaborative economy come Uber richiedono quadri normativi chiari sulla concorrenza a livello nazionale ed europeo <ref name="brigante2021it" />.

== Basi Giuridiche ==
* '''[[Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana]]''': Articolo 3 (Principio di Uguaglianza) <ref name="brigante2021it" />; Articolo 32 (Diritto alla Salute) <ref name="brigante2021it" />; Articolo 97 (Imparzialità e Buon Andamento) <ref name="brigante2021it" />.
* '''Diritto Amministrativo e Digitale Italiano''': [[Codice dell'Amministrazione Digitale]] (CAD / D.Lgs. 82/2005) Articoli 1 e 7 <ref name="brigante2021it" />; [[Legge 241/1990]] modificata dal D.L. 76/2020 (Legge 120/2020 - Decreto Semplificazioni) <ref name="brigante2021it" />; D.P.C.M. 27 gennaio 1994 e D.L. 163/1995 (Carta dei Servizi) <ref name="brigante2021it" />.
* '''Diritto dell'Unione Europea e Giurisprudenza''': Regolamento (UE) 2016/679 (GDPR) Considerandi 34, 35 e 52 <ref name="brigante2021it" />; [[Corte Costituzionale]] Sentenza n. 265/2016 <ref name="brigante2021it" />; Corte di Giustizia dell'Unione Europea ([[CGUE]]) Causa C-434/15 (''Élite Taxi v. Uber'') <ref name="brigante2021it" />; [[Garante per la Protezione dei Dati Personali]] Autorizzazione n. 8/2016 <ref name="brigante2021it" />.

== Disposizioni Principali e Analisi ==
1. '''Carta dei Servizi Digitali''': Garantisce la continuità del servizio (accesso 24/7) e l'imparzialità esterna, evidenziando al contempo il rischio di spostare le barriere discriminatorie alla fase d'accesso a causa del divario digitale (''digital divide'') <ref name="brigante2021it" />.
2. '''Privacy in Sanità Digitale (E-Health)''': Il trattamento dei dati sanitari deve soddisfare quattro parametri fondamentali stabiliti dal Garante Privacy: finalità, necessità, proporzionalità e non eccedenza, ancorati al principio dell'autodeterminazione informatica <ref name="brigante2021it" />.
3. '''Mobilità Intelligente e Giurisprudenza Uber''': A seguito delle sentenze della [[Corte Costituzionale]] (n. 265/2016) e della [[CGUE]] (Causa C-434/15), le piattaforme come Uber sono qualificate come servizi di trasporto soggetti alla normativa nazionale ed europea sulla concorrenza <ref name="brigante2021it" />.
4. '''Riforme Amministrative''': Sottolinea la necessità di un quadro normativo armonizzato a livello UE sull'intelligenza artificiale e la cessazione della prassi dei decreti di digitalizzazione a cascata privi di reali stanziamenti di bilancio <ref name="brigante2021it" />.

'''Three Governance Paradigms Framework: Law 1.0, Law 2.0, Law 3.0 and Legal Metrics''' is a theoretical and policy framework developed by Roger Brownsword to map the evolution of legal governance across three paradigms—Law 1.0 (doctrinal coherentism), Law 2.0 (rule-based regulatory), and Law 3.0 (techno-regulatory / technological management)—as well as analyzing the role, ambivalence, and transformation of legal metrics from measuring human/institutional performance to measuring machine performance and automated technologies <ref>Brownsword, R. (2024). Legal Metrics: Getting the Measure of Good Governance. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 10(1-2), 5–20.</ref>.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Roger Brownsword]], Professor of Law at [[King's College London]] and [[Bournemouth University]], this paper presents a critical response to the symposium volume ''Comparative Legal Metrics'' edited by M. Bussani et al. (Leiden: Brill, 2023) <ref>Brownsword (2024), p. 5.</ref>. Brownsword argues that the growth of legal metrics corresponds to a shift in governance from pure legal doctrine (*Law 1.0*), to instrumental policy-based regulation (*Law 2.0*), and now into technology-driven governance (*Law 3.0*) where machines replace human rule-makers and enforcers <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 6, 8, 12, 17.</ref>.

== Legal Basis & Foundations ==
The framework draws upon key instruments in legal theory, regulation, and international jurisprudence:
* '''[[Law 1.0, 2.0, and 3.0 Theoretical Framework]]''': Roger Brownsword's mapping of the three legal governance paradigms <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 6, 8.</ref>.
* '''[[Comparative Legal Metrics]] (Bussani et al. eds, 2023)''': An international comparative study on the application of quantitative metrics in legal systems <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 5, 6.</ref>.
* '''[[EU AI Act & UK Pro-Innovation AI Approach]]''': Comparative analysis of risk-based AI regulation in the EU versus the UK's pro-innovation stance <ref>Brownsword (2024), p. 10.</ref>.
* '''[[High Court of Kenya Ruling on NIIMS]]''': Unconstitutionality ruling on the National Integrated Identity Management System due to inadequate safeguard frameworks <ref>Brownsword (2024), p. 15.</ref>.
* '''[[UN Sustainable Development Goals]] (SDGs 13–16)''': Global governance parameters for climate protection, justice, and strong institutions <ref>Brownsword (2024), p. 16.</ref>.

== Background & The Three Governance Paradigms ==
The evolution of legal governance is divided into three primary paradigms:
1. *Law 1.0 (Doctrinal Coherentism)*: Focuses on internal doctrinal coherence, legal precedent, and the pure Rule of Law. Metrics and new technologies play no specific role <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 7, 8.</ref>.
2. *Law 2.0 (Rule-Based Regulatory)*: Focuses on regulatory effectiveness, institutional efficiency, and instrumental policy goals. Legal metrics measure human and judicial performance <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 8, 9, 13.</ref>.
3. *Law 3.0 (Techno-Regulatory & Technological Management)*: Utilizes automated technologies and ex-ante technological management to replace rules and human supervision. Metrics shift to assessing machine performance <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 8, 10, 11, 17.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Identify the utility and risks of legal metrics within regulatory governance (*Law 2.0*) <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 5, 13.</ref>.
* Anticipate the shifting role of metrics as governance transitions to automated machine execution (*Law 3.0*) <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 6, 17, 18.</ref>.
* Ensure technological governance respects three essential imperatives (*good governance imperatives*): safeguarding *planetary boundaries*, guaranteeing *peaceful co-existence*, and respecting *human agency and autonomy* <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 15, 16.</ref>.

== Scope ==
The scope encompasses comparative legal theory, philosophy of technology, judicial reform (Brazil, India, Switzerland, Kenya), administrative automation (Japanese Digital Agency), and global AI/data governance <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 5–20.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & Policy Implications ==
* '''Automated Management & Shift of Supervision (Law 3.0)''': Initiatives such as the Japanese Digital Agency reviewing over 10,000 statutes to replace human oversight with AI, robotics, and automated systems <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 17, 18.</ref>.
* '''Dangers of Quantification (Omnimetric Society)''': As conceptualized by Teresa Rodriguez de las Heras Ballell, unchecked quantification risks replacing veracity with popularity <ref>Brownsword (2024), p. 18.</ref>.
* '''Managerial Justice Distortions''': Lessons from Brazil's *Justice in Numbers* project, where judicial work shifted toward template-based output to fulfill performance targets <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 12, 13.</ref>.

== Policy Issues & Unresolved Challenges ==
* '''Risk of Regulatory Capture''': The discontinuation of the World Bank's *Doing Business* report due to data integrity concerns and indicator gaming <ref>Brownsword (2024), p. 6.</ref>.
* '''Merton & Ellul Warning''': A critical warning against endlessly perfecting means (*continually improved means*) without rigorously evaluating ends (*carelessly examined ends*) <ref>Brownsword (2024), p. 20.</ref>.

'''Quadro dei Tre Paradigmi di Governance Giuridica e Metriche Legali''' (''Three Governance Paradigms Framework: Law 1.0, Law 2.0, Law 3.0 and Legal Metrics'') è un quadro teorico e politico sviluppato da Roger Brownsword per mappare l'evoluzione della governance giuridica attraverso tre paradigmi—Law 1.0 (coerentismo dottrinale), Law 2.0 (regolamentazione basata su regole) e Law 3.0 (gestione tecno-regolatoria / gestione tecnologica)—analizzando il ruolo, l'ambivalenza e la trasformazione delle metriche legali (''legal metrics'') da strumenti di misurazione delle prestazioni umane e istituzionali a misuratori delle prestazioni delle macchine e delle tecnologie automatizzate <ref>Brownsword, R. (2024). Legal Metrics: Getting the Measure of Good Governance. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 10(1-2), 5–20.</ref>.

== Sinossi ==
Scritto da [[Roger Brownsword]], Professore di Diritto presso il [[King's College London]] e la [[Bournemouth University]], l'articolo presenta una risposta critica al volume del simposio ''Comparative Legal Metrics'' curato da M. Bussani et al. (Leiden: Brill, 2023) <ref>Brownsword (2024), p. 5.</ref>. Brownsword sostiene che la crescita delle metriche legali corrisponda a un passaggio della governance dalla pura dottrina giuridica (*Law 1.0*), alla regolamentazione basata su politiche strumentali (*Law 2.0*), fino a giungere alla governance guidata dalla tecnologia (*Law 3.0*) in cui le macchine sostituiscono l'uomo nella creazione e nell'applicazione delle norme <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 6, 8, 12, 17.</ref>.

== Basi Giuridiche e Fondamenti ==
Il quadro si basa su strumenti chiave della teoria del diritto, della regolamentazione e della giurisprudenza internazionale:
* '''[[Quadro Teorico di Law 1.0, 2.0 e 3.0]]''': Mappatura dei tre paradigmi di governance giuridica stilata da Roger Brownsword <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 6, 8.</ref>.
* '''[[Comparative Legal Metrics]] (Bussani et al. ed., 2023)''': Studio comparato internazionale sull'applicazione delle metriche quantitative nei sistemi giuridici <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 5, 6.</ref>.
* '''[[Regolamento UE sull'IA & Approccio Pro-Innovazione del Regno Unito]]''': Analisi comparata tra la regolamentazione dell'IA basata sul rischio nell'UE e l'approccio orientato all'innovazione del Regno Unito <ref>Brownsword (2024), p. 10.</ref>.
* '''[[Sentenza della Corte Suprema del Kenya sul NIIMS]]''': Dichiarazione di incostituzionalità del National Integrated Identity Management System per assenza di un adeguato quadro regolatorio di tutela <ref>Brownsword (2024), p. 15.</ref>.
* '''[[Obiettivi di Sviluppo Sostenibile dell'ONU]] (SDG 13–16)''': Parametri di governance globale per la tutela del clima, la giustizia e istituzioni solide <ref>Brownsword (2024), p. 16.</ref>.

== Contestualizzazione e i Tre Paradigmi di Governance ==
L'evoluzione della governance giuridica si suddivide in tre paradigmi principali:
1. *Law 1.0 (Coerentismo Dottrinale)*: Si concentra sulla coerenza dottrinale interna, sui precedenti legali e sul puro Stato di Diritto (Rule of Law). Le metriche e le nuove tecnologie non svolgono alcun ruolo specifico <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 7, 8.</ref>.
2. *Law 2.0 (Regolamentazione Basata su Regole)*: Si concentra sull'efficacia regolatoria, sull'efficienza istituzionale e sul raggiungimento di obiettivi di politica strumentale. Le metriche legali misurano le prestazioni umane e giudiziarie <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 8, 9, 13.</ref>.
3. *Law 3.0 (Gestione Tecno-Regolatoria e Tecnologica)*: Utilizza tecnologie automatizzate e la gestione tecnologica ex-ante (*technological management*) per sostituire le regole e la supervisione umana. Le metriche si spostano sulla valutazione delle prestazioni delle macchine <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 8, 10, 11, 17.</ref>.

== Obiettivi ==
* Identificare l'utilità e i rischi delle metriche legali all'interno della governance regolatoria (*Law 2.0*) <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 5, 13.</ref>.
* Anticipare l'evoluzione del ruolo delle metriche durante la transizione verso la governance gestita da macchine automatizzate (*Law 3.0*) <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 6, 17, 18.</ref>.
* Garantire che la governance tecnologica rispetti i tre imperativi essenziali per una buona governance (*good governance imperatives*): la salvaguardia dei *limiti planetari*, la garanzia della *coesistenza pacifica* e il rispetto per l'*autonomia e agenzia umana* <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 15, 16.</ref>.

== Ambito di Applicazione ==
L'ambito comprende la teoria del diritto comparato, la filosofia della tecnologia, la riforma giudiziaria (Brasile, India, Svizzera, Kenya), l'automazione burocratica (Agenzia Digitale Giapponese) e la governance globale di IA e dati <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 5–20.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Chiave e Implicazioni Politiche ==
* '''Gestione Automatizzata e Spostamento della Supervisione (Law 3.0)''': Iniziative come la revisione da parte dell'Agenzia Digitale Giapponese di oltre 10.000 leggi per sostituire la supervisione umana con IA, robotica e sistemi automatizzati <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 17, 18.</ref>.
* '''I Pericoli della Quantificazione (Società Omnimetrica)''': Come concettualizzato da Teresa Rodriguez de las Heras Ballell, una quantificazione incontrollata rischia di sostituire la veridicità con la popolarità <ref>Brownsword (2024), p. 18.</ref>.
* '''Distorzioni della Giustizia Manageriale''': L'esperienza del progetto *Justice in Numbers* in Brasile, dove l'attività giudiziaria è stata riorientata verso l'efficienza basata su modelli predefiniti per soddisfare gli indicatori chiave di prestazione (KPI) <ref>Brownsword (2024), pp. 12, 13.</ref>.

== Politiche Critiche e Questioni Irrisolte ==
* '''Rischio di Regulatory Capture''': La dismissione del rapporto *Doing Business* della Banca Mondiale a causa di manipolazioni dei dati e degli indicatori <ref>Brownsword (2024), p. 6.</ref>.
* '''L'Avvertimento di Merton ed Ellul''': Un monito fondamentale per evitare il perfezionamento continuo dei mezzi (*continually improved means*) senza un esame critico dei fini (*carelessly examined ends*) <ref>Brownsword (2024), p. 20.</ref>.

'''Do government invitations to consultations shape stakeholder participation in public policymaking?''' is an empirical comparative political science and public administration research paper authored by Adriana Bunea and Idunn Nørbech of the University of Bergen (Norway), published in the ''European Journal of Political Research'' (EJPR) in 2025.

== Summary ==
This study examines whether and how formal government invitations to online public consultations (OPCs) affect the volume and diversity of stakeholder participation in public policymaking. Drawing on a comprehensive dataset covering 251,153 stakeholder submissions (104,460 from citizens and 146,693 from organizations) across 4,062 public consultations held by Norwegian government ministries between 2009 and 2023, the study demonstrates that a higher number of government invitations leads to greater participation volume and greater diversity of interest groups involved.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This document is an academic political science research study and is not based on any specific statutory or judicial legislative instrument [1–116].
* '''Norwegian Public Consultation Scheme (*Høyringar*):''' Norway's executive administrative governance procedure requiring the collection of public input before a policy proposal is finalized.

== Background ==
Online public consultations are used by government bureaucracies to involve citizens and organizations in policy formulation, aiming to reduce bias in interest representation and strengthen procedural legitimacy. In Scandinavian countries such as Norway, public consultation — historically rooted in traditional corporatist arrangements — has increasingly shifted toward pluralist patterns of representation. However, the effectiveness of bureaucratic outreach efforts through formal invitations in shaping public participation had not previously been tested systematically at scale.

== Objectives ==
1. Test whether the number of government invitations increases both the total level of participation and the diversity of interests represented (Hypotheses 1.1 & 1.2).
2. Test the moderating effect of policy act type on the relationship between invitations and participation (Hypotheses 2.1 & 2.2).
3. Analyze how invitations directed at organizations can drive individual citizen mobilization (the "activation belt" effect).

== Scope ==
The research covers all 4,062 online public consultations held by every executive ministry in Norway between 2009 and 2023.

== Key Provisions / Findings ==
* '''Hypothesis 1.1 Supported (Participation Volume):''' Each additional government invitation increases stakeholder participation by '''0.5%''' (IRR = 1.005, p < 0.01). A one-standard-deviation increase in invitations (+84 invitations) yields an average additional '''+31.3 submissions''' for legislative proposals (+16.3 from organizations and +16.4 from citizens).
* '''Hypothesis 1.2 Supported (Stakeholder Diversity):''' The number of invitations is significantly positively associated with the diversity index of interest types (β = +0.005, p < 0.01).
* '''Policy Act Moderation Effects (Hypotheses 2.1 & 2.2):''' The positive effect of invitations on both participation volume and diversity is strongest for legislative proposals (*Lov*) and government reports (*NOU/Rapport*), while the effect is considerably more moderate for government regulations (*Forskrift*) and EU directives.
* '''Organizations as an "Activation Belt" for Citizens:''' Although invitations are sent almost exclusively to organizations and institutions, an increase in organizational invitations significantly raises both the probability (p < 0.01) and frequency (p < 0.01) of individual citizen participation. For example, in a 2022 seabed mineral-mining consultation, the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) forwarded the ministry's invitation to its network, mobilizing 980 individual citizen submissions.

== Implementation ==
The methodology was implemented through negative binomial regression models, hurdle models for citizen participation, and OLS regression for the Laakso-Taagepera diversity index [50–52, 85]. Replication data and code are stored openly on DataverseNO at `doi:10.18710/HZIBBH`.

== Policy Issues ==
1. The risk of "consultation fatigue," in which a high volume of simultaneous invitations may strain the resources of stakeholder organizations.
2. High baseline participation inequality on technical or non-legislative issues (such as EU directives), which require additional bureaucratic outreach effort.

== Reform / Implications ==
The study demonstrates that formal bureaucratic outreach through invitations is an effective, low-cost institutional instrument for democratizing public policymaking.
