'''Understanding unequal representation''' is a symposium introductory article and comparative political science analytical framework authored by Brian Burgoon (University of Amsterdam), Noam Lupu (Vanderbilt University), Jonas Pontusson (University of Geneva), and Wouter Schakel (University of Amsterdam), published in the ''European Journal of Political Research'' (EJPR) in 2022.

== Summary ==
This article presents the analytical framework for an EJPR Symposium examining income and class biases in political representation across liberal democracies. The paper conceptualizes unequal representation through two central approaches — congruence and responsiveness — and identifies the mediating conditions and moderating conditions that link wealth to political influence. The study demonstrates that affluence bias in representation is not merely a distinctively American phenomenon, but a common feature across many democracies.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This document is an academic research article and is not based on any specific statutory or judicial legislative instrument [1–36].

== Background ==
Since the 1980s, elected governments in OECD countries have rarely taken new initiatives to compensate low- and middle-income citizens for the concentration of wealth at the top, with state redistribution actually declining across the US and Western Europe. Populist rhetoric claiming that policymaking favors elite interests has found strong resonance among working-class and lower-middle-class citizens.

== Objectives ==
1. Advance a comparative approach to the study of unequal political representation.
2. Map the chain of political representation into three stages: pre-electoral (candidate recruitment and party platforms), electoral (campaigns and voter choice), and post-electoral (legislative bargaining and lobbying).
3. Distinguish the causal mechanisms between mediating conditions and moderating conditions.

== Scope ==
The research synthesizes six comparative studies drawing on cross-national data (33–39 countries), longitudinal public opinion survey data (>800 policy proposals in Germany), historical cabinet minister data (18 democracies since 1945), and conjoint candidate choice experiments.

== Key Provisions & Symposium Findings ==
* '''Ideological Congruence:''' Elected representatives across 33 countries are consistently more closely aligned with the preferences of wealthy citizens than poor citizens.
* '''Policy Responsiveness:''' Public policy outputs (as observed in Germany and across 18 democracies) consistently respond more to the preferences of business owners and high-status groups than to those of unskilled workers.
* '''Agenda-Setting Bias:''' Legislative activity is significantly higher in policy domains prioritized by high-status occupational groups.
* '''Descriptive Misrepresentation & Candidate Recruitment:''' Middle-class voters tend to disfavor working-class candidates, contributing to the shortage of working-class representatives in parliament.
* '''Party Platforms:''' Political parties' budgetary commitments (especially among right-wing parties) more closely reflect the spending preferences of wealthy citizens.
* '''Moderating Conditions:''' Corruption, clientelism, and economic growth moderate representation bias. However, proportional electoral systems and economic globalization were '''not''' found to eliminate representation bias.

== Implementation ==
The article outlines a methodological framework based on comparative macro-statistical analysis, machine learning techniques, and conjoint experiments. The research was funded by the European Research Council (ERC Advanced Grant No. 741538), NWO (Grant No. 406-15-089), and the Amsterdam Center for Inequality Studies (AMCIS).

== Policy Issues ==
1. The deficit of political influence among low-income and working-class citizens in shaping redistributive policy.
2. The hidden influence of high-income elite groups through legislative agenda-setting and cabinet composition.

== Reform / Future Research Directions ==
1. Integrating measurement of policy positions with issue salience.
2. Broadening class comparisons to include skilled versus unskilled workers and intersections with gender and ethnicity.
3. Measuring citizens' awareness of representation inequality and its effect on populist voting behavior.

'''Policy Framework on Irish Constitutional Traditions, Judicial Independence, and Fundamental Rights''' (''Laporan Kebijakan Tradisi Konstitusi, Independensi Peradilan, dan Hak-Hak Fundamental Irlandia'') is a comparative constitutional law and doctrinal framework authored by Ciarán Burke. It examines the concept and evolution of "constitutional traditions" in the Republic of Ireland under the 1937 Constitution (''Bunreacht na hÉireann''), covering judicial supremacy, popular sovereignty versus natural law, judicial independence and political patronage in judicial appointments (JAAB/JAC), proportionality and rationality tests in limiting fundamental rights, and harmonization between domestic law, European Union law, and the ECHR <ref>Burke, C. (2022). Comparative Constitutional Traditions Project - Report on Ireland. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 14(1), 151–187.</ref>.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Ciarán Burke]] (Professor of International Law and Legal Officer at the EFTA Surveillance Authority), this report provides a comprehensive mapping of Irish constitutional traditions under the 1937 Constitution <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 151, 153.</ref>. Burke outlines how Ireland merges common law traditions with a written constitution holding supreme normative status <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 153, 165, 172.</ref>. The policy analysis examines judicial review, the interaction between popular sovereignty and natural law, systemic weaknesses in judicial appointments (JAAB), and practical applications regarding freedom of expression and movement <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 158, 162, 181–185.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
Ireland's constitutional framework rests on key domestic and international instruments:
* '''[[Bunreacht na hÉireann]] (Constitution of Ireland 1937)''':
** *Preamble & Articles 1, 5, 6*: Affirmation of popular sovereignty and foundational values <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 151, 158, 159.</ref>.
** *Articles 13.9, 13.11, 35.1, & 35.4*: Judicial appointment and impeachment mechanisms <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 181, 184.</ref>.
** *Articles 34–37*: Single court hierarchy and power of judicial review <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 151, 186.</ref>.
** *Articles 40.1, 40.3, 40.4, 40.6.1*: Guarantees of equality, personal liberty, expression, assembly, and association <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 162, 167, 172, 179.</ref>.
* '''[[Courts and Court Officers Act 1995]]''': Establishment of the Judicial Appointments Advisory Board (JAAB) <ref>Burke (2022), p. 181.</ref>.
* '''[[European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003]]''': Incorporation of the ECHR into domestic Irish law <ref>Burke (2022), p. 172.</ref>.
* '''Key Jurisprudence''':
** *State (Burke) v Lennon (1940)*: Recognition of judicial power to invalidate unconstitutional legislation <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 152, 158.</ref>.
** *Heaney v Ireland (1994)*: Formulation of the three-part proportionality test <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 167, 168.</ref>.
** *Finn v AG (1983) & Riordan v Taoiseach (1999)*: Absolute popular sovereignty over constitutional amendments <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 159, 160.</ref>.
** *Maguire v Ardagh / Abbeylara (2001)*: Protection of judicial functions against parliamentary fact-finding <ref>Burke (2022), p. 183.</ref>.

== Background & Living Document Doctrine ==
The 1937 Constitution established a decentralized system of judicial review early in its history <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 153, 155, 186.</ref>. Irish courts interpret the Constitution as a "living document" that adapts to contemporary social values <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 153, 161.</ref>. This dynamic approach is reflected in successful constitutional referendums authorizing same-sex marriage (2015), the legalization of abortion (2018), and the removal of the offense of blasphemy (2018) <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 156, 161, 171.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & Proportionality ==
* '''Three-Part Proportionality Test (Heaney Test)''':
# *Pressing and Substantial Objective*: Legislative limits must serve a pressing and substantial goal <ref>Burke (2022), p. 167.</ref>.
# *Rational Connection & Minimal Impairment*: Restrictions must be rationally connected to the objective and impair rights as little as possible <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 167, 168.</ref>.
# *Proportional Effect*: The severity of the restriction must be proportional to the objective <ref>Burke (2022), p. 168.</ref>.
* '''Absolute Popular Sovereignty''': Because the Irish electorate exercises supreme power through referendums, the doctrine of "unconstitutional constitutional amendments" is rejected <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 159, 160.</ref>.
* '''Judicial Appointment Reform''': The JAAB framework (1995) failed to prevent political patronage due to executive discretion <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 181, 182.</ref>. The Judicial Appointments Commission Bill 2017 proposed creating an independent body with a lay majority <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 183, 187.</ref>.

== Policy Challenges ==
* '''Judicial Discipline Scandals''': The absence of an internal disciplinary body led to crises such as the Sheedy Affair (1998) and the Curtin case (2002–2006) <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 184, 185.</ref>, spurring the passage of the Judicial Council Bill <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 183, 188.</ref>.

== Cross-Entity Relationships ==

'''Quadro Politico sulle Tradizioni Costituzionali Irlandesi, l'Indipendenza Giudiziaria e i Diritti Fondamentali''' (''Rapporto sulle Tradizioni Costituzionali Irlandesi'') è un quadro di analisi dottrinale e diritto costituzionale comparato redatto da Ciarán Burke. Esamina il concetto e l'evoluzione delle "tradizioni costituzionali" nella Repubblica d'Irlanda sotto la Costituzione del 1937 (''Bunreacht na hÉireann''), coprendo la supremazia giudiziaria, la sovranità popolare rispetto al diritto naturale, l'indipendenza giudiziaria e il patronato politico nelle nomine dei giudici (JAAB/JAC), i test di proporzionalità e razionalità nella limitazione dei diritti fondamentali, e l'armonizzazione tra diritto interno, diritto dell'Unione Europea e CEDU <ref>Burke, C. (2022). Comparative Constitutional Traditions Project - Report on Ireland. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 14(1), 151–187.</ref>.

== Panoramica ==
Redatto da [[Ciarán Burke]] (Professore di Diritto Internazionale e Funzionario Giuridico presso l'EFTA Surveillance Authority), questo rapporto fornisce una mappatura completa delle tradizioni costituzionali irlandesi ai sensi della Costituzione del 1937 <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 151, 153.</ref>. Burke descrive come l'Irlanda unisca la tradizione della *Common Law* con una costituzione scritta avente valore normativo supremo <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 153, 165, 172.</ref>. L'analisi esamina il controllo di costituzionalità, l'interazione tra sovranità popolare e diritto naturale, le debolezze sistemiche nelle nomine giudiziarie (JAAB) e le applicazioni pratiche riguardanti la libertà di espressione e di movimento <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 158, 162, 181–185.</ref>.

== Basi Giuridiche ==
Il quadro costituzionale irlandese si basa su fondamentali strumenti nazionali e internazionali:
* '''[[Bunreacht na hÉireann]] (Costituzione dell'Irlanda del 1937)''':
** *Preambolo e Articoli 1, 5, 6*: Affermazione della sovranità popolare e dei valori fondanti <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 151, 158, 159.</ref>.
** *Articoli 13.9, 13.11, 35.1 e 35.4*: Meccanismi di nomina e impeachment dei giudici <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 181, 184.</ref>.
** *Articoli 34–37*: Gerarchia giudiziaria e potere di controllo di costituzionalità giudiziaria <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 151, 186.</ref>.
** *Articoli 40.1, 40.3, 40.4, 40.6.1*: Garanzie di uguaglianza, libertà personale, espressione, associazione e assemblea <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 162, 167, 172, 179.</ref>.
* '''[[Courts and Court Officers Act 1995]]''': Istituzione della Commissione Consultiva per le Nomine Giudiziarie (JAAB) <ref>Burke (2022), p. 181.</ref>.
* '''[[European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003]]''': Incorporazione della CEDU nel diritto interno irlandese <ref>Burke (2022), p. 172.</ref>.
* '''Giurisprudenza Chiave''':
** *State (Burke) v Lennon (1940)*: Riconoscimento del potere giudiziario di annullare leggi incostituzionali <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 152, 158.</ref>.
** *Heaney v Ireland (1994)*: Formulazione del test di proporzionalità in tre fasi <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 167, 168.</ref>.
** *Finn v AG (1983) e Riordan v Taoiseach (1999)*: Sovranità popolare assoluta sugli emendamenti costituzionali <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 159, 160.</ref>.
** *Maguire v Ardagh / Abbeylara (2001)*: Tutela delle funzioni giudiziarie contro le indagini parlamentari sui fatti <ref>Burke (2022), p. 183.</ref>.

== Contestualizzazione e Dottrina del "Living Document" ==
La Costituzione del 1937 ha stabilito un sistema decentralizzato di controllo di costituzionalità fin dalle sue origini <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 153, 155, 186.</ref>. I tribunali irlandesi interpretano la Costituzione come un "documento vivente" (*living document*) che si adatta ai valori sociali contemporanei <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 153, 161.</ref>. Questo approccio è evidenziato dai referendum costituzionali che hanno approvato il matrimonio tra persone dello stesso sesso (2015), la legalizzazione dell'aborto (2018) e la depenalizzazione della bestemmia (2018) <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 156, 161, 171.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Principali e Proporzionalità ==
* '''Test di Proporzionalità in Tre Fasi (Test Heaney)''':
# *Obiettivo Urgente e Sostanziale*: Le limitazioni legislative devono rispondere a un obiettivo urgente e rilevante <ref>Burke (2022), p. 167.</ref>.
# *Connessione Razionale e Minima Ingerenza*: Le restrizioni devono essere razionalmente collegate all'obiettivo e limitare i diritti il meno possibile <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 167, 168.</ref>.
# *Effetto Proporzionato*: La severità della restrizione deve essere proporzionata all'obiettivo perseguito <ref>Burke (2022), p. 168.</ref>.
* '''Sovranità Popolare Assoluta''': Poiché l'elettorato irlandese esercita il potere supremo tramite referendum, la dottrina degli "emendamenti costituzionali incostituzionali" è respinta <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 159, 160.</ref>.
* '''Riforma delle Nomine Giudiziarie''': Il sistema JAAB (1995) non è riuscito a impedire il patronato politico a causa della discrezionalità dell'esecutivo <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 181, 182.</ref>. Il disegno di legge Judicial Appointments Commission Bill 2017 ha proposto la creazione di un organo indipendente a maggioranza laica <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 183, 187.</ref>.

== Criticità e Riforme ==
* '''Scandali sulla Disciplina Giudiziaria''': L'assenza di un organo disciplinare interno ha portato a crisi come lo Sheedy Affair (1998) e il caso Curtin (2002–2006) <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 184, 185.</ref>, accelerando l'approvazione del Judicial Council Bill <ref>Burke (2022), pp. 183, 188.</ref>.

'''Gender Balance in Corporate Bodies: Notes on the Recent Amendments to the Equal Opportunities Code and the Final Approval of the Women on Boards Directive''' (Original Title: ''Why Diversity? Gender Balance in Corporate Bodies: Notes on the Recent Amendments to the Equal Opportunities Code and the Final Approval of the Women on Boards Directive'') is a legal and corporate governance analysis framework formulated by Mia Callegari, Eva R. Desana, and Fabiana Massa Felsani in *The Italian Law Journal* (Vol. 08 – No. 02/2022, pp. 715–744).<ref>Callegari, M., Desana, E.R., & Massa Felsani, F. (2022). Why Diversity? Gender Balance in Corporate Bodies: Notes on the Recent Amendments to the Equal Opportunities Code and the Final Approval of the Women on Boards Directive. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 8(2), 715–744.</ref> The study evaluates the evolution and regulatory fragmentation of corporate gender quotas in Italy, tracing developments from ''Law 12 July 2011 n. 120 (Golfo-Mosca Law)''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 716, 717.</ref>, ''Law 27 December 2019 n. 160 (Budget Law 2020)''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), p. 718.</ref>, the ''Consolidated Act on State-Owned Enterprises (TUSPP / D.Lgs. 175/2016)''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 718, 719.</ref>, and ''Law 5 November 2021 n. 162 (Amendments to the Equal Opportunities Code / D.Lgs. 198/2006)''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 715, 719, 721.</ref>, to European Union harmonization via the ''Women on Boards Directive (Directive (EU) 2022/2381)''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 715, 737, 740.</ref>.

It examines the application of 2/5 (40%) or 33% mandatory gender quotas across administrative and supervisory bodies in listed companies, publicly controlled companies, banking institutions (''Banca d'Italia Update 35 to Circular 285'')<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 719, 720.</ref>, and insurance firms (''IVASS Research Paper 22 & MISE Decree 88/2022'')<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 720, 721.</ref>. Furthermore, it analyzes gender equality certification instruments (gender diversity ratings), National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) certification criteria (Mission 5 / D.L. 77/2021)<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 715, 729, 735.</ref>, tax relief/public procurement incentive mechanisms<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 735, 736.</ref>, and judicial oversight and sanctions<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 725, 727, 731.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Authored by [[Mia Callegari]], [[Eva R. Desana]] (both Full Professors of Commercial Law at the University of Turin), and [[Fabiana Massa Felsani]] (Full Professor of Commercial Law at the University of Naples 'Federico II'), this work reviews a decade of mandatory gender quota regulations in Italy following the enactment of the ''Golfo-Mosca Law (Law 120/2011)''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 715, 716.</ref>. The authors analyze the effect of increasing board quotas from 1/3 to 2/5 (40%) under ''Budget Law 2020'' and ''Law 162/2021'', which successfully increased female representation on listed company boards to over 41%<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 716, 718, 721, 722.</ref>.

However, the study highlights critical legislative oversights—such as omitting board of statutory auditor quotas for public companies—the persistent scarcity of women in executive leadership roles (CEOs), and anomalies in sanction regimes<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 724, 726, 728, 733.</ref>. It commends the introduction of gender diversity rating certifications under the PNRR framework and the EU-wide adoption of the ''Women on Boards Directive (EU) 2022/2381''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 729, 735, 737, 741.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
=== Italian National Legislation & Constitution ===
* '''Constitution of the Italian Republic''': Article 3 (Substantive Equality) and Article 51 (Equal Access to Public Offices)<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 723, 732.</ref>.
* '''Law 12 July 2011 n. 120 (Golfo-Mosca Law)'''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), p. 716.</ref>.
* '''Consolidated Law on Finance (TUF / D.Lgs. 24 February 1998 n. 58)''': Arts. 147-ter para 1-ter, 147-quater para 1-bis, 148 paras 1-bis & 4-bis (as amended by Law 160/2019 / Budget Law 2020)<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 717, 718.</ref>.
* '''Consolidated Act on State-Owned Enterprises (TUSPP / D.Lgs. 19 August 2016 n. 175)''': Article 11 para 4<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 718, 719.</ref>.
* '''Law 5 November 2021 n. 162''': Amendments to the Equal Opportunities Code (D.Lgs. 11 April 2006 n. 198)<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 715, 721, 735.</ref>.
* '''D.P.R. 30 November 2012 n. 251''': Implementing Regulation of the Golfo-Mosca Law for Public Companies<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), p. 718.</ref>.
* '''Decree-Law 31 May 2021 n. 77 (Art. 47)''' & '''Ministerial Decree 29 April 2022''' (PNRR Procurement & Gender Certification)<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 729, 735, 736.</ref>.

=== Financial & Insurance Regulatory Frameworks ===
* '''Banca d'Italia Notice 285/2013 (Update 35 / 30 June 2021)''': Mandatory 33% quota for underrepresented gender in bank administrative and control bodies<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 719, 720.</ref>.
* '''Ministry of Economic Development (MISE) Decree 2 May 2022 n. 88 (Art. 11)''': Mandatory 33% quota for insurance corporate bodies<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), p. 720.</ref>.

=== European Union & International Directives ===
* '''Directive (EU) 2022/2381 (Women on Boards Directive)''': 40% non-executive or 33% overall director quota by 2026<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 715, 737, 740.</ref>.
* '''Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU''' (Arts. 21, 23) & '''TFEU''' Art. 157(3)<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 739, 740.</ref>.
* '''UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs Goal 5 / 2030 Agenda)'''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 717, 730.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & Three Policy Pillars ==
1. '''Quota Increase to 2/5 (40%) for Listed and Public Companies''': Law 160/2019 and Law 162/2021 raised reserved seats for the underrepresented gender from 1/3 to 2/5 (40%) across six consecutive terms (18 years) for administrative boards of listed and publicly controlled companies<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 718, 721, 722.</ref>.
2. '''Sectoral Expansion in Banking and Insurance''': Banca d'Italia and MISE established a 33% mandatory threshold for management and supervisory organs in all banks and insurance entities to enhance risk management and board diversity<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 719, 720, 721.</ref>.
3. '''Gender Equality Certification and PNRR Incentives''': Law 162/2021 introduced a certified gender diversity rating framework tied to PNRR Mission 5, providing social security tax relief for employers (up to €50,000/year) and bonus score points in public procurement tenders<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 715, 729, 735, 736.</ref>.

== Institutional and Individual Relationships ==
* '''[[Mia Callegari]]''': Lead Author & Full Professor of Commercial Law, University of Turin<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 715, 722.</ref>.
* '''[[Eva R. Desana]]''': Lead Author & Full Professor of Commercial Law, University of Turin<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 715, 718.</ref>.
* '''[[Fabiana Massa Felsani]]''': Lead Author & Full Professor of Commercial Law, University of Naples 'Federico II'<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 715, 717.</ref>.
* '''[[CONSOB]]''': Italian Financial Conduct Authority supervising corporate governance data<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 716, 731.</ref>.
* '''[[Banca d'Italia]]''': Central Bank of Italy issuing banking gender quota rules<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 719, 730.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 715–744.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pp. 715–744.</ref>

'''Quadro di Politica per l'Equilibrio di Genere negli Organi Societari: Note sulle Recenti Modifiche al Codice delle Pari Opportunità e l'Approvazione della Direttiva Women on Boards''' (Titolo originale: ''Why Diversity? Gender Balance in Corporate Bodies: Notes on the Recent Amendments to the Equal Opportunities Code and the Final Approval of the Women on Boards Directive'') è un quadro di analisi giuridica e di corporate governance formulato da Mia Callegari, Eva R. Desana e Fabiana Massa Felsani su *The Italian Law Journal* (Vol. 08 – N. 02/2022, pagg. 715–744).<ref>Callegari, M., Desana, E.R., & Massa Felsani, F. (2022). Why Diversity? Gender Balance in Corporate Bodies: Notes on the Recent Amendments to the Equal Opportunities Code and the Final Approval of the Women on Boards Directive. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 8(2), 715–744.</ref> Lo studio valuta l'evoluzione e la frammentazione normativa delle quote di genere in Italia, partendo dalla ''Legge 12 Luglio 2011 n. 120 (Legge Golfo-Mosca)''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 716, 717.</ref>, dalla ''Legge 27 Dicembre 2019 n. 160 (Legge di Bilancio 2020)''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pag. 718.</ref>, dal ''Testo Unico delle Società a Partecipazione Pubblica (TUSPP / D.Lgs. 175/2016)''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 718, 719.</ref> e dalla ''Legge 5 Novembre 2021 n. 162 (Modifiche al Codice delle Pari Opportunità / D.Lgs. 198/2006)''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 715, 719, 721.</ref>, fino all'armonizzazione a livello europeo tramite la ''Direttiva Women on Boards (Direttiva (UE) 2022/2381)''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 715, 737, 740.</ref>.

Esamina l'applicazione della quota obbligatoria del 2/5 (40%) o del 33% negli organi di amministrazione e controllo di società quotate, società a controllo pubblico, settore bancario (''Banca d'Italia Aggiornamento 35 alla Circolare 285'')<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 719, 720.</ref> e assicurativo (''IVASS Research Paper 22 & D.M. MISE 88/2022'')<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 720, 721.</ref>. Analizza inoltre la certificazione di parità di genere (gender diversity rating), i criteri di certificazione PNRR (Missione 5 / D.L. 77/2021)<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 715, 729, 735.</ref>, gli incentivi fiscali e negli appalti pubblici<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 735, 736.</ref>, nonché il sistema sanzionatorio e di vigilanza giudiziaria<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 725, 727, 731.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Redatto da [[Mia Callegari]], [[Eva R. Desana]] (entrambe Professoresse Ordinarie di Diritto Commerciale all'Università degli Studi di Torino) e [[Fabiana Massa Felsani]] (Professoressa Ordinaria di Diritto Commerciale all'Università degli Studi di Napoli 'Federico II'), questo studio esamina un decennio di regolamentazione sulle quote di genere in Italia a seguito della ''Legge Golfo-Mosca (L. 120/2011)''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 715, 716.</ref>. Le autrici analizzano l'impatto dell'innalzamento della quota da 1/3 a 2/5 (40%) introdotto dalla ''Legge di Bilancio 2020'' e dalla ''L. 162/2021'', che ha portato la presenza femminile nei consigli di amministrazione delle società quotate oltre il 41%<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 716, 718, 721, 722.</ref>.

Ciononostante, lo studio evidenzia significative sviste legislative—come l'omesso riferimento agli organi di controllo delle società pubbliche—la persistente scarsità di donne in ruoli esecutivi apicali (CEO) e le anomalie nel regime sanzionatorio<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 724, 726, 728, 733.</ref>. Il lavoro accoglie con favore l'introduzione della certificazione della parità di genere nel PNRR e l'approvazione della ''Direttiva Europea Women on Boards (UE) 2022/2381''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 729, 735, 737, 741.</ref>.

== Basi Giuridiche ==
=== Normativa Nazionale e Costituzione Italiana ===
* '''Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana''': Articolo 3 (Uguaglianza Sostanziale) e Articolo 51 (Pari Opportunità nell'Accesso agli Uffici Pubblici)<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 723, 732.</ref>.
* '''Legge 12 Luglio 2011 n. 120 (Legge Golfo-Mosca)'''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pag. 716.</ref>.
* '''Testo Unico della Finanza (TUF / D.Lgs. 24 Febbraio 1998 n. 58)''': Art. 147-ter comma 1-ter, 147-quater comma 1-bis, 148 commi 1-bis & 4-bis (modificato dalla L. 160/2019 / Legge di Bilancio 2020)<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 717, 718.</ref>.
* '''Testo Unico delle Società a Partecipazione Pubblica (TUSPP / D.Lgs. 19 Agosto 2016 n. 175)''': Articolo 11 comma 4<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 718, 719.</ref>.
* '''Legge 5 Novembre 2021 n. 162''': Modifiche al Codice delle Pari Opportunità (D.Lgs. 11 Aprile 2006 n. 198)<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 715, 721, 735.</ref>.
* '''D.P.R. 30 Novembre 2012 n. 251''': Regolamento di attuazione della Legge Golfo-Mosca per le società pubbliche<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pag. 718.</ref>.
* '''Decreto-Legge 31 Maggio 2021 n. 77 (Art. 47)''' e '''D.M. 29 Aprile 2022''' (Certificazione di Genere negli Appalti PNRR)<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 729, 735, 736.</ref>.

=== Normativa Settoriale Bancaria e Assicurativa ===
* '''Banca d'Italia Disposizioni 285/2013 (Aggiornamento 35 / 30 Giugno 2021)''': Quota minima del 33% per il genere meno rappresentato negli organi di amministrazione e controllo delle banche<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 719, 720.</ref>.
* '''Decreto Ministero dello Sviluppo Economico (MISE) 2 Maggio 2022 n. 88 (Art. 11)''': Quota minima del 33% per gli organi delle imprese di assicurazione<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pag. 720.</ref>.

=== Direttive dell'Unione Europea e Internazionali ===
* '''Direttiva (UE) 2022/2381 (Direttiva Women on Boards)''': Target del 40% per amministratori non esecutivi o 33% sul totale degli amministratori entro il 2026<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 715, 737, 740.</ref>.
* '''Carta dei Diritti Fondamentali dell'UE''' (Art. 21, 23) e '''TFUE''' Art. 157(3)<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 739, 740.</ref>.
* '''Obiettivi di Sviluppo Sostenibile dell'ONU (SDGs Goal 5 / Agenda 2030)'''<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 717, 730.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Chiave e Tre Pilastri di Politica ===
1. '''Innalzamento della Quota al 2/5 (40%) per Società Quotate e Pubbliche''': La L. 160/2019 e la L. 162/2021 hanno elevato la riserva di posti per il genere meno rappresentato dal 1/3 al 2/5 (40%) per sei mandati consecutivi (18 anni) negli organi amministrativi delle società quotate e a controllo pubblico<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 718, 721, 722.</ref>.
2. '''Estensione Settoriale a Banche e Assicurazioni''': Banca d'Italia e MISE hanno stabilito la soglia minima del 33% negli organi di gestione e controllo di tutte le banche e compagnie assicurative per migliorare la governance del rischio<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 719, 720, 721.</ref>.
3. '''Certificazione della Parità di Genere e Incentivi PNRR''': La L. 162/2021 ha introdotto la certificazione della parità di genere (gender diversity rating) legata alla Missione 5 del PNRR, che prevede lo sgravio contributivo per i datori di lavoro (fino a €50.000/anno) e premialità nei punteggi dei bandi di gara pubblici<ref>Callegari et al. (2022), pagg. 715, 729, 735, 736.</ref>.

'''Framing Migration, Population and Legal Orders: The Integration Puzzle in Italy Policy Framework''' (officially translated into Indonesian as ''Kerangka Kebijakan Hukum dan Peradilan Integrasi Migrasi, Demografi, dan Tata Kelola Administrasi di Italia dan Uni Eropa'') is a comparative administrative law and policy framework authored by Hilde Caroli Casavola to examine structural barriers, regulatory gaps (the "multiple gaps scenario"), and bureaucratic dysfunction in migrant integration across Italy and the European Union <ref>Caroli Casavola, H. (2023). Framing Migration, Population and Legal Orders: The Integration Puzzle in Italy. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 15(2), 201–253.</ref>. The framework evaluates the interaction between the EU asylum regime (Dublin System, New European Pact on Asylum and Migration), Italian national policy (Consolidated Immigration Act/UTI, Decreto Flussi, Decreto Salvini, Decreto Lamorgese), depopulation in interior and rural areas (inner areas / small municipalities), the reception system (SAI and CAS), and collaborative governance models (''amministrazione condivisa'') with the Third Sector (''Terzo Settore'') based on Italian Constitutional Court Judgments No. 131/2020 and No. 52/2021 <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 201, 205, 226, 234, 250.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Authored by [[Hilde Caroli Casavola]], Professor of Administrative Law at the [[University of Molise]], this study analyzes the complex interaction between migration, demographic decline, and the legal frameworks for integration in Italy and the EU <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), p. 201.</ref>. The framework highlights a "multiple gaps scenario" comprising labor law gaps, demographic gaps, and social welfare gaps in Italy <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 226, 231, 234, 241.</ref>. The author advocates for shifting from short-term emergency approaches toward long-term structural integration planning that links migrant settlement to the revitalization of depopulated inner areas through collaborative public administration with the Third Sector (''amministrazione condivisa'') <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 234, 240, 249, 250.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
The policy and legal foundation of this framework rests upon EU supranational instruments and Italian constitutional jurisprudence:
* '''[[Treaty on European Union]] (Articles 79 & 80 TEU)''' & '''[[Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union]] (Article 298 TFEU)''': Governs EU competence in immigration/asylum policies and the principle of European administrative efficiency <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 205, 253.</ref>.
* '''[[Constitution of Italy|1948 Constitution of the Italian Republic]]''':
** ''Articles 2 & 3'': Guarantees inviolable human rights and substantive equality <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 222, 242.</ref>.
** ''Articles 32, 34, & 38'': Guarantees rights to health, education, and social assistance <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 242, 243.</ref>.
** ''Articles 117 & 118'': Legislative competence allocation between State and Regions and the principle of horizontal subsidiarity <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 242, 250.</ref>.
* '''[[Consolidated Law on Immigration]] (Legislative Decree No. 286/1998 - UTI)''': Primary Italian immigration statute (specifically Articles 5-bis, 22, 40) <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 228, 231, 245.</ref>.
* '''[[Regulation (EU) 2021/2115]] (CAP Strategic Plans)''': Article 14 / Amendment No. 732 establishing the Social Conditionality Clause to combat agricultural labor exploitation (''caporalato'') <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 232, 233.</ref>.
* '''Key Jurisprudence''':
** ''Italian Constitutional Court'': Judgment No. 252/2001 (core right to health for all), Judgments No. 106/2018 & 44/2020 (striking down discriminatory residence length requirements for social housing), Judgment No. 186/2020 (right to civil registry enrollment for asylum seekers), and Judgments No. 131/2020 & 52/2021 (legitimizing ''amministrazione condivisa'') <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 243, 244, 245, 250.</ref>.
** ''Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU)'': Case C-502/10 (''Mangat Singh'') and Case C-303/19 (equal access to family allowances) <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 223, 244.</ref>.

== Background & Dublin System Failures ==
The EU Dublin System, which assigns primary responsibility to the member state of first entry, creates an asymmetric burden on coastal Mediterranean states such as Italy, Greece, Spain, and Malta <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 207, 208, 217.</ref>. The failure of mandatory relocation mechanisms and delays surrounding the New European Pact on Asylum and Migration leave thousands of migrants in prolonged legal limbo <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 209, 212, 215.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Address the "multiple gaps scenario" across labor market access, demographic renewal, and welfare rights in Italy <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 226, 231, 241.</ref>.
* Integrate migrant settlement into the National Strategy for Inner Areas (NSIA/SNAI) to counter depopulation in small rural municipalities <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 234, 239, 240.</ref>.
* Implement collaborative governance models (''amministrazione condivisa'') between public institutions and the Third Sector based on horizontal subsidiarity <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 249, 250.</ref>.

== Scope & Key Provisions ==
* '''Critique of Decreto Flussi & Labor Gaps''': The quota-based ''Decreto Flussi'' system and the requirement for job offers prior to entry (Art. 22 UTI) are unrealistic, causing severe administrative backlogs at local Prefectures (''Prefetture'') and pushing workers into informal employment <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 228, 231, 248.</ref>.
* '''Reception Regimes (SAI vs. CAS)''': The municipal-based System for Reception and Integration (''SAI'') offers comprehensive support, but remains underutilized compared to the emergency-driven Temporary Reception Centers (''CAS''), which lack long-term integration services <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 236–240.</ref>.
* '''Collaborative Governance (Judgment No. 131/2020)''': Confirms that public bodies can directly co-design and co-program social integration services with Third Sector entities outside standard commercial procurement models <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), p. 250.</ref>.

== Administrative Dysfunctions ==
* '''Prefectural Bottlenecks''': Delays in issuing work authorizations (''nulla-osta'') by Prefectures lead to situations where migrant workers who have completed pre-departure training programs in Africa are unable to obtain entry visas in time, harming domestic business operations <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 247, 248, 249.</ref>.

== Focus Named Entities & Related Entities ==
* '''[[Hilde Caroli Casavola]]''': Main author and Professor of Administrative Law at the University of Molise <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), p. 201.</ref>.
* '''[[SAI]] (Sistema di accoglienza e integrazione)''': Municipal-led reception and integration system <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 234, 238, 240.</ref>.
* '''[[European Union Agency for Asylum]] (EUAA)''': EU asylum regulatory agency <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 219, 220.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 201–253.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 201–253.</ref>

'''Framing Migration, Population and Legal Orders: The Integration Puzzle in Italy Policy Framework''' (denominato ufficialmente in italiano ''Kerangka Kebijakan Hukum dan Peradilan Integrasi Migrasi, Demografi, dan Tata Kelola Administrasi di Italia dan Uni Eropa'') è un quadro di analisi di diritto amministrativo comparato e politiche pubbliche elaborato da Hilde Caroli Casavola per esaminare gli ostacoli strutturali, i vuoti normativi (il "scenario dei divari multipli") e le disfunzioni burocratiche nell'integrazione dei migranti in Italia e nell'Unione Europea <ref>Caroli Casavola, H. (2023). Framing Migration, Population and Legal Orders: The Integration Puzzle in Italy. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 15(2), 201–253.</ref>. Il quadro valuta l'interazione tra il regime di asilo dell'UE (Sistema di Dublino, Nuovo Patto europeo sulla migrazione e l'asilo), la normativa nazionale italiana (Testo Unico sull'Immigrazione, Decreto Flussi, Decreto Salvini, Decreto Lamorgese), l'impatto dello spopolamento nelle aree interne e rurali (piccoli comuni), il ruolo del sistema di accoglienza (SAI e CAS) e i modelli di amministrazione condivisa con il Terzo Settore sulla base delle Sentenze della Corte Costituzionale n. 131/2020 e n. 52/2021 <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 201, 205, 226, 234, 250.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Scritto da [[Hilde Caroli Casavola]], Professoressa di Diritto Amministrativo presso l'[[Università degli Studi del Molise]], questo studio analizza le complesse interrelazioni tra migrazione, calo demografico e quadro giuridico dell'integrazione in Italia e nell'UE <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), p. 201.</ref>. La ricerca evidenzia il "scenario dei divari multipli" (divario lavorativo, demografico e di welfare) <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 226, 231, 234, 241.</ref>. L'autrice propone il passaggio da un approccio emergenziale di breve termine a una programmazione strutturale dell'integrazione, integrando i migranti nelle strategie di rivitalizzazione delle aree interne tramite la collaborazione tra amministrazione pubblica e Terzo Settore (amministrazione condivisa) <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 234, 240, 249, 250.</ref>.

== Basi Giuridiche ==
Il quadro di politica giuridica trova fondamento negli strumenti sovranazionali dell'UE e nel diritto costituzionale italiano:
* '''[[Trattato sull'Unione Europea]] (Articoli 79 e 80 TUE)''' e '''[[Trattato sul Funzionamento dell'Unione Europea]] (Articolo 298 TFUE)''': Regolano le competenze dell'UE in materia di immigrazione/asilo e il principio dell'efficienza amministrativa europea <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 205, 253.</ref>.
* '''[[Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana|Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana del 1948]]''':
** ''Articoli 2 e 3'': Garanzia dei diritti inviolabili dell'uomo e uguaglianza sostanziale <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 222, 242.</ref>.
** ''Articoli 32, 34 e 38'': Diritto alla salute, all'istruzione e all'assistenza sociale <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 242, 243.</ref>.
** ''Articoli 117 e 118'': Riparto della potestà legislativa Stato-Regioni e principio di sussidiarietà orizzontale <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 242, 250.</ref>.
* '''[[Testo Unico sull'Immigrazione]] (Decreto Legislativo 25 luglio 1998, n. 286 - TUI)''': Normativa fondamentale in materia di immigrazione (in particolare gli artt. 5-bis, 22, 40) <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 228, 231, 245.</ref>.
* '''[[Regolamento (UE) 2021/2115]] (Piani Strategici della PAC)''': Articolo 14 / Emendamento n. 732 relativo alla clausola di condizionalità sociale per contrastare il caporalato <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 232, 233.</ref>.
* '''Giurisprudenza Principale''':
** ''Corte Costituzionale'': Sentenza n. 252/2001 (nucleo irriducibile del diritto alla salute), Sentenze n. 106/2018 e n. 44/2020 (illegittimità dei requisiti di residenza prolungata per l'edilizia residenziale pubblica), Sentenza n. 186/2020 (iscrizione anagrafica per i richiedenti asilo) e Sentenze n. 131/2020 e n. 52/2021 (amministrazione condivisa) <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 243, 244, 245, 250.</ref>.
** ''Corte di Giustizia dell'Unione Europea (CGUE)'': Causa C-502/10 (''Mangat Singh'') e Causa C-303/19 (parità di trattamento negli assegni familiari) <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 223, 244.</ref>.

== Contesto e Criticità del Sistema di Dublino ==
Il Sistema di Dublino dell'UE, imponendo la responsabilità al paese di primo ingresso, genera uno squilibrio sproporzionato a carico dei paesi costieri del Mediterraneo (Italia, Grecia, Spagna, Malta) <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 207, 208, 217.</ref>. La mancanza di meccanismi effettivi di ricollocazione obbligatoria e i ritardi nell'adozione del Nuovo Patto europeo sulla migrazione e l'asilo lasciano migliaia di migranti in una condizione di incertezza giuridica <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 209, 212, 215.</ref>.

== Obiettivi ==
* Superare il "scenario dei divari multipli" nell'accesso al mercato del lavoro, nella demografia e nei diritti sociali in Italia <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 226, 231, 241.</ref>.
* Integrare l'accoglienza dei migranti nella Strategia Nazionale per le Aree Interne (SNAI) per contrastare lo spopolamento dei piccoli comuni <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 234, 239, 240.</ref>.
* Sviluppare modelli di amministrazione condivisa tra istituzioni pubbliche e Terzo Settore fondati sulla sussidiarietà orizzontale <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 249, 250.</ref>.

== Ambito e Disposizioni Principali ==
* '''Critica al Decreto Flussi e Divario Lavorativo''': Il sistema delle quote del Decreto Flussi e il requisito della chiamata dall'estero (Art. 22 TUI) si dimostrano irrealistici, causando ritardi burocratici presso le Prefetture e alimentando il lavoro sommerso <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 228, 231, 248.</ref>.
* '''Accoglienza SAI vs. CAS''': Il Sistema di Accoglienza e Integrazione (''SAI''), gestito dai comuni, garantisce servizi completi di integrazione, ma risulta ridimensionato rispetto ai Centri di Accoglienza Straordinaria (''CAS''), a carattere prevalente ed emergenziale <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 236–240.</ref>.
* '''Amministrazione Condivisa (Sentenza n. 131/2020)''': La Corte Costituzionale conferma la legittimità della co-programmazione e co-progettazione tra enti pubblici e Terzo Settore per i servizi di integrazione sociale al di fuori delle logiche di mercato e degli appalti pubblici <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), p. 250.</ref>.

== Disfunzioni Burocratiche ==
* '''Colli di Bottiglia nelle Prefetture''': I ritardi nel rilascio dei nulla-osta da parte delle Prefetture impediscono l'arrivo tempestivo di lavoratori stranieri formatisi nei paesi d'origine, arrecando danno al tessuto produttivo nazionale <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 247, 248, 249.</ref>.

== Entità Correlate e Stato degli Individui ==
* '''[[Hilde Caroli Casavola]]''': Autrice principale e Professoressa di Diritto Amministrativo presso l'Università degli Studi del Molise <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), p. 201.</ref>.
* '''[[SAI]] (Sistema di accoglienza e integrazione)''': Sistema di accoglienza gestito dagli enti locali <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 234, 238, 240.</ref>.
* '''[[European Union Agency for Asylum]] (EUAA)''': Agenzia dell'Unione europea per l'asilo <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 219, 220.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Non presente nelle fonti disponibili.]]'' <ref>Caroli Casavola (2023), pp. 201–253.</ref>

'''Keynote Speech by Marta Cartabia: Restorative Justice Paradigm in Italian Criminal Justice Reform Framework''' is a policy keynote address delivered by Marta Cartabia at the NYU School of Law Convocation Day (May 18, 2023, at Madison Square Garden) and published in the ''Italian Journal of Public Law'' (Vol. 15 Issue 2/2023). The speech details a reconceptualization of criminal justice policy from a retributive, "either-or" approach toward a restorative justice paradigm ("both-and" approach) <ref>Cartabia, M. (2023). Keynote Speech. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 15(2), 159–164.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Delivered by [[Marta Cartabia]], Professor of Constitutional Law at [[Bocconi University]] Milan, former President of the [[Italian Constitutional Court]], and former Minister of Justice of Italy, the address synthesizes policy reflections behind the Italian criminal justice system reform <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 159, 162–163.</ref>. Cartabia contends that justice must not be confined to a rigid retributive dichotomy ("an eye for an eye"), but must simultaneously deliver justice to victims while offering a second chance to offenders in service of human dignity and public safety <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 161–163.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
The framework is anchored in national constitutional norms and international recommendations:
* '''[[Constitution of the Italian Republic (1948)]]''': Guarantees human dignity, democratic institutions, separation of powers, and the Rule of Law <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 161.</ref>.
* '''[[Italian Criminal Justice Reform]]''': Codifies the restorative justice paradigm into statutory national criminal law <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 163.</ref>.
* '''[[European Union Recommendations on Restorative Justice]]''': Directives and policy instruments from EU institutions supporting restorative mechanisms <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 163.</ref>.

== Background & Historical Inspiration ==
The reform framework draws inspiration from three major historical milestones:
1. *European Integration (1948)*: The vision of [[Konrad Adenauer]], [[Robert Schuman]], and [[Alcide De Gasperi]] to build a legal community centered on solidarity rather than humiliation of defeated nations <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 160–161.</ref>.
2. *South African Reconciliation Experience*: The philosophy of [[Albie Sachs]] ("Soft Vengeance") and the South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission rejecting pure retributive revenge <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 161–163.</ref>.
3. *Italian Red Brigades Dialogue*: An 8-year mediated dialogue between victims and perpetrators of 1970s–80s terrorism (including the assassination of [[Aldo Moro]]) seeking memory restoration and social healing <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 162.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Shift criminal justice policy from a retributive "either/or" model to a restorative "both/and" approach <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 162, 163.</ref>.
* Address victims' need for timely justice while humanizing correctional conditions for offenders <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 163.</ref>.
* Refine judicial reasoning language through rights balancing and inter-institutional dialogue <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 162.</ref>.

== Scope ==
The framework spans Italian constitutional law, criminal justice reform, judicial interpretation, restorative justice, and European Union policy <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 159–164.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & Judicial Approach ==
* '''"Both/And" Judicial Reasoning''': Hard cases before courts must be resolved through balancing rights and reasonable accommodation rather than strict binary outcomes <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 162, 163.</ref>.
* '''Codification of Restorative Path''': Formalizing restorative mediation tracks as a complementary dimension within statutory criminal procedures <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 163.</ref>.

== Implementation ==
Operationalized through the enactment of the Italian Criminal Justice Reform under Cartabia's tenure as Minister of Justice, alongside constitutional rights-balancing jurisprudence rendered by the Italian Constitutional Court <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 162, 163.</ref>.

== Policy Issues & Unresolved Challenges ==
* '''Penitentiary Conditions and Human Rights''': The imperative to align prison conditions with fundamental human dignity standards <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 163.</ref>.
* '''Victim Satisfaction & Social Peace''': Ensuring restorative processes adequately resolve victim trauma without causing secondary victimization <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 161, 163.</ref>.

== Related Entities ==
* '''[[Marta Cartabia]]''': Keynote Speaker, Bocconi University Professor, and former Minister of Justice <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 159, 163.</ref>.
* '''[[Italian Constitutional Court]]''': Judicial body where Cartabia served as Judge and President <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 159, 162.</ref>.
* '''[[NYU School of Law]]''': Venue of the 2023 Convocation Day Keynote Address <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 159.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 159–164.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 159–164.</ref>

'''Il Discorso Inaugurale di Marta Cartabia: Il Paradigma della Giustizia Riparativa nella Riforma della Giustizia Penale Italiana''' (titolo originale inglese: ''Keynote Speech by Marta Cartabia: Restorative Justice Paradigm in Italian Criminal Justice Reform Framework'') è un discorso di indirizzo politico e accademico pronunciato da Marta Cartabia durante il Convocation Day della NYU School of Law (18 maggio 2023 presso il Madison Square Garden) e pubblicato nella rivista ''Italian Journal of Public Law'' (Vol. 15 Issue 2/2023). Il discorso illustra la riconcettualizzazione della politica criminale da un approccio puramente retributivo ("either-or approach") verso un paradigma di giustizia riparativa ("both-and approach") <ref>Cartabia, M. (2023). Keynote Speech. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 15(2), 159–164.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Tenuto da [[Marta Cartabia]], Rettrice e Professoressa di Diritto Costituzionale presso l'[[Università Bocconi]] di Milano, già Presidente della [[Corte Costituzionale]] e già Ministra della Giustizia della Repubblica Italiana, il discorso sintetizza la riflessione alla base della riforma del sistema penale italiano <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 159, 162–163.</ref>. Cartabia sostiene che la giustizia non debba ridursi a una rigida dicotomia punitiva ("occhio per occhio"), ma debba garantire il soddisfacimento dei diritti delle vittime offrendo contemporaneamente una seconda possibilità (*second chance*) al reo, a tutela della dignità umana e della sicurezza collettiva <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 161–163.</ref>.

== Basi Giuridiche ==
Il quadro di riferimento trova fondamento in principi costituzionali nazionali e atti sovranazionali:
* '''[[Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana (1948)]]''': Tutela la dignità della persona, le istituzioni democratiche, la separazione dei poteri e lo Stato di diritto (*Rule of Law*) <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 161.</ref>.
* '''[[Riforma della Giustizia Penale Italiana]]''': Integra il paradigma della giustizia riparativa all'interno del codice e del sistema processuale penale <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 163.</ref>.
* '''[[Raccomandazioni dell'Unione Europea sulla Giustizia Riparativa]]''': Atti e direttive delle istituzioni europee volti a promuovere i percorsi riparativi nei paesi membri <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 163.</ref>.

== Contesto e Ispirazione Storica ==
La visione alla base della riforma si articola su tre momenti storici fondamentali:
1. *L'Integrazione Europea (1948)*: L'iniziativa di [[Konrad Adenauer]], [[Robert Schuman]] e [[Alcide De Gasperi]] volta a fondare una comunità giuridica basata sulla solidarietà e sul superamento della logica di punizione dei vinti <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 160–161.</ref>.
2. *L'Esperienza Sudafricana di Riconciliazione*: Il pensiero di [[Albie Sachs]] (*Soft Vengeance*) e il lavoro della Commissione per la Verità e la Riconciliazione in Sudafrica <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 161–163.</ref>.
3. *Il Dialogo sulle Brigate Rosse in Italia*: Il percorso d'incontro durato 8 anni tra vittime e responsabili del terrorismo degli anni '70 e '80 (incluso il caso dell'assassinio di [[Aldo Moro]]) per la ricomposizione della memoria e delle ferite sociali <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 162.</ref>.

== Obiettivi ==
* Superare il modello di giustizia puramente punitivo (*either/or*) in favore di un approccio integrato (*both/and approach*) <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 162, 163.</ref>.
* Rispondere alle istanze di giustizia delle vittime garantendo al contempo la rieducazione e l'umanizzazione delle pene <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 163.</ref>.
* Arricchire il linguaggio del ragionamento giudiziario attraverso il bilanciamento dei diritti e il dialogo interistituzionale <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 162.</ref>.

== Ambito di Applicazione ==
Il discorso ricomprende temi di diritto costituzionale italiano, riforma della giustizia penale, ermeneutica giudiziaria, giustizia riparativa e diritto dell'Unione Europea <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 159–164.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Principali e Approccio Giudiziario ==
* '''Ragionamento Giudiziario "Both/And"''': La risoluzione dei casi complessi (*hard cases*) deve avvenire non mediante opzioni binarie escludenti, bensì attraverso il bilanciamento dei diritti e il ragionevole accomodamento <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 162, 163.</ref>.
* '''Istituzionalizzazione della Giustizia Riparativa''': L'introduzione formale di percorsi di mediazione riparativa paralleli al processo penale ordinario <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 163.</ref>.

== Attuazione ==
Tradotto in norma attraverso l'approvazione della Riforma della Giustizia Penale promossa durante il mandato di Cartabia come Ministra della Giustizia, unitamente all'applicazione dei principi di bilanciamento dei diritti nella giurisprudenza della Corte Costituzionale <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 162, 163.</ref>.

== Questioni Politiche e Problemi Aperti ==
* '''Condizioni Detentive e Diritti Umani''': La necessità di garantire condizioni carcerarie conformi al senso di umanità e alla dignità della persona <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 163.</ref>.
* '''Tutela delle Vittime e Pace Sociale''': Assicurare che la giustizia riparativa offra riposte concrete al dolore delle vittime evitando nuove forme di vittimizzazione <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 161, 163.</ref>.

== Entità Correlate ==
* '''[[Marta Cartabia]]''': Autrice del Discorso Inaugurale, Professoressa alla Bocconi e già Ministra della Giustizia <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 159, 163.</ref>.
* '''[[Corte Costituzionale]]''': Organo giudiziario in cui Cartabia ha svolto le funzioni di Giudice e Presidente <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 159, 162.</ref>.
* '''[[NYU School of Law]]''': Sede della cerimonia di laurea in cui è stato pronunciato il discorso <ref>Cartabia (2023), p. 159.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITÀ NON VERIFICABILE|Non presente nelle fonti disponibili.]]'' <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 159–164.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITÀ NON VERIFICABILE|Non presente nelle fonti disponibili.]]'' <ref>Cartabia (2023), pp. 159–164.</ref>

== 3. POLICY ANALYSIS ==

* '''Background:''' [FACT] Judicial decision-making has historically been viewed as a purely deliberative, rational application of legal rules. However, cutting-edge social cognitive neuroscience and cognitive psychology demonstrate that human brains rely heavily on automatic, unconscious processing to manage information overload. Building on a 2007 American Judges Association white paper on procedural fairness, Casey, Burke, and Leben synthesized neurocognitive science to provide trial and appellate judges with actionable strategies for mindful decision-making.
* '''Policy Problem / Cognitive Failures in Courts:''' [FACT] Judges working under heavy dockets, crowded calendars, and pressing emergency motions frequently default to automatic, reflexive thinking. This reliance on unexamined cognitive schemas introduces systematic errors:
 ''Faulty Heuristics:'' Judges succumb to anchoring (e.g., being swayed by arbitrary prosecutor demands or loaded dice throws in German sentencing experiments), narrow bracketing/streaks (judges reluctant to grant consecutive favorable decisions), framing, hindsight bias, and egocentric overconfidence.
 ''Implicit Biases:'' Unconscious racial and social stereotypes operate below conscious awareness, affecting white judges' reaction times on Implicit Association Tests (IAT) and influencing sentencing outcomes.
 ''Decision Fatigue & Resource Depletion:'' Sleep deprivation, multitasking, and low blood glucose levels degrade reflective capacity. The famous Israeli parole board study demonstrated that judges defaulted to denying parole as cases progressed, but reverted to granting parole immediately after meal breaks replenished glucose stores.
 ''Loss of Procedural Fairness:'' Distracted or rushed judges fail to give litigants "Voice" (an active, respectful hearing), undermining public compliance with court orders and trust in the judiciary.
* '''Legal / Policy Gap:''' [FACT / INTERPRETATION] Traditional judicial education lacked cognitive science integration, leaving judges unaware of how subconscious reflexive defaults, physical exhaustion, and docket-clearing pressures undermine procedural fairness and legal accuracy.
* '''Objectives:''' [FACT] Transform courtroom administration from a mechanical "case processing" model to a "mindful" procedural justice model that minimizes cognitive biases and maximizes litigant perceptions of fairness.
* '''Implementation & Actionable Strategies:''' [FACT] The paper details 5 specific reform strategies for judges and court administrators:

# ''Focusing on Purpose:'' Shift perspective from moving docket volume to delivering fair, individualized justice (e.g., Judge Judy Harris Kluger taking 2–3 extra minutes in community court to look defendants in the eye).

# ''Formalizing Decision Heuristics:'' Expose informal "rules of thumb" (such as matching heuristics in bail decisions) to critical review, standardization, and transparency.

# ''"Reading the Dials" & Mindfulness:'' Monitor physical distractions, fatigue, and courtroom temperature; adopt brief mindfulness pauses such as the STOP Meditation (Stop, Take a breath, Observe thoughts/feelings, Proceed with awareness).

# ''Using Decision Aids:'' Implement substantive and procedural checklists (modeled on Atul Gawande's medical checklists) and actuarial Risk and Needs Assessment tools to anchor reflective reasoning.

# ''Seeking Feedback & Fostering Accountability:'' Utilize CourTools survey measures, videotaped peer feedback, and mandatory written opinion writing ("asking why at each step") to heighten accuracy motivation.

* '''Evidence / Empirical Findings:''' [FACT]
 ''Procedural Fairness Impact:'' Litigants who feel heard (activating brain reward centers) exhibit significantly higher compliance with court orders and greater public satisfaction.
 ''Bias Suppression Capability:'' When judges are consciously aware of the need to monitor for implicit racial bias and are motivated to suppress it, they successfully eliminate bias in decision outcomes.
 ''Disfluency & Reflective Activation:'' Presenting information in harder-to-read formats or introducing metacognitive difficulty prompts the brain's reflective system to engage in deliberative processing.
 ''Actuarial vs. Intuitive Superiority:'' Statistical risk assessments consistently outperform intuitive judicial predictions by preventing reliance on spurious correlations or unrepresentative base rates.
* '''Impact:''' [FACT / INFERENCE] Serves as a foundational policy roadmap for state court systems across the United States to integrate implicit bias training, procedural justice benchcards, and mindfulness techniques into judicial education programs.
* '''Evaluation & Unresolved Issues:''' [FACT / INTERPRETATION] Challenges remain in overcoming judicial misconceptions that mindfulness is mystical or incompatible with legal skepticism, and in ensuring busy trial courts avoid using checklists as mechanical "box-checking" exercises without genuine litigant engagement.

'''One more constrained than the other: Asymmetrical ideological alignment and its implications for polarization''' is an empirical comparative political science and public policy research paper authored by Tadeas Cely of Masaryk University (Czech Republic), published in the ''European Journal of Political Research'' (EJPR) in 2025.

== Summary ==
This study tests the asymmetry of ideological alignment and belief constraint between left- and right-wing partisan camps across 15 European countries. Based on an analysis of 23,586 partisans from 131 political parties, using data from the European Social Survey (ESS 2008 & 2016), the Chapel Hill Expert Survey (CHES), and the Manifesto Project, the study demonstrates that left-wing partisans consistently show stronger belief alignment on economic issues than right-wing partisans. It further develops a theoretical model showing that the real extent of disagreement between two opposing partisan camps is bounded by the camp with weaker ideological alignment (the right).

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This document is an academic political science research study and is not based on any specific statutory or judicial legislative instrument [1–148].

== Background ==
Classic political science research assumed that ideological alignment makes voting decisions easier for citizens. However, recent scholarship shows that overly tight belief constraint fuels political stereotyping, the formation of echo chambers, and rising affective polarization. Prior literature generally assumed that ideological alignment is symmetric between left and right camps, without accounting for how asymmetry in belief structure affects the depth of political conflict.

== Objectives ==
1. Test the Ideological Asymmetry Hypothesis: ideological alignment is weaker among supporters of right-pole parties than left-pole parties (Hypothesis 1).
2. Test the Position Blurring Hypothesis: ideological alignment is stronger among supporters of parties with clearer ideological positions (Hypothesis 2).
3. Test the Programmatic Nicheness Hypothesis: ideological alignment is stronger among supporters of niche parties (Hypothesis 3).
4. Identify the implications of ideological asymmetry for the expansion and depth of partisan conflict in society.

== Scope ==
The research covers an analysis of 23,586 partisan respondents from 131 political parties across 15 European countries, divided into 7 party families: Radical Left, Green, Socialist, Liberal, Christian Democratic, Conservative, and Radical Right.

== Key Provisions / Findings ==
* '''Economic Dimension Asymmetry (Hypothesis 1 Supported):''' On the economic dimension, a 1-point rightward shift on a 10-point ideology scale reduces individual ideological alignment by B = -0.32 (SE = 0.07, p < 0.01), equivalent to disconnecting 1.5 policy attitudes from the party line.
* '''2016 Sociocultural Realignment:''' Sociocultural alignment showed strong left-wing asymmetry in 2008 (B = -0.43, SE = 0.09), but shifted to a symmetric, parabolic shape by 2016, in which extreme right-wing partisans reached a high alignment level (0.7) matching that of extreme left-wing partisans (0.6).
* '''Belief Network Interconnectedness (GEI):''' Left-wing party families show belief-network interconnectedness that is '''10% to 47% higher''' than right-wing families. The Radical Left recorded the highest network density (GEI = 7.69, 61% significant ties), followed by Socialists (GEI = 7.18) and Greens (GEI = 6.63). The Radical Right recorded the lowest density (GEI = 5.22, only 27% significant ties; p < 0.001).
* '''Limited Effects of Position Blurring and Nicheness:''' Position blurring significantly reduced economic alignment in 2016 (B = -1.1, SE = 0.33) but had no effect on sociocultural alignment. Programmatic nicheness showed only a modest non-linear effect on economic alignment.
* '''Model of Partisan Conflict Containment:''' The overall breadth of substantive disagreement between two opposing camps is determined by the belief density of the '''less-aligned camp''' (the right). Political polarization can only expand to cover more issues if belief constraint deepens within right-wing partisan camps.

== Implementation ==
The methodology was implemented through three-level multilevel linear regression (individuals, parties, countries) and Gaussian graphical belief-network modeling using EBIC glasso regularization and NetworkComparisonTest. Replication code and data are published openly on GitHub at `https://github.com/tadeascely/one_more_constrained`.

== Policy Issues ==
1. Rising intergroup intolerance driven by group homogeneity and echo-chamber formation within the highly aligned left camp.
2. The potential expansion of political conflict into sociocultural domains as ideological alignment increases within the radical right.

== Reform / Implications ==
The study shows that understanding mass polarization requires accounting for asymmetry in belief structure, in which the consolidation of a comprehensive narrative on the political right is the key determinant of escalating partisan conflict.

'''European Commission for the Efficiency of Justice''' (*Commission Européenne Pour l'Efficacité de la Justice* – '''CEPEJ''') is an intergovernmental body headquartered in Strasbourg, France, established by the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe. CEPEJ is tasked with gathering knowledge, facilitating the exchange of operational analysis, and improving the efficiency, quality, and timeliness of national justice systems across the Council of Europe's 47 member states (including all 27 EU member states), with the ultimate goal of reducing case backlogs at the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) without lowering standards of legal protection.

== Summary ==
Established around 2002, CEPEJ was formed in response to a workload crisis at the ECtHR, where the number of applications surged from 8,400 cases in 1999 to 57,200 cases in 2009, with a total backlog reaching 119,300 applications. In its operations, CEPEJ established the Centre for the Study and Analysis of Judicial Time Use Research Network (SATURN) and a Working Group on Quality of Justice. CEPEJ employs a methodology of close collaboration among academics, judges, and judicial civil servants, led by its Bureau (Fausto de Santis and John Stacey) and Secretariat (Stéphane Leyenberger).

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Resolution of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe:''' The basis for establishing CEPEJ as a judicial efficiency commission headquartered in Strasbourg.
* '''European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR):''' The international legal framework guaranteeing the right to a fair and timely trial.
* '''Protocol No. 14 to the European Convention on Human Rights:''' Entered into force on 10 June, enabling the ECtHR to adapt its internal organization and proceedings to manage a massive volume of applications.

== Background & Policy Issues ==
The backlog crisis at the ECtHR threatened the effectiveness of Europe's human rights protection system. ECtHR jurisprudence consistently affirms that, while timeliness and fairness of trial fall under ECHR oversight, the internal organization of courts remains within the sovereign authority of individual member states. CEPEJ was created to bridge this gap by helping modernize judicial organization at the national level.

=== ECtHR Application Backlog Statistics (1999–2009) ===
* '''1999:''' 8,400 applications allocated.
* '''2003:''' 27,200 applications allocated; ~65,000 applications pending.
* '''2009:''' 57,200 applications allocated; total backlog rose to '''119,300 applications'''.

== Scope & Key Initiatives ==
1. '''Judicial Time Use Research Network (SATURN):''' A center for analytical study of case-processing time and duration in courts.
2. '''Working Group on Quality of Justice:''' Develops quality standards for judicial management and service delivery.
3. '''Tripartite Collaboration:''' Fosters ongoing cooperation among academics, judges, and Ministry of Justice officials.
4. '''Public Repository:''' All CEPEJ analyses and guidelines are published openly at `www.coe.int/cepej`.

== Policy Issues ==
* The need to balance improved judicial administrative efficiency with maintaining high standards of legal protection.
* The diversity of legal infrastructures across 47 member states, most of which follow civil law traditions.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Council of Europe & ECtHR:''' The parent organization and the tribunal that is the subject of the efficiency assistance.
* '''IJCA & IACA:''' Scholarly publishing and international court administration research partners.

'''The European Commission for the Efficiency of Justice (CEPEJ) Reform & Judicial Evaluation Framework''' is a policy framework, statistical evaluation mechanism, and judicial reform instrument established by the Council of Europe (CoE) via Resolution Res(2002)12. It was created to formulate standards, indicators, and time management tools to optimize the quality, effectiveness, and speed of judicial systems across the 47 CoE member states, based on the standards of Articles 5, 6, and 13 of the ''European Convention on Human Rights'' (ECHR) [1–3, 7–8, 11–12].

== Summary ==
Published by Prof. dr. juris Jon T. Johnsen (University of Oslo) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this policy framework evaluates the first decade of CEPEJ's operations since its establishment in 2002. Formed in response to a backlog crisis at the ''European Court of Human Rights'' (ECtHR) related to trial delays, CEPEJ performs functions such as collecting comparative judicial statistical data (''GT-EVAL'') and drafting trial time management guidelines (''SATURN Centre'') [1, 2, 5, 17–19, 43]. This framework triggered the application of reasonable time trial standards across 47 CoE member states without acting as a rigid supervisory body (''non-supervisory body'').

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe Resolution Res(2002)12:''' The founding statute of CEPEJ, adopted on September 18, 2002.
* '''European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR):'''
** ''Article 6:'' The right to a fair trial and the resolution of cases within a reasonable time.
** ''Article 5:'' The right to liberty and security of person.
** ''Article 13:'' The right to an effective remedy at the national level.
* '''ECtHR Jurisprudence:''' Landmark judgments such as ''Hadjidjanis v. Greece (2005)'', ''Scordino v. Italy (2006)'', and ''Airy v. Ireland (1979)'' [11, 66, 78–79].
* '''EU Accession Criteria (Copenhagen Criteria):''' CEPEJ judicial standards are used as a benchmark for the eligibility of EU candidate states.

== Background ==
In the early 2000s, the ECtHR experienced a functional crisis due to a backlog of over 72,000 cases. The vast majority of these complaints originated from citizens protesting the excessive length of judicial proceedings in Southern and Eastern Europe [5–6]. The paradox that the very court designed to protect ECHR rights could not fulfill the principle of a speedy trial prompted the Council of Europe to establish CEPEJ to reform national judicial systems from their roots.

== Objectives ==
1. Examine the results achieved by different judicial systems through reliable statistical evaluation methods.
2. Identify problems and facilitate the exchange of experiences in court governance.
3. Formulate time management instruments to combat trial delays.
4. Provide technical assistance to member states requiring adjustments to meet ECHR standards.

== Scope ==
This policy encompasses the 47 member states of the Council of Europe (covering >800 million citizens). The biennial statistical evaluation (''European Judicial Survey'') collects over 2.5 million data entries from 46 participating states [18–19].

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Four Main Organs of CEPEJ:''' The Plenary (gathering representatives from all member states twice a year), the Bureau (4 elected members), Expert Working Groups (such as GT-EVAL and SATURN), and the CoE Secretariat.
* '''Reasonable Time Benchmarks:''' ECtHR standards set tolerance limits: Ordinary criminal cases (<5 years); Priority civil cases (<2 years); Complex civil cases (<8 years).
* '''EUGMONT & Time Management Checklist:''' Standardized statistical guidelines for monitoring case workflows and providing early warnings of potential delays [48–49].
* '''Legal Aid Principles:''' Based on ''Airy v. Ireland'', legal aid must be provided to impoverished citizens in complex civil and criminal cases.

== Implementation ==
* '''SATURN Centre (Judicial Time Management):''' Drafted the ''Framework Programme'', optimum duration guidelines, and a ''Best Practice Compendium'' based on pilot court research.
* '''Application of Gentle Persuasion:''' Encouraging voluntary national judicial reforms without the direct application of legal sanctions.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Legal Aid Shortcoming:''' CEPEJ is criticized for not prioritizing legal aid schemes, leading to extreme disparities (e.g., Albania allocated €0.01 per capita while Northern Ireland allocated €54 per capita).
* '''Unavailability of Real Time Data:''' The majority of member states do not yet record the ''real handling time'' of each case, forcing reliance on ''disposition time'' estimates [56–57, 61–62].

== Reform / Change ==
* Shifting CEPEJ's strategic focus from drafting new guidelines toward prioritizing the implementation of existing instruments in the field [13, 64–65].
* Strengthening direct dialogue between CEPEJ and the ECtHR so that SATURN instruments are consistently referenced in judgments concerning Article 6 ECHR violations.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Council of Europe (CoE):''' The parent organization that founded CEPEJ.
* '''European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR):''' The judicial body enforcing the ECHR, which references CEPEJ instruments [5, 78–79].
* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]:''' ''Not found in the available sources.'' [FACT] [1–85].
