'''The CEPEJ European Judicial Systems Evaluation Policy Framework''' is a transnational judicial evaluation policy framework and comparative performance benchmarking model developed by the European Commission for the Efficiency of Justice (CEPEJ) and reviewed by Ingo Keilitz (CourtMetrics & College of William and Mary, 2015) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA). Based on the ''European Judicial Systems – Edition 2014 (2012 Data)'' report (521 pages, 45 Council of Europe member states), it establishes a 208-indicator survey utilizing home-grown evidence-based data to measure efficiency, budget allocation, e-justice, leadership, and the quality of judicial services [2–6, 12–13].

== Summary ==
Published by Ingo Keilitz in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this policy framework evaluates the fifth edition of the CEPEJ Report, ''European Judicial Systems – Edition 2014 (2012 Data)''. Collecting data from 45 Council of Europe countries through a verified 208-indicator survey, the report presents an in-depth analysis of judicial budgets, e-justice, procedural simplification, case clearance rates, and the glass ceiling constraints faced by female judges. Keilitz demonstrates the superiority of the CEPEJ methodology, which relies on valid, home-grown government data, compared to global donor indices (such as WJP or UNDP) [12–13]. This methodology was successfully replicated to benchmark the judicial reform project in Kenya (''Judicial Performance Improvement Project'') under Chief Justice Willy Mutunga.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Statute of the Council of Europe & CEPEJ Mandate:''' The institutional foundation establishing CEPEJ as the expert body for European judicial evaluation.
* '''CEPEJ 208-Item Survey Framework:''' The standardized instrument for measuring judicial efficiency and quality.
* '''Kenya Judicial Performance Improvement Project (2012):''' The judicial transformation framework of Kenya based on CEPEJ benchmarks.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
The critical need for transparent and measurable judicial performance data prompted the Council of Europe to establish CEPEJ. The CEPEJ biennial report has become the primary reference for policymakers and legal researchers worldwide [2–3].

== Objectives ==
1. Provide a verified database regarding judicial efficiency and quality across 45 European countries [2–3].
2. Facilitate comparative analysis (benchmarking) of judicial performance at both regional and global levels [10–11].
3. Encourage the utilization of home-grown data to support sustainable judicial reforms [12–13].

== Scope ==
This policy encompasses the evaluation of judicial systems across 45 Council of Europe member states, budgetary indicators, e-court operations, and the comparative application of judicial performance metrics outside Europe (specifically, Kenya).

== Key Provisions ==
* '''208-Indicator Evaluation Methodology:'''
** Measurements include the supply side (e.g., budgets and court buildings) as well as the demand side (e.g., case clearance rates and disposition times).
** Data is collected by national correspondents and directly verified by the CEPEJ expert team.
* '''Key Trends Output (Chapter 18 of the CEPEJ Report):'''
# Judicial budgets remain a public priority despite economic crises, though investments are uneven.
# Expansion of e-justice and e-courts (e-filing, automated case registration, electronic signatures, and jurisprudence databases).
# Implementation of simplified procedures for undisputed civil claims and minor criminal offenses.
# The excessive length of judicial proceedings remains a primary challenge.
# The glass ceiling phenomenon for women in the judiciary persists.

== Implementation ==
* '''Publication of the 2014 CEPEJ Report:''' A 521-page biennial evaluation containing over 250 tables and figures [2–3].
* '''Benchmarking the Kenyan Judiciary:''' Replication of the CEPEJ methodology by Ingo Keilitz to measure the performance of the ''Judicial Performance Improvement Project'' under Chief Justice Willy Mutunga.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Excessive Length of Proceedings:''' Delays in case handling that severely disrupt access to justice.
* '''Dominance of Top-down Donor Indicators:''' The risk of reform failure due to the reliance on third-party global indices (WJP/UNDP) that fail to reflect local realities [12–13].

== Reform / Change ==
* The adoption of home-grown performance management systems by national judiciaries.
* The critical need for procedural simplification and the expansion of e-court automation.

'''How do parties react to defections? Electoral strategies after a valence loss''' is an empirical comparative political science and public policy research paper authored by Andrea Ceron (University of Milan) and Elisa Volpi (University of Geneva), published in the ''European Journal of Political Research'' (EJPR) in 2022.

== Summary ==
This study analyzes how political parties across 14 Western European democracies respond to parliamentary defections in shaping their election manifestos. Treating defections as a form of "valence loss" that damages leadership reputation, credibility, and party brand, the study tests changes in manifesto strategy across 135 political parties through an analysis of 1,131 manifestos spanning 1945 to 2015. The findings show that parties experiencing defections respond by strengthening their emphasis on competence, increasing programmatic clarity, reducing issue diversity, and focusing on the core issues they already own [7, 42, 45, 53–54].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This document is an academic political science research study and is not based on any specific statutory or judicial legislative instrument [1–95].
* '''Parliamentary Party Discipline Rules:''' The study analyzes parliamentary defection within the framework of the Responsible Party Government model and electoral accountability [4, 11, 51–52].

== Background ==
Internal cohesion is a crucial asset for political parties in delivering on campaign promises and maintaining electoral accountability. When MPs switch parties or form new groupings, voters and prospective coalition partners face greater uncertainty about the party's true positions and commitments. Classic spatial competition literature generally examined only shifts along the left-right ideological spectrum. This research fills that gap by examining the non-positional manifesto strategies parties use to repair damaged valence reputation.

== Objectives ==
1. Test Hypothesis 1: the greater the extent of defections a party suffers, the higher the emphasis on competence in its next manifesto.
2. Test Hypothesis 2: the greater the extent of defections a party suffers, the greater the programmatic clarity of its next manifesto.
3. Test Hypotheses 3A & 3B: defections reduce issue diversity and increase emphasis on the party's core issues [28–29, 38].

== Scope ==
The research covers a cross-national database of 2,053 legislators involved in 611 annual defection episodes across 14 Western European countries (Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom) between 1945 and 2015.

== Key Provisions / Findings ==
* '''Hypothesis 1 Supported (Competence Emphasis):''' Past defections significantly increase the share of manifesto content devoted to competence to govern (β = +3.18, p < 0.05; IV model p < 0.01).
* '''Hypothesis 2 Supported (Programmatic Clarity):''' Defections increase programmatic clarity (β = +4.70, p < 0.10; IV model p < 0.05), showing that damaged parties abandon ambiguity in favor of clear commitments.
* '''Hypotheses 3A & 3B Supported (Streamlining & Issue Specialization):''' Defections significantly reduce issue diversity (β = -2.30, p < 0.05) and increase focus on the party's owned core issues (β = +5.79, p < 0.05).
* '''Latent Reputation Index:''' Defections have a strong positive effect on the composite reputation index (β = +0.73, p < 0.001).

== Implementation ==
The methodology was implemented through three-level linear random-intercept models (manifestos, parties, countries) with control variables including RILE placement, government status, party size, party age, and electoral volatility [41–42, 45–46]. Endogeneity was addressed using an Instrumental Variable approach (`Switches IV`) based on structural defection determinants. Manifesto data were sourced from MARPOR/CMP (WZB Berlin).

== Policy Issues ==
1. Damage to party brand and label caused by leadership's inability to maintain parliamentary cohesion.
2. The risk of ambiguous "broad-appeal" strategies failing for fractured parties, as illustrated by the UK Labour Party's 2019 election on Brexit [22–23, 56–58].

== Reform / Implications ==
1. Encouraging parties that experience defections to adopt streamlined, clear campaign messaging focused on governing competence.
2. Strengthening specialization in owned core issues to rebuild trust among voters and prospective coalition partners.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''European Consortium for Political Research (ECPR) & John Wiley & Sons Ltd.:''' Publisher of the EJPR journal.
* '''WZB Berlin / Manifesto Project (CMP/MARPOR):''' Provider of manifesto data.
* '''Cecep Mustafa:''' Not found in the available sources [1–95].

'''The CFMnet Project & Dutch Judicial Quality and Innovation Policy Framework''' is a civil caseflow management governance policy and evaluation framework assessing the added value of the European Union research project 'CFMnet' (''Towards European Caseflow Management Development Network'') for the civil and administrative judicial reform program ''Kwaliteit en Innovatie'' (KEI/QAI) in the Netherlands. Formulated by Thomas de Weers (Utrecht University, 2016) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), Vol. 8 No. 1, it maps European caseflow best practices—such as financial incentives for mediation, centralized judicial expert management, real-time performance monitoring, and audio-visual courtroom recordings—to address cost overruns, schedule delays, and digitalization hurdles in the Dutch judiciary [1–36].

== Summary ==
Published by Thomas de Weers in the IJCA (October 2016), this policy framework evaluates the practical utility of the EU's caseflow management research (the ''CFMnet Project'') for the Dutch civil justice reform program named ''Kwaliteit en Innovatie'' (KEI/QAI) [1–4]. Managed by the Ministry of Security and Justice and the Council for the Judiciary (''Raad voor de Rechtspraak''), the KEI program aimed to replace the paper- and fax-based judicial system with an integrated digital procedure via the ''MijnZaak'' and ''MijnWerkomgeving'' portals [8–10, 14–16]. However, the KEI project faced legislative delays, opposition from the Netherlands Bar Association (NOvA), and a severe ICT budget blowout escalating from €60 million to €200 million [15–20]. De Weers categorizes the practices from the ''CFMnet Handbook'' into four groups for the Netherlands: (1) ''Quick Wins'' (e.g., daily internal publication of judge performance statistics from Germany and audio-visual recordings replacing written transcripts from Spain/Portugal); (2) ''Long-Term High-Value Innovations'' (e.g., centralized judicial expert management from Antwerp and real-time timeframe alarm systems from Finland); (3) Practices already implemented in the Netherlands; and (4) Irrelevant practices such as the restriction of appeal rights [21–31].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''KEI/QAI Reform Program (Kamerstukken II 2014-15, 34 059, no. 3):''' The legislative act simplifying and digitizing civil procedure, passed by the Dutch Senate on July 12, 2016.
* '''EU CFMnet Research Project (EU Action Grant JUST/2013):''' The European Union framework for identifying and disseminating civil caseflow best practices across 12 member states.
* '''Wetboek van Burgerlijke Rechtsvordering (Rv) & Algemene wet bestuursrecht (Awb):''' The Dutch Code of Civil Procedure and General Administrative Law Act.
* '''CEPEJ Saturn Guidelines (Council of Europe):''' International reference frameworks for judicial time and caseflow management.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
Despite ranking 1st globally in civil justice according to the World Justice Project 2015, the Dutch judiciary lagged significantly in digitalization, relying heavily on physical paper files and fax machines for daily communications compared to other European nations.

== Objectives ==
1. Transform complicated, expensive, and time-consuming Dutch civil procedures into standardized, user-friendly digital processes.
2. Unify the summons procedure (''dagvaardingsprocedure'') and application procedure (''verzoekschriftprocedure'') into a single, uniform basic procedure [10, 13–14, 18].
3. Identify and absorb caseflow best practices from the CFMnet Handbook to resolve operational weaknesses in the Dutch judiciary [4, 19, 27–31].

== Scope ==
This policy encompasses the evaluation of civil caseflow governance in Dutch courts and the comparative assessment of best practices across 12 civil law countries in the European Union.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Unified Basic Digital Procedure:'''
** Merging disparate legal proceedings into a single digital claim pipeline via the ''MijnZaak'' portal for litigants and ''MijnWerkomgeving'' for court staff.
* '''Classification of CFMnet Best Practices:'''
** '''Category 1 (Quick Wins):''' Internal daily judge performance publications and treating audio/video recordings as official court records [27–28].
** '''Category 2 (High-Value Innovations):''' Centralized expert monitoring units, real-time timeframe alarm systems, and 50% court fee refunds for successful mediation [23–25].
** '''Category 3 (Already Implemented):''' Summary proceedings and the division of labor between judges and court clerks.
** '''Category 4 (Irrelevant):''' Rigid backlog reduction instruments like restricting appeal rights.

== Implementation ==
* '''Establishment of Digital Portals:''' The development of ''MijnZaak'' for litigants and ''MijnWerkomgeving'' as a digital workspace for court staff.
* '''Adoption of Real-Time Monitoring and Expert Management:''' Proposals to integrate early warning delay indicators and civil expert oversight units into the judiciary's IT systems.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''KEI ICT Budget Blowout:''' Project costs skyrocketing uncontrollably from an initial estimate of €60 million to €200 million.
* '''Risks of Merging Legal and IT Reforms:''' Warnings from the Council of State (''Raad van State'') that coupling procedural law reform with digitalization poses a high risk that an IT failure could paralyze the entire legal reform [15–16, 19–20].

== Reform / Change ==
* Integrating real-time monitoring instruments directly into the Dutch judicial digital infrastructure (''MijnWerkomgeving'').
* Establishing a centralized registration and monitoring system for the quality of civil judicial experts (''court experts register'').

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Council for the Judiciary (Raad voor de Rechtspraak):''' The authority managing judicial IT implementation and innovation in the Netherlands.
* '''Utrecht University & LUT Finland:''' The academic institutions orchestrating the CFMnet research consortium.
* '''Court of First Instance Antwerp:''' The pioneer court for the centralized judicial expert monitoring system model.

The '''Administrative Corruption Prevention Policy Framework Based on a Regulatory Perspective''' (''Corruption from a Regulatory Perspective: Regulatory Anticorruption Toolkit'') is an analytical framework of administrative law and regulatory studies formulated in Edoardo Chiti's review of Maria De Benedetto's work (*Corruption from a Regulatory Perspective*, Oxford: Hart, 2021). It defines administrative corruption as an issue of regulatory effectiveness (a ''regulatory issue'') rooted in the bad quality or bad functioning of rules <ref>Chiti, E. (2022). Book Review: Maria De Benedetto, Corruption from a Regulatory Perspective, Oxford, Hart, 2021. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 14(2), 606–612.</ref>; articulates a *regulatory anticorruption* model focusing on managing the rules' life-cycle, structuring regulatory stock, and controlling regulatory flow <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 606, 609.</ref>; utilizes the *corruptibility assessment* instrument <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 610.</ref>; and positions public trust as a primary intangible factor in the effectiveness of administrative law <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 607, 610, 611, 612.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Authored by [[Edoardo Chiti]] (Full Professor of Administrative Law at Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna, Pisa), this review analyzes the monograph written by [[Maria De Benedetto]] <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 606, 607.</ref>. The author emphasizes that administrative corruption is fundamentally a regulatory issue, as it is intrinsically linked to abuses of power arising from poor legal design <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 606, 607.</ref>. Compared to conventional criminal law enforcement (*conventional anticorruption*) or behavioural interventions (*behavioural anticorruption*), the *regulatory anticorruption* model offers a more functional ex-ante and ex-post strategy <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 608, 609.</ref>. It relies on managing regulatory stock (simplifying authorization regimes and enhancing anti-corruption agency advocacy) and regulating regulatory flow through tailored regulatory impact assessments <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 609.</ref>. The analysis concludes by underscoring public trust as an indispensable social fabric securing legal compliance <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 610, 611.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''International & Global Standards''':
** *Transparency International Corruption Perceptions Index (1995)* <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 608.</ref>.
** *United Nations Convention against Corruption / UNCAC (2003)* <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 608.</ref>.
** *OECD Recommendations on Transparency and Integrity in Public Action* <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 608.</ref>.
* '''Comparative Domestic Frameworks''':
** Anti-corruption prevention regimes of France, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Italy (including the *Italian National Recovery and Resilience Plan / PNRR*) <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 608.</ref>.
* '''Doctrinal Works & Related Literature''':
** Maria De Benedetto, *Corruption from a Regulatory Perspective* (Hart, 2021) <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 606.</ref>.
** Maria De Benedetto, Guido Corso, Nicoletta Rangone, *Diritto amministrativo effettivo* (Mulino, 2022) <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 612.</ref>.
** Marco d’Alberti (ed.), *Corruzione e pubbliche amministrazioni* (2017) <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 606, 611.</ref>.

== Core Provisions & Three Strategic Pillars ==
1. '''Definition of Corruption as a Regulatory Issue''': Corruption encompasses any abuse of public power for private gain induced by dysfunctional rules or poor regulatory draftsmanship <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 607.</ref>. Regulatory effectiveness hinges on normative certainty, low compliance costs, and tangible public outcomes <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 607.</ref>.
2. '''Tripartite Control Structure (Principal-Agent-Client)''':
* *Principal–Agent* (State/Citizens vs. Public Officials): Internal administrative oversight <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 607.</ref>.
* *Principal–Client* (State vs. Private Actors): Public oversight of private economic activities <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 607, 608.</ref>.
* *Agent–Client* (Public Officials vs. Private Actors): Ex-post criminal enforcement <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 608.</ref>.
3. '''Corruptibility Assessment Protocol''': An evaluation tool measuring the corruptibility risk of legislation by examining legal incentive structures, wording patterns in administrative authorizations, and criminal record databases <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 610.</ref>.

== Relationships with Related Entities ==
* '''[[Edoardo Chiti]]''': Review Author & Full Professor of Administrative Law at Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 606, 607.</ref>.
* '''[[Maria De Benedetto]]''': Monograph Author & Regulatory Studies Scholar <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 606, 612.</ref>.
* '''[[Marco d'Alberti]]''': Administrative Law Scholar and Pioneer in Corruption and Regulatory Studies <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 606, 611.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 606–612.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 606–612.</ref>

Il '''Quadro Politico per la Prevenzione della Corruzione Amministrativa in una Prospettiva Regolatoria''' (''Corruption from a Regulatory Perspective: Regulatory Anticorruption Toolkit'') è un quadro analitico di diritto amministrativo e studi regolatori formulato nella recensione di Edoardo Chiti all'opera di Maria De Benedetto (*Corruption from a Regulatory Perspective*, Oxford: Hart, 2021) per definire la corruzione amministrativa come un problema di efficacia regolatoria (un ''regulatory issue'') derivante dalla cattiva qualità o dal cattivo funzionamento delle regole <ref>Chiti, E. (2022). Book Review: Maria De Benedetto, Corruption from a Regulatory Perspective, Oxford, Hart, 2021. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 14(2), 606–612.</ref>; articolare un modello di *regulatory anticorruption* incentrato sulla gestione del ciclo di vita delle regole, la strutturazione dello *stock* regolatorio e il controllo del *flusso* regolatorio <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 606, 609.</ref>; impiegare lo strumento del *corruptibility assessment* <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 610.</ref>; e posizionare la fiducia pubblica (*trust*) come fattore intangibile primario per l'efficacia del diritto amministrativo <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 607, 610, 611, 612.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Scritta da [[Edoardo Chiti]] (Professore Ordinario di Diritto Amministrativo presso la Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna di Pisa), questa recensione analizza la monografia di [[Maria De Benedetto]] <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 606, 607.</ref>. L'autore sottolinea che la corruzione amministrativa è fondamentalmente un problema regolatorio, poiché è intrinsecamente legata all'abuso di potere derivante da una scarsa qualità della disciplina normativa <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 606, 607.</ref>. Rispetto all'approccio penalistico tradizionale (*conventional anticorruption*) o alle strategie comportamentali (*behavioural anticorruption*), il modello di *regulatory anticorruption* offre una soluzione funzionale basata sulla gestione ex-ante ed ex-post delle regole <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 608, 609.</ref>. Questo approccio interviene sullo *stock* regolatorio (attraverso programmi di semplificazione e potenziamento dell'avvocatura/advocacy delle autorità anticorruzione) e sul *flusso* regolatorio (tramite analisi di impatto della regolamentazione mirate) <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 609.</ref>. L'analisi si conclude evidenziando la fiducia pubblica (*trust*) come collante sociale indispensabile per garantire il rispetto della legge <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 610, 611.</ref>.

== Base Giuridica ==
* '''Standard e Iniziative Internazionali''':
** *Indice di Percezione della Corruzione di Transparency International (1995)* <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 608.</ref>.
** *Convenzione delle Nazioni Unite contro la Corruzione / UNCAC (2003)* <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 608.</ref>.
** *Raccomandazioni OCSE sulla Trasparenza e l'Integrità nella Pubblica Amministrazione* <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 608.</ref>.
* '''Quadri Normativi Nazionali Comparati''':
** Modelli di prevenzione della corruzione di Francia, Spagna, Regno Unito e Italia (incluso il *Piano Nazionale di Ripresa e Resilienza / PNRR*) <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 608.</ref>.
* '''Opere Dottrinali e Letteratura Affine''':
** Maria De Benedetto, *Corruption from a Regulatory Perspective* (Hart, 2021) <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 606.</ref>.
** Maria De Benedetto, Guido Corso, Nicoletta Rangone, *Diritto amministrativo effettivo* (Mulino, 2022) <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 612.</ref>.
** Marco d’Alberti (a cura di), *Corruzione e pubbliche amministrazioni* (2017) <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 606, 611.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Principali e Tre Pilastri Strategici ==
1. '''Definizione di Corruzione come Problema Regolatorio''': La corruzione include qualsiasi abuso di potere pubblico per vantaggio privato causato da difetti funzionali o da un cattivo disegno normativo <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 607.</ref>. L'efficacia regolatoria dipende da certezza del diritto, bassi costi di conformità (*compliance costs*) e risultati sostanziali (*outcomes*) <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 607.</ref>.
2. '''Struttura di Controllo Tripartita (Principale-Agente-Cliente)''':
* *Principale–Agente* (Stato/Cittadini vs. Funzionari Pubblici): Controllo amministrativo interno <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 607.</ref>.
* *Principale–Cliente* (Stato vs. Attori Privati): Controllo pubblico sulle attività economiche private <ref>Chiti (2022), pp. 607, 608.</ref>.
* *Agente–Cliente* (Funzionari Pubblici vs. Attori Privati): Repressione penale ex-post <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 608.</ref>.
3. '''Protocollo di Corruptibility Assessment''': Strumento di valutazione per misurare il rischio di corruttibilità di una norma legislativa analizzando gli incentivi giuridici, il linguaggio delle autorizzazioni amministrative e i database giudiziari <ref>Chiti (2022), p. 610.</ref>.

'''Rule of Law: A Normative Ideal and Its Implications for the Italian Public Administration''' (Indonesian: ''Kerangka Kebijakan Negara Hukum (Rule of Law) dan Implikasinya terhadap Administrasi Publik Italia'') is an administrative law analysis and legal theory policy framework formulated by Edoardo Chiti and Gianluigi Palombella. It reconceptualizes the Rule of Law not merely as passive compliance with the principle of legality or the formal state structure (''Stato di diritto'' / ''Rechtsstaat''), but as a normative ideal built upon a core "duality"—the interaction and beneficial tension between law created by political power (''gubernaculum'') and "other law" beyond the reach of public power (''jurisdictio''/rights/transnational norms). Furthermore, it evaluates the operationalization of this ideal within Italian public administration through judicial review, the duty to give reasons, procedural fairness, and the governance of inter-legality <ref>Chiti, E., & Palombella, G. (2024). Rule of Law: A Normative Ideal and Its Implications for the Italian Public Administration. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 10(1–2), 57–72.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Co-authored by [[Edoardo Chiti]] (Full Professor of Administrative Law) and [[Gianluigi Palombella]] (Full Professor of Applied Legal Theory) at the [[Sant'Anna School of Advanced Studies]] in Pisa, this study provides a deep deconstruction of how the Rule of Law applies to the Italian public administration <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pp. 57, 58.</ref>. The authors assert that the Rule of Law is substantially richer than simple statutory compliance (''rule by law'' / ''Stato di diritto'') <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), p. 60.</ref>. The core of the Rule of Law lies in "duality"—the existence of countervailing legal norms (''jurisdictio'') that cannot be overridden by the political will of sovereign power (''gubernaculum'') <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pp. 61, 64.</ref>. Within Italian administration, this ideal is operationalized across three practical pillars: judicial review, the duty to give reasons, and procedural fairness <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pp. 68, 69.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Supranational EU & International Law''':
** ''Treaty on European Union (TEU) Article 2'': Establishes the Rule of Law as a foundational value of the European Union <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), p. 58.</ref>.
** ''Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (EUCFR) Article 47'' & ''ECHR Article 6'': Guarantees procedural fairness and the right to an effective judicial remedy <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), p. 70.</ref>.
* '''Italian Constitutional & Administrative Law''':
** ''Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana (Articles 24 & 113)'': Constitutional right to judicial review against administrative acts <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), p. 68.</ref>.
** ''Legge 7 agosto 1990, n. 241 (Italian Administrative Procedure Act)'': Article 3 (Mandatory Duty to Give Reasons) <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), p. 68.</ref> and Articles 7–13 (Procedural Fairness & Right to be Heard) <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), p. 68.</ref>.
* '''Key Jurisprudence''':
** ''CJEU Joined Cases C-584/10 P et al. (Kadi I)'': Affirms the Rule of Law as an autonomous constitutional guarantee overriding international administrative acts <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), p. 70.</ref>.
** ''Taricco Saga (CJEU Case C-105/14 jo. Italian Constitutional Court Order n. 24/2016)'': Illustrates the dialectic between supranational EU Rule of Law principles and national criminal legality guarantees <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), p. 67.</ref>.
** ''Tribunale di Roma Judgment n. 35542/2024 (Giudizio Universale)'': Delimitates the scope of judicial review in climate litigation under the political question doctrine <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), p. 65.</ref>.

== Core Policy Provisions & Legal Duality ==
1. '''Duality of Legality (Gubernaculum vs. Jurisdictio)''': Political authority (''gubernaculum'') holds the mandate to enact policy, but must remain bounded by independent, countervailing norms (''jurisdictio'') safeguarding individual rights and minorities <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), p. 61.</ref>.
2. '''Operationalization via Administrative Pillars''': Administrative compliance is not measured solely by statutory conformity, but by whether public decisions ensure transparent reasoning and fair procedural participation for citizens <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pp. 68, 71.</ref>.
3. '''Governance of Inter-Legality''': Public administrators operating in multi-layered legal environments (national, European, and global) must actively reconcile competing norms rather than deferring strictly to domestic legislative mandates <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pp. 62, 72.</ref>.

'''Rule of Law: A Normative Ideal and Its Implications for the Italian Public Administration''' (in italiano: ''Quadro Politico sullo Stato di Diritto (Rule of Law) e le sue Implicazioni per la Pubblica Amministrazione Italiana'') è un quadro di analisi del diritto amministrativo e della teoria del diritto formulato da Edoardo Chiti e Gianluigi Palombella per riconcettualizzare lo *Rule of Law* non come mera obbedienza passiva al principio di legalità o alla forma di stato (*Stato di diritto* / *Rechtsstaat*), bensì come un ideale normativo (*normative ideal*) fondato su una struttura di "dualità" (*duality*)—ovvero l'interazione e la tensione feconda (*beneficial tension*) tra il diritto creato dal potere politico (*gubernaculum*) e "un altro diritto" al di fuori della portata del potere pubblico (*jurisdictio*/diritti/norme transnazionali). Inoltre, lo studio valuta l'operazionalizzazione di questo ideale nella pubblica amministrazione italiana attraverso il controllo giurisdizionale, l'obbligo di motivazione degli atti amministrativi, il giusto procedimento (*procedural fairness*) e la gestione delle situazioni di inter-legalità (*inter-legality*) <ref>Chiti, E., & Palombella, G. (2024). Rule of Law: A Normative Ideal and Its Implications for the Italian Public Administration. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 10(1–2), 57–72.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Redatto da [[Edoardo Chiti]] (Professore Ordinario di Diritto Amministrativo) e [[Gianluigi Palombella]] (Professore Ordinario di Teoria del Diritto Applicata) presso la [[Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna]] di Pisa, questo studio offre una decostruzione approfondita dell'applicazione dello *Rule of Law* nella burocrazia italiana <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pagg. 57, 58.</ref>. Gli autori affermano che lo *Rule of Law* è concettualmente più ricco del semplice rispetto formale della legge (*rule by law* / *Stato di diritto*) <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pag. 60.</ref>. L'essenza dello *Rule of Law* risiede nella "dualità", ossia nella presenza di norme di bilanciamento (*jurisdictio*) che il potere politico (*gubernaculum*) non può sopprimere o prevaricare <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pagg. 61, 64.</ref>. Nell'amministrazione italiana, questo ideale si concretizza attraverso tre pilastri pratici: il controllo giurisdizionale (*judicial review*), l'obbligo di motivazione dei provvedimenti e le garanzie partecipative e procedurali <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pagg. 68, 69.</ref>.

== Base Giuridica ==
* '''Diritto Supranazionale dell'Unione Europea e Internazionale''':
** ''Trattato sull'Unione Europea (TUE) Articolo 2'': Sancisce lo *Rule of Law* come valore fondante dell'Unione Europea <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pag. 58.</ref>.
** ''Carta dei Diritti Fondamentali dell'Unione Europea (CDFUE) Articolo 47'' & ''CEDU Articolo 6'': Garantiscono il diritto a un equo processo e a un ricorso effettivo <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pag. 70.</ref>.
* '''Diritto Costituzionale e Amministrativo Italiano''':
** ''Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana (Articoli 24 e 113)'': Diritto costituzionale alla tutela giurisdizionale contro gli atti della pubblica amministrazione <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pag. 68.</ref>.
** ''Legge 7 agosto 1990, n. 241'': Articolo 3 (Obbligo di motivazione del provvedimento amministrativo) <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pag. 68.</ref> e Articoli 7–13 (Giusto procedimento e diritto di partecipazione) <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pag. 68.</ref>.
* '''Giurisprudenza Chiave''':
** ''CGUE Cause Riunite C-584/10 P e a. (Kadi I)'': Afferma lo *Rule of Law* come garanzia costituzionale autonoma dell'UE prevalente sugli atti internazionali <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pag. 70.</ref>.
** ''Saga Taricco (CGUE C-105/14 e Corte Cost. Ordinanza n. 24/2016)'': Illustra la dialettica tra lo *Rule of Law* sovranazionale e il principio di legalità penale nazionale <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pag. 67.</ref>.
** ''Tribunale di Roma Sentenza n. 35542/2024 (Giudizio Universale)'': Delimita i confini del sindacato giurisdizionale nelle controversie climatiche in base alla dottrina della *political question* <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pag. 65.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Principali e Dualità della Legalità ==
1. '''Dualità della Legalità (Gubernaculum vs. Jurisdictio)''': Il potere politico (*gubernaculum*) ha la facoltà di fissare gli indirizzi di governo, ma deve rimanere limitato da norme autonome (*jurisdictio*) poste a tutela dei diritti individuali e delle minoranze <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pag. 61.</ref>.
2. '''Operazionalizzazione nei Pilastri Amministrativi''': La legalità amministrativa non si valuta solo sulla conformità formale al testo legislativo, ma dalla misura in cui le decisioni pubbliche garantiscono la trasparenza delle motivazioni e la giusta partecipazione dei cittadini <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pagg. 68, 71.</ref>.
3. '''Gestione dell'Inter-Legalità''': I funzionari pubblici che operano in contesti normativi multilivello (nazionale, europeo e globale) devono bilanciare attivamente le diverse fonti del diritto anziché adagiarsi su una mera applicazione meccanica delle norme interne <ref>Chiti & Palombella (2024), pagg. 62, 72.</ref>.

'''The Treatment of Citizens' Complaints in the Justice Field: Is an Ombudsman Necessary? Framework''' is a policy framework and comparative-constitutional analysis of the handling of citizens' complaints regarding administrative and operational dysfunctions within the justice system in France and other European countries. It evaluates the urgency, scope, and institutionalization options between an Ombudsman (or ''Médiateur'') versus a Superior Council of the Judiciary (''CSM''), ensuring that such mechanisms do not violate the principles of judicial independence and the separation of powers [1, 3, 5, 9, 10, 17, 24, 41–48].

== Summary ==
Published by Prof. Hélène Pauliat (University of Limoges) in ''Ethique publique'' (2007) and the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this policy framework dissects the mechanisms for handling public complaints against the judiciary. Drawing lessons from the crisis of public confidence following the ''Affaire d'Outreau'' scandal in France, the study asserts that citizen complaints are crucial signals for measuring the quality of judicial services. However, unlike general public services (such as electricity or transportation), the judiciary is a constitutional power protected by judicial independence. This framework presents a complaint classification matrix, introduces the role of an ''Internal Complaint Manager'', and proposes two national institutional integration scenarios by strengthening either the ''Conseil supérieur de la magistrature'' (CSM) or the ''Médiateur de la République'' [12, 26, 41–45].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''French Code of Judicial Organization (Code de l'organisation judiciaire - COJ):''' ''Article L. 141-1'' (formerly Art. L. 781-1), which regulates state liability for gross negligence (''faute lourde'') or a denial of justice (''déni de justice'').
* '''Organic Law No. 2007-287 of March 5, 2007:''' French organic law concerning the recruitment, training, and accountability of judges.
* '''Decision of the Conseil constitutionnel No. 2007-551 DC (March 1, 2007):''' Invalidated the clause allowing direct citizen complaints to the executive, as it could trigger executive intervention against judges.
* '''European Charter on the Status of Judges (1998):''' A European charter obligating member states to provide citizen complaint procedures regarding judicial accountability.
* '''Council of Europe Recommendations R(85)13 & R(86)12:''' Regulates the function of the Ombudsman and measures to prevent backlogs in judicial workloads.

== Background ==
The wrongful arrest and detention scandal of the ''Affaire d'Outreau'' exposed the vulnerabilities of the French judiciary, triggering a crisis of citizen confidence due to slow trial processes, complex legal language, and the lack of a clear complaint channel. Because judges are constitutionally independent, evaluating judicial quality cannot be equated with managing a regular public enterprise. A complaint handling mechanism is required that can distinguish between disputes over the content of a judgment and administrative service dysfunctions.

== Objectives ==
1. Build a transparent citizen complaint handling mechanism to restore public trust.
2. Distinctly separate complaints regarding the content of judicial decisions (appellate remedies) from complaints regarding operational dysfunctions and ethical violations.
3. Establish the position of an ''Internal Complaint Manager'' in every local court for rapid response.
4. Formulate a national integrated complaint institutional model based on either the CSM or an Ombudsman [41–45].

== Scope ==
This policy includes a comparative analysis of judicial complaint systems in France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Canada, Spain, England & Wales, Sweden, Finland, Poland, Slovenia, Italy, and Portugal.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Complaint Classification Matrix (Belgium & Canada):'''
** ''Complaints against the Content of a Judicial Decision:'' Strictly the authority of appellate/cassation judges; Ombudsmen are prohibited from handling these.
** ''Operational Dysfunctions:'' Scheduling negligence, information delays, and staff unfriendliness, which are handled by the Ombudsman or Complaint Manager.
** ''Ethical/Disciplinary Faults of Judges:'' Handled by the disciplinary panel of the CSM or the Canadian Judicial Council.
* '''Internal Complaint Manager Position:''' A judge appointed at the district level to collect, clarify, and directly respond to citizens' operational complaints.
* '''CEPEJ Case Delay Compensation Data:''' 22 European countries provide compensation for trial delays, 44 countries for illegal detention, and 43 countries for illegal conviction.

== Implementation ==
* '''Scenario 1 (CSM-Centric):''' Establishing the CSM as the central registry, conducting preliminary examinations via the ''Inspection générale'', and publishing annual judicial complaint reports.
* '''Scenario 2 (Médiateur-Centric):''' Utilizing the ''Médiateur'' as the linchpin to filter complaints, forwarding cases to the CSM, the Chief of Court, or professional organizations.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Institutional Fragmentation:''' Separate handling of complaints by the ''Médiateur'', the ''Direction des services judiciaires'', and the ''CSM'' without a unified annual report [33–38].
* '''Risk of Political Intervention:''' Adopting a direct complaint channel through the Minister of Justice risks becoming a tool for political pressure against judges.

== Reform / Change ==
* Institutionalization of an ''Internal Complaint Manager'' in local courts to cut through complaint bureaucracy.
* Strengthening the CSM as an independent body responsible for transparency and judicial ethics.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Conseil supérieur de la magistrature (CSM):''' The independent supervisory body for the discipline and ethics of French judges.
* '''Médiateur de la République:''' The French national Ombudsman handling administrative dysfunctions.
* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]:''' Cecep Mustafa is identified as a judicial judge (Hakim Yustisial) at the Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy (Pustrajak) within the Supreme Court of the Republic of Indonesia and a postgraduate lecturer at Universitas Ibnu Chaldun. [private person] is a law student at UPN "Veteran" Jakarta (NIM: 2410611102) [FACT].

=== Deutsch (Schweizer Hochdeutsch) ===
'''Behandlung von Bürgerbeschwerden im Justizbereich: Ist ein Ombudsmann erforderlich?'''
Dieser von Prof. Hélène Pauliat (Universität Limoges) im ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA, 2007/2013) veröffentlichte Rahmen analysiert die Bearbeitung von Bürgerbeschwerden gegen die Justiz in Frankreich und Europa. Die Studie, die durch den Vertrauensverlust nach der Outreau-Affäre motiviert wurde, fordert die klare Trennung von Beschwerden über Urteilsinhalte und administrativen Fehlfunktionen. Sie schlägt die Einrichtung eines internen Beschwerdemanagers sowie die Stärkung des Obersten Justizrates (CSM) oder des Ombudsmanns vor, um die Rechenschaftspflicht zu erhöhen, ohne die richterliche Unabhängigkeit zu verletzen.
* '''Rechtsgrundlage:''' Code de l'organisation judiciaire (Art. L. 141-1), Loi organique n° 2007-287, Europäische Charta über das Statut der Richter (1998).

=== Français ===
'''Le traitement des plaintes des citoyens dans le domaine de la justice : Un médiateur est-il nécessaire ?'''
Publié par la Prof. Hélène Pauliat (Université de Limoges) dans la revue ''Éthique publique'' et l' ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA, 2007/2013), ce cadre analyse le traitement des plaintes des citoyens contre les dysfonctionnements judiciaires en France et en Europe. Tirant les leçons de l'affaire d'Outreau, l'étude souligne la nécessité de séparer strictement les plaintes concernant le contenu des décisions judiciaires de celles portant sur les dysfonctionnements administratifs. Elle propose la création d'un poste de gestionnaire interne des plaintes et le renforcement du Conseil supérieur de la magistrature (CSM) ou du Médiateur pour garantir la transparence sans violer l'indépendance de la justice.
* '''Base Légale:''' Code de l'organisation judiciaire (Art. L. 141-1), Loi organique n° 2007-287, Charte européenne sur le statut des juges (1998).

'''Il trattamento dei reclami dei cittadini nel settore della giustizia: È necessario un Mediatore?'''
Pubblicato dalla Prof.ssa Hélène Pauliat (Università di Limoges) nell' ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA, 2007/2013), questo quadro analizza la gestione dei reclami dei cittadini contro le disfunzioni giudiziarie in Francia e in Europa. A seguito dello scandalo di Outreau, lo studio richiede una rigorosa separazione tra i reclami sul contenuto delle sentenze e quelli sui malfunzionamenti amministrativi. Propone l'istituzione di un gestore interno dei reclami e il rafforzamento del Consiglio superiore della magistratura (CSM) o del Mediatore per garantire la trasparenza senza violare l'indipendenza giudiziaria.

The '''Collegiate Collaboration and Procedural Guidelines Framework''' (also known as the ''Relying on the Courts Framework'') is a judicial management policy framework that proposes the strengthening of horizontal collegiate collaboration and the creation of procedural guidelines (''procesreglementen'') by judges. It acts as a counterbalance to strict professional hierarchies to protect internal judicial independence, increase efficiency, ensure timeliness, and maintain consistency in judicial decisions [1, 2, 5, 11, 97–99].

== Overview ==
Issued by Prof. Dr. Philip Langbroek in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (2024), this framework analyzes the negative impact of rigid judicial hierarchies that suppress the professional autonomy of judges. Through comparative studies in the Netherlands, Ukraine, and Greece, the framework demonstrates that horizontal collaboration—specifically through the drafting of procedural guidelines—can limit the use of trial postponement tactics by lawyers, strengthen internal independence, and boost public trust.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR):''' Guarantees the right to a fair, predictable, and timely trial.
* '''Dutch Supreme Court Ruling (Hoge Raad, June 3, 2022, ECLI:NL:HR:2022:824):''' Acknowledges the legal legitimacy of procedural guidelines (''procesreglementen'') established by judicial panels.
* '''Opinion of Advocate-General Ruth de Bock (ECLI:NL:PHR:2021:1228):''' Provides a comprehensive analysis regarding the legal nature and boundaries of judicial procedural guidelines.
* '''Dutch Judiciary Organization Act 2001 (''Wet op de rechterlijke organisatie 2001''):''' Statutory foundation for court organization in the Netherlands.
* '''Article 90 of the Greek Constitution:''' Governs the appointment of judicial leadership and the inspection system by the ''Areios Pagos'' (Supreme Court).

== Background and Policy Problems ==
The reliable administration of justice requires a balance between organizational hierarchy and social cohesion (horizontal collaboration). Without horizontal cohesion, judicial hierarchies are often exploited to control judges' behavior through the threat of disciplinary sanctions and career promotion control, which ultimately undermines internal judicial independence. 

In strictly hierarchical judicial systems lacking collegiate collaboration, judges work in isolation and are vulnerable to political intervention and fear of sanctions. Lawyers and prosecutors exploit this systemic weakness to manipulate procedures via repeated postponement requests and unjustified judicial recusals. Consequently, disposition times become unpredictable and severely delayed. Furthermore, under the traditional separation of powers doctrine, judges are often perceived as lacking rule-making authority. Without explicit legislative delegation, procedural guidelines drafted by judges are vulnerable to challenges of overstepping authority.

== Implementation and Comparative Analysis ==
The management policy was evaluated across three European jurisdictions:

* '''The Netherlands:''' Operating within a high-trust society, procedural guidelines (''procesreglementen'') are widely utilized across civil, criminal, and immigration courts. This practice is supported by the ''Raad voor de Rechtspraak'' (Council for the Judiciary) and affirmed by Hoge Raad jurisprudence. Internal cohesion has maintained public trust in judges at approximately 70%.
* '''Ukraine (Odesa & Kyiv Oblast):''' The MATRA/CILC project (2019–2023) successfully facilitated local judges in drafting procedural guidelines alongside bar associations and local NGOs (Second of May Group). This was backed by the High Council of Justice to protect judges from disciplinary sanctions. The guidelines successfully restricted unjustified recusals and tightened postponement requirements (e.g., mandating substitute counsel if a lawyer is unavailable) [49–51].
* '''Greece:''' Attempts to draft procedural guidelines in Piraeus and Athens (2019–2022) were actively obstructed and sabotaged by the leadership of the ''Areios Pagos'' (Maria Georgiou) and judges' associations. This resistance, driven by a rigid hierarchical inspection system, led to extreme case backlogs (disposition times reaching 559–610 days), negative regulatory inflation (''polynomia'' and ''kakanomy''), and unilateral dismissals of judges by the Supreme Court leadership.

== Key Provisions and Proposed Reforms ==
* '''Judges as Procedural Rule-Makers:''' Judicial panels directly draft trial procedure agreements, setting document submission deadlines, speaking durations, and strict requirements for trial postponements.
* '''Limiting Trial Postponements:''' Mandating that absent lawyers appoint substitute counsel, except in proven emergencies.
* '''Autonomy in Concrete Cases:''' Judges retain the authority to deviate from procedural guidelines in specific cases if necessary in the interest of justice.
* '''Multidisciplinary Organization Test:''' Proposed paradigm shift from traditional rule-of-law tests to evaluating the judicial organization's characteristics based on its level of collegiate collaboration.
* '''Reform of Disciplinary Inspections:''' Explicit protection for internal judicial independence, urging the separation of disciplinary inspection functions from Supreme Court leadership to align with European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) jurisprudence.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Utrecht University & Center for International Legal Cooperation (CILC):''' Academic institutions and judicial reform project implementers.
* '''Hoge Raad & Areios Pagos:''' The Supreme Courts of the Netherlands and Greece, respectively.
* '''High Council of Justice Ukraine & Venice Commission:''' Institutional bodies involved in European and Ukrainian judicial oversight.
* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]:''' Not found in the available sources [1–123].

== References ==

Relying on the Courts: About Collegiate Collaboration in Courts as a Counterbalance to Professional Hierarchy and as a Necessary Precondition for Efficiently Delivering, Timely and Consistent Justice. ''International Journal for Court Administration'', 15(2), 5. DOI: https://doi.org/10.36745/ijca.527.
* Bovend'Eert, P. P. T. (2016). The Legal Nature of Procedural Rules and Other Court Regulations. ''Nederlands Juristenblad'', 5, 257–326.
* Sillen, J. (2019). The Concept of 'Internal Judicial Independence' in the Case Law of the European Court of Human Rights. ''European Constitutional Law Review'', 15, 104–133.

The '''Comparative Legal Metrics and Performance Quantification Framework''' (officially titled ''Comparative Legal Metrics: Quantification of Performance as a Regulatory Technique Framework'') is a comparative legal analysis and policy framework that evaluates the application of quantitative instruments and performance measurement as regulatory techniques designed to steer behavior, enhance public accountability, and evaluate the efficiency of judicial systems, educational institutions, policy-making processes, and markets at national and transnational levels <ref>Napolitano, G. (2024). Comparative Legal Metrics: An Introduction. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 10(1-2), 1–4; Bussani, M., Cassese, S., & Infantino, M. (Eds.). (2023). ''Comparative Legal Metrics. Quantification of Performance as a Regulatory Technique''. Leiden: Brill.</ref>.

== Overview ==
Based on a symposium review authored by [[Giulio Napolitano]], Full Professor of Administrative Law at [[Roma Tre University]], the trend of quantitative performance measurement driven by the digital revolution has become a global phenomenon across both public and private sectors <ref>Napolitano (2024), pp. 1–2.</ref>. Originating from the 21st General Congress of the [[International Academy of Comparative Law]] held in Asunción, Paraguay, the compiled volume edited by Mauro Bussani, Sabino Cassese, and Marta Infantino demonstrates that performance quantification substantially alters how law is understood and applied via carrot-and-stick incentive structures, reporting duties, and standardizations of performance <ref>Napolitano (2024), pp. 1–3.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
This framework is rooted in several regulatory approaches and quantitative mechanisms:
* '''[[Performance-Based Regulatory Measures]]''': Regulatory techniques using quantitative indicators, algorithms, and reporting requirements to direct public and private behavior <ref>Napolitano (2024), pp. 2–3.</ref>.
* '''[[Corporate Social Responsibility Compliance Metrics]]''': Hard law and soft law corporate governance and self-regulatory instruments designed to measure compliance with Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) and Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) standards <ref>Napolitano (2024), p. 3.</ref>.
* '''[[International Organizations Legal Metrics]]''': Standardized legal metrics produced by international organizations to evaluate and influence national policy-making and legislative choices <ref>Napolitano (2024), p. 3.</ref>.

== Background ==
Driven by the digital revolution over recent decades, quantitative performance measurement has expanded rapidly across various jurisdictions seeking to establish evidence-based public policies and streamline administrative efficiency <ref>Napolitano (2024), p. 2.</ref>. Despite the wide adoption of quantification across education, health, justice, and financial markets, legal research addressing this phenomenon had previously remained minimal <ref>Napolitano (2024), p. 2.</ref>. This comparative framework addresses this gap by gathering contributions from international scholars examining legal systems including Brazil, Mexico, India, Switzerland, South Africa, Poland, China, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the European Union <ref>Napolitano (2024), p. 2.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Analyze comparatively how quantitative performance instruments function as regulatory interventions across sectors and regions <ref>Napolitano (2024), pp. 2, 3.</ref>.
* Examine the actors producing legal metrics and map their regulatory effects on domestic and transnational law <ref>Napolitano (2024), pp. 2–3.</ref>.
* Identify the structural limits and errors in the elaboration of quantitative standards to prevent bureaucratic distortions <ref>Napolitano (2024), p. 3.</ref>.

== Scope ==
The scope of this framework is divided into three primary functional areas:
# '''Core Domestic Functions (Justice & Education)''': Judicial performance indicators in Brazil (quantified justice & managerial judges), Mexico, India, and Switzerland, as well as admission algorithms and educational metrics in South Africa and Poland <ref>Napolitano (2024), pp. 2–3.</ref>.
# '''National Policy-Making''': Digitalization of public administration in Africa, performance governance in China and Japan, and human rights indicators by the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) in the United Kingdom <ref>Napolitano (2024), pp. 2–3.</ref>.
# '''Transnational Market Activities & Global Metrics''': Mass algorithmic profiling in Africa, digital platform reputation feedback systems in Europe, corporate CSR metrics, and legal indices generated by international organizations <ref>Napolitano (2024), p. 3.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & Quantitative Instruments ==
* '''Judicial Performance Assessment (Quantified Justice)''': Deployment of tools such as the ''Judicial Performance Index'' in India and the managerial judge framework in Brazil, Mexico, and Switzerland to evaluate court efficiency and judicial output <ref>Napolitano (2024), pp. 2–3.</ref>.
* '''Quantity vs. Quality Distortion''': Reliance on quantitative indicators risks creating a shift toward prioritizing "quantity over quality" and "form over substance," potentially undermining substantive justice <ref>Napolitano (2024), p. 2.</ref>.
* '''Human Rights Quantification''': Application of metric-based frameworks to measure compliance with fundamental rights and equality benchmarks, such as those evaluated by the UK EHRC <ref>Napolitano (2024), p. 3.</ref>.

== Implementation ==
Operationalized through national public policy initiatives, judicial evaluation metrics, public sector algorithmic decision-making systems, corporate compliance obligations, and international ranking instruments <ref>Napolitano (2024), pp. 2–3.</ref>.

== Policy Issues ==
* '''Formalistic Distortions''': The risk that regulatory focus shifts toward merely satisfying numeric targets rather than improving the actual quality of public administration and legal output <ref>Napolitano (2024), p. 2.</ref>.
* '''Standardization Errors''': Structural vulnerabilities arising when uniform quantitative metrics are applied without accounting for specific sectoral contexts and local legal cultures <ref>Napolitano (2024), p. 3.</ref>.

== Proposed Reforms ==
The framework promotes a critical analytical approach to avoid "naive enthusiasm" regarding quantification and algorithms. Legal scholars and policy-makers are urged to explicitly identify error risks in standard elaboration and adapt quantitative tools to local legal systems <ref>Napolitano (2024), p. 3.</ref>.

== Related Entities ==
* '''[[Giulio Napolitano]]''': Symposium Review Author and Professor of Administrative Law at Roma Tre University <ref>Napolitano (2024), pp. 1, 2.</ref>.
* '''[[Mauro Bussani]]''': Lead Editor of *Comparative Legal Metrics* <ref>Napolitano (2024), pp. 1, 2.</ref>.
* '''[[Sabino Cassese]]''': Lead Editor of *Comparative Legal Metrics* <ref>Napolitano (2024), pp. 1, 2.</ref>.
* '''[[Marta Infantino]]''': Lead Editor of *Comparative Legal Metrics* <ref>Napolitano (2024), pp. 1, 2.</ref>.

'''The Li & Verschoof Comparative Judicial Mediation Policy Framework''' is a comparative judicial mediation policy and empirical socio-legal evaluation model concerning the practice of mediating judges (judges encouraging settlement) in the Netherlands and China. Formulated by Dr. Yedan Li and Prof. Rick Verschoof in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), Vol. 9 No. 1 (December 2017), the framework compares the striking similarities in judicial mediation techniques (facilitating negotiation, narrow/evaluative intervention, and broad/therapeutic intervention) against the stark contrast in litigant perceptions. It reveals high satisfaction among Dutch litigants versus deep mistrust among Chinese litigants, attributing these divergent outcomes to differences in judicial independence, bureaucratic performance incentives, mediation frequency, and the unregulated use of ''caucuses'' [1–21, 36–43, 62–68].

== Summary ==
Published by Dr. Yedan Li and Prof. Rick Verschoof in the IJCA (December 2017), this policy framework examines the global convergence of "multi-tasking judges" who combine the roles of adjudicator and mediator [1–5]. Utilizing comparative empirical data from 100 civil cases in the Netherlands (involving 37 judges across 5 courts) and 49 labor cases in China (across 2 local courts), the study reveals that judges in both countries employ highly similar mediation techniques based on the Riskin Grid (facilitating, narrow/evaluative, and broad/therapeutic) [17–35]. However, the litigants' responses are diametrically opposed: Dutch litigants are highly satisfied, whereas Chinese litigants experience profound mistrust [1, 7, 36–39]. The authors demonstrate that this divergence is rooted in institutional disparities. In the Netherlands, judges are independent, mediation occurs during open, single-session court hearings adhering to ''audi et alteram partem'' (the right to be heard equally), and caucuses are strictly prohibited. In contrast, mediation in China is driven by bureaucratic case quality evaluation incentives, fears of ''guanxi'' (informal relational influence), repetitive mediation leading to inconsistent opinions, and the use of opaque, unregulated caucuses that trigger perceptions of judicial bias [45–48, 50–57].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Dutch Code of Civil Procedure (Wetboek van Burgerlijke Rechtsvordering - Rv) Articles 87 & 88:''' The 2002 revised rules of Dutch civil procedure that obligate judges to explore opportunities for settlement during oral hearings.
* '''Principle of Audi et Alteram Partem (Article 6 ECHR):''' A fundamental principle of European procedural law ensuring the right of both parties to be present and heard equally during all court interventions.
* '''PRC Civil Procedure Law Articles 9, 94, 133, 142, & 201:''' The foundation of Chinese civil procedural law governing the mediation authority of judges and guaranteeing the principle of voluntariness.
* '''SPC Opinions on Priority to Mediation (2010 Notice) & SPC Code of Conduct (2010 Art. 39):''' Guidelines issued by the Supreme People's Court of China regarding the prioritization of mediation and the prohibition of forced settlements.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
Global judicial reforms are pushing civil law judges to transition from rigid legal adjudicators into problem-solving judges. However, implementing this "multi-tasking" role triggers distinctly different neutrality challenges in developing nations compared to developed nations.

== Objectives ==
1. Empirically compare the techniques, strategies, and interventions of mediating judges in the Netherlands and China based on the Riskin grid.
2. Identify the socio-legal factors causing the stark divergence in litigant satisfaction and trust toward judicial mediation.
3. Formulate ethical standards and procedural boundaries to ensure that the mediator-judge role does not undermine judicial independence and procedural fairness.

== Scope ==
This policy encompasses the empirical evaluation of civil judicial mediation across 5 first-instance courts in the Netherlands and labor dispute mediation in 2 local courts in China.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Three Categories of Judicial Mediation Intervention (Riskin Grid):'''
** '''Facilitating Negotiation:''' Providing a platform, facilitating communication, and encouraging independent negotiation (up to 25–30 interventions per hearing in the Netherlands).
** '''Narrow/Evaluative Intervention:''' Proposing compromise figures, evaluating the strength/weakness of arguments, providing a ''provisional judicial opinion'', or showing a draft judgment.
** '''Broad/Therapeutic Intervention:''' Exploring underlying interests beyond formal legal claims (e.g., apologies, repairing neighborly relations).
* '''Divergence in Institutional Practices:'''
** '''Dutch Model:''' Mediation is conducted once during an open court hearing, adheres strictly to ''audi et alteram partem'', and absolutely forbids caucusing.
** '''Chinese Model:''' Mediation is repetitive, tied to bureaucratic performance evaluations, and utilizes opaque, unregulated caucuses.

== Implementation ==
* '''Execution of Empirical Observation & Interviews:''' Data collection spanning 100 Dutch cases (257 interviews) and 49 Chinese cases (96 interviews) between 2011 and 2014.
* '''Integration of the Provisional Opinion:''' Dutch judges openly present a provisional legal opinion in front of both parties to anchor negotiations in the shadow of the law.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Breakdown of the Dispute Resolution Triad due to Caucusing:''' One-sided caucusing in China makes litigants feel the judge is colluding with their opponent; if mediation fails, the subsequent judgment is perceived as fundamentally unfair (the triad breaks down into "two against one").
* '''Distortion by Bureaucratic Performance Incentives:''' Evaluating Chinese judges based on their mediation settlement rates pressures them to aggressively coerce litigants just to clear dockets or avoid writing difficult decisions.

== Reform / Change ==
* Eliminating rigid bureaucratic incentives that tie a judge's performance evaluation to pure mediation settlement percentages.
* Formulating procedural regulations and ethical codes that prohibit unregulated, non-transparent caucuses to strictly uphold the ''audi et alteram partem'' principle.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Utrecht University Law School & Bielefeld University:''' The academic institutions executing the comparative judicial mediation research.
* '''Courts of First Instance of the Netherlands (Rechtbanken):''' The courts where ''audi et alteram partem''-based mediations were observed.
* '''Supreme People's Court of China (SPC):''' The publisher of judicial mediation policy guidelines in China.
* '''[private person]:''' A Law student specializing in Constitutional Law (Hukum Tata Negara) at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta. The procedural fairness, due process guarantees (''audi et alteram partem''), and the constitutional boundaries of judicial independence discussed in this comparative framework align profoundly with her academic studies. Cecep Mustafa is not found in the available sources [FACT] [1–68].

== Multilingual Summaries (Swiss National Languages) ==

=== Deutsch (Schweizer Hochdeutsch) ===
'''Vergleichender politischer Rahmen zur richterlichen Mediation von Li & Verschoof'''
Dieser von Dr. Yedan Li und Prof. Rick Verschoof im ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA, 2017) veröffentlichte Rahmen vergleicht die Praxis der richterlichen Mediation in den Niederlanden und China. Die empirische Studie zeigt, dass Richter in beiden Ländern ähnliche Mediationstechniken (basierend auf dem Riskin-Grid) anwenden, die Reaktionen der Prozessparteien jedoch extrem unterschiedlich ausfallen: In den Niederlanden herrscht hohe Zufriedenheit, in China tiefes Misstrauen. Die Autoren führen diese Divergenz auf institutionelle Unterschiede zurück. Während in den Niederlanden das Prinzip des rechtlichen Gehörs (audi et alteram partem) in offenen Anhörungen ohne Einzelgespräche (Caucuses) gilt, wird die Mediation in China durch bürokratische Leistungsanreize, intransparente Caucuses und die Angst vor informellen Beziehungen ("Guanxi") verzerrt.
* '''Rechtsgrundlage:''' Niederländische Zivilprozessordnung Art. 87 & 88; EMRK Art. 6; Chinesisches Zivilprozessrecht; SPC-Richtlinien 2010.

=== Français ===
'''Cadre politique comparatif de la médiation judiciaire de Li & Verschoof'''
Publié par la Dre Yedan Li et le Prof. Rick Verschoof dans l' ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA, 2017), ce cadre compare la pratique de la médiation par les juges aux Pays-Bas et en Chine. L'étude empirique montre que les juges des deux pays utilisent des techniques de médiation très similaires (basées sur la grille de Riskin), mais que les réactions des plaideurs sont diamétralement opposées : grande satisfaction aux Pays-Bas, méfiance profonde en Chine. Les auteurs attribuent cette divergence à des différences institutionnelles. Aux Pays-Bas, le principe du contradictoire (audi et alteram partem) est respecté lors d'audiences publiques sans apartés (caucuses). En Chine, la médiation est faussée par des incitations bureaucratiques liées à l'évaluation des performances, des apartés opaques et la crainte des relations informelles ("Guanxi").
* '''Base Légale:''' Code de procédure civile néerlandais Art. 87 & 88 ; CEDH Art. 6 ; Loi de procédure civile chinoise ; Lignes directrices de la SPC (2010).

=== Italiano ===
'''Quadro politico comparativo della mediazione giudiziaria di Li & Verschoof'''
Pubblicato dalla Dott.ssa Yedan Li e dal Prof. Rick Verschoof nell' ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA, 2017), questo quadro confronta la pratica della mediazione da parte dei giudici nei Paesi Bassi e in Cina. Lo studio empirico mostra che i giudici in entrambi i paesi utilizzano tecniche di mediazione molto simili (basate sulla griglia di Riskin), ma le reazioni dei litiganti sono diametralmente opposte: grande soddisfazione nei Paesi Bassi, profonda sfiducia in Cina. Gli autori attribuiscono questa divergenza a differenze istituzionali. Nei Paesi Bassi viene rispettato il principio del contraddittorio (audi et alteram partem) in udienze pubbliche senza incontri separati (caucus). In Cina, la mediazione è distorta da incentivi burocratici di valutazione delle prestazioni, caucus opachi e il timore di relazioni informali ("Guanxi").
* '''Base Legale:''' Codice di procedura civile olandese Art. 87 & 88; CEDU Art. 6; Legge di procedura civile cinese; Linee guida della SPC (2010).

=== Rumantsch ===
'''Ramma politica cumparegliativa da la mediaziun giudiziala da Li & Verschoof'''
Publitgà da la Dr. Yedan Li e dal Prof. Rick Verschoof en l' ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA, 2017), cumpareglia quest cadro la pratica da la mediaziun tras derschaders en ils Pajais Bass ed en China. Il studi empiric mussa ch'ils derschaders dad omadus pajais utiliseschan tecnicas da mediaziun fitg sumegliantas (basadas sin la rait da Riskin), ma las reacziuns dals litigants èn diametralmain oppostas: auta satisfacziun en ils Pajais Bass, profunda disfidanza en China. Ils auturs attribueschan questa divergenza a differenzas instituziunalas. En ils Pajais Bass vegn respectà il princip da l'audiziun eguala (audi et alteram partem) en audienzas publicas senza discurs separads (caucuses). En China vegn la mediaziun falsifitgada tras impuls burocratics da valitaziun da prestaziun, caucuses opacs e la tema da relaziuns informalas ("Guanxi").
* '''Basa Legala:''' Cudesch da procedura civila ollandais Art. 87 & 88; CEDH Art. 6; Lescha da procedura civila chinaisa; Lingias directivas da la SPC (2010).

The '''Assessment Policy Framework for Insurance Sustainability and Corporate Governance (EU–Italy)''' (officially published as ''The Assessment of Sustainability in Insurance Activity: Corporate and Products Governance. The Perspective of the European Union and the Effects on Italian Insurance Regulations'') is a comprehensive legal and policy analysis framework formulated by Prof. Ciro G. Corvese in ''The Italian Law Journal'' (Vol. 10 – Nos. 01-02/2024, pp. 575–598)<ref>Corvese, C.G. (2024). The Assessment of Sustainability in Insurance Activity: Corporate and Products Governance. The Perspective of the European Union and the Effects on Italian Insurance Regulations. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 10(1-2), 575–598.</ref>. 

The framework evaluates the systemic integration of sustainability risks, sustainability factors, and sustainability preferences into the corporate governance and distribution systems of insurance and reinsurance undertakings<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 575, 576, 578, 580.</ref>. It examines the structural adjustments to the ''Solvency II'' regime (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/35 as amended by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/1256) and the ''Insurance Distribution Directive (IDD)'' (Commission Delegated Regulations (EU) 2017/2358 & 2017/2359 as amended by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/1257)<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 577, 578, 585, 588.</ref>. 

Furthermore, the framework addresses Product Oversight and Governance (POG), the Prudent Person Principle (Article 132 Solvency II / Article 275a Delegated Reg 2015/35), rules of conduct, advisory processes for Insurance-Based Investment Products (IBIPs), and safeguards against greenwashing and mis-selling<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 583, 584, 585, 589.</ref>. It also details national implementation and regulatory harmonization in Italy led by the Institute for the Supervision of Insurance (IVASS) via Provision No. 131/2023, which amended IVASS Regulations Nos. 24/2016, 38/2018, 40/2018, and 45/2020<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 592, 593, 595, 596.</ref>.

== Overview & Executive Summary ==
Authored by [[Ciro G. Corvese]] (Associate Professor of Business Law and Corporate Law at the University of Siena), this policy framework analyzes the mandatory incorporation of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) principles into European Union and Italian insurance regimes<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 575, 576.</ref>. Rather than enacting standalone primary regulations, the European Union embedded sustainability factors, risks, and client preferences directly into existing foundational insurance pillars (Solvency II and IDD) through Delegated Regulations (EU) 2021/1256 and 2021/1257<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 577, 578.</ref>.

These amendments structurally reform risk management, actuarial functions, executive remuneration policies, and update the application of the Prudent Person Principle<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 581, 582, 584.</ref>. For distributors of Insurance-Based Investment Products (IBIPs), advisors are required to explicitly record customer sustainability preferences while maintaining a strict sequence: financial risk profiles and investment objectives must be determined prior to assessing sustainability preferences to prevent greenwashing and mis-selling<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 588, 589, 591.</ref>. In Italy, IVASS Provision No. 131/2023 harmonized national regulatory standards across four key operational regulations<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 592, 593.</ref>.

== Legal Basis & Regulatory Framework ==
* '''European Union Regulations & Directives''':
** ''EU Sustainable Finance Action Plan (COM(2018) 97 final)''<ref>Corvese (2024), p. 575.</ref>.
** ''Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR / Regulation (EU) 2019/2088)'': Statutory definitions of sustainability risk (Art. 2(22)), sustainability factors (Art. 2(24)), and sustainable investments (Art. 2(17))<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 576, 580.</ref>.
** ''EU Taxonomy Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2020/852)'': Environmentally sustainable economic activities (Art. 2(1))<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 577, 580.</ref>.
** ''Solvency II Framework (Directive 2009/138/EC & Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/35)'': Articles 44(2) & 48(1)(g) Directive 2009/138/EC; Articles 260, 269, 272, 275, 275a Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/35<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 577, 579, 581.</ref>.
** ''Insurance Distribution Directive (IDD / Directive (EU) 2016/97)'': Articles 17(1), 28, 30(1)<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 577, 587, 591.</ref>.
** ''Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/1256'': Amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/35 regarding the integration of sustainability risks in governance<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 578, 585.</ref>.
** ''Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/1257'': Amending Delegated Regulations (EU) 2017/2358 & 2017/2359 regarding sustainability factors, risks, and preferences in POG and IBIP business conduct<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 578, 588.</ref>.
** ''Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD / Directive (EU) 2024/1760)'': Article 15(3) on executive remuneration alignment with climate targets<ref>Corvese (2024), p. 583.</ref>.
* '''Italian Insurance Supervisory Authority (IVASS) Regulations''':
** ''IVASS Provision of May 10, 2023, No. 131''<ref>Corvese (2024), p. 592.</ref>.
** ''IVASS Regulation No. 24/2016'' (Investments and Asset Management)<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 592, 593.</ref>.
** ''IVASS Regulation No. 38/2018'' (Corporate Governance System and Risk Management)<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 592, 593, 594.</ref>.
** ''IVASS Regulation No. 40/2018'' (Insurance Distribution and IBIP Rules of Conduct)<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 592, 595.</ref>.
** ''IVASS Regulation No. 45/2020'' (Product Oversight and Governance / POG)<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 593, 596.</ref>.
** ''Consob Regulation No. 20307/2018'' (Intermediaries Regulation)<ref>Corvese (2024), p. 595.</ref>.
* '''Institutional Guidelines & Supervisory Guidance''':
** ''EIOPA Technical Advice & Guidelines on System of Governance (EIOPA-BoS-14/253EN & EIOPA-BoS-19/172)''<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 578, 582.</ref>.
** ''EIOPA Guidance on Customer's Sustainability Preferences in Suitability Assessment under IDD (EIOPA-BoS-22-391)''<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 584, 591.</ref>.
** ''UN Principles for Responsible Investment (UNPRI) & UN Principles for Sustainable Insurance (UNPSI)''<ref>Corvese (2024), p. 576.</ref>.

== Three Main Pillars of Policy Analysis ==
1. '''Integration of Sustainability Risks into Solvency II Corporate Governance''': Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/1256 mandates that risk management (Art. 269), actuarial functions (Art. 272), remuneration policies (Art. 275), and the Prudent Person Principle (Art. 275a) explicitly incorporate sustainability risks to guarantee long-term asset-liability stability<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 580, 581, 582, 584.</ref>.
2. '''Product Governance (POG) and IBIP Suitability Assessments''': Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/1257 requires manufacturers and distributors to embed sustainability objectives within Target Market (TM) identification. Customers without sustainability preferences are classified as neutral rather than part of a negative target market. Advising on IBIPs requires prior evaluation of financial risk tolerance before collecting sustainability preferences to prevent greenwashing<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 585, 586, 588, 589, 596.</ref>.
3. '''Italian Domestic Harmonization via IVASS Provision 131/2023''': IVASS aligned four major national regulations (Reg. 24/2016, 38/2018, 40/2018, and 45/2020) to enforce policy restructuring across investment strategies, distributor incentive structures, pre-contractual disclosures, and mandatory ESG training networks<ref>Corvese (2024), pp. 592, 593, 594, 595, 596.</ref>.

title: Judicial-policy-cosenza-ppo-governance-2011

{{Infobox
