Il '''Quadro Politico di Riforma Giudiziaria, Indipendenza della Magistratura e Stato di Diritto in Ucraina''' (''Judicial Reform, Judicial Independence, and Rule of Law Policy Framework in Ukraine'') è un modello di analisi giuridica comparata e politica giudiziaria sviluppato da Larry A. Di Matteo, Galyna Mykhailiuk e Nina Mykhailiuk per valutare la trasformazione del sistema giudiziario ucraino post-2014 <ref>Di Matteo, L. A., Mykhailiuk, G., & Mykhailiuk, N. (2021). Advancing the Rule of Law: Creating an Independent and Competent Judiciary. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 07(01), 61–93.</ref>. Il quadro analizza l'istituzione di nuovi organi specializzati ([[High Anti-Corruption Court]] / HACC, [[High Court for Intellectual Property]] / HCIP), la selezione dei giudici della nuova [[Supreme Court of Ukraine|Corte Suprema]], il ruolo dei consigli indipendenti ([[High Qualification Commission of Judges]] / HQCJ, [[High Council of Justice]] / HCJ, [[Public Integrity Council]] / PIC, [[Public Council of International Experts]] / PCIE), gli emendamenti costituzionali del 2016 che hanno revocato le competenze politiche del Parlamento e del Presidente sulle nomine giudiziarie, e l'allineamento con gli standard della [[Commissione di Venezia]] e dell'[[Unione Europea]] <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 61, 63, 77, 78, 81, 83, 88.</ref>.

== Descrizione Generale ==
Elaborato da [[Larry A. Di Matteo]], [[Galyna Mykhailiuk]] (Deputata del Parlamento ucraino) e [[Nina Mykhailiuk]], lo studio presenta un'analisi approfondita della riforma giudiziaria ucraina successiva alla Rivoluzione Maidan del 2014 <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 61, 63.</ref>. Gli autori esaminano le misure adottate dall'Ucraina per ripristinare la fiducia pubblica e soddisfare i criteri europei dello Stato di diritto <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 61, 65, 76.</ref>. Tra i temi principali figurano la spoliticizzazione delle nomine giudiziarie, l'integrazione di esperti internazionali (PCIE) nella selezione dei giudici anticorruzione e le sfide operative legate all'esecuzione delle norme <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 78, 83, 88, 91.</ref>.

== Base Giuridica ==
Il quadro normativo della riforma si fonda su strumenti costituzionali nazionali, leggi ordinarie e pareri internazionali:
* '''[[Costituzione dell'Ucraina]] (Emendamenti del 30 settembre 2016)''': Ha rimosso il potere politico del Parlamento e del Presidente sulle nomine e sui licenziamenti dei giudici, abolendo il periodo di prova di 5 anni per i giudici di nuova nomina <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 78, 88.</ref>.
* '''[[Law on Ensuring the Right to a Fair Trial 2015|Legge sul Diritto a un Equo Processo 2015]] (Legge N. 192-VIII)''' e '''[[Law on the Judiciary and Status of Judges 2016|Legge sull'Ordinamento Giudiziario e lo Status dei Giudici 2016]] (Legge N. 1402-VIII)''': Norme fondamentali sull'amministrazione della giustizia e sui requisiti professionali <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 77, 88.</ref>.
* '''[[Law on the High Council of Justice 2016|Legge sull'Alto Consiglio della Magistratura 2016]] (Legge N. 1798-VIII)''': Ha trasferito la competenza disciplinare sui giudici all'Alto Consiglio della Magistratura (HCJ) <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 81, 88.</ref>.
* '''[[Law on the High Anti-Corruption Court 2018|Legge sull'Alta Corte Anticorruzione 2018]] (Legge N. 2447-VIII)''': Ha istituito l'Alta Corte Anticorruzione (HACC) e il Consiglio Pubblico di Esperti Internazionali (PCIE) <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 76, 83.</ref>.
* '''Standard Internazionali''': Pareri della [[Commissione di Venezia]] (N. 801/2015 e N. 904/2017) <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 73, 76, 88.</ref>.

== Contesto e Spoliticizzazione ==
Dopo il 2014, il livello di fiducia dei cittadini ucraini nella magistratura è crollato a causa della corruzione sistemica e delle ingerenze politiche <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 63, 72.</ref>. Attraverso l'Accordo di Coalizione ''European Ukraine'' e la ''Strategia Ukraine-2020'', il governo ha posto la riforma giudiziaria come condizione essenziale per l'integrazione europea <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 74, 76.</ref>. La rimozione delle prerogative parlamentari nelle nomine è stata fondamentale per prevenire fenomeni di ''judicial capture'', analizzati anche in prospettiva comparata con i casi di Turchia e Polonia <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 73, 88.</ref>.

== Obiettivi ==
* Garantire un corpo giudiziario indipendente, competente ed esente da corruzione sistemica <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 61, 63.</ref>.
* Depoliticizzare le procedure di reclutamento, valutazione e disciplina dei giudici <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 67, 88.</ref>.
* Aumentare la fiducia delle istituzioni e soddisfare i requisiti di adesione all'Unione Europea <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 61, 73, 77.</ref>.

== Ambito di Applicazione ==
Include il diritto costituzionale ucraino, le procedure concorsuali per la nuova Corte Suprema, l'istituzione dei tribunali specializzati (HACC e HCIP), l'analisi comparata con i sistemi giudiziari degli Stati Uniti, della Polonia e della Turchia, e le funzioni degli organi di valutazione (HQCJ, HCJ, PIC, PCIE) <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 65, 73, 78–87.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Principali e Organi di Valutazione ==
* '''Abolizione del Controllo Politico''': Gli emendamenti costituzionali del 2016 hanno trasferito in via esclusiva all'Alto Consiglio della Magistratura (HCJ) la gestione delle nomine, dei trasferimenti e delle sanzioni disciplinari dei magistrati <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), p. 88.</ref>.
* '''High Qualification Commission of Judges (HQCJ) e Public Integrity Council (PIC)''': L'HQCJ gestisce i concorsi e le valutazioni, affiancata dal PIC, un organo della società civile incaricato di verificare l'integrità etica e patrimoniale dei candidati <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 79, 81.</ref>.
* '''Public Council of International Experts (PCIE)''': Organismo composto da esperti legali internazionali con potere di veto congiunto con l'HQCJ per escludere candidati privi dei requisiti di integrità per l'HACC <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), p. 83.</ref>.

== Criticità e Sfide Operative ==
* '''Carenza di Giudici''': Le dimissioni di massa e la lentezza delle valutazioni hanno generato una grave carenza di organico nei tribunali di primo e secondo grado <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), p. 81.</ref>.
* '''Decisioni della Corte Costituzionale''': La sentenza N. 2-p/2020 della Corte Costituzionale ha annullato alcune disposizioni della riforma, evidenziando la fragilità delle riforme non pienamente blindate a livello costituzionale <ref>Di Matteo et al. (2021), pp. 91, 93.</ref>.

'''Policy Framework on Generative AI Regulation, Data Protection, and Digital Vulnerability''' (''ChatGPT: Challenges and Legal Issues in Advanced Conversational AI'') is a comparative private law and data protection regulatory policy framework formulated by Amalia Diurni and Giovanni Maria Riccio. It analyzes the legal challenges, privacy risks (web scraping, data confidentiality, machine accuracy/hallucinations, minor age verification), and digital vulnerability arising from conversational and generative artificial intelligence systems (such as ChatGPT and Replika). Furthermore, it evaluates enforcement actions by the Italian Data Protection Authority (''Garante per la Protezione dei Dati Personali'') and the establishment of supranational regulatory standards including the EU AI Act, the EDPB Task Force, the G7 Hiroshima Process, and the Bletchley Declaration <ref>Diurni, A., & Riccio, G.M. (2023). ChatGPT: Challenges and Legal Issues in Advanced Conversational AI. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 9(2), 473–498.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Authored by [[Amalia Diurni]] (Full Professor of Comparative Private Law at the University of Rome "Tor Vergata") and [[Giovanni Maria Riccio]] (Full Professor of Comparative Law at the University of Salerno), this study evaluates the legal and societal risks associated with the mass deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 473, 474.</ref>. 

The analysis highlights the emergence of a new legal concept termed "digital vulnerability", wherein users become ontologically vulnerable to the illusion of empathy and the manipulation of "meaningless narratives" produced by conversational AI <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 473, 481.</ref>. The authors review the provisional ban imposed on ChatGPT by the Italian Data Protection Authority (''Garante Privacy'') in March 2023 due to GDPR non-compliance, and advocate for an adaptive, human-centric regulatory framework centered on transparency, risk assessment, and algorithmic explainability <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 483, 486, 489.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''[[General Data Protection Regulation]] (GDPR / Regulation EU 2016/679)''':
** ''Article 3'': Territorial scope <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 489.</ref>.
** ''Articles 5 & 6'': Principles of data accuracy and the lack of a lawful basis for mass training data collection via web scraping <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 489, 491.</ref>.
** ''Article 8'': Protection of minors' personal data and age verification mandates <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 489, 494.</ref>.
** ''Article 15'': Right of access by the data subject <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 493.</ref>.
** ''Articles 16 & 17'': Right to rectification and right to erasure (''right to be forgotten'') within machine learning parameter weights <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 493, 494.</ref>.
** ''Article 22'': Automated individual decision-making and profiling constraints <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 489.</ref>.
** ''Article 58(2)(f)'': Investigative and corrective powers to impose temporary or definitive limitations/bans on processing <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 489.</ref>.
* '''[[EU AI Act]] (Proposal COM(2021) 206 final / Amendments of 14 June 2023)''': Recitals 60g and 60h, Article 28b (transparency obligations for foundation generative models, prevention of illegal content generation, and mandatory public summaries of copyrighted training data) <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 484, 485.</ref>.
* '''Supranational Policy Frameworks''': The [[Bletchley Declaration]] (UK AI Safety Summit 2023) <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 485.</ref>, the G7 Hiroshima AI Process (Guiding Principles & Code of Conduct) <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 485.</ref>, and the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 485.</ref>.

== Three AI Profiles and Risk Dimensions ==
1. '''Pre-trained AI (Algorithmic Training Phase)''': High risk of unauthorized web scraping, massive processing of unverified personal data, and systematic data representation bias <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 475, 477.</ref>.
2. '''Generative AI (Deep Learning & Output Generation)''': High risk of "machine hallucinations" where false or misleading statements harm personal identity and reputation, potential copyright infringement, and mass automated disinformation <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 477, 479, 491.</ref>.
3. '''Communicative AI (Human-Machine Interaction)''': Risk of emotional manipulation driven by the AI's imitation of natural language, exploiting users' digital vulnerability and diminishing critical pluralism <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 480, 481.</ref>.

== Policy Implementation & Technical Barriers ==
* '''Garante Privacy Enforcement (March 2023)''': The Italian authority issued a provisional limitation against OpenAI due to: i) lack of a privacy notice; ii) lack of a legal basis for mass web scraping; iii) generation of inaccurate personal data; iv) lack of an age verification mechanism for minors <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 489, 491, 494.</ref>. A similar order was issued against Luka Inc. (Replika app) on 2 February 2023 under Article 58(2)(f) GDPR <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 489.</ref>.
* '''The Machine Unlearning Dilemma''': Fulfilling the right to rectification (Art. 16 GDPR) and the right to erasure (Art. 17 GDPR) poses a fundamental technical barrier in neural networks, as removing specific personal data points without retraining the entire model from scratch remains a complex technical hurdle <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 493, 494.</ref>.
* '''Enforcement Limitations''': Administrative bans imposed unilaterally show structural limitations when users bypass geographic restrictions using Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), reinforcing the necessity of supranational coordination <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 483, 489.</ref>.

== Related Entities & Focus Status ==
* '''[[Amalia Diurni]]''': Lead Author; Full Professor of Comparative Private Law at the University of Rome "Tor Vergata" <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 473.</ref>.
* '''[[Giovanni Maria Riccio]]''': Lead Author; Full Professor of Comparative Law at the University of Salerno <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 473.</ref>.
* '''[[Garante per la Protezione dei Dati Personali]]''': Italian Data Protection Authority <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 489.</ref>.
* '''[[European Data Protection Board]] (EDPB)''': Established the dedicated ChatGPT Task Force on 13 April 2023 <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 483.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 473–498.</ref>
* '''Geovanny Widya Berlianty P''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 473–498.</ref>

Il '''Quadro Politico sulla Regolamentazione dell'IA Generativa, Protezione dei Dati e Vulnerabilità Digitale''' (''ChatGPT: Challenges and Legal Issues in Advanced Conversational AI'') è un quadro analitico di diritto privato comparato e regolamentazione della protezione dei dati formulato da Amalia Diurni e Giovanni Maria Riccio. Il quadro esamina le sfide giuridiche, i rischi per la privacy (web scraping, riservatezza dei dati, accuratezza/allucinazioni della macchina, verifica dell'età dei minori) e la vulnerabilità digitale (''digital vulnerability'') derivanti dall'uso dell'intelligenza artificiale conversazionale e generativa (come ChatGPT e Replika). Valuta inoltre le azioni di applicazione della legge da parte dell'Autorità Garante per la Protezione dei Dati Personali e la creazione di standard normativi sopranazionali (EU AI Act, EDPB Task Force, G7 Hiroshima Process, Dichiarazione di Bletchley) <ref>Diurni, A., & Riccio, G.M. (2023). ChatGPT: Challenges and Legal Issues in Advanced Conversational AI. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 9(2), 473–498.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Scritto da [[Amalia Diurni]] (Professoressa Ordinaria di Diritto Privato Comparato presso l'Università degli Studi di Roma "Tor Vergata") e [[Giovanni Maria Riccio]] (Professore Ordinario di Diritto Comparato presso l'Università degli Studi di Salerno), lo studio valuta i rischi legali e sociali legati al dispiegamento di massa dei modelli linguistici di grandi dimensioni (LLM) come ChatGPT <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 473, 474.</ref>.

L'analisi evidenzia l'emergere del nuovo concetto giuridico di "vulnerabilità digitale", in cui gli utenti diventano ontologicamente vulnerabili all'illusione dell'empatia e alla manipolazione di narrazioni "prive di significato" (''meaningless narratives'') generate dall'IA conversazionale <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 473, 481.</ref>. Gli autori esaminano la limitazione provvisoria imposta a ChatGPT dal Garante per la Protezione dei Dati Personali nel marzo 2023 per non conformità al GDPR, e propongono un quadro normativo adattivo e antropocentrico basato su trasparenza, valutazione del rischio e spiegabilità algoritmica (''explainability'') <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 483, 486, 489.</ref>.

== Base Giuridica ==
* '''[[Regolamento Generale sulla Protezione dei Dati]] (GDPR / Regolamento UE 2016/679)''':
** ''Articolo 3'': Ambito di applicazione territoriale <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 489.</ref>.
** ''Articoli 5 e 6'': Principi di esattezza dei dati e assenza di una base giuridica idonea per la raccolta massiva di dati di addestramento tramite web scraping <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 489, 491.</ref>.
** ''Articolo 8'': Condizioni applicabili al consenso dei minori in relazione ai servizi della società dell'informazione <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 489, 494.</ref>.
** ''Articolo 15'': Diritto di accesso dell'interessato <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 493.</ref>.
** ''Articoli 16 e 17'': Diritto di rettifica e diritto alla cancellazione (''diritto all'oblio'') all'interno dei pesi parametrici della rete neurale <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 493, 494.</ref>.
** ''Articolo 22'': Processo decisionale automatizzato relativo alle persone fisiche e profilazione <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 489.</ref>.
** ''Articolo 58, par. 2, lett. f'': Poteri correttivi di imporre una limitazione provvisoria o definitiva al trattamento <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 489.</ref>.
* '''[[EU AI Act|Proposta di Regolamento sull'IA dell'UE]] (COM(2021) 206 final / Emendamenti del 14 giugno 2023)''': Considerandi 60g e 60h, Articolo 28b (obblighi di trasparenza per i modelli di IA generativa fondativi, prevenzione della generazione di contenuti illeciti e sintesi dettagliata dei dati protetti dal diritto d'autore usati per l'addestramento) <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 484, 485.</ref>.
* '''Iniziative Sopranazionali''': La [[Dichiarazione di Bletchley]] (2023) <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 485.</ref>, il G7 Hiroshima AI Process <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 485.</ref> e la Raccomandazione UNESCO sull'Etica dell'Intelligenza Artificiale <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 485.</ref>.

== Profilazione dei Rischi dell'IA ==
1. '''IA Pre-addestrata (Pretrained AI)''': Rischi derivanti dalla raccolta massiva non autorizzata di dati personali dal web e bias di rappresentazione dei dati <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 475, 477.</ref>.
2. '''IA Generativa (Generative AI)''': Rischi di "allucinazioni della macchina" (''machine hallucinations'') che generano informazioni false dannose per l'identità personale, violazioni del diritto d'autore e disinformazione automatizzata <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 477, 479, 491.</ref>.
3. '''IA Conversazionale (Communicative AI)''': Rischi di manipolazione emotiva dovuti all'imitazione del linguaggio umano, con conseguente sfruttamento della vulnerabilità digitale degli utenti e riduzione del pluralismo critico <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 480, 481.</ref>.

== Attuazione della Politica e Ostacoli Tecnici ==
* '''Intervento del Garante Privacy (Marzo 2023)''': L'autorità italiana ha disposto la limitazione provvisoria nei confronti di OpenAI per: i) mancanza di informativa sulla privacy; ii) assenza di idonea base giuridica per il web scraping; iii) inesattezza dei dati personali elaborati; iv) assenza di un sistema di verifica dell'età dei minori <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 489, 491, 494.</ref>. Un provvedimento analogo è stato emesso contro Luka Inc. (app Replika) il 2 febbraio 2023 ai sensi dell'Art. 58(2)(f) del GDPR <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 489.</ref>.
* '''Problema Tecnico dell'Unlearning''': L'esercizio del diritto di rettifica (Art. 16 GDPR) e di cancellazione (Art. 17 GDPR) incontra un limite tecnico complesso nelle reti neurali, poiché rimuovere singoli dati senza riaddestrare l'intero modello dall'inizio (''machine unlearning barrier'') rimane una sfida irrisolta <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 493, 494.</ref>.
* '''Limiti dell'Esecuzione Territoriale''': I divieti amministrativi nazionali mostrano limiti pratici se gli utenti aggirano le restrizioni tramite reti private virtuali (VPN), evidenziando la necessità di un'azione regolatoria coordinata a livello globale <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 483, 489.</ref>.

== Entità Correlate e Stato degli Individui ==
* '''[[Amalia Diurni]]''': Autrice principale; Professoressa Ordinaria di Diritto Privato Comparato presso l'Università degli Studi di Roma "Tor Vergata" <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 473.</ref>.
* '''[[Giovanni Maria Riccio]]''': Autore principale; Professore Ordinario di Diritto Comparato presso l'Università degli Studi di Salerno <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 473.</ref>.
* '''[[Garante per la Protezione dei Dati Personali]]''': Autorità Garante per la Privacy in Italia <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 489.</ref>.
* '''[[Comitato Europeo per la Protezione dei Dati]] (EDPB)''': Ha istituito la Task Force dedicata a ChatGPT il 13 aprile 2023 <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), p. 483.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Non trovato nelle fonti disponibili.]]'' <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 473–498.</ref>
* '''Geovanny Widya Berlianty P''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Non trovato nelle fonti disponibili.]]'' <ref>Diurni & Riccio (2023), pp. 473–498.</ref>

'''Decree of the President of the Council of Ministers April 22, 2022, n. 54''' (''Decreto del Presidente del Consiglio dei Ministri 22 aprile 2022, n. 54'') is an Italian executive decree amending DPCM n. 84/2015 and DPCM n. 100/2019 to establish the ''Department for the Digital Transition of Justice, Statistical Analysis and Cohesion Policies'' (''Dipartimento per la transizione digitale della giustizia, l'analisi statistica e le politiche di coesione'') within the Italian Ministry of Justice <ref>DPCM 22 aprile 2022, n. 54, Art. 1 para. 1.</ref>; reorganize key General Directorates (including DGSIA, Statistics, Cohesion Policies, and Penitentiary Infrastructure) <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 1 para. 1 subparas. c, d.</ref>; and execute the personnel staff quota redistribution for managerial and administrative judicial personnel <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 3 and Annexes I–IV.</ref>.

== Executive Summary ==
Promulgated by the President of the Council of Ministers Mario Draghi upon the proposal of the Minister of Justice Marta Cartabia, this decree restructures the Italian Ministry of Justice to support the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) and accelerate judicial digital transformation <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Preamble and Art. 5.</ref>. The cornerstone of this reorganization is the creation of the Department for Digital Transition, which oversees DGSIA (designated as the single digital transition office pursuant to Art. 17 of the Digital Administration Code), the General Directorate for Statistics and Organizational Analysis, and the General Directorate for the Coordination of Cohesion Policies <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 1 para. 1 subpara. c (Art. 5-bis DPCM 84/2015).</ref>. Additionally, a new General Directorate was created within the Department of Penitentiary Administration (DAP) specifically tasked with managing assets, services, and prison infrastructure projects <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 1 para. 1 subpara. d.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Primary Statutes & Legislative Mandates''':
** ''Law August 23, 1988, n. 400 (Art. 17)'' <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Preamble.</ref>.
** ''Decree-Law November 6, 2021, n. 152 (converted with amendments by Law December 29, 2021, n. 233, Art. 35)'' <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Preamble.</ref>.
** ''Legislative Decree July 30, 1999, n. 300 (Arts. 4, 5, 16–19)'' <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Preamble.</ref>.
** ''Legislative Decree March 7, 2005, n. 82 (Digital Administration Code - Art. 17)'' <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 1 para. 1 subpara. c.</ref>.
** ''DPCM June 15, 2015, n. 84'' and ''DPCM June 19, 2019, n. 100'' <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Arts. 1, 2.</ref>.

== Key Provisions ==
=== 1. Establishment of the Digital Transition Department (Art. 5-bis DPCM 84/2015) ===
* '''General Directorate for Automated Information Systems (DGSIA)''': Responsible for digitization strategies, cybersecurity, server room management, and performing single-office digital transition duties under Art. 17 CAD <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 1 para. 1 subpara. c.</ref>.
* '''General Directorate of Statistics and Organizational Analysis''': Manages SISTAN, judicial statistics databases, and relations with ISTAT and international bodies <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 1 para. 1 subpara. c.</ref>.
* '''General Directorate for the Coordination of Cohesion Policies''': Coordinates EU cohesion programs, fund monitoring, and state aid compliance <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 1 para. 1 subpara. c.</ref>.

=== 2. General Directorate for Prison Infrastructure (DAP) ===
Directly manages public and patrimonial real estate assets, needs analysis, and infrastructure project execution across penal institutions <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 1 para. 1 subpara. d.</ref>.

=== 3. Personnel Quota Redistribution (Annexes I–IV) ===
* '''Judicial Administration''': 345 Executive/Managerial staff and 43,123 Area staff (Total: 43,468) <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Annex II (Table D).</ref>.
* '''Department of Penitentiary Administration (DAP)''': 346 Executive staff and 4,789 Area staff (Total: 5,135) <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Annex III (Table E).</ref>.
* '''Juvenile and Community Justice''': 62 Executive staff and 3,478 Area staff (Total: 3,540) <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Annex IV (Table F).</ref>.

'''Decreto del Presidente del Consiglio dei Ministri 22 aprile 2022, n. 54''' è un regolamento esecutivo della Repubblica Italiana che modifica il DPCM n. 84/2015 e il DPCM n. 100/2019 al fine di istituire il ''Dipartimento per la transizione digitale della giustizia, l'analisi statistica e le politiche di coesione'' presso il Ministero della Giustizia <ref>DPCM 22 aprile 2022, n. 54, Art. 1 comma 1.</ref>; riorganizzare le Direzioni Generali chiave (tra cui DGSIA, Statistica, Politiche di Coesione ed Edilizia Penitenziaria) <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 1 comma 1 lett. c, d.</ref>; e disporre la ridistribuzione delle dotazioni organiche del personale dirigenziale e amministrativo della giustizia <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 3 e Allegati I-IV.</ref>.

== Sintesi Esecutiva ==
Emanato dal Presidente del Consiglio dei Ministri Mario Draghi su proposta del Ministro della Giustizia Marta Cartabia, il decreto riorganizza la struttura ministeriale per garantire il raggiungimento degli obiettivi del Piano Nazionale di Ripresa e Resilienza (PNRR) e accelerare la transizione digitale della giustizia <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Preambolo e Art. 5.</ref>. Il fulcro della riforma è rappresentato dalla creazione del Dipartimento per la Transizione Digitale, dal quale dipendono la DGSIA (quale ufficio unico per la transizione digitale ai sensi dell'Art. 17 del Codice dell'Amministrazione Digitale), la Direzione Generale di Statistica e Analisi Organizzativa e la Direzione Generale per il Coordinamento delle Politiche di Coesione <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 1 comma 1 lett. c (Art. 5-bis DPCM 84/2015).</ref>. Viene inoltre istituita presso il Dipartimento dell'Amministrazione Penitenziaria (DAP) una nuova Direzione Generale dedicata alla gestione dei beni, dei servizi e dell'edilizia penitenziaria <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 1 comma 1 lett. d.</ref>.

== Basi Giuridiche ==
* '''Normativa Primaria e Decreti Attuativi''':
** ''Legge 23 agosto 1988, n. 400 (Art. 17)'' <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Preambolo.</ref>.
** ''Decreto-Legge 6 novembre 2021, n. 152 (convertito con modificazioni dalla Legge 29 dicembre 2021, n. 233, Art. 35)'' <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Preambolo.</ref>.
** ''Decreto Legislativo 30 luglio 1999, n. 300 (Artt. 4, 5, 16–19)'' <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Preambolo.</ref>.
** ''Decreto Legislativo 7 marzo 2005, n. 82 (Codice dell'amministrazione digitale - Art. 17)'' <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 1 comma 1 lett. c.</ref>.
** ''DPCM 15 giugno 2015, n. 84'' e ''DPCM 19 giugno 2019, n. 100'' <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Artt. 1, 2.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Principali ==
=== 1. Istituzione del Dipartimento per la Transizione Digitale (Art. 5-bis DPCM 84/2015) ===
* '''Direzione Generale per i Sistemi Informativi Automatizzati (DGSIA)''': Competente per le strategie di digitalizzazione, la cybersicurezza, la gestione dei data center e le funzioni di Responsabile per la transizione digitale ex Art. 17 CAD <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 1 comma 1 lett. c.</ref>.
* '''Direzione Generale di Statistica e Analisi Organizzativa''': Gestisce il SISTAN, le banche dati statistiche della giustizia e i rapporti con l'ISTAT e gli organismi internazionali <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 1 comma 1 lett. c.</ref>.
* '''Direzione Generale per il Coordinamento delle Politiche di Coesione''': Coordina i programmi di coesione europea, il monitoraggio dei fondi e la materia degli aiuti di Stato <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 1 comma 1 lett. c.</ref>.

=== 2. Direzione Generale per la Gestione dell'Edilizia Penitenziaria (DAP) ===
Sovraintende alla gestione del patrimonio immobiliare, all'analisi dei fabbisogni e alla programmazione degli interventi di edilizia penitenziaria <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Art. 1 comma 1 lett. d.</ref>.

=== 3. Ridistribuzione delle Dotazioni Organiche (Allegati I–IV) ===
* '''Amministrazione Giudiziaria''': 345 Dirigenti e 43.123 Unità di personale delle aree (Totale: 43.468) <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Allegato II (Tabella D).</ref>.
* '''Dipartimento Amministrazione Penitenziaria (DAP)''': 346 Dirigenti e 4.789 Unità di personale delle aree (Totale: 5.135) <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Allegato III (Tabella E).</ref>.
* '''Giustizia Minorile e di Comunità''': 62 Dirigenti e 3.478 Unità di personale delle aree (Totale: 3.540) <ref>DPCM 54/2022, Allegato IV (Tabella F).</ref>.

The '''Policy Framework on Dual Preliminarity and Italian-EU Triangular Judicial Dialogue''' (Italian: ''Doppia Pregiudizialità e Dialogo Segitiga Peradilan Italia-UE'') governs the doctrinal and procedural relationship between ordinary national courts, the [[Italian Constitutional Court]] (Corte Costituzionale / ItCC), and the [[Court of Justice of the European Union]] (ECJ / CJEU). It addresses scenarios of "dual preliminarity" (''doppia pregiudizialità''), where a domestic legal provision is alleged to simultaneously violate both the national Constitution and EU Law or the [[Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union]] (CFR). The doctrine evolved from the historical *Granital model* (Judgment No. 170/1984) to the *obiter dictum* of Judgment No. 269/2017 (which prioritized the "first word" of the Constitutional Court), and was subsequently refined into the *tempered 269 model* (Judgments No. 20/2019, No. 63/2019, No. 54/2022, and No. 67/2022) to guarantee national courts the freedom to refer questions to the ECJ under Article 267 TFEU and to disapply conflicting national legislation <ref>Amalfitano, C., & Cecchetti, L. (2023). The ECJ’s Approach to Dual Preliminarity 5 Years After the ITCC’s Judgment No. 269/2017. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 15(1), 86–120.</ref>.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Chiara Amalfitano]] (Full Professor of EU Law at the University of Milan) and [[Lorenzo Cecchetti]] (Postdoctoral Fellow in EU Law at Luiss University), the framework analyzes the ECJ's jurisprudence on Italian dual preliminarity five years following the landmark Judgment No. 269/2017 of the Italian Constitutional Court <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 86–87.</ref>. Initial concerns that Judgment No. 269/2017 would restrict ordinary courts from directly accessing the ECJ were resolved through the "tempered 269 model" established in Judgments No. 20/2019 and No. 63/2019 <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 87, 96–97.</ref>. The framework ensures full compliance with the core principles (''noyau dur'') of EU judicial protection while strengthening fundamental rights protection in Europe <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 86, 98, 117–120.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
The framework operates at the intersection of EU supranational law and Italian constitutional law:
* '''[[Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union]] (Article 267 TFEU)''': Establishes the preliminary reference procedure, securing the right and duty of national courts to refer questions of EU law to the ECJ <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 89–90.</ref>.
* '''[[Treaty on European Union]] (Article 4(2) & Article 19 TEU)''': Mandates respect for national constitutional identities and guarantees effective judicial protection <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 115–116.</ref>.
* '''[[Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union]] (CFR)''': Standard catalog of fundamental rights applicable when Member States implement EU law <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 94, 105.</ref>.
* '''[[Constitution of Italy]] (Articles 3, 11, 117, and 134)''': Grounds the integration of international/EU legal obligations and centralized constitutional review <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 94, 116, 118.</ref>.
* '''Key Jurisprudence''':
** ''ECJ'': *Simmenthal* (Case 106/77), *Melki and Abdeli* (Joined Cases C-188/10 & C-189/10), *A v B* (Case C-112/13), *O.D. and Others v INPS* (Case C-350/20), *IS* (Case C-564/19), *RS* (Case C-430/21) <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 89, 91, 98, 107, 111.</ref>.
** ''Italian Constitutional Court'': Judgment No. 170/1984 (*Granital*), Judgment No. 269/2017 (*Obiter Dictum*), Judgment No. 20/2019, Judgment No. 63/2019, Judgment No. 54/2022, Judgment No. 67/2022 <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 93–97, 118.</ref>.

== Background & Evolution of the Model ==
Dual preliminarity arises when a statute violates both constitutional norms and EU law <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), p. 88.</ref>. Under the *Granital Model* (1984), ordinary courts were required to directly disapply national statutes in conflict with directly effective EU law without prior referral to the Constitutional Court <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), p. 93.</ref>. Judgment No. 269/2017 attempted to invert this priority by inviting ordinary courts to submit questions of constitutionality first ("first word") <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), p. 94.</ref>. To align this with EU law standards, the ItCC adopted the *tempered 269 model* in Judgments No. 20/2019 and No. 63/2019, clarifying that referrals to the ItCC are an invitation and do not strip ordinary courts of their power to refer to the ECJ or disapply conflicting legislation <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 87, 96–97.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & Tempered 269 Model ==
* '''Three Core ECJ Requirements (Melki and A v B Case Law)''':
# National courts must remain free to submit preliminary references to the ECJ at any stage of proceedings <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 91–92.</ref>.
# National courts must be permitted to adopt interim protective measures <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), p. 92.</ref>.
# National courts must retain the power to disapply national legislation contrary to directly effective EU law <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), p. 92.</ref>.
* '''Refinements Under the Tempered Model''':
** *Judgment No. 20/2019*: Reconciles priority by defining the preliminary referral to the ItCC as an opportunity/invitation rather than an absolute restriction <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), p. 96.</ref>.
** *Judgment No. 63/2019*: Confirms the inherent power of ordinary judges to disapply non-compliant provisions <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), p. 97.</ref>.
** *ECJ Endorsement in O.D. v INPS (2021)*: The ECJ recognized the ItCC's preliminary reference under a presumption of relevance, resolving it within 13 months to preserve procedural economy <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 98–99.</ref>.

== Policy Analysis & Comparative Impact ==
Unlike the rule of law conflicts seen in Hungary (*IS*) and Romania (*RS*)—where national apex courts attempted to prohibit preliminary references under threat of disciplinary proceedings <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 107, 110–114</ref>—the Italian *tempered 269 model* fosters a cooperative framework between domestic constitutional review and EU judicial primacy <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 115–118</ref>.

Il '''Quadro Politico sulla Doppia Pregiudizialità e Dialogo Triangolare Italia-UE''' (inglese: ''Policy Framework on Dual Preliminarity and Italian-EU Triangular Judicial Dialogue'') disciplina la dottrina e le dinamiche procedurali tra i giudici comuni nazionali, la [[Corte costituzionale della Repubblica Italiana]] e la [[Corte di Giustizia dell'Unione Europea]] (CGUE / CEJ). Esso regola le ipotesi di "doppia pregiudizialità", vale a dire i casi in cui una norma nazionale sia sospettata di violare contemporaneamente la Costituzione italiana e il diritto dell'Unione europea o la [[Carta dei diritti fondamentali dell'Unione Europea]] (CDFUE). Il modello si è evoluto dal classico *modello Granital* (sentenza n. 170/1984) all''*obiter dictum* della sentenza n. 269/2017 (volto ad assicurare la "prima parola" alla Corte costituzionale), fino al perfezionamento nel *modello 269 temperato* (sentenze n. 20/2019, n. 63/2019, n. 54/2022 e n. 67/2022) per garantire la libertà del giudice comune di adire la CGUE ex art. 267 TFUE e di disapplicare la legge nazionale difforme <ref>Amalfitano, C., & Cecchetti, L. (2023). The ECJ’s Approach to Dual Preliminarity 5 Years After the ITCC’s Judgment No. 269/2017. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 15(1), 86–120.</ref>.

== Panoramica ==
Elaborato da [[Chiara Amalfitano]] (Professoressa Ordinaria di Diritto dell'UE presso l'Università degli Studi di Milano) e [[Lorenzo Cecchetti]] (Assegnista di ricerca in Diritto dell'UE presso la Luiss Guido Carli), il quadro analizza la giurisprudenza della CGUE sulla doppia pregiudizialità italiana a cinque anni dalla sentenza n. 269/2017 della Corte Costituzionale <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 86–87.</ref>. Le preoccupazioni iniziali circa un'eventuale limitazione delle prerogative dei giudici ordinari sono state superate con l'introduzione del "modello 269 temperato" nelle sentenze n. 20/2019 e n. 63/2019 <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 87, 96–97.</ref>. Tale quadro garantisce il rispetto del nucleo essenziale (''noyau dur'') della tutela giurisdizionale dell'UE, rafforzando contemporaneamente la protezione dei diritti fondamentali in Europa <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 86, 98, 117–120.</ref>.

== Basi Giuridiche ==
Il quadro opera all'intersezione tra il diritto sovranazionale dell'UE e il diritto costituzionale italiano:
* '''[[Trattato sul funzionamento dell'Unione europea]] (Articolo 267 TFUE)''': Fondamento del rinvio pregiudiziale, che assicura il diritto e l'obbligo dei giudici nazionali di adire la CGUE <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 89–90.</ref>.
* '''[[Trattato sull'Unione europea]] (Articoli 4(2) e 19 TUE)''': Tutela dell'identità nazionale degli Stati membri e garanzia di una tutela giurisdizionale effettiva <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 115–116.</ref>.
* '''[[Carta dei diritti fondamentali dell'Unione Europea]] (CDFUE)''': Parametro per la valutazione della compatibilità dei diritti fondamentali <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 94, 105.</ref>.
* '''[[Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana]] (Articoli 3, 11, 117 e 134)''': Fondamento dell'adeguamento dell'ordinamento interno al diritto dell'UE e del sindacato accentrato di costituzionalità <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 94, 116, 118.</ref>.
* '''Giurisprudenza Chiave''':
** *CGUE*: *Simmenthal* (Causa 106/77), *Melki e Abdeli* (Cause riunite C-188/10 e C-189/10), *A c. B* (Causa C-112/13), *O.D. e altri c. INPS* (Causa C-350/20), *IS* (Causa C-564/19), *RS* (Causa C-430/21) <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 89, 91, 98, 107, 111.</ref>.
** *Corte Costituzionale*: Sentenza n. 170/1984 (*Granital*), Sentenza n. 269/2017 (*Obiter Dictum*), Sentenza n. 20/2019, Sentenza n. 63/2019, Sentenza n. 54/2022, Sentenza n. 67/2022 <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 93–97, 118.</ref>.

== Evoluzione del Modello ==
La doppia pregiudizialità sorge quando una legge nazionale viola sia la Costituzione che il diritto dell'UE <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), p. 88.</ref>. Sotto il *modello Granital* (1984), il giudice comune era tenuto a disapplicare direttamente le norme interne contrastanti con il diritto dell'UE dotato di efficacia diretta <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), p. 93.</ref>. Con la sentenza n. 269/2017, la Consulta ha suggerito di sollevare prima la questione di legittimità costituzionale ("prima parola") <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), p. 94.</ref>. Per garantire la piena compatibilità con l'ordinamento dell'UE, la Corte costituzionale ha introdotto il *modello 269 temperato* (sentenze n. 20/2019 e n. 63/2019), chiarificando che il previo ricorso alla Consulta costituisce una facoltà/invito e non preclude al giudice comune la facoltà di adire la CGUE o di disapplicare la norma interna <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 87, 96–97.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Principali e Modello 269 Temperato ==
* '''I Tre Requisiti del Noyau Dur (Giurisprudenza Melki e A c. B)''':
# Il giudice nazionale deve rimanere libero di adire la CGUE in qualsiasi fase del processo <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 91–92.</ref>.
# Il giudice nazionale deve poter adottare qualsiasi misura provvisoria cautelare necessaria <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), p. 92.</ref>.
# Il giudice nazionale deve conservare il potere di disapplicare le disposizioni nazionali contrarie al diritto dell'UE con effetto diretto <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), p. 92.</ref>.
* '''Affinamenti nel Modello Temperato''':
** *Sentenza n. 20/2019*: Definisce il previo rinvio alla Consulta come un'opportunità o invito e non un obbligo assoluto <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), p. 96.</ref>.
** *Sentenza n. 63/2019*: Conferma il potere del giudice ordinario di disapplicare le norme nazionali difformi <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), p. 97.</ref>.
** *Riconoscimento della CGUE nella causa O.D. c. INPS (2021)*: La CGUE ha accolto il rinvio pregiudiziale della Corte costituzionale avvalendosi della presunzione di rilevanza e decidendo il caso entro 13 mesi <ref>Amalfitano & Cecchetti (2023), pp. 98–99.</ref>.

'''The Bridges Built By Judges: Justice And Credibility Policy Framework''' is a policy framework and socio-legal analysis examining the gap between the perceptions of the Dutch public and the Judiciary regarding justice and punitiveness. It outlines a strategy to balance two dimensions (cognitive and normative) to build the public credibility of the judiciary (''judicial credibility'') [FACT].

== Summary ==
Published by Prof. Gabriël van den Brink in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA) with the support of the Netherlands Council for the Judiciary (''Raad voor de rechtspraak''), this policy framework dissects the phenomenon of the gap between judges and society. Based on research data from the ''Social and Cultural Planning Office'' (SCP) and studies by Elffers, De Keijser, and Wagenaar, the majority of the public considers criminal sentences in the Netherlands to be too lenient. This framework maps this gap along two axes (cognitive and normative) and offers four dimensions of credibility for judges to build communicative "bridges" without sacrificing judicial independence.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Article 1 of the Dutch Constitution (Grondwet):''' Guarantees the principle of equality and the prohibition of discrimination in legal services.
* '''Article 1 of the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure (Wetboek van Strafvordering):''' Establishes the principle of legality while providing judicial discretion for judges to fill legal gaps.
* '''Judiciary Organization Act 2002 (Wet op de rechterlijke organisatie):''' The foundation for the reorganization of the judicial structure and the establishment of the Netherlands Council for the Judiciary.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the text [FACT].

== Background ==
Although the Netherlands is classified as a ''high-trust society'' (61% of the public trusts the judiciary), public trust fluctuates due to media coverage of judicial scandals (such as the 2000 Schiedam Park murder and the Lucia de B. case). Judges face societal demands for harsher punishments, while professional legal reasoning remains bound by strict formal evidentiary criteria.

== Objectives ==
1. Understand the sociological roots of the gap between public perception and judicial legal reasoning.
2. Analyze the differences between ''legal truth'' and ''media logic''.
3. Map citizen profiles based on education levels and normative attitudes (''active, awaiting, anxious citizens'').
4. Formulate strategies to increase the public credibility of judges based on four leadership dimensions.

== Scope ==
This policy evaluates the Dutch criminal justice system, the interaction between judicial panels and society, the role of mass media, and a comparison of public trust levels across European countries.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''The Punitiveness Gap:''' Experiments prove that laypeople who do not receive full information impose criminal sentences 3 to 4 times harsher than professional judges.
* '''Cognitive Axis:'''
** ''Legal Truth Policy:'' Based on rational arguments, formal evidence, and the state's monopoly on prosecution.
** ''Media Logic:'' Based on framing, the personalization of scapegoats, dramatization, and emotion.
* '''Normative Axis:'''
** ''Active Citizens:'' Highly educated, tolerant, and comprehend legal rationality (the profile of the majority of judges).
** ''Anxious Citizens:'' Less educated, anxious, and demand life imprisonment or strong authoritative leaders.

== Implementation ==
* '''Four Dimensions of Judicial Credibility (Kouzes & Posner Model):'''
# ''Interactive Dimension:'' Judges explain the reasoning of their verdicts directly to the public/media.
# ''Normative Dimension:'' Open explanation of the moral standards and legal principles underlying the sentence.
# ''Performative Dimension:'' The use of narratives, stories, and rhetoric that can be understood by the general public.
# ''Cognitive Dimension:'' Understanding the lived realities of the lower class and affected minority groups.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Inaccessibility of Legal Language:''' The use of overly technical legal reasoning language makes it difficult for the public and journalists to understand.
* '''Limited Effectiveness of Harsher Sentences:''' Mechanically increasing the severity of criminal sentences does not automatically increase the trust of less-educated citizens (''anxious citizens'').

== Reform / Change ==
* Strengthening ''victims' rights'' in trials to bridge citizens' experiences.
* Developing direct normative communication by judges outside the judicial "ivory tower."

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Netherlands Council for the Judiciary (Raad voor de rechtspraak):''' The institution that commissioned the public trust research.
* '''[private person]:''' A Law student at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta (NIM: 2410611102), enrolled in the 2024/2025 academic year, specializing in Constitutional Law (Hukum Tata Negara). Cecep Mustafa is not found in the available sources [FACT].

== Multilingual Summaries (Swiss National Languages) ==

=== Deutsch (Schweizer Hochdeutsch) ===
'''Gerechtigkeit und Glaubwürdigkeit: Über von Richtern gebaute Brücken'''
Dieser von Prof. Gabriël van den Brink im ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA, 2008) veröffentlichte Rahmen analysiert die soziologisch-rechtliche Kluft zwischen der niederländischen Öffentlichkeit und der Justiz in Bezug auf Strafmass (Punitiveness Gap) und Gerechtigkeit. Die Studie zeigt, dass eine rein mechanische Verschärfung von Strafen das Vertrauen "ängstlicher Bürger" (anxious citizens) nicht stärkt. Stattdessen schlägt der Rahmen vier Dimensionen richterlicher Glaubwürdigkeit vor, um die Lücke zwischen professioneller "rechtlicher Wahrheit" und emotionaler "Medienlogik" zu schliessen, ohne die richterliche Unabhängigkeit zu gefährden.
* '''Rechtsgrundlage:''' Niederländische Verfassung (Grondwet Art. 1); Strafprozessordnung (Art. 1); Gesetz über die Gerichtsorganisation 2002.

=== Français ===
'''Justice et crédibilité : Des ponts construits par les juges'''
Publié par le Prof. Gabriël van den Brink dans l' ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA, 2008), ce cadre analyse le fossé socio-juridique entre le public néerlandais et la magistrature concernant la sévérité des peines (punitiveness gap) et la justice. L'étude montre que l'alourdissement mécanique des peines ne renforce pas la confiance des « citoyens anxieux ». Au lieu de cela, le cadre propose quatre dimensions de crédibilité judiciaire pour combler l'écart entre la « vérité juridique » professionnelle et la « logique médiatique » émotionnelle, sans compromettre l'indépendance de la justice.
* '''Base Légale:''' Constitution néerlandaise (Grondwet Art. 1) ; Code de procédure pénale (Art. 1) ; Loi sur l'organisation judiciaire de 2002.

=== Italiano ===
'''Giustizia e credibilità: Ponti costruiti dai giudici'''
Pubblicato dal Prof. Gabriël van den Brink nell' ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA, 2008), questo quadro analizza il divario socio-legale tra il pubblico olandese e la magistratura in merito alla severità delle pene (punitiveness gap) e alla giustizia. Lo studio dimostra che un inasprimento meccanico delle pene non rafforza la fiducia dei "cittadini ansiosi". Invece, il quadro propone quattro dimensioni di credibilità giudiziaria per colmare il divario tra la "verità legale" professionale e la "logica dei media" emotiva, senza compromettere l'indipendenza giudiziaria.
* '''Base Legale:''' Costituzione olandese (Grondwet Art. 1); Codice di procedura penale (Art. 1); Legge sull'organizzazione giudiziaria del 2002.

'''Giustia e credibladad: Punts construidas da derschaders'''
Publitgà dal Prof. Gabriël van den Brink en l' ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA, 2008), analisescha quest cadro la largia socio-giuridica tranter il public ollandais ed ils derschaders pertutgant la severitad da las painas (punitiveness gap) e la giustia. Il studi mussa ch'in augment mecanic da las painas na rinforza betg la fidanza dals "burgais anxius". Empè da quai propona il cadro quatter dimensiuns da credibladad giudiziala per surmuntar la differenza tranter la "vardad giuridica" professiunala e la "logica da las medias" emoziunala, senza periclitar l'independenza giudiziala.
* '''Basa Legala:''' Constituziun ollandaisa (Grondwet Art. 1); Cudesch da procedura penala (Art. 1); Lescha davart l'organisaziun da las dretgiras 2002.

'''The e-CODEX Framework and Greek European Payment Order (EPO) Pilot Implementation''' is a transnational European Union e-Justice interoperability policy framework and electronic court system architecture model (e-CODEX - ''e-Justice Communication via Online Data Exchange''). Formulated by Prof. George Pangalos, Ioannis Salmatzidis, and Ioannis Pagkalos (Informatics Laboratory, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki / AUTH, 2014), it establishes decentralized interoperability standards (''e-Delivery, e-Signature DSS-Tool, e-ID, e-Document XML''), connecting the EU e-Justice Portal with national judicial systems, and operationalizes the European Payment Order (EPO) pilot system in Greece (at the Athens Court of First Instance) based on EU Regulations No. 1896/2006 and No. 936/2012 [1, 7–15, 20, 23].

== Summary ==
Published by Prof. George Pangalos, Ioannis Salmatzidis, and Ioannis Pagkalos in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this policy framework outlines the e-CODEX system architecture and the execution of the European Payment Order (EPO) pilot in Greece. e-CODEX is an EU Large Scale e-Justice project that designs decentralized infrastructure to link the EU e-Justice Portal with the national judicial systems of 20 member states. Utilizing four decentralized components (''Gateway, National Connector, National System/CMS, and e-Justice Portal''), e-CODEX enables paperless electronic filing of cross-border debt recovery claims [9–12, 13]. The Greek EPO pilot, centered at the Athens Court of First Instance, has been fully operational since June 2014, eliminating physical mail delivery and circumventing language barriers via automated XML data conversion.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Regulation (EC) No. 1896/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council:''' The foundational regulation creating the European Order for Payment (EPO) procedure for undisputed cross-border financial claims [13–14, 33].
* '''Regulation (EU) No. 936/2012:''' The regulation updating the EPO procedure standards and application forms across the EU [13–14].
* '''EU ICT Policy Support Program:''' The European Union funding framework financing the e-CODEX project for 50 months starting in 2012.
* '''Circle of Trust Agreement:''' An agreement ensuring data confidentiality, encryption, and mutual trust signed by all participating e-CODEX ministries of justice.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text.

== Background ==
The increasing economic integration and mobility of EU citizens have led to a rapid growth in cross-border legal procedures. Traditional manual, paper-based legal communication caused protracted delays, opaque case statuses, and exorbitant costs. In the commercial sector, cross-border debt payment delays triggered SME bankruptcies. To combat this, the EU launched the e-Justice initiative and funded the e-CODEX project.

== Objectives ==
1. Facilitate cross-border access to justice for EU citizens, enterprises, and legal professionals.
2. Build a decentralized, secure, and content-agnostic electronic delivery platform (''e-Delivery'') based on the ebMS 3.0 standard.
3. Operationalize the electronic European Payment Order (EPO) pilot integrated between the Greek judicial system and other EU member states.
4. Eliminate reliance on physical registered mail and reduce language barriers in case filings [1, 7, 9–10, 13–14].

== Scope ==
This policy covers the implementation of the e-CODEX architecture across 20 EU member states, with a specific focus on the EPO Pilot operations at the Athens Court of First Instance and the involvement of Greek lawyers.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Four Components of the e-CODEX Architecture:'''
# ''e-CODEX Gateway'': The secure data transmission hub using the ebMS 3.0 standard (Holodeck b2b messaging) and ETSI REM.
# ''National Connector'': The local module for semantic mapping, XML document conversion, and digital signature validation.
# ''National System (CMS)'': The internal court case management application (Athens Court of First Instance).
# ''European e-Justice Portal'': The single EU portal communicating directly with the Gateway.
* '''Three Main Building Blocks:'''
** ''e-Delivery'': Encrypted message transportation between Gateways.
** ''e-Signature'': Electronic signature verification based on the DSS-Tool to issue a ''trust-ok token''.
** ''e-ID'': User identity authentication via national portals (e.g., the Greek ''Ermis'' portal) or ''Find a Lawyer 2''.
* '''Phased Roll-out Strategy:'''
** The pilot implementation was initially restricted to lawyers (''lawyers first'') registered with the Athens Bar Association and Thessaloniki Bar Association before expanding to the general public.

== Implementation ==
* '''Operationalization of the Greek EPO Pilot:''' Fully functional since June 2014 at the Athens Court of First Instance (which manages ~60% of the national caseload).
* '''Automated Testing Tool:''' Use of an automated testing application to simulate random message transmissions to validate the reliability of the National Connector prior to full deployment.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Cross-Border Access Deficit:''' 63% of small cross-border financial claims in the EU were abandoned because the estimated handling costs exceeded the financial value claimed.
* '''Non-Technical Systemic Limitations:''' e-CODEX cannot resolve national regulatory differences regarding court fee payment methods, official defendant notification rules, and difficulties in identifying foreign court jurisdictions.

== Reform / Change ==
* Expansion of the e-CODEX pilot into 8 other legal domains, including Small Claims (SC), European Arrest Warrants (EAW), and the recognition of financial penalties [12–13].
* Plans to open direct e-filing access to ordinary citizens following the lawyer stabilization phase.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''European Commission (e-Justice Portal):''' The executive body managing the single EU justice portal.
* '''Aristotle University of Thessaloniki (AUTH):''' The scientific coordinator and technical developer of e-CODEX Greece.
* '''[private person]:''' A Law student at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta (NIM: 2410611102), specializing in Constitutional Law (Hukum Tata Negara). Cecep Mustafa is not found in the available sources.

'''The ECtHR Judicial Performance Measurement Policy Framework''' is a governance and judicial performance evaluation framework concerning the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR). Formulated through the critical research of Elizabeth Lambert Abdelgawad (2017) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), Vol. 8 No. 2, the framework evaluates the ECtHR's paradigm shift from individual human rights protection (''pro victima'') toward a quantitative, Results-Based Management (RBM/RBB) orientation. This managerial shift prioritizes efficiency, case disposal quotas, and the rapid rejection of single applications by single judges. The policy model identifies the negative impacts of tightening quantitative criteria, notably the erosion of the right of individual application (Article 34 of the ECHR), the decline of judicial legitimacy, and the neglect of qualitative standards regarding judicial reasoning [1–35].

== Summary ==
Published by Elizabeth Lambert Abdelgawad (2017) in the IJCA, this policy framework critiques the application of the ''Results-Based Budgeting'' (RBB) managerial model at the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) [1–3, 6–7]. To overcome a massive case backlog (peaking at 151,000 pending cases in 2011) amid the Council of Europe's zero-growth budget policy, the ECtHR adopted a single-judge filtering mechanism under Protocol 14 and tightened the formal requirements of Rule 47. While these reforms successfully increased the quantitative output of case rejections—with 95% of applications declared inadmissible and 90% of those decided by a single judge without legal reasoning (''unreasoned decisions'')—Abdelgawad asserts that this obsession with quantitative productivity has eroded the constitutional right of individual petition (Article 34 ECHR) and blatantly ignored the qualitative justice criteria developed by the CEPEJ.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR):''' Article 19 (the Court's mission to ensure the observance of the Convention), Article 6 (Right to a Fair Trial), Article 13 (Right to an Effective Remedy), and Article 34 (Right of Individual Application).
* '''Protocol No. 14 to the ECHR:''' Provisions establishing the Single-Judge mechanism for the rapid rejection of clearly inadmissible applications.
* '''Rule 47 of the Rules of Court:''' Court regulations imposing strict formal requirements for lodging new applications.
* '''Intergovernmental Declarations (Interlaken 2010, Brighton 2012, Brussels 2015):''' Political agreements among state parties directing the managerial reform of the ECtHR.
* '''Council of Europe Budget Rules (Results-Based Budgeting / RBB):''' The results-based budget management framework implemented since 1999–2000.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
The explosion of individual petitions following the expansion of the Council of Europe into Eastern Europe was not matched by budget increases. The Court became a "victim of its own success," leading major donor states to demand strict managerial accountability and the aggressive slashing of operational costs.

== Objectives ==
1. Overcome the severe backlog crisis in Strasbourg.
2. Meet stringent productivity and efficiency targets under the Results-Based Budgeting (RBB) scheme.
3. Develop a balanced performance measurement framework that integrates both quantitative and qualitative indicators of justice.

== Scope ==
This policy covers the evaluation of judicial governance and case administration at the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) for the 47 member states of the Council of Europe.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Single-Judge Filtering Mechanism:'''
** The authority of a single judge to rapidly disqualify inadmissible applications without a contradictory process.
* '''Priority Policy:'''
** Categorizing cases based on urgency (Categories I–III for core rights and matters of public interest).
* '''Tightening of Rule 47 Formal Requirements:'''
** The automatic dismissal of applications if they fail to meet the strict administrative requirements set by the Court.
* '''Integration of Qualitative Justice Criteria:'''
** The necessity of providing brief legal reasoning for rejections and conducting regular applicant satisfaction surveys.

== Implementation ==
* '''Operationalization of Protocol 14 (2011–2015):''' The processing of hundreds of thousands of applications by single-judge formations, significantly reducing the backlog.
* '''Application of Brief Reasoning (2016):''' The adoption of formal judicial decisions with brief reasoning to replace registry letters for single-judge rejections, following the Brussels Declaration.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Erosion of Individual Petition Rights:''' The transformation of the ECtHR from a victim-protecting court into an abstract standard-setting body.
* '''Neglect of Quality and Transparency:''' The absence of adequate legal aid and the lack of judicial reasoning in mass rejections, triggering a severe crisis of legitimacy among applicants and lawyers.

== Reform / Change ==
* Adopting CEPEJ qualitative criteria and conducting periodic applicant satisfaction surveys.
* Establishing Information Offices in the countries that contribute the most cases to filter and improve applications before they reach the Court.
* Pressuring member states to fully execute ''leading judgments'' at the domestic level to stem the flood of repetitive cases [32–33].

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR):''' The primary subject of the judicial performance evaluation.
* '''Council of Europe (CEPEJ & Committee of Ministers):''' The governing bodies setting the budget policies and European justice standards.
* '''[private person]:''' A Law student at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta (NIM: 2410611102), specializing in Constitutional Law (Hukum Tata Negara). As constitutional frameworks intersect heavily with human rights adjudication, the ECtHR’s balance between individual petition rights and judicial efficiency presents a vital comparative model for constitutional legal studies. Cecep Mustafa is not found in the available sources [FACT] [1–35].

'''The European Cooperation in Court Administration Studies Framework''' (''EGPA Study Group & Swiss Sinergia Project'') is a policy framework and international academic-practitioner network that facilitates empirical-interdisciplinary research, judicial public administration cooperation, and court management modernization through the integration of the ''European Group for Public Administration'' (EGPA) Permanent Study Group on Justice and Court Administration, the ''Swiss Sinergia Project'' (funded by the ''Swiss National Science Foundation''), and the ''International Association for Court Administration'' (IACA) [FACT].

== Summary ==
Published in a special issue of the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this research policy framework was formulated by Philip Langbroek, Markus Zimmer, Andreas Lienhard, Luis Palma, Marco Fabri, and Daniel Kettiger. The framework marks a fundamental transition in the management of courts in Europe, moving away from the exclusive domain of rigid formalistic law toward organizational analysis, public management, and open governance (''shift from law to organization and governance''). Supported by the ''Swiss Sinergia Project'', which commenced on May 1, 2012, and the EGPA network, this framework integrates interdisciplinary approaches (law, sociology, economics, psychology, history, and political science) to generate practical solutions for judicial workloads.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Not found in the available sources''': This document serves as a public policy research framework and international scientific network, rather than a statutory law or formal government regulation [FACT].

== Background ==
Since the mid-1990s, democracies in Europe have experienced a fundamental shift in which courts are no longer viewed merely as closed legal forums, but rather as public institutions that must be accountable and transparent. However, empirical data-driven research on judicial administration in Europe has lagged significantly behind the United States, Canada, and Australia. In 1999, the EGPA initiated a judicial administration study group in Bergen, which was subsequently strengthened by the disbursement of research funds for the ''Swiss Sinergia Project'' by the ''Swiss National Science Foundation'' in May 2012.

== Objectives ==
1. Expand the research network of judicial administration academics and practitioners across Europe and internationally.
2. Encourage empirical and interdisciplinary research to comprehend the complexities of court governance.
3. Facilitate a platform for the exchange of experiences among judges, court administrators, and academic researchers through the IACA and EGPA platforms.
4. Develop integrated management models to enhance judicial efficiency without compromising the enforcement of the rule of law.

== Scope ==
This policy and research network encompasses various prominent institutions in Europe:
* '''Center of Competence for Public Management (Univ. of Bern, Switzerland):''' The lead institution for the ''Sinergia'' project, working in collaboration with the Universities of Zurich, Lucerne, St. Gallen, and IDHEAP.
* '''Montaigne Centre (Utrecht Law School, Netherlands):''' A primary research partner in European judicial administration.
* '''Italian & Spanish Research Centers:''' IRSIG-CNR (Bologna), ''Research Centre for Judicial Studies'' (Bologna), ''Observatory on Justice'' (Coimbra, Portugal), and the ''Institute of Law and Technology'' (UAB Barcelona).
* '''Menu For Justice Project:''' Involves over 30 institutes researching the training needs of judges and lawyers in Europe.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Two Facets of Judicial Independence:''' Differentiates between the individual judge's independence in deciding cases without intimidation (''adjudicative independence'') and the institutional autonomy of the court itself (''institutional autonomy'').
* '''Absolute Interdisciplinary Approach:''' Studying the judiciary from a purely legal angle is insufficient; it must incorporate sociological, macroeconomic, psychological, historical, and political science perspectives.
* '''Courts as Complex Public Organizations:''' Adopts Willoughby's (1929) concept that courts are complex public organizations that share characteristics with other public institutions.
* '''Pragmatic Compromise of Values:''' Resolves conflicts between management efficiency values and the administration of justice flexibly and pragmatically, avoiding rigid artificial logic.

== Implementation ==
* '''EGPA Conference in Bergen (September 2012):''' Served as a presentation platform for European judicial administration research papers.
* '''Publication of the IJCA Special Issue (2013):''' Presented 10 research articles from authors across 7 countries (Australia, Switzerland, Italy, France, Finland, Norway, USA).
* '''Support from International Volunteer Teams:''' Involved teams of proofreaders and editors from Australia, Ireland, Brazil, the UK, Germany, and the US under the direction of Technical Editor Linda Wade-Bahr.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Isolation of Formalist Legal Traditions:''' The limitation of judicial studies due to the tendency of legal academics to separate courts from public administration science.
* '''Risk of Political Oversight:''' The potential disruption of judicial independence when executive political authorities hold control over court budgets and management.

== Reform / Change ==
* Modernization of judicial management practices as an absolute necessity for the future.
* Integration of academic platforms (''EGPA/IJCA'') with the operational needs of court practitioners in the field.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''International Association for Court Administration (IACA):''' Publication partner and provider of the research exchange platform.
* '''Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF):''' The grant-providing institution for the ''Sinergia Project''.
* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]:''' ''Not found in the available sources'' [FACT].

The journal is published four times a year on behalf of the European Consortium for Political Research (ECPR) by John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

== Summary ==
This document sets out EJPR's editorial leadership structure, led by three editors (Isabelle Engeli, Emiliano Grossman, and Sofia Vasilopoulou), the technical guidelines for article submission ("Notes for Contributors"), and the full table of contents for Volume 61, Issue 4, comprising 16 scholarly works (13 full research articles and 3 research notes). This issue covers major topics in comparative European politics, including the legitimacy-conferring capacity of constitutional courts, the effect of repeated electoral defeat on political trust, party manifesto responses to defections, and populism's relationship with intra-party democracy.

'''The European Judicial Training Network Policy Framework for the Europeanization of National Judges''' is a transnational judicial training and governance policy framework regarding the Europeanization of national judges. Formulated by Simone Benvenuti (University of Rome "La Sapienza" & iCourts Copenhagen, 2015) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), it analyzes the structure, funding, and operationalization of the European Judicial Training Network (EJTN / ''Réseau Européen de Formation Judiciaire''). The framework is based on four core principles—''Co-operation, Decentralization, Complementarity, and Targeting''—as well as the concept of European Added Value (EAV), the Aiakos Exchange Programme, and knowledge management instruments (EU Law Court Coordinators such as ''Eurinfra'' in the Netherlands and ''European Gaius'' in Italy) to build the European Area of Freedom, Security and Justice [1–6, 14–16, 23–24, 28–31, 45–46].

== Summary ==
Published by Simone Benvenuti in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this policy framework reviews the evolution of the European Judicial Training Network (EJTN) as the primary platform for judicial training in the European Union. Based on Articles 81 and 82 of the Lisbon Treaty and the 2011 European Commission Communication, the EU targeted training for 50% of legal practitioners by 2020. Benvenuti demonstrates that while the European Commission's massive scale targets were somewhat unrealistic, the EJTN has successfully executed its transnational coordination function effectively through a decentralized model based on 4 principles (Co-operation, Decentralization, Complementarity, Targeting) and the concept of European Added Value (EAV) [2, 28–31, 38–39]. Beyond the ''Aiakos'' exchange program, the long-term success of the Europeanization of judges is heavily determined by the development of transnational judicial networks and the establishment of EU Law Court Coordinators (such as the ''Eurinfra'' project in the Netherlands and ''European Gaius'' in Italy) [24, 43–46].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Articles 81 & 82 TFEU (Lisbon Treaty):''' The formal legal foundation of the European Union for the development of judicial training in civil and criminal matters.
* '''2011 European Commission Communication:''' The policy document titled "Building trust in EU-wide justice: a new dimension to European judicial training."
* '''Council Decision 2007/126/JHA:''' The basis for providing operating grants to the EJTN from the European Union budget [14–15].
* '''Bordeaux Charter (2000):''' The foundational document for the establishment of the ''Réseau de Bordeaux'' network.
* '''European Parliament Resolutions 2008 & 2012 (2012/2864(RSP)):''' Mandates supporting EU law coordinators in national courts [31, 45–46].
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text.

== Background ==
The creation of the European Area of Justice requires a uniform understanding of EU law among national judges. The EJTN was established to coordinate national judicial training institutions without eroding the legal autonomy of member states [2, 8, 30–31].

== Objectives ==
1. Foster the creation of a common European judicial culture.
2. Coordinate judicial training standards and needs based on the principle of European Added Value (EAV) [4, 38–39].
3. Organize cross-border judicial exchange programs (''Exchange Programme & Aiakos'') [23–25].
4. Build knowledge management instruments through the network of EU Law Court Coordinators at the local court level [45–46].

== Scope ==
This policy covers the governance of judicial training across the 28 EU Member States, national judicial schools (e.g., ENM France, CSM Italy, Escuela Judicial Spain), the Academy of European Law (ERA Trier), and transnational judicial associations.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Four EJTN Governance Principles:'''
# *Co-operation*: Close collaboration between the EJTN, the European Commission, and professional judicial networks [28–29].
# *Decentralization*: The planning and execution of training remain in the hands of national judicial schools [29–31].
# *Complementarity*: European training complements rather than replaces the primary responsibilities of member states [31, 37–38].
# *Targeting*: Determining specific and effective target activities, such as the exchange programs.
* '''Funding Mechanisms and Organizational Structure:'''
** EU operating grants cover up to 95% of the EJTN’s total budget (€7.88 million in 2015) [15–16].
** The Permanent Secretariat is located in Brussels with 3 Working Groups and specialized sub-working groups (Civil, Criminal, Administrative, Linguistics, Trainers) [14, 19–20].
* '''EU Law Court Coordinators Instrument:'''
** The establishment of specialized judges acting as EU law coordinators in local courts (the Dutch ''Eurinfra'' & Italian ''European Gaius'' models) to disseminate knowledge at the grassroots level.

== Implementation ==
* '''Aiakos Exchange Program:''' Facilitates reciprocal 2-week exchanges for young and future judges [24–25].
* '''Coordinator Network Development:''' The institutionalization of EU law coordinator judges in the Netherlands, Italy, Slovenia, Croatia, and Hungary.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Unrealistic Commission Targets:''' The imbalance between the European Commission's massive targets and the actual capacity for large-scale training [2, 36–37].
* '''Risks of Executive Intervention:''' Attempts by executive agencies (such as EASO) to train judges, which face opposition for threatening judicial independence [32–33].

== Reform / Change ==
* Establishing the European Added Value (EAV) criteria as the primary filter for transnational training budget allocation [38–39].
* Forming strategic partnerships with transnational judicial associations (such as the AEAJ) and institutionalizing court coordinators [43–46].

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''European Judicial Training Network (EJTN):''' The primary executing body for European judicial training policies.
* '''University of Rome "La Sapienza" & iCourts Copenhagen:''' The academic institutions of the primary author.
* '''[private person]:''' A Law student at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta (NIM: 2410611102), specializing in Constitutional Law. Cecep Mustafa is not found in the available sources [1–46].
