'''The Sousa, Kettiger & Lienhard Comparative E-Justice Policy Framework''' is an empirical e-justice policy and cross-national comparative court innovation evaluation model formulated by Marcos Sousa, Dr. Daniel Kettiger, and Prof. Dr. Andreas Lienhard in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), Vol. 13 No. 2 (August 2022). It analyzes the antecedents (drivers and hinderers at the environmental, organizational, innovation feature, and individual levels), the impacts, and the operational results of the integrated e-justice portal "Justitia 4.0" (''Justitia.Swiss'') in Switzerland compared with the Electronic Judicial Process system "PJe" (''Processo Judicial Eletrônico'') in Brazil. The framework is based on 47 in-depth interviews conducted across 7 cantons/7 states and the supreme/federal courts of both nations [1–15, 37–48, 60–128].

== Summary ==
Published by Marcos Sousa, Daniel Kettiger, and Andreas Lienhard in the IJCA (August 2022), this policy framework addresses the transnational research gap regarding ICT adoption strategies in judiciaries with distinct governance traditions [1–13]. Comparing two federal republics with civil law traditions, the study evaluates the "Justitia 4.0" single-portal project in Switzerland and the "PJe" system in Brazil [2, 10–12, 59]. Utilizing 47 qualitative interviews, the research maps innovation drivers and barriers across four levels of analysis [41–48, 60]. In Switzerland, the federalism of 26 cantons and 4 official languages necessitates a consensus-based approach that requires a lengthy implementation timeline (2018–2026) [83–90]. In Brazil, top-down centralization by the National Council of Justice (CNJ) rapidly digitized >95% of case files but triggered complaints regarding poor usability and the loss of local customization autonomy [55, 95–97, 102]. Both countries report significant positive impacts on processing speed, the eradication of processual ''dead time'', and the facilitation of judicial telework [105–108, 118–121].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Swiss Federal Constitution Article 191c:''' The constitutional guarantee of Swiss judicial independence that restricts unilateral executive interference in court administration.
* '''Swiss Civil and Criminal Procedure Codes Revision:''' The foundational legal harmonization required to mandate electronic communication within the ''Justitia 4.0'' framework.
* '''CNJ Resolutions No. 185/2013 & No. 335/2020 (Brazil):''' The National Council of Justice regulations establishing PJe as the mandatory national standard for electronic justice systems.
* '''CNJ Resolution No. 298/2019 (Brazil):''' The regulatory framework governing the implementation of remote work (telework) within the Brazilian judiciary.
* '''European Convention on Human Rights Article 6:''' The international standard guaranteeing the right to a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
Modern judiciaries are compelled to adopt ICT to combat case backlogs and enhance access to justice, yet national governance structures (federal consensus vs. top-down centralization) heavily dictate how these technologies are adopted and received by users.

== Objectives ==
1. Comparatively analyze the drivers and hinderers of national-scale e-justice adoption across environmental, organizational, innovation feature, and individual levels.
2. Measure the actual impacts of digitalization on workflow speed, operational costs, system usability, and procedural fairness.
3. Formulate evidence-based strategic recommendations for policymakers executing nationwide judicial ICT rollouts.

== Scope ==
This policy covers a comparative evaluation of e-justice implementations across 7 Swiss Cantons (including the ''Bundesgericht'') and 7 Brazilian States (including the TRF1).

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Four Levels of Innovation Antecedent Analysis:'''
** '''Environmental Level:''' The impact of Swiss cantonal federalism vs. Brazilian CNJ centralization, mandatory legislation, and ICT infrastructure.
** '''Organizational Level:''' The timeline of adoption, the use of ''sandboxes'' (pilot testing), training programs, and integration with legacy IT systems.
** '''Innovation Feature Level:''' The stringent data privacy/security demands in Switzerland vs. the persistent usability (user-friendliness) issues of Brazil's PJe.
** '''Individual Level:''' Addressing resistance to change, the generation gap, and overall digital literacy.
* '''Primary Impacts of E-Justice Adoption:'''
** '''Speed & Dead Time Reduction:''' The elimination of manual file transport and search times down to milliseconds.
** '''Simultaneous Access & Telework:''' Enabling concurrent document access by multiple parties and sustaining court operations via telework during the COVID-19 pandemic.

== Implementation ==
* '''Sandbox Methodology in Switzerland:''' Conducting controlled pilot tests in specific cantons before executing the national rollout of Justitia 4.0.
* '''Institutionalization of PJe in Brazil:''' The aggressive integration of PJe across all state and federal courts under the strict oversight of the CNJ.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Complexities of Swiss Cantonal Consensus:''' The slow pace of securing uniform agreements across 26 autonomous cantons and 4 language regions.
* '''Rigid CNJ Centralization & PJe Usability Gaps:''' The loss of regional autonomy to adapt software interfaces and the lack of court-provided physical infrastructure (e.g., dual monitors) for teleworking staff.

== Reform / Change ==
* Mainstreaming the ''sandbox'' methodology for large-scale judicial software development to ensure usability before national mandates.
* Improving judicial ICT interfaces to be highly user-friendly while providing adequate home-office infrastructure for judicial teleworkers.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Swiss Federal Supreme Court (Bundesgericht):''' The judicial leader of the Justitia 4.0 public-law cooperation project.
* '''National Council of Justice (CNJ Brazil):''' The central regulatory authority governing the PJe system.
* '''International Journal for Court Administration (IJCA):''' The publisher of this comparative e-justice study.
* '''[private person]:''' A nineteen-year-old Law student specializing in Constitutional Law (Hukum Tata Negara) at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta for the 2024/2025 academic year. The comparative analysis of how constitutional federalism (Swiss Cantonal Autonomy vs. Brazilian CNJ Centralization) dictates the implementation of national e-justice platforms offers an excellent comparative perspective for her constitutional law studies. Cecep Mustafa is not found in the available sources [FACT] [1–131].

'''Kerangka Kebijakan Pelembagaan Ketidakpastian Pemilu dan Kelangsungan Rezim Otoriter Bernhard, Edgell & Lindberg''' (''Bernhard, Edgell & Lindberg's Institutionalising Electoral Uncertainty Policy Framework'') adalah kerangka kebijakan politik-hukum dan model evaluasi pelembagaan pemilu multipartai dalam rezim otoriter yang dirumuskan oleh Michael Bernhard, Amanda B. Edgell, dan Staffan I. Lindberg dalam *European Journal of Political Research* (EJPR, 2019/2020), yang menganalisis bagaimana pengulangan pemilu (*reiterated elections*) dan tingkat persaingan politik memengaruhi kelangsungan (*survival*), demokratisasi (*democratisation*), atau penggantian rezim (*authoritarian replacement*) pada 262 rezim otoriter (1946–2010) melalui analisis riwayat peristiwa multinomial logit (*discrete-time multinomial logistic regression*) [FACT] [1, 5, 26–28].

== Ringkasan ==
Dipublikasikan oleh Michael Bernhard, Amanda B. Edgell, dan Staffan I. Lindberg di EJPR (2019/2020), kerangka kebijakan ini menjawab perdebatan teoritis mengenai apakah pemilu multipartai memperkuat atau mengancam rezim otoriter [1–5]. Menggunakan data 262 rezim otoriter periode 1946–2010, studi ini menemukan bahwa dampak pemilu tergantung pada tingkat kompetisi politik dan pelembagaan ketidakpastian. Pada pemilu multipartai kompetitif, rezim otoriter menghadapi risiko kegagalan dan demokratisasi paling tinggi pada 1–3 pemilu pertama (*double-edged sword hypothesis*). Jika rezim mampu bertahan melampaui fase awal ini, risiko demokratisasi menurun dan kelangsungan hidup rezim terlembagakan. Sebaliknya, pemilu hegemoni secara konsisten meningkatkan stabilitas rezim sejak awal [5, 53–55].

== Dasar Hukum ==
* '''Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) Dataset v8''': Kerangka pengukuran indikator pemilu multipartai, tingkat persaingan, dan kebebasan sipil global.
* '''Autocratic Regimes Dataset (Geddes, Wright & Frantz, 2014)''': Klasifikasi ilmiah tipe rezim otoriter dan variabel hasil kegagalan rezim.
* '''Not found in the available sources''': Regulasi undang-undang formal spesifik lainnya tidak disebutkan dalam teks sumber [FACT].

== Latar Belakang ==
Adopsi pemilu multipartai oleh rezim otoriter pasca-Perang Dingin sebagai strategi peniruan demokrasi (*democratic emulation*) yang membawa dilema ketidakpastian politik.

== Tujuan ==
1. Menguji dampak pengulangan pemilu (*reiterated elections*) terhadap kelangsungan rezim otoriter, transisi demokrasi, dan penggantian otoriter.
2. Membedakan secara empiris efek pemilu hegemoni versus pemilu kompetitif.
3. Menyediakan analisis riwayat peristiwa multinomial logit bebas bias endogenitas melalui *Control Function model*.

== Ruang Lingkup ==
Kebijakan ini mencakup evaluasi empiris terhadap 262 rezim otoriter di 110 negara (4.232 tahun-negara) rentang tahun 1946 hingga 2010.

== Ketentuan Utama ==
* '''Hipotesis Pedang Bermata Dua (*Double-Edged Sword Hypothesis*)''':
** **Fase Kerentanan Awal**: Tiga pemilu kompetitif pertama memicu lonjakan risiko transisi demokrasi.
** **Fase Pelembagaan**: Pengulangan pemilu kompetitif setelah titik infleksi menurunkan risiko kegagalan dan meningkatkan stabilitas rezim.
* '''Klasifikasi Pemilu Otoriter''':
** **Pemilu Hegemoni**: Memiliki kecurangan sistematis atau pembatasan hak pilih (<25%), berfungsi menstabilkan otoriterisme.
** **Pemilu Kompetitif**: Memiliki persaingan nyata dan hak pilih ≥25%, berisiko tinggi memicu demokratisasi di awal.

== Implementasi ==
* **Penerapan Discrete-Time Multinomial Logit**: Pemisahan hasil kegagalan rezim menjadi demokratisasi vs penggantian otoriter.
* **Uji Validitas Control Function (CF) Model**: Penggunaan *V-Dem Party Institutionalisation Index* sebagai variabel instrumen untuk mengontrol endogenitas.

== Permasalahan Kebijakan ==
* **Kerentanan Penguasa Otoriter di Masa Awal**: Tingginya risiko penggulingan petahana saat membuka pemilu kompetitif pertama.
* **Kelangkaan Otoriterisme Kompetitif Jangka Panjang**: Sangat sedikit rezim yang mampu bertahan lama dalam kondisi kompetitif murni.

== Reformasi / Perubahan ==
* Mendorong gerakan pro-demokrasi untuk memfokuskan mobilisasi pada 1–3 siklus pemilu awal pasca-pembukaan politik.
* Mengadaptasi strategi bantuan demokrasi internasional berdasarkan tingkat persaingan pemilu di negara sasaran.

The '''ELI Research Framework on Common Constitutional Traditions in Europe''' (''Kerangka Penelitian Tradisi Konstitusional Bersama di Eropa'') is a transnational scientific research framework conducted under the auspices of the European Law Institute (ELI) to analyze and map common constitutional traditions across EU Member States as a foundational source of general principles of EU law pursuant to Article 6(3) TEU <ref>della Cananea, G. (2021). The ELI Research on ‘Common Constitutional Traditions in Europe’: Research in Progress. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 13(1), 1–4.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Authored by [[Giacinto della Cananea]], this report outlines the progress of a transnational research project proposed by [[Sabino Cassese]] and [[Mario Comba]] within the [[European Law Institute]] (ELI) <ref>della Cananea (2021), p. 1.</ref>. The initiative brings together European legal scholars to examine common constitutional traditions not only through statutory legal texts, but also through practical implementation and underlying legal cultures <ref>della Cananea (2021), pp. 1–2.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
This framework is grounded in primary European legal instruments:
* '''[[Article 6(3) TEU]]''': Establishes that fundamental rights resulting from the common constitutional traditions of Member States constitute general principles of EU law <ref>della Cananea (2021), p. 2.</ref>.
* '''[[European Convention on Human Rights|European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR)]]''': Serves as the primary reference standard for human rights protection across Europe <ref>della Cananea (2021), p. 2.</ref>.

== Background ==
This project marked a major institutional shift for ELI, expanding its research scope beyond private law into transnational public and constitutional law <ref>della Cananea (2021), p. 1.</ref>. Participating scholars include Piotr Bogdanowicz, Iain Cameron, Riccardo De Caria, Jörg Fedtke, Michele Graziadei, Francis Jacobs, Jeffrey Jowell, Andras Sajo, Guy Scoffoni, Takis Tridimas, Daria De Pretis, and Jacques Ziller <ref>della Cananea (2021), p. 1.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Define the scope and core elements of common constitutional traditions using case law and legal doctrine <ref>della Cananea (2021), p. 3.</ref>.
* Test common tradition hypotheses through targeted domains, notably freedom of expression and judicial independence <ref>della Cananea (2021), p. 3.</ref>.
* Provide conceptual clarity regarding national identities within European legal integration <ref>della Cananea (2021), p. 3.</ref>.

== Scope ==
The research encompasses transnational EU constitutional law, comparative methodology, fundamental human rights guarantees, and judicial dialogue between the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) and domestic courts <ref>della Cananea (2021), pp. 1–3.</ref>.

== Research Streams & Deliverables ==
* '''General Concepts Project''': Baseline conceptual research published in *Rivista trimestrale di diritto pubblico* (n. 4/2017) and IJPL <ref>della Cananea (2021), p. 3.</ref>.
* '''Freedom of Expression Report''': Official ELI report published on the ELI website, accompanied by national reports in IJPL <ref>della Cananea (2021), p. 3.</ref>.
* '''Judicial Independence Stream''': Studies on the rule of law and judicial autonomy in Europe published in IJPL (notably issue n. 2/2020) <ref>della Cananea (2021), p. 3.</ref>.

== Implementation ==
Operationalized through judicial references made by domestic courts to the CJEU under the preliminary reference procedure <ref>della Cananea (2021), p. 2.</ref>.

== Policy Issues ==
* '''Comparative Methodology''': Developing comparative legal methods specifically tailored to the European legal area <ref>della Cananea (2021), pp. 2–3.</ref>.
* '''Harmonization vs. National Identity''': Balancing EU legal integration with constitutional respect for Member State national identities <ref>della Cananea (2021), p. 3.</ref>.

== Related Entities ==

* '''[[Sabino Cassese]] & [[Mario Comba]]''': Project Proposers <ref>della Cananea (2021), p. 1.</ref>.

'''Judiciary In Times Of Scarcity: Retrenchment And Reform''' is a comparative policy research report prepared by Frans van Dijk and Horatius Dumbrava under the auspices of the European Network of Councils for the Judiciary (ENCJ), analyzing the impact of the economic crisis and budget cuts on judicial systems across Europe.

== Summary ==
The report documents the "double bind" phenomenon experienced by European judiciaries during the economic recession: a surge in financial and social disputes occurring simultaneously with operating budget cuts of up to 20%. The study evaluates various short-term austerity measures alongside structural reforms (digitalization, procedure simplification, judicial map consolidation, and output-based budgeting) against the core values of the judiciary.

== Legal Basis ==

* '''Not found in the available sources:''' The report operates as an independent comparative study endorsed by ENCJ and is not established under any specific statutory legislative instrument.
* '''Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR):''' Guarantees the right to a fair trial and access to an independent and impartial tribunal.
* '''Vilnius Declaration (2011):''' An ENCJ declaration on protecting the judicial function and access to justice amid economic crises.

== Background ==
Banking crises and economic recessions in Europe triggered public finance crises. Governments across various European countries implemented drastic budget cuts, while caseloads for civil disputes, bankruptcies, and labor matters increased sharply.

== Objectives ==
1. Identify and evaluate judicial reform measures across EU member states. 2. Analyze the causal relationship between the quality of legal/judicial infrastructure and national economic growth. 3. Provide ENCJ recommendations for preserving judicial independence and access to justice during periods of budget austerity.

== Scope ==
The study covers EU member states and ENCJ observer countries, including the Netherlands, Romania, Greece, Portugal, Ireland, the United Kingdom, Denmark, Lithuania, Latvia, Spain, Italy, Germany, Austria, Belgium, Poland, Turkey, and Sweden.

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Economic Impact of Case Delay:''' Inefficiency and delay in civil justice reduce annual GDP growth by up to 1.0% in Italy, while high-quality justice in the Netherlands contributes 0.8% to annual GDP.
* '''Protection of Judicial Salaries:''' Judicial salary cuts can only be justified under exceptional economic conditions if applied equally across the entire public sector, are time-limited, and are governed by law to prevent executive interference.
* '''Access to Justice (Article 6 ECHR):''' Increases in court fees must not obstruct citizens' right to bring legitimate cases before a court.
* '''Output-Based Budgeting System:''' Court funding allocation directly linked to workload volume and projected case output (as demonstrated by the model in the Netherlands).

== Implementation ==
Reform implementation focuses on:

* Digitalization and e-courts (e-filing, e-tracking, video recording of hearings in Sweden, remote hearings).
* Simplification of civil and commercial procedures (9–12 week procedures in Ireland).
* Redistribution of tasks from judges to qualified legal assistants (*Rechtspfleger* in Germany/Austria, judicial fellows in Ireland).
* Judicial map consolidation for operational efficiency.

== Policy Problems ==
1. The "double bind" phenomenon: rising case volumes amid cuts to operating budgets. 2. Risk of erosion of judicial independence due to discretionary salary cuts imposed by the executive. 3. Closure of local courts potentially reducing geographical access to justice. 4. Judges' concerns regarding output-based budgeting systems perceived as overly "technocratic."

== Reform / Change ==

* A shift from destructive short-term cost-cutting toward long-term structural modernization.
* Use of ICT to replace physical court presence without reducing the quality of justice.
* Active involvement of judicial bodies in all stages of the budgeting and legal reform process.

'''The Access to Environmental Justice in Brazil Policy Framework''' is a judicial governance policy and evaluation model concerning the right of access to environmental justice in Brazil. Formulated by Dr. Mariana Almeida Passos de Freitas (Court Clerk at the Federal Justice in Curitiba/PR & Doctor of Environmental Law) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), Special Issue, Vol. 8 No. 3 (July 2017), the framework analyzes the effectiveness of collective procedural instruments—specifically the ''Ação Popular'' (Popular Action) and the ''Ação Civil Pública'' (Public Civil Action). It evaluates their success in breaking down objective and subjective barriers for citizens, guaranteeing environmental citizenship, and measures the impact of environmental court specialization [1–17].

== Summary ==
Published by Dr. Mariana Almeida Passos de Freitas in the IJCA (July 2017), this policy framework evaluates the transformation of access to environmental justice in Brazil following the 1988 Federal Constitution [1–3]. Enforcing Article 225 of the 1988 Constitution, which guarantees an ecologically balanced environment for present and future generations, the study outlines how the Brazilian judiciary has responded to executive inactivity by adopting collective procedural instruments [1–3, 6, 15]. Two primary instruments—the ''Ação Popular'' (Law 4,717/65 & Article 5 LXXIII of the Constitution) and the ''Ação Civil Pública'' (Law 7,347/85)—fractured traditional individualistic legal procedures by exempting plaintiffs from court fees and suspending expert witness costs. Freitas asserts that access to environmental justice is fundamentally "access to power," requiring the elimination of objective barriers (costs/time) and subjective barriers (informational/psychological asymmetry), alongside the strengthening of ''environmental court specialization''.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Brazilian Federal Constitution of 1988 Article 225:''' The constitutional mandate guaranteeing the right to an ecologically balanced environment and the shared duty to preserve it.
* '''Brazilian Federal Constitution of 1988 Article 5 LXXIII:''' The constitutional foundation for the ''Ação Popular'' (Popular Action), guaranteeing the exemption of legal fees.
* '''Law No. 4,717/65 (Lei da Ação Popular):''' The statute regulating the Popular Action procedure to annul acts damaging the environment and public heritage.
* '''Law No. 7,347/85 (Lei da Ação Civil Pública):''' Procedural law for civil liability concerning damages to the environment, consumers, and diffuse rights.
* '''Aarhus Convention (1998):''' The international standard regarding the rights of access to information, public participation, and access to justice in environmental matters.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
The inability of executive administrations to prevent environmental disasters and predatory exploitation forced the Brazilian judiciary to become the primary arena for resolving ecological conflicts.

== Objectives ==
1. Eliminate the objective barriers (costs/time) and subjective barriers (information asymmetry) that prevent citizens from accessing environmental justice.
2. Facilitate the protection of diffuse and supra-individual rights through collective procedural instruments.
3. Actualize ''environmental citizenship'' and accelerate the specialization of environmental courts.

== Scope ==
This policy encompasses the evaluation of environmental judicial governance, the ''Ação Popular'' and ACP instruments, and the specialization of courts in Brazil.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Collective Procedural Instruments:'''
** '''Ação Popular:''' A citizen's lawsuit to annul environmental damages, featuring the exemption of court fees unless bad faith is proven.
** '''Ação Civil Pública (ACP):''' A lawsuit for environmental damage liability initiated by the Public Prosecution Service or community associations.
* '''Incentives and Fee Exemptions:'''
** The exemption of court registration fees and the suspension of expert witness fees until the final judgment, shifting the burden to the losing party.
* '''Environmental Court Specialization:'''
** The establishment of specialized environmental chambers and courts to enhance professionalism and the efficient handling of complex ecological cases.

== Implementation ==
* '''Operationalization of Fee Exemptions:''' Applying the non-condemnatory cost rule for environmental plaintiffs to encourage public participation.
* '''Strengthening Judicial Capacity:''' Conducting environmental awareness training and establishing specialized environmental courts (''Varas Ambientais Especializadas'').

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Environmental Discrimination and Injustice:''' The burden of environmental risks is disproportionately borne by socio-economically weak and minority communities.
* '''Subjective Informational Barriers:''' The lack of access to information, leaving vulnerable citizens unaware that their environmental rights are being violated.

== Reform / Change ==
* Expanding the establishment of specialized environmental courts at both the first and second-instance levels.
* Increasing public information provision and environmental citizenship education programs.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Federal Justice of Brazil:''' The judicial institution executing environmental legal governance.
* '''Superior Court of Justice (STJ):''' The apex court generating key environmental jurisprudence (e.g., Justice Herman Benjamin).
* '''Public Prosecution Service (Ministério Público):''' The primary initiator of the ''Ação Civil Pública''.
* '''[private person]:''' A Law student at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta (NIM: 2410611102), specializing in Constitutional Law (Hukum Tata Negara). As environmental justice relies heavily on constitutional guarantees (such as Article 225 of the 1988 Brazilian Constitution), this framework serves as a vital comparative model for her academic studies. Cecep Mustafa is not found in the available sources [FACT] [1–17].

'''2024 Rule of Law Report – Country Chapter on the Rule of Law Situation in Italy''' (''Commission Staff Working Document SWD(2024) 812 final'') is an annual evaluation report published by the [[European Commission]] on 24 July 2024. It maps and evaluates judicial reforms, anti-corruption frameworks, media pluralism, and institutional checks and balances in the Italian Republic throughout 2023–2024 <ref>European Commission, '2024 Rule of Law Report – Country Chapter on the rule of law situation in Italy', SWD(2024) 812 final (24 July 2024), p. 1.</ref>. The document examines the implementation of judicial reform framework laws (Law 71/2022 and Legislative Decree 44/2024), constitutional reform proposals regarding the separation of careers of judges and prosecutors, the repeal of the offence of abuse of public office (''abuso d'ufficio''), civil and criminal justice digitalisation, backlog management, and challenges surrounding media freedom and journalist protection <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 1, 3, 4, 5, 10, 15.</ref>.

== Executive Summary ==
This Commission Staff Working Document provides a comprehensive assessment across four central pillars of the rule of law in Italy <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 1, 3.</ref>. Under the judicial pillar, Italy demonstrated progress in digitalising civil justice, reducing disposition times, and recruiting staff for the ''Office of the Trial'' (''Ufficio del Processo'') in accordance with PNRR commitments <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 1, 10, 12, 13.</ref>. However, the Commission noted concerns regarding proposed constitutional reforms (separation of careers and drawing lots for CSM members) <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 5, 6.</ref>, the abrogation of ''abuso d'ufficio'' under Draft Law A.C. 1718 <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 15, 16.</ref>, legislative restrictions on publishing pre-trial detention orders (the ''Costa amendment'') <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 28, 29.</ref>, and the extensive reliance on emergency ''law decrees'' <ref>European Commission (2024), p. 33.</ref>. The Commission issued seven specific policy recommendations for the Italian Republic <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 2, 3.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''European Union Law & Frameworks''':
** Articles 2 and 7 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU) and the EU Rule of Law Mechanism <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 1, 2.</ref>.
** National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR / ''Piano Nazionale di Ripresa e Resilienza'') <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 3, 7, 10, 13, 17.</ref>.
* '''Italian Constitutional & Statutory Framework''':
** ''Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana'': Articles 21, 49, 77, 102, 104, 105, 106(1), 135 <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 3, 5, 6, 21, 24, 31, 33.</ref>.
** ''Law 17 June 2022, No. 71'' and ''Legislative Decree 28 March 2024, No. 44 (LD 44/2024)'' & ''LD 45/2024'' <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 4, 5.</ref>.
** ''Legislative Decree 31 March 2023, No. 36'' (New Public Procurement Code) <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 14, 23.</ref>.
** ''Law Decree 3 July 2024, No. 92'' (Introducing Art. 314-bis Criminal Code / ''peculato per distrazione'') <ref>European Commission (2024), p. 16.</ref>.
** ''Draft Constitutional Law A.C. 1921'' (Direct Election of Prime Minister / ''Premierato'') <ref>European Commission (2024), p. 32.</ref>.
** ''Draft Law A.C. 1718 / A.S. 808'' (Abrogation of ''Abuso d'Ufficio'' & Reform of Trading in Influence) <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 15, 16.</ref>.

== Four Core Pillars & Policy Analysis ==
=== 1. Justice System ===
The enactment of Legislative Decree 44/2024 introduced psycho-aptitude evaluations for judicial recruits, evaluation files (''fascicolo personale''), and structural court management adjustments <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 4, 5.</ref>. Concurrently, government-backed constitutional reform proposals aim to separate the careers of judges and prosecutors, create two separate High Councils of the Judiciary (CSM), introduce a lot system for council selection, and establish a High Disciplinary Court <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 5, 6.</ref>. Civil justice digitalisation achieved full operationality, though criminal justice software (APP) faces stability and usability critiques <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 10–12.</ref>.

=== 2. Anti-Corruption Framework ===
ANAC updated the National Anti-Corruption Plan (PNA 2023) to align with public procurement digitization under LD 36/2023 <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 14, 15.</ref>. However, the parliament's approval of Draft Law A.C. 1718 repealing ''abuso d'ufficio'' (abuse of office) and narrowing trading in influence generated criticism regarding compliance with international anti-corruption standards (UNCAC and Council of Europe) <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 15, 16.</ref>. Law Decree 92/2024 introduced Article 314-bis to criminalise unlawful diversion of public funds <ref>European Commission (2024), p. 16.</ref>.

=== 3. Media Pluralism and Media Freedom ===
While AGCOM's regulatory independence remains solid, governance structures and license fee reductions for public broadcaster RAI raised concerns over financial autonomy <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 24–26.</ref>. The adoption of the ''Costa Amendment'' restricts journalists from publishing full pre-trial detention orders prior to trial conclusions <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 28, 29.</ref>. Anti-SLAPP measures and criminal defamation law reform remain pending <ref>European Commission (2024), p. 29.</ref>.

=== 4. Institutional Checks and Balances ===
The government proposed Draft Constitutional Law A.C. 1921 (''Premierato'') to establish the direct election of the Prime Minister <ref>European Commission (2024), p. 32.</ref>. Emergency executive decrees accounted for roughly 50% of acts passed during the legislative period <ref>European Commission (2024), p. 33.</ref>. Italy continues to lack a accredited National Human Rights Institution (NHRI) under UN Paris Principles and has 71 ECtHR judgments pending execution <ref>European Commission (2024), pp. 33, 34.</ref>.

'''Relazione sullo Stato di Diritto 2024 – Capitolo sulla Situazione dello Stato di Diritto in Italia''' (''Commission Staff Working Document SWD(2024) 812 final'') è un rapporto annuale di valutazione pubblicato dalla [[Commissione Europea]] il 24 luglio 2024. Il documento analizza le riforme giudiziarie, il quadro anticorruzione, il pluralismo dei media e il sistema di bilanciamento dei poteri (''checks and balances'') nella Repubblica Italiana per il periodo 2023–2024 <ref>Commissione Europea, 'Relazione sullo Stato di Diritto 2024 – Capitolo sulla situazione dello Stato di Diritto in Italia', SWD(2024) 812 final (24 luglio 2024), p. 1.</ref>. Il rapporto evidenzia l'attuazione delle leggi quadro di riforma della giustizia (Legge 71/2022 e Decreto Legislativo 44/2024), la proposta di riforma costituzionale sulla separazione delle carriere tra giudici e PM, l'abrogazione del reato di abuso d'ufficio, la digitalizzazione del processo civile e penale, l'efficienza nella gestione dell'arretrato e le sfide relative alla libertà di stampa e alla tutela dei giornalisti <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 1, 3, 4, 5, 10, 15.</ref>.

== Sintesi Esecutiva ==
Il documento di lavoro dello staff della Commissione Europea fornisce una valutazione approfondita sui quattro pilastri fondamentali dello Stato di diritto in Italia <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 1, 3.</ref>. Nel settore della giustizia, l'Italia ha registrato progressi nella digitalizzazione civile, nella riduzione dei tempi di attraversamento delle cause (''disposition time'') e nell'assunzione di personale per l'[[Ufficio per il Processo]] ai sensi degli obiettivi del PNRR <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 1, 10, 12, 13.</ref>. Tuttavia, la Commissione ha espresso riserve sulla proposta di riforma costituzionale (separazione delle carriere e sorteggio dei componenti del CSM) <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 5, 6.</ref>, sull'abrogazione dell'abuso d'ufficio prevista dal ddl A.C. 1718 <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 15, 16.</ref>, sulle restrizioni alla pubblicazione delle ordinanze di custodia cautelare (emendamento Costa) <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 28, 29.</ref> e sull'uso estensivo dei decreti-legge d'urgenza <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), p. 33.</ref>. La Commissione ha indirizzato 7 raccomandazioni specifiche alle autorità italiane <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 2, 3.</ref>.

== Basi Giuridiche ==
* '''Diritto dell'Unione Europea e Meccanismi''':
** Articoli 2 e 7 del Trattato sull'Unione Europea (TUE) e Meccanismo UE sullo Stato di Diritto <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 1, 2.</ref>.
** Piano Nazionale di Ripresa e Resilienza (PNRR) <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 3, 7, 10, 13, 17.</ref>.
* '''Ordinamento Costituzionale e Legislativo Italiano''':
** ''Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana'': Articoli 21, 49, 77, 102, 104, 105, 106(1), 135 <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 3, 5, 6, 21, 24, 31, 33.</ref>.
** ''Legge 17 giugno 2022, n. 71'' e ''Decreto Legislativo 28 marzo 2024, n. 44 (D.Lgs. 44/2024)'' e ''D.Lgs. 45/2024'' <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 4, 5.</ref>.
** ''Decreto Legislativo 31 marzo 2023, n. 36'' (Nuovo Codice dei Contratti Pubblici) <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 14, 23.</ref>.
** ''Decreto-Legge 3 luglio 2024, n. 92'' (Introduzione dell'Art. 314-bis c.p. / ''peculato per distrazione'') <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), p. 16.</ref>.
** ''Disegno di Legge Costituzionale A.C. 1921'' (Elezione diretta del Presidente del Consiglio / ''Premierato'') <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), p. 32.</ref>.
** ''Disegno di Legge A.C. 1718 / A.S. 808'' (Abrogazione dell'Abuso d'Ufficio e Riforma del Traffico di Influenze Illecite) <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 15, 16.</ref>.

== I Quattro Pilastri e Analisi delle Politiche ==
=== 1. Sistema Giudiziario ===
L'approvazione del D.Lgs. 44/2024 ha introdotto i test psico-attitudinali per l'accesso in magistratura, il fascicolo personale del magistrato e miglioramenti nella gestione organizzativa dei tribunali <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 4, 5.</ref>. Parallelamente, la proposta di riforma costituzionale intende separare le carriere dei giudici e dei PM, istituire due distinti Consigli Superiori della Magistratura, introdurre il sorteggio per l'elezione dei membri e creare una Alta Corte Disciplinare <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 5, 6.</ref>.

=== 2. Quadro Anticorruzione ===
L'ANAC ha aggiornato il Piano Nazionale Anticorruzione (PNA 2023) coordinandosi con la digitalizzazione degli appalti pubblici ex D.Lgs. 36/2023 <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 14, 15.</ref>. Tuttavia, l'abrogazione del reato di abuso d'ufficio e la ridefinizione del traffico di influenze (ddl A.C. 1718) hanno sollevato critiche in relazione agli standard internazionali anticorruzione (UNCAC e Consiglio d'Europa) <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 15, 16.</ref>. Il D.L. 92/2024 ha introdotto l'Articolo 314-bis c.p. per punire la destinazione indebita di denaro o beni pubblici <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), p. 16.</ref>.

=== 3. Pluralismo e Libertà dei Media ===
Nonostante l'indipendenza dell'AGCOM, la governance della RAI e le riduzioni del canone d'abbonamento sollevano preoccupazioni sull'autonomia finanziaria del servizio pubblico <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 24–26.</ref>. L'approvazione dell'emendamento Costa vieta la pubblicazione del testo delle ordinanze di custodia cautelare fino al termine dell'udienza preliminare <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 28, 29.</ref>. Rimangono pendenti la riforma della diffamazione a mezzo stampa e le tutele contro le azioni legali intimidatorie (SLAPP) <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), p. 29.</ref>.

=== 4. Bilanciamento dei Poteri (Checks and Balances) ===
È stato presentato il disegno di legge costituzionale A.C. 1921 (''Premierato'') relativo all'elezione diretta del Presidente del Consiglio <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), p. 32.</ref>. I decreti-legge d'urgenza hanno rappresentato circa il 50% delle leggi approvate durante la legislatura corrente <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), p. 33.</ref>. L'Italia non ha ancora istituito una Istituzione Nazionale per i Diritti Umani (NHRI) conforme ai Principi di Parigi ONU ed ha 71 sentenze della Corte EDU in attesa di esecuzione <ref>Commissione Europea (2024), pp. 33, 34.</ref>.

| issuing_authority = Filippo Donati / University of Florence / Italian Journal of Public Law
| legal_basis = Art. 19(1) TEU; Art. 47 CFR; Art. 2 TEU; Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2020/2092; Decision 2006/928
| date = 2021 (Editorial Publication); February 27, 2018 (ASJP Judgment); December 16, 2020 (Conditionality Reg); February 16, 2022 (CJEU Twin Judgments)
| status = Operational / Active
}}

The '''Judicial Independence, Primacy of EU Law, and Rule of Law Mechanism Framework''' is a European legal policy and constitutional doctrine framework that mandates all European Union (EU) Member States to ensure national judicial independence and uphold the primacy of EU law over conflicting domestic legislation and constitutional provisions.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Filippo Donati]], Full Professor of Constitutional Law at the [[University of Florence]], this editorial analysis evaluates the escalating jurisdictional conflict between the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) and the Constitutional Courts of several Member States (notably Poland and Romania) regarding judicial independence and the hierarchy of EU law <ref>Donati, F. (2021). Rule of Law, Independence of the Judiciary and Primacy of EU Law. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 13(2), 323–327.</ref>. The CJEU affirmed that Article 19(1) TEU and Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights (CFR) possess direct effect, requiring national courts to disapply domestic rules—including national constitutional provisions—if they breach judicial independence <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 323–324.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
The framework relies on key European Union legal instruments:
* '''[[Article 19(1) TEU]] & [[Article 47 CFR]]''': Mandates Member States to provide effective judicial protection and guarantees independent courts in fields covered by EU law <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 323–324.</ref>.
* '''[[Article 2 TEU]] & [[Article 4(3) TEU]]''': Establishes the foundational values of the Rule of Law and the principle of sincere cooperation <ref>Donati (2021), p. 323.</ref>.
* '''[[EU Budget Conditionality Regulation|Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2020/2092]]''': Establishes general rules for a conditionality regime to protect the EU budget from systemic Rule of Law breaches <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 326–327.</ref>.
* '''[[Romanian CVM Mechanism|Decision 2006/928]]''': Cooperation and Verification Mechanism for monitoring judicial reform and anticorruption progress in Romania <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 325–326.</ref>.

== Background ==
Landmark CJEU jurisprudence—starting with ''Associação Sindical dos Juízes Portugueses'' (C-64/16), ''A.K. and Others'' (Joined Cases C-585/18 et al.), and ''A.B. and Others'' (C-824/18)—triggered a severe constitutional backlash in Poland and Romania <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 323–325.</ref>. The Polish Constitutional Tribunal (in Cases P 7/20 and K 3/21) declared an ECtHR judgment (*Xero Flor*) "non-existent" and held Articles 1, 2, 4(3), and 19(1) TEU unconstitutional to the extent they demanded primacy of EU law over the Polish Constitution <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 324–325.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Ensure courts across all EU Member States satisfy uniform standards of independence and impartiality <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 323–324.</ref>.
* Uphold the principle of primacy of EU law over domestic legislative and constitutional rules that infringe fundamental rights <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 323–325.</ref>.
* Leverage financial sanctions (*financial leverage*) to safeguard EU budget funds from democratic backsliding <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 326–327.</ref>.

== Scope ==
The scope of this framework covers European constitutional law, national judicial independence, infringement procedures, and financial conditionality enforcement across EU jurisdictions—including Poland, Romania, Hungary, and Portugal <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 323, 326–327.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & Jurisprudential Interpretations ==
* '''Direct Effect & Primacy of EU Law''': National courts are obligated to disapply any domestic legislative provision or constitutional ruling that undermines judicial independence <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 323–324, 326.</ref>.
* '''Prohibition of Disciplinary Sanctions against Judges''': EU law prohibits subjecting national judges to disciplinary proceedings or penalties for applying EU law or assessing national law compatibility with EU law (*RS* Case C-430/21) <ref>Donati (2021), p. 326.</ref>.
* '''Financial Conditionality Instrument''': Compliance with Rule of Law standards is a prerequisite for receiving EU budget disbursements (Upheld in CJEU Twin Judgments C-156/21 and C-157/21) <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 326–327.</ref>.

== Implementation ==
Operationalized through European Commission infringement actions, daily financial penalties imposed by the CJEU (such as the €1 million daily penalty against Poland regarding its Disciplinary Chamber), and the freeze of EU budget allocations under Conditionality Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2020/2092 <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 324–327.</ref>.

== Policy Issues ==
* '''Article 7 TEU Unanimity Obstacle''': Sanction mechanisms under Article 7(2) TEU are politically paralyzed because targeted Member States (Poland, Hungary) use mutual vetoes to shield each other <ref>Donati (2021), p. 326.</ref>.
* '''Domestic Constitutional Defiance''': Direct refusal by national constitutional courts to abide by binding rulings of the CJEU and the ECtHR <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 324–326.</ref>.

== Proposed Reforms ==
The European Commission is urged to combine rigorous new infringement procedures with immediate financial leverage under the Guidelines of March 2, 2022 (C(2022) 1382 final) on the Conditionality Regulation <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 326–327.</ref>.

== Related Entities ==
* '''[[Filippo Donati]]''': Author and Full Professor of Constitutional Law at the University of Florence <ref>Donati (2021), p. 323.</ref>.
* '''[[Court of Justice of the European Union]]''': Supreme judicial authority of the European Union <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 323–327.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 323–327.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>Donati (2021), pp. 323–327.</ref>

| legal_basis = Article 6 ECHR; Magna Charta of Judges (2010); CCJE Opinions 6, 7, 11
| date = November 2011 (CCJE) / 2013 (IJCA Publication)
| status = Active Advisory Policy & European Judicial Governance Standards

'''The European Judicial Information Technology Policy Framework: CCJE Opinion No. 14 (2011) on Justice and Information Technologies''' is a policy framework and IT governance guideline for the administration of justice in Europe. Formulated by the ''Consultative Council of European Judges'' (CCJE) of the Council of Europe, it aims to leverage information technology (IT) to enhance access to justice, case management, transparency, and efficiency. Concurrently, it ensures the absolute protection of the right to a fair trial, judicial independence, and procedural safeguards in accordance with Article 6 of the ''European Convention on Human Rights'' (ECHR) [1–3, 18–19, 26, 29].

== Summary ==
Prepared with the support of Dr. Dory Reiling (Judge at the First Instance Court of Amsterdam) as a supporting expert and published in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this policy framework evaluates the status of IT adoption across 47 member states of the Council of Europe, drawing on longitudinal data from the ''European Commission for the Efficiency of Justice'' (CEPEJ) [1, 4, 5, 8–9]. The framework asserts that IT must facilitate access to justice and case management without diminishing procedural safeguards, replacing the decision-making role of the judge, or eroding judicial independence [3, 18–19, 29].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR):''' Guarantees the right to a fair trial, access to a court, impartiality, judicial independence, and the resolution of cases within a reasonable time.
* '''Magna Charta of Judges (CCJE 2010):''' Codifies the principles of judicial transparency and the obligation to publish information.
* '''CCJE Opinions No. 6, 7, and 11:''' Provides guidelines on the dissemination of judicial information, transparency, and the quality of judicial decisions.
* '''Council of the EU Decision on the European Case Law Identifier (ECLI):''' Establishes cross-border standards for numbering and accessing European jurisprudence.
* '''ECtHR Videoconferencing Jurisprudence:''' Foundational judgments regarding remote proceedings, such as ''Marcello Viola v. Italy'' (2006) and ''Asciutto v. Italy'' (2007).

== Background ==
The implementation of IT in European judiciaries has grown rapidly, evolving from basic office administration tools into strategic informational mechanisms. However, this rapid adoption has triggered concerns regarding the potential dehumanization of the judicial process, threats to the independence of individual judges, and the systemic marginalization of judges in national IT decision-making and governance.

== Objectives ==
1. Promote the use of IT to expand access to justice, accountability, and case file workflow management.
2. Ensure that all judicial IT applications strictly comply with ''fair hearing safeguards'' under Article 6 of the ECHR [3, 9, 18–19].
3. Guarantee that judicial IT governance decisions fall under the authority of the Council for the Judiciary or an equivalent independent body, with active judicial participation.
4. Develop open jurisprudence publications to strengthen the ''shadow function of courts''.

== Scope ==
This policy encompasses the 47 member states of the Council of Europe, which are categorized by CEPEJ into three tiers of IT adoption:
* '''High Level (17 countries):''' Implementing IT for direct support, court management, and external communication (e.g., Austria, Finland, Estonia, France, Switzerland).
* '''Medium Level (20 countries):''' Implementing IT for direct support and court management, but with limited external interaction (e.g., Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, Spain, Sweden, UK-England & Wales).
* '''Low Level (8 countries):''' IT adoption remains in its nascent stages (e.g., Moldova, Greece, Serbia).

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Protection of the Judge's Role:''' IT must be viewed strictly as an ''ancillary aid''. It must not replace the judge's fundamental role in evaluating evidence, interpreting the law, or adjudicating cases.
* '''Authority over Physical Presence:''' Judges retain full authority to order the physical presence of parties, demand original documents, and hear witnesses in person whenever necessary.
* '''Videoconferencing Safeguards:''' The deployment of videoconferencing facilities must not diminish the ''guarantees of the defense'' or compromise the qualitative perception of the trial.
* '''4-Stage EU E-Government Benchmark Model:''' Encourages the evolution of court electronic communication from Stage 1 (Online Information) and Stage 2 (Downloadable Forms) toward Stage 3 (Two-Way E-filing) and Stage 4 (Full Electronic Transactions, e.g., MCOL-PCOL).
* '''Judges' Participation in IT Governance:''' IT procurement and system architecture decisions must actively involve judges and remain under the supervision of an independent judicial body.

== Implementation ==
* '''New Legal Information Market Structure:''' The direct publication of jurisprudence by courts via the internet (standardized by ECLI) alters the legal information market, transforming courts from mere adjudicators into primary, direct information producers for the public.
* '''CEPEJ Longitudinal Data (2004–2008):''' Demonstrated a significant increase in the presence of jurisprudence databases (from 33 to 41 countries) and word processing at the judge's desk (40 to 45 countries). However, comprehensive electronic file systems (''e-files'') remained experimental in most nations, with Austria being a notable exception implementing it extensively.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Exclusion of Judges in IT Decisions:''' In more than half of the member states, critical IT decisions are dictated by the Ministry of Justice or the executive bureaucracy without inclusive judicial participation.
* '''Risk of Dehumanization & Rigid Standardization:''' The widespread use of automated, system-based forms risks creating a rigid judiciary that is less sensitive to the unique, individual circumstances of citizens.

== Reform / Change ==
* Institutionalizing mandatory initial and ongoing IT training for all judges and court administrative staff.
* Transferring the authority for IT decision-making from executive branches to the Council for the Judiciary or a similar independent body.
* Documenting and facilitating the structured ''exchange of experiences'' and institutional experimentation regarding IT applications across CoE member states.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Consultative Council of European Judges (CCJE):''' Recruited Dr. Dory Reiling as a supporting expert for drafting Opinion 14.
* '''European Commission for the Efficiency of Justice (CEPEJ):''' Provided the longitudinal statistical data defining the baseline of judicial IT usage across Europe [4, 6–8].
* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]:''' ''Not found in the available sources.'' [FACT] [1–37].

'''The Langbroek European Court Administration and Judicial Professional Space Policy Framework''' is a judicial administration policy framework and court management model in Europe. Formulated by Prof. Dr. Philip M. Langbroek (Managing Editor of the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' / IJCA) in the IJCA, Special Issue, Vol. 8 No. 3 (July 2017), the framework analyzes the centralized nature of European court administration based on the Napoleonic legacy. It assesses the position of judges as civil servants versus office holders and examines the dilemma between the economic approach/productivity pressure and the preservation of the "judicial professional space" to safeguard judicial independence and judicial legitimacy [1–7].

== Summary ==
Published by Prof. Dr. Philip M. Langbroek in the IJCA (July 2017), this policy framework details the unique characteristics of court administration in Europe [1–3]. In contrast to the United States, court administration in Europe is consistently organized on a centralized national scale, where the European Union only possesses limited authority over transnational coordination rules for criminal and cross-border insolvency cases. Influenced by the Napoleonic legacy, judges in continental Europe are positioned as civil servants subject to hierarchical disciplinary supervision. Langbroek warns that the dominance of an economic approach emphasizing rigid productivity risks eroding the "judicial professional space." Without adequate time allocated for legal training, peer review, and stakeholder interaction, judicial independence will dissolve into bureaucratic routine, threatening the long-term legitimacy of the judiciary [6–7].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''EU Transnational Cooperation Rules:''' European Union provisions regarding cooperation in criminal matters, cross-border insolvencies, and the execution of civil judgments.
* '''Continental Legal Tradition / Napoleonic Legacy:''' The historical framework placing local courts under detailed national regulations concerning budgets, personnel, and security.
* '''Establishment of the UK Ministry of Justice (2005):''' The adaptation of a centralized court administration structure at the ministerial level within a common law jurisdiction.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
The increasing administrative burden and demands for economic efficiency in European courts possess the potential to suppress the independent conscience of judges.

== Objectives ==
1. Maintain the balance between the demands of administrative efficiency and the provision of judicial professional space.
2. Ensure judges have the allocated time to differentiate between routine cases and cases requiring special attention.
3. Preserve the legitimacy and independence of the judiciary from the dangers of bureaucratic routinization.

== Scope ==
This policy covers the evaluation of court administration in Continental Europe, the European Union, England, Wales, and offers comparisons with the United States.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Characteristics of European Court Administration:'''
** Centralized national organization under the Ministry of Justice or the Administrative Council for the Judiciary.
** The status of judges as civil servants under national hierarchical disciplinary supervision.
* '''Development of the Judicial Professional Space:'''
** Reserving dedicated time outside the courtroom for legal courses, peer review, jurisprudence analysis, and stakeholder interaction.
* '''Risks of the Economic Approach Pitfalls:'''
** Excessive productivity pressures erode a judge's ability to choose wisely between routine handling and in-depth analysis (room for conscience).

== Implementation ==
* '''Management of 7 Administrative Domains:''' Integrated management covering personnel, information, organization, finance, ICT, security, and facilities.
* '''NACM-IACA Joint Conference (2017):''' Dissemination of European court administration research at the Arlington, Virginia conference.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Limited Autonomy of Local Courts:''' The strict binding of regional courts to detailed national budgeting and accounting rules.
* '''Threat of Independence Dissolving into Routine:''' The risk of judges adjudicating cases automatically without profound analysis due to the pursuit of productivity targets.

== Reform / Change ==
* Formulating court management policies that guarantee time allocation for the judicial professional space.
* Granting judges the freedom of conscience to differentiate and triage cases.

* '''National Association for Court Management (NACM):''' The co-organizer of the 2017 worldwide court excellence conference.
* '''European Commission (Department for Justice):''' The institution executing evaluation studies on the effectiveness of European judicial coordination.
* '''[private person]:''' A Law student at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta (NIM: 2410611102), specializing in Constitutional Law (Hukum Tata Negara). As the constitutional structures of the state shape judicial independence, Langbroek's analysis of the Napoleonic legacy versus judicial professional space provides a highly relevant comparative framework for her academic specialization. Cecep Mustafa is not found in the available sources [FACT] [1–7].

'''The MEDEL European Judicial Governance Policy & Institutional Survey Framework''' is a comparative judicial governance policy framework and institutional survey model formulated through research conducted by MEDEL (''Magistrats européens pour la démocratie et les libertés'', 2014). Published in the book ''Judicial Governance in Europe'' (Edições Almedina, 2015) and reviewed by Markus Zimmer in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA, 2016), Vol. 7 No. 2, this framework evaluates the structures of supreme judicial councils, their institutional independence from the executive and legislative branches, their human resources management powers over judges and prosecutors (recruitment, selection, performance assessment, promotion, transfer, discipline, and training), and the degree to which judicial council functions are formalized in public law [1–5].

== Summary ==
Published by José Mouraz Lopes, Gualtiero Michelini, and António Cluny (2015) and reviewed by Markus Zimmer in the IJCA (2016), this policy framework summarizes the results of the 2014 survey conducted by MEDEL (''Magistrats européens pour la démocratie et les libertés'') [1–2]. The survey evaluates institutional judicial independence and the structures of supreme judicial councils across 11 European countries and Turkey [3–4]. The report maps the allocation of council membership by profession as well as HR authorities encompassing recruitment, performance assessment, promotion, salary administration, and disciplinary procedures. Markus Zimmer evaluates this compilation as highly useful for court administration researchers, although he notes several methodological shortcomings, such as the absence of comparative tables and an index [3–4].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Public Laws Enshrining Supreme Judicial Council Functions:''' The public law frameworks within respective European countries that guarantee the structure, authority, and independence of supreme judicial councils.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
MEDEL was established in June 1985 by European judges and prosecutors as a professional advocacy/guild association. This research was undertaken to map the state of institutional judicial independence across Europe [1–2].

== Objectives ==
1. Map the structures and functions of the primary governing organs of the judicial branch (supreme judicial councils).
2. Study the execution of human resources authority pertaining to judges and prosecutors.
3. Strengthen the institutional independence of the judiciary from the executive and legislative branches.

== Scope ==
This policy encompasses comparative studies across 11 European Union member states, Turkey, and the Czech Republic [1, 3–4].

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Structure and Allocation of Judicial Council Membership:'''
** Regulating the proportional allocation of council membership among judges, prosecutors, lawyers, academics, civil society representatives, the legislature, and ministers.
* '''Execution of Human Resources Management Authority:'''
** The council's authority in recruitment, selection, performance evaluation, salary administration, promotion, transfer, disciplinary actions, and training.
* '''Mapping of Formalization in Public Law:'''
** Assessing the degree to which the functions of judicial councils are officially recognized within national public laws.

== Implementation ==
* '''Execution of the 2014 MEDEL Survey:''' The collection of responses from 14 MEDEL member associations (averaging 10–30+ pages per country).
* '''Publication of the E-Book (2015):''' The publication of the book by Edições Almedina in Coimbra, Portugal.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Vulnerability of Institutional Independence:''' The risk of executive political interference in the appointment and promotion of judges and prosecutors.
* '''Methodological Weaknesses in Data Presentation:''' The absence of the original questionnaire, comparative summary tables, and an index, which diminishes the research's utility as a reference tool.

== Reform / Change ==
* Standardizing the comparative judicial survey methodology by involving professional researchers and utilizing integrated matrix formats.
* Strengthening the formalization of supreme judicial council functions within public law to guarantee judicial autonomy.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''MEDEL:''' The organization that designed and conducted the judicial governance survey.
* '''Edições Almedina:''' The official publisher of the research book.
* '''International Journal for Court Administration (IJCA):''' The journal that published Markus Zimmer's policy review.

'''The Green Paper for a European Rechtspfleger''' is a policy framework, qualification standard, and model position description formulated by the ''European Union of Rechtspfleger'' (EUR) (completed in November 2008) to standardize the position of the European Rechtspfleger across member states of the European Union and the Council of Europe. Its purpose is to independently transfer routine judicial tasks from judges to independent legal administrative officers to improve judicial efficiency and guarantee the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time (Article 6 of the ECHR) [1, 3–8, 13, 15].

== Summary ==
Published by Thomas Kappl and the EUR executive board in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this Green Paper is designed to spark academic and public discussion regarding the establishment of standardized qualifications for the European Rechtspfleger. Responding to the surge in caseloads across European courts, the document proposes the independent delegation of routine judicial tasks to higher-level judicial civil servants possessing a minimum of 3 years of legal education. This transfer has proven to free judges to focus on complex cases, thereby producing higher-quality judgments.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Model Statute for a European Rechtspfleger (1995 EUR Congress, Spain):''' The primary foundation for the professional framework of the European Rechtspfleger.
* '''Recommendation No. R (86) 12 of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe:''' Recommendation regarding measures to prevent and reduce the excessive workload in the courts.
* '''Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR):''' The guarantee of everyone's right to a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time.
* '''Recommendation No. R (80) 3 of the Council of Europe:''' Recommendation concerning teaching, research, and training in the field of "Computers and Law" (Electronic Data Processing - EDP).
* '''EC Directive 89/48/EEC:''' Provisions on a general system for the recognition of higher-education diplomas awarded on completion of professional education and training of at least three years' duration.

== Background ==
As caseloads increase in European courts, judges face serious obstacles as they spend significant time and resources handling administrative and routine judicial tasks. This condition threatens the fulfillment of the Article 6 ECHR mandate. The EUR, an international organization founded in 1967 encompassing associations of higher-level judicial civil servants in 16 European countries and several non-European countries (e.g., Japan, Mali, Morocco, Tunisia), initiated the drafting of the Green Paper. Led by EUR President Thomas Kappl, the EUR Commission drafted this document throughout 2007–2008 and officially submitted it to the Directorate-General for Justice, Freedom and Security of the European Commission in Brussels (Dec 2, 2008) and the CEPEJ Plenary Session in Strasbourg (Dec 11, 2008).

== Objectives ==
1. Liberalize and relieve judges of routine judicial tasks so they can focus on severe cases that generate higher-quality judgments.
2. Standardize minimum educational qualifications (a Bachelor of Law / minimum 3 years of higher education) for prospective European Rechtspflegers across all EU countries.
3. Develop a model position description that can be independently applied across various types and levels of courts.
4. Foster public discussion and consensus among the Ministries of Justice of EU and Council of Europe member states.

== Scope ==
This policy covers the judicial systems in the member states of the European Union and the 47 member states of the Council of Europe.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Judicial Independence of the Rechtspfleger:''' The Rechtspfleger is an objective and independent officer of the judicature. In making decisions, they are bound only by the law and the principles of justice.
* '''Uniform Education Standards:''' Prospective Rechtspflegers must complete a specialized legal higher education program of at least 3 years (Bachelor of Law or equivalent) based on a standardized curriculum.
* '''Model Position Description:''' Standardizing functions and responsibilities across all levels of courts to optimize the efficiency of legal administration based on a standard EUR questionnaire.
* '''Integration of ICT / EDP:''' Mandatory provision of basic and advanced training in electronic data processing (EDP) for all judicial officers.

== Implementation ==
* '''Submission to the European Commission (December 2, 2008):''' Submitted directly by the EUR Delegation led by Thomas Kappl to Mrs. Lana Papamichalopoulou (Head of Unit, DG Justice) in Brussels in 5 languages (French, English, Italian, Romanian, German) for distribution to all EU Ministries of Justice.
* '''Submission to CEPEJ (December 11, 2008):''' Submitted by EUR Secretary General Adelheid Hell and Jean-Jacques Kuster to CEPEJ President Fausto De Santis during the Plenary Session in Strasbourg.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Variations in Domestic Training Systems:''' Differences in the duration and content of Rechtspfleger training across EU member states requiring curriculum harmonization.
* '''Excessive Judicial Workload:''' The lack of routine authority delegation causing delays in sentencing and adjudication in several member states.

== Reform / Change ==
* Harmonization of professional qualifications based on the European diploma equivalency standard (Directive 89/48/EEC).
* Expansion of the use of electronic data processing (EDP/e-Justice) in executing Rechtspfleger duties in accordance with Recommendation No. R (80) 3.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

'''The Thomas Kappl European Rechtspfleger Proposal Framework''' is a judicial governance and harmonization policy framework for senior non-judge judicial officers (''Rechtspfleger'') in Europe. Formulated by Thomas Kappl (Former President of the European Union of Rechtspfleger / EUR) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), Vol. 8 No. 1 (October 2016), the framework proposes the creation of a ''European Rechtspfleger'' to handle cross-border uncontested legal matters, European land and commercial registries, the execution of judgments, and the management of court backlogs caused by the economic crisis in Europe [1–6].

== Summary ==
Published by Thomas Kappl in the IJCA (October 2016), this policy framework proposes the establishment of a transnational senior judicial officer position (the ''European Rechtspfleger''). Although European integration in the fields of economics and immigration has developed rapidly, the resolution of uncontested legal matters that cross national borders remains time-consuming, complicated, and expensive. The EUR formulated the ''Green Paper for a European Rechtspfleger'', which was discussed with justice ministries across 17 European countries and presented by EUR President Jean-Jacques Kuster to the Legal Committee of the European Parliament. This policy aims to grant the ''Rechtspfleger'' the authority to manage property registrations, business registrations, European Inheritance Certificates, and cross-border judgment executions directly from a citizen's hometown.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''EUR Green Paper for a European Rechtspfleger:''' The primary policy document championed by the EUR to initiate discussions on the harmonization of the ''Rechtspfleger'' profession in Europe.
* '''CEPEJ Report "European Judicial Systems – 2014 Edition":''' The official report by the Council of Europe that included discussions on the ''European Rechtspfleger'' proposal.
* '''European Union Legal Harmonization Initiatives:''' The framework for establishing European Inheritance Certificates, the European Commercial Registry, and the European Land Registry.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
European citizens conducting cross-border transactions (such as purchasing a home in another country or opening a branch office) face bureaucratic hurdles in civil law that are disjointed across borders.

== Objectives ==
1. Facilitate fast, affordable, and transparent access to justice for European citizens in uncontested matters.
2. Encourage the establishment of integrated European land and commercial registries.
3. Assist courts in untangling the backlog of insolvency cases and forced sales resulting from the European economic crisis.

== Scope ==
This policy encompasses 17 member states of the European Union/Europe and 2 non-European countries (Japan and South Korea) involved in the EUR discussions.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Jurisdiction over Uncontested Matters:'''
** Transferring authority over family law, probate/inheritance, property registration, and business licensing from judges to the ''Rechtspfleger''.
* '''The "Live Europe" Principle:'''
** Empowering citizens to complete foreign legal transactions through a ''Rechtspfleger'' located in their city of residence.
* '''Integrated Registry Harmonization:'''
** The creation of a unified European Land Register and European Commercial Register.

== Implementation ==
* '''Submission to the European Parliament:''' The presentation of the ''EUR Green Paper'' by Jean-Jacques Kuster to the Legal Committee of the European Parliament.
* '''Formulation of the EUR White Paper:''' The drafting of concrete proposals as the next step in public and professional discourse.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Court Backlogs:''' A surge in applications for forced sales and insolvencies following the European economic crisis.
* '''Disparate Legal Systems:''' Not all EU member states currently recognize the position of a ''Rechtspfleger'' within their judicial systems (e.g., common law systems).

== Reform / Change ==
* Drafting concrete proposals in the ''EUR White Paper'' to establish formal EU regulations.
* Accelerating the harmonization of electronic, integrated land and business registration procedures.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''European Union of Rechtspfleger (EUR):''' The association designing the ''European Rechtspfleger'' proposal.
* '''CEPEJ (Council of Europe):''' The judicial efficiency review body discussing the EUR proposal.
* '''[private person]:''' Not found in the available sources. [FACT] [1–6].
* '''Cecep Mustafa:''' Not found in the available sources. [FACT] [1–6].

'''''Sustainability and Remedial Regime in the Sale of Consumer Goods''''' is an EU and Italian civil and consumer law analytical framework formulated by Andrea Fantini in ''The Italian Law Journal'' (Vol. 10 Nos. 01-02/2024, pp. 149–173) <ref>Fantini, A. (2024). Sustainability and Remedial Regime in the Sale of Consumer Goods. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 10(1-2), 149–173.</ref>. The work analyzes the relationship between private law, sustainability, and the right to repair within consumer protection schemes <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 149, 162, 169.</ref>; examines the regime of conformity of goods under ''Directive (EU) 2019/771'' and the ''Italian Consumer Code (Codice del Consumo)'' (Arts. 129, 135-bis, 135-ter) <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 158, 163, 164, 167.</ref>; criticizes the lack of a remedial hierarchy prioritizing repair over replacement <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 165, 166.</ref>; and provides an analysis of EU/French policy reforms (such as ''Loi n° 2020-105 / Indice de réparabilité'') alongside tax and guarantee incentive techniques to advance the circular economy <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 168, 171, 172.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Authored by [[Andrea Fantini]] (PhD and Research Fellow in Civil Law at the University of Salento), this study examines how European Union and Italian consumer law can be transformed to support the circular economy and the UN 2030 Agenda <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 149, 153, 158.</ref>. The author criticizes ''Directive (EU) 2019/771'' and the ''Codice del Consumo'' for failing to establish a clear remedial hierarchy prioritizing repair over replacement, despite incorporating "durability" as an objective requirement of conformity <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 164, 165.</ref>. The paper evaluates practical manufacturer obstacles (such as pentalobe security screws and software repair locks), analyzes pioneer legislation such as France's Anti-Waste Law (''Loi anti-gaspillage n° 2020-105'') introducing the Repairability Index (''Indice de réparabilité'') <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 168, 171.</ref>, and stresses the importance of establishing a "new balance" bridging the individual economic interest (''homo oeconomicus'') with ecological solidarity values (''homo ecologicus'') <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 161, 172, 173.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
=== Primary EU Law ===
* '''Treaty on European Union (TEU)''': Article 3(3) & (5) (Sustainable Development & Environmental Protection Objectives) <ref>Fantini (2024), p. 160.</ref>.
* '''Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU)''': Article 11 (Environmental Protection Integration) & Article 12 (Consumer Protection Integration) <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 160, 173.</ref>.
* '''Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (CFREU)''': Article 37 (High Level of Environmental Protection) <ref>Fantini (2024), p. 160.</ref>.

=== Secondary EU & National Legislation ===
* '''Directive (EU) 2019/771''' (Consumer Sales Directive) <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 159, 162.</ref> & '''Directive (EU) 2019/770''' (Digital Content/Services), replacing Directive 1999/44/EC <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 163, 164.</ref>.
* '''Italian Consumer Code (Codice del Consumo)''': Articles 129, 135-bis, 135-ter (as amended by Legislative Decree 4 November 2021, n. 170) <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 163, 164, 167.</ref>.
* '''Constitution of the Italian Republic''': Article 9, Article 118 (Subsidiarity), and principles of solidarity (Art. 2) and human dignity <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 155, 156.</ref>.
* '''French Law n° 2020-105''' (Loi anti-gaspillage et pour l'économie circulaire; Code de l'Environnement Art. L. 541-9-2 & Code de la Consommation Arts. L. 217-9, L. 441-3) <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 171, 172.</ref>.
* '''European Parliament Resolutions''': Resolution of 25 November 2020 (2020/2021(INI)) & Resolution of 7 April 2022 (2022/2515(RSP)) on the Right to Repair <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 160, 169, 170.</ref>.

=== Key Jurisprudence ===
* '''Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU)''': Case C-404/06 ''Quelle AG v. Bundesverband der Verbraucherzentralen'' (Prohibition of charging consumers for the use of defective goods prior to replacement) <ref>Fantini (2024), p. 167.</ref>.
* '''International Court of Justice (ICJ)''': ''Gabcikovo-Nagymaros Project'' Case (Hungary v. Slovakia) 1997 (Hermeneutic role of sustainable development) <ref>Fantini (2024).</ref>.
* '''National Courts''': Supreme Court of Norway Judgment (2006) (Refusing product replacement on environmental grounds) <ref>Fantini (2024), p. 166.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & Policy Pillars ==
# '''Objective Conformity & Durability Requirement''': Directive (EU) 2019/771 and Article 129 of the Italian Consumer Code establish "durability" as an objective conformity criterion, obligating manufacturers to maintain product functionality over a reasonable lifespan <ref>Fantini (2024), p. 164.</ref>.
# '''Lack of Remedial Hierarchy (Repair vs. Replacement)''': Current statutory frameworks place repair and replacement on equal footing (Article 13 Directive 2019/771), creating a systemic bias toward full replacement rather than repair <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 164–166.</ref>.
# '''Reform Innovations & Right to Repair''': Introducing repairability indices (such as France's ''Indice de réparabilité''), extended repair warranties, and tax reductions (such as Swedish VAT cuts on repair services) are key to overcoming technical barriers (e.g., proprietary screws) and combatting greenwashing <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 164, 168, 171, 172.</ref>.

== Entity Relationships ==
* '''[[Andrea Fantini]]''': Lead Author & Research Fellow at the University of Salento <ref>Fantini (2024), p. 149.</ref>.
* '''[[European Parliament]]''': EU Legislative institution issuing resolutions on the Right to Repair <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 160, 169, 170.</ref>.
* '''[[AGCM (Autorità Garante della Concorrenza e del Mercato)]]''': Italian competition authority prosecuting greenwashing and misleading commercial practices <ref>Fantini (2024), p. 164.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 149–173.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Fantini (2024), pp. 149–173.</ref>
