'''Kerangka Kebijakan Produktivitas Yudisial dan Reformasi Pengadilan India''' (''Judicial Productivity in India Policy Framework'') adalah kerangka kebijakan dan studi komparatif produktivitas yudisial yang dirumuskan oleh Barry Walsh (konsultan pengembangan sektor peradilan Australia / ADB) yang membandingkan efisiensi peradilan antara Wilayah Ibu Kota Nasional Delhi (India) dan Australia untuk membuktikan bahwa penumpukan perkara (''backlog'') di India bukan semata disebabkan oleh kurangnya jumlah hakim, melainkan oleh rendahnya produktivitas peradilan akibat rendahnya tingkat penyelesaian damai (''settlement rates'' ~5% vs ~70%), rendahnya pengakuan bersalah (''guilty plea rates''), tingginya frekuensi penundaan persidangan (''adjournment rates'' 20–40 kali vs 0,3–6,3 kali), ketiadaan persidangan berkelanjutan (''continuous trials''), serta metode pencatatan persidangan manual yang lambat.

== Ringkasan ==
Dipublikasikan oleh Barry Walsh dalam ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), studi komparatif empiris ini menantang pandangan konvensional bahwa penumpukan perkara di India hanya dapat diatasi dengan menambah jumlah hakim. Berdasarkan data empiris proyek ADB di Delhi dan Australia, Walsh menunjukkan bahwa hakim Australia memiliki kapasitas penyelesaian perkara (''disposal capacity'') dua kali lipat dibanding hakim di Delhi (1.511 vs 701 perkara per tahun). Penyebab utamanya adalah sistem peradilan India yang jarang menyelesaikan perkara secara damai (~5%), tidak memiliki kepastian tanggal putusan (''outcome date certainty''), merutinkan penundaan persidangan (20–40 kali per perkara), memfragmentasi persidangan ke dalam 5 tahap terpisah, dan mengandalkan diktasi manual stenografer.

== Dasar Hukum ==
* '''Konstitusi India (Constitution of India):''' Mengatur sistem peradilan common law terkodifikasi tiga tingkat di tingkat federal dan negara bagian.
* '''Indian Code of Civil Procedure & Code of Criminal Procedure:''' Regulasi tata cara persidangan perdata dan pidana, aturan pembuktian, serta kewenangan diskresi penundaan persidangan oleh hakim.
* '''Penghapusan Sistem Juri (1956):''' Perubahan hukum acara pidana yang menghapuskan persidangan berbasis juri di India.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Regulasi undang-undang formal spesifik lainnya tidak disebutkan dalam teks sumber.

== Latar Belakang ==
Wacana reformasi peradilan di India selalu berfokus pada tuntutan penambahan alokasi jumlah hakim per populasi. Melalui studi ADB di High Court dan District Courts Delhi, Walsh melakukan evaluasi produktivitas yudisial untuk menguji validitas asumsi tersebut dibanding kriteria ''best practice'' internasional.

== Tujuan ==
1. Membuktikan secara empiris perbedaan kapasitas produktivitas antara hakim India dan standar internasional.
2. Mengidentifikasi hambatan struktural yang menyebabkan rendahnya angka penyelesaian damai dan pengakuan bersalah di India.
3. Mendorong pengadopsian persidangan berkelanjutan (''continuous trials'') dan pencatatan suara elektronik (''electronic sound recording'').

== Ruang Lingkup ==
Kebijakan ini mencakup analisis komparatif peradilan di Wilayah Ibu Kota Nasional Delhi (High Court & District Courts) dan pengadilan di Australia.

== Ketentuan Utama ==
* '''Perbandingan Indikator Produktivitas Utama''':
** ''Rasio Penyelesaian per Hakim per Tahun'': Delhi = **701 perkara** vs Australia = **1.511 perkara**.
** ''Kebutuhan Hakim per 100.000 Penyelesaian (Lakh of Disposals)'': Delhi = **153 hakim** vs Australia = **66 hakim**.
** ''Tingkat Penyelesaian Damai Perdata'': India = **~5%** vs Australia/Kanada = **>70–90%**.
** ''Rata-rata Penundaan Persidangan (Adjournments)'': India = **20–40 kali** per perkara vs Australia = **0,3–6,3 kali**.
* '''Lima Tahapan Persidangan Terfragmentasi di India''':
# Penetapan Isu dan Dakwaan (''Issues and charges'').
# Pembuktian Penggugat/Penuntut (''Plaintiff/Petitioner evidence'').
# Pembuktian Tergugat/Terdakwa (''Defendant/Respondent evidence'').
# Argumen Akhir (''Final argument'').
# Putusan (''Order and judgment'').
* '''Ketiadaan Outcome Date Certainty''': Ketidakmampuan pengadilan menentukan tanggal pasti penyelesaian perkara yang menghilangkan dorongan para pihak untuk berdamai.

== Implementasi ==
* **Data Proyek ADB di Delhi (TA4153-IND & TA4437-IND)**: Pengumpulan data rutin internal dari 21 pengadilan tingkat pertama dan High Court Delhi pada 2004–2005.

= 'Digital Acceleration During Covid-19 Pandemic: How the Indonesian Constitutional Court Brings the Citizens Justice' (Muhidin et al., 2023) =

=== Wiki Entity Page ===
{{Infobox

}}

The '''Indonesian Constitutional Court Digital Acceleration Framework''' (''Kerangka Akselerasi Digital Mahkamah Konstitusi Republik Indonesia'') is a digital judicial transformation and ICT governance policy implemented by the Constitutional Court of the Republic of Indonesia (MKRI) to guarantee the continuity of public access to constitutional justice during the COVID-19 pandemic. This framework combines online application registration through the Electronic Case Handling Information System (''Sistem Informasi Penanganan Perkara Elektronik'' / SIMPEL), remote trials based on Zoom and mini courtrooms across 34 universities, digital decision signing with the National Cyber and Crypto Agency (BSSN), and live broadcasting via YouTube channels.

== Summary ==
Authored by Muhidin, Eman Suparman, Indra Perwira, and M. Guntur Hamzah in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (2023), this study outlines how the MKRI responded to the Large-Scale Social Restrictions (PSBB) policy and the closure of court buildings. Holding firmly to the principle "Justice delayed is justice denied," the MKRI launched PMK No. 1/2021 on Remote Trials, allowing parties to litigate from their homes, offices, or workspaces. During the 2020–2022 period, the MKRI's case resolution efficiency increased by 18% (resolving 132 out of 143 cases in 2022) and delivered five landmark decisions that restored citizens' constitutional rights [65, 66, 67–77].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''1945 Constitution of the Republic of Indonesia (UUD 1945):''' Article 23(2), Article 24(3), Article 27(1), and Article 28D(1) (guaranteeing constitutional rights, the rule of law, and fair trials).
* '''Health Emergency & SPBE Framework:''' Presidential Decrees No. 11/2020 & No. 12/2020; Perppu No. 1/2020; and Presidential Regulation No. 95/2018 on Electronic-Based Government Systems (SPBE).
* '''Constitutional Court Regulations (PMK):'''
** ''PMK No. 18/2008 & PMK No. 18/2009:'' Guidelines for Electronic Filing and Remote Trial Examination.
** ''PMK No. 9/2020 & PMK No. 2/2021:'' Rules of Procedure for Judicial Review.
** ''PMK No. 1/2021:'' Implementation of Remote Trials (permitting the use of Zoom from the applicant's domicile).

== Background & Policy Problems ==
The COVID-19 pandemic forced the MKRI to halt face-to-face hearings for nearly two months (March 17 – May 13, 2020). Postponing hearings risked neglecting human rights and allowing executive emergency measures to proceed without constitutional checks and balances. To overcome geographical constraints and internet disparities in Indonesia, the MKRI accelerated the transition from conventional methods to modern ICT-based justice.

== Main Components of the MKRI E-Justice Ecosystem ==
1. '''SIMPEL (Electronic Case Handling Information System):''' A web portal for online application registration, file monitoring, receiving trial summons, and downloading decision copies for free.
2. '''Remote Hearings (Virtual Trials):''' The use of Zoom Meetings and the provision of smartboard mini courtrooms in collaboration with 34 universities across Indonesia.
3. '''Judicial Administration System (JAS) & General Administration System (GAS):''' Management of e-Minutasi, digital case tracking, portal management (`www.mkri.id`), and trial broadcasting via YouTube.
4. '''BSSN Digital Signatures:''' Implementation of electronic signature certification with the BSSN for judges and registrars, allowing decisions to be uploaded within hours of pronouncement.

== Application of Procedural Justice Theory (Tom R. Tyler) ==
* '''Voice:''' Fulfills the principle of ''audi et alteram partem'' by hearing statements from all parties virtually.
* '''Neutrality:''' Provides equal digital access for ordinary citizens and state institutions (President/DPR).
* '''Respect:''' Provides free e-court facilities as a form of respect for citizens' constitutional rights.
* '''Trust:''' Enhances public transparency through live broadcasts of hearings and open-access downloads.

== Five Landmark Decisions During the Pandemic ==
1. '''Decision No. 70/PUU-XVII/2019 (KPK Supervisory Board):''' Affirmed that the KPK Supervisory Board is not authorized to grant ''pro justitia'' permits (wiretapping/searches) and set a two-year investigation time limit.
2. '''Decision No. 37/PUU-XVIII/2020 (COVID-19 Finance Law):''' Limited the validity period of Law No. 2/2020 to a maximum of 2 years and established good-faith standards in state budget usage.
3. '''Decision No. 91/PUU-XVIII/2020 (Job Creation Law Formal Review):''' Granted the formal review and declared Law No. 11/2020 ''conditionally unconstitutional'' due to procedural flaws in its formation [71–73].
4. '''Decision No. 72/PUU-XVII/2019 (Taspen/BPJS Pension Funds):''' Canceled the mandatory transfer of civil servant pension fund management from PT Taspen to BPJS Employment.
5. '''Decision No. 21/PUU-XIX/2021 (Child Sexual Abuse Reporting):''' Expanded the reporting subjects of child sexual abuse under Article 293(2) of the Criminal Code so that parents or guardians can represent victims.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''MKRI & Padjadjaran University:''' The judicial institution and the researchers' home university.
* '''National Cyber and Crypto Agency (BSSN) & PT Telkom:''' Digital signature security partner and super-fast network provider.
* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]:''' Not found in the available sources [1–113].

'''Access to Justice and Court Administration Reform in Indonesia's Religious Courts''' (''Program Keadilan untuk Semua'' / Justice for All Program) is a series of judicial administration policies and legal reforms launched by the Directorate General of the Religious Courts (Badilag) of the Supreme Court of the Republic of Indonesia. This policy aims to expand the reach of justice for the poor, female heads of household, and populations in remote areas by waiving court fees (''prodeo''), conducting circuit courts (''sidang keliling''), and providing Legal Aid Posts (''Posbakum'').

== Summary ==
Following the transfer of organizational and financial authority to the Supreme Court under the "One Roof System" (Law No. 35 of 1999), the Religious Courts pioneered evidence-based public service reforms (*Access and Equity Study*). This program successfully eliminated financial and geographical barriers for tens of thousands of poor citizens, increased public trust, and linked family law registration with access to national social protection programs.

== Legal Basis ==
The implementation of access to justice reforms within the Religious Courts is based on the following legal foundations:
* '''Law No. 7 of 1989 jo. Law No. 50 of 2009''' on Religious Courts (Article 60 regarding legal aid).
* '''Law No. 48 of 2009''' on Judicial Power (Articles 56 and 57 regarding the right of the poor to obtain free legal aid).
* '''Law No. 35 of 1999''' on Amendments to the Law on Judicial Power (One Roof System).
* '''Presidential Instruction No. 3 of 2010''' on Equitable Development Programs (focusing on justice for women and children).
* '''Supreme Court Circular (SEMA) No. 10 of 2010''' on Guidelines for Providing Legal Aid in the Judiciary.
* '''Presidential Regulation No. 5 of 2010''' on the National Medium-Term Development Plan (RPJMN) 2010–2014.
* '''National Access to Justice Strategy''' (Bappenas, 2009).

== Background ==
Following the fall of President Soeharto in 1998, Indonesia's judicial institutions generally experienced a crisis of public confidence due to corruption and inefficiency. However, an Asia Foundation survey (2001) found that Religious Courts were considered the most honest and effective government institutions. Through the ''One Roof'' reform, Religious Courts utilized their autonomous authority to improve case administration and respond to the legal needs of the poor.

== Objectives ==
1. Waive court fees for justice seekers who are financially incapable (''prodeo'').
2. Bring judicial services closer to residential areas in remote regions through circuit courts.
3. Provide free legal advisory and information services within court buildings (''Posbakum'').
4. Integrate the legality of family legal status (marriage/divorce) with the right to register children's birth certificates and access pro-poor social assistance.

== Scope ==
This policy covers the jurisdiction of Religious Courts at the regency/city level (343 working units) and High Religious Courts / Mahkamah Syar'iyah (29 working units), which handle Islamic family law cases including:
* Marriage and Divorce (accounting for 74% of all national civil cases).
* Marriage Legalization (''Isbat Nikah'').
* Inheritance, Wills, Grants, Endowments (''Waqf''), Alms (''Zakat''), and Shari'ah Economics.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Court Fee Waivers (Prodeo):''' The court covers the costs of summoning witnesses and administration for citizens living below the poverty line.
* '''Circuit Courts (Sidang Keliling):''' Panels of judges and registrars travel to remote locations to hold hearings outside the court building.
* '''Legal Aid Posts (Posbakum):''' Provision of advocates/paralegals from Legal Aid Organizations (LBH) or Universities within the court premises.
* '''SMS Reporting System:''' The use of automated monthly SMS technology to monitor the usage of access to justice budgets in real-time across 372 judicial working units.

== Implementation ==
* '''Budget Increases:''' The state budget (APBN) increased Badilag's allocation for prodeo and circuit courts 18-fold, from <Rp 1 billion (2007) to Rp 24 billion (2008), which continued in the 2010–2014 RPJMN.
* '''Service Achievements (2011):''' In the first 7 months of 2011, 6,243 poor citizens received ''prodeo'' facilities, 13,860 citizens were served by ''circuit courts'', and 16,390 people consulted at 46 ''Posbakum'' posts.
* '''Caseload Increase:''' The caseload of Religious Courts increased by 77% in the 2006–2010 period as an indicator of growing accessibility and public trust.

== Policy Problems ==
* The average cost of a divorce case (Rp 800,000) prior to the reform was equivalent to 4 times the monthly per capita income of the poor.
* The lack of a Divorce Certificate prevented female heads of household (''PEKKA'') from proving their legal status to receive Raskin, BLT, and Jamkesmas.
* Without marriage legalization (''isbat nikah''), approximately 56%–60% of children from unrecorded marriages could not obtain a Birth Certificate.

== Reform / Change ==
* Transformation from isolated judicial institutions into national judicial reform leaders.
* Recognition within the Supreme Court Reform Blueprint 2010–2035.
* Replication of Badilag's service model to the General Courts under Bappenas.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Supreme Court of the Republic of Indonesia:''' The parent institution overseeing administrative and judicial matters.
* '''Bappenas & Ministry of Finance:''' National strategy planners and state budget allocators.
* '''Family Court of Australia & AusAID:''' International donor partners in drafting empirical studies and technical assistance.
* '''PEKKA:''' NGO partner supporting female heads of household.
* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]:''' Not found in the available sources [1–66].

'''A General Theory on International Courts and Compliance with International Agreements Policy & Analytical Framework''' is a comprehensive theoretical and empirical framework regarding the extent to which international judicial institutions (specifically the European Court of Justice - ECJ) can influence national government behavior and drive compliance with international agreements. Developed by Clifford J. Carrubba and Matthew J. Gabel (2015) in their book *International Courts and the Performance of International Agreements* (Cambridge University Press) and critically reviewed by Giacomo Di Federico (2016) in the *International Journal for Court Administration* (IJCA), this framework utilizes game theory to model international adjudication. It empirically tests 1,098 judgments involving defendant governments and 1,808 government litigation rulings between 1960 and 1999 to evaluate the *Political Sensitivity Hypothesis* and the *Conditional Effectiveness Hypothesis* [1–13].

== Summary ==
Published by Carrubba and Gabel (2015) and reviewed by Giacomo Di Federico (2016) in the IJCA, this policy framework employs formal game theory modeling to test the effectiveness of international court adjudication [1–3]. The study analyzes a comprehensive dataset of ECJ rulings between 1960 and 1999 (annulment, infringement, and preliminary rulings) along with intra-EU trade data (1970–1993). The findings confirm two primary hypotheses: the *Political Sensitivity Hypothesis* (the ECJ is more likely to rule against a government if there is a net balance of third-party briefs from other member states supporting that outcome) and the *Conditional Effectiveness Hypothesis* (an ECJ ruling is only effective in altering national policy if supported by the intervention of other member states) [3, 7–9]. Di Federico's review highlights post-1999 legal developments (such as Article 260(3) TFEU of the Lisbon Treaty) that have further altered the landscape of EU legal compliance [12–13].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), Articles 258 & 259:''' Infringement proceedings against member states for failing to fulfill treaty obligations.
* '''TFEU Article 263:''' Annulment proceedings reviewing the legality of legislative acts.
* '''TFEU Article 267:''' Preliminary reference procedures from national courts to the ECJ.
* '''TFEU Article 260(3) (Lisbon Treaty):''' The European Commission's authority to request immediate financial penalties for the failure to notify measures transposing a directive.
* '''Statute of the Court of Justice of the European Union (Post-Nice Treaty):''' Reform provisions allowing cases to be decided without an Advocate General's opinion if they do not raise new points of law.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
Compliance with international agreements remains highly debated in transnational legal literature. Because international courts lack an autonomous, coercive enforcement mechanism, the effectiveness of their rulings relies heavily on the voluntary compliance of member states, which is dictated by the rational calculation between short-term compliance costs and long-term cooperation benefits [2–3].

== Objectives ==
1. Model the strategic conditions that determine the effectiveness of international court adjudication.
2. Test the influence of third-party government briefs on the political sensitivity of the ECJ.
3. Demonstrate the tangible economic impact of ECJ trade liberalization rulings on intra-EU import flows [8–9].

== Scope ==
This policy covers the adjudication analysis of the Court of Justice of the European Union (ECJ) and the compliance behaviors of the six founding EU member states from 1960 to 1999.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Political Sensitivity Hypothesis:'''
** The Court is more likely to rule against a defendant government when there is a larger proportion of third-party briefs opposing that government.
* '''Conditional Effectiveness Hypothesis:'''
** A Court ruling against a government is more effective at altering policy if it is supported by net third-party briefs that are economically significant (measured via log GDP).
* '''Measuring Legal Merits via AG Opinions:'''
** Utilizing the Advocate General's opinions as an objective benchmark for pure legal merits, isolated from political pressures.

== Implementation ==
* '''Testing 1,098 Defendant Government Rulings:''' Mathematical confirmation of the ECJ's political sensitivity in infringement and preliminary rulings (1960–1999).
* '''Intra-EU Trade Analysis (1970–1993):''' Demonstrating that preliminary rulings have a broader trade policy impact than infringement rulings when supported by third-party briefs [8–9].

== Policy Problems ==
* '''The Legitimacy Dilemma:''' The severe risk of legitimacy loss if the ECJ issues a ruling that is subsequently ignored or openly defied by a national government.
* '''Short-Term Compliance Costs:''' The tendency of national governments to defect from agreements when the immediate costs of compliance outweigh the long-term benefits of cooperation.

== Reform / Change ==
* '''Implementation of Article 260(3) TFEU (Lisbon Treaty):''' Strengthening the deterrent effect through automatic financial sanctions for delays in directive transposition.
* '''Flexibility of AG Opinions (Nice Treaty):''' Eliminating the requirement for an AG opinion in routine cases to expedite adjudication.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Court of Justice of the European Union (ECJ):''' The primary subject of the empirical study on adjudication and compliance.
* '''University of Bologna:''' The academic institution of reviewer Giacomo Di Federico.
* '''[private person]:''' A Law student at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta (NIM: 2410611102), specializing in Constitutional Law (Hukum Tata Negara). Cecep Mustafa is not found in the available sources [FACT] [1–13].

The '''Internationalisation of Constitutional Law and Multilevel Rights Protection Framework''' (''Kerangka Kebijakan Internasionalisasi Hukum Konstitusi dan Perlindungan Hak Bertingkat'') is a constitutional law policy and theoretical framework examining the "de-provincialisation" of the 1948 Constitution of the Italian Republic, the integration of international and European Union norms into domestic law, and the multilevel protection of fundamental rights <ref>Onida, V. (2012). The Constitution Yesterday and Today. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 4(1), 15–37.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Authored by [[Valerio Onida]], Professor Emeritus of Constitutional Law at the [[University of Milan]], this framework posits that the 1948 Italian Constitution was not merely a local post-fascist political compromise, but a foundational document born out of the global experience of World War II and universal human rights movements <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 15–17.</ref>. Drawing upon the ideas of [[Giuseppe Dossetti]], Onida highlights that the Italian Constitution embodies universal human values that transcend local ideological boundaries <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 16–17.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
This framework rests upon national constitutional provisions and international legal instruments:
* '''[[Articles 10 & 11 of the Italian Constitution]]''': Mandates automatic compliance with customary international law and permits limitations of national sovereignty to promote international peace and justice <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 20, 24.</ref>.
* '''[[Article 117 of the Italian Constitution]]''': Binds national and regional legislative power to EU law and international treaty obligations (as amended in 2001) <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 23, 26.</ref>.
* '''[[Universal Declaration of Human Rights|UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)]] & [[European Convention on Human Rights|ECHR (1950)]]''': Establishes international and European baseline standards for fundamental human rights protection <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 18, 21–22.</ref>.
* '''Jurisprudence of the Italian Constitutional Court''': *Sentenza* No. 170/1984 (primacy of Community law) and *Sentenze* No. 348 and 349 of 2007 (establishing the ECHR as a constitutional parameter) <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 20–21, 24.</ref>.

== Background ==
Contemporary constitutionalism is defined by a universalist vocation: the recognition that every human being possesses inherent dignity and inalienable rights <ref>Onida (2012), p. 17.</ref>. Inspired by [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]]'s "Four Freedoms" speech (1941), the post-war order linked peace to international human rights protection <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 19, 30.</ref>. In Italy, cross-ideological dialogue between Catholic-Democrats ([[Giorgio La Pira]], [[Alcide De Gasperi]]) and Marxist/Leftist factions ([[Palmiro Togliatti]]) forged the "strong core" of the 1948 Constitution <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 27–29.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Advance a constitutional interpretation open to supranational human rights contributions <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 21, 24.</ref>.
* Counter the erosion of social rights and the welfare state caused by unchecked market globalization <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 31–33.</ref>.
* Protect democratic institutions from populist erosion and power concentration disguised as executive "governability" <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 35–37.</ref>.

== Scope ==
The scope covers Italian constitutional law, EU supranational law, the European Court of Human Rights system, social rights within the welfare state, and comparative constitutional studies involving Germany, France, and the United States <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 20–22, 28–29, 33–34.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & Legal Implications ==
* '''Multilevel Protection of Rights''': Harmonious integration of national constitutional rights, EU law, and ECHR case law without reducing higher domestic protection standards <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 21, 24.</ref>.
* '''Rejection of Rigid Originalism''': Human rights provisions must be interpreted dynamically rather than restricted to historical originalist perspectives <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 24–25.</ref>.
* '''Parity of Social Rights''': Social rights (work, health, social security—encompassing ''freedom from want'') share equal constitutional status with traditional civil and political liberties <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 31–34.</ref>.

== Implementation ==
Operationalized through Constitutional Court judgments, including the prohibition of extradition in capital punishment cases (*Sentenze* No. 54/1979 & No. 223/1996) and the enforcement of prisoners' fundamental rights (*Sentenza* No. 73/2001) <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 25, 26.</ref>.

== Policy Issues ==
* '''Threats of Free Market Globalization on Social Rights''': Critique of extreme fiscal austerity that undermines the social functions of the state <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 32–33.</ref>.
* '''Democratic Depreciation via Populism''': The risk of power concentration and simplified consensus mechanisms that erode the separation of powers <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 35–36.</ref>.

== Reform & Proposed Changes ==
Promotes the adoption of "constitutional patriotism" and executive stability reforms based on the [[Tommaso Perassi|Tommaso Perassi Agendum]] (1946) while maintaining strict institutional checks and balances <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 36, 37.</ref>.

== Related Entities ==
* '''[[Valerio Onida]]''': Author and Constitutional Law Professor <ref>Onida (2012), p. 15.</ref>.
* '''[[Giuseppe Dossetti]]''': Constituent Assembly Leader Quoted in Text <ref>Onida (2012), p. 16.</ref>.
* '''[[Franklin D. Roosevelt]]''': Architect of the "Four Freedoms" Concept <ref>Onida (2012), p. 19.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 15–37.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Onida (2012), pp. 15–37.</ref>

'''The Establishing Justice In Iraq & Post-Conflict Judicial Assessment Framework''' is a policy framework and empirical analysis of the reconstruction of Iraq's criminal and civil justice systems following the 2003 coalition invasion. Compiled by a 13-member US legal assessment team (including judges, prosecutors, public defenders, and court administrator Luther D. "Dan" Thomas) under the ''Coalition Provisional Authority'' (CPA), it diagnoses the destruction of judicial infrastructure and the legacy of Ba'ath Party corruption and manipulation. It establishes emergency human rights safeguards and sets forth 14 judicial reform recommendations [1–3, 15, 24–27, 34–40].

== Summary ==
Published by Luther D. “Dan” Thomas in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this policy framework documents the journey of the US Department of Justice Judicial Assessment Mission to Iraq in May–June 2003. Operating under the ''Coalition Provisional Authority'' (CPA) led by Ambassador L. Paul Bremer, the team found total paralysis of court buildings due to mass looting, alongside a dominant practice of torture and corruption inherited from Saddam Hussein's regime [1–4, 15, 24]. The team successfully formulated four emergency human rights safeguards that were immediately enacted by the CPA, and submitted 14 structural reform recommendations covering judicial ''vetting'', the reform of the inquisitorial system, legal aid for the poor, and an administrative land claims procedure [25, 27, 34–40].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Geneva Convention:''' Authorized the Coalition Forces/CPA to restore public order and conduct the removal of Ba'ath Party officials for security purposes.
* '''CPA Orders & Decrees (May 2003):''' The De-Ba'athification Decree and the order establishing four ''Emergency Human Rights Safeguards'' by Amb. L. Paul Bremer.
* '''1925 & 1970 Iraqi Constitutions:''' The foundation of the Iraqi civil law system, the separation of powers, and the establishment of the Council of Judges.
* '''Code of Hammurabi (1700 BC):''' The historical reference for the oldest written law in the Mesopotamian region.

== Background ==
Following the 2003 coalition invasion, Iraq experienced a severe legal vacuum due to Saddam Hussein's release of thousands of violent criminals and the disbandment of the security apparatus. Courthouses were looted down to their electrical wiring. A US DOJ assessment team was dispatched to evaluate the condition of 12 Courts of Appeal and the Court of Cassation, and to design the restoration of the ''Rule of Law'' [1–4, 9, 10].

== Objectives ==
1. Diagnose the physical and institutional damage to the Iraqi justice system across four main regions.
2. Halt human rights violations in criminal investigations (such as torture and the denial of the right to remain silent).
3. Cleanse the judicial system of Ba'ath Party politicization and corruption.
4. Draft a framework for infrastructure reconstruction, salary increases, and legal aid [36–39].

== Scope ==
This policy evaluates all levels of the judiciary in Iraq: the Court of Cassation, 12 Courts of Appeal (in Baghdad, Basrah, Mosul, Hillah, Kirkuk, Irbil, Najaf, Nasiriyah), Courts of First Instance, Criminal Courts, Special Courts (Personal Status, Labor, Juvenile), and the dissolution of the Revolutionary Courts [8–13].

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Four Emergency Human Rights Safeguards (Bremer Safeguards):'''
# ''Absolute Ban on Torture Confessions:'' The absolute prohibition on the use of confessions obtained through torture.
# ''Advice of Rights:'' The obligation to advise suspects of their rights according to international standards upon arrest.
# ''Right to Counsel Since Investigation:'' The right to be accompanied by a lawyer from the initial investigation stage by the investigating judge.
# ''Right to Remain Silent:'' The guarantee of the right to remain silent at all stages of the criminal justice process.
* '''The "Baghdad is Silent" Phenomenon:''' The passive attitude of judges who were reluctant to hold trials because they were accustomed to waiting for bureaucratic instructions from the Ministry of Justice.
* '''Low Pay & Systemic Corruption:''' Public defenders were only paid $2–$3 per serious criminal case, driving widespread bribery at the lower levels [18–20].

== Implementation ==
* '''Distribution of Emergency Advocate Funds:''' The distribution of over $80,000 in coalition funds by Dan Thomas to Iraqi lawyers who were assisting in the search for victims of abduction/enforced disappearance.
* '''Dissolution of Revolutionary Courts:''' The abolition of Ba'ath political courts in the summer of 2003.
* '''Reorganization of the Inquisitorial System:''' The transfer of partial authority from the ''Investigating Judge'' to the ''Public Prosecutor'' to ensure an independent prosecution function.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Mass Land Disputes:''' The forced displacement of ethnic Kurds and Shia by the Ba'ath regime created dual ownership claims that could not be resolved by ordinary civil courts.
* '''Security Threats to Personnel:''' The rampant terrorism attacks against court facilities and the assassination of local translators.

== Reform / Change ==
* Implementation of the 14 structural reform recommendations for the Iraqi judiciary [34–40].
* Increased salary incentives for prosecutors to equal those of judges to eradicate corruption.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Coalition Provisional Authority (CPA):''' The transitional government that issued the emergency human rights decrees.
* '''U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ):''' Dispatched the 13-member judicial assessment team.
* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]:''' ''Not found in the available sources.'' [FACT] [1–40].

'''The Irish Courts Service Model''' (''Management of the Courts: The Irish Courts Service Model'') is a policy and court administration governance framework in Ireland based on an ''independent agency model''. Established via the ''Courts Service Act, 1998'', it transferred the authority of court management from the executive branch (''Department of Justice, Equality and Law Reform'') to an autonomous body (the ''Courts Service''). This body is led by a Board with a judicial majority (9 out of 17 members) and managed by a Chief Executive Officer (CEO) who is accountable to the Parliament (''Oireachtas'') [FACT].

== Summary ==
Published by P.J. Fitzpatrick (the first CEO of the Irish Courts Service) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this policy framework analyzes the fundamental transformation of judicial administration in Ireland. Ending the "Ministry of Justice" governance system that had been in place since 1924, the 1996 report of the ''Working Group on a Courts Commission'', chaired by Justice Denham, spurred the enactment of the ''Courts Service Act, 1998''. This model delegates court operations, building management, ICT, and budget allocation to the ''Courts Service'', an autonomous statutory body that combines the leadership of judges, legal professionals, staff, and public representatives.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Courts Service Act, 1998:''' The primary statute establishing the ''Courts Service'', regulating its organizational functions (Section 5), reform proposal authority (Section 6F), Board governance (Sections 13-15), CEO accountability, and judicial independence safeguards (Sections 9, 20, 21).
* '''Courts of Justice Act 1924 & Courts (Establishment and Constitution) Act 1961:''' Early foundational statutes structuring the Irish judicial organization post-independence.
* '''Courts (Supplemental Provisions) Act 1961 (Eighth Schedule):''' Regulated the administrative authority of the Minister of Justice prior to 1998.

== Background ==
For over 70 years following independence, the administration of the Irish judiciary was under the full control of the Department of Justice, with no formal input from judges regarding resource allocation. This lack of autonomy prompted the establishment of the ''Working Group on a Courts Commission'' in October 1995. The Working Group recommended creating an independent agency to shift the judicial philosophy from merely a "court system" to a public-oriented "court service."

== Objectives ==
1. Independently manage and administer all levels of courts in Ireland.
2. Provide high-quality support facilities for judges to perform their judicial duties.
3. Provide adequate information and courthouse facilities for the public and court users.
4. Ensure that judicial administration does not interfere with the adjudicative independence of judges.

== Scope ==
This policy applies nationally, encompassing all levels of courts in Ireland: the ''Supreme Court'', ''High Court'', ''Circuit Court'', and ''District Court'', as well as 1,100 judicial staff employees.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Courts Service Board Composition:''' The Board consists of 17 members, with a judicial majority of 9 (Chief Justice, 3 Court Presidents, 1 Expert Judge, and 4 elected Judges), plus 8 non-judicial members (CEO, barrister, solicitor, staff representative, ministry official, consumer representative, trade union representative, and a business expert).
* '''CEO Accountability to Parliament:''' The CEO acts as the ''Accounting Officer'' before the ''Public Accounts Committee'' of the Parliament (''Oireachtas''), but is legally exempted from answering questions related to the exercise of judicial adjudicative functions (''Section 21'').
* '''Protection of Judicial Independence (Section 9):''' Explicitly states that no authority of the ''Courts Service'' may be used to interfere with court proceedings or erode judicial independence.

== Implementation ==
* '''Drafting the 3-Year Strategic Plan:''' The formulation of a 3-Year Strategic Plan, which must be approved by the Minister and laid before Parliament, detailing budget utilization targets and Irish language bilingualism policies.
* '''Management of Beneficial Funds (€1.062 Billion):''' The professional management of trust funds for litigants and minors by the Board.
* '''ICT & Building Infrastructure Construction:''' The construction of the ''Criminal Courts Complex'' in Dublin and the modernization of trial facilities.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Limits of Parliamentary Examination Authority:''' The risk of breaching judicial independence when the CEO is examined by Parliamentary Committees, addressed via a dispute testing clause to the High Court (''Section 21'').
* '''Annual Budget Dependency:''' The persistent need for the budget to be dependent on the annual appropriation vote by ''Dáil Éireann''.

== Reform / Change ==
* Granting official statutory advisory rights (''Section 6F'') to the ''Courts Service'' to propose changes to procedural law and the redistribution of court jurisdiction.
* Establishment of the ''Judicial Support Unit'' and structuring support units for the ''Courts Rules Committees''.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Department of Justice, Equality and Law Reform:''' The executive partner responsible for the annual budget allocation funding.
* '''Oireachtas (Irish Parliament):''' The legislative body receiving the annual reports and the 3-year strategic plans.
* '''[private person]:''' A Law student at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta (NIM: 2410611102), enrolled in the 2024/2025 academic year, with documented administrative records in her university's Student Senate (SEMA FH UPNVJ). Cecep Mustafa is not found in the available sources [FACT].

'''Italian and EU Cybersecurity Administrative Governance Framework''' (''Kerangka Kebijakan Tata Kelola Keamanan Siber Nasional Italia dan Uni Eropa'') is a public administrative law and governance framework regulating institutional structures, regulatory powers, sanctioning mechanisms, and technical-operational coordination for critical digital infrastructure protection across the European Union (via ENISA) and nationally in Italy (via the ''Agenzia per la Cybersicurezza Nazionale'' / ACN), positioning the Prime Minister of Italy (''Presidente del Consiglio dei Ministri'' / PCM) as the central node of national policy control <ref>Rossa, S. (2022). Administrative Law Reflections on Cybersecurity, and on its Institutional Actors, in the European Union and Italy. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 14(2), 426–450.</ref>.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Stefano Rossa]], Assistant Professor of Administrative Law at the [[University of Eastern Piedmont]], the analysis examines the administrative law implications of public cybersecurity policies across the European Union and Italy <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 426, 427.</ref>. The study reviews the re-defined mandate of the [[European Union Agency for Cybersecurity]] (ENISA) under the EU Cybersecurity Act (Regulation EU 2019/881) and the creation of Italy's national cybersecurity authority, the [[Agenzia per la Cybersicurezza Nazionale]] (ACN), enacted under the government of Prime Minister [[Mario Draghi]] in 2021 <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 429, 431, 434, 435.</ref>. Rossa highlights executive centralization within the Prime Minister's Office (PCM) and proposes a participatory cybersecurity framework based on public-private collaboration for institutional sustainability <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 440, 445, 447, 448.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
The policy and institutional architecture rests on national and European legal instruments:
* '''[[Regulation (EU) 2019/881]] (Cybersecurity Act)''': Establishes ENISA's permanent mandate as the EU center of cybersecurity expertise and introduces the EU cybersecurity certification framework for ICT products <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 431, 432.</ref>.
* '''[[Directive (EU) 2016/1148]] (NIS Directive)''': Mandates that every EU Member State designate national cybersecurity competent authorities and single points of contact <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 431, 434.</ref>.
* '''[[Decreto-Legge 14 giugno 2021 n. 82]] (Legge 109/2021)''': Establishes ACN as an autonomous agency protecting national cybersecurity interests <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 434, 435, 436.</ref>.
* '''[[Decreto-Legge 21 settembre 2019 n. 105]] (Legge 133/2019)''': Defines the National Cybersecurity Perimeter (''Perimetro di Sicurezza Nazionale Cibernetica'' - PSNC) to secure public and private entities managing essential functions <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 435, 436.</ref>.
* '''[[Legge 3 agosto 2007 n. 124]]''': Italian intelligence reform law placing national security policy coordination under the Prime Minister <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 441, 442.</ref>.

== Background & Hybrid Warfare ==
The evolution of modern conflict has given rise to hybrid warfare, in which cyberattacks on digital networks cause severe real-world disruption to physical infrastructure and national stability <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 426, 428.</ref>. In response, Italy instituted the PSNC framework and consolidated fragmented cybersecurity competencies under a single dedicated administrative body, ACN <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 434–436.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Build a responsive, integrated system of cyber resilience across the European Union <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 431, 432.</ref>.
* Safeguard vital state functions and essential public services against major cyber disruptions <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 429, 435, 436.</ref>.
* Harmonize cybersecurity standards and certification schemes across the European single market <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 432, 434.</ref>.
* Align public cybersecurity governance with UN Sustainable Development Goal 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions) <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 449, 450.</ref>.

== Scope ==
The scope covers administrative law governance, EU and national cybersecurity institutions, ICT product certification, mandatory incident notification protocols, and regulatory oversight of essential service operators <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 428, 429, 436, 438.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & ACN Governance ==
* '''Institutional Architecture and Autonomy''': ACN possesses regulatory, administrative, financial, and accounting autonomy under the direct oversight and policy direction of the Prime Minister (PCM) <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 436, 440.</ref>.
* '''Key Coordinating Organs''':
** ''Nucleo per la Cybersicurezza (NC)'': Provides operational support to the Prime Minister during national cyber crises <ref>Rossa (2022), p. 443.</ref>.
** ''Comitato Interministeriale per la Cybersicurezza (CIC)'': Formulates strategic policy guidance, oversees national strategy implementation, and coordinates inter-ministerial cyber affairs <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 443, 444.</ref>.
* '''Administrative Penalties''': ACN holds statutory authority to impose financial fines ranging from €12,000 to €150,000 for NIS regulation non-compliance <ref>Rossa (2022), p. 439</ref>, and €200,000 to €1,800,000 for violations of PSNC requirements <ref>Rossa (2022), p. 439</ref>.

== ENISA Star Network & Participatory Model ==
* '''Star Network Model''': Relations between ENISA and EU national authorities operate on a decentralized star network model, with ENISA acting as the central coordination hub and exercise host (e.g., ''Cyber Europe 2022'') <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 445, 446.</ref>.
* '''Participatory Cybersecurity''': Addresses the risk of public sector technical lock-in by incorporating Open Government principles, academic partnerships, and civic participation <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 447, 448, 449.</ref>.

== Policy Challenges & Reforms ==
* '''Executive Centralization Risk''': Concentrating cyber governance within the Prime Minister's Office limits parliamentary oversight (primarily conducted via COPASIR) and exposes national policy continuity to cabinet instability <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 444, 449.</ref>.

== Entity Relationships ==
* '''[[Stefano Rossa]]''': Study author and Assistant Professor of Administrative Law <ref>Rossa (2022), p. 426.</ref>.
* '''[[Agenzia per la Cybersicurezza Nazionale]] (ACN)''': Italian National Cybersecurity Agency <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 434, 436.</ref>.
* '''[[European Union Agency for Cybersecurity]] (ENISA)''': EU Cybersecurity Agency <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 429, 431.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''Not found in the available sources.'' <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 426–450.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''Not found in the available sources.'' <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 426–450.</ref>

Il '''Quadro di Governance Amministrativa della Sicurezza Cibernetica in Italia e nell'Unione Europea''' (''Administrative Law Reflections on Cybersecurity, and on its Institutional Actors, in the European Union and Italy'') è un quadro di diritto amministrativo e politiche pubbliche che disciplina l'architettura istituzionale, i poteri regolatori, i meccanismi sanzionatori e il coordinamento tecnico-operativo per la protezione delle infrastrutture digitali critiche a livello dell'Unione Europea (tramite l'ENISA) e nazionale in Italia (tramite l'[[Agenzia per la Cybersicurezza Nazionale]] / ACN), ponendo il Presidente del Consiglio dei Ministri (PCM) al centro del controllo della politica nazionale <ref>Rossa, S. (2022). Administrative Law Reflections on Cybersecurity, and on its Institutional Actors, in the European Union and Italy. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 14(2), 426–450.</ref>.

== Descrizione ==
Redatto da [[Stefano Rossa]], Ricercatore di Diritto Amministrativo presso l'[[Università degli Studi del Piemonte Orientale]], lo studio esamina le implicazioni di diritto amministrativo legate alle politiche pubbliche di sicurezza cibernetica nell'Unione Europea e in Italia <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 426, 427.</ref>. L'analisi approfondisce il mandato ridefinito dell'[[European Union Agency for Cybersecurity]] (ENISA) ai sensi dell'''EU Cybersecurity Act'' (Regolamento UE 2019/881) e l'istituzione dell'autorità unica italiana, l'[[Agenzia per la Cybersicurezza Nazionale]] (ACN), creata sotto il governo del Presidente del Consiglio [[Mario Draghi]] nel 2021 <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 429, 431, 434, 435.</ref>. Rossa evidenzia la centralizzazione dell'esecutivo in capo alla Presidenza del Consiglio dei Ministri (PCM) e propone un modello di ''participatory cybersecurity'' fondato sulla collaborazione pubblico-privata per garantire la sostenibilità istituzionale <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 440, 445, 447, 448.</ref>.

== Base Giuridica ==
Il quadro normativo e istituzionale si fonda su fonti europee e nazionali:
* '''[[Regolamento (UE) 2019/881]] (Cybersecurity Act)''': Conferisce un mandato permanente all'ENISA quale centro di competenza cibernetica dell'UE e introduce il quadro europeo di certificazione della sicurezza cibernetica per i prodotti ICT <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 431, 432.</ref>.
* '''[[Direttiva (UE) 2016/1148]] (Direttiva NIS)''': Impone a ciascuno Stato membro dell'UE di designare autorità nazionali competenti in materia di sicurezza cibernetica <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 431, 434.</ref>.
* '''[[Decreto-Legge 14 giugno 2021 n. 82]] (Legge 109/2021)''': Dispone l'istituzione dell'ACN quale organismo autonomo preposto alla tutela della sicurezza cibernetica nazionale <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 434, 435, 436.</ref>.
* '''[[Decreto-Legge 21 settembre 2019 n. 105]] (Legge 133/2019)''': Definisce il Perimetro di Sicurezza Nazionale Cibernetica (PSNC) per tutelare soggetti pubblici e privati che gestiscono funzioni essenziali dello Stato <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 435, 436.</ref>.
* '''[[Legge 3 agosto 2007 n. 124]]''': Legge di riforma dei servizi di informazione per la sicurezza che attribuisce al Presidente del Consiglio l'alta direzione delle politiche di sicurezza <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 441, 442.</ref>.

== Contesto e Guerra Ibrida ==
L'evoluzione dei conflitti moderni ha portato all'affermazione della guerra ibrida (''hybrid warfare''), in cui gli attacchi cibernetici alle reti digitali producono impatti devastanti sulle infrastrutture fisiche e sulla stabilità dello Stato <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 426, 428.</ref>. In risposta a queste minacce, l'Italia ha istituito il PSNC e consolidato le competenze amministrative frammentate all'interno di un'unica autorità dedicata, l'ACN <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 434–436.</ref>.

== Obiettivi ==
* Realizzare un sistema integrato e reattivo di resilienza cibernetica nell'Unione Europea <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 431, 432.</ref>.
* Proteggere le funzioni essenziali dello Stato e i servizi pubblici fondamentali da incidenti cibernetici ad alto impatto <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 429, 435, 436.</ref>.
* Armonizzare gli standard di sicurezza e i regimi di certificazione per i prodotti e servizi ICT nel mercato unico europeo <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 432, 434.</ref>.
* Integrare la sicurezza cibernetica nell'Obiettivo 16 dell'Agenda ONU per lo Sviluppo Sostenibile (Pace, Giustizia e Istituzioni Solide) <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 449, 450.</ref>.

== Ambito di Applicazione ==
L'ambito comprende il diritto amministrativo applicato alla sicurezza cibernetica, la governance delle istituzioni europee e nazionali, i regimi di certificazione dei prodotti ICT, gli obblighi di notifica degli incidenti e la vigilanza amministrativa sugli operatori di servizi essenziali <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 428, 429, 436, 438.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Chiave e Governance ACN ==
* '''Architettura Istituzionale e Autonomia dell'ACN''': L'ACN gode di autonomia regolamentare, amministrativa, finanziaria e contabile ed è posta sotto la diretta alta direzione del Presidente del Consiglio dei Ministri (PCM) <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 436, 440.</ref>.
* '''Organi di Coordinamento''':
** ''Nucleo per la Cybersicurezza (NC)'': Assicura il supporto operativo al Presidente del Consiglio nella gestione delle crisi cibernetiche nazionali <ref>Rossa (2022), p. 443.</ref>.
** ''Comitato Interministeriale per la Cybersicurezza (CIC)'': Svolge funzioni di consulenza strategica, monitoraggio della strategia nazionale e coordinamento interministeriale <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 443, 444.</ref>.
* '''Sanzioni Amministrative''': L'ACN è titolare del potere sanzionatorio amministrativo, con sanzioni pecuniarie da €12.000 a €150.000 per violazione della normativa NIS <ref>Rossa (2022), p. 439</ref>, e da €200.000 a €1.800.000 per violazioni relative al PSNC <ref>Rossa (2022), p. 439</ref>.

== Modello a Stella ENISA e Sicurezza Cibernetica Partecipativa ==
* '''Star Network Model''': Le relazioni tra l'ENISA e le autorità nazionali europee seguono un modello a stella decentralizzato, in cui l'ENISA funge da hub di coordinamento e organizza esercitazioni congiunte (es. ''Cyber Europe 2022'') <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 445, 446.</ref>.
* '''Participatory Cybersecurity''': Previene il rischio di divario tecnologico del settore pubblico (''lock-in effect'') promuovendo i principi dell'Open Government, l'integrazione con il settore accademico e la collaborazione pubblico-privata <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 447, 448, 449.</ref>.

== Criticità Politiche e Riforma ==
* '''Rischio di Centralizzazione dell'Esecutivo''': La forte concentrazione di poteri in capo alla Presidenza del Consiglio riduce lo spazio per il controllo parlamentare (esercitato principalmente tramite il COPASIR) ed espone l'azione amministrativa alla volatilità politica dei governi <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 444, 449.</ref>.

== Relazioni tra Entità ==
* '''[[Stefano Rossa]]''': Autore dello studio e Ricercatore di Diritto Amministrativo <ref>Rossa (2022), p. 426.</ref>.
* '''[[Agenzia per la Cybersicurezza Nazionale]] (ACN)''': Autorità Nazionale di Sicurezza Cibernetica dell'Italia <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 434, 436.</ref>.
* '''[[European Union Agency for Cybersecurity]] (ENISA)''': Agenzia dell'Unione Europea per la Sicurezza Cibernetica <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 429, 431.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''Non presente nelle fonti disponibili.'' <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 426–450.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''Non presente nelle fonti disponibili.'' <ref>Rossa (2022), pp. 426–450.</ref>

}}

The '''Italian Administrative Procedure Act Policy Framework''' (officially centered on ''Law no. 241 of August 7, 1990 / Legge 7 agosto 1990, n. 241'') is the foundational statutory and policy framework in Italian administrative law governing adjudicatory administrative procedures, transparency, public participation, administrative simplification, and principles of good governance <ref>Sandulli, A. (2012). The Italian Administrative Procedure Act: Back to the Future. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 4(2), 202–206.</ref>.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Aldo Sandulli]], Full Professor of Administrative Law at [[University "Suor Orsola Benincasa" of Naples]], this analysis evaluates the two-decade evolutionary trajectory of Law no. 241 of 1990 <ref>Sandulli (2012), p. 202.</ref>. Drafted by an expert academic commission appointed in 1979 by Minister for Civil Service [[Massimo Severo Giannini]] and chaired by [[Mario Nigro]], the Act fundamentally transformed the relationship between public administration and citizens from an authoritarian paradigm to a transparent, participatory, and structured interaction <ref>Sandulli (2012), pp. 202–203.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''[[Legge 7 agosto 1990, n. 241|Law no. 241 of August 7, 1990]]''': The core Italian administrative procedure statute establishing statutory rights to public participation, document access, strict procedural deadlines, and administrative simplification mechanisms <ref>Sandulli (2012), pp. 202–203.</ref>.

== Background ==
The original bill was completed by the Nigro Commission in 1982, but faced an eight-year political and bureaucratic delay before enactment by the Italian Parliament in 1990 <ref>Sandulli (2012), pp. 202–203.</ref>. The statutory architecture of Law no. 241/1990 established general principles focused on adjudicatory administrative procedures affecting individual legal positions, while general regulatory acts were intentionally excluded from its direct scope <ref>Sandulli (2012), p. 203.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Guarantee transparency via public access to administrative documents (*accesso agli atti*) and ensure public participation in administrative decision-making <ref>Sandulli (2012), pp. 202–204.</ref>.
* Maintain a structural balance between administrative efficiency (*simplification*) and citizen rights (*guarantees*) <ref>Sandulli (2012), pp. 203–204.</ref>.
* Uphold constitutional principles of impartiality and good administration (*imparzialità e buon andamento*) <ref>Sandulli (2012), p. 205.</ref>.

== Scope ==
Applies across all individual adjudicatory administrative procedures in Italy. However, general administrative and regulatory acts, emergency measures, and specified large-scale infrastructure projects are excluded or subject to special regimes <ref>Sandulli (2012), pp. 203, 204–205.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & Mechanisms ==
* '''Participation and Transparency Rights''': Mandates advance notice of administrative proceedings (*comunicazione di avvio del procedimento*) and establishes a general right of access to administrative documents <ref>Sandulli (2012), pp. 202–203.</ref>.
* '''Conference of Services (Conferenza di Servizi)''': A statutory coordination mechanism enabling multiple administrative bodies to make collective determinations efficiently <ref>Sandulli (2012), pp. 202, 204.</ref>.
* '''Procedure Officer (Responsabile del Procedimento - RUP)''': Requires the designation of a specific individual officer responsible for guiding each procedure to timely completion <ref>Sandulli (2012), p. 202.</ref>.

== Implementation ==
Operationalized throughout Italian public administration bodies and routinely reviewed and interpreted by administrative courts, primarily the Italian Council of State (*Consiglio di Stato*) <ref>Sandulli (2012), pp. 202, 205.</ref>.

== Policy Issues ==
* '''Patchwork Effect''': Frequent piecemeal amendments by the legislature have eroded the original structural coherence and spirit of the Act <ref>Sandulli (2012), pp. 203–205.</ref>.
* '''Marginalization of Democratic Guarantees''': A shifting procedural focus prioritizing economic acceleration and litigation reduction over citizen procedural guarantees <ref>Sandulli (2012), p. 204.</ref>.
* '''Flight from General Rules''': Increasing statutory exemptions created for emergency procedures and major infrastructure, allowing administration to bypass standard Law 241/1990 guarantees <ref>Sandulli (2012), pp. 204–205.</ref>.

== Proposed Reforms (De Jure Condendo) ==
Aldo Sandulli recommends three structural reform steps:
# Implement a moratorium on makeshift emergency legislative amendments <ref>Sandulli (2012), p. 205.</ref>.
# Conduct empirical mapping and comparative legal research on contemporary Italian administrative practices <ref>Sandulli (2012), p. 205.</ref>.
# Establish a new expert academic commission (modeled on the Nigro Commission) to draft a balanced modern Administrative Procedure Act <ref>Sandulli (2012), p. 205.</ref>.

== Related Entities ==
* '''[[Aldo Sandulli]]''': Author of the analysis and Professor of Administrative Law <ref>Sandulli (2012), p. 202.</ref>.
* '''[[Massimo Severo Giannini]]''': Minister for Civil Service who initiated the 1979 Commission <ref>Sandulli (2012), p. 202.</ref>.
* '''[[Mario Nigro]]''': Chair of the Commission that drafted the 1982 bill <ref>Sandulli (2012), p. 202.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>Sandulli (2012), pp. 202–206.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>Sandulli (2012), pp. 202–206.</ref>

| status = Operational / Active
}}

The '''Comparative Framework of the Italian Administrative Procedure and Rights Act''' (officially centered on the work ''Administrative Procedures and Rights in Italy: A Comparative Approach'') is a comparative legal evaluation framework analyzing the Italian Administrative Procedure Act of 1990 (Law no. 241/1990). It examines the codification of judge-made law, participatory rights, public record access, due process guarantees, and the utilitarian balance between protecting individual liberty and maintaining administrative efficiency <ref>della Cananea, G. (2010). Administrative Procedures and Rights in Italy: A Comparative Approach. ''Forward / Essay'', 207–219.</ref>.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Giacinto della Cananea]], Professor of Administrative Law at the University "Federico II" of Naples, this study evaluates two decades of implementation of Law no. 241/1990 in Italy using comparative law benchmarks and European due process standards <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 207, 212.</ref>. Citing constitutional theories by [[Charles McIlwain]] and [[Thomas Paine]], the framework underscores how administrative procedure acts function as a legal limitation on government power to prevent despotism <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 207, 219.</ref>. Law no. 241/1990 codified key judicial principles, such as the duty to state reasons, public participation rights, and access to public documents, while continuing to face persistent bureaucratic resistance <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 208, 210.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
The framework is grounded in key national, supranational, and international legal instruments:
* '''[[Italian Administrative Procedure Act of 1990|Italian Administrative Procedure Act of 1990 (Law no. 241/1990)]]''': Codification of general administrative procedure principles, participation rights, and access to public records in Italy <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 208–209.</ref>.
* '''[[Article 21-octies Amendment|Article 21-octies Amendment (2005)]]''': A statutory provision limiting the annulment of administrative acts due to technical formal deficiencies <ref>della Cananea (2010), p. 216.</ref>.
* '''[[Italian Constitution of 1947]]''': Established general principles of good governance (*buon andamento*) <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 207–208.</ref>.
* '''[[Article 6 ECHR]] & [[EU General Principles of Law]]''': European standards governing fair trial guarantees, procedural protection, and the duty to give reasons <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 214–215.</ref>.
* '''[[Aarhus Convention]]''': An international treaty influencing public access rights to environmental information <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 215, 217.</ref>.

== Background ==
Unlike the post-1970s Iberian constitutions (Spain and Portugal), which explicitly codified procedural rights, the 1947 Italian Constitution provided only general principles for administrative organization <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 207–208.</ref>. In 1990, the Italian Parliament enacted Law no. 241/1990 to respond to public demands for transparent governance by codifying judge-made case law <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 208, 210.</ref>. However, the civil service persistently resisted procedural restrictions, successfully lobbying in subsequent amendments to extend the default administrative decision-making deadline from 30 days to 90 days <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 209, 217.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Evaluate the efficacy of Law no. 241/1990 in securing due process protections for individuals against administrative authorities <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 208, 212.</ref>.
* Measure the performance of Italian public authorities against comparative European and international standards <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 212–214.</ref>.
* Analyze the utilitarian balance between individual freedoms and administrative efficiency/social welfare <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 215–216.</ref>.

== Scope ==
The scope covers Italian administrative law, procedural competence sharing between central and regional governments, comparative analysis with US administrative law (APA 1946 / FOIA 1966), German law (VwVfG 1976), Austrian law (1925), Swedish acts (1971/1986), and the impact of European Union law <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 212–216.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & Comparative Issues ==
* '''Lack of Explicit Right to Oral Hearing''': While Law no. 241/1990 guarantees written submissions and record access, it lacks an explicit statutory right to an oral hearing <ref>della Cananea (2010), p. 215.</ref>.
* '''Exemption of Rule-Making Procedures''': Statutory requirements bind individual adjudicative acts but explicitly exclude general rule-making, leaving notice-and-comment mechanisms absent unlike under the US APA (Article 13) <ref>della Cananea (2010), p. 215.</ref>.
* '''Erosion of Duty to State Reasons via Article 21-octies''': The 2005 amendment preventing decision annulment for purely formal flaws risks misinterpretation where courts treat omitted reasons as mere procedural defects <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 216–217.</ref>.

== Implementation ==
Implemented through mandatory designation of a responsible procedure officer (*responsabile del procedimento*) across public agencies, statutory deadline enforcement, and administrative court judicial review <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 209, 215–216.</ref>.

== Policy Issues ==
* '''Bureaucratic Resistance''': Continuous opposition from traditional civil service bodies viewing procedural constraints as operational burdens <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 209, 216.</ref>.
* '''Regional Autonomy vs. Procedural Rights''': Risk of fragmented individual protections due to regional rule variation following the 2001 constitutional reform <ref>della Cananea (2010), p. 217.</ref>.

== Proposed Reforms (De Jure Condendo) ==
* Expand public record access rights in alignment with the Aarhus Convention <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 215, 217.</ref>.
* Extend the duty to give reasons and notice requirements to general rule-making actions <ref>della Cananea (2010), p. 215.</ref>.
* Prevent judicial misapplication of Article 21-octies that reduces the duty to state reasons to a formal obstacle <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 216–217.</ref>.

== Related Entities ==
* '''[[Giacinto della Cananea]]''': Author and Professor of Administrative Law at University "Federico II" of Naples <ref>della Cananea (2010), p. 207.</ref>.
* '''[[Massimo Severo Giannini]]''': Italian Legal Scholar <ref>della Cananea (2010), p. 215.</ref>.
* '''[[Sabino Cassese]]''': Public Law Expert <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 208, 219.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 207–219.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>della Cananea (2010), pp. 207–219.</ref>

'''Policy Framework for the Reform of Italian Class Actions and Collective Injunctions''' (''Legge 12 aprile 2019 n. 31'') is a civil procedural law policy framework in Italy introduced via Law 12 April 2019 no. 31. The framework inserted Title VIII-bis (''Dei procedimenti collettivi'') into the Italian Code of Civil Procedure (''Codice di procedura civile'' - Arts. 840-bis to 840-sexiesdecies), replacing the previous consumer class action regime (Article 140-bis of the Consumer Code). It expands standing to sue to any individual and entity representing homogeneous individual rights through a three-phase simplified proceeding based on an opt-in mechanism <ref>De Santis, A.D. (2019). The New Italian Class Action: Hope Springs Eternal. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 05(02), 757–771.</ref>.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Angelo Danilo De Santis]], Associate Professor of Civil Procedure at the [[University of Roma Tre]], the analysis examines the fundamental overhaul of collective redress in Italy <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 757, 758.</ref>. Law 12 April 2019 no. 31 repealed former consumer class action provisions in the Consumer Code (Articles 139, 140, and 140-bis) and incorporated them directly into the Code of Civil Procedure to offer broader, more effective judicial protection in mass dispute scenarios <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 757–760.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
The framework relies on national procedural instruments as well as European legal bases:
* '''Law 12 April 2019 no. 31''': Introduced Title VIII-bis (Arts. 840-bis to 840-sexiesdecies) into the Italian Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) and Title V-bis of the CPC Implementing Provisions (Arts. 196-bis and 196-ter) <ref>De Santis (2019), p. 757.</ref>.
* '''Code of Civil Procedure (Arts. 702-bis, 702-ter, 702-quater)''': Establishes the simplified proceedings regime governing class action lawsuits <ref>De Santis (2019), p. 758.</ref>.
* '''Consumer Code (Arts. 37, 139, 140, 140-bis)''': Repealed Articles 139, 140, and 140-bis while retaining Article 37 regarding unfair terms injunctions <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 757, 760.</ref>.
* '''Regulation (EU) No. 1215/2012 (Brussels I Recast) & Legislative Decree 19 January 2017 no. 3''': Governs European jurisdictional rules and documentary disclosure standards modeled on private antitrust enforcement <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 758, 761, 765.</ref>.

== Background & Paradigm Shift ==
The previous consumer class action regime introduced in 2009 (Art. 140-bis Consumer Code) failed to deliver widespread mass redress due to procedural hurdles and high cost barriers <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 758, 766.</ref>. Law no. 31/2019 enacted a major paradigm shift by removing the requirement for consumer status: any individual, commercial enterprise, or registered non-profit organization now possesses standing to seek judicial remedies for mass harm <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 759, 760.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Provide an efficient and equal access to justice mechanism for all aggrieved parties in Italy <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 758, 759.</ref>.
* Enhance the deterrent effect against corporate misconduct and public service providers <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 766, 770.</ref>.
* Streamline evidentiary proceedings through judicial disclosure orders and shifting technical expert fees to defendants <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 764, 765.</ref>.

== Scope ==
The policy framework encompasses class actions for damages as well as collective actions for injunctive and declaratory relief filed against corporate entities or public service operators <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 757, 759, 770, 771.</ref>.

== Three-Phase Procedural Structure ==
* '''Phase I: Admissibility Assessment''': The Specialized Section of the Tribunal reviews whether the claim is not clearly groundless, the rights are homogeneous, no conflict of interest exists, and the claimant is an adequate representative <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 758, 761–764.</ref>.
* '''Phase II: Merits & Liability Phase''': The court examines common liability issues and determines defendant liability. Defendants can be ordered to advance technical expert expenses <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 758, 759, 764, 765.</ref>.
* '''Phase III: Adhesion Proceedings''': Voluntary opt-in claims are registered via the Ministry of Justice public portal. A court-appointed Class Representative Administrator verifies member submissions and handles distribution <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 759, 765–770.</ref>.

== Collective Injunctions (Art. 840-sexiesdecies) ==
Parallel to damages claims, collective injunctive actions allow individuals or registered non-profit organizations to seek orders restraining unlawful conduct or mandating corrective action (''facere''). Proceedings are conducted in chambers (Arts. 737–739 CPC) with mandatory intervention by the Public Prosecutor (''Pubblico Ministero'') and enforced via Art. 614-bis CPC <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 770, 771.</ref>.

== Policy Issues & Criticisms ==
* '''Opt-in System Limitations''': Retaining a voluntary opt-in mechanism rather than an opt-out model is viewed as a hurdle that limits class participation and global dispute settlements <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 759, 766.</ref>.
* '''Transitional Gap''': The repeal of Consumer Code provisions risks creating a legal vacuum for unlawful acts that occurred prior to the effective date of Law no. 31/2019 <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 757, 760.</ref>.

== Entity Relationships ==
* '''[[Angelo Danilo De Santis]]''': Study author and Associate Professor of Civil Procedure <ref>De Santis (2019), p. 757.</ref>.
* '''[[University of Roma Tre]]''': Academic affiliation of the author <ref>De Santis (2019), p. 757.</ref>.
* '''[[Italian Parliament]]''': Legislative authority that enacted Law 12 April 2019 no. 31 <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 757, 758.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''Not found in the available sources.'' <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 757–771.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''Not found in the available sources.'' <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 757–771.</ref>

Il '''Quadro Politico di Riforma dell'Azione di Classe e dell'Ingiunzione Collettiva in Italia''' (''Legge 12 aprile 2019 n. 31'') rappresenta la riforma della tutela giurisdizionale collettiva introdotta con la Legge 12 aprile 2019 n. 31. Tale normativa ha inserito il Titolo VIII-bis (''Dei procedimenti collettivi'') all'interno del Codice di procedura civile italiano (Art. 840-bis a 840-sexiesdecies c.p.c.), sostituendo il precedente regime dell'azione di classe consumeristica (Art. 140-bis del Codice del Consumo) ed estendendo la legittimazione ad agire a chiunque sia titolare o rappresentante di diritti individuali omogenei attraverso un procedimento semplificato articolato in tre fasi e basato sul meccanismo dell'opt-in <ref>De Santis, A.D. (2019). The New Italian Class Action: Hope Springs Eternal. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 05(02), 757–771.</ref>.

== Descrizione ==
Redatto da [[Angelo Danilo De Santis]], Professore Associato di Diritto Processuale Civile presso l'[[Università degli Studi Roma Tre]], lo studio analizza la revisione strutturale della tutela collettiva (''collective redress'') in Italia <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 757, 758.</ref>. La Riforma del 2019 ha abrogato la disciplina dell'azione di classe contenuta nel Codice del Consumo (Art. 139, 140 e 140-bis), collocandola direttamente all'interno del Codice di procedura civile al fine di garantire una tutela processuale uniforme e ad ampio spettro <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 757–760.</ref>.

== Base Giuridica ==
Il quadro normativo si fonda su fonti interne e sovranazionali:
* '''Legge 12 aprile 2019 n. 31''': Ha inserito il Titolo VIII-bis (Art. 840-bis a 840-sexiesdecies) nel Codice di procedura civile e il Titolo V-bis nelle Disposizioni di attuazione del c.p.c. (Art. 196-bis e 196-ter) <ref>De Santis (2019), p. 757.</ref>.
* '''Codice di procedura civile (Art. 702-bis, 702-ter, 702-quater)''': Regola la struttura del procedimento sommario/semplificato applicabile all'azione di classe <ref>De Santis (2019), p. 758.</ref>.
* '''Codice del Consumo (Art. 37, 139, 140, 140-bis)''': Abrogazione degli Art. 139, 140 e 140-bis, mantenendo in vigore l'Art. 37 sulle clausole vessatorie <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 757, 760.</ref>.
* '''Regolamento (UE) N. 1215/2012 (Bruxelles I bis) & D.Lgs. 19 gennaio 2017 n. 3''': Disciplina della competenza giurisdizionale europea e norme sull'esibizione delle prove documentali (''disclosure'') mutuate dal settore antitrust <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 758, 761, 765.</ref>.

== Contesto e Cambio di Paradigma ==
Il precedente modello di azione di classe risalente al 2009 (Art. 140-bis Codice del Consumo) si era rivelato inefficace a causa di rigidità procedurali e ostacoli economici <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 758, 766.</ref>. La Legge n. 31/2019 ha superato il limite soggettivo della qualifica di consumatore: la legittimazione ad agire è ora riconosciuta a qualsiasi persona fisica, impresa o ente no-profit iscritto nell'elenco ministeriale <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 759, 760.</ref>.

== Obiettivi ==
* Garantire un effettivo accesso alla giustizia per la riparazione dei danni di massa a tutti i soggetti dell'ordinamento <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 758, 759.</ref>.
* Rafforzare la funzione deterrente nei confronti di condotte illecite poste in essere da imprese o gestori di servizi pubblici <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 766, 770.</ref>.
* Agevolare l'istruzione probatoria mediante l'ordine di esibizione documentale e l'anticipazione delle spese di consulenza tecnica a carico del convenuto <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 764, 765.</ref>.

== Ambito di Applicazione ==
Il quadro normativo comprende sia l'azione di classe risarcitoria sia l'azione inibitoria collettiva e dichiarativa nei confronti di imprese o enti gestori di servizi pubblici <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 757, 759, 770, 771.</ref>.

== Articolazione del Procedimento in Tre Fasi ==
* '''Fase I: Ammissibilità''': La Sezione Specializzata del Tribunale valuta se il ricorso non sia manifestamente infondato, se i diritti siano omogenei e se non sussista un conflitto di interessi <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 758, 761–764.</ref>.
* '''Fase II: Merito e Accertamento della Responsabilità''': Il giudice decide sulle questioni comuni e accerta la responsabilità del convenuto, ponendo eventualmente a suo carico le spese per la consulenza tecnica d'ufficio <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 758, 759, 764, 765.</ref>.
* '''Fase III: Adesione e Liquidazione''': Fase di pendenza delle adesioni volontarie (''opt-in'') gestita tramite il portale telematico del Ministero della Giustizia. Un rappresentante dei common aderenti nomina e verifica i crediti ai fini del risarcimento <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 759, 765–770.</ref>.

== Inibitoria Collettiva (Art. 840-sexiesdecies) ==
Unitamente all'azione risarcitoria, è prevista l'azione inibitoria collettiva volta a far cessare una condotta illecita o a ordinarne la rimozione (''facere''). Il procedimento si svolge in camera di consiglio (Art. 737–739 c.p.c.) con l'intervento obbligatorio del Pubblico Ministero ed è eseguibile coattivamente ex Art. 614-bis c.p.c. <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 770, 771.</ref>.

== Criticità Politiche e Riforma ==
* '''Limiti del Sistema Opt-in''': Il mantenimento dell'adesione volontaria (''opt-in'') in luogo dell'adesione automatica con facoltà di recesso (''opt-out'') è considerato un ostacolo ad una risoluzione globale delle controversie di massa <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 759, 766.</ref>.
* '''Vuoto Normativo Transitorio''': L'abrogazione delle norme del Codice del Consumo rischia di creare dubbi applicativi per gli illeciti commessi prima dell'entrata in vigore della Legge n. 31/2019 <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 757, 760.</ref>.

== Relazioni tra Entità ==
* '''[[Angelo Danilo De Santis]]''': Autore dello studio e Professore Associato di Diritto Processuale Civile <ref>De Santis (2019), p. 757.</ref>.
* '''[[Università degli Studi Roma Tre]]''': Affiliazione accademica dell'autore <ref>De Santis (2019), p. 757.</ref>.
* '''[[Parlamento Italiano]]''': Organo legislativo che ha emanato la Legge 12 aprile 2019 n. 31 <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 757, 758.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''Non presente nelle fonti disponibili.'' <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 757–771.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''Non presente nelle fonti disponibili.'' <ref>De Santis (2019), pp. 757–771.</ref>
