= 'Efficiency of the Judicial System in Protecting Citizens against Administrative Judicial Acts: The Case of Macedonia' (Pelivanova & Dimeski, 2011/2013) =

=== Wiki Entity Page ===
{{Infobox
| stable_id = judicial-policy-macedonia-administrative-justice-2006
| name = Macedonian Administrative Judicial System (2006/2010 Reforms)
| type = Specialized Administrative Judicial Reform Framework / Court Efficiency Evaluation
| issuing_authority = Parliament of the Republic of Macedonia / Administrative Court / St. Kliment Ohridski University
| legal_basis = Constitution of Macedonia Art. 50(2) & Amends 15/21/101; Law on Courts; Law on Administrative Disputes 2006/2010
| date = Reform 2006 / Court Operational Dec 5, 2007 / Amending Act 2010
| status = Active / Statutory Framework in Effect
}}

'''Macedonian Administrative Judicial System & Reforms''' is a specialized judicial reform framework in the Republic of Macedonia established under the Law on Administrative Disputes (2006) and its 2010 amendments. This reform transitioned the administrative oversight system from an "Anglo-Saxon Model" (oversight by the Administrative Chamber of the Supreme Court) to a "European-Continental Model" based on specialized dual-instance courts (the ''Administrative Court'' which commenced operations on December 5, 2007, and the ''Higher Administrative Court'' established in 2010/2011). The reform aimed to resolve systematic delays, severe case backlogs, and the erosion of public confidence in the legal protection of citizens.

== Summary ==
Based on the empirical study by Dr. Natasa Pelivanova and Dr. Branko Dimeski of St. Kliment Ohridski University (Bitola), the transition from the Supreme Court to a specialized Administrative Court has not successfully resolved the backlog problem. Although the number of judges was increased from 22 in 2008 to 25 in 2009, the number of unresolved cases actually increased from '''9,154 cases (2008)''' to '''10,340 cases (2009)'''. The primary causes of these delays include spatial and IT technology constraints, a crisis in judicial assistance (only 18 assistants for 25 judges in 2009), and the lack of practical experience in administrative law among the appointed judges.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Constitution of the Republic of Macedonia (1991):''' Article 50(2) (guaranteeing judicial review of administrative acts), Amendment 15 (independent judicial power), Amendment 21 (right to appeal), and Amendment 101 (status of the Supreme Court).
* '''Law on Courts (Official Gazette No. 58/06, 35/08, 150/10):''' Articles 22 and 34 defining the court hierarchy and the jurisdiction of the Administrative Court.
* '''Law on Administrative Disputes (2006 & Amending Act 2010):''' The foundational basis establishing the Administrative Court and the Higher Administrative Court.
* '''Constitutional Court Decision U.No. 231/2008-0-1 (2009):''' Mandated the availability of two-instance judicial protection in administrative disputes.

== Organization & Six Specialized Departments ==
The Administrative Court of Macedonia organizes its caseload into 6 specialized departments and 8 chambers/councils:
1. '''Department I:''' Real Estate, Cadastre, and Education.
2. '''Department II:''' Denationalization, Expropriation, and Transformation.
3. '''Department III:''' Urbanism/Construction, Water, Agriculture, Economy, Transport, and Broadcasting.
4. '''Department IV:''' Pensions, Disability Insurance, Social Welfare, Health Insurance, and Labor Rights.
5. '''Department V:''' Public Procurement, Unemployment Rights, Taxes, Competition, and Public Information Access.
6. '''Department VI:''' Customs, Levies, Passports/Travel, Weapons, Energy, Concessions, and Intellectual Property.

== Key Problems & Causes of Delay ==
1. '''Escalating Case Backlogs:''' Unresolved cases rose from 9,154 in 2008 to 10,340 in 2009.
2. '''Shortage of Judicial Assistants:''' In 2008, the court had '''0 judicial assistants''', and in 2009, there were only 18 assistants for 25 judges (less than 1 assistant per judge).
3. '''Lack of Administrative Law Specialization:''' Most appointed judges had backgrounds in civil, criminal, or private law without prior practical experience in administrative law.
4. '''Inadequate Infrastructure & IT:''' Deplorable spatial constraints and outdated technical equipment impaired court workflow.

== Comparison with the French Model ==
The French Model (European-Continental Model) relies on specialized education at the ''École Nationale d'Administration'' (ENA), career mobility between courts and the bureaucracy, and consultative functions that accelerate case resolution. Pelivanova and Dimeski recommend continuous training, budget increases, hiring more judicial assistants, and reducing political intervention in judicial appointments.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''St. Kliment Ohridski University & IJCA:''' The researchers' home institution and the publishing journal.
* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]:''' Not found in the available sources [1–22].

'''Subsidiarity and the New Frontiers of Freedom of Contract''' (Italian: ''Kerangka Kebijakan Subsidiariasitas dan Batas Baru Kebebasan Berkontrak'') is an analytical framework spanning private and public law formulated by [[Filippo Maisto]]. The framework provides legal justification for the binding force of contracts created in place of public acts (*contracts in place of public acts*) on the basis of vertical and horizontal subsidiarity principles <ref>Maisto, F. (2021). Subsidiarity and the New Frontiers of Freedom of Contract. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 7(2), 731–742.</ref>. It expands freedom of contract into three new domains (contracts replacing administrative acts, alternative judicial dispute settlement contracts, and contracts as sources of legal rules) and demonstrates that subsidiarity functions as a "revolving door" that bridges the rigid dichotomy between private law (*diritto privato*) and public law (*diritto pubblico*) <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 731, 741–742.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Authored by [[Filippo Maisto]] (Full Professor of Private Law at the [[University of Calabria]]), the study refutes classical theories concerning the "death of contract" (e.g., Grant Gilmore) and the collapse of contractual freedom (e.g., P.S. Atiyah), as well as traditional Italian doctrines asserting that contracts cannot pursue public interests <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 731, 737.</ref>. The author proves that horizontal subsidiarity grants legal legitimacy to private agreements replacing public acts <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 731, 735.</ref>.

Through this framework, freedom of contract is expanded into three distinct domains:
# '''Contracts Substitutive of Administrative Measures''' (e.g., *convenzioni urbanistiche* and environmental settlements under Art. 306-bis of the Environmental Code) <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 735–736.</ref>;
# '''Contracts Alternative to Judicial Dispute Resolution''' (authorizing arbitration and ADR mechanisms in public-interest disputes) <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 736.</ref>;
# '''Contracts as Sources of Legal Rules''' (acknowledging the normative effect of collective labor agreements, sports regulations, professional codes of ethics, and condominium bylaws upon third parties) <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 736, 738.</ref>.

The framework proposes a shift from formalistic subsumption (*Begriffsjurisprudenz*) toward an axiological decision-making method aligned with constitutional values and the direct application of constitutional principles (''Drittwirkung'') <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 738, 741–742.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
=== European Union Law ===
* '''[[Treaty on European Union]] (TEU)''': Article 5 (Principle of Subsidiarity) <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 732.</ref>.

=== Constitution of the Italian Republic ===
* '''Article 3 & Article 23''': Resource allocation mechanisms and distributive justice <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 738.</ref>.
* '''Article 41 & Article 42''': Freedom of private economic initiative and social function of property <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 738.</ref>.
* '''Article 117(2)(l)''': Exclusive state legislative competence over private law (''ordinamento civile'') <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 734.</ref>.

=== Italian Codes and Statutes ===
* '''Codice Civile''': Article 1372(2) (Privity of contract / effects on third parties) <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 738.</ref>; Article 1987 (Unilateral promises / ''promesse unilaterali'') <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 734.</ref>.
* '''Legge 7 agosto 1990, n. 241''': Article 11 (Administrative agreements and *convenzioni urbanistiche*) <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 735.</ref>.
* '''Decreto Legislativo 3 luglio 2017, n. 117''': Third Sector Code (''Codice del Terzo Settore'') <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 733.</ref>.
* '''Decreto Legislativo 3 aprile 2006, n. 152''': Article 306-bis (Environmental transactions / *transazione ambientale*) <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 736.</ref>.
* '''Decreto Legislativo 12 aprile 2006, n. 163''': Article 241(1) (Arbitration limits in public contracts) <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 736.</ref>.

=== Key Jurisprudence ===
* '''[[Corte Costituzionale]] (Italian Constitutional Court)''':
** ''Sentenza n. 303/2003 & n. 6/2004'': Established *chiamata in sussidiarietà* in legislative allocations <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 733.</ref>.
** ''Sentenza n. 300/2003, n. 301/2003, n. 287/2016'': Private status of banking foundations <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 733.</ref>.
** ''Sentenza n. 185/2018'': Application of horizontal subsidiarity to Third Sector organizations <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 733.</ref>.
** ''Sentenza n. 228/2016, n. 6/2013, n. 77/2011, n. 41/2017'': Regional civil law limits vs. *ordinamento civile* <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 734.</ref>.
* '''Supranational Jurisprudence (CJEU)''': Case C-353/06 (*Grunkin-Paul*); Case C-148/02 (*Garcia Avello*); Case C-219/91 (*Bellone v. Yokohama*) <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 732, 734.</ref>.

== Three New Frontiers of Freedom of Contract ==
# '''Contracts Substitutive of Administrative Measures''': Public-private agreements are categorized as true civil contracts subject to private law remedies, including rules on defects of consent (*vizi del consenso*), pre-contractual liability (*responsabilità precontrattuale*), and breach damages <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 735–736.</ref>.
# '''Contracts Alternative to Judicial Settlements''': Freedom of contract expands into arbitration agreements and alternative dispute resolution (ADR) involving administrative or public interests <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 736.</ref>.
# '''Contracts as Sources of Legal Rules''': Private agreements that generate binding legal rules for third parties, departing from strict privity of contract (Art. 1372(2) Codice Civile) to fulfill overriding public objectives <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 736, 738.</ref>.

'''Sussidiarietà e Nuove Frontiere della Libertà Contrattuale''' (in inglese: ''Subsidiarity and the New Frontiers of Freedom of Contract''; identificativo: `judicial-policy-maisto-subsidiarity-contract-2021`) è un quadro analitico tra diritto privato e diritto pubblico formulato da [[Filippo Maisto]]. Il quadro fornisce la giustificazione giuridica della forza vincolante dei contratti stipulati in sostituzione di provvedimenti amministrativi (*contracts in place of public acts*) sulla base dei principi di sussidiarietà verticale e orizzontale <ref>Maisto, F. (2021). Subsidiarity and the New Frontiers of Freedom of Contract. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 7(2), 731–742.</ref>. L'opera estende la libertà contrattuale a tre nuove forme (contratti sostitutivi di provvedimenti amministrativi, contratti di risoluzione alternativa delle controversie giudiziarie e contratti come fonti di regole giuridiche) e dimostra che la sussidiarietà funziona come una "porta girevole" (*revolving door*) che supera la rigida dicotomia tra diritto privato e diritto pubblico <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 731, 741–742.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Scritto da [[Filippo Maisto]] (Professore Ordinario di Diritto Privato presso l'[[Università della Calabria]]), lo studio confuta le teorie classiche sulla "morte del contratto" (Grant Gilmore) e sul "crollo della libertà contrattuale" (P.S. Atiyah), nonché le tesi tradizionali che negavano la capacità del contratto di perseguire interessi pubblici <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 731, 737.</ref>. L'autore dimostra che il principio di sussidiarietà orizzontale attribuisce legittimità giuridica agli accordi privati che sostituiscono l'azione pubblica <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 731, 735.</ref>.

Attraverso questo quadro analitico, la libertà contrattuale viene ampliata in tre distinti settori:
# '''Contratti sostitutivi di provvedimenti amministrativi''' (es. *convenzioni urbanistiche* ed ex Art. 306-bis del Codice dell'Ambiente per la transazione ambientale) <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 735–736.</ref>;
# '''Contratti alternativi alla risoluzione giudiziale''' (che legittimano l'arbitrato e i meccanismi ADR nelle controversie di interesse pubblico) <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 736.</ref>;
# '''Contratti come fonti di regole giuridiche''' (riconoscendo l'efficacia normativa dei contratti collettivi di lavoro, degli statuti sportivi, dei codici deontologici e dei regolamenti condominiali nei confronti dei terzi) <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 736, 738.</ref>.

Lo studio propone il passaggio dal formalismo sussuntivo (*Begriffsjurisprudenz*) a un metodo decisionale assiologico orientato ai valori costituzionali e all'applicazione diretta dei principi costituzionali (''Drittwirkung'') <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 738, 741–742.</ref>.

== Basi Giuridiche ==
=== Diritto dell'Unione Europea ===
* '''[[Trattato sull'Unione Europea]] (TUE)''': Articolo 5 (Principio di Sussidiarietà) <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 732.</ref>.

=== Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana ===
* '''Articoli 3 e 23''': Allocazione delle risorse e giustizia distributiva <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 738.</ref>.
* '''Articoli 41 e 42''': Libertà di iniziativa economica privata e funzione sociale della proprietà <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 738.</ref>.
* '''Articolo 117, comma 2, lett. l''': Competenza legislativa esclusiva dello Stato in materia di *ordinamento civile* <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 734.</ref>.

=== Codici e Leggi Italiane ===
* '''Codice Civile''': Articolo 1372, comma 2 (Efficacia del contratto rispetto ai terzi) <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 738.</ref>; Articolo 1987 (Promesse unilaterali) <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 734.</ref>.

** ''Sentenze n. 228/2016, n. 6/2013, n. 77/2011, n. 41/2017'': Limiti del diritto privato regionale rispetto all'ordinamento civile <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 734.</ref>.
* '''Giurisprudenza Sovranazionale (CGUE)''': Causa C-353/06 (*Grunkin-Paul*); Causa C-148/02 (*Garcia Avello*); Causa C-219/91 (*Bellone c. Yokohama*) <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 732, 734.</ref>.

== Tre Nuove Frontiere della Libertà Contrattuale ==
# '''Contratti sostitutivi di provvedimenti amministrativi''': Gli accordi pubblico-privati sono qualificati come veri e propri contratti di diritto privato, soggetti ai rimedi civilistici quali i vizi del consenso, la responsabilità precontrattuale e il risarcimento del danno per inadempimento <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 735–736.</ref>.
# '''Contratti alternativi alla risoluzione giudiziale''': Estensione dell'autonomia negoziale alle convenzioni arbitrali e agli strumenti ADR aventi ad oggetto interessi pubblici <ref>Maisto (2021), p. 736.</ref>.
# '''Contratti come fonti di regole giuridiche''': Accordi privati capaci di generare vincoli normativi nei confronti dei terzi, derogando al principio di relatività del contratto (Art. 1372 co. 2 Cod. Civ.) per il perseguimento di interessi generali prevalenti <ref>Maisto (2021), pp. 736, 738.</ref>.

'''The Law of the Algorithmic State in Bulgaria Policy Framework''' (officially: ''Kerangka Kebijakan Hukum Negara Algoritmik, Otomasi Administrasi, dan Tata Kelola AI di Bulgaria'') is an administrative policy framework and judicial legal analysis formulated by Deyana Marcheva and Sylvia Tsoneva. It examines the legal basis, practical application, and regulatory gaps concerning algorithmic automation and artificial intelligence (AI) within public administration bodies in Bulgaria <ref>Marcheva, D., & Tsoneva, S. (2025). The Law of the Algorithmic State in Bulgaria. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 17(2), 529–563.</ref>.

The framework provides an analysis of the reduction of the "algorithmic state" to mere e-Government and ICT infrastructures <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 529, 532.</ref>, the general framework of e-Government (E-Government Act, RegiX, Open Data Portal, INSPIRE) <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 535, 543, 544.</ref>, sector-specific automation (such as electronic traffic tickets, National Revenue Agency tax audit systems, judicial SJC/AIS systems, AFIS, EURODAC, and the INSAIT BgGPT language model) <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 538, 548, 550, 558.</ref>, fundamental rights protection gaps in the Administrative Procedure Code <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 553, 556, 557.</ref>, and alignment with the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) and GDPR <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 529, 535, 554.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Authored by [[Deyana Marcheva]] and [[Sylvia Tsoneva]] (Associate Professors at New Bulgarian University), the framework presents a comprehensive mapping of public sector automation and AI integration in Bulgaria <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), p. 529.</ref>. The authors identify that Bulgarian administrative law lags behind in integrating human rights safeguards against automated decision-making <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 529, 553.</ref>.

Through an empirical survey under the Access to Public Information Act (APIA), the study reveals that public automation in Bulgaria is currently concentrated on general e-government infrastructure, automated traffic enforcement, and tax data digitalization, while the general administrative law lacks explicit recognition of human intervention standards <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 546, 548, 556, 558.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
The legal framework governing automation and AI in Bulgaria rests on European Union regulations and national legislation:
=== European Union Law ===
* '''[[EU Artificial Intelligence Act]] (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)''': EU harmonized rules on AI, fully applicable as of August 2026 <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 529, 530.</ref>.
* '''[[General Data Protection Regulation]] (Regulation (EU) 2016/679 / GDPR)''': Provides data protection principles and restricts automated decision-making without human oversight (Articles 22 & 35) <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 535, 554.</ref>.
* '''[[Open Data Directive]] (Directive (EU) 2019/1024)''' and '''[[INSPIRE Directive]] (Directive 2007/2/EC)'''.
* '''[[eIDAS Regulation]] (Regulation (EU) No 910/2014)'''.

=== National Legislation of Bulgaria ===
* '''[[E-Government Act 2007]] (EGA / Prom. SG. 46/2007)''': Governs electronic document exchange, public registries, and system interoperability <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 535, 536.</ref>.
* '''[[Administrative Procedure Code 2006]] (APC / Prom. SG. 30/2006)''': General administrative law, currently containing a regulatory gap regarding automated decisions <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), p. 556.</ref>.
* '''[[Protection of Personal Data Act 2002]] (PPDA / Prom. SG. 1/2002)''': Articles 52 (prohibition of sole automated legal decisions) and 64 (mandatory DPIA) <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 554, 555.</ref>.
* '''[[Road Traffic Act 1999]] (Prom. SG. 20/1999)''': Article 189 & § 1 p. 63 regulating electronic traffic ticket issuance <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 558, 559.</ref>.
* '''[[Labour Code 1986]] (2024 Amendment)''': Article 107h par. 11 & 12 governing algorithmic management in remote work <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 531, 555.</ref>.
* '''[[Judiciary Act 2007]]''', '''[[Cyber Security Act 2018]]''', and '''[[State and Municipal Liability for Damage Act 1988]]'''.

== Background & E-Government Perception ==
The deployment of AI and algorithms in Bulgaria has developed within public digital transformation strategies <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 531, 535.</ref>. Under the ''Concept for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in Bulgaria until 2030'', the government established an AI vision aligned with EU policies <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 531, 532.</ref>. However, administrative practice has largely reduced the "algorithmic state" to e-Government infrastructure (such as the RegiX inter-registry system and government cloud systems), neglecting the human rights implications of automated decisions <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 529, 543, 553.</ref>.

== Key Objectives ==
* Establish a transparent, inclusive, and accountable legal administrative framework for AI and public automation <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), p. 562.</ref>.
* Ensure Bulgarian public authorities comply with the EU AI Act and GDPR frameworks <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 529, 554.</ref>.
* Guarantee citizens' right to human involvement and meaningful explanations regarding automated administrative acts <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 554, 556.</ref>.

== Scope & Application ==
The policy scope encompasses digital administrative law, RegiX data exchange infrastructure, automated tax audit processes at the National Revenue Agency (NRA), police biometric automation (AFIS/EURODAC), electronic traffic enforcement, deployment of the [[INSAIT]] BgGPT Bulgarian language model, and judicial case law <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 529–563.</ref>.

== Key Legal Findings & Case Law ==
* '''Lack of Human Intervention Standard in APC''': The Bulgarian APC contains no general rules acknowledging output from automated systems, nor does it mandate human intervention when automated systems issue binding decisions <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), p. 556.</ref>.
* '''Electronic Traffic Tickets as Machine Statements''': Electronic tickets are machine-generated without human administrative intervention or official signatures <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 558, 559.</ref>.
* '''SAC Interpretative Decision No. 1/2014''': The Supreme Administrative Court ruled that short-track electronic ticketing is lawful only when infractions are captured by stationary automated devices <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 559, 560.</ref>.
* '''BgGPT Open Language Model''': The INSAIT institute integrated the open-source BgGPT model (Mistral-7B) for adoption by the National Revenue Agency and municipal services <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 550, 551.</ref>.

== Policy Issues & "Black Box Administration" ==
* '''Risk of Administrative Arbitrariness''': The absence of algorithm disclosure obligations and the non-recognition of code as an administrative document risks creating a "black box administration" <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 556, 557.</ref>.
* '''Police & Law Enforcement Secrecy''': AI and biometric usage by police forces is classified, impeding public scrutiny and legal redress <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 546, 557.</ref>.

== Entity Relationships & Focus Entities Status ==
* '''[[Deyana Marcheva]]''': Primary Author / Associate Professor at New Bulgarian University <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), p. 529.</ref>.
* '''[[Sylvia Tsoneva]]''': Primary Author / Associate Professor at New Bulgarian University <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), p. 529.</ref>.
* '''[[INSAIT]]''': Bulgarian AI Research Institute, developer of BgGPT <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), p. 550.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available source documents.]]'' <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 529–563.</ref>

Il '''Quadro di Politica Giuridica sullo Stato Algoritmico, l'Automazione Amministrativa e la Governance dell'IA in Bulgaria''' (ufficialmente in lingua inglese: ''The Law of the Algorithmic State in Bulgaria Policy Framework'') è un quadro di politica amministrativa e un'analisi giuridica formulata da Deyana Marcheva e Sylvia Tsoneva per esaminare i fondamenti giuridici, l'uso pratico e le lacune normative relative all'automazione algoritmica e all'intelligenza artificiale (IA) da parte della pubblica amministrazione in Bulgaria <ref>Marcheva, D., & Tsoneva, S. (2025). The Law of the Algorithmic State in Bulgaria. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 17(2), 529–563.</ref>.

Il quadro analizza la riduzione dello "stato algoritmico" a mera infrastruttura di e-Government e ICT <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 529, 532.</ref>, il quadro generale del governo elettronico (E-Government Act, RegiX, Portale Open Data, INSPIRE) <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 535, 543, 544.</ref>, l'automazione nei settori specifici (come le sanzioni stradali elettroniche, l'Agenzia Nazionale delle Entrate, i sistemi giudiziari SJC/AIS, AFIS, EURODAC e il modello linguistico INSAIT BgGPT) <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 538, 548, 550, 558.</ref>, le lacune di tutela dei diritti fondamentali nel Codice di Procedura Amministrativa <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 553, 556, 557.</ref>, nonché l'allineamento con il Regolamento Europeo sull'IA (EU AI Act / Regolamento (UE) 2024/1689) e il GDPR <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 529, 535, 554.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Scritto da [[Deyana Marcheva]] e [[Sylvia Tsoneva]] (Professoresse Associate presso la New Bulgarian University), lo studio presenta una mappatura completa dell'automazione pubblica e dell'integrazione dell'IA in Bulgaria <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), p. 529.</ref>. Le autrici evidenziano che il diritto amministrativo bulgaro è in ritardo nell'integrare le garanzie dei diritti umani contro le decisioni automatizzate <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 529, 553.</ref>.

Attraverso un'indagine empirica condotta ai sensi dell'Access to Public Information Act (APIA), lo studio rivela che l'automazione pubblica in Bulgaria è attualmente concentrata sull'e-government, sul sanzionamento stradale automatizzato e sulla digitalizzazione fiscale, mentre il diritto amministrativo generale è privo di standard normativi sull'intervento umano (*human intervention*) <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 546, 548, 556, 558.</ref>.

== Base Giuridica ==
Il quadro giuridico dell'automazione e dell'IA in Bulgaria si fonda sulla normativa dell'Unione Europea e sulla legislazione nazionale bulgara:
=== Diritto dell'Unione Europea ===
* '''[[EU Artificial Intelligence Act]] (Regolamento (UE) 2024/1689)''': Regolamento armonizzato sull'IA, pienamente applicabile ad agosto 2026 <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 529, 530.</ref>.
* '''[[General Data Protection Regulation]] (Regolamento (UE) 2016/679 / GDPR)''': Principi sulla protezione dei dati e divieto di decisioni automatizzate prive di intervento umano (Articoli 22 e 35) <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 535, 554.</ref>.
* '''[[Direttiva Open Data]] (Direttiva (UE) 2019/1024)''' e '''[[Direttiva INSPIRE]] (Direttiva 2007/2/CE)'''.
* '''[[Regolamento eIDAS]] (Regolamento (UE) n. 910/2014)'''.

=== Legislazione Nazionale Bulgara ===
* '''[[Legge sul Governo Elettronico 2007]] (EGA / Prom. SG. 46/2007)''': Regola lo scambio di documenti elettronici, i registri pubblici e l'interoperabilità dei sistemi <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 535, 536.</ref>.
* '''[[Codice di Procedura Amministrativa 2006]] (APC / Prom. SG. 30/2006)''': Legge procedurale generale, attualmente affetta da una lacuna normativa riguardante le decisioni automatizzate <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), p. 556.</ref>.
* '''[[Legge sulla Protezione dei Dati Personali 2002]] (PPDA / Prom. SG. 1/2002)''': Articoli 52 (divieto di decisioni giuridiche uniche automatizzate) e 64 (obbligo di DPIA) <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 554, 555.</ref>.
* '''[[Legge sulla Circolazione Stradale 1999]] (Prom. SG. 20/1999)''': Articolo 189 & § 1 p. 63 per l'emissione automatizzata di verbali elettronici <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 558, 559.</ref>.
* '''[[Codice del Lavoro 1986]] (Emendamento 2024)''': Articolo 107h par. 11 & 12 sulla gestione algoritmica nel lavoro a distanza <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 531, 555.</ref>.

== Contesto e Percezione dell'E-Government ==
L'adozione dell'IA e degli algoritmi in Bulgaria si è sviluppata all'interno delle strategie di trasformazione digitale della pubblica amministrazione <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 531, 535.</ref>. Nella ''Concept for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in Bulgaria until 2030'', il governo ha fissato una visione conforme al quadro europeo <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 531, 532.</ref>. Tuttavia, la prassi amministrativa ha ridotto lo "stato algoritmico" alla sola infrastruttura di e-Government (come la piattaforma RegiX e il cloud statale), trascurando la valutazione dell'impatto delle decisioni automatizzate sui diritti fondamentali dei cittadini <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 529, 543, 553.</ref>.

== Obiettivi Principali ==
* Creare un quadro giuridico amministrativo trasparente, inclusivo e responsabile per l'uso dell'IA e dell'automazione <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), p. 562.</ref>.
* Garantire la conformità delle autorità pubbliche bulgare all'EU AI Act e al GDPR <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 529, 554.</ref>.
* Garantire ai cittadini il diritto all'intervento umano (*right to human involvement*) e alla spiegazione dei provvedimenti amministrativi automatizzati <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 554, 556.</ref>.

== Ambito e Applicazione ==
L'ambito di applicazione comprende il diritto amministrativo digitale, la piattaforma di interoperabilità RegiX, i processi di verifica fiscale dell'Agenzia Nazionale delle Entrate (NRA), l'automazione biometrica delle forze dell'ordine (AFIS/EURODAC), i verbali stradali elettronici, l'uso del modello linguistico bulgaro [[INSAIT]] BgGPT e la giurisprudenza amministrativa <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 529–563.</ref>.

== Principi Giuridici e Giurisprudenza ==
* '''Assenza di Standard sull'Intervento Umano nell'APC''': Il Codice di Procedura Amministrativa bulgaro non disciplina l'uso dei sistemi automatizzati e non impone l'intervento umano quando il sistema emette atti vincolanti <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), p. 556.</ref>.
* '''Dichiarazioni di Macchina e Verbali Elettronici''': I verbali elettronici sono generati automaticamente dal sistema senza l'intervento diretto o la firma di un funzionario <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 558, 559.</ref>.
* '''Decisione Interpretativa della Corte Suprema Amministrativa n. 1/2014''': La Corte ha stabilito che la procedura sanzionatoria abbreviata per verbale elettronico è legittima solo se l'infrazione è rilevata da dispositivi automatici stazionari <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 559, 560.</ref>.
* '''Modello Linguistico BgGPT''': L'istituto INSAIT ha sviluppato il modello open-source BgGPT (basato su Mistral-7B) destinato all'uso da parte dell'Agenzia delle Entrate e dei comuni <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 550, 551.</ref>.

== Criticità di Politica e "Black Box Administration" ==
* '''Rischio di Arbitrio Amministrativo''': La mancanza di obblighi di trasparenza sugli algoritmi e il mancato riconoscimento del codice sorgente come documento amministrativo rischiano di creare una "amministrazione scatola nera" (*black box administration*) <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 556, 557.</ref>.
* '''Segretezza nei Settori di Polizia''': L'uso di IA e biometria da parte delle forze dell'ordine è classificato come informazione riservata, limitando il controllo pubblico e i rimedi giurisdizionali <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 546, 557.</ref>.

== Relazioni tra Entità e Stato delle Entità di Focus ==
* '''[[Deyana Marcheva]]''': Autrice principale / Professoressa Associata presso la New Bulgarian University <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), p. 529.</ref>.
* '''[[Sylvia Tsoneva]]''': Autrice principale / Professoressa Associata presso la New Bulgarian University <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), p. 529.</ref>.
* '''[[INSAIT]]''': Istituto bulgaro di ricerca sull'IA, sviluppatore di BgGPT <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), p. 550.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Non presente nelle fonti disponibili.]]'' <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 529–563.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Non presente nelle fonti disponibili.]]'' <ref>Marcheva & Tsoneva (2025), pp. 529–563.</ref>

| legal_basis = Organic Law No. 2009-1523 (France); Special Law of 6 Jan 1989 (Belgium); B-VG Art. 140 (Austria); Grundgesetz Art. 100.1 (Germany); Constitución Española Art. 93; Art. 267 TFEU
| date = 2023 (Publication in Italian Journal of Public Law Vol. 15 Issue 1)

}}

'''Comparative Dual Preliminarity Judicial Policy Framework''' (''Doktrin dan Kerangka Kebijakan Peradilan Dual Preliminarity dalam Hukum Komparatif'') is a comparative legal analysis framework formulated by Giuseppe Martinico to examine the phenomenon of dual preliminarity (*doppia pregiudizialità*), a situation in which doubts regarding the constitutional legitimacy (*question of constitutional legitimacy*) and conformity with European Union law (*conformity with EU law*) of the same national legal provision are raised simultaneously in judicial proceedings <ref>Martinico, G. (2023). Dual Preliminarity in Comparative Law. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 15(1), 121–138.</ref>. The framework maps priority mechanisms (*priority criteria*) among apex courts through two legal formants (*legal formants*): the *legislative formant* (France and Belgium) and the *judicial formant* (Austria, Germany, and Spain), alongside an analysis of interpretative competition (*interpretative competition*) and judicial dialogue <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 121, 123, 124, 130.</ref>.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Giuseppe Martinico]] (Full Professor of Comparative Public Law at Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna Pisa), this work presents a comparative analysis of dual preliminarity across five EU Member States (France, Belgium, Austria, Germany, and Spain) and offers comparison with Italy <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 121, 123.</ref>. The author investigates how national constitutional courts and the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) manage competing interpretations over fundamental rights <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 123, 133, 137.</ref>. The study highlights the landmark *Melki* jurisprudence (Cases C-188/10 & C-189/10) as a guiding framework that preserves the effectiveness of EU law without invalidating national constitutional review <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 125–129, 137.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
The dual preliminarity judicial policy framework is grounded in national statutory instruments and supranational jurisprudence:
* '''[[France]]''': *Organic Law No. 2009-1523* amending *Ordonnance No. 58-1067* (Articles 23-2 and 23-5) introducing the Priority Question of Constitutionality (*Question Prioritaire de Constitutionnalité* / QPC) <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 124, 125.</ref>.
* '''[[Belgium]]''': *Special Law of 6 January 1989 on the Cour d'Arbitrage* (Article 26, as amended in 2009) <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 129.</ref>.
* '''[[Austria]]''': Article 140 of the Federal Constitutional Law (*Bundes-Verfassungsgesetz* / B-VG) and *Verfassungsgerichtshof* Jurisprudence (Judgments U 466/11 & U 1836/11) <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 130, 131.</ref>.
* '''[[Germany]]''': Article 100.1 of the Basic Law (*Grundgesetz*) and *Bundesverfassungsgericht* Jurisprudence (Decision 1 BvL 3/08 and *Right to be Forgotten* cases) <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 135.</ref>.
* '''[[Spain]]''': Articles 93, 96.1, and 10.2 of the Spanish Constitution (*Constitución Española*) and *Tribunal Constitucional* Jurisprudence (Auto 168/2016) <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 135, 136.</ref>.
* '''[[European Union Law]]''': Article 267 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) and CJEU Jurisprudence (*Simmenthal* Case 106/77; *Melki* Cases C-188/10 & C-189/10; *Chartry* Case C-457/09; *A v B* Case C-112/13) <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 123, 125, 128, 129, 131.</ref>.

== Background & Interpretative Competition ==
National judges in Europe operate within a multilevel legal order that entails multiple loyalties <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 121.</ref>. Following the binding application of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights (CFR), an interpretative competition (*inter-court competition*) emerged between national constitutional courts and the CJEU over the monopoly of interpreting equivalent norms <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 123, 133.</ref>. The phenomenon of dual preliminarity represents a central arena for resolving priority rules between constitutional review and EU law preliminary references <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 123, 124.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Map solutions to dual preliminarity tensions in Europe based on the distinction between the *legislative formant* and the *judicial formant* <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 121, 124.</ref>.
* Ensure that national priority constitutional review procedures do not compromise the supremacy and immediate applicability of EU law <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 125, 128, 137.</ref>.
* Identify the function of EU law as a shield to preserve judicial independence against risks of *judicial capture* <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 138.</ref>.

== Scope ==
The scope of this policy framework encompasses comparative constitutional law in France, Belgium, Austria, Germany, Spain, and Italy, CJEU preliminary reference procedures, application of the CFR versus the ECHR, and national constitutional court review mechanisms <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 121–138.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & The Melki Criteria ==
* '''Legal Formants''':
** *Legislative Formant*: France and Belgium established priority constitutional review mechanisms through statutory legislation <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 121, 124, 129.</ref>.
** *Judicial Formant*: Austria, Germany, and Spain addressed priority relationships through constitutional court case law <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 121, 130, 135.</ref>.
* '''Melki Guidance (CJEU Cases C-188/10 & C-189/10)''': The CJEU established that Article 267 TFEU does not preclude national priority constitutional review procedures, PROVIDED ordinary courts remain free to:
# Submit preliminary references to the CJEU at any stage of the proceedings <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 128.</ref>.
# Adopt any measure necessary to guarantee provisional judicial protection <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 128.</ref>.
# Disapply national statutory provisions incompatible with EU law at the conclusion of the procedure <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 128.</ref>.

== Policy Issues & Shield Against Judicial Capture ==
* '''Melki Doctrine as a Democratic Shield''': In the context of rule-of-law crises in Poland (*Rzecznik Praw Obywatelskich*, C-521/21) and Romania (*Euro Box Promotion*, C-357/19), the *Melki* doctrine enabled ordinary judges to maintain preliminary references to the CJEU when national constitutional courts experienced political capture <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 138.</ref>.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''[[Giuseppe Martinico]]''': Lead Author and Full Professor at Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna Pisa <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 121.</ref>.
* '''[[Court of Justice of the European Union]] (CJEU)''': Supranational Court of the European Union <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 123, 125.</ref>.
* '''[[Conseil Constitutionnel]]''': Constitutional Council of France <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 124, 125.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 121–138.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 121–138.</ref>

'''Quadro di Politica Giudiziaria sulla Doppia Pregiudizialità nel Diritto Comparato''' (''Comparative Dual Preliminarity Judicial Policy Framework'') è un quadro di analisi giuscomparatistica formulato da Giuseppe Martinico per esaminare il fenomeno della *doppia pregiudizialità* (*dual preliminarity*), ossia la situazione in cui i dubbi sulla legittimità costituzionale (*question of constitutional legitimacy*) e sulla conformità al diritto dell'Unione Europea (*conformity with EU law*) di una medesima disposizione nazionale sorgono contemporaneamente all'interno di un processo giudiziario <ref>Martinico, G. (2023). Dual Preliminarity in Comparative Law. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 15(1), 121–138.</ref>. Il quadro mappa i meccanismi di priorità (*priority criteria*) tra le corti supreme attraverso due formanti giuridici (*legal formants*): il *legislative formant* (Francia e Belgio) e il *judicial formant* (Austria, Germania e Spagna), unitamente all'analisi della competizione interpretativa (*interpretative competition*) e del dialogo giurisdizionale <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 121, 123, 124, 130.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Redatto da [[Giuseppe Martinico]] (Professore Ordinario di Diritto Pubblico Comparato presso la Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna di Pisa), lo studio presenta un'analisi comparativa della doppia pregiudizialità in cinque Stati membri dell'UE (Francia, Belgio, Austria, Germania e Spagna) offrendo un confronto con l'Italia <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 121, 123.</ref>. L'autore analizza come le corti costituzionali nazionali e la Corte di Giustizia dell'Unione Europea (CGUE) gestiscano la competizione interpretativa sui diritti fondamentali <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 123, 133, 137.</ref>. La ricerca evidenzia la fondamentale giurisprudenza *Melki* (Cause C-188/10 e C-189/10) quale modello guida per preservare l'efficacia del diritto UE senza annullare il controllo di costituzionalità nazionale <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 125–129, 137.</ref>.

== Basi Giuridiche ==
Il quadro politico-giuridico sulla doppia pregiudizialità si fonda su fonti legislative nazionali e sulla giurisprudenza sovranazionale:
* '''[[Francia]]''': *Legge Organica N. 2009-1523* che modifica l'*Ordonnance N. 58-1067* (Articoli 23-2 e 23-5) introducendo la Question Prioritaire de Constitutionnalité (QPC) <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 124, 125.</ref>.
* '''[[Belgio]]''': *Legge Speciale del 6 gennaio 1989 sulla Cour d'Arbitrage* (Articolo 26, modificato nel 2009) <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 129.</ref>.
* '''[[Austria]]''': Articolo 140 della Legge Costituzionale Federale (*Bundes-Verfassungsgesetz* / B-VG) e Giurisprudenza del *Verfassungsgerichtshof* (Sentenze U 466/11 e U 1836/11) <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 130, 131.</ref>.
* '''[[Germania]]''': Articolo 100.1 della Legge Fondamentale (*Grundgesetz*) e Giurisprudenza del *Bundesverfassungsgericht* (Decisione 1 BvL 3/08 e casi sul *Diritto all'Oblio*) <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 135.</ref>.
* '''[[Spagna]]''': Articoli 93, 96.1 e 10.2 della Costituzione Spagnola (*Constitución Española*) e Giurisprudenza del *Tribunal Constitucional* (Auto 168/2016) <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 135, 136.</ref>.
* '''[[Diritto dell'Unione Europea]]''': Articolo 267 del Trattato sul Funzionamento dell'Unione Europea (TFUE) e Giurisprudenza della CGUE (*Simmenthal* Causa 106/77; *Melki* Cause C-188/10 e C-189/10; *Chartry* Causa C-457/09; *A v B* Causa C-112/13) <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 123, 125, 128, 129, 131.</ref>.

== Contesto e Competizione Interpretativa ==
I giudici nazionali in Europa operano all'interno di un ordine giuridico multilivello che comporta lealtà multiple <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 121.</ref>. In seguito al valore vincolante della Carta dei Diritti Fondamentali dell'UE (CDFUE), è emersa una competizione interpretativa (*inter-court competition*) tra le corti costituzionali nazionali e la CGUE per il monopolio interpretativo di norme equivalenti <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 123, 133.</ref>. Il fenomeno della doppia pregiudizialità costituisce un'arena centrale per la risoluzione delle regole di priorità tra controllo di costituzionalità e rinvio pregiudiziale UE <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 123, 124.</ref>.

== Obiettivi ==
* Mappare le soluzioni alle tensioni da doppia pregiudizialità in Europa sulla base della distinzione tra *formante legislativo* e *formante giurisprudenziale* <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 121, 124.</ref>.
* Garantire che le procedure nazionali d'esame incidente di costituzionalità non compromettano il primato e la diretta applicabilità del diritto UE <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 125, 128, 137.</ref>.
* Individuare la funzione del diritto UE quale scudo per la tutela dell'indipendenza dei giudici rispetto a rischi di *judicial capture* <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 138.</ref>.

== Ambito di Applicazione ==
L'ambito di applicazione di questo quadro include il diritto costituzionale comparato in Francia, Belgio, Austria, Germania, Spagna e Italia, la procedura di rinvio pregiudiziale dinanzi alla CGUE, l'applicazione della CDFUE rispetto alla CEDU e i meccanismi di controllo delle corti costituzionali nazionali <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 121–138.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Chiave e i Criteri Melki ==
* '''Formanti Giuridici (Legal Formants)''':
** *Formante Legislativo*: Francia e Belgio hanno introdotto meccanismi di priorità del controllo di costituzionalità mediante fonti legislative <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 121, 124, 129.</ref>.
** *Formante Giurisprudenziale*: Austria, Germania e Spagna hanno regolato i rapporti di priorità attraverso l'elaborazione giurisprudenziale delle rispettive corti costituzionali <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 121, 130, 135.</ref>.
* '''Orientamento Melki (CGUE Cause C-188/10 e C-189/10)''': La CGUE ha stabilito che l'Articolo 267 TFUE non osta a procedure nazionali di controllo prioritario di costituzionalità, A CONDIZIONE CHE i giudici ordinari rimangano liberi di:
# Sottoporre rinvii pregiudiziali alla CGUE in qualsiasi fase del processo <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 128.</ref>.
# Adottare qualsiasi misura necessaria per garantire la tutela giurisdizionale provvisoria <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 128.</ref>.
# Disapplicare la disposizione nazionale contrastante con il diritto UE al termine della procedura <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 128.</ref>.

== Profili Politico-Giuridici e Protezione contro la Cattura Giudiziaria ==
* '''Dottrina Melki come Scudo Democratico''': Nel contesto delle crisi dello Stato di diritto in Polonia (*Rzecznik Praw Obywatelskich*, C-521/21) e Romania (*Euro Box Promotion*, C-357/19), la dottrina *Melki* ha consentito ai giudici ordinari di formulare rinvii pregiudiziali alla CGUE anche a fronte di corti costituzionali nazionali soggette a cattura politica (*judicial capture*) <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 138.</ref>.

== Relazioni con Altre Entità ==
* '''[[Giuseppe Martinico]]''': Autore Principale e Professore Ordinario presso la Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna di Pisa <ref>Martinico (2023), p. 121.</ref>.
* '''[[Corte di Giustizia dell'Unione Europea]] (CGUE)''': Corte Sovranazionale dell'Unione Europea <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 123, 125.</ref>.
* '''[[Conseil Constitutionnel]]''': Consiglio Costituzionale della Repubblica Francese <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 124, 125.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Non presente nelle fonti disponibili.]]'' <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 121–138.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Non presente nelle fonti disponibili.]]'' <ref>Martinico (2023), pp. 121–138.</ref>

'''Participation in Rulemaking in Italy''' (Indonesian title: ''Kerangka Kebijakan Partisipasi Masyarakat dalam Pembentukan Peraturan Administrasi di Italia'') is an administrative law analytical framework formulated by Bernardo Giorgio Mattarella to examine the legal regime and practical implementation of public participation in administrative rulemaking (*regolamenti*) and general administrative acts (*atti amministrativi generali*) in Italy; evaluate the explicit exemption of rulemaking from the Italian Administrative Procedure Act (*Law 241/1990*); distinguish between procedural, informal, and organic participation; and critique governmental escape strategies achieved through detailed technical statutes, emergency orders (*ordinanze di urgenza*), and privatization <ref>Mattarella, B.G. (2010). Participation in Rulemaking in Italy. *Workshop Participation in Rulemaking in Europe*, Osnabrück, 339–352.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Authored by [[Bernardo Giorgio Mattarella]] (Professor of Administrative Law at the University of Siena), this study provides a comprehensive mapping of the structural limitations surrounding public participation in Italian administrative rulemaking <ref>Mattarella (2010), p. 339.</ref>. Under traditional Italian administrative doctrine, public participation in rulemaking is not recognized as a general principle, as *Law 241/1990* explicitly excludes the enactment of regulations and general administrative acts from statutory information and consultation rights <ref>Mattarella (2010), p. 341.</ref>. Nevertheless, participatory procedures such as notice and comment and Regulatory Impact Assessment (*RIA*) have expanded significantly at the regional level (e.g., Tuscany) and within independent regulatory authorities (e.g., Bank of Italy, Consob, Energy, and Telecommunications) <ref>Mattarella (2010), pp. 341, 343.</ref>. The author highlights a growing gap between theory and practice: while formal mechanisms are expanding in specific sectors, executive authorities frequently bypass administrative procedure requirements through statutory inflation (enacting detailed primary legislation) and emergency orders (*ordinanze di urgenza*) <ref>Mattarella (2010), pp. 346, 350, 351.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''[[Law 241/1990]] (Italian Administrative Procedure Act)''': Governs participation rights for individual administrative decisions, but explicitly exempts administrative regulations and general administrative acts <ref>Mattarella (2010), p. 341.</ref>.
* '''[[Law 262/2005]] (Savings Protection & Financial Regulation Law)''': Mandates transparency, notice and comment procedures, and RIA for the Bank of Italy and Consob <ref>Mattarella (2010), p. 343.</ref>.
* '''[[Constitution of Italy]]''': Provisions on regulatory authority distribution post-2001 Title V reform <ref>Mattarella (2010), p. 341.</ref>; constitutional guarantee of unrestricted judicial review against administrative acts <ref>Mattarella (2010), pp. 339, 340.</ref>.
* '''Regional & Sectoral Legislation''': Tuscany Regional Law 2007 (establishing public participation protection authorities and *débat public*) <ref>Mattarella (2010), pp. 341, 342.</ref>; Urban Planning Law of 1942 (statutory right to submit objections / *osservazioni*) <ref>Mattarella (2010), p. 342.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & Classification of Participation ==
1. '''Statutory Exclusions in Law 241/1990''': Administrative participation in Italian legal tradition is primarily conceived as a defensive mechanism to protect individual rights (*defensive tool*) rather than a direct democratic instrument for policy drafting <ref>Mattarella (2010), pp. 341, 346.</ref>.
2. '''Procedural vs. Informal vs. Organic Participation''':
* *Procedural*: Open notice and comment procedures initiated by independent regulatory agencies <ref>Mattarella (2010), p. 343.</ref>.
* *Informal*: Unregulated back-channel negotiations between government officials and trade unions or industry associations, creating risks of corruption and unequal access <ref>Mattarella (2010), pp. 344, 345.</ref>.
* *Organic*: Appointment of professional interest group representatives (lawyers, doctors, engineers) directly to administrative boards <ref>Mattarella (2010), p. 345.</ref>.
3. '''Legal Escape Strategies''': Government reliance on primary statutory legislation and emergency decrees (*ordinanze di urgenza*) to enact detailed administrative rules while bypassing open administrative procedures <ref>Mattarella (2010), pp. 350, 351.</ref>.

'''Participation in Rulemaking in Italy''' (titolo indonesiano: ''Kerangka Kebijakan Partisipasi Masyarakat dalam Pembentukan Peraturan Administrasi di Italia'') è un quadro analitico di diritto amministrativo formulato da Bernardo Giorgio Mattarella per esaminare il regime giuridico e la prassi applicativa della partecipazione del pubblico alla formazione degli atti normativi amministrativi (*rulemaking / regolamenti*) e degli atti amministrativi generali in Italia; valutare l'esclusione esplicita del *rulemaking* dalla Legge sul Procedimento Amministrativo (*Legge 241/1990*); distinguere tra partecipazione procedimentale, informale e organica; e criticare le strategie di evasione o fuga (*escape strategies*) del governo attraverso leggi dettagliate, ordinanze di urgenza e privatizzazioni <ref>Mattarella, B.G. (2010). Participation in Rulemaking in Italy. *Workshop Participation in Rulemaking in Europe*, Osnabrück, 339–352.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Redatto da [[Bernardo Giorgio Mattarella]] (Professore Ordinario di Diritto Amministrativo presso l'Università degli Studi di Siena), lo studio offre una ricognizione organica dei limiti della partecipazione pubblica alla funzione regolamentare in Italia <ref>Mattarella (2010), p. 339.</ref>. Tradizionalmente, il diritto amministrativo italiano non riconosce la partecipazione al *rulemaking* come principio generale, in quanto la *Legge 241/1990* esclude espressamente l'adozione di atti normativi e amministrativi generali dalle garanzie di partecipazione e trasparenza <ref>Mattarella (2010), p. 341.</ref>. Tuttavia, istituti quali il *notice and comment* e l'Analisi di Impatto della Regolamentazione (*AIR / RIA*) si sono sviluppati ampiamente a livello regionale (es. Regione Toscana) e presso le Autorità Indipendenti (es. Banca d'Italia, Consob, ARERA, AGCOM) <ref>Mattarella (2010), pp. 341, 343.</ref>. L'autore evidenzia il paradosso per cui, a fronte dell'espansione dei meccanismi partecipativi in specifici settori, l'amministrazione pubblica ricorre frequentemente a strategie di elusione del procedimento amministrativo mediante l'ipertrofia legislativa (leggi-provvedimento) e l'uso improprio delle ordinanze di urgenza <ref>Mattarella (2010), pp. 346, 350, 351.</ref>.

== Basi Giuridiche ==
* '''[[Legge 241/1990]] (Legge sul Procedimento Amministrativo)''': Disciplina la partecipazione al procedimento per provvedimenti individuali, ma esclude espressamente l'attività diretta all'emanazione di atti normativi e generali <ref>Mattarella (2010), p. 341.</ref>.
* '''[[Legge 262/2005]] (Legge sulla Tutela del Risparmio)''': Impone obblighi di consultazione pubblica (*notice and comment*) e Analisi di Impatto della Regolamentazione per Banca d'Italia e Consob <ref>Mattarella (2010), p. 343.</ref>.
* '''[[Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana]]''': Riparto della potestà regolamentare tra Stato ed Enti Territoriali ex art. 117 post-riforma 2001 <ref>Mattarella (2010), p. 341.</ref>; garanzia della tutela giurisdizionale contro gli atti della P.A. ex art. 113 <ref>Mattarella (2010), pp. 339, 340.</ref>.
* '''Leggi Regionali e Settoriali''': Legge Regionale Toscana n. 69/2007 (promozione della partecipazione e *débat public*) <ref>Mattarella (2010), pp. 341, 342.</ref>; Legge Urbanistica del 1942 (presentazione di osservazioni ed opposizioni) <ref>Mattarella (2010), p. 342.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Chiave e Classificazione della Partecipazione ==
1. '''Esclusione Statutaria ex Legge 241/1990''': La partecipazione nel diritto amministrativo italiano è storicamente concepita come strumento di difesa del privato di fronte all'esercizio del potere (*defensive tool*), anziché come garanzia democratica di condivisione delle scelte generali <ref>Mattarella (2010), pp. 341, 346.</ref>.
2. '''Partecipazione Procedimentale vs. Informale vs. Organica''':
* *Procedimentale*: Consultazioni pubbliche trasparenti avviate dalle Autorità Indipendenti <ref>Mattarella (2010), p. 343.</ref>.
* *Informale*: Trattative riservate tra governo, sindacati e associazioni di categoria con rischi di opacità e disparità di trattamento <ref>Mattarella (2010), pp. 344, 345.</ref>.
* *Organica*: Presenza di rappresentanti degli ordini professionali negli organi collegiali delle istituzioni pubbliche <ref>Mattarella (2010), p. 345.</ref>.
3. '''Strategie di Fuga dal Procedimento (Escape Strategies)''': Impiego di leggi dettagliate e ordinanze contingibili e urgenti da parte dell'esecutivo per disciplinare materie amministrative senza adempiere alle garanzie procedimentali <ref>Mattarella (2010), pp. 350, 351.</ref>.

{{Infobox|stable_id=judicial-policy-mcdonnell-youthwings-2025|name=Young radicals, moderates and aligned: Ideological congruence and incongruence in party youth wings|type=Comparative Political Research Paper & Party Organization Study|issuing_authority=Duncan McDonnell et al. / Griffith University / EJPR|legal_basis=Not found in the available sources.|date=2025|status=Published / Active}}

'''Young radicals, moderates and aligned: Ideological congruence and incongruence in party youth wings''' is a comparative empirical research paper authored by Duncan McDonnell (Griffith University) together with an international research team, published in the ''European Journal of Political Research'' (EJPR) in 2025 [1–2].

== Summary ==
This study examines the ideological relationship between party youth wing members and senior party leaderships. Analyzing survey data from the YOUMEM project covering 4,679 members across 12 party youth wings in six Western countries (Australia, Austria, Germany, Italy, Spain, and Sweden), the study proposes a tripartite typology: *radicals* (members who place themselves more extreme than the party), *moderates* (members more moderate than the party), and *aligned* (members who match the party). The findings show that radicals make up a majority of members (58.3%), but their proportion is far higher in centre-left youth wings than in centre-right ones.

== Legal Basis ==

* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This document is an academic political science research study and is not established under any statutory or judicial legislative instrument [1–106].

== Background ==
Since the classic literature of Ostrogorski, Michels, and Duverger through to May (1973), grassroots members — particularly youth wing members — have been regarded as the most ideologically pure and radical group compared to pragmatic party elites. However, previous research had not distinguished the *direction* of incongruence, nor the socialization factors that shape it.

== Objectives ==
1. Propose a new typology of ideological congruence (*radicals*, *moderates*, *aligned*). 2. Test the effect of membership length on radicalism (Hypothesis 1a/1b). 3. Test the impact of political career ambitions (office-seeking) on ideological alignment (Hypothesis 2) [20–21]. 4. Analyze ideological differences between centre-left and centre-right youth wings (Hypothesis 3) [21–22]. 5. Measure the effect of a senior party's government vs. opposition status on member perceptions (Hypothesis 4) [22–25].

== Scope ==
The research covers 12 youth wings of major parties in 6 countries: Australia (AYL, YL), Austria (SJÖ, JVP), Germany (Jusos, JU), Italy (GD, FIG), Spain (JSE, NNGG), and Sweden (SSU, MUF) [25, 29–33].

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Congruence Typology:''' Calculated from the mathematical difference between respondents' self-placement and their placement of the senior party on a 1–10 left-right scale.
* '''Group Proportions:''' *Radicals* make up 58.3%, *Aligned* 25.3%, and *Moderates* 16.5%.
* '''Centre-Left Radical Dominance (Hypothesis 3 Supported):''' Centre-left youth members have a much higher probability of being radical (~75%) compared to centre-right (<50%) (p < 0.001) [50–52, 57]. Austria's SJÖ has the highest proportion of radicals (90.5%).
* '''Role of Political Ambition (Hypothesis 2 Partially Supported):''' Members who aspire to stand for office are more likely to be aligned than radical [50–52, 55].
* '''Effect of Membership Length (Hypothesis 1a Partially Supported):''' The longer someone has been a member, the higher their probability of being radical rather than aligned, due to intensive socialization within peer circles [48, 50–52, 54].
* '''Government Status (Hypothesis 4 Not Supported):''' The senior party's government/opposition status did not significantly affect members' ideological alignment [50–51, 58].

== Implementation ==
The methodology was implemented through online surveys via LimeSurvey and Qualtrics (2018–2022), multinomial logistic regression estimation with country-clustered standard errors, and extensive robustness testing [25–26, 47, 50–52, 65–69]. Data is publicly deposited on Harvard Dataverse.

== Policy Problems ==
1. Internal tension between radical youth members and party leaders pursuing median voters. 2. The risk of member dissatisfaction leading to inactivity or exit from the party. 3. Obstacles to recruiting electoral candidates who align with the official party platform.

== Reform / Change ==
Rejects the thesis that grassroots members have become passive or homogeneous, demonstrating instead that internal ideological dynamics remain characterized by friction between radical youth and pragmatic elites [72–73].

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''Griffith University & ECPR:''' The authors' institution and the publisher.
* '''Harvard Dataverse:''' Repository for the YOUMEM research data.
* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]:''' Not found in the available sources [1–106].

The individual-level drivers of attitudes towards party repositioning|type=Comparative Political Research Paper & Public Opinion Study|issuing_authority=Maurits J. Meijers & Ruth Dassonneville / Radboud University / EJPR|legal_basis=Not found in the available sources.|date=2025|status=Published / Active}}

'''Who accepts party policy change? The individual-level drivers of attitudes towards party repositioning''' is a comparative empirical research paper authored by Maurits J. Meijers (Radboud University Nijmegen) and Ruth Dassonneville (Université de Montréal / KU Leuven), published in the ''European Journal of Political Research'' (EJPR) in 2025.

== Summary ==
This study examines the individual-level determinants of public acceptance or rejection of political party policy repositioning. Analyzing survey data from over 12,000 respondents across five European countries (Germany, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, and the United Kingdom), the study finds that a majority of citizens support the principle that parties should be able to change their policy positions. However, populist attitudes and right-wing extremism are strongly associated with rejecting policy change, as these groups view repositioning as a form of political elite opportunism.

== Legal Basis ==

* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This document is an academic political science research study and is not established under any statutory or judicial legislative instrument [1–117].

== Background ==
Political parties frequently change policy positions in response to public opinion, competing party strategy, or external crises. Prior research has produced contradictory results as to whether voters view policy repositioning as democratic, pragmatic flexibility or as dishonest, opportunistic "flip-flopping" [2–4, 14, 20].

== Objectives ==
1. Measure the public's principled level of acceptance of party policy change directly, using a 1–7 scale. 2. Analyze the influence of political interest on acceptance of policy change (Hypothesis 1). 3. Test the impact of technocratic attitudes on acceptance of repositioning (Hypothesis 2). 4. Test the influence of ideological extremism on rejection of change (Hypothesis 3). 5. Test the impact of populist attitudes on rejection of party policy change (Hypothesis 4).

== Scope ==
This comparative study covers five European countries with varying electoral systems and government configurations: Germany, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, and the United Kingdom.

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Overall Level of Acceptance:''' A majority of voters across the 5 countries tend to support party flexibility (median score of 4 in DE, PL, ES; score of 5 in NL, UK).
* '''Effect of Populist Attitudes (Strongest Predictor):''' Populist attitudes have a strongly statistically significant negative effect on acceptance of policy change across all 5 countries (b = -0.428, p < 0.001). Populist voters view policy repositioning as evidence of power-seeking elite opportunism [9, 23–25, 69, 76].
* '''Role of Political Interest:''' High political interest increases acceptance of policy change (b = 0.131, p < 0.001), as informed voters better understand shifting context and political dynamics [9, 15–16, 45, 47].
* '''Dynamics of Ideological Extremism:''' The negative effect of ideological extremism is driven specifically by right-wing extremist groups; left-wing extremism shows no significant negative effect.
* '''Open-Text Analysis Findings:''' Pro-change respondents use words such as "circumstances" and "new insights," while anti-change respondents use words like "power," "interests," and "benefit."

== Implementation ==
The methodology was implemented through weighted quota surveys by YouGov and ElectionCompass, OLS regression analysis (pooled and country-specific), and automated text analysis (Quanteda and the DeepL API) applied to open-ended responses. Replication data is publicly deposited on Harvard Dataverse.

== Policy Problems ==
1. The challenge political parties face in making governing-coalition compromises without triggering perceptions of elite betrayal among populist voters. 2. The risk of reputational and credibility erosion arising from accusations of opportunism and pure power-seeking.

== Reform / Change ==
A shift from assessing the aggregate electoral impact of repositioning toward understanding the psychological determinants and individual-level voter attitudes underlying acceptance of policy flexibility [4, 5, 8, 72–74].

* '''Radboud University, Université de Montréal & KU Leuven:''' The authors' home institutions.
* '''Dutch Organisation for Scientific Research (NWO):''' Funding body for the Veni Grant research.
* '''YouGov & ElectionCompass:''' Survey fieldwork providers across the 5 countries.
* '''Harvard Dataverse:''' Repository for the replication data.
* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]:''' Not found in the available sources [1–117].

Meijers, Robert A. Huber & Andrej Zaslove / EJPR|legal_basis=Not found in the available sources.|date=2025|status=Published / Active}}

'''The anatomy of populist ideology: How political parties define 'the people' and 'the elite''' is a comparative empirical research paper authored by Maurits J. Meijers (Radboud University / University of Antwerp), Robert A. Huber (University of Salzburg), and Andrej Zaslove (Radboud University), published in the ''European Journal of Political Research'' (EJPR) in 2025.

== Summary ==
This study examines how political parties in 31 European countries define the two core concepts of populist ideology: "the people" and "the elite." Using data from the 2023 wave of the Populism and Political Parties Expert Survey (POPPA), the study finds that conceptions of "the people" are driven primarily by host ideology — nativism for the cultural dimension and economic ideology for the economic dimension — while populism itself is the main predictor determining who is considered part of "the elite."

== Legal Basis ==

* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This document is an academic political science research study and is not established under any statutory or judicial legislative instrument [1–78].

== Background ==
Populist ideology centers on the opposition between "the honest people" and "the corrupt elite." However, both "the people" and "the elite" function as empty signifiers — concepts without fixed meaning that are filled in by political parties according to their own worldviews.

== Objectives ==
1. Identify comparative cross-national patterns in how societal groups are classified as "the people" or "the elite." 2. Distinguish the influence of populism from host ideologies such as nativism and left-right economic position. 3. Analyze how left-wing and right-wing populist parties construct notions of political, media, economic, and socio-structural elites.

== Scope ==
This comparative study covers 312 political parties across 31 European countries, using the 2023 POPPA expert survey.

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Cultural Conception of "The People":''' Nativism is the primary explanatory variable excluding "citizens with a migration background" from the definition of the people (b = -0.80), with right-wing populism reinforcing this exclusion.
* '''Economic Conception of "The People":''' Left-right economic ideology determines the inclusion/exclusion of "very wealthy citizens," with left-wing populists explicitly excluding the wealthy from the definition of the people.
* '''Conception of "The Elite":''' Populism is the main predictor determining which groups are seen as elites. Right-wing populists specifically target media elites (journalists) and socio-structural elites (academics), while left-wing populists target economic elites (corporate CEOs).

== Implementation ==
The methodology was implemented by collecting survey data from 324 political experts across Europe, using 0–10 scales for populism and ideology components, and estimating OLS linear regression models with country-fixed effects.

== Policy Problems ==
1. The challenge of understanding how political parties direct mobilization rhetoric and define legitimate "popular sovereignty." 2. The risk of attacks on media independence and academic freedom from right-wing populist movements.

== Reform / Change ==
Provides the first comparative empirical evidence separating the effect of populism from nativism and economic ideology in the construction of political identity.

'''Policy Framework on Public Participation in Administrative Procedures in Spain and Italy''' (''Participation in Administrative Procedures: Lessons from the Spanish Experience'') is a comparative administrative law framework formulated by Oriol Mir Puigpelat. It examines citizen participation in administrative procedures (individual adjudication and rulemaking), distinguishes between the Rule of Law (''Rechtsstaat'') defensive function and the Democratic Principle (''participatory democracy'') function of public participation, and evaluates instruments such as ''audiencia'', ''información pública'', and ''terminación convencional'' in Spain and Italy <ref>Mir Puigpelat, O. (2010). Participation in Administrative Procedures: Lessons from the Spanish Experience. In *Administrative Procedures and Rights*, 330–336.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Authored by [[Oriol Mir Puigpelat]] (Professor of Administrative Law at the University of Barcelona), this study provides a comparative analysis of public participation mechanisms within Spanish and Italian administrative law <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 330.</ref>.

The analysis establishes that citizen participation does not exclusively serve a democratic function; rather, it often operates as a Rule of Law mechanism designed to protect subjective individual rights against administrative actions <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 335.</ref>. However, in administrative rulemaking and discretionary policy decisions affecting broader public interest, public participation (through notice-and-comment mechanisms and representational associations) directly enhances participatory democracy <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), pp. 335, 336.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Spanish Constitutional Law''':
** ''Spanish Constitution of 1978'' (''Constitución Española de 1978''): Article 105.a (guarantee of citizen and association participation in rulemaking) <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 333.</ref>; Article 105.c (guarantee of the right to a hearing/''audiencia'' for interested parties in administrative procedures) <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 331.</ref>.
* '''Spanish General Administrative Legislation''':
** ''Ley 30/1992'' (''LRJPAC / Common Administrative Procedure Act''): Article 31 (collective interests) <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 331.</ref>; Article 34 (procedural communications) <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 331.</ref>; Article 86 (''Información Pública'' / Notice and Comment Procedure) <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 332.</ref>; Article 88 (''Terminación Convencional'' / Procedural Agreements) <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 333.</ref>.
** ''Ley de Procedimiento Administrativo de 17 de julio de 1958'' (LPA): Articles 23, 83, and 91 (right to a hearing under the Franco era for subjective rights and individual interests) <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 331.</ref>.
** ''Ley 50/1997 del Gobierno'': Article 24 (rulemaking procedures of the central government) <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 333.</ref>.
** ''Ley 7/1985 de bases del régimen local'': Article 49 (public consultation at local government level) <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 333.</ref>.
* '''Italian Administrative Law (Comparative Benchmark)''':
** ''Legge 7 agosto 1990, n. 241'': Articles 7 and 8.3 (procedural notification) <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 331.</ref>; Article 11 (procedural agreements) <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 333.</ref>; Article 13 (explicit exclusion of rulemaking from general participation rights) <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 333.</ref>.

== Policy Instruments & Implementation ==
1. '''Audiencia del Interesado (Right to a Hearing)''': Established under the LPA 1958 and expanded by LRJPAC 1992 to encompass collective interests. It functions primarily as a written right to comment and be heard for defense of subjective rights <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 331.</ref>.
2. '''Información Pública (Notice and Comment)''': Open to the general public (''uti cives''). Regulated under Article 86 LRJPAC, requiring official publication, access to case files, a minimum 20-day comment period, and a reasoned administrative response <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 332.</ref>.
3. '''Terminación Convencional (Procedural Agreements)''': Governed by Article 88 LRJPAC. Unlike the broader scope under Italian law (Art. 11 Legge 241/1990), Spanish law restricts procedural settlements to instances explicitly authorized by sectoral legislation <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 333.</ref>.

== Related Entities & Focus Status ==
* '''[[Oriol Mir Puigpelat]]''': Author; Professor of Administrative Law at the University of Barcelona <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 330.</ref>.
* '''[[Roberto Caranta]]''': Italian Administrative Law Scholar (Comparative reference) <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 330.</ref>.
* '''[[Giacinto della Cananea]]''': Italian Administrative Law Scholar (Referenced) <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), p. 330.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), pp. 330–336.</ref>
* '''Geovanny Widya Berlianty P''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Mir Puigpelat (2010), pp. 330–336.</ref>
