| legal_basis = EU Charter Art. 34(3); Directive 2014/36/EU (Art. 20); Regulation (EU) 2019/1149 (ELA); Italian Immigration Code (TUI / DLgs 286/1998); Italian Law 199/2016 (Art. 603-bis CP)
| date = 2021 (Publication IJPL Vol. 13 Issue 2); 2014 (Directive 2014/36/EU); 2016 (DLgs 203/2016 & Law 199/2016); 2019 (Regulation ELA)
| status = Operational / Active
}}

'''EU and Italian Multilevel Policy Framework on the Right to Accommodation for Cross-Border Seasonal Agricultural Workers''' (Indonesian: ''Kerangka Kebijakan Multilevel Perlindungan Hak atas Akomodasi dan Hak-Hak Sosial Pekerja Musim Pertanian Lintas Batas di Uni Eropa dan Italia'') is a multilevel legal and public policy analysis framework formulated by Alessandro Nato and Elisabetta Tatì to evaluate the effectiveness of guaranteeing social rights—specifically the right to adequate accommodation—for cross-border seasonal agricultural workers across the European Union and Italy (including EU citizens, Third-Country Nationals, registered, and irregular workers) <ref>Nato, A., & Tatì, E. (2021). Where Does Social Europe Lay? Looking for Social Europe Among the Worker, Resident and Human Being Statuses with the Help of the Right to Accommodation in the Multilevel System. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 13(2), 511–568.</ref>. The framework examines the collision between three legal statuses (*worker-status*, *resident-status*, and *human being-status*), evaluates key EU secondary legal instruments (Directive 2014/36/EU, Directive 2011/98/EU, Directive 2009/52/EC, Directive 2018/957/EU, ELA Regulation (EU) 2019/1149), Italian legislative frameworks (*Testo Unico sull'Immigrazione / TUI* in conjunction with *DLgs 203/2016*, *Law 199/2016* on anti-*caporalato* in conjunction with *Article 603-bis of the Italian Penal Code*), and jurisprudence from the Court of Justice of the European Union (*CJEU: Tümer, Kamberaj, INPS v. WS*) and the Italian Constitutional Court <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 512, 515, 520, 534, 538, 540, 552, 560, 567.</ref>.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Alessandro Nato]] and [[Elisabetta Tatì]] (Postdoctoral Researchers at LUISS Guido Carli University, Rome), this study presents an in-depth analysis of the fulfillment of the right to adequate accommodation for seasonal agricultural workers in the EU and Italy <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 511, 512.</ref>. The authors argue that despite formal EU statutory mandates (such as Directive 2014/36/EU), most agricultural workers continue to face severe exploitation and inhabit informal settlements or ghettos due to declining national labour inspection regimes and market-efficiency paradigms <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 521, 523, 536, 542.</ref>. The framework proposes a paradigm shift away from pure *worker-status* or *resident-status* toward a *human being-status* anchored in European social citizenship based on territorial presence <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 515, 565, 566.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
The protection framework for cross-border seasonal agricultural workers relies on supranational human rights instruments, EU directives, and national legislation:
* '''[[Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union]] (EU Charter)''': Article 34(3) (Social assistance and housing help) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 532, 533.</ref>; Article 5 (Prohibition of forced labour and human trafficking) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), p. 526.</ref>; Article 31 (Fair and just working conditions) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), p. 526.</ref>.
* '''[[Directive 2014/36/EU]] (Seasonal Workers Directive)''': Article 20 (Proof of adequate accommodation and prohibition of automatic rent deductions) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 534, 535.</ref>; Article 23 (Equal treatment principle) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), p. 522.</ref>; Article 24 (Risk assessment-based inspections) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 536, 537.</ref>.
* '''[[Regulation (EU) 2019/1149]] (European Labour Authority / ELA)''': Coordinates cross-border joint labour inspections <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 537, 538.</ref>.
* '''Italian National Law''':
** *Legislative Decree n. 286/1998 (TUI)* as amended by *DLgs n. 203/2016*: Articles 5-bis and 24 governing the *contratto di soggiorno* and standard accommodation requirements for seasonal workers <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 540, 544.</ref>.
** *Law n. 199/2016*: Amending Article 603-bis of the Italian Criminal Code to criminalize illegal intermediaries (*caporali*) and exploitative employers, while introducing corporate liability <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 552, 553.</ref>.

== Background & Collision of the Three Legal Statuses ==
The structure of agri-food supply chains in Southern Europe relies heavily on flexible, low-cost labor <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 518, 524.</ref>. This dynamic exposes a fundamental tension among three legal statuses:
# '''Worker-Status''': Social rights are conditioned on employment market participation, which is often compromised by market efficiency logics <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 514, 517.</ref>.
# '''Resident-Status''': Rights are tied to lawful residency, which is frequently weaponized to exclude irregular workers <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 514, 515.</ref>.
# '''Human Being-Status''': The ideal constitutional approach guaranteeing fundamental human rights (including housing) solely on the basis of physical presence within a territory (*territorial presence*) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 515, 565, 566.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Ensure seasonal agricultural workers (EU and non-EU) access accommodation that meets occupational health, safety, and human dignity standards <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 521, 532, 535.</ref>.
* Eliminate abusive rent extraction, *caporalato* illegal intermediation, and labor exploitation in agriculture <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 524, 552.</ref>.
* Strengthen national and cross-border labor inspection regimes through the coordination of the European Labour Authority (ELA) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 537, 538.</ref>.

== Key Jurisprudence & Statutory Directives ==
* '''Landmark CJEU Ruling (Tümer Case C-311/13)''': The CJEU affirmed that EU labor safeguards apply to all workers regardless of irregular residence status, establishing that public immigration control cannot override fundamental labor protections <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 515, 516.</ref>.
* '''Italian TUI Housing Mandates (DLgs 203/2016)''': Employers hiring foreign seasonal workers must demonstrate proof of standard accommodation meeting minimum social housing criteria and cover return transportation costs <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), p. 544.</ref>.
* '''Italian Constitutional Court Jurisprudence (Judgments n. 44/2020 & n. 9/2021)''': The Constitutional Court struck down regional length-of-residency requirements (e.g., in Lombardy and Abruzzo) for accessing public social housing as unconstitutionally discriminatory <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), p. 560.</ref>.

== Enforcement Deficits ==
* '''Decline in Labor Inspections''': Total agricultural labor inspections in Italy decreased from 14,397 in 2006 to 7,265 in 2017, severely impairing state capacity to detect housing abuses <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), p. 551.</ref>.
* '''Mandate Limitations of the ELA''': Regulation (EU) 2019/1149 does not grant the European Labour Authority independent, unannounced inspection powers within Member States without prior national consent <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 538, 539.</ref>.

== Entity Relationships ==
* '''[[Alessandro Nato]]''': Lead Author & Postdoctoral Researcher, LUISS Guido Carli <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 511, 512.</ref>.
* '''[[Elisabetta Tatì]]''': Lead Author & Postdoctoral Researcher, LUISS Guido Carli <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 511, 512.</ref>.
* '''[[European Labour Authority]] (ELA)''': EU body coordinating cross-border labor inspection enforcement <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 537, 538.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 511–568.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 511–568.</ref>

}}

Il '''Quadro Politico Multilivello dell'UE e Italiano sul Diritto all'Alloggio per i Lavoratori Agricoli Stagionali Transfrontalieri''' (titolo originale in inglese: ''Where Does Social Europe Lay? Looking for Social Europe Among the Worker, Resident and Human Being Statuses with the Help of the Right to Accommodation in the Multilevel System'') è un quadro di analisi giuridica e di politica pubblica multilivello formulato da Alessandro Nato ed Elisabetta Tatì per valutare l'efficacia della garanzia dei diritti sociali, in particolare il diritto ad un alloggio adeguato (*right to accommodation*), per i lavoratori agricoli stagionali transfrontalieri nell'Unione Europea e in Italia (inclusi cittadini dell'UE, cittadini di paesi terzi, lavoratori regolari e irregolari) <ref>Nato, A., & Tatì, E. (2021). Where Does Social Europe Lay? Looking for Social Europe Among the Worker, Resident and Human Being Statuses with the Help of the Right to Accommodation in the Multilevel System. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 13(2), 511–568.</ref>. Il quadro analizza il conflitto tra tre status giuridici (*worker-status*, *resident-status* e *human being-status*), valuta gli strumenti di diritto derivato dell'UE (Direttiva 2014/36/UE, Direttiva 2011/98/UE, Direttiva 2009/52/CE, Direttiva 2018/957/UE, Regolamento ELA (UE) 2019/1149), la normativa italiana (*Testo Unico sull'Immigrazione / TUI* in combinato disposto con il *DLgs 203/2016*, la *Legge 199/2016* sul contrasto al *caporalato* e l'*Articolo 603-bis del Codice Penale*), nonché la giurisprudenza della Corte di Giustizia dell'Unione Europea (*CGUE: Tümer, Kamberaj, INPS c. WS*) e della Corte Costituzionale italiana <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 512, 515, 520, 534, 538, 540, 552, 560, 567.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Scritto da [[Alessandro Nato]] ed [[Elisabetta Tatì]] (ricercatori post-doc presso l'Università LUISS Guido Carli di Roma), questo studio offre un'analisi approfondita sull'effettività del diritto all'alloggio per i lavoratori stagionali in agricoltura nell'UE e in Italia <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 511, 512.</ref>. Gli autori evidenziano che, nonostante gli obblighi normativi europei (come la Direttiva 2014/36/UE), la maggior parte dei lavoratori agricoli versa in condizioni di grave sfruttamento e vive in insediamenti informali o "ghetti" a causa del declino delle ispezioni del lavoro e della prevalenza delle logiche di mercato <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 521, 523, 536, 542.</ref>. Lo studio propone un cambio di paradigma dal mero *worker-status* o *resident-status* verso uno *human being-status* fondato sulla cittadinanza sociale europea legata alla presenza territoriale (*territorial presence*) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 515, 565, 566.</ref>.

== Basi Giuridiche ==
La tutela dei lavoratori agricoli stagionali transfrontalieri si fonda su strumenti sovranazionali sui diritti umani, direttive europee e legislazione nazionale italiana:
* '''[[Carta dei Diritti Fondamentali dell'Unione Europea]] (Carta dell'UE)''': Articolo 34 comma 3 (Assistenza sociale e abitativa) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 532, 533.</ref>; Articolo 5 (Proibizione della schiavitù e del lavoro forzato) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), p. 526.</ref>; Articolo 31 (Condizioni di lavoro giuste ed eque) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), p. 526.</ref>.
* '''[[Direttiva 2014/36/UE]] (Direttiva Lavoratori Stagionali)''': Articolo 20 (Requisito di un alloggio adeguato e divieto di detrazione automatica del canone dal salario) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 534, 535.</ref>; Articolo 23 (Principio di parità di trattamento) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), p. 522.</ref>; Articolo 24 (Ispezioni basate sulla valutazione del rischio) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 536, 537.</ref>.
* '''[[Regolamento (UE) 2019/1149]] (Autorità Europea del Lavoro / ELA)''': Disciplina il coordinamento delle ispezioni congiunte transfrontaliere <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 537, 538.</ref>.
* '''Legislazione Nazionale Italiana''':
** *Decreto Legislativo 25 luglio 1998, n. 286 (TUI)* modificato dal *DLgs n. 203/2016*: Articoli 5-bis e 24 relativi al *contratto di soggiorno* e ai requisiti dell'alloggio per i lavoratori stagionali <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 540, 544.</ref>.
** *Legge 29 ottobre 2016, n. 199*: Riforma dell'Articolo 603-bis del Codice Penale per la punibilità dell'intermediazione illecita (*caporalato*), dello sfruttamento lavorativo e l'introduzione della responsabilità amministrativa degli enti <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 552, 553.</ref>.

== Contesto e Conflitto dei Tre Status Giuridici ==
La catena del valore agroalimentare nell'Europa meridionale richiede manodopera flessibile e a basso costo <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 518, 524.</ref>. Questa struttura genera una tensione diretta tra tre status:
# '''Worker-Status''': I diritti sociali sono subordinati all'inserimento nel mercato del lavoro, spesso sacrificati per logiche di competitività aziendale <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 514, 517.</ref>.
# '''Resident-Status''': I diritti sono vincolati alla regolarità del soggiorno, usata come barriera per escludere i lavoratori irregolari <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 514, 515.</ref>.
# '''Human Being-Status''': L'approccio costituzionale ideale che garantisce i diritti umani fondamentali (incluso l'alloggio) sulla mera base della presenza fisica sul territorio (*territorial presence*) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 515, 565, 566.</ref>.

== Obiettivi ==
* Garantire ai lavoratori agricoli stagionali (UE ed extra-UE) alloggi conformi agli standard di igiene, sicurezza e dignità umana <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 521, 532, 535.</ref>.
* Contrastare le trattenute illecite sugli stipendi, le pratiche di *caporalato* e lo sfruttamento lavorativo in agricoltura <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 524, 552.</ref>.
* Rafforzare i controlli ispettivi nazionali e transfrontalieri tramite l'Autorità Europea del Lavoro (ELA) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 537, 538.</ref>.

== Giurisprudenza e Disposizioni Chiave ==
* '''Sentenza della CGUE (Causa Tümer C-311/13)''': La Corte ha affermato che le tutele del lavoro dell'UE si applicano a tutti i lavoratori indipendentemente dalla regolarità del soggiorno, stabilendo che le esigenze di controllo dell'immigrazione non possono annullare i diritti del lavoro <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 515, 516.</ref>.
* '''Requisiti Abitativi TUI (DLgs 203/2016)''': Il datore di lavoro che assume un lavoratore stagionale straniero deve dimostrare la disponibilità di un alloggio idoneo conforme agli standard minimi dell'edilizia residenziale pubblica <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), p. 544.</ref>.
* '''Giurisprudenza della Corte Costituzionale Italiana (Sentenze n. 44/2020 e n. 9/2021)''': La Corte ha dichiarato incostituzionali i requisiti regionali di residenza prolungata (es. Regione Lombardia e Abruzzo) per l'accesso all'edilizia residenziale pubblica (*social housing*) <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), p. 560.</ref>.

== Criticità e Deficit Ispettivi ==
* '''Calo delle Ispezioni''': Le ispezioni nel settore agricolo in Italia sono diminuite da 14.397 nel 2006 a 7.265 nel 2017, riducendo l'efficacia del contrasto agli abusi abitativi <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), p. 551.</ref>.
* '''Limiti del Mandato ELA''': Il Regolamento (UE) 2019/1149 non conferisce all'Autorità Europea del Lavoro il potere di condurre ispezioni autonome nei Paesi membri senza il preventivo consenso nazionale <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 538, 539.</ref>.

== Relazioni tra le Entità ==
* '''[[Alessandro Nato]]''': Autore Principale e Ricercatore Post-Doc, LUISS Guido Carli <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 511, 512.</ref>.
* '''[[Elisabetta Tatì]]''': Autrice Principale e Ricercatrice Post-Doc, LUISS Guido Carli <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 511, 512.</ref>.
* '''[[European Labour Authority]] (ELA)''': Organismo UE per il coordinamento delle ispezioni sul lavoro <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 537, 538.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Non presente nelle fonti disponibili.]]'' <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 511–568.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Non presente nelle fonti disponibili.]]'' <ref>Nato & Tatì (2021), pp. 511–568.</ref>

'''High Performance Court Framework (HPC Framework)''' is an organizational and administrative management framework developed by the National Center for State Courts (NCSC) in Williamsburg, Virginia. Aimed at courts of first instance, the framework guides court leadership toward achieving and sustaining high administrative quality through five core concepts: Administrative Principles, Managerial Culture, Performance Measurement, Performance Management, and the Quality Cycle.

== Summary ==
Developed by Dr. Roger Hanson, Dr. Brian Ostrom, and Dr. Matthew Kleiman, the HPC Framework addresses challenges shared by trial-court judges worldwide, such as heavy caseloads, sole judicial decision-making, and the need to manage caseflow alongside adjudicative duties. Rather than offering a one-size-fits-all solution, the framework provides a scientific methodology for measuring performance through 10 CourTools indicators, diagnosing court culture, and running a continuous quality cycle.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This framework is an organizational management policy guide published by NCSC researchers, not a statutory enactment [1–4].

== Background & Common Conditions of Trial Courts ==
Trial-court judges across different legal traditions (civil law, common law, customary law, Sharia) share similar working conditions:
1. Handling high volumes of civil, criminal, and family cases.
2. Acting as final arbiters of fact.
3. Facing pressure to manage caseflow so it does not accumulate into backlog.

== The Five Core Concepts of the Framework ==

=== 1. Administrative Principles ===
* '''Individual Attention to Every Case:''' Ensuring each case receives sufficient time for accurate legal decision-making.
* '''Proportionality to Caseload Need:''' Complex, demanding cases receive more time/resources than routine ones.
* '''Procedural Justice:''' Ensuring court proceedings are perceived as fair, transparent, and respectful of the rights of the parties.
* '''Judicial Control over the Legal Process:''' Judges and administrators actively manage caseflow rather than leaving it to attorneys.

=== 2. Managerial Culture ===
Analyzed along two dimensions: '''Solidarity''' (shared commitment to common goals) and '''Sociability''' (cordial engagement). Divided into 4 cultural types:
# '''Communal:''' High Sociability / Low Solidarity.
# '''Networked:''' High Sociability / High Solidarity.
# '''Autonomous:''' Low Sociability / Low Solidarity.
# '''Hierarchical:''' Low Sociability / High Solidarity.

=== 3. Performance Measurement (CourTools) ===
Uses 10 core NCSC CourTools indicators:
# ''Access and Fairness'' (Access & Fairness Survey).
# ''Clearance Rates'' (Case Resolution Rate).
# ''Time to Disposition'' (Time to Judgment).
# ''Age of Active Pending Caseload'' (Age of Active Backlog).
# ''Trial Date Certainty'' (Certainty of Trial Scheduling).
# ''Reliability and Integrity of Court Files'' (Case File Reliability).
# ''Collection of Monetary Penalties'' (Fee/Penalty Collection).
# ''Effective Use of Jurors'' (Jury Utilization Efficiency).
# ''Court Employee Satisfaction'' (Court Staff Satisfaction).
# ''Cost Per Case'' (Cost per Case).

=== 4. Performance Management ===
The court's "administratively activist" action in using performance measurement data to change business processes, train staff, and adjust services.

=== 5. The Quality Cycle ===
A repeating 5-step system: (1) Defining the Scope of the Problem → (2) Data Gathering → (3) Analysis & Interpretation → (4) Taking Action → (5) Evaluating Results [18–20].

== International Application ==
* '''Transitional Court Systems (e.g., Afghanistan, Kosovo, Nigeria):''' Helps design court organizations and training curricula for judges/staff based on core working values [23–25].
* '''Consolidated Court Systems (e.g., Canada, Singapore, Australia):''' Provides tools for public accountability and helps build a cadre of high-performance-oriented judges.

'''Case Processing Time Standards''' in American state and local trial courts is a judicial management policy framework developed by the National Center for State Courts (NCSC), the American Bar Association (ABA), the Conference of Chief Justices (CCJ), and the Conference of State Court Administrators (COSCA). The framework sets reasonable timelines for resolving civil, criminal, domestic relations, juvenile delinquency, child protection, and probate cases, aiming to eliminate unnecessary delay and ensure public accountability.

== Summary ==
Adopted gradually since the 1970s to cover 41 states and the District of Columbia by 2007, time standards serve as a tool for motivation, measurement, management, and the development of court information systems. The standards distinguish between intermediate time standards for each procedural stage and overall time standards spanning from filing to disposition.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''US State Court Administrative Rules:''' Applied across 41 states and Washington, D.C., either mandatorily or as advisory/elective guidelines.
* '''Federal Child Protection Statute (ASFA 1997):''' The Adoption and Safe Families Act of 1997 (P.L. 105-89; 42 U.S.C. § 675(5)(B)), which mandates limits on the duration a child may remain in foster care.
* '''ABA Standards Relating to Trial Courts:''' 1992 Edition, Sections 2.50, 2.51C, 2.52, and 2.55.
* '''Trial Court Performance Standards (TCPS 1990):''' Developed by the NCSC and the Bureau of Justice Assistance (BJA) of the US Department of Justice.

== Background ==
National research in the US demonstrates that court delay is unrelated to court size or the number of filings per judge, but instead depends on the court leadership's commitment to effective caseflow management. Simply adding new judgeships without effective caseflow management does not resolve case backlogs.

== Objectives ==
1. Ensure prompt and fair justice that meets public expectations.
2. Reduce the volume and age of the pending case inventory (backlog).
3. Ensure trial date certainty and control the cost of access to justice.
4. Maintain a balance between procedural speed and substantive fairness (speedy justice without sacrificing substantive fairness).

== Scope & ABA Standards Table ==

=== Overall Time Standards (ABA) ===
{| class="wikitable"
|-
! Case Type !! 90% Completed !! 98% Completed !! 100% Completed
|-
| '''General Civil''' || 12 Months || 18 Months || 24 Months
|-
| '''Domestic Relations''' || 3 Months || 6 Months || 12 Months
|-
| '''Felony''' || 120 Days || 180 Days || 365 Days
|-
| '''Misdemeanor''' || 30 Days || -- || 90 Days
|}

=== Child Protection Cases (ASFA 1997 & NCJFCJ) ===
* Preliminary protective hearing: Must be held within 72 hours of a child's removal from parental custody.
* Adjudication: Must be completed within 60 days of removal.
* Permanency planning hearing: Must be held within 12–14 months.
* Petition for termination of parental rights: Mandatory when a child has been in foster care for 15 of the last 22 months.

== Key Provisions & Management Tools ==
* '''Strict Continuance Policy:''' Postponements are granted only for good cause shown, submitted in writing. A continuance rate exceeding 20% indicates excessive court leniency that undermines attorney preparedness.
* '''Differentiated Case Management (DCM):''' A "triage" system distinguishing simple, standard, and complex cases so that judicial resource allocation is properly targeted.
* '''Four Core NCSC CourTools Measures:'''
# '''Clearance Rate:''' The percentage of outgoing cases relative to incoming cases.
# '''Time to Disposition:''' The percentage of cases resolved within the established time standard.
# '''Age of Pending Caseload:''' The average age of currently active pending cases.
# '''Certainty of Trial Date:''' The certainty of the scheduled trial date and evidence submission.

== Policy Issues ==
1. '''Saturation Point of Capacity:''' Even a highly efficient court can reach a saturation point if a surge in caseload is not matched by adequate support staffing.
2. '''Continuance Abuse:''' Lax continuance policies increase attorney costs, waste witnesses' time, and fuel public frustration.
3. '''Risk of "Foster Care Drift":''' Children risk being left adrift in the temporary care system without a clear path to adoption if permanency timelines are not strictly enforced.

== Reform / Implications ==
* Institutionalization of time standards across 41 US states, along with the integration of NCSC's CourTools indicators for the ongoing performance evaluation of judicial panels.
* Implementation of ASFA regulations across all 50 states by 2007 to ensure permanency certainty for children.

'''The Judicial Trust and Access to Justice Policy Framework in Nepal''' (''Judicial Trust in Nepal: Demand- and Supply-Side Perspectives'') is a judicial policy framework and empirical evaluation regarding the level of public trust and confidence and access to justice in Nepal, analyzed from two perspectives: the ''demand-side'' (justice seekers and vulnerable groups) and the ''supply-side'' (judges, advocates, and judicial officials).

== Summary ==
Published in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (2025) by Dr. Bidhya Chapagain, this policy framework reveals the existence of a significant "trust deficit" towards the Nepalese judiciary. Qualitative research involving 52 stakeholders demonstrates that from the ''demand-side'', the public complains about political intervention in judicial appointments, a backlog of 165,000 cases, and the alienation of vulnerable groups (''Dalits, Madhesi, PwD, rural women'') [2, 6, 21, 25, 27–28]. From the ''supply-side'', judges confirm the destructive impact of politicization and propose public-oriented (''people-centered'') reforms [30–32, 36–37].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Constitution of Nepal 2015''': Guarantees the right to equal justice and an independent judiciary.
* '''Five-Year Strategic Plans of the Nepali Judiciary''': Strategic Plan I (2004–2009), Plan II (2009–2014), Plan III (2014–2019), and Plan IV (2019–2023) [12, 32–33, 62–64].
* '''Reports of the Supreme Court High-Level Probe Commissions (2015, 2021)''': Official reports addressing irregularities, malpractices, and corruption within the judiciary.
* '''Sustainable Development Goal 16 (SDG 16)''': Equal access to justice for all.

== Background ==
Although Nepal has transitioned to a federal structure, the judiciary continues to operate under a centralized unitary model. Political instability and recurring judicial scandals have exacerbated public skepticism. Judicial reforms thus far have tended to be "inward-looking," focusing solely on internal procedural efficiency without directly engaging the community [9, 11–12].

== Objectives ==
1. Map the root causes of the judicial trust deficit in Nepal from both demand and supply perspectives.
2. Overcome systemic barriers to access to justice for marginalized groups.
3. Encourage transparent, merit-based judicial appointments to eliminate political intervention.
4. Reduce the backlog of 165,000 cases through modernization and judicial transparency.

== Scope ==
The study encompasses empirical research in Kathmandu and three rural districts in Nepal, involving 30 community members in 3 ''Focus Group Discussions'' (FGDs) and 22 in-depth interviews with judges, court officials, and advocates [15–19].

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Dual-Sided Evaluation of Judicial Trust''':
# ''Demand-Side (Justice Seekers)'': Views the judiciary as a distant, expensive institution influenced by political affiliation and social status [2, 21, 23, 27–29].
# ''Supply-Side (Judicial Actors)'': Acknowledges the importance of integrity and communication transparency, but complains about the courtroom insulation of judges [30–32, 34–36].
* '''Case Backlog Findings''': The Supreme Court of Nepal resolves only 17% of total annual cases, leaving a backlog of >27,000 cases in the Supreme Court and 165,000 cases across all judicial levels.
* '''Access Distrust Level''': 72% of female victims of sexual violence in Nepal do not seek formal legal protection due to a lack of trust and social stigma.

== Implementation ==
* '''Community Outreach Strategy''': Encouraging the implementation of community engagement programs and public communication to demystify the judicial process [31–33, 46, 53].
* '''Judicial Appointment Reform''': Enforcing ethical standards and transparency in judicial recruitment under the supervision of the Judicial Council.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Politicization of Judicial Appointments''': Public trust collapsed due to the perception that court decisions are influenced by political party loyalty [2, 27–29].
* '''Barriers for Marginalized Groups''': Dalits, Madhesis, persons with disabilities, and rural women face double discrimination and legal language alienation.

== Reform / Change ==
* '''Digital Courts''': Adopting digital justice system technologies similar to those in Estonia and Singapore.
* '''Mobile Courts''': Implementing Kenya's ''mobile courts'' model to bring justice closer to rural areas.
* '''Community Legal Education''': Expanding clinical legal education modeled after practices in Indonesia.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Supreme Court of Nepal''': The apex of judicial leadership and the creator of the five-year strategic plans.
* '''National Judicial Academy (NJA)''': Nepal's judicial research and training institution.
* '''Cecep Mustafa / [private person]''': ''Not found in the available sources.'' [FACT] [1–66].

'''The Policy Framework for the Performance and Economic Impact of the Netherlands Judiciary''' (''Performance of the Netherlands Judiciary & Economic Impact Policy Framework'') is a judicial performance evaluation and macro/microeconomic impact policy framework formulated by Dr. Frans van Dijk (Director of the Council for the Judiciary, Netherlands). It evaluates a 15-year transformation of the Dutch judiciary (1998–2013) following the Leemhuis Commission Report and the 2002 Reorganization Act (the establishment of the *Raad voor de rechtspraak* and *gerechtsbesturen*), measures court delay reductions, user satisfaction, and calculates realized societal economic gains of €795M–€970M per year (0.13%–0.16% of GDP).

== Summary ==
Published by Dr. Frans van Dijk in the *International Journal for Court Administration* (IJCA), this empirical policy framework provides a retrospective evaluation of Dutch judicial reforms between 1998 and 2013. Initiated by the *Leemhuis Commission Report* (1998) and the establishment of the *Council for the Judiciary* (*Raad voor de rechtspraak*) in 2002, the Dutch judiciary implemented output-based management, quality and lead-time standards, and a judicial map restructuring (*Herziening Rechterlijke Kaart 2013*). Van Dijk's evaluation demonstrates that civil trial duration reductions (190 days faster) and administrative streamlining successfully generated tangible societal economic gains ranging from €795M to €970M annually.

== Legal Basis ==

* '''Wet op de rechterlijke organisatie / 2002 Judiciary Governance Reform Act:''' Established the Council for the Judiciary and transferred operational court management responsibilities to integrally responsible court boards (*gerechtsbesturen*).
* '''Crisis- en herstelwet (2010 Crisis and Recovery Law):''' Instituted expedited procedures and strict statutory deadlines for administrative litigation involving infrastructure projects.
* '''Wet op de herziening van de rechterlijke kaart (2013 New Judicial Map Law):''' Restructured judicial jurisdictions by consolidating 21 first-instance courts into 11, and 5 appeal courts into 4.
* '''2011 Small Claims Jurisdiction Regulations:''' Increased the monetary threshold for small claims courts (*kantonrechter*) from €5,000 to €25,000.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text.

== Background ==
In 1998, the Dutch Ministry of Justice examined the economic impacts of court inefficiencies. Three primary categories of societal losses were identified: transaction costs, investment postponement costs, and capital uncertainty costs.

== Objectives ==

1. Reduce court delays for major civil disputes by up to 8 months and administrative cases by up to 6 months.
2. Improve judicial reasoning clarity and the uniform application of the law.
3. Lower courtroom waiting times from 1–2 hours to less than 30 minutes.
4. Realize potential societal economic gains of up to 0.24% of GDP.

== Scope ==
This policy covers the evaluation of Civil Law and Administrative Law litigation across First-Instance Courts and Courts of Appeal in the Netherlands.

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Three Categories of Economic Losses from Court Delays:'''

# *Transaction Costs:* Litigation fees, attorney remuneration, and productive time losses.

# *Costs of Postponing Activities:* Freezing investment projects and business permits due to ongoing disputes.

# *Costs of Uncertainty:* Reserving liquidity capital buffers to hedge against judicial outcome unpredictability.

* '''Efficiency Gains and Realized Economic Value (1998–2013):'''
 *Major Civil Disputes:* Duration reduced by 190 days (from 626 to 436 days). Realized economic gain: **€530M per year**.
 *Administrative Cases:* Duration reduced by 2–4 months (down to 259 days) via the *Nieuwe zaaksbehandeling* method. Realized economic gain: **€175M–€350M per year**.
 *Courtroom Waiting Times:* Decreased from 1–2 hours to ~30 minutes. Realized economic gain: **€90M per year**.
 *Total Realized Societal Gains:* **€795M–€970M per year** (0.13%–0.16% of GDP).
* '''New Administrative Case-Handling Method (Nieuwe zaaksbehandeling 2011/12):'''
 Mandatory initial hearings within 13 weeks where judges integrate mediation techniques to resolve disputes on the spot.

== Implementation ==

* '''Customer Satisfaction Surveys (Prisma & Synovate Regioplan 2011):''' Satisfaction with legal reasoning rose from 59% to 83% for litigants and 52% to 67% for legal professionals; satisfaction regarding uniform law application climbed from 38% to 56%.
* '''2013 New Judicial Map:''' Jurisdictional consolidation to foster within-court specialization among judges.

== Policy Problems ==

* '''Emerging Digital Access Bottleneck (KEI Program):''' Growing public demand for e-filing, digital archives, and automated hearing schedules that remains partially unfulfilled.
* '''Court Fee Barriers:''' Government-mandated increases in court fees that risk restricting access to justice.

== Reform / Change ==

* Civil procedural simplification and full digital transformation (*KEI Program 2013–2017*).
* Governance adjustments anchored in public performance accountability.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''Council for the Judiciary (Raad voor de rechtspraak):''' The independent administrative body managing the Dutch court system.
* '''Leemhuis Commission:''' The committee that drafted the foundational 1998 judicial reform report.
* '''[private person]:''' A Law student at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta (NIM: 2410611102), specializing in Constitutional Law. Cecep Mustafa is not found in the available sources.

2. '''Civil Procedural Simplification for a 6-Month Duration Target:''' Develop more informal and rapid civil procedures so that major civil dispute durations can be shortened further from 436 days down to 6 months (180 days), yielding potential extra economic value of €480M–€630M.
3. '''Expansion of Nieuwe Zaaksbehandeling Implementation in Administrative Cases:''' Ensure that all administrative courts consistently apply the 13-week initial hearing method to fully realize the potential economic gains of €350M annually.

| type = European & Italian Administrative Law Policy Framework / Paradigm Shift in European Administrative Law
| issuing_authority = Aldo Sandulli / Italian Journal of Public Law
| legal_basis = Next Generation European Union (NGEU); Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF); European Semester Mechanism; National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP/PNRR)
| date = 2022 (Publication Vol. 14 Issue 1/2022)
| status = Operational / Active
}}

The '''NGEU-NRRP Economic Planning and Administrative Transformation Framework''' (officially centered on the work ''Economic Planning and Administrative Transformations in the NGEU and NRRP: A Paradigm Shift'') is a supranational European and Italian administrative law and economic planning policy framework. Originating from the Next Generation European Union (NGEU) recovery plan and the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), it redirects state economic planning under the central oversight of the European Commission and induces an organizational transformation in public administration from a process-based model to project-based management <ref>Sandulli, A. (2022). Economic Planning and Administrative Transformations in the NGEU and NRRP: A Paradigm Shift. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 14(1), 3–8.</ref>.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Aldo Sandulli]], Professor of Administrative Law, this study outlines how the NGEU and RRF funding mechanisms triggered a paradigm shift in European and national administrative law <ref>Sandulli (2022), pp. 3–5.</ref>. Drawing upon the scholarship of [[Sabino Cassese]] regarding the evolution of European integration through crisis response, the framework highlights how NGEU revived state economic planning functions under European Commission guidance while restructuring Italian public bureaucracy from rigid process-oriented workflows to project-based management <ref>Sandulli (2022), pp. 3, 5–6, 8.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
The framework is grounded in key supranational instruments and national planning frameworks:
* '''[[Next Generation European Union]] (NGEU)''': The European Union recovery package funding grants and loans through joint debt issuance <ref>Sandulli (2022), pp. 3–4.</ref>.
* '''[[Recovery and Resilience Facility]] (RRF)''': The core mechanism of NGEU establishing targets for ecological transition, digital transformation, and social cohesion <ref>Sandulli (2022), p. 4.</ref>.
* '''[[European Semester Mechanism]]''': The EU financial coordination framework and financial conditionality system <ref>Sandulli (2022), p. 4.</ref>.
* '''[[National Recovery and Resilience Plan]] (NRRP / PNRR)''': Italy's national recovery plan approved by the Council of the European Union <ref>Sandulli (2022), pp. 5, 6.</ref>.

== Background ==
The COVID-19 pandemic and the conflict in Ukraine accelerated European integration through the establishment of NGEU <ref>Sandulli (2022), p. 3.</ref>. For decades prior, national economic planning capacity in Member States was marginal, as European economic governance deferred development choices to regulated markets <ref>Sandulli (2022), p. 6.</ref>. NGEU reintroduced public economic planning under European institutional direction <ref>Sandulli (2022), p. 5.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Accelerate ecological and digital transitions while bolstering territorial and social cohesion across the EU <ref>Sandulli (2022), p. 4.</ref>.
* Align national economic development planning with supranational strategic priorities <ref>Sandulli (2022), pp. 5, 8.</ref>.
* Enhance the speed and operational efficiency of public investment absorption via administrative reform <ref>Sandulli (2022), pp. 6–7.</ref>.

== Scope ==
The scope covers European administrative law, national economic planning, Italian bureaucratic organization, public project management, and public financial oversight <ref>Sandulli (2022), pp. 3–8.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & Administrative Structure ==
* '''Central Role of the European Commission''': The Commission performs semi-annual verifications of milestones and targets before disbursing funds, holding the authority to suspend funding in cases of non-compliance or rule-of-law violations <ref>Sandulli (2022), p. 5.</ref>.
* '''Parallel Administration in Italy''': Establishment of a Control Room (*Cabina di Regia*) within the Presidency of the Council of Ministers, expanded responsibilities for the State General Accounting Office (*Ragioneria Generale dello Stato*), and dedicated Mission Units (*Unità di Missione*) across ministries <ref>Sandulli (2022), p. 6.</ref>.
* '''Project-Based Organization''': Transitioning from rigid traditional administrative procedures to corporate project management techniques, turning the Single Responsible Officer (*RUP*) into an active project manager <ref>Sandulli (2022), pp. 7–8.</ref>.
* '''Concomitant Audit by the Court of Auditors''': Strengthening real-time external oversight (*concomitant control*) by the Italian Court of Auditors (*Corte dei Conti*) throughout project implementation <ref>Sandulli (2022), p. 8.</ref>.

== Implementation ==
Implemented across all Italian ministries and regional authorities as the primary beneficiary of NGEU funds through strict semi-annual performance schedules <ref>Sandulli (2022), pp. 5–6.</ref>.

== Policy Issues ==
* '''Procedural Time Constraints''': Public performance evaluations risk shifting focus away from substantive investment quality toward strict compliance with time constraints <ref>Sandulli (2022), pp. 6–7.</ref>.
* '''Organizational Strain''': Demanding deadlines impose significant workloads on administrative staff, raising risks of human resource allocation conflicts across concurrent projects <ref>Sandulli (2022), pp. 7–8.</ref>.

== Proposed Reforms ==
Integrates corporate project management and business engineering methodologies into the public sector while leveraging concomitant external controls by the *Corte dei Conti* to secure timely target fulfillment <ref>Sandulli (2022), pp. 7, 8.</ref>.

== Related Entities ==
* '''[[Aldo Sandulli]]''': Author and Professor of Administrative Law <ref>Sandulli (2022), p. 3.</ref>.
* '''[[Sabino Cassese]]''': Cited Legal Scholar <ref>Sandulli (2022), p. 3.</ref>.
* '''[[European Commission]]''': Primary Oversight and Controlling Authority for NGEU <ref>Sandulli (2022), p. 5.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>Sandulli (2022), pp. 3–8.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>Sandulli (2022), pp. 3–8.</ref>

=== '''Wiki Entity Page''' ===
{{Infobox
| stable_id = judicial-policy-nigeria-virtual-court-proceedings-2020
| name = Virtual Court Proceedings (VCP) Framework in Nigeria
| type = Judicial Administration Policy & Legal Technology Strategy
| issuing_authority = National Judicial Council (NJC) of Nigeria & Heads of Judicial Bodies
| legal_basis = NJC Circular No. NJC/CIR/HOC/II/656 (2020); Practice Directions 2020; Evidence (Amendment) Act 2023; ACJL Lagos 2021
| date = April 2020 – Present
| status = Implemented / Active (Under Development)
}}

'''The Virtual Court Proceedings (VCP) Framework in Nigeria''' is a judicial administration policy and legal technology operational framework in the Federal Republic of Nigeria that permits the remote conduct of civil and criminal court proceedings through the utilization of audio-visual links (AVL) and digital communication platforms.

== Summary ==
Initiated in April 2020 by the National Judicial Council (NJC) as a response to the Covid-19 pandemic crisis, the VCP evolved from a mere emergency instrument into a permanent judicial modernization strategy. Although it has received broad support from legal practitioners for increasing efficiency and saving time, the implementation of VCP in Nigeria still faces serious challenges in the form of a national electricity crisis, uneven internet access, technophobia, and technical conflicts with public document evidentiary rules.

== Legal Basis ==
The implementation of VCP in Nigeria is based on a series of circulars, practice directions, and national legislation:
* '''NJC Circular No. NJC/CIR/HOC/II/656''' (April 6, 2020) regarding the prevention of the spread of Covid-19 and the use of VCP.
* '''Practice Direction for Remote Hearing of Cases in the Lagos State Judiciary 2020'''.
* '''High Court of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) Abuja Covid-19 Practice Direction 2020'''.
* '''Federal High Court of Nigeria Practice Direction for Sitting During Covid-19 Period 2020'''.
* '''National Industrial Court of Nigeria (NICN) Practice Direction 2020'''.
* '''Administration of Criminal Justice (Amendment) Law of Lagos State 2021''' (Section 12(2) which recognizes VCP in criminal trials).
* '''Court of Appeal of Nigeria (Civil Procedure) Rules 2021'''.
* '''Evidence (Amendment) Act of Nigeria 2023''' (Sections 1–10 regarding the recognition of digital oaths, computer evidence, and electronic signatures).
* '''Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999''' (Section 36 regarding the right to a fair and public hearing).

== Background ==
Prior to 2020, the application of technology in the Nigerian judiciary only covered e-filing and e-service in certain state courts. The outbreak of the Covid-19 pandemic forced the cessation of physical court operations. To prevent case backlogs, the NJC issued a national instruction for judicial bodies to utilize audio-visual networks to hold remote hearings.

== Objectives ==
1. Ensure business continuity of judicial functions under both emergency and normal conditions.
2. Increase the efficiency and speed of legal dispute resolution in courts.
3. Cut travel costs and risks for advocates, witnesses, and litigants.
4. Modernize the Nigerian judiciary to align with international judicial standards (such as in Singapore, Australia, and the UK) [31–37].

== Scope ==
The VCP policy applies across all Federal and State judicial jurisdictions in Nigeria, with trial focus points in two main legal hubs:
* '''Lagos State:''' The national commercial center with the highest case volume.
* '''Federal Capital Territory (FCT) Abuja:''' The center for high-level judicial institutions (Supreme Court, Court of Appeal, Federal High Court, NICN).

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Conduct of Digital Hearings:''' The use of video conferencing platforms (such as Zoom and WebEx) to hear statements from parties, witnesses, and legal arguments.
* '''Digital Oaths and Access:''' Recognition of oaths taken via video link and the electronic transmission of trial files.
* '''Ethics and Courtroom Decorum:''' The obligation to maintain lawyer-client confidentiality, official advocate attire, and the orderliness of the virtual courtroom.

== Implementation ==
* '''Participation Levels:''' Based on a 2024 empirical study of 353 advocates, 46.5% of respondents stated they had direct experience leading/participating in VCP hearings [48–51].
* '''Advanced Regulatory Phase:''' The passage of the ''Evidence (Amendment) Act 2023'' strengthened the legal legitimacy of electronic evidence and digital signatures used in the VCP.

== Policy Problems ==
1. '''Basic Infrastructure:''' The electricity supply crisis (where 92 million citizens lack stable electricity) and weak internet networks are the biggest barriers to VCP (agreed upon by 85% of respondents).
2. '''Constitutional Debate:''' Claims emerged that virtual trials violate the requirement for a public hearing under Section 36 of the 1999 Constitution. An attempted constitutional amendment failed in the Senate in March 2022.
3. '''Evidentiary Procedure Conflicts:''' Section 90(1)(c) of the Evidence Act 2011 still requires the submission of physical Certified True Copies (CTC) of public documents, complicating document tendering in virtual trials.
4. '''Technophobia & Skills:''' 45.5% of advocates/judges experience fear of new technology (technophobia) and 34.9% lack IT skills.

== Reform / Change ==
* The need for comprehensive harmonization between VCP Practice Directions and the Civil Procedure Rules of each respective court.
* Recommendation to amend Section 90(1)(c) of the Evidence Act so that electronic copies of public document CTCs can be legally admitted as secondary evidence.
* The need for planned investment from judicial institutions and the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA) in IT training and the provision of hardware facilities in court buildings.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''National Judicial Council (NJC):''' The oversight body and primary catalyst for the VCP policy in Nigeria.
* '''Lagos State Judiciary & High Court FCT Abuja:''' Key pioneers in the trials and issuance of VCP Practice Directions.
* '''Babcock University School of Law:''' The academic institution conducting the empirical evaluation study of VCP.
* '''Cecep Mustafa / [private person]:''' *Not found in the available sources* [FACT] [1–102].

== See Also ==
* [[National Judicial Council of Nigeria]]
* [[Evidence (Amendment) Act 2023]]
* [[Digital Access to Justice]]
* [[International Journal for Court Administration]]

== References ==
* Davies, A., Olugasa, O., & Odunaike, D. A. (2024). Experimental Trials of the Virtual Court Proceedings in Nigeria: An Empirical Perspective. ''International Journal for Court Administration'', 15(2), 4. DOI: https://doi.org/10.36745/ijca.550.
* Olugasa, O. & Davies, A. (2022). Remote Court Proceedings: Justice Online or Justice on the line. ''International Journal for Court Administration'', 13(2).
* National Judicial Council (NJC). (2020). Circular No. NJC/CIR/HOC/II/656: Preventive Measures On The Spread Of Corona Virus (Covid-19).
* Lagos State Judiciary. (2020). Practice Direction for Remote Hearing of Cases in the Lagos State Judiciary 2020.

'''The Framework for Development and Evaluation of Community Engagement at the Neighbourhood Justice Centre''' is a policy framework, a five-phase developmental model, and a community engagement evaluation model implemented at the Neighbourhood Justice Centre (NJC) in the City of Yarra, Melbourne, Australia [1–4, 18–20].

== Summary ==
Published by Tim Haslett, Chris Ballenden, Louise Bassett, Saroj Godbole, and Kerry Walker in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this policy framework formulates the governance and evaluation of community engagement at Australia's first multi-jurisdictional community court. Utilizing a systems thinking approach (Causal Loop Diagrams - CLD), the framework maps the shift in resource allocation across five developmental phases to demonstrate the effectiveness of crime prevention and restorative justice interventions to the government.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Department of Justice Victoria Policy Framework (2007):''' ''The Neighbourhood Justice Centre: Community Justice in Action in Victoria''.
* '''UK Ministry of Justice Report (2009):''' ''Engaging Communities in Criminal Justice'' (8 Principles of Community Justice).
* '''Victoria Multi-jurisdictional Statutes:''' The consolidation of authority from the ''Magistrates' Court'', ''Children's Court (Criminal Division)'', ''Victims of Crime Assistance Tribunal'' (VOCAT), and ''Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal'' (VCAT).
* '''Comparative Public Participation Models:''' ''Ladder of Citizen Participation'' (Arnstein, 1969), ''IAP2 Spectrum'', and ''Varieties of Participation'' (Fung, 2006) [4–8].

== Background ==
The NJC was established in 2007 to create a justice system that is more integrated, responsive, accessible, and effective in addressing the root causes of criminal behavior in the City of Yarra. However, after four years of operation, the NJC faced challenges, including the absence of a single agreed-upon definition of community engagement and demands from funding authorities for accountability in measuring qualitative impacts.

== Objectives ==
1. Maximize the capacity of the Yarra community to prevent and manage the impacts of crime.
2. Enhance conflict resolution through Appropriate Dispute Resolution (ADR) and restorative justice.
3. Provide efficient, transparent, and inclusive judicial services at the local level.
4. Function as an "incubator" to transfer community justice practices to the mainstream justice system.

== Scope ==
This policy applies to all NJC operations in the City of Yarra, Melbourne, encompassing four multi-jurisdictional judicial bodies, professional communities (Client Services / rehabilitation service providers), and local communities (Neighbourhood Houses and public housing estate committees).

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Three Dimensions of Integrated Justice:''' Integrating community justice, restorative justice, and therapeutic jurisprudence.
* '''Two-Way Process:''' Community engagement evolves from the initial outreach of the court to the active participation of the community in determining how justice is administered.
* '''Problem Solving Conferences:''' Deliberation sessions involving stakeholders and defendants to formulate recovery agreements as alternatives to imprisonment.
* '''Respected Community Members Panels:''' Conflict resolution skills training for community leaders to proactively extinguish potential ethnic clashes.

== Implementation (Five Phases of Development) ==
1. '''Phase 1 (Establishing the NJC Concept):''' Establishing initial contact with professional and local community organizations.
2. '''Phase 2 (Development of Communities):''' Organizing ''Problem Solving Conferences'' and formally engaging the community [24–26].
3. '''Phase 3 (Independence and Resilience of Local Communities):''' Building the resilience and independent governance of local partner organizations.
4. '''Phase 4 (Systemic and Policy Related Interventions):''' Collaborating on crime prevention policies with Victoria Police, local government, universities, and the Office of Housing.
5. '''Phase 5 (Change within the Justice System):''' Disseminating NJC's best practices throughout the Victoria justice system.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Difficulty in Qualitative Measurement:''' Crime prevention and community building activities are difficult to evaluate using conventional quantitative metrics.
* '''Shifts in Political Support:''' A change in the Victoria government in 2010 resulted in the loss of its primary sponsor (Attorney General Rob Hulls) and brought demands to accelerate the transfer of practices to mainstream courts.

== Reform / Change ==
* Adoption of a developmental evaluation questions matrix at the end of each phase [23, 27–28, 31, 34, 38].
* Institutionalization of systems thinking (Causal Loop Diagrams) to transparently manage the shifting allocation of resources.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Department of Justice Victoria:''' The parent organization that established the NJC.
* '''University of Queensland & Ponte Consulting:''' Partners in formulating the evaluation framework.
* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]:''' ''Not found in the available sources.'' [FACT] [1–39].

== See Also ==
* [[Neighbourhood Justice Centre]]
* [[Community Justice]]
* [[Therapeutic Jurisprudence]]
* [[International Journal for Court Administration]]

== References ==
* Haslett, T., Ballenden, C., Bassett, L., Godbole, S., & Walker, K. (2010). Framework for Development and Evaluation of Community Engagement. ''International Journal for Court Administration'', 3(1), 1–15.
* Department of Justice (Victoria). (2007). ''The Neighbourhood Justice Centre: Community Justice in Action in Victoria''. Melbourne: Department of Justice.

| legal_basis = Courts Legislation (Neighbourhood Justice Centre) Act 2006 (Act No. 51/2006); Attorney-General's 2004 Justice Statement

'''Neighbourhood Justice Centre (NJC) in Yarra''' is Australia's first community justice centre, established in the suburb of Collingwood, City of Yarra, Melbourne, Victoria. Set up as a specialized division of the Magistrates' Court of Victoria and the Children's Court of Victoria under the '''Courts Legislation (Neighbourhood Justice Centre) Act 2006''', the NJC integrates multi-jurisdictional court proceedings with on-site legal aid, correctional, rehabilitation, and mediation services. The NJC applies a therapeutic jurisprudence and restorative justice approach, and adopts systems thinking methodology (process mapping, causal loop diagrams/CLDs, and simulation modeling) to understand caseflow dynamics and prevent reoffending.

== Summary ==
Announced in April 2005 under the ''A Fairer Victoria'' initiative, the NJC was designed to address high crime rates in Collingwood, which stood at six times the Victorian state average (52,754 per 100,000 residents). Drawing inspiration from the Red Hook Community Justice Center in New York, the NJC combines court proceedings with community outreach, targeting a 50/50 balance between adjudication and crime prevention activities. A 2008 systems thinking intervention by Ponte Consulting helped NJC management address the emerging tendency toward excessive "court-centricity" and predicted a workload crisis in correctional services caused by the lagged effect of community-sentence supervision [3, 9, 31–33].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Courts Legislation (Neighbourhood Justice Centre) Act 2006 (Act No. 51/2006):''' Received Royal Assent on 15 August 2006, establishing the NJC Court as a new division of the Magistrates' Court and Children's Court.
* '''Attorney-General's 2004 Justice Statement & A Fairer Victoria Policy:''' The Victorian government's policy framework for improving access to justice and modernizing courts.
* '''CBO & ICO Statutory Framework:''' The arrangements governing Community Based Orders (CBO) and Intensive Correction Orders (ICO) as non-custodial sentences.

== Background & International Inspiration ==
The NJC's development was informed by the success of community court models abroad, particularly the Red Hook Community Justice Center in Brooklyn, New York. Evaluation data from Red Hook showed a 50% increase in compliance with community sanctions, a contribution of 79,000 hours of community service, a 300% increase in public confidence, and a decline in serious crime (murders -48%, rapes -79%, robberies -25%).

== Scope & Systems Thinking Methodology ==

=== Three Core Systems Thinking Tools ===
1. '''Process Mapping:''' Developed 23 micro-level process maps based on 28 interviews with operational staff, shifting the mindset from case-by-case thinking to process-based thinking.
2. '''Causal Loop Diagrams (CLDs):''' Mapped the cause-and-effect relationships between perceptions of court fairness, public trust, and reductions in crime rates [12–17].
3. '''Stock-Flow Simulation Modeling:''' Modeled caseflow across 4 sub-systems (Magistrates' Court, Crimes/Family Violence, VCAT, VOCAT) and HR dynamics to forecast operational capacity limits.

=== Three Core Strategic Goals ("Elevator Statements") ===
In an organizational learning workshop, NJC staff formulated three new goals:
1. ''A Fair Go for All''.
2. ''Reducing Re-Offending''.
3. ''Taking the Law Back to the Village''.

== Policy Issues & Workload Dynamics ==
1. '''The "Court-Centricity" Problem:''' A gradual surge in court caseload consumed staff time, preventing community outreach activities from reaching the intended 50% target.
2. '''Lagged Corrections Workload Effect:''' While the client-services assessment unit processes cases within 2 weeks, the corrections unit supervises CBO/ICO clients for 12 to 18 months. A temporary surge in court mentions creates a correctional-capacity crisis felt up to 18 months later [31–33].
3. '''Loss of Organizational Memory ("Rookies and Pros" Model):''' High staff turnover (e.g., losing 3 of 5 registry staff within 6 months) created a "rookie factor" that slowed institutional learning and process maturity.
4. '''Use of 2D Tools for 3D Problems:''' The limitations of conventional (2D) administrative tools in handling the complex, interconnected dynamics (3D) of judicial policy.

== Reform & Organizational Learning ==
Applying systems thinking allowed NJC leadership to restructure and streamline court scheduling, identify operational capacity limits, and reallocate staff time toward crime-prevention programs and local community engagement.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Magistrates' Court of Victoria & Department of Justice, Victoria:''' Parent organization and budget oversight body for the NJC.
* '''Cecep Mustafa:''' Not found in the available sources [1–41].
* '''[private person]:''' Not found in the available sources [1–41].

'''The Data-Informed Case Management for Special Immigrant Juvenile Status Cases Policy Framework''' is a judicial governance and data-informed case management framework for handling Special Immigrant Juvenile Status (SIJS) predicate finding requests in state trial courts. Formulated by Danielle Fox, Hisashi Yamagata, Lili Khozeimeh, Marianne Hendricks, Madeleine Jones, and Rick Dabbs (Montgomery County Circuit Court, Maryland, USA) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), Vol. 8 No. 3 (July 2017), the framework analyzes the transformation of custody and guardianship case management for unaccompanied alien children (UAC). It traces the evolution from a single-judge handling model (pre-2014) and a two-judge model (2014–2015), to a ''three-judicial officer model'' (2015–2016) driven by a dedicated SIJS database and automated scheduling to guarantee legal certainty, drastically reduce case backlogs, and uphold the rule of law [1–36].

== Summary ==
Published by the management and research team of the Montgomery County Circuit Court (Maryland) in the IJCA (July 2017), this policy framework evaluates the state trial court's response to the massive influx of Unaccompanied Alien Children (UAC) requesting factual predicate findings for Special Immigrant Juvenile Status (SIJS) [1–5]. Based on federal laws (INA 1990 and TVPRA 2008) and state legislation (Maryland Law Chapter 96 of 2014), state courts are mandated to issue predicate orders confirming the impossibility of parental reunification due to abuse, neglect, or abandonment [5–8]. Analyzing 939 SIJS cases (May 2013–September 2016), the study maps the evolution of case management from a reactive, attorney-driven single-judge model to a highly structured '''Three-Judicial Officer Model''' (two judges for guardianship and one magistrate for custody). This model is supported by court-managed automated scheduling (within a 125-day timeframe) and the generation of automated ''critical review sheets'' [13–22, 25]. These reforms successfully catapulted the court's clearance rate from 32% to 90% and slashed the average age of pending cases by 44% (from 233 days to 130 days).

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) of 1990 (8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(27)(J)) & TVPRA 2008:''' US federal regulations establishing SIJS immigration relief for immigrant children subjected to parental abuse, neglect, or abandonment.
* '''Maryland Code, Family Law § 1-201(b)(10) & Maryland Law Chapter 96 (2014):''' State legislation expanding the equity jurisdiction of Maryland courts up to the age of 21 specifically for SIJS factual predicate findings.
* '''Maryland Rules of Procedure (Rules 2-121–2-126, 10-201, & 16-307):''' Court rules governing the service of process (including international service), guardianship procedures, and the authority of family case managers.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
A surge in unaccompanied child immigration from Central America triggered a massive influx of SIJS requests in Maryland family courts. This influx threatened to overwhelm the court's docket capacity if not aggressively managed using data-informed strategies.

== Objectives ==
1. Ensure the issuance of SIJS factual predicate findings is timely, consistent, and accurate to support the rule of law.
2. Slash the accumulation of case backlogs and reduce the age of pending cases to comply with Maryland’s family case time standards.
3. Transform judicial administration through Differentiated Case Management (DCM) and the active utilization of performance data.

== Scope ==
This policy encompasses the evaluation of the governance of custody and guardianship cases involving SIJS requests at the Montgomery County Circuit Court, Maryland, from 2013 to 2016.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Three-Judicial Officer Model:'''
** Assigning two independent judges specifically for guardianship + SIJS cases, and one dedicated magistrate for custody + SIJS cases.
* '''Court-Managed Automated Scheduling:'''
** Reclaiming scheduling control from attorneys; the IT system automatically schedules custody and SIJS hearings within 125 days after valid service of process is achieved.
* '''Pre-Trial File Verification & Critical Review Sheets:'''
** Rigorous screening of international service and translated documents by case managers, followed by the generation of automated critical review sheets prior to hearings.

== Implementation ==
* '''Evolution of the Case Management System:''' The transition from a single-judge model (2007–2013), to a two-judge approach (2014–2015), and finally to the three-judicial officer model with special dockets (2015–2016).
* '''Development of a Dedicated SIJS Database:''' The creation of a secondary support database that pulls data from the court's main system to automate reporting and generate critical working documents.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Challenges with International Service of Process:''' The extreme difficulty of lawfully serving legal summons to parents residing in foreign countries.
* '''Vulnerability to Staff Turnover:''' Operational disruptions and temporary dips in case closures resulting from the turnover of key case management personnel.

== Reform / Change ==
* Establishing a cross-functional Technical Advisory Board to continuously identify business efficiency gaps and monitor data.

The '''Northern European Independent Judicial Agency & Integrated Court Governance Framework''' is a court governance and administration framework that proposes the establishment of an independent judicial agency (''sui generis'' non-departmental public body) and the implementation of an "Integrated Management" system to separate court administration from executive ministries [1, 13, 16, 21–23].

== Summary ==
Issued by Tin Bunjevac in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (2013) based on comparative research on court governance, this framework analyzes the structural failures of the traditional "executive/departmental model." The executive model causes a misalignment between authority and responsibility, stifles long-term strategic planning, and exacerbates case backlogs. This framework recommends adopting the "Northern European Model" (found in Sweden and the Netherlands), which combines an independent agency providing macro-level resources with integrated management at the local court level [13, 16, 21–25].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Dutch Judiciary (Organization) Act''': Section 85 (board nomination procedures), Section 94 (legal quality mandate), and Section 106 (minister's limited intervention rights).
* '''Irish Courts Service Act 1998''': Section 11 (stakeholder board composition) and Section 13 (compliance with general government policy).
* '''Swedish Appropriations Directions for Courts & Freedom of Information Laws''': Regulations on the autonomy of independent bodies and public information transparency in Sweden.
* '''Her Majesty’s Courts and Tribunals Service Framework Document 2011''' (England & Wales).

== Background ==
In the traditional departmental model, courts depend on the Ministry of Justice for budgeting, human resources, and operations. The physical separation of the executive bureaucracy leaves judges without access to analytical data and planning infrastructure. Simultaneously, there has been a surge in caseloads (>30%), increased legal complexity, and growing demands for public transparency. The culture of judicial individuality further weakens internal court coordination.

== Objectives ==
1. Separate court administrative operations from the executive ministerial bureaucracy.
2. Implement an integrated management system where courts independently manage finances, human resources, and workflows.
3. Guarantee judicial independence while strengthening soft accountability and organizational transparency.
4. Improve the efficiency and quality of legal services for the public.

== Jurisdiction & Scope ==
This governance policy is analyzed comparatively across various jurisdictions:
* '''Australia''': Victoria, New South Wales, South Australia, and the Federal Court of Australia.
* '''Northern & Western Europe''': Sweden (SNCA), Netherlands (Raad voor de Rechtspraak), Ireland (Courts Service), England & Wales (HMCTS), Denmark, Norway, and Germany.
* '''North America''': Canada and the United States.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Independent Judicial Agency (Sui Generis Body)''': An independent public body outside the ministry tasked with providing budgets, ICT, physical infrastructure, and research development without interfering in daily judicial decisions.
* '''Integrated Management System''': The consolidation of financial, HR, administrative, and case flow management under the leadership of a Chief Judge and a professional court administrator.
* '''Diverse Board Composition''': The supervisory board consists of both judges and public/non-judicial representatives to ensure social accountability.
* '''Diminished Ministerial Responsibility''': The reduction of direct ministerial oversight, replaced by public transparency, freedom of information laws, annual reports, and Ombudsman oversight.

== Implementation ==
* '''Sweden (SNCA / Domstolsverket)''': Since 1975, the SNCA has operated as an independent agency providing ICT systems, training, budgeting, and physical facilities for all Swedish courts.
* '''Netherlands (Raad voor de Rechtspraak)''': Since 2002, the Dutch Council for the Judiciary has managed the judicial budget, conducted judicial quality research (RechtspraaQ system), and coordinated legal updates.
* '''Federal Court of Australia''': Implementation of integrated management under the leadership of a Chief Judge and a Chief Court Administrator.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Misalignment of Authority & Responsibility''': The executive model separates those responsible for outcomes (judges) from those holding budget and HR authority (ministries).
* '''Over-sized Judges' Councils''': Courts managed by councils of >15 judges (like the 19th-century Council of Judges) have proven managerially ineffective.
* '''Judicial Individuality & Passive Administration''': The resistance of some judges to comply with integrated organizational management directives, resulting in a fragmented organization.

== Evaluation & Reform ==
The Northern European independent agency system is evaluated as superior and more flexible than departmental models. Recommended reforms include:
* Establishing compact management boards (4–9 members) with fixed-term appointments based on merit.
* Institutionalizing soft accountability through public information openness and customer appreciation surveys.
* Elevating judicial quality standards via compliance research, peer-review evaluations, and continuous training.
* Clearly delineating macro-level infrastructure support from micro-level local court management autonomy.

== Unresolved Issues ==
Tensions remain between judicial individuality and demands for organizational uniformity. There are also challenges in defining the exact demarcation of authority between the central judicial agency and local court leaders, as well as the risk of politicization in board nomination processes if not managed by an independent recommendation committee.

'''The Reiling ODR & Court Digitalization Policy Framework''' is a judicial technology policy framework and evaluation model for the integration of Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) into the justice system. Formulated by Dr. Dory Reiling (Senior Judge at the Amsterdam First Instance Court and former Product Owner of the Dutch Digital Civil Procedure) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), Vol. 8 No. 2 (May 2017), the framework analyzes the ''eKantonrechter'' experiment (a Dutch digital small claims civil procedure based on Article 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure). It critically evaluates the transition from mere "court digitalization" toward an integrated, user-centric ODR model based on the real-world needs of justice seekers [1–21].

== Summary ==
Published by Dr. Dory Reiling in the IJCA (May 2017), this policy framework evaluates the lessons learned from the development of the ''eKantonrechter'' digital civil procedure in the Netherlands, launched in May 2014 [1–4, 10–11]. Designed to adjudicate small claims disputes (<€25,000), as well as employment and consumer matters based on Article 96 of the Dutch Code of Civil Procedure (Rv), the procedure utilized DigiD and eHerkenning authentication alongside a structured form interface [4, 7–10]. However, evaluations revealed that the ''eKantonrechter'' experienced total user rejection (zero usage in 2016). Reiling exposes that this failure was rooted in the consensual requirement of Article 96 Rv, which necessitated both parties to submit the dispute jointly—a romantic academic assumption that contradicts the reality of litigation, where a claimant typically wants the court to assert their rights over an uncooperative defendant. Reiling argues that judicial ODR must shift from a technology-centric approach to a user-centric design that maps out citizens' actual "justice moments" and integrates ODR directly into the standard contentious court proceedings [13, 15–17].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Wetboek van Burgerlijke Rechtsvordering (Rv) Article 96:''' A provision in the Dutch Code of Civil Procedure that serves as the basis for consensual small claims procedures without mandatory legal representation.
* '''Technology for Justice Guidelines (Reiling, 2010):''' Guiding principles for judicial web accessibility based on an understanding of citizens' information needs.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
Court digitalization innovations frequently fail because they are designed around the internal assumptions of judges and technocrats rather than the real-world behaviors and needs of the public seeking to resolve legal problems.

== Objectives ==
1. Transform judicial digitalization from the mere computerization of physical files into user-centric ODR integration.
2. Provide digital access to justice that is fair, fast, accessible, and sustainable.
3. Actively transfer the "ownership of the problem" back to the litigating parties.

== Scope ==
This policy encompasses an evaluation of the ''eKantonrechter'' procedure in the Netherlands and provides a comparative analysis of international ODR systems (CyberSettle, DemanderJustice, Rechtwijzer, CRT British Columbia).

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Evaluation of eKantonrechter and Consensuality Failure:'''
** The consensual digital civil procedure failed to attract users (zero usage in 2016) because claimants refused to register jointly with defendants, combined with high court fees and the lack of an appeal mechanism.
* '''Paradigm Shift to User-Centric Design:'''
** Judicial IT design must be rooted in mapping the users' "justice moments" rather than institutional technocratic assumptions.
* '''Network/Cloud Problem-Solving Model:'''
** Recognizing that citizens' dispute resolution pathways are non-linear and require various ODR instruments seamlessly integrated with formal court processes.

== Implementation ==
* '''Development of eKantonrechter (2014):''' The creation of a Digital Justice Kiosk utilizing DigiD/eHerkenning authentication with a mix of structured and unstructured questionnaire forms.
* '''Integration of ODR and Formal Courts:''' Adopting resolutions from the ODR2016 conference in The Hague to fuse pre-trial ODR instruments into the official judicial litigation chain.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Reluctance of Defendants to Participate:''' The inherent difficulty of inducing a defendant to voluntarily join an ODR process without legal pressure or incentives.
* '''High Costs of Digital Litigation:''' Maintaining high official court fees serves as a disincentive for citizens considering formal digital ODR platforms.

== Reform / Change ==
* Abandoning the purely consensual ODR model in favor of integrating ODR into contentious (non-voluntary) court proceedings.
* Expanding socio-legal research (e.g., ''Paths to Justice'') to thoroughly understand the actual routes society takes to resolve disputes.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Netherlands Judiciary (De Rechtspraak):''' The developer and administrator of the ''eKantonrechter'' procedure.
* '''Dutch Consumers Union (Consumentenbond):''' The testing partner for the digital form user panels.
* '''HIIL & ODR2016:''' The organizers of the 15th International ODR Conference at the Peace Palace in The Hague.
* '''[private person]:''' A Law student at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta (NIM: 2410611102), specializing in Constitutional Law. The structural implementation of e-justice and user-centric procedural rights discussed in this framework offer vital comparative perspectives for modern constitutional legal studies. Cecep Mustafa is not found in the available sources [FACT] [1–22].

Die Studie zeigt auf, warum das Verfahren im Jahr 2016 nicht genutzt wurde (Zero Usage): Die Anforderung der Einvernehmlichkeit (Artikel 96 Rv), bei der Kläger und Beklagter den Streit gemeinsam einreichen müssen, widerspricht der rechtlichen Realität. L'étude explique pourquoi la procédure n'a pas été utilisée en 2016 (utilisation nulle) : l'exigence de consensualité (article 96 Rv), qui oblige le demandeur et le défendeur à soumettre conjointement le litige, contredit la réalité juridique. Reiling soutient que les tribunaux doivent abandonner une approche centrée sur la technologie au profit d'un modèle ODR centré sur l'utilisateur, axé sur les véritables « moments de justice » des citoyens, et intégrer directement l'ODR dans les procédures judiciaires contentieuses.
* '''Base Légale:''' Code de procédure civile (Rv) Art. 96 ; Lignes directrices sur la technologie pour la justice (2010).

=== Italiano ===
'''Quadro di digitalizzazione dei tribunali e risoluzione online delle controversie (ODR) di Reiling'''
Pubblicato dalla Dott.ssa Dory Reiling nell' ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA, 2017), questo quadro valuta la procedura civile digitale olandese ''eKantonrechter''. Lo studio rivela i motivi per cui la procedura ha registrato un utilizzo nullo nel 2016: il requisito della consensualità (Articolo 96 Rv), che obbliga attore e convenuto a presentare congiuntamente la controversia, contraddice la realtà legale. Reiling sostiene che i tribunali devono passare da un approccio tecno-centrico a un modello ODR incentrato sull'utente, basato sui veri "momenti di giustizia" dei cittadini, integrando l'ODR direttamente nei procedimenti giudiziari contenziosi.
* '''Base Legale:''' Codice di procedura civile (Rv) Art. 96; Linee guida sulla tecnologia per la giustizia (2010).
