| '''Group 3: Settlement (Settlement Support)''' || Uncertain Outcome / ''Win-Win'' (Active disputes encouraged to settle) || '''9%''' || Web prelodgement forms, asynchronous communication (email), & negotiation software || Adelaide prelodgement notices (Australia), e@dr Singapore, & ''Cybersettle.com'' New York City [19–21].
|-
| '''Group 4: Judgment (Judicial Adjudication)''' || Uncertain Outcome / ''Zero-Sum'' (Contradictory civil disputes) || '''8%''' || Electronic case files (e-case file), multimedia evidence search, & knowledge management || Complex digital files in the US, Netherlands, and Australia [22–25].
|-
| '''Other / Supervisory''' || Bankruptcies, juvenile justice, register supervision || 23% || ''Not categorized as dispute resolution'' || Commercial and land registration.
|}

== Caseflow Re-engineering Strategy ("Shifting Left and Down") ==
* '''Simplification (Shifting Left):''' Creating routines and standard legal formulas reduces case uncertainty, moving cases from Group 4 (Judgment) to Group 2 (Notarial) or Group 1 (Title).
* '''Early Intervention (Shifting Down):''' Facilitating early mediation and providing ''golden legal nuggets'' (practical, jargon-free legal guidance - Susskind) encourages parties to settle disputes out of court.

== Application of Party Litigation Theory (Galanter: One-Shotters vs. Repeat Players) ==
* '''Repeat Players:''' Financial institutions or corporations that frequently act as plaintiffs in Group 1 (Title). Courts benefit by opening channels for bulk electronic data entry.
* '''One-Shotters:''' Ordinary citizens who rarely litigate in court. Courts are obligated to provide clear web portals to improve procedural justice for them.

'''Policy Framework on Comparative Legal Metrics, Transnational Actor Accountability, and EU Digital Extraterritoriality''' (''The Power of Numbers and the Role of Law: On the Way to the Global Accountability of Transnational Actors?'') is a comparative law and legal philosophy analytical framework authored by Giorgio Resta in ''The Italian Law Journal'' (Vol. 10 Nos. 01-02/2024, pp. 43–55) <ref>Resta, G. (2024). The Power of Numbers and the Role of Law: On the Way to the Global Accountability of Transnational Actors?. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 10(1-2), 43–55.</ref>. The work reviews the comparative monograph ''Comparative Legal Metrics: Quantification of Performances as Regulatory Technique'' (2023, edited by M. Bussani, S. Cassese, and M. Infantino) <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 43, 44.</ref>; analyzes the transformation of "quantification of performance" into an instrument of governance (''governance by numbers'') and a subtle, generative, and opaque Foucauldian form of power <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 43, 45, 46.</ref>; examines domestic and transnational actor accountability mechanisms through Global Administrative Law <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 46, 48.</ref>; and dissects the extraterritoriality trends of European Union digital regulations (GDPR, DMA, DSA, Data Act, Data Governance Act, and AI Act) alongside their impacts on digital sovereignty, jurisdictional conflicts (''US CLOUD Act'' vs ''Art. 48 GDPR''), and technological inequality/digital colonialism towards developing countries (Global South) <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 49, 50, 52, 54, 55.</ref>.

== Executive Summary ==
Authored by [[Giorgio Resta]] (Full Professor of Comparative Law at Roma Tre University), this article analyzes performance quantification (''legal metrics'') as a novel instrument of power in global society <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 43, 44.</ref>. Applying a theoretical framework derived from Michel Foucault, Resta demonstrates that power based on metrics and quantitative indicators (such as World Bank rankings or university ratings) operates not through vertical repression, but as a generative and opaque mechanism <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 45, 46.</ref>. In response to algorithmic opacity in artificial intelligence systems and the regulatory immunity of transnational actors, the European Union has extended its jurisdiction extraterritorially through digital regulation (the ''Brussels Effect''), including the GDPR, DMA, DSA, Data Act, and EU AI Act <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 47, 50, 51, 52.</ref>. However, Resta cautions that uncalibrated extraterritorial reach risks igniting jurisdictional conflicts with the ''US CLOUD Act'' while creating trade barriers and digital neocolonialism for developing nations in the Global South <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 53, 54, 55.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''European Union Digital Frameworks''':
** ''General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) (Regulation (EU) 2016/679)'': Article 3 (Targeting Criterion/Jurisdiction), Articles 15 & 22 (Access Rights & Automated Decision-Making/Profiling), Article 27 (EU Representative Obligation), Article 48 (Anti-FISA Clause), Recital 63 (Trade Secrets & Intellectual Property Boundaries) <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 46, 47, 50, 51, 54.</ref>.
** ''Directive 95/46/EC'': Article 4(1)(a) (Place of Establishment) & Article 25 (Adequate Level of Protection) <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 50, 51.</ref>.
** ''Digital Markets Act (DMA) (Regulation (EU) 2022/1925)'': Article 1(2) (Core Platform Services & Targeting) <ref>Resta (2024), p. 51.</ref>.
** ''Digital Services Act (DSA) (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065)'': Article 2(1) (Intermediary Services & Location) <ref>Resta (2024), p. 51.</ref>.
** ''Data Governance Act (DGA) (Regulation (EU) 2022/868)'': Article 5(9)–(11) & Article 31 (Anti-FISA Clause) <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 51, 52, 54.</ref>.
** ''Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854)'': Article 1(3) & Article 32(2) (Anti-FISA / Conflict of Laws) <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 51, 52, 54.</ref>.
** ''Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act) (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)'': Article 2(1)(a)–(c) (Extraterritorial Scope & Output Used in EU), Article 5 (Prohibitions), Article 22 (EU Representative Obligation), Recital 22 <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 46, 52, 53, 54.</ref>.
* '''Foreign Statutes & Key Jurisprudence''':
** ''US CLOUD Act (Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data Act)'' <ref>Resta (2024), p. 54.</ref>.
** ''State v Loomis 881 N.W.2d 749 (Wis. 2016)'' (Algorithmic Risk Assessment & Trade Secrets) <ref>Resta (2024), p. 47.</ref>.
** ''CJEU Jurisprudence'': Case C-131/12 ''Google Spain / Costeja Gonzalez''; Case C-507/17 ''Google v CNIL''; Case C-362/14 ''Schrems I''; Case C-311/18 ''Schrems II'' <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 50, 51.</ref>.

== Core Policy Pillars & Analysis ==
=== 1. Quantification as Foucauldian Power ===
Performance metrics substitute traditional hierarchical authority with horizontal, self-enforcing compliance incentives <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 43, 45.</ref>. Modern machine-learning systems introduce algorithmic opacity (''fallacy of inscrutability'') where decision rationale is concealed behind proprietary trade secrets, undermining procedural due process rights as seen in ''State v Loomis'' <ref>Resta (2024), p. 47.</ref>.

=== 2. Extraterritoriality & The Brussels Effect ===
The EU projects regulatory standards globally by applying the targeting criterion across its digital legislative suite <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 50, 51.</ref>. Notably, Article 2(1)(c) of the EU AI Act extends jurisdiction to third-country providers whose AI output is utilized within the European Union, making EU standards de facto global benchmarks <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 52, 53.</ref>.

=== 3. Jurisdictional Conflicts and Impact on the Global South ===
Direct conflicts emerge between US extraterritorial demands under the ''CLOUD Act'' and EU statutory prohibitions against non-treaty foreign data transfers under Anti-FISA clauses (Art. 48 GDPR, Art. 31 DGA, Art. 32 Data Act) <ref>Resta (2024), p. 54.</ref>. Furthermore, heavy compliance mandates—such as appointing EU representatives under Art. 27 GDPR and Art. 22 AI Act—disproportionately penalize tech startups in developing countries, worsening digital colonialism <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 54, 55.</ref>.

'''Quadro Politico sulla Metrica Giuridica Comparata, Responsabilità degli Attori Transnazionali ed Estraterritorialità Digitale dell'UE''' (''The Power of Numbers and the Role of Law: On the Way to the Global Accountability of Transnational Actors?'') è un quadro di analisi di diritto comparato e filosofia del diritto formulato da Giorgio Resta in ''The Italian Law Journal'' (Vol. 10 Nos. 01-02/2024, pp. 43–55) <ref>Resta, G. (2024). The Power of Numbers and the Role of Law: On the Way to the Global Accountability of Transnational Actors?. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 10(1-2), 43–55.</ref>. L'opera recensisce la monografia comparativa ''Comparative Legal Metrics: Quantification of Performances as Regulatory Technique'' (2023, a cura di M. Bussani, S. Cassese e M. Infantino) <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 43, 44.</ref>; analizza la trasformazione della "quantificazione delle prestazioni" in uno strumento di governance (''governance by numbers'') e in una forma di potere foucaultiano sottile, generativo e opaco <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 43, 45, 46.</ref>; esamina i meccanismi di responsabilità degli attori interni e transnazionali attraverso il Diritto Amministrativo Globale <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 46, 48.</ref>; e scompone le tendenze di estraterritorialità dei regolamenti digitali dell'Unione Europea (GDPR, DMA, DSA, Data Act, Data Governance Act e AI Act) unitamente ai loro impatti sulla sovranità digitale, sui conflitti di giurisdizione (''US CLOUD Act'' vs ''Art. 48 GDPR'') e sulla disuguaglianza tecnologica/colonialismo digitale nei confronti dei paesi in via di sviluppo (Global South) <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 49, 50, 52, 54, 55.</ref>.

== Sintesi Esecutiva ==
Redatto da [[Giorgio Resta]] (Professore Ordinario di Diritto Comparato presso l'Università degli Studi Roma Tre), questo articolo esamina la quantificazione delle prestazioni (''legal metrics'') come nuovo strumento di potere nella società globale <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 43, 44.</ref>. Utilizzando il quadro teorico di Michel Foucault, Resta dimostra che il potere basato su metriche e indicatori quantitativi (come le classifiche della Banca Mondiale o i rating universitari) non opera in modo verticale o repressivo, ma attraverso un meccanismo generativo e opaco <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 45, 46.</ref>. Per contrastare l'opacità algoritmica nei sistemi di intelligenza artificiale e l'immunità normativa degli attori transnazionali, l'Unione Europea ha esteso la propria giurisdizione in via estraterritoriale tramite la regolamentazione digitale (il cosiddetto ''effetto Bruxelles''), includendo GDPR, DMA, DSA, Data Act e EU AI Act <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 47, 50, 51, 52.</ref>. Tuttavia, Resta avverte che un'estensione estraterritoriale non calibrata rischia di innescare conflitti giurisdizionali con l'''US CLOUD Act'' e di creare barriere commerciali e neocolonialismo digitale per i paesi del Sud del Mondo <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 53, 54, 55.</ref>.

== Basi Giuridiche ==
* '''Regolamentazione Digitale dell'Unione Europea''':
** ''Regolamento Generale sulla Protezione dei Dati (GDPR) (Regolamento (UE) 2016/679)'': Articolo 3 (Criterio del Targeting/Giurisdizione), Articoli 15 e 22 (Diritti di Accesso e Processi Decisionali Automatizzati/Profilazione), Articolo 27 (Obbligo del Rappresentante UE), Articolo 48 (Clausola Anti-FISA), Considerato 63 (Limiti del Segreto Commerciale e Proprietà Intellettuale) <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 46, 47, 50, 51, 54.</ref>.
** ''Direttiva 95/46/CE'': Articolo 4(1)(a) e Articolo 25 <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 50, 51.</ref>.
** ''Digital Markets Act (DMA) (Regolamento (UE) 2022/1925)'': Articolo 1(2) <ref>Resta (2024), p. 51.</ref>.
** ''Digital Services Act (DSA) (Regolamento (UE) 2022/2065)'': Articolo 2(1) <ref>Resta (2024), p. 51.</ref>.
** ''Data Governance Act (DGA) (Regolamento (UE) 2022/868)'': Articolo 5(9)–(11) e Articolo 31 (Clausola Anti-FISA) <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 51, 52, 54.</ref>.
** ''Data Act (Regolamento (UE) 2023/2854)'': Articolo 1(3) e Articolo 32(2) (Anti-FISA / Conflitto di Leggi) <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 51, 52, 54.</ref>.
** ''Legge sull'Intelligenza Artificiale (EU AI Act) (Regolamento (UE) 2024/1689)'': Articolo 2(1)(a)–(c) (Ambito Estraterritoriale ed Output Utilizzato nell'UE), Articolo 5 (Divieti), Articolo 22 (Nomina del Rappresentante UE), Considerato 22 <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 46, 52, 53, 54.</ref>.
* '''Normative Straniere e Giurisprudenza Chiave''':
** ''US CLOUD Act (Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data Act)'' <ref>Resta (2024), p. 54.</ref>.
** ''State v Loomis 881 N.W.2d 749 (Wis. 2016)'' (Valutazione Algoritmica del Rischio e Segreto Commerciale) <ref>Resta (2024), p. 47.</ref>.
** ''Giurisprudenza della Corte di Giustizia dell'UE (CGUE)'': Causa C-131/12 ''Google Spain / Costeja Gonzalez''; Causa C-507/17 ''Google v CNIL''; Causa C-362/14 ''Schrems I''; Causa C-311/18 ''Schrems II'' <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 50, 51.</ref>.

== Pilastri delle Politiche e Analisi ==
=== 1. Quantificazione come Potere Foucaultiano ===
Le metriche giuridiche sostituiscono le tradizionali gerarchie con incentivi di conformità orizzontali e autoinflitti <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 43, 45.</ref>. L'apprendimento automatico nei sistemi di IA genera opacità algoritmica (''fallacy of inscrutability''), dove la motivazione della decisione è protetta dal segreto industriale, limitando le garanzie del giusto processo come nel caso ''State v Loomis'' <ref>Resta (2024), p. 47.</ref>.

=== 2. Estraterritorialità ed Effetto Bruxelles ===
L'UE proietta i propri standard normativi su scala globale adottando il criterio del targeting nella sua legislazione digitale <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 50, 51.</ref>. L'Articolo 2(1)(c) dell'EU AI Act estende l'applicazione ai fornitori di paesi terzi qualora l'output generato dall'IA sia utilizzato nell'Unione Europea <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 52, 53.</ref>.

=== 3. Conflitti di Giurisdizione e Impatto sul Sud Globale ===
Sussiste un contrasto diretto tra le richieste estraterritoriali statunitensi previste dal ''CLOUD Act'' e le disposizioni UE che vietano il trasferimento di dati ad autorità straniere senza trattati internazionali (Art. 48 GDPR, Art. 31 DGA, Art. 32 Data Act) <ref>Resta (2024), p. 54.</ref>. Inoltre, i costi elevati per la conformità (come la nomina di un rappresentante ex Art. 27 GDPR e Art. 22 AI Act) svantaggiano le start-up dei paesi in via di sviluppo, alimentando il colonialismo digitale <ref>Resta (2024), pp. 54, 55.</ref>.

'''Training and Recruitment of Judges in Germany''' is a judicial policy study and legal education system monograph authored by Johannes Riedel (Chief Justice / President of the Court of Appeal in Cologne, Germany) and published in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), Vol. 5, No. 2, October 2013 (ISSN 2156-7964) [1–3].

== Summary ==
This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the recruitment procedures, state examinations, competence profiles (''Anforderungsprofile''), and initial training for career judges in the Federal Republic of Germany [1–5]. The German judicial system utilizes a uniform legal qualification concept (''Einheitsjurist''), meaning all registered legal professions (judges, prosecutors, lawyers, and legal civil servants) undergo the exact same university education and practical training (''Vorbereitungsdienst''). The selection of career judges is conducted independently by the 16 states (''Länder'') through the Ministries of Justice, Higher Regional Courts, and Judicial Electoral Committees (''Richterwahlausschüsse'').

== Legal Basis ==
* '''German Constitution (Grundgesetz - GG):'''
** ''Article 33(2):'' Ensures every citizen's right to equal access to public office based solely on aptitude, qualifications, and professional ability (''Eignung, Befähigung und fachliche Leistung'').
** ''Articles 92 & 95:'' Regulate the separation of judicial powers between the Federation and the 16 ''Länder''.
* '''German Judiciary Act (Deutsches Richtergesetz - DRiG):'''
** ''Sections 5 & 7:'' Regulate academic qualifications and state examinations (''Befähigung zum Richteramt'').
** ''Section 9:'' Requires German citizenship, loyalty to the democratic legal order, judicial qualifications, and '''social competence''' (added during the 2002 reform).
* '''State Legal Training Acts:''' Such as the ''Juristenausbildungsgesetz Nordrhein-Westfalen'' (JAG NRW).

== Legal Education System & State Examinations ==
1. '''University Studies & First State Examination (Erstes Staatsexamen):''' Theoretical legal studies at a university averaging 4 years, culminating in the First Examination divided between a state board exam and a university faculty exam.
2. '''Preparatory Service (Vorbereitungsdienst):''' A 2-year paid practical training period that includes rotations in civil courts (5 months), criminal courts/prosecution (3 months), administrative agencies (3 months), and law firms (10 months).
3. '''Second State Examination (Zweites Staatsexamen):''' A practical graduation exam focusing on drafting judgments, indictments, and lawyer pleadings.
4. '''Passing Threshold:''' Only about '''15% of graduates''' successfully achieve an "above average" score ($\ge 9.00$ points / ''vollbefriedigend'' out of an 18-point scale), serving as the primary threshold to be invited for a judicial recruitment interview.

== Competence Profiles & Selection Procedures ==
The ''Länder'' Ministries of Justice utilize competence profiles (''Anforderungsprofile'') encompassing four main categories:
* '''Professional Competence:''' Mastery of the law, ability to apply it in practice, mature judgment, and understanding of judicial duties.
* '''Personal Competence:''' Natural authority, physical/mental resilience under pressure, ability to make swift decisions, and awareness of personal weaknesses.
* '''Social Competence:''' Teamwork ability, communication, conflict resolution/mediation, and public service awareness.
* '''Leadership Competence:''' Clarity of instructions and trust in staff.

=== Assessment Center Model (Cologne Court of Appeal District Example) ===
The 1-day selection process includes [32–36]:
1. '''Group Discussion:''' Debating a legal policy issue to test structured discussion skills and openness to other opinions.
2. '''Working Test (10 Cases):''' Completing 10 concise civil/criminal procedure tasks under time pressure to test prioritization and decision-making speed.
3. '''Self-Reference (Visitenkarte):''' A written reflection on personal achievements and motivations.
4. '''Multi-Stakeholder Panel Interview:''' Interviewed by the President of the Court of Appeal, President of the Regional Court, Head of Human Resources, Equal Opportunity/Gender Representative, and a Staff Council Representative.

== Initial Training of New Judges ==
Newly appointed probationary judges (averaging 28–30 years old) undergo a probationary period of 3–5 years before receiving a lifetime appointment. Initial training includes [43–46]:
* Assignment to a 3-judge panel (''Landgericht'') to share responsibilities with senior judges.
* An initial workload reduction (50%–70%) in certain administrations.
* A compulsory 3-day seminar covering trial techniques, witness examination, time management, and communication psychology.

== Policy Problems ==
1. '''Interview Bias:''' The risk of selection panels favoring highly eloquent candidates over thoughtful, quieter candidates, requiring a balanced evaluation against their multi-year academic track record.
2. '''Lack of Transparency in Federal Judicial Selection:''' The election of federal supreme court judges by the ''Richterwahlausschuss'' at the federal level is conducted without open public job advertisements (''Ausschreibung'').
3. '''Impact of Single-Judge Reforms:''' Changes to procedural codes mandating first-instance trials be decided by single judges reduce opportunities for young judges to learn within panels.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

'''The Romanian Judicial Training in Sentencing and Lifelong Learning Policy Framework''' is an empirical judicial training policy framework and lifelong experiential learning model for judges and prosecutors ("magistrates") regarding sentencing. Formulated by Diana Richards (University College London / UCL, 2015) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), it is based on an empirical study of 510 respondents operating under the Romanian National Institute of Magistracy (NIM). The framework compares the recruitment pathways for recent graduates (the ''NIM route'') with those for experienced practitioners (the ''direct route/induction''), and examines the levels of appreciation for initial training, continuous training, e-learning, and the development of "judicial craft" as judicial experience increases [1–3, 14–17, 27–30, 51–56].

== Summary ==
Published by Diana Richards in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this policy framework reviews the empirical findings regarding Romanian magistrates' attitudes toward sentencing training. Using a sample of 510 respondents governed by the National Institute of Magistracy (NIM), the study discovered that 93% of magistrates consider initial training to be highly useful for their careers. A key finding highlights the dynamic that "appreciation comes with experience," meaning that the appreciation for initial training and university legal education significantly increases as magistrates accumulate judicial experience [31–32, 51–52]. Junior judges desperately require direct practical experience through 2nd-year court internships and job-shadowing, whereas senior judges prefer normative legal discussion seminars, complex case studies, and live online Q&A sessions [33–35, 38–41, 52–55].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Romanian Judicial Recruitment and Training Framework:''' The legal framework regulating the hybrid recruitment tracks consisting of the ''NIM Route'' (2 years of training) and the ''Direct Route'' (2 months of induction training) [14–16, 25–28].
* '''EJTN Lot 1 Study on Best Practices in Training of Judges and Prosecutors (2014):''' The official European Commission report officially recognizing the four best practices of the Romanian NIM.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
Research on judicial decision-making requires a developmental dimension. Romania's hybrid system provides a unique opportunity to compare inexperienced judges with former practicing lawyers within the same training environment at the NIM [14–17].

== Objectives ==
1. Empirically measure the perceptions of judges and prosecutors regarding the effectiveness of initial, induction, and continuous training [1, 23–24].
2. Map teaching method preferences based on levels of judicial experience (experiential learning) [31–35, 51–54].
3. Evaluate the feasibility of teaching "judicial craft" and assess the effectiveness of e-learning [46–50, 55–56].

== Scope ==
This policy covers the judicial training models in Romania, with a specific focus on criminal judges and public prosecutors operating under the oversight of the NIM.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''The NIM Hybrid Recruitment Routes:'''
** ''NIM Route:'' A 2-year training program for recent law graduates without practical legal experience [18, 25–28].
** ''Direct Route:'' A 2-month intensive induction training for practitioners with a minimum of 5 years of legal experience [25–28, 30].
* '''Training Method Preferences Based on Experience:'''
** ''New Judges:'' Prioritize court internships and job-shadowing over in-class sessions [33–35, 52, 54].
** ''Senior Judges:'' Prioritize seminars discussing legal stipulations, complex case studies, and live online Q&A sessions [38–41, 54–55].
** ''The Unpopularity of Mock Trials:'' Trial simulations are largely unpopular due to the dominance of "passive watchers" who find the exercise frustrating [33–34, 53].
* '''Perspectives on Judicial Craft:'''
** 57% of respondents believe that judicial craft can be developed through training, whereas 42% consider it a skill that can only be cultivated through actual trial experience.

== Implementation ==
* '''Empirical Field Survey (2014):''' The collection of 510 questionnaires and the observation of 11 training sessions at the Romanian NIM [27–29].
* '''E-Learning Module Development:''' The implementation of an integrated e-learning platform providing direct access to legislation alongside live Q&A sessions.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Theoretical Oversaturation among New Judges:''' The intense desire of junior judges to immediately practice law in the courtroom rather than enduring extensive theoretical lectures.
* '''Challenges of the New 2014 Legal Codes:''' The necessity of mastering the new criminal code and criminal procedure code without the benefit of established older precedents [41–42].

== Reform / Change ==
* Tailoring training methods to align with the participants' level of experience (''experience-tailored training'').
* Prioritizing real-world court internships over mock trial simulations.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''National Institute of Magistracy (NIM):''' The primary judicial training institution in Romania.
* '''University College London (UCL) Judicial Institute:''' The academic institution conducting the empirical research.
* '''[private person]:''' A Law student at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta (NIM: 2410611102), specializing in Constitutional Law (Hukum Tata Negara). Cecep Mustafa is not found in the available sources [FACT] [1–58].

'''Differentiated Use of Electronic Case Management Systems''' is an analytical framework and judicial ICT policy study authored by Dr. Erwin J. Rooze (former adviser to the Netherlands Council for the Judiciary). Based on international qualitative research (2006–2008) across European countries and Australia, the framework applies '''contingency theory''' to classify judicial ICT applications into three levels of sophistication (Basic, Medium, Advanced), four operational components (Administrative, Logistics, Procedural, Content Management), and three caseflow tracks (Mass, Regular, Complex Caseflows) in order to optimize judicial efficiency and procedural justice [1, 2, 4, 10–15, 25–28, 34, 35].

== Summary ==
Drawing on empirical experience in the Netherlands, Austria, England, Singapore, and Western Australia, Dr. Rooze argues that no single ICT system suits every type of case ("no one best way to organize"). Courts must align ICT investment with the specific characteristics of their caseload: mass caseflows require advanced logistics automation to the point of forming a fully-fledged e-court, while complex caseflows require advanced digital content management, which has been shown to cut judges' analysis time by '''50%''' [10–12, 27, 28, 33, 36, 37].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This document is an academic research article and policy assessment, not a statutory enactment [1–45].
* '''Analyzed Standards Framework:''' Procedural justice standards, efficiency indicators from the European Commission for the Efficiency of Justice (CEPEJ), and the US Department of Justice's Differentiated Case Management (DCM) guidelines.

== Background & Contingency Theory ==
The concept of case management originated in the United States to shift control of case progress from lawyers to the courts. Drawing on organizational contingency theory (Lawrence & Lorsch 1967; Galbraith 1973), Rooze argues that a court's structure and ICT support needs depend on its external environment and its specific area of law (civil, criminal, commercial, administrative) [9–13].

== The Four Components of Case Management (ECMS) ==
1. '''Administrative Management:''' Case registration, unique case-number assignment, file location tracking, and management reporting.
2. '''Logistics Management:''' Guiding caseflow from intake to archiving, milestone planning, capacity allocation (courtrooms, judges, staff), and tracking/tracing.
3. '''Procedural Management:''' Enforcing procedural rules, verifying jurisdiction, checking court fee payments, milestone signaling, and automated notifications.
4. '''Content Management:''' Dynamic text templates, official document drafting, audio/video recording, digital archiving, and automated decision-making for uncontested claims.

== Three Levels of ICT Sophistication ==
* '''Basic Level (Electronic Case Administration):''' Focused on reliable electronic databases, schedule printing, and basic reporting.
* '''Medium Level (Caseflow Support):''' Integrating calendars and judge/staff data to automate milestone tracking and backlog alerts.
* '''Advanced Level (Digital Handling & e-Court):''' Fully paperless digital file handling, self-service web filing, and automated document generation.

== Differentiation by Caseflow Track ==
{| class="wikitable"
|-
! Caseflow Track !! Case Characteristics !! Key ICT Component !! Real-World Examples
|-
| '''Mass Caseflow''' || High volume, low complexity (e.g., traffic violations, small money claims). || Advanced Logistics Management & e-Court Automation || Money Claim Online (England) & Mahnverfahren (Austria).
|-
| '''Complex Caseflow''' || Low volume, high complexity (e.g., intellectual property, international cybercrime). || Advanced Content Management & Digital File Analysis || 50% reduction in judicial analysis time in the Netherlands & Western Australia.
|-
| '''Regular Caseflow''' || Medium volume, medium complexity. || Procedural Management to maintain standard scheduling || Use of advanced web forms in Singapore.
|}

== Policy Issues & Implementation Realism ==
1. '''Failure of Judicial ICT Projects:''' Many judicial ICT projects in Europe have failed due to excessive optimism and rigid system designs that ignore case-type contingency (Velicogna 2007).
2. '''Preventing Wasted Investment:''' High-tech ICT investment in mass caseflows should focus on administrative efficiency, while investment in complex caseflows should focus on judges' knowledge work [31–33].

'''Policy Framework for the Italian and European Economic Constitutions Post-COVID-19 Pandemic and Ukraine War Crises''' (''Kerangka Kebijakan Konstitusi Ekonomi Italia dan Uni Eropa Pasca-Krisis Pandemi COVID-19 dan Perang Ukraina'') is a comparative public law and constitutional analytical framework formulated by Monica Rosini and Marta Tomasi to examine the transformation of the Italian Economic Constitution (Articles 35–47 of the 1948 Italian Constitution) and the European Union Economic Constitution following the dual crises of the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine <ref>Rosini, M., & Tomasi, M. (2023). The European and Italian Economic Constitution(s) After the Recent Crises: Towards a New Role for State Powers?. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 15(2), 293–326.</ref>. This framework evaluates the paradigm shift from budgetary discipline/austerity models toward an enhanced active role for the state (*State as promoter, investor, and shareholder*), the activation of the general escape clause of the *Stability and Growth Pact (SGP)*, temporary State Aid frameworks (*Temporary Framework & Temporary Crisis Framework*), collective financing instruments under *NextGenerationEU / Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF)* / *Italian PNRR* (€191.5 billion), the *Patrimonio Rilancio* mechanism (CDP / MEF), and the normative convergence between Article 41(3) of the Italian Constitution and Article 3(3) TEU regarding the highly competitive social market economy <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 295, 298, 301, 303, 312, 314, 319, 325.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Authored by [[Monica Rosini]] (Associate Professor of Public Law at the Free University of Bozen-Bolzano) and [[Marta Tomasi]] (Assistant Professor of Comparative Public Law at the University of Trento), this study presents a comprehensive evaluation of how pandemic and energy shocks reshaped the relationship between the state and the economy in Italy and the European Union <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), p. 295.</ref>. The authors establish that market failures during ecosystemic shocks necessitated unprecedented EU solidarity mechanisms (*NextGenerationEU*) and triggered the revival of the Italian state as a primary investor and major shareholder in strategic economic sectors <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 301, 311, 314, 324.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
The economic constitutional framework in Italy and the European Union rests on national constitutional provisions, primary EU treaty law, and emergency secondary legislation:
* '''[[Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana]]''':
** *Article 3*: Substantive equality and social dignity guarantee <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), p. 297.</ref>.
** *Articles 35–47*: Title III of Part I governing Economic Relations <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), p. 295.</ref>.
** *Article 41*: Private economic initiative freedom, limited by social utility and environmental protection, alongside economic planning powers <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 297, 318.</ref>.
** *Article 43*: Legal basis for nationalization and state assistance to strategic enterprises <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), p. 297.</ref>.
* '''[[Treaty on European Union]] (TEU)''': Article 3(3) establishing the EU commitment to a highly competitive social market economy <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), p. 325.</ref>.
* '''[[Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union]] (TFEU)''': Article 122 (solidarity principle) and Article 106 (State Aid rules) <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 301, 309.</ref>.
* '''EU Recovery Regulations''': Regulation (EU) 2021/241 establishing the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 302, 316.</ref>.
* '''Italian Emergency Legislation''': Decreto-Legge 19 maggio 2020 n. 34 (*Decreto Rilancio*) Article 27 establishing *Patrimonio Rilancio* <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 312, 313.</ref>; Decreto MEF 3 febbraio 2021 n. 261 <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), p. 313.</ref>.

== Background & Paradigm Shift ==
Prior to the 2020 pandemic, the European Economic Constitution was dominated by strict SGP budgetary rules and fiscal discipline that frequently conflicted with the open and mixed nature of the Italian Economic Constitution <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 296, 298.</ref>. The COVID-19 outbreak and the Ukrainian war forced the EU to activate the SGP *general escape clause* and issue common debt via *NextGenerationEU* <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 300, 302.</ref>. This shift re-evaluated the role of the state from a mere market guardian into an active director of economic development <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 320, 324.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Mitigate health and energy crisis impacts through direct grants, liquidity guarantees, and social rights preservation <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 299, 310.</ref>.
* Rebuild the Italian economy via the execution of the *Italian PNRR*, oriented toward green and digital transitions <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 316, 319.</ref>.
* Align economic growth goals with substantive social equality and environmental sustainability <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 318, 325.</ref>.

== Scope ==
The scope of this policy framework includes the flexibility analysis of the Italian Constitution, ECB monetary interventions (PEPP), the SURE scheme, NGEU/RRF/PNRR funding, the creation of CDP's *Patrimonio Rilancio*, the expansion of golden powers, and EU energy price regulations (REPowerEU and Market Correction Mechanism) <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 293–326.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & Patrimonio Rilancio Structure ==
* '''SGP Escape Clause & Temporary State Aid''': Suspending SGP rules enabled Italy to approve budget variations exceeding €150 billion <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 300, 309, 310.</ref>.
* '''Patrimonio Rilancio Scheme (Art. 27 DL 34/2020)''':
# Government bond allocation of up to €44 billion managed by Cassa Depositi e Prestiti (CDP) over a 12-year duration <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 312, 313.</ref>.
# Divided into 3 dedicated sub-funds (Decreto MEF 261/2021): FNST (Temporary Emergency Support), SNSF (National Strategic Fund for capital injections in firms with turnover >€50 million), and FNRI (Corporate Restructuring Fund) <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), p. 313.</ref>.
* '''Italian PNRR Architecture (€191.5 Billion)''': Distributed across 6 key Missions, accompanied by mandatory Horizontal Reforms (judiciary and public administration), Enabling Reforms, and Sectoral Reforms <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 316, 319, 321.</ref>.

== Policy Challenges & Post-Crisis Fiscal Discipline ==
* '''Temporary NGEU vs. Structural Needs''': NextGenerationEU remains a temporary instrument maturing in 2058 without granting permanent independent taxing powers to the EU, thus falling short of a full "Hamiltonian Moment" <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 302, 303.</ref>.
* '''Post-2023 Uncertainty''': Whether state interventions and social rights priorities will solidify long-term or revert to strict fiscal austerity rules remains an ongoing legal and political debate <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 306, 326.</ref>.

''''Quadro Politico della Costituzione Economica Italiana ed Europea Post-Crisi Pandemica da COVID-19 e Guerra in Ucraina'''' (''The European and Italian Economic Constitution(s) After Recent Crises Policy Framework'') è un quadro analitico di diritto pubblico e costituzionale comparato formulato da Monica Rosini e Marta Tomasi per esaminare la trasformazione della Costituzione Economica Italiana (Articoli 35–47 della Costituzione Italiana del 1948) e della Costituzione Economica dell'Unione Europea a seguito delle doppie crisi della pandemia da COVID-19 e della guerra in Ucraina <ref>Rosini, M., & Tomasi, M. (2023). The European and Italian Economic Constitution(s) After the Recent Crises: Towards a New Role for State Powers?. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 15(2), 293–326.</ref>. Questo quadro valuta il cambio di paradigma dal modello di disciplina di bilancio/austerità verso un rafforzato ruolo attivo dello Stato (*State as promoter, investor, and shareholder*), l'attivazione della clausola di salvaguardia generale (*general escape clause*) del *Patto di Stabilità e Crescita (PSC)*, i quadri temporanei per gli Aiuti di Stato (*Temporary Framework & Temporary Crisis Framework*), gli strumenti di finanziamento collettivo *NextGenerationEU / Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF)* / *PNRR Italiano* (pari a 191,5 miliardi di euro), lo strumento del *Patrimonio Rilancio* (CDP / MEF) e la convergenza normativa tra l'Articolo 41 comma 3 della Costituzione Italiana e l'Articolo 3(3) TUE riguardante l'economia sociale di mercato fortemente competitiva <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 295, 298, 301, 303, 312, 314, 319, 325.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Scritto da [[Monica Rosini]] (Professoressa Associata di Diritto Pubblico presso la Libera Università di Bolzano) e [[Marta Tomasi]] (Ricercatrice di Diritto Pubblico Comparato presso l'Università di Trento), questo studio presenta una valutazione complessiva di come gli shock pandemico ed energetico abbiano ridefinito il rapporto tra lo Stato e l'economia in Italia e nell'Unione Europea <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), p. 295.</ref>. Le autrici evidenziano che i fallimenti del libero mercato durante shock ecosistemici hanno reso necessari inediti strumenti di solidarietà europea (*NextGenerationEU*) e hanno determinato il ritorno dello Stato italiano quale investitore primario e azionista di riferimento nei settori economici strategici <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 301, 311, 314, 324.</ref>.

== Basi Giuridiche ==
Il quadro della costituzione economica in Italia e nell'Unione Europea si fonda su disposizioni costituzionali nazionali, sul diritto primario dell'UE e su regolamenti d'urgenza:
* '''[[Costituzione della Repubblica Italiana]]''':
** *Articolo 3*: Uguaglianza sostanziale e garanzia della dignità sociale <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), p. 297.</ref>.
** *Articoli 35–47*: Titolo III della Parte I relativo ai Rapporti Economici <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), p. 295.</ref>.
** *Articolo 41*: Libertà dell'iniziativa economica privata, limitata dall'utilità sociale e dalla tutela ambientale, unitamente ai poteri di programmazione economica <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 297, 318.</ref>.
** *Articolo 43*: Base giuridica per nazionalizzazioni e aiuti alle imprese strategiche <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), p. 297.</ref>.
* '''[[Trattato sull'Unione Europea]] (TUE)''': Articolo 3(3) che stabilisce l'impegno dell'UE per un'economia sociale di mercato fortemente competitiva <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), p. 325.</ref>.
* '''[[Trattato sul Funzionamento dell'Unione Europea]] (TFUE)''': Articolo 122 (principio di solidarietà) e Articolo 106 (norme sugli Aiuti di Stato) <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 301, 309.</ref>.
* '''Regolamenti UE sulla Ripresa''': Regolamento (UE) 2021/241 che istituisce il Dispositivo per la Ripresa e la Resilienza (RRF) <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 302, 316.</ref>.
* '''Legislazione d'Urgenza Italiana''': Decreto-Legge 19 maggio 2020 n. 34 (*Decreto Rilancio*) Articolo 27 relativo all'istituzione del *Patrimonio Rilancio* <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 312, 313.</ref>; Decreto MEF 3 febbraio 2021 n. 261 <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), p. 313.</ref>.

== Contesto ed Evoluzione del Paradigma ==
Prima della pandemia del 2020, la Costituzione Economica Europea era dominata dalle rigide regole del PSC e dalla disciplina di bilancio, che spesso entravano in conflitto con la natura aperta e mista della Costituzione Economica Italiana <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 296, 298.</ref>. L'emergenza COVID-19 e il conflitto in Ucraina hanno costretto l'UE ad attivare la *clausola di salvaguardia generale* del PSC e a emettere debito comune con *NextGenerationEU* <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 300, 302.</ref>. Questa evoluzione ha rivalutato la funzione dello Stato, trasformandolo da mero custode del mercato in un vero e proprio regolatore dello sviluppo economico <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 320, 324.</ref>.

== Obiettivi ==
* Attenuare gli impatti delle crisi sanitaria ed energetica attraverso contributi diretti, garanzie di liquidità e salvaguardia dei diritti sociali <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 299, 310.</ref>.
* Rilanciare l'economia italiana tramite l'attuazione del *PNRR Italiano*, orientato verso le transizioni ecologica e digitale <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 316, 319.</ref>.
* Armonizzare la crescita economica con la giustizia sociale e la sostenibilità ambientale <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 318, 325.</ref>.

== Ambito di Applicazione ==
L'ambito di questo quadro politico comprende l'analisi della flessibilità della Costituzione Italiana, gli interventi monetari della BCE (PEPP), il programma SURE, i finanziamenti NGEU/RRF/PNRR, la creazione del *Patrimonio Rilancio* di CDP, l'estensione del *golden power* e la regolamentazione europea sui prezzi dell'energia (REPowerEU e Meccanismo di Correzione del Mercato) <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 293–326.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Chiave e Struttura del Patrimonio Rilancio ==
* '''Attivazione della Clausola del PSC ed Aiuti di Stato Flessibili''': La sospensione del PSC ha consentito all'Italia di approvare scostamenti di bilancio superiori a 150 miliardi di euro <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 300, 309, 310.</ref>.
* '''Struttura del Patrimonio Rilancio (Art. 27 DL 34/2020)''':
# Assegnazione di titoli di Stato fino a 44 miliardi di euro gestiti da Cassa Depositi e Prestiti (CDP) con durata di 12 anni <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 312, 313.</ref>.
# Articolato in 3 sotto-fondi (Decreto MEF 261/2021): FNST (Fondo Nascita e Sviluppo Temporaneo), SNSF (Sotto-fondo Nazionale Strategico per interventi in aziende con fatturato >50 milioni di euro) e FNRI (Fondo Nazionale Ristrutturazione Imprese) <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), p. 313.</ref>.
* '''Architettura del PNRR Italiano (191,5 Miliardi di Euro)''': Suddiviso in 6 Missioni chiave, accompagnato da Riforme Orizzontali obbligatorie (giustizia e pubblica amministrazione), Riforme Abilitanti e Riforme Settoriali <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 316, 319, 321.</ref>.

== Criticità Politiche e Disciplina di Bilancio Post-Crisi ==
* '''Natura Temporanea di NGEU vs Bisogni Strutturali''': NextGenerationEU rimane uno strumento temporaneo con scadenza nel 2058 senza la concessione di poteri fiscali autonomi all'UE, non configurando un vero e proprio "Momento Hamiltoniano" <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 302, 303.</ref>.
* '''Incertezza Post-2023''': Rimane aperto il dibattito se l'intervento pubblico e la centralità dei diritti sociali si consolideranno permanentemente o se vi sarà un ritorno alla rigida disciplina di bilancio <ref>Rosini & Tomasi (2023), pp. 306, 326.</ref>.

'''The Assessing The Courts In Russia: Parameters Of Progress Under Putin Framework''' is a policy framework and qualitative-comparative analysis of judicial administration in the Russian Federation. It evaluates the progress and challenges of court reform from the era of Boris Yeltsin through the Presidency of Vladimir Putin based on seven main criteria (judicial independence, fair procedural law, judicial power/jurisdiction, accountability, accessibility, workflow efficiency, and public perception) [1, 2, 9, 15–17, 23–26].

== Summary ==
Published by Prof. Peter H. Solomon, Jr. (University of Toronto) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this policy framework dissects the journey of judicial reform in the Russian Federation. Addressing the Soviet legacy that left courts weak and dependent, Yeltsin-era reforms provided life tenure for judges and established the Judicial Department. Entering President Vladimir Putin's era, the government allocated tens of billions of rubles through Federal Targeted Programs to raise judicial salaries, expand the network of ''Justices of the Peace'', enact new Criminal and Civil Procedure Codes, and increase public transparency via court websites [15–21]. However, the study underlines that the absolute power of ''court chairmen'' and ''accusatorial bias'' remain major challenges.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Constitution of the Russian Federation (1993):''' Guarantees the principles of judicial independence and the separation of powers.
* '''Conception of Judicial Reform 1991:''' The foundational document for post-Soviet judicial reform.
* '''Criminal Procedure Code of 2001 & Civil Procedure Code of 2002:''' Established adversarial trial principles and shortened procedures (''plea bargaining'').
* '''Federal Targeted Programs (2002–2006 & 2007–2011):''' The budgetary foundation for modeling and modernizing national courts.

== Background ==
Following the collapse of the Soviet Union, the Russian judiciary faced severe budget constraints and the absence of modern procedural laws. During Putin's era, available state coffers were utilized to unblock stalled Yeltsin-era reforms, raising minimum judicial salaries to $1,000/month, and building an accountability system without sacrificing judicial independence.

== Objectives ==
1. Evaluate the achievements of Russian judicial reform using 7 qualitative criteria.
2. Address case delays by strengthening the role of the ''Justices of the Peace''.
3. Enhance transparency and public accountability by publishing decisions on court websites.
4. Formulate 10 future improvement indicators to fully uphold the ''Rule of Law'' [37–42].

== Scope ==
This policy evaluates all pillars of the judiciary in Russia: Courts of General Jurisdiction, Arbitrazh (Commercial) Courts, the Constitutional Court, Justices of the Peace, and the Judicial Department.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Seven Judicial Evaluation Criteria (Solomon):''' (1) Judicial independence; (2) Procedural law ensuring equality of parties; (3) Court power/jurisdiction; (4) Accountability systems; (5) Accessibility; (6) Performance efficiency; (7) Public attitudes and trust.
* '''Absolute Power of Court Chairmen:''' Court chairmen hold the authority to assign case files, control bonuses/facilities, and propose the dismissal of judges to the JQC, making them a potential channel for informal intervention.
* '''Accusatorial Bias & Shortened Procedures:''' Acquittal rates by single judges remain below 1%, while the ''shortened procedure'' is used in 37.5% of cases in District Courts and 47% in Justices of the Peace.

== Implementation ==
* '''Strengthening the Justices of the Peace Network:''' Handling 65% of civil cases and 30% of criminal cases nationwide to reduce the burden on District Courts.
* '''Judicial Salary Increases & Computerization:''' Setting a base judicial salary of at least $1,000/month and launching a national court website system.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Low Salaries for Court Staff:''' Wage disparity between judges and administrative staff triggers high staff turnover rates.
* '''Obstacles to Enforcing Judgments:''' The failure of bailiffs to execute civil/business judgments encourages the widespread use of private collection services.

== Reform / Change ==
* Recommendations to limit term lengths and introduce peer election for court chairmen.
* Abolition of rigid statistical metrics of "judicial error" in the performance evaluation of judges.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Supreme Court & High Arbitrazh Court:''' The apex pillars of Russia's general and commercial judiciaries.
* '''Ministry of Economic Development and Trade (MERT):''' Initiator of the proposed judicial accountability law.
* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]:''' ''Not found in the available sources.'' [FACT] [1–44].

'''Rwanda’s Gacaca Courts Transitional Justice Policy Framework''' is a transitional justice policy framework and Rwandan indigenous community court model reviewed by Markus Zimmer (Executive Editor of the IJCA, 2014) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA). It is based on a 10-year experiment (2002–2012) to try mid- and lower-level perpetrators following the 1994 genocide through a panel of 9 lay judges (respected community elders) without the presence of lawyers. The framework prioritized reconciliation, healing, and community service without violating the necessity of enforcing justice [2, 6–8].

== Summary ==
Published by Markus Zimmer in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this policy framework reviews the successes and challenges of the Gacaca Courts in Rwanda. Following the 1994 genocide, the ''International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda'' (ICTR) in Arusha only prosecuted top-level ringleaders. The mass detention of tens of thousands of lower-level perpetrators paralyzed Rwanda's formal justice system. As a solution, the Rwandan Government revived the indigenous Gacaca courts—a justice system without lawyers, led by panels of 9 lay judges chosen from respected community elders. Operating in open-air settings, these proceedings prioritized reconciliation and community service sentences. Despite possessing flaws when compared to 21st-century Western judicial standards, the Gacaca Courts, which officially closed on June 17–18, 2012, are globally recognized as a bold and innovative transitional justice experiment.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Official Transitional Justice Policy of the Republic of Rwanda:''' The national legal framework governing the establishment and operationalization of the Gacaca Courts.
* '''United Nations Mandate & ICTR Arusha:''' The international legal foundation for handling the Rwandan genocide crimes at the elite leadership level.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
The failure of the international justice system to try lower-level perpetrators and the operational paralysis of Rwanda's formal prisons prompted the birth of this community-based judicial innovation [4–6].

== Objectives ==
1. Independently and inclusively try tens of thousands of mid- and lower-level post-genocide perpetrators.
2. Realize social reconciliation and community healing over the spirit of vengeance.
3. Alleviate the severe burden on the national prison system through community service sentences.

== Scope ==
This policy encompasses the prosecution of mid- and lower-level genocide crimes across villages and towns throughout the Republic of Rwanda.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Panel of 9 Lay Judges:''' Trials were presided over by nine respected community elders without the involvement or representation of lawyers.
* '''Open Community Proceedings:''' Hearings were conducted outdoors in public spaces, attended by local residents and survivors to confirm or refute the defendants' confessional testimonies.
* '''Community Service Sentences:''' A strong preference for community service penalties to restore the community and reintegrate the perpetrators into their original environments.

== Implementation ==
* '''10-Year Operationalization (2002–2012):''' The processing of tens of thousands of genocide suspects through thousands of localized Gacaca panels.
* '''Official Closing Ceremony:''' The formal termination of the Gacaca Courts by the Government of Rwanda on June 17–18, 2012.

== Policy Problems ==

'''The Rwanda Integrated Electronic Case Management System (IECMS) Policy Framework''' is a comprehensive e-justice digitalization and cross-agency case management policy framework developed and implemented by the Ministry of Justice of Rwanda (MoJ) in partnership with Synergy International Systems, Inc. between 2015 and 2017. Documented by Adam Watson, Regis Rukundakuvuga, and Khachatur Matevosyan in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), Special Issue, Vol. 8 No. 3 (July 2017), the system fully integrates the data and case file workflows across the five primary institutions of the justice sector (National Police, Prosecution, Judiciary, Correctional Services, and Civil Litigation Service). Utilizing a Sector Wide Approach (SWAp), the framework was designed to eradicate case backlogs, increase transparency, accelerate contract enforcement, and ensure automated compliance with civil and criminal procedural law [1–17, 20–22].

== Summary ==
Published by Adam Watson, Regis Rukundakuvuga, and Khachatur Matevosyan in the IJCA (July 2017), this policy framework evaluates the successful digital transformation of Rwanda's justice sector through the implementation of the ''Integrated Electronic Case Management System'' (IECMS) [1–3]. Addressing the legacy of case delays, massive paper backlogs, and transparency vulnerabilities post-1994 genocide, the Ministry of Justice spearheaded the development of the IECMS based on a Sector Wide Approach (SWAp) [2, 4–6, 18]. The system seamlessly integrates the processing of criminal and civil cases across five institutions: the Police, Prosecution (NPPA), Judiciary, Correctional Services (RCS), and Civil Litigation [4, 10–11]. Engineered through a rigorous Business Process Reengineering (BPR) phase that produced a 500-page System Design Document, the IECMS was operationalized using a unique strategic triad: ''Developing from the Beginning'' (from Police to Corrections), ''Deploying from the End'' (deploying the courts first to "pull" data), and ''Focusing Forward'' (only processing new cases to prevent overwhelming staff with legacy paper files) [8–9, 20–22]. The IECMS notably catapulted Rwanda's ranking in the World Bank's ''Doing Business'' Enforcing Contracts index by 22 positions, earning Rwanda the highest Quality of Judicial Processes score in Sub-Saharan Africa.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Rwanda Justice Sector Strategic Plan (JRLOS Strategic Plan 2013):''' The strategic planning document mandating the automation of case management across the justice sector.
* '''Rwandan Civil and Criminal Procedural Law:''' The procedural laws that dictate the technical workflow and routing rules programmed into the IECMS.
* '''Legal Provisions for Rwanda's Justice Sector Organizations:''' The foundational laws establishing the National Police (2000), the Judiciary & Prosecution (2004), and the Correctional Services (2010).
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
Fragmented, paper-based justice systems fueled severe case backlogs, execution delays, and corruption risks, prompting the Rwandan government to position ICT as the central enabler of national justice sector development.

== Objectives ==
1. Provide a single, integrated digital point of entry for managing cases from the point of arrest through to sentence execution.
2. Enhance transparency, accountability, equality before the law, and automatic compliance with procedural law.
3. Equip the sector with Business Intelligence and M&E tools (based on international CourTools standards) to measure clearance rates and caseloads per judge accurately.

== Scope ==
This policy encompasses the integration of IT systems across the 5 primary justice sector institutions throughout the entire judicial territory of the Republic of Rwanda.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Integration of 5 Justice Sector Institutions:'''
** Automated data exchange between the Police, Public Prosecution, Courts, Correctional Services, and Civil Litigation via single case IDs and QR codes.
* '''Specialized Deployment Strategy:'''
** '''Developing from the Beginning:''' Software development progressing chronologically from the Police to Corrections.
** '''Deploying from the End:''' Launching the court application first to trigger a "data pull" necessity from Prosecution and Police.
** '''Focusing Forward:''' Processing only new cases electronically to free staff from the burden of digitizing old historical files.
* '''Community-Based eJustice Infrastructure:'''
** Recruiting affordable youth facilitators and establishing e-services kiosks in cybercafés and "smart villages" to assist citizens lacking internet access.

== Implementation ==
* '''BPR and System Design Document Formulation (2015):''' The creation of a 500-page operational prototype by Synergy International Systems and the NCSC.
* '''ToT Execution and Phased Rollout (2016–2017):''' Training 40 technical trainers, launching a 15-court pilot in Kigali (Jan 2016), culminating in a nationwide rollout across all courts (June 2017).

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Limited Citizen Internet Access:''' Only approximately 20% of the population has access to reliable internet, hindering direct public digital engagement.
* '''Institutional Resistance and Work Culture Change:''' Resistance to technological adaptation from senior judges and court staff accustomed to paper-based workflows.

== Reform / Change ==
* Amending procedural law to formalize electronic summons and eliminate obsolete physical/manual procedural requirements.
* Interfacing the IECMS with external agencies such as Court Bailiffs, the National Identification Agency (NIDA), the Rwanda Development Board (RDB), and the Law Reform Commission.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Ministry of Justice of Rwanda (MoJ):''' The primary owner and administrator of the IECMS project.
* '''Synergy International Systems, Inc.:''' The technical software developer of the IECMS.
* '''World Bank:''' The international body that evaluated the positive impact of the IECMS on the ''Doing Business Enforcing Contracts'' index.
* '''[private person]:''' A nineteen-year-old Law student specializing in Constitutional Law (Hukum Tata Negara) at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta for the 2024/2025 academic year. The systemic procedural integration and constitutional due process enhancements analyzed in this framework offer pertinent comparative perspectives for her academic specialization. Cecep Mustafa is not found in the available sources [FACT] [1–34].

The '''Rodolfo Sacco's Comparative Law Method and Legal Formants Framework''' (officially titled ''Rodolfo Sacco’s Conception of The Comparative Law Method'') is a comparative legal science methodology framework that establishes procedures for analyzing comparative legal systems, the doctrine of legal formants (*elementi costitutivi del diritto*), and interdisciplinary comparative research principles.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Katharina Boele-Woelki]], President of [[Bucerius Law School]] and Chair of the [[Commission on European Family Law]], this review evaluates the scholarship of prominent Italian comparative legal scholars [[Rodolfo Sacco]] and [[Piercarlo Rossi]] in their treatise ''Einführung in die Rechtsvergleichung''. The framework emphasizes that comparative law is not merely a single "pure method," but rather a structured combination of methodological approaches designed to identify similarities and differences across jurisdictions, explain their underlying causes, and evaluate normative solutions.

== Legal Basis ==
This methodological framework is rooted in foundational scholarly works and harmonization instruments:
* '''[[Einführung in die Rechtsvergleichung]] (2017)''': The 3rd edition comparative methodology textbook authored by Rodolfo Sacco and Piercarlo Rossi, published by Nomos Verlagsgesellschaft.
* '''[[Legal Formants: A Dynamic Approach to Comparative Law]] (1991)''': The landmark article by Rodolfo Sacco published in the *American Journal of Comparative Law* detailing the theory of legal formants.
* '''[[Principles of European Family Law]]''': Harmonization instruments drafted by the Commission on European Family Law (CEFL) utilizing a combined comparative methodology.

== Background ==
Rodolfo Sacco made a fundamental contribution to comparative legal science by dismantling the myth of national legal homogeneity. Sacco demonstrated that a legal system does not consist of a single, uniform rule, but rather a multiplicity of coexisting and often conflicting elements known as "legal formants" (*formanti del diritto*)—such as statutory provisions, judicial decisions, and scholarly doctrine. Katharina Boele-Woelki's review synthesizes Sacco's core methodological precepts for future generations of comparatists.

== Objectives ==
* Prevent comparative research from predetermining its results (*ex-ante conclusions*).
* Affirm the comparability of legal rules and systems across jurisdictions with different economic foundations.
* Promote integrated interdisciplinary comparative research (*synchronized comparative research*).
* Provide evaluative guidance for European legal harmonization by balancing the search for a common core (*Common Core*) against selecting the best solution (*Better Law*).

== Scope ==
The scope encompasses comparative private law methodology, family law, commercial transactions, interdisciplinary legal studies, and comparative legal translation studies.

== Key Provisions & Five Methodological Principles ==
# '''Methodological Pluralism''': Comparative law is not a single pure method, but a scientific process comprising four distinct stages: description, analysis, explanation, and evaluation.
# '''Absence of Predetermination''': Comparative research is a "journey of discovery" where researchers must not predetermine findings or outcomes prior to conducting the inquiry.
# '''Comparability Across Economic Systems''': Different legal systems remain comparable through establishing a *tertium comparationis* based on structure, function, and consequences, while strictly avoiding superficial quick scans.
# '''Synchronized Interdisciplinary Research''': Promotes *synchronized comparative research*, in which legal scholars and experts from other social sciences conduct simultaneous research in the same jurisdiction.
# '''Balancing Common Core and Better Law''': Harmonization projects should neither blindly chase a common core nor seek unneeded novelty, but must justify adopting a "better law" approach through explicit value-oriented argumentation.

== Implementation ==
Implemented across comparative law curricula at Bucerius Law School, scholarly activities of the International Academy of Comparative Law, and drafting practices for family law principles by the Commission on European Family Law (CEFL).

== Policy Issues ==
* '''Risk of Superficial Quick Scans''': The tendency to scan multiple legal systems rapidly without deep context risks misinterpreting how rules function within local legal cultures.
* '''Challenges of Synchronized Research''': Significant time and resource constraints make fully integrated, multi-jurisdictional *synchronized comparative research* difficult compared to single-jurisdiction *restricted comparative research*.

== Proposed Reforms ==
Encouraging the formation of cross-disciplinary, international research teams to carry out synchronized comparative studies, alongside enforcing transparency in value justifications whenever selecting a *Better Law* standard.

== Related Entities ==
* '''[[Katharina Boele-Woelki]]''': Review Author and President of Bucerius Law School.
* '''[[Rodolfo Sacco]]''': Primary Figure and Originator of the Legal Formants Doctrine.
* '''[[Piercarlo Rossi]]''': Co-author of *Einführung in die Rechtsvergleichung*.

| type = Labor Law, Antidiscrimination & Algorithmic Governance Judicial Policy Framework
| issuing_authority = Raffaello Santagata de Castro / Università degli Studi della Campania 'Luigi Vanvitelli' / The Italian Law Journal
| legal_basis = Codice Civile Art. 1345; D.Lgs. 215/2003 & 216/2003; Statuto dei Lavoratori Art. 15 & 28; Council Directives 2000/43/EC & 2000/78/EC
| date = 2021 (Publication in ItaLJ Vol. 07 No. 02); 2020 (Deliveroo Bologna Court Order)
| status = Operational / Active Jurisprudential & Doctrinal Framework
}}

'''Italian Judicial Policy Framework on Antidiscrimination Law and Algorithmic Decision-Making in Employment''' is a judicial policy framework and doctrinal analysis formulated by Raffaello Santagata de Castro to evaluate the transformation of antidiscrimination law enforcement within Italian labor courts <ref>Santagata de Castro, R. (2021). Antidiscrimination Law in the Italian Courts: New Frontiers on the Topic in the Age of Algorithms. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 07(02), 843–872.</ref>. The framework examines the jurisprudential shift from the traditional civil law model based on unlawful motive (*motivo illecito* - Article 1345 of the Italian Civil Code) toward the European Union antidiscrimination law regime (Directives 2000/43/EC and 2000/78/EC as transposed by Legislative Decrees No. 215/2003 and No. 216/2003). It addresses the shift of the burden of proof, indirect discrimination in automated decision-making and algorithmic management (exemplified by the Deliveroo "Frank" algorithm ruling by the Labour Court of Bologna in 2020), and the procedural legal standing of trade unions and collective interest bodies under Article 28 of the Workers' Statute (*Statuto dei Lavoratori*, Law No. 300/1970) and Class Action Law No. 31/2019 <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 843, 846, 847, 850, 852, 854, 855, 864, 870.</ref>.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Raffaello Santagata de Castro]] (Associate Professor of Labor Law at Università degli Studi della Campania 'Luigi Vanvitelli'), this work analyzes key developments in antidiscrimination jurisprudence within Italian courts <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), p. 843.</ref>. The author highlights the transition from a restrictive application of general civil law principles (*motivo illecito* under Art. 1345 CC) to full alignment with EU antidiscrimination standards <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 846, 847, 854.</ref>. Special emphasis is given to algorithmic discrimination in digital platform work—marked by the landmark decision of the Court of Bologna regarding Deliveroo—and collective enforcement mechanisms led by trade unions <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 854, 855, 869, 870.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
The judicial policy framework relies on both Italian domestic statutes and European Union law instruments:
* '''[[Italian Civil Code]] (Codice Civile, Art. 1345)''': General provision on unlawful motive (*motivo illecito*), historically misapplied to discriminatory dismissals <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 846, 847.</ref>.
* '''[[Workers' Statute]] (Statuto dei Lavoratori, Law No. 300/1970)''':
** ''Article 15'': Nullity of discriminatory measures in employment <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), p. 847.</ref>.
** ''Article 28'': Emergency procedure against anti-union conduct <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 852, 870.</ref>.
* '''[[Legislative Decree No. 215/2003]] & [[Legislative Decree No. 216/2003]]''': Transposition of EU Directives 2000/43/EC and 2000/78/EC into Italian law <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 852, 864.</ref>.
* '''[[Law No. 31/2019]]''': Reform of class action and collective redress mechanisms in Italy <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 844, 864.</ref>.
* '''Key Case Law''':
** ''Italian Court of Cassation'': Judgment No. 6575/2016 (decoupling discriminatory dismissal from subjective intent/unlawful motive) and Judgment No. 1/2020 (applying the shift of burden of proof to collective anti-union actions) <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 848, 870.</ref>.
** ''Labour Court of Bologna'': Order of 31 December 2020 (*Nidil CGIL et al. v. Deliveroo Italy S.r.l.*) on algorithmic indirect discrimination <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 854, 855.</ref>.
** ''Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU)'': *Case C-507/18 (NH v. Associazione Avvocatura per i diritti LGBTI - Rete Lenford)* on collective legal standing without identifiable victims <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 868, 869.</ref>.

== Background & Doctrinal Paradigm Shift ==
Historically, Italian labor courts avoided applying EU antidiscrimination statutory frameworks, analyzing discriminatory dismissals through the lens of Article 1345 of the Civil Code (*motivo illecito*) <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 846, 847.</ref>. This required workers to prove that unlawful intent was the sole determining factor of the employer's decision <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), p. 847.</ref>. In Judgment No. 6575/2016, the Court of Cassation corrected this approach, establishing that discriminatory measures are objectively illegal regardless of the employer's subjective state of mind <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 848, 854.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Eliminate subjective intent requirements (*motivo illecito*) in discriminatory employment litigation <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 847, 854.</ref>.
* Enforce the shift of the burden of proof (*shift of burden of proof*) based on prima facie statistical or factual evidence <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 862, 864, 870.</ref>.
* Extend antidiscrimination oversight to automated decision-making and digital platform algorithms <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 844, 854, 855.</ref>.
* Empower trade unions and collective entities to initiate legal proceedings without an identifiable individual victim <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 868, 870.</ref>.

== Key Issues & The Deliveroo Case ==
* '''Objective Nature of Discrimination''': Alignment with EU standards dictates evaluating adverse effects rather than subjective employer motives <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), p. 854.</ref>.
* '''Deliveroo "Frank" Algorithm (Bologna Labour Court, 2020)''': The Court held that penalizing delivery riders' reputation scores and booking priorities for canceling shifts—even due to participation in strikes or illness—constituted indirect discrimination <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 854, 855.</ref>. The algorithm was ruled "blind" to legitimate reasons for absence <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 855, 856.</ref>.
* '''Burden of Proof in Collective Actions''': Cassation Judgment No. 1/2020 affirmed that procedural rules shifting the burden of proof apply universally, including in collective disputes under Art. 28 of the Workers' Statute <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 862, 870.</ref>.

== Critiques & Unresolved Policy Issues ==
* '''Indirect Discrimination vs. Objective Justification''': Academic scholars noted that classifying algorithmic discrimination strictly as "indirect" allows employers to claim business necessity or objective justification defenses <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 855, 856.</ref>.
* '''Black Box Algorithms & Information Asymmetry''': The absence of a general right to disclosure under CJEU jurisprudence (*Meister*, C-415/10) creates evidentiary hurdles for workers attempting to inspect proprietary code <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 855, 863.</ref>.
* '''Regulatory Horizon''': The proposed EU Artificial Intelligence Act (COM(2021) 206 final) aims to introduce ex-ante compliance and audit standards for high-risk AI recruitment and workforce management systems <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), p. 844.</ref>.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''[[Raffaello Santagata de Castro]]''': Principal Author and Associate Professor at Università degli Studi della Campania 'Luigi Vanvitelli' <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), p. 843.</ref>.
* '''[[Deliveroo Italy S.r.l.]]''': Defendant Platform Company in the Algorithmic Discrimination Lawsuit <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 854, 855.</ref>.
* '''[[Court of Cassation (Italy)|Corte di Cassazione]]''': Italian Supreme Court of Cassation <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 848, 870.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 843–872.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Santagata de Castro (2021), pp. 843–872.</ref>
