The '''United Kingdom Supreme Court''' ('''UKSC''') is the highest court of appeal in the United Kingdom for civil matters across all UK jurisdictions (England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland) and for criminal matters (from England, Wales, and Northern Ireland). Established pursuant to Part 3 of the '''Constitutional Reform Act 2005''', it formally assumed the appellate jurisdiction of the House of Lords on October 1, 2009. The Court operates as an independent, non-ministerial executive department housed in the Middlesex Guildhall on Parliament Square, London.

== Summary ==
Authored by Prof. Gavin Drewry of Royal Holloway, University of London, this case study reviews the background and structural innovation of the UKSC's establishment. The reform was fundamentally triggered by the necessity to meet the standards of objective judicial independence mandated by Article 6(1) of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) and corresponding Strasbourg Court jurisprudence (''Procola v Luxembourg''; ''McGonnell v UK''), which demand a strict physical and constitutional separation between the legislature and the judiciary. Administratively, the UKSC applies New Public Management (NPM) principles, managed by a Chief Executive (Jenny Rowe) who acts as the Accounting Officer and answers directly to the Public Accounts Committee of the House of Commons.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Constitutional Reform Act 2005 (c. 4):''' The primary statutory authorization establishing the Supreme Court, defining its jurisdiction, governance structure, independence, and rulemaking powers (Supreme Court Rules 2009).
* '''Appellate Jurisdiction Act 1876:''' The historical predecessor statute that created the judicial House of Lords and Lords of Appeal in Ordinary (superseded and repealed by the CRA 2005).
* '''Human Rights Act 1998 & ECHR (Article 6(1)):''' The statutory and treaty-based requirement for objective judicial independence and tribunal impartiality.

== Background & Policy Problems ==
For over a century following the Appellate Jurisdiction Act 1876, the highest court of appeal in the UK was embedded inside the non-elected second chamber of the national legislature—the House of Lords. Although judicial functions were separated from legislative business in practice (especially after the creation of the Appellate Committee in 1948), the Law Lords remained voting members of Parliament. On June 12, 2003, Prime Minister Tony Blair unexpectedly announced the creation of an independent UK Supreme Court to resolve ongoing constitutional anomalies.

=== Main Anomalies Addressed ===
1. '''Violation of Separation of Powers:''' ECHR jurisprudence dictated that housing the highest appellate judges within the legislature created a perceived conflict of interest, requiring structural separation.
2. '''Government as a Litigant Party:''' The UK Government is a party in over '''50% of cases''' coming before the top court, making it critical that court administration be free from Ministry of Justice oversight to protect judicial independence.
3. '''Erosion of Historical Caseload Focus:''' The Court's docket shifted dramatically from a tax-heavy focus in the 1950s (>30% tax cases) to a public law and human rights docket (37% in 2003/04; 24% ECHR in 2009), demanding modern administrative handling.

== New Public Management (NPM) Governance Structure ==
* '''Chief Executive & Accounting Officer:''' Jenny Rowe was appointed in January 2008 to oversee the budget and operations, entirely distinct from the Courts Service agency of the Ministry of Justice.
* '''Efficiency Mandate (Section 51 CRA 2005):''' Statutorily mandates that court resources be managed to achieve an "efficient, effective, and economic" system.
* '''Bifurcated Organizational Structure:'''
** ''Corporate Resources Directorate:'' Manages HR, finance, communications, and health & safety.
** ''Judicial Services:'' Led by a legal Registrar, managing case filing, listing, and 7 temporary judicial assistants.
* '''Staffing:''' 38.4 Full-Time Equivalent (FTE) staff.

== Common Law Constitutionalism & Constitutional Statutes ==
Although the UK lacks a codified written constitution, Supreme Court jurisprudence has fostered common law constitutional doctrines:
* '''Constitutional Statutes:''' Laws LJ in ''Thoburn v Sunderland City Council'' defined "constitutional statutes" as laws regulating the fundamental relationship between the citizen and the state (e.g., Magna Carta, Bill of Rights 1689, HRA 1998, ECA 1972).
* '''Qualification of Parliamentary Sovereignty:''' In ''Jackson v Attorney General'', Lord Steyn stated ''obiter'' that if Parliament attempted to abolish judicial review, the court might qualify parliamentary sovereignty to protect fundamental legal principles.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''House of Lords & JCPC:''' Institutional predecessor and co-located appellate court sharing judges and infrastructure.
* '''Ministry of Justice (MoJ) / DCA:''' Executive funding and oversight bodies, though the UKSC operates distinctly as a non-ministerial department.
* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]:''' Not found in the available sources [1–62].

'''The United Kingdom Supreme Court Administration and Judicial-Administrative Governance Framework''' is a judicial administration governance policy framework for the UK Supreme Court (UKSC). Formulated by William Arnold (Director of Corporate Services UKSC, 2014) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), it is based on a historical and juridical analysis of the implementation of the Constitutional Reform Act 2005 (CRA) and the Crime and Courts Act 2013. This framework establishes a strict separation of powers between the President/Justices and the Chief Executive (CE) to maintain institutional independence from the Executive (Lord Chancellor / Ministry of Justice) and the Legislature, while insulating judges from parliamentary budgetary scrutiny through the role of the Chief Executive as an independent Accounting Officer [1–13, 23–24].

== Summary ==
Published by William Arnold in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this policy framework reviews the transformation of the United Kingdom's highest appellate judicial system from the Appellate Committee of the House of Lords to the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom (UKSC) under the Constitutional Reform Act 2005. Officially operating since October 1, 2009, at the Middlesex Guildhall, the UKSC implements a unique administrative structure independent of the Ministry of Justice. The position of Chief Executive was established statutorily as an Accounting Officer directly responsible to Parliament (Public Accounts Committee), thereby protecting the Justices from political budgetary scrutiny [13, 23–24]. The Crime and Courts Act 2013 amendments further strengthened this independence by transferring the authority to appoint the Chief Executive and determine staff terms directly to the President of the UKSC and the Chief Executive [7, 9–10].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Constitutional Reform Act 2005 (CRA):''' The separation of powers legislation that established the UKSC (effective October 1, 2009), separated judicial authority from the House of Lords, established the statutory Chief Executive office (Section 48), and set its budget as a Non-Ministerial Department [4, 7–11].
* '''Crime and Courts Act 2013:''' An amendment that removed the Lord Chancellor's involvement in the appointment of the Chief Executive and the determination of staff working terms at the UKSC [7, 9–10].
* '''Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010 (Section 7):''' Affirms that civil servants at the UKSC are specifically accountable to the UKSC/Chief Executive and not to Executive Ministers [21–22].
* '''Appellate Jurisdiction Act 1876:''' The former legal basis for the appointment of Lords of Appeal in Ordinary (Law Lords) in the House of Lords prior to the 2009 reform.
* '''Judicial Committee Act 1833 (Section 4):''' The legal foundation for the referral jurisdiction of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC).
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
The separation of judicial and legislative roles from the House of Lords was announced in June 2003 to reaffirm the separation of powers between the Executive, Legislature, and Judiciary. Since 2009, the UKSC has handled the apex appellate functions and was merged with the administration of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC) [4, 6–7].

== Objectives ==
1. Ensure the tangible independence of the apex judiciary from Executive (Ministry of Justice) and Legislative interventions.
2. Insulate the Supreme Court Justices from parliamentary political/budgetary scrutiny by designating the Chief Executive as the independent Accounting Officer [13, 23–24].
3. Secure an independent judicial budget under a Non-Ministerial Department status (ring-fenced budget) through a direct Treasury Estimate [11, 19–20].
4. Establish an efficient dualistic governance structure between the Corporate Services and Registry divisions [13–14].

== Scope ==
This policy covers the governance of the apex judiciary for England & Wales, Northern Ireland, Scottish civil cases, and the Commonwealth and Crown Dependencies jurisdictions under the JCPC [2, 5–7, 25].

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Statutory Role of the Chief Executive (Miss Jenny Rowe):'''
** Acts as an independent Accounting Officer responsible to Parliament for the use of the judicial budget.
** Appointed by the President of the UKSC and oversees all civil servants at the UKSC [8–9].
* '''Ring-Fenced Budget Mechanism (Non-Ministerial Department):'''
** UKSC budget proposals are sent directly to the Treasury via the Lord Chancellor (who acts only as an official conduit without the authority to alter the proposed figures) [19–20].
* '''Dualistic Administrative Organizational Structure:'''
# *Corporate Services* (William Arnold): Manages facilities, finance, HR, ICT, libraries, communications, and the Management Board secretariat [13–14].
# *Registry* (Registrar - Senior Lawyer): Manages case administration, Permission to Appeal (PTA) applications, judgment publications, and supervises Judicial Assistants with a dual accountability line (juridical to the President and administrative to the CE).

== Implementation ==
* '''Non-Ministerial Department Operations:''' Execution of an independent budget estimate from the Consolidated Fund since April 1, 2010.
* '''JCPC Administrative Merger:''' The consolidation of the JCPC administration under the UKSC Chief Executive since April 2011, improving operational efficiency without disrupting either institution's independent functions.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Risk of Financial Intervention:''' The constant need to ensure the government does not breach statutory commitments during 4-year Spending Reviews from the Treasury [20–21].
* '''Theoretical Tension of Section 48(4) CRA:''' Potential clashes between the UKSC President's authority to give official directions and the Chief Executive's direct statutory responsibility as an Accounting Officer to Parliament.

== Reform / Change ==
* The transfer of the Chief Executive appointment authority from the Lord Chancellor to the UKSC President through the Crime and Courts Act 2013 [8–9].
* Plans to adopt an integrated Permission to Appeal (PTA) system for cases from Scotland to replace the Advocates' certification mechanism.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''UK Supreme Court (UKSC):''' The target apex judicial body of the policy.
* '''Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC):''' The Commonwealth appellate court operating under the integrated administration of the UKSC.
* '''[private person]:''' A Law student at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta (NIM: 2410611102), specializing in Constitutional Law (Hukum Tata Negara). Cecep Mustafa is not found in the available sources [FACT] [1–26].

'''The European and Italian Unjust Enrichment Comparative Restitution Framework''' refers to the judicial policy structure and comparative private law framework mapping the historical evolution, circulation of legal models, and structural divergence between French-derived civil law systems and Anglo-Germanic legal systems in the realm of restitution and unjustified enrichment (''arricchimento senza causa'') <ref>Albanese, A. (2023). The Historical Background to Unjust Enrichment in Italy and in Europe. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 9(2), 425–449.</ref>.

== Overview ==
The rules governing restitution in Europe are the product of the historical circulation of three primary legal models: Roman-French, Roman-Germanic, and English Common Law <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 425–426.</ref>. Formulated through comparative scholarship by [[Antonio Albanese]], Associate Professor of Private Law at the [[University of Bologna]], this framework divides European systems into two main operational models:
# '''Franco-Italian Model''': Requires five cumulative elements: defendant enrichment, plaintiff damage/impoverishment, correlation between enrichment and loss, lack of legal cause (''lack of cause''), and strict subsidiarity <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 427, 430, 445.</ref>.
# '''Anglo-Germanic Model''': Focuses on three primary elements: defendant enrichment, gain obtained at the expense of/from the rights of the plaintiff (''auf dessen Kosten''), and lack of legal justification, without requiring direct out-of-pocket financial loss or strict subsidiarity <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 426, 432–433, 445–448.</ref>.

== Statutory and Legal Basis ==
The primary statutory and transnational instruments governing this framework include:
* '''[[Italian Civil Code]] (1942)''': Article 2041 (general unjust enrichment clause) and Article 2042 (mandatory subsidiary character) <ref>Italian Civil Code, Arts. 2041, 2042; Albanese (2023), pp. 427, 438, 443.</ref>.
* '''[[Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch]] (German BGB)''': Section 812 (general clause and ''Eingriffskondiktion'') and Section 852 (restitution following the expiration of tort claims) <ref>BGB, §§ 812, 852; Albanese (2023), pp. 432, 448.</ref>.
* '''[[Principles of European Unjustified Enrichment Law]] (PEUEL)''': Article 2:101 (justification requirement) and Article 7:102 (concurrent obligations) <ref>PEUEL, Arts. 2:101, 7:102; Albanese (2023), p. 449.</ref>.

== Historical Background ==
The historical circulation of European legal models demonstrates that the 1927 Italian-French Draft Code of Obligations (Art. 73) influenced codifications in Albania (1927), Romania (1934), and Greece (1940) <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 426–427.</ref>. Conversely, the 1900 German BGB model (§ 812) influenced codes in Sweden, Switzerland, Portugal, Brazil, the Soviet Union, Hungary, Japan, and China <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 426, 446–447.</ref>. In France, the unjust enrichment action was first established through landmark jurisprudence in the ''arrêt Boudier'' case (1892) by the French Court of Cassation <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 427, 429–430.</ref>.

== Objectives ==
* Map the functional differentiation between performance-based enrichment actions (''Leistungskondiktion'') and interference-based enrichment actions (''Eingriffskondiktion'') <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 432–433.</ref>.
* Facilitate mechanisms for the disgorgement of illicit profits resulting from intellectual property infringement or unauthorized asset usage <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 425, 444–446.</ref>.
* Advance the harmonization of European restitution law under a unified principle of legal justification <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 425, 449.</ref>.

== Scope ==
The scope of this framework covers private contract and obligations law, tort liability, intellectual property rights, unauthorized asset exploitation, and comparative private law across European Union member states <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 425–426, 439, 445.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & Principles ==
* '''Abstract Subsidiarity Rule (Art. 2042 Italian Civil Code)''': Precludes an unjust enrichment claim if the plaintiff abstractly had another action available to obtain compensation, even if that primary action has expired or failed on procedural grounds <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 443–444.</ref>.
* '''Profit Disgorgement via Eingriffskondiktion''': Under BGB § 812 and German Federal Court of Justice (BGH) jurisprudence (such as the 1971 ''Flugreiseentscheidung'' case), gains derived from invading another party's protected legal sphere must be surrendered, even if the owner suffered zero out-of-pocket financial loss <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 432, 445–446.</ref>.
* '''Compensation vs. Restitution Distinction''': Tort compensation focuses on indemnifying the plaintiff's loss (''neminem laedere''), whereas unjust enrichment focuses on stripping the defendant's unmeritorious gain <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 443–445.</ref>.

== Implementation ==
The framework is implemented through statutory codification and judicial interpretation across key bodies: the [[Italian Supreme Court of Cassation]] (''Corte di Cassazione''), the [[German Federal Court of Justice]] (''BGH''), the [[French Court of Cassation]] (''Cour de Cassation''), and the UK [[House of Lords]] <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 427, 430, 438, 444, 446.</ref>.

== Policy Challenges ==
* '''Rigidity of Italian Subsidiarity''': The doctrine of "abstract subsidiarity" in Italy hinders the practical utility of Article 2041 and marginalizes unjustified enrichment claims compared to other European jurisdictions <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 443–444.</ref>.
* '''Failure to Disgorge Illicit Profits''': Requiring proof of "patrimonial decrease" (out-of-pocket loss) allows bad-faith actors to retain profits earned through bad-faith rights exploitation whenever direct loss cannot be demonstrated <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 444–445.</ref>.

== Proposed Reforms ==
Legal scholars advocate reinterpreting the "patrimonial decrease" requirement to align with "at the expense of" (''auf dessen Kosten''), transitioning from abstract subsidiarity to "concrete subsidiarity," and permitting concurrent claims in tort and restitution <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 443–445.</ref>.

== Focus Entities Status ==
* '''[[Antonio Albanese]]''': Lead Author and Associate Professor of Private Law at the University of Bologna <ref>Albanese (2023), p. 425.</ref>.
* '''[[University of Bologna]]''': Author's affiliated academic institution <ref>Albanese (2023), p. 425.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 425–449.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''' (Stable ID: `Geovanny Widya Berlianty P`): ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]'' <ref>Albanese (2023), pp. 425–449.</ref>

The '''U.S. Federal Courts Case Management/Electronic Case Files - CM/ECF and PACER Framework''' is a policy framework, technical architecture, and implementation strategy for electronic case filing and management systems (''CM/ECF'') and public access to court electronic records (''PACER'') across the entire United States Federal Courts system [1–3, 25].

== Summary ==
Published by J. Michael Greenwood and Gary Bockweg in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (2012), this policy framework evaluates the key success factors of the national implementation of the CM/ECF and PACER systems. Developed since 1995 by the ''Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts'' (AOUSC), the system successfully eliminated conventional paper files and replaced them with standard PDF electronic documents as official court records (''official record''), processing tens of millions of docket entries and hundreds of millions of public accesses annually.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''U.S. E-Government Act of 2002 & 28 U.S.C. § 1913:''' Regulates the authority to collect PACER fees to fund court automation and expand public access.
* '''Federal Rules of Civil, Criminal, and Bankruptcy Procedure (e.g., FRCP Rule 5):''' Establishes technical provisions and the legal validity of electronic case filing (''e-filing'').
* '''Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act of 2005:''' Regulatory basis for handling mass bankruptcy cases.
* '''Judicial Conference Policy on Public Access to Electronic Court Records:''' Policy on the openness of court records and data privacy protection.

== Background ==
Prior to CM/ECF, the U.S. Federal Courts, consisting of 758 court facilities, relied on a traditional paper filing system that was expensive, slow, and prone to loss. The project was developed gradually, starting from an asbestos case prototype in Ohio (1995) and bankruptcy cases in New York (1996), until it eventually covered all first-instance and appellate courts in 2005.

== Objectives ==
1. Integrate online filing (''e-filing''), file management (''e-files''), docket entries (''e-docket''), notifications (''e-noticing''), and public access (''PACER'') into a single unified database.
2. Establish PDF-based electronic documents as the official court record.
3. Ensure the operational reliability of the system 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year.
4. Facilitate transparent access to court records for advocates, the public, and the media.

== Scope ==
This policy applies nationally across all levels of the U.S. Federal Courts:
* 12 Courts of Appeals.
* 94 District Courts (Civil & Criminal).
* 90 Bankruptcy Courts.
* U.S. Court of International Trade.
* *(Exception)*: The U.S. Supreme Court manages a separate, independent ICT system.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Single PDF Mandatory Standard:''' All documents must be uploaded in PDF/A format verified by a validation program.
* '''Password & Hash Table Authentication:''' Logins and passwords are legally recognized as valid electronic signatures (''legal signature''), protected by ''hash table'' security stamp encryption.
* '''Notice of Electronic Filing (NEF):''' Automated notifications sent via email within seconds of registration, functionally replacing the conventional legal process of service.
* '''Self-Redaction Privacy System:''' Filers are required to redact sensitive data (social security numbers, bank accounts) before files are made public on PACER.
* '''Self-Sustaining PACER Fees:''' Nominal query fees ($0.08–$0.10/page) are reinvested to fund the maintenance of judicial ICT systems.

== Implementation ==
* '''Data Processing Functions (DPF):''' Adoption of a PERL/Java-based mini-programming language that allows non-technical court staff to modify entry templates according to local rules.
* '''Disaster Resilience:''' The system proved to remain fully operational without loss of official records during the 9/11/2001 terrorist crisis in New York and Hurricane Katrina in 2005 in New Orleans.
* '''U.S. Treasury Integration:''' Filing fee payments are directly linked to the online payment systems of the U.S. Department of the Treasury.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''2005 Bankruptcy Caseload Surge:''' Amendments to the Bankruptcy Act triggered case filing increases of up to 1000% in some districts, which the system handled successfully without delays.
* '''Data Security and Privacy:''' The need for ''layered protection'' oversight to prevent hacking and ensure the protection of distributed/sealed documents.

== Reform / Change ==
* Establishment of ''Court User Development Committees'' that periodically evaluate system needs.
* Implementation of a mentoring program between senior courts and newly adopting courts.
* Adoption of the ''NextGen CM/ECF'' system, which includes full-text searching and judicial conflict checking features.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts (AOUSC):''' The developer and central manager of CM/ECF.
* '''U.S. Department of the Treasury:''' Partner in online financial transaction processing.

'''The Drug Treatment Courts and Their Progeny in the U.S. Policy Framework''' is a therapeutic criminal justice and long-term evaluation policy framework concerning Drug Treatment Courts (DTC) and their derivatives (such as Juvenile Drug Courts, Family Treatment Courts, Tribal Healing to Wellness Courts, and Veterans Treatment Courts) in the United States. Formulated by Caroline Cooper (American University Justice Programs Office) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), Vol. 8 No. 3 (July 2017), the framework analyzes the 25+ year evolution since the founding of the Miami Drug Court in 1989. It evaluates the application of Differentiated Case Management (DCM) and the NADCP/BJA's 10 Key Components, proposing reforms to rebalance legal supervision with the principles of therapeutic jurisprudence [1–9, 14–18, 28–32].

== Summary ==
Published by Caroline Cooper in the IJCA (July 2017), this policy framework evaluates the 25+ year journey of Drug Treatment Courts (DTC) in the United States since their inception in Miami in 1989 [1–3]. Developed as a pragmatic response to the crisis of mandatory sentencing laws and the "revolving door" cycle of incarcerating drug addicts, the DTC model applies Differentiated Case Management (DCM) and therapeutic jurisprudence by providing intensive outpatient treatment as a diversion from prosecution [1–5, 9]. The DTC model eventually spawned four primary derivatives: Juvenile Drug Courts, Family Treatment Courts (driven by ASFA 1997), Tribal Healing to Wellness Courts, and Veterans Treatment Courts [14–18]. However, Cooper identifies severe challenges, including the erosion of fidelity to the NADCP/BJA's 10 Key Components, a problematic shift toward a probation-based model that strips defendants of public defender representation, subjective selection processes that trigger racial disparities, and the persistent rejection of Medication Assisted Treatment (MAT) [11–13, 19–27]. The proposed reforms emphasize drafting a ''Unifying Mission Statement'', securing felony record expungements, and integrating therapeutic jurisprudence into university curricula and Continuing Legal Education (CLE) [30–39].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Sixth Amendment & Due Process Clause (U.S. Constitution):''' Constitutional guarantees of the right to a speedy and public trial, a fair hearing, and the assistance of counsel.
* '''Mandatory Sentencing Laws (1980s Federal & State Laws):''' Strict sentencing regulations that triggered mass incarceration and catalyzed the creation of the alternative DTC model.
* '''Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA) of 1997 (Public Law 105-89):''' The legal foundation enforcing strict 15/22-month timelines for foster care, which spurred the creation of Family Drug Treatment Courts.
* '''Defining Drug Courts: The 10 Key Components (NADCP/BJA 1997):''' The foundational national standard defining the mandatory elements for operating a DTC in the United States.
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
The failure of mass incarceration policies to rehabilitate drug addicts compelled judicial leaders in Miami in 1989 to leverage the coercive power of the criminal justice system to mandate participation in medical treatment.

== Objectives ==
1. Halt the revolving-door cycle of incarcerating drug addicts through intensive medical rehabilitation backed by judicial supervision.
2. Ensure the protection of defendants' constitutional rights and legal sovereignty within a non-adversarial team approach.
3. Eliminate the collateral consequences of permanent criminal records for participants who successfully graduate from the program.

== Scope ==
This policy covers the evaluation of DTCs at the Federal, State, and Tribal levels within the US, as well as their international adoption in over 20 countries.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''The 10 Key Components (NADCP/BJA):'''
** Integrating drug treatment with criminal justice processing, maintaining a non-adversarial approach, ensuring early intervention, conducting frequent abstinence testing, and providing continuous evaluation.
* '''Four DTC Progeny Permutations:'''
** Juvenile Drug Courts (focusing on adolescent development), Family Treatment Courts (ASFA 1997), Tribal Healing to Wellness Courts (10 Tribal Components), and Veterans Courts (addressing trauma & PTSD).
* '''Medication Assisted Treatment (MAT) Mandate:'''
** A federal mandate prohibiting DTCs from denying participants the use of certified medical treatments (e.g., methadone/buprenorphine).

== Implementation ==
* '''Enforcement of Evidence-Based Eligibility Criteria:''' Abolishing subjective selection or "team voting" and replacing it with scientific risk/need assessment instruments.
* '''Academic Partnerships and CLE Training:''' Integrating DTC principles into law schools, medical schools, public health programs, and Continuing Legal Education.

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Loss of Public Defender Representation in the Probation Model:''' Probationers in DTCs often lack public defender representation, making them highly vulnerable to program termination and incarceration without due process.
* '''Racial and Demographic Disparities:''' Unsystematic and subjective selection criteria have led to disproportionately low enrollment rates for minority groups (particularly African Americans).

== Reform / Change ==
* Redrafting a ''Unifying Mission Statement'' and establishing clear pathways for the expungement of felony records.
* Expanding the indicators of success from mere recidivism rates to comprehensive prosocial recovery indicators (desistance measures).

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''American University (Justice Programs Office):''' The research institution executing national technical assistance for DTCs.
* '''National Association of Drug Court Professionals (NADCP):''' The authors of the 10 Key Components and Adult Best Practice Standards.
* '''U.S. Department of Justice (BJA/OJJDP/DCPO):''' The federal agencies providing grants and national guidance for DTCs.
* '''[private person]:''' A Law student at Universitas Pembangunan Nasional "Veteran" Jakarta (NIM: 2410611102), specializing in Constitutional Law (Hukum Tata Negara). The intersection of constitutional due process rights and therapeutic jurisprudence explored in this framework provides a highly relevant comparative case study for her academic focus. Cecep Mustafa is not found in the available sources [FACT] [1–47].

Dieser von Caroline Cooper im ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA, 2017) veröffentlichte Rahmen bewertet die 25-jährige Entwicklung von Drogenbehandlungsgerichten (DTC) in den USA, die 1989 in Miami begannen. Das DTC-Modell, eine Alternative zu den strengen "Mandatory Sentencing Laws", verbindet gerichtliche Aufsicht mit intensiver medizinischer Behandlung (Therapeutic Jurisprudence). '''The US Federal Courts NextGen Case Management / Electronic Case Files Policy Framework''' is an e-filing and case management system governance policy framework developed by the Administrative Office of the United States Courts (AOUSC) and reviewed by John Brinkema and Dr. J. Michael Greenwood (2015) in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA). It outlines the replacement of the legacy CM/ECF system (operational since 1996 across 200+ federal courts) with a centralized cloud/Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA). Key innovations include Central Sign-On (CSO), XML/NIEM integration, Electronic Self-Representation (eSR) for ''pro se'' filers, and a measured, incremental technological transition driven by Agile development methodologies [1–15, 25–31].

== Summary ==
Published by John Brinkema and Dr. J. Michael Greenwood in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this policy framework analyzes the evolution, architecture, and transition management challenges from the legacy CM/ECF to the NextGen CM/ECF in the United States Federal Courts. Managing over 47 million cases and 600 million PDF documents, the old decentralized system was replaced by a centralized architecture (cloud & SOA) to reduce operational costs and consolidate infrastructure [2–3, 25–26]. NextGen introduced Central Sign-On (CSO), Electronic Self-Representation (eSR) for ''pro se'' bankruptcy filers, and enhanced judicial support tools (Judicial Workspace & Calendar) [11–21, 28–29]. The authors expose major project challenges, including a 2+ year schedule delay due to "Death March" syndrome, the crippling impact of budget sequestration, the 2013 AOUSC restructuring that destroyed institutional knowledge, and the absence of a General API [33–39, 43–46].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Administrative Office of the US Courts Act 1939:''' The statutory foundation granting the AOUSC authority to provide administrative and technological support to federal courts.
* '''Judicial Conference of the US & CACM Steering Group Mandates:''' Official directives guiding the collection of 10,000+ functional requirements for NextGen [4–5].
* '''NIEM & Federal XML Data Exchange Standards:''' Automated data encoding standards for inter-agency information exchange [21, 28–29].
* '''U.S. Budget Sequestration Act (2011/2014):''' Federal budget cut policies that forced cloud centralization and restructuring [37–39].
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' Other specific formal statutory regulations are not mentioned in the source text [FACT].

== Background ==
The legacy e-filing system (Legacy CM/ECF) launched in 1996 successfully managed e-docketing across 200 federal courts. However, an accumulation of thousands of Modification Requests (MRs), the burden of multiple local login credentials, and severe budget constraints triggered the necessary transition to a centralized NextGen system.

== Objectives ==
1. Consolidate the IT infrastructure of 200 decentralized courts into a centralized data center architecture (cloud/SOA) [25–26].
2. Provide a unified Central Sign-On (CSO) module for attorneys and the public [11–13].
3. Facilitate ''pro se'' case filing through data-enabled XML/NIEM electronic forms (eSR) [21, 25, 28–29].
4. Develop integrated judicial support modules (Workspace, Calendar, Judge Review Packets) [15–21].

== Scope ==
This policy encompasses all US Federal Courts, including the Courts of Appeals, District Courts, Bankruptcy Courts, and Specialized Courts.

== Key Provisions ==
* '''Centralized Architecture and Cloud Computing:'''
** Operation of two data centers (East/West) based on cloud computing and Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) to guarantee service continuity [25–26].
* '''Central Sign-On (CSO) & JENIE Infrastructure:'''
** Integration of a unified national credentialing system that eliminates the need for separate registrations in each judicial district [11–13].
* '''Measured Step Transition & Agile Methodology:'''
** Incremental recoding without shutting down the legacy system (zero downtime tolerance), and shifting from ''waterfall'' to ''agile development'' methodologies [6–8, 28, 31].
* '''Electronic Self-Representation (eSR) Functionality:'''
** Simplifying ''pro se'' bankruptcy filings using NIEM XML-structured e-forms [21, 25, 28–29].

== Implementation ==
* '''Requirements Gathering Process (2009–2012):''' The identification of 10,000+ functional requirements by a specialized CACM committee [4–5].
* '''Rejection of Commercial Off-The-Shelf (OTS) Solutions:''' The AOUSC's definitive decision to continue building and maintaining the system ''in-house'' rather than relying on commercial software [6–7].

== Policy Problems ==
* '''Death March Project Syndrome:''' A schedule delay of at least 2 years resulting from a gross underestimation of system complexity [31, 33–34].
* '''Impact of the 2013 AOUSC Reorganization:''' The disbanding of senior IT teams, the loss of hundreds of years of institutional knowledge, and an excessive reliance on outside contractors [34–38].
* '''Absence of a General API:''' Hurdles in internal and external data integration due to the lack of a standardized general application programming interface [43–46].

== Reform / Change ==
* Establishing the absolute necessity of maintaining organizational stability and institutional knowledge during massive IT projects [47–48].
* Implementing strict filtering between actual testable requirements (''real requirements'') and mere ''user wants''.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==
* '''Administrative Office of the US Courts (AOUSC):''' The executive agency developing NextGen CM/ECF.
* '''Judicial Conference Committee on Court Administration and Case Management (CACM):''' The body responsible for defining functional requirements.

'''Mind the gap: How party–voter incongruence fuels the entry and support of new parties''' is an empirical comparative political science and public policy research paper authored by Marc van de Wardt (Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Ghent University, & ULB) and Simon Otjes (Leiden University & University of Groningen), published in the ''European Journal of Political Research'' (EJPR) in 2021 (print edition Vol. 61, pages 194–213, 2022).

== Summary ==
This study analyzes how ideological incongruence — the gap between voters' policy positions and the positions of established parties along the left–right spectrum — drives the emergence of new political parties in parliamentary elections and fuels voter support for those new parties. Testing a core assumption of spatial voting theory, the study consists of two parts: Study 1 examines new party entry rates across 47 elections in 17 Western European countries (2000–2016), and Study 2 examines individual-level voting decisions among 18,323–23,338 voters across 11 countries (1996–2015). The findings demonstrate that '''representational gaps significantly increase the number of new parties entering elections and drive voters toward the new party that is ideologically closer to them'''.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This document is an academic political science research study and is not based on any specific statutory or judicial legislative instrument [1–95].

== Background ==
In representative democracy, voters control public policy by electing the party closest to their own views. When established parties shift toward the center or converge, representational gaps emerge. Political figures such as Pablo Iglesias (Podemos, Spain), Thierry Baudet (Forum voor Democratie, Netherlands), and Emmanuel Macron (En Marche, France) have openly stated that they founded new parties to fill ideological space abandoned by established parties. Spatial theory (Downs 1957) assumes this dynamic, but a comprehensive, large-scale cross-national empirical test had not previously been carried out.

== Objectives ==
1. Test Hypothesis 1 (New Party Entry): the rate of new party entry in elections will be higher when party–voter incongruence is higher.
2. Test Hypothesis 2 (New Party Voting): voters will be more likely to vote for a new party when that party is perceived as ideologically closer than the nearest established party.
3. Compare the effect of policy proximity against democratic dissatisfaction (protest voting).

== Scope ==
The research covers a sample of 17 consolidated Western European democracies between 1996 and 2016, drawing on data from the Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES), ParlGov, and national election records.

== Key Provisions / Findings ==
* '''Hypothesis 1 Supported (New Party Entry):''' Party–voter incongruence has a statistically significant positive effect on the number of new parties (p < 0.05). An increase in incongruence from the 25th to the 75th percentile raises the number of new parties from '''6.22 to 11.54'''.
* '''Hypothesis 2 Supported (New Party Voting Behavior):''' The relative proximity of a new party significantly increases a voter's probability of voting for it (p < 0.01). Moving relative proximity from the 25th to the 75th percentile increases the predicted probability of a new-party vote from '''0.01 to 0.07'''.
* '''Valence Advantage of Established Parties:''' When a new party and an established party are equally close ideologically to a voter, the probability of voting for the new party is only '''0.15''', while the probability of voting for the established party is '''0.85'''. This shows that established parties hold a strong reputational and track-record advantage.
* '''Policy Motivation vs. Protest Voting:''' Ideological proximity has a much stronger effect than dissatisfaction with democracy, demonstrating that new-party voters are primarily driven by policy considerations ("policy voters") rather than simply casting protest votes.

== Implementation ==
The methodology was implemented through Poisson regression for event counts in Study 1, using the Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) incongruence measure, and logistic regression with clustered standard errors in Study 2. The research was funded by the Research Foundation – Flanders (FWO Grant FWO16/PDO/198) and F.R.S.-FNRS (Grant 28091302).

== Policy Issues ==
1. Representational gaps arising from established parties shifting away from voter preferences.
2. The valence disadvantage that makes it difficult for new parties to compete unless they offer a clearly distinct ideological position.

== Reform / Implications ==
1. Integrating short-term party–voter incongruence variables into theoretical models of strategic party entry.
2. Recognizing that voters possess sufficient rationality and political information to assess parties' ideological proximity.

* '''European Consortium for Political Research (ECPR) & John Wiley & Sons Ltd.:''' Publisher of the EJPR journal.
* '''Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES):''' Provider of election survey data.

title: Judicial-policy-vapnek-costsaving-2013
wikitext:
{{Infobox|stable_id=judicial-policy-vapnek-costsaving-2013|name=21 Cost-Saving Measures For The Judiciary|type=Research Paper & Policy Guide|issuing_authority=Jessica Vapnek / Tetra Tech DPK|legal_basis=Not found in the available sources.|date=2012–2013|status=Active / Published}}

'''21 Cost-Saving Measures For The Judiciary''' is a policy paper and practical guide by Jessica Vapnek (Tetra Tech DPK) providing a comprehensive set of strategies for judiciaries facing budget cuts and limited resources.

== Summary ==
The guide sets out 21 operational cost-saving steps for the judiciary, grouped into three main categories: operational measures, staffing and salary measures, and court and case management measures. It emphasizes balancing administrative efficiency with the protection of access to justice and due process.

== Legal Basis ==

* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This document operates as a comparative policy guide and is not established under a single statutory legislative instrument [1–45].
* '''Article III of the US Constitution (Judicial Compensation Clause):''' An example of constitutional protection against reductions to federal judicial salaries.
* '''California Government Code § 68543.5 & Florida Statutes § 29.018:''' Examples of state legislation governing the use of retired judges and the sharing of operating costs.

== Background ==
Courts around the world, particularly in developing countries and some US states, face budget crises driven by fiscal austerity. Successful legal reforms often increase the number of filed cases, further straining judicial workloads amid limited funding.

== Objectives ==
1. Identify practical steps to reduce non-essential expenditures and eliminate redundant bureaucratic processes. 2. Provide a taxonomy of 21 cost-saving measures without sacrificing the quality and independence of the judiciary. 3. Promote accountability and efficiency in court budget management.

== Scope ==
The paper covers case studies and practical examples from developing countries (such as Afghanistan, Albania, Colombia, Costa Rica, DRC, Guatemala, the Philippines, Rwanda, Serbia, and Vietnam) as well as developed countries (the United States and Europe).

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Operational Measures (Measures 1–6):''' Energy savings, centralized customer call centers (New Hampshire), inter-agency cost-sharing of operations (Florida), e-filing, videoconferenced hearings (Minnesota), publication of digital legal databases (Albania, Vietnam), and decentralized budget analysis (Rwanda, DRC).
* '''Staffing & Salary Measures (Measures 7–12):''' Cross-training of staff, salary freezes/cuts and temporary furloughs, use of retired judges as Judicial Hearing Officers (New York, California), use of law student volunteers (Macedonia), and adoption of performance standards (Colombia).
* '''Court & Case Management Measures (Measures 13–21):''' Shared courtrooms, continuous trial assignments (Iowa), establishment of specialized courts (Singapore), emphasis on oral procedures (Latin America), anti-corruption measures through fee transparency, mandatory mediation/ADR (Italy, Guatemala), expansion of small claims courts (Philippines), and diversion of minor disputes to administrative tribunals (New York City).

== Implementation ==
Implementation proceeds in phases, prioritizing less disruptive measures first to avoid public and staff backlash. Quality is evaluated using national/international standards such as *CourTools* (NCSC) and the *International Framework for Court Excellence* (ICCE) [3, 26–27].

== Policy Problems ==
1. Risk of declining decision quality if efficiency indicators are applied rigidly without quality oversight. 2. Negative effects of long-term salary freezes on the retention of experienced judges (e.g., 10% annual judge departures in New York). 3. Potential increase in corruption in developing countries if staff/judicial salaries are cut drastically. 4. Reduced access to justice resulting from cuts to court operating hours.

== Reform / Change ==
A shift from fragmented, paper-based administration toward digital technology automation, strengthened non-litigation mediation pathways (ADR), simplified small-claims procedures, and modernized judicial budgeting.

* '''Tetra Tech DPK & USAID:''' Donor and implementing bodies for judicial reform projects.
* '''World Bank & UNODC:''' Developers of judicial databases and integrity guidance.
* '''National Center for State Courts (NCSC) & ICCE:''' Providers of court performance measurement standards [11, 26–27].
* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]:''' Not found in the available sources [1–45].

'''Policy Framework on the International Protection of Young Male Noncombatants under IHL and IHRL''' (official title: ''Gaza’s Young Adult Male Noncombatant as a Legitimised Target Under Patriarchal Laws of War: Probing the Routine Killing of Civilian Men Amid Feminist Abstention, Terrorism Ambiguities, and Genocidal Tensions'') is a critical and humanitarian legal policy framework formulated by Riccardo Vecellio Segate and published in ''The Italian Law Journal'' (Vol. 10 Nos. 01-02/2024, pp. 387–450).<ref>Vecellio Segate, R. (2024). Gaza’s Young Adult Male Noncombatant as a Legitimised Target Under Patriarchal Laws of War: Probing the Routine Killing of Civilian Men Amid Feminist Abstention, Terrorism Ambiguities, and Genocidal Tensions. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 10(1-2), 387–450.</ref> The work examines the normalisation of the mass killing of young adult male civilians (noncombatants) under the Laws of War (LoW);<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 387, 388, 392, 394.</ref> analyzes contradictions within mainstream "women and children" narratives that exclude men from the category of vulnerability;<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 387, 390, 391, 397, 398.</ref> evaluates stereotypical constructions of men as perpetual potential combatants or "military-age males";<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 392, 406, 409, 411.</ref> and provides a detailed legal case study on the 2023–2024 Gaza conflict.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 393, 440–445.</ref>

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Riccardo Vecellio Segate]] (Postdoctoral Researcher in Epistemic Justice at the [[University of Groningen]]), this study offers a critical assessment of disparities in international protection accorded to civilian men in armed conflict.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 387, 388.</ref> The author demonstrates how military commanders, policymakers, and media outlets have displaced core principles of International Humanitarian Law (IHL) and International Human Rights Law (IHRL) to establish a de facto hierarchy of civilian protection.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 387, 390, 397.</ref> Under this informal hierarchy, young adult civilian men are routinely categorised as potential terrorists or "military-age males" (MAMs), thereby rendering their deaths acceptable or less publicly condemned.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 392, 406, 409.</ref> Segate investigates this phenomenon through critical feminist legal theory (incorporating [[Adriana Cavarero]]'s concept of ''Horrorism''),<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 387, 407, 408.</ref> gender-based mandatory military conscription,<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 403, 404.</ref> and empirical evidence from the Srebrenica massacre, Bucha, and algorithmic targeting systems (e.g., ''Lavender'') deployed in Gaza.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 418, 436, 440, 443.</ref>

== Legal Basis ==
* '''International Humanitarian Law (IHL / Ius in Bello)''':
** ''1949 Geneva Conventions & Additional Protocols (AP I & II)'': The Principle of Distinction between combatants and noncombatants;<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 388, 395, 410, 443.</ref> the Principles of Proportionality and Precaution in Attack.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), p. 443.</ref>
* '''International Human Rights Law (IHRL)''':
** ''International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR)'': Right to Life and the Principles of Equality and Non-Discrimination.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 388, 390, 395.</ref>
** ''UN Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW)''.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), p. 402.</ref>
* '''International Criminal Law (ICL) & Jurisprudence''':
** ''Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC)'': War Crimes, Crimes Against Humanity, and the Crime of Genocide under the 1948 Genocide Convention.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 393, 401, 406, 409, 436, 437.</ref>
** ''International Case Law'': International Court of Justice ([[International Court of Justice|ICJ]]) cases including ''South Africa v. Israel'', ''Gambia v. Myanmar'', and ''Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro'';<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 408, 437, 441.</ref> International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia ([[International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia|ICTY]]) jurisprudence (e.g., ''Prosecutor v. Krstić'').<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 406, 437.</ref>

== Core Policy Analysis ==
1. '''Hierarchical Differentiation of Civilian Protection''': The pervasive deployment of the phrase "women and children" in military and journalistic reports implicitly legitimises the killing of the remaining 60% of casualties (civilian men) as an acceptable collateral cost.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 387, 397, 435, 440, 447.</ref>
2. '''Stereotypical Construction & AI Algorithmic Targeting''': Autonomous weapons systems and AI targeting software (such as ''Lavender'' and ''Where's Daddy?'') encode gender biases that automatically classify military-age males (MAMs) as terrorist targets without individualised verification.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 392, 410, 411, 418, 443.</ref>
3. '''Critique of the "Sparing Women" Presumption''': Permitting the routine extermination of noncombatant men does not protect women and children; rather, it destroys family support structures, induces intergenerational epigenetic trauma, and facilitates broader genocidal dynamics.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 412, 418, 419, 439, 444.</ref>

== Related Entities ==
* '''[[Riccardo Vecellio Segate]]''': Lead Author and Postdoctoral Researcher in Epistemic Justice at the [[University of Groningen]].<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), p. 387.</ref>
* '''[[Adriana Cavarero]]''': Italian feminist philosopher who conceptualised the theory of ''Horrorism''.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 387, 407, 408.</ref>
* '''[[International Court of Justice]]''': Judicial body adjudicating international genocide disputes.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 408, 441.</ref>
* '''[[Francesca Albanese]]''': UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territories occupied since 1967.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 440, 442, 445.</ref>
* '''Cecep Mustafa''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]''<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 387–450.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in the available sources.]]''<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 387–450.</ref>

Il '''Quadro Politico-Giuridico per la Protezione Internazionale dei Non Combattenti Maschi Giovani''' (titolo originale: ''Gaza’s Young Adult Male Noncombatant as a Legitimised Target Under Patriarchal Laws of War: Probing the Routine Killing of Civilian Men Amid Feminist Abstention, Terrorism Ambiguities, and Genocidal Tensions'') è un quadro di analisi giuridico-umanitaria e critica formulato da Riccardo Vecellio Segate e pubblicato in ''The Italian Law Journal'' (Vol. 10 Nos. 01-02/2024, pp. 387–450).<ref>Vecellio Segate, R. (2024). Gaza’s Young Adult Male Noncombatant as a Legitimised Target Under Patriarchal Laws of War: Probing the Routine Killing of Civilian Men Amid Feminist Abstention, Terrorism Ambiguities, and Genocidal Tensions. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 10(1-2), 387–450.</ref> L'opera analizza la normalizzazione dell'uccisione di massa di civili maschi giovani (non combattenti) nel Diritto di Guerra (Laws of War / LoW);<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 387, 388, 392, 394.</ref> esamina le contraddizioni della narrazione dominante "donne e bambini" che esclude gli uomini dalla categoria di vulnerabilità;<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 387, 390, 391, 397, 398.</ref> valuta la costruzione stereotipata degli uomini come potenziali combattenti perpetui ("military-age males");<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 392, 406, 409, 411.</ref> e presenta uno studio di caso giuridico sul conflitto di Gaza del 2023–2024.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 393, 440–445.</ref>

== Sintesi ==
Redatto da [[Riccardo Vecellio Segate]] (Ricercatore Postdoc in Giustizia Epistemica presso l'[[Università di Groninga]]), questo studio offre una critica approfondita delle disparità nella protezione internazionale accordata ai civili maschi nei conflitti armati.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 387, 388.</ref> L'autore dimostra come i comandi militari, i responsabili politici e i mezzi di informazione abbiano progressivamente alterato i principi del Diritto Internazionale Umanitario (DIU) e del Diritto Internazionale dei Diritti Umani (DIDU), creando una gerarchia di fatto nella protezione dei civili.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 387, 390, 397.</ref> In questo sistema informale, i civili maschi giovani vengono automaticamente classificati come "maschi in età militare" o potenziali terroristi, rendendo la loro eliminazione accettabile o meno soggetta a riprovazione pubblica.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 392, 406, 409.</ref> Segate analizza questo fenomeno attraverso la teoria giuridica femminista critica (incorporando il concetto di ''Horrorism'' di [[Adriana Cavarero]]),<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 387, 407, 408.</ref> la leva militare obbligatoria basata sul genere,<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 403, 404.</ref> ed evidenze empiriche tratte dal massacro di Srebrenica, da Buča e dai sistemi di targeting algoritmico (come ''Lavender'') impiegati a Gaza.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 418, 436, 440, 443.</ref>

== Basi Giuridiche ==
* '''Diritto Internazionale Umanitario (DIU / Ius in Bello)''':
** ''Convenzioni di Ginevra del 1949 e Protocolli Aggiuntivi'': Principio di Distinzione tra combattenti e non combattenti;<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 388, 395, 410, 443.</ref> Principi di Proporzionalità e Precauzione nell'attacco.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), p. 443.</ref>
* '''Diritto Internazionale dei Diritti Umani (DIDU)''':
** ''Patto Internazionale sui Diritti Civili e Politici (PIDCP)'': Diritto alla Vita e Principi di Uguaglianza e Non Discriminazione.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 388, 390, 395.</ref>
** ''Convenzione ONU sull'eliminazione di ogni forma di discriminazione della donna (CEDAW)''.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), p. 402.</ref>
* '''Diritto Penale Internazionale (DPI) e Giurisprudenza''':
** ''Statuto di Roma della Corte Penale Internazionale (CPI)'': Crimini di Guerra, Crimini contro l'Umanità e Crimine di Genocidio ai sensi della Convenzione sul Genocidio del 1948.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 393, 401, 406, 409, 436, 437.</ref>
** ''Giurisprudenza Internazionale'': Cause presso la Corte Internazionale di Giustizia ([[Corte Internazionale di Giustizia|CIG]]) tra cui ''Sudafrica c. Israele'', ''Gambia c. Myanmar'' e ''Bosnia ed Erzegovina c. Serbia e Montenegro'';<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 408, 437, 441.</ref> giurisprudenza del Tribunale Penale Internazionale per l'ex-Jugoslavia ([[Tribunale Penale Internazionale per l'ex-Jugoslavia|TPIJ]]) (es. ''Prosecutor v. Krstić'').<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 406, 437.</ref>

== Analisi Politico-Giuridica Fondamentale ==
1. '''Differenziazione Gerarchica della Protezione Civile''': L'uso sistematico della formula "donne e bambini" nei report militari e mediatici legittima implicitamente l'uccisione del restante 60% delle vittime (civili maschi) come un costo collaterale accettabile.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 387, 397, 435, 440, 447.</ref>
2. '''Costruzione Stereotipata e Targeting Algoritmetico via IA''': I sistemi d'arma autonomi e i software di intelligence (come ''Lavender'' e ''Where's Daddy?'') incorporano bias di genere che classificano automaticamente i maschi in età militare quali bersagli terroristici, senza verifica individuale.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 392, 410, 411, 418, 443.</ref>
3. '''Critica della Presunzione di Salvaguardia delle Donne''': Tollerare la distruzione sistematica degli uomini non combattenti non protegge le donne e i bambini; al contrario, distrugge la struttura economica e sociale delle famiglie, genera traumi epigenetici intergenerazionali e facilita le dinamiche genocidarie.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 412, 418, 419, 439, 444.</ref>

* '''[[Adriana Cavarero]]''': Filosofa femminista italiana, autrice del concetto di ''Horrorism''.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 387, 407, 408.</ref>
* '''[[Corte Internazionale di Giustizia]]''': Organo giudiziario competente per le controversie internazionali sul genocidio.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 408, 441.</ref>
* '''[[Francesca Albanese]]''': Relatrice speciale delle Nazioni Unite sulla situazione dei diritti umani nei territori palestinesi occupati dal 1967.<ref>Vecellio Segate (2024), pp. 440, 442, 445.</ref>

How parties strategically use commitments to gain credibility in an increasingly competitive political landscape|type=Comparative Political Research Paper & Policy Strategy Study|issuing_authority=Mathias Bukh Vestergaard / Aarhus University / EJPR|legal_basis=Not found in the available sources.|date=2025|status=Published / Active}}

'''Why all these promises? How parties strategically use commitments to gain credibility in an increasingly competitive political landscape''' is a comparative empirical research paper authored by Mathias Bukh Vestergaard (Aarhus University) and published in the ''European Journal of Political Research'' (EJPR) in 2025.

== Summary ==
This study examines why political parties strategically make policy commitments (campaign promises) in election manifestoes despite the risk of voter punishment if those promises are broken by post-election compromises. By analyzing 330,850 quasi-sentences from manifestoes in 11 Western countries (1984–2019), the study finds that the proportion of commitments has doubled over the last four decades, mainstream parties promise more than niche parties, and increased emphasis on an issue drives higher commitment-making to build credibility.

== Legal Basis ==

* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This document is an academic political science research study and is not established under any statutory or judicial legislative instrument [1–119].

== Background ==
Over the past 50 years, the Western political landscape has undergone major transformation: the emergence of new parties, weakening traditional voter loyalty, rising electoral volatility, and intensified issue competition. Political parties use policy commitments as a costly signal to persuade an increasingly fluid electorate [1, 3, 11–14].

== Objectives ==
1. Test the time trend of policy commitment strategy usage from 1984 to 2019. 2. Analyze differences in commitment usage between mainstream and niche parties [22–27, 60]. 3. Measure the impact of changes in issue saliency on commitment intensity [28–33, 61]. 4. Test the effect of the effective number of parties on election promise-making [19–22, 59].

== Scope ==
The research covers 11 Western countries (the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, Switzerland, Germany, Luxembourg, Austria, Ireland, and Denmark), representing a range of electoral systems and party configurations.

== Key Provisions ==

* '''Definition of a Policy Commitment:''' A statement in which a party takes on high responsibility for future policy (e.g., "We will increase X" or "We pledge to implement Y").
* '''Time Trend:''' The proportion of policy commitments rose from ~10% in 1984 to ~20% in 2019.
* '''Mainstream vs. Niche Parties:''' Mainstream parties have a commitment ratio 1.39 times higher than niche parties, offsetting niche parties' reputation for being more committed on their core issues.
* '''Issue Saliency Dynamics:''' Increased focus on an issue is followed by an increase in the proportion of commitments on that issue (rising from ~11% to over 20%) [61–62, 67].
* '''Effect of Effective Number of Parties (Counter-Hypothesis Result):''' As the number of parties in a system increases, the proportion of commitments actually *decreases* (falling from ~33% in two-party systems to under 10% in multi-party systems) in order to preserve post-election coalition negotiation flexibility [59–60, 65, 70].

== Implementation ==
The methodology was implemented through the development of a coding scheme, training of 8 human coders on 65,630 quasi-sentences, and use of the ELECTRA language model to automatically code 330,850 quasi-sentences [7, 37–38].

== Policy Problems ==
1. The dilemma between pre-election vote-seeking and the flexibility needed for post-election government formation (office-seeking) [15–16, 70, 76]. 2. The risk of electoral punishment and negative media coverage if commitments are broken due to coalition compromises or economic crises. 3. The difficulty voters face in enforcing democratic accountability within fragmented multi-party systems.

== Reform / Change ==
A shift from ambiguous electoral communication toward binding commitment signals aimed at winning voter credibility amid political uncertainty.

== Relationships with Other Entities ==

* '''Aarhus University & ECPR:''' The author's institution and the sponsoring academic association.
* '''European Research Council (ERC):''' Research funding body (Grant No. 817855).
* '''Comparative Manifesto Project (CMP) / WZB Berlin:''' Provider of the election manifesto corpus.
* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]:''' Not found in the available sources [1–119].

'''Reconceptualizing Security Strategies For Courts: Developing A Typology For Safer Court Environments''' is a judicial policy study and court design framework authored by Prof. Anne Wallace (Edith Cowan University), Prof. Deborah Blackman (University of Canberra), and Dr. Emma Rowden (University of Technology Sydney), published in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA, Vol. 5, No. 2, October 2013, ISSN 2156-7964).

== Summary ==
This study reconceptualizes court security strategies by moving beyond traditional perimeter security approaches (such as X-ray scanners, metal detectors, and CCTV cameras). Utilizing the results of a three-year research project funded by the ''Australian Research Council'' (ARC Linkage Project LP0882179), the authors developed a four-quadrant typology that combines "Place vs. Process" dimensions and "Hard vs. Soft Systems" analysis to ensure physical, psychological, cultural safety, and accessibility for all court users [1, 4, 5, 14–17].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This document is an academic research article and court administration policy framework, not a specific statutory or judicial legislative instrument [1–27].
* '''Related Policy Instruments Analyzed:''' The ''Family Violence Strategy 2004–2005'' of the Family Court of Australia, which established the principle of the "primacy of safety".

== Background ==
Over the past 30 years, Australian courts experienced heightened security concerns following violent courtroom incidents, the assassination of Judge David Louis Opas at his home, and post-9/11 and Bali Bombings terrorism threats. Government responses focused on massive funding for reactive, "airport-style" perimeter security. However, this approach is limited and neglects the psychological safety, cultural safety, and accessibility needs of court users [2–4].

== Policy Objectives ==
1. Distinguish clearly between the concept of "Safety" (a holistic, broad state of the user) and "Security" (technical/procedural mechanisms).
2. Develop a four-quadrant typology to analyze and design holistic court safety strategies [14–17].
3. Promote the "co-creation of safety" through collaboration among court administrators, architects, and court users.

== Scope & Methodology ==
The research involved 87 semi-structured interviews with judges, magistrates, security staff, lawyers, and victim advocates, as well as 66 "user jury" participants in focus groups evaluating court buildings across 5 jurisdictions in Australia and New Zealand.

== The Four Quadrants of Court Safety Typology ==
The typology combines two classification axes [14–18]:
1. '''Inflexible Environments (Hard Place):''' Architectural layouts, perimeter screening points, and physical segregation zones.
2. '''Regulatory Systems (Hard Process):''' Official rules, security personnel presence, breach reporting procedures, and queuing rules.
3. '''Flexible Environments (Soft Place):''' User-centric waiting spaces, clear wayfinding signage, witness support rooms, and accessible drinking water and toilets.
4. '''Supportive Practices (Soft Process):''' Intelligence gathering and integrated case scheduling, pre-hearing briefings, non-verbal intimidation detection, and collaborative practices.

== Implementation & Domestic Violence Case Study ==
The study analyzes the dilemma of domestic violence victims in courts who often feel like "sitting ducks" in open waiting rooms monitored by CCTV, or risk being "cornered" and intimidated in hidden public corners out of sight of security. The best solution combines hard approaches (perimeter screening) with soft approaches (special scheduling for domestic violence cases, pre-hearing briefings, and the detection of non-verbal intimidation signals) [8, 18–21].

== Policy Problems ==
1. The dominance of a "fortress approach" that triggers anxiety and psychological stress for victims and witnesses [2–4, 23].
2. A lack of training for security personnel to detect non-verbal intimidation codes.

== Reform / Change ==

'''Budgeting in the Era of Judicial Independence''' is an academic policy study and empirical economic analysis authored by Jesper Wittrup. The study tests the relationship between perceived judicial independence and national economic growth across 95 countries (1980–2003), and evaluates the two main models of judicial budgeting in Europe: the traditional Ministry of Justice model and the independent Judicial Council model.

== Summary ==
This study empirically demonstrates that public and business perception of judicial independence has a strong, significant positive effect on national economic growth (R² = 0.411, p < 0.01). However, formal (*de jure*) indicators show no correlation with economic growth. Wittrup analyzes the budget governance challenges of the Ministry of Justice model (risk of accusations of political manipulation or budget freezing) and the Judicial Council model (risk of accusations of internal favoritism and lack of public accountability). As a solution, Wittrup recommends the use of objective, transparent statistical workload indicators.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This document is an academic research article and policy assessment, not a statutory enactment.
* '''Statutory & Constitutional Frameworks Analyzed:'''
** '''Magna Carta (1215):''' A legal compromise between King John and the English nobility.
** '''English Bill of Rights (1689):''' Limits placed on monarchical power following the Glorious Revolution.
** '''Danish Courts Administration Act (Domstolsstyrelsen 1999):''' The legal basis for establishing Denmark's independent judicial budget management body.

== Background & the Fundamental Political Dilemma ==
The economic perspective of North and Weingast identifies a "fundamental political dilemma": a government strong enough to protect citizens' property rights is also strong enough to confiscate their wealth. Judicial independence functions as a neutral third-party enforcer that guarantees government commitment, thereby encouraging investment and economic growth.

== Empirical Research Findings & Budgeting Models ==

=== 1. Economic Growth Regression (1980–2003) ===
* Uses data from the Penn World Table v6.2 and the World Economic Forum's 2006 survey of 11,000+ business executives across 95 countries.
* Adding the perceived-judicial-independence variable increases the model's explanatory power from R² = 0.267 to '''R² = 0.411'''.
* The Feld & Voigt *de jure* index shows that merely copying formal rules on paper, without real independence, does not generate economic growth.

=== 2. Comparison of Judicial Budgeting Models in Europe ===
{| class="wikitable"
|-
! Budgeting Model !! Key Characteristics !! Governance Risk !! Countries Applying It (2006)
|-
| '''Ministry of Justice Model (MoJ Model)''' || The Ministry of Justice manages and allocates court budgets. || Rumors of political punishment/reward (e.g., the Tvind case in Denmark) or rigid budget allocation. || England, Germany, Finland, France, Spain, Italy, Croatia, etc.
|-
| '''Judicial Council Model''' || An independent council / courts administration manages the judicial budget. || Risk of accusations of favoritism among judges and challenges to public accountability. || Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Netherlands, Ireland, Hungary, etc.
|}

== Oversight & Accountability (Danish Model) ==
In Denmark, the transfer of budget authority to the *Domstolsstyrelsen* (1999) is balanced by oversight from the General Public Auditor. If serious financial criticism arises, the Minister of Justice and the Auditor agree on corrective instructions; failure to comply empowers the Minister of Justice to dismiss the entire independent Board of Governors.

== Policy Issues ==
1. Loss of budget efficiency due to the Ministry of Justice's reluctance to reallocate funds between courts.
2. The risk of internal conflict among judges over budget priorities under the Judicial Council model.
3. The need to balance judicial independence with public financial accountability.

== Reform / Implications ==
* The development and implementation of transparent, objective statistical workload indicators in Denmark, Germany, Finland, Norway, and the Netherlands to provide a fair basis for budget allocation.

'''Voter preferences as a source of descriptive (mis)representation by social class''' is an empirical comparative political science and public policy research paper authored by Reto Wüest (University of Bergen) and Jonas Pontusson (University of Geneva), published in the ''European Journal of Political Research'' (EJPR) in 2022.

== Summary ==
This study analyzes why democratically elected legislators consistently come from wealthier, more highly educated social strata than the citizens they represent (descriptive misrepresentation). Drawing on an online conjoint survey experiment involving 4,500+ Swiss citizens and an analysis of observational candidate data from the 2007 and 2011 Swiss National Council elections, the study tests whether this representational gap stems from voter demand or party supply. The findings show that voters generally reject routine working-class candidates and upper-middle-class candidates alike, favoring skilled working-class and lower-middle-class candidates instead.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This document is an academic political science research study and is not based on any specific statutory or judicial legislative instrument [1–102].
* '''Swiss National Council Electoral Rules (*Nationalrat*):''' The study is set within Switzerland's open-list proportional representation system, which allows voters to express direct candidate preferences through cumulation and list deletion.

== Background ==
Unequal policy responsiveness toward lower-income groups has become a central issue in comparative politics. Across many democracies, legislators' occupational backgrounds have been shown to shape their voting behavior and legislative agenda-setting. In Switzerland, nearly one-third of parliamentarians in 2000 and 2010 were lawyers or entrepreneurs (compared to 13% of the active workforce), and 86% of elected MPs had household incomes above the national median.

== Objectives ==
1. Test Hypothesis 1: on average, voters prefer skilled working-class (SWC) and lower-middle-class (LMC) candidates over routine working-class (RWC) and upper-middle-class (UMC) candidates.
2. Test Hypothesis 2: middle-class voters hold no bias against upper-middle-class (UMC) candidates relative to SWC or LMC candidates.
3. Analyze the roles of perceived competence ("competence bonus") and empathy ("understanding penalty") in candidate evaluation, based on Fiske et al.'s social psychology model.

== Scope ==
The research comprises a conjoint experiment run on the LINK Institute's online panel with 4,500+ Swiss voters (May 2017), evaluating 8 candidate attributes (occupation, education, income, party, ideology, parliamentary experience, gender, and residence), alongside an analysis of observational candidate data from the FORS Selects surveys (2007 & 2011) [28, 33–37, 39, 75, 90].

== Key Provisions / Findings ==
* '''Hypothesis 1 Supported (Voter Preferences):''' Overall, voters give the highest support to skilled working-class (SWC) and lower-middle-class (LMC) candidates, while rejecting routine working-class (RWC) and upper-middle-class (UMC) candidates.
* '''Hypothesis 2 Supported (Class-Divided Voter Preferences):'''
** Working-class voters strongly reject UMC candidates, viewing them as out of touch with ordinary people's problems ("understanding penalty").
** Middle-class voters show '''no bias against UMC candidates''' relative to SWC candidates, while strongly rejecting RWC candidates.
* '''Competence Bonus vs. Empathy Penalty (Fiske Model):''' SWC, LMC, and UMC candidates all enjoy a significant "competence bonus" relative to RWC candidates. However, UMC candidates suffer an "understanding/empathy penalty," being perceived as disconnected from ordinary citizens' lives.
* '''Turnout Inequality Mechanism:''' Survey data show a substantially higher turnout rate among middle-class citizens ('''81.4%–89.5%''') than among working-class citizens ('''63.2%–79.3%'''). Because working-class citizens — who dislike UMC candidates — vote less often, middle-class voters, who are not biased against UMC candidates, end up dominating actual election outcomes.
* '''Real-World Election Results:''' In real elections, routine working-class (RWC) candidates face very low chances of being elected, even when placed high on party lists. UMC candidates, by contrast, face no such penalty in practice, benefiting from significantly larger campaign budgets (an average of CHF 17,327 compared to CHF 2,230 for RWC candidates) and strategic party list placement (pre-cumulation).

== Implementation ==
The methodology was implemented through Marginal Means (MMs) and Average Marginal Component Effects (AMCEs) estimated via OLS regression with respondent-clustered standard errors, along with multilevel logistic regression for the observational data. Replication data are held by FORS, with funding support from the SNSF (Grant No. 100017_166238) and the ERC (Grant No. 741538).

== Policy Issues ==
1. Unequal responsiveness of public policy to low-income groups due to the scarcity of working-class representatives.
2. Systemic bias in candidate selection by party selectorates, which tend to favor highly educated, high-status candidates.

== Reform / Implications ==
1. Increasing working-class voter turnout is the most effective way to reduce the dominance of upper-middle-class elites in parliament.
2. Campaign finance transparency reforms could help limit the advantage of wealthier candidates' larger campaign budgets.
