'''European Judicial Motivation and Quality Benchmarks Framework''' is a law and economics policy analysis and evaluation authored by Dr. Katarina Zajc and Dr. Mitja Kovač (University of Ljubljana). Prepared for the 2010 EGPA Conference and published in the ''International Journal for Court Administration'' (IJCA), this framework analyzes judicial motivation, incentive structures, and caseload backlogs in European civil law countries using principal-agent theory, Posner's utility maximization model (''Homo Economicus''), the ''carrots and sticks'' mechanism, and an economic evaluation of the Finnish Quality Benchmarks [1–3, 7, 24].

== Summary ==
This study addresses the puzzle of why case backlogs persist in Europe despite continuous efforts to improve decision quality. In continental European judicial bureaucracies, society acts as the ''Principal'' while the court/judge acts as the ''Agent''. Because monitoring judges' performance is extremely costly and information is asymmetric ($C_d > B_p$), judges tend to engage in ''shirking''. Zajc & Kovač prove that increasing the salaries of already employed judges is ineffective at increasing productivity. Instead, judicial motivation can be enhanced through non-financial incentives (''carrots'') such as promotion prospects (rank-order tournaments), peer reputation/awards, and legal legacy [11, 13–16]. The exclusive use of punishments (''sticks'') is rejected because the ''multiplication effect'' can threaten judicial independence [20–22, 37].

== Legal Basis ==
* '''Not found in the available sources:''' This document is an academic research article, not a statutory legislative instrument [1–4].
* '''Analyzed Standard Frameworks:''' Finnish Quality Benchmarks (Rovaniemi Quality Project); promotion criteria of the Slovenian Judicial Service Act; CEPEJ Evaluation Guidelines; and Trial Court Performance Standards (TCPS/NCSC).

== Core Theory & Economic Analysis ==

=== 1. Principal-Agent Theory & Information Asymmetry ===
In civil law judiciaries, society (Principal) grants authority to the court/judge (Agent). Because human capital-based work is difficult to measure, detection costs ($C_d$) exceed prevention benefits ($B_p$), triggering ''moral hazard'' and ''shirking''.

=== 2. Judicial Utility Model (Posner - Homo Economicus) ===
Judges are ''utility maximizers'' who prefer high salaries, reasonable workloads, reputation, and the freedom to make decisions without interference.

=== 3. Carrots vs. Sticks & The Multiplication Effect ===
* '''Carrots (Positive Incentives):'''
** ''Promotion Prospects & Rank-Order Tournaments:'' Judges compete to achieve high scores (number of decisions, citation rates, clearance speed, reversal ratios) to gain promotions [11–14].
** ''Reputation & Awards:'' "Judge of the Year" awards, top 10% lists, or public appreciation.
** ''Legal Legacy:'' The desire to influence legal development and create jurisprudence.
* '''The Danger of Sticks (Sanctions/Punishments) & The Multiplication Effect (Dari-Mattiacci & De Geest):'''
Although sanctions (threats of dismissal, salary cuts, criminal prosecution) appear strong, applying ''sticks'' to non-verifiable performance carries a high risk of abuse by authoritarian rulers and undermines judicial independence [20–22, 37].

== Six Aspects of the Finnish Quality Benchmarks ==
The research evaluates the Finnish Rovaniemi Quality Project model, which consists of 6 aspects and 40 criteria:
1. '''The Process:''' Transparency, independence, expediency, settlement encouragement, flexibility, and public access.
2. '''The Decision:''' Fair, lawful, convincing reasoning, systematic, easily understood, and correct language.
3. '''Treatment of Parties:''' Respect for human dignity, fair advice, prompt service, and communication/PR.
4. '''Promptness:''' Optimum processing time, case importance context, and adherence to deadlines.
5. '''Competence & Skills:''' Continuous training, annual personal development interviews, and thorough preparation.
6. '''Organization & Management:''' Professional management, methodical case assignment, monitoring delayed cases, and preventing workload overload.

== Comparative Empirical Findings from European Countries ==
* '''Finland:''' Annual court budget negotiations with the Ministry of Justice encourage efficiency; individual sanctions are very rare (only 2 reprimands in 2006 out of 901 judges).
* '''Germany:''' Court presidents evaluate case volumes for promotions; there were 20 professional inadequacy proceedings and 22 criminal cases in 2006 out of 20,138 judges.
* '''Sweden:''' Processing time targets are agreed upon annually with the National Courts Administration; only 2 reprimands in 2006 out of 1,039 judges.
* '''Netherlands:''' Targets are set at the court level; the Supreme Court only handles 1–2 judicial dismissals per year.
* '''Slovenia:''' Promotion is governed by 9 statutory criteria under the Judicial Service Act. A 2009/10 financial incentive scheme faced opposition from some judges citing interference with independence.

* '''Cecep Mustafa & [private person]:''' Not found in the available sources [1–49].

'''Policy Framework on Labour Law Transparency and Comprehensibility of Automated Decision Systems''' (''Transparency and Comprehensibility of Working Conditions and Automated Decisions: Is It Possible to Open the Black Box?'') is a digital labour law framework formulated by Loredana Zappalà. It examines the boundaries of transparency and comprehensibility in algorithmic management, evaluates the transposition of Directive (EU) 2019/1152 into Italian law (''Decreto Trasparenza'' / Legislative Decree 104/2022 in conjunction with ''Decreto Lavoro'' / Decree-Law 48/2023), compares these developments with Article 22 of the GDPR and the proposed EU Platform Work Directive, and highlights the role of collective bargaining and trade unions in opening the "black box" of workplace automated decision-making <ref>Zappalà, L. (2023). Transparency and Comprehensibility of Working Conditions and Automated Decisions: Is It Possible to Open the Black Box?. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 9(2), 623–652.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Authored by [[Loredana Zappalà]] (Associate Professor of Labour Law at the University of Catania), this study evaluates the impact of automated decision-making and algorithmic management on workers' rights and human dignity <ref>Zappalà (2023), pp. 623, 625.</ref>. 

The analysis highlights that algorithmic transparency must go beyond simple information disclosure to guarantee both "knowability" and "comprehensibility"—translating complex mathematical formulas into understandable legal and operational rules <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 630.</ref>. Although Italy introduced Article 1-bis into Legislative Decree 152/1997 via the ''Decreto Trasparenza'' to require employers to disclose algorithmic logic, this protection was weakened by the 2023 ''Decreto Lavoro'', which restricted disclosure obligations strictly to "fully automated" systems <ref>Zappalà (2023), pp. 639, 643.</ref>. The author argues that collective bargaining and trade union co-determination remain essential to negotiate algorithmic parameters and prevent automated workplace discrimination <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 651.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''European Union Law''':
** ''Directive (EU) 2019/1152'' (Transparent and Predictable Working Conditions) <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 634.</ref>.
** ''General Data Protection Regulation'' (GDPR / Regulation EU 2016/679): Articles 13, 14, 15, and Article 22 (automated individual decision-making and the right to explanation) <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 629.</ref>.
** ''Proposed EU Platform Work Directive'' (COM(2021) 762 final): Articles 6, 7, and 8 (human monitoring and review of automated systems) <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 635.</ref>.
** ''Proposed EU Artificial Intelligence Act'' (COM(2021) 206 final) <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 635.</ref>.
* '''Italian Labour Legislation''':
** ''Legislative Decree 27 June 2022, n. 104'' (''Decreto Trasparenza''): Inserted Article 1-bis into Legislative Decree 152/1997, mandating employer information duties for automated decision/monitoring systems <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 639.</ref>.
** ''Decree-Law 4 May 2023, n. 48'' (''Decreto Lavoro''), converted into ''Law 85/2023'': Restricted the scope of Article 1-bis strictly to "fully automated" systems <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 643.</ref>.
** ''Workers' Statute'' (''Statuto dei Lavoratori'' / Law 20 May 1970, n. 300): Article 4 (remote monitoring and audiovisual surveillance) and Article 8 (prohibition of collecting non-relevant personal data) <ref>Zappalà (2023), pp. 644, 650.</ref>.
* '''Key Jurisprudence''':
** ''Consiglio di Stato'': Judgment 13 December 2019, n. 8472 (School Teacher Transfer Case: principles of algorithmic openness, comprehensibility, and Human-in-the-Loop) <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 630.</ref>.
** ''Tribunale di Bologna'': Judgment 31 December 2020 (Frank Algorithm - Deliveroo Italy Case) <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 636.</ref>.
** ''Garante per la Protezione dei Dati Personali'': Decision 10 June 2021, n. 234 (Foodinho) and Deliveroo Decision <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 638.</ref>.
** ''Court of Appeal of Amsterdam'' (''Gerechtshof Amsterdam''): Rulings 4 April 2023 (Uber & Ola Cabs Algorithmic Transparency Cases) <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 637.</ref>.
** ''Tribunale di Palermo'': Judgments 31 March 2023 (Filcams-CGIL v. Uber Eats) and 20 June 2023 (Filcams-CGIL v. Foodinho/Glovo) <ref>Zappalà (2023), pp. 646, 647.</ref>.
** ''Tribunale di Torino'': Judgment 5 August 2023 <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 648.</ref>.

== Policy Analysis & Implementation ==
* '''The Opacity of the "Black Box"''': Complex algorithmic models and machine learning systems create significant opacity in worker evaluations and task assignments, risking biased or discriminatory outcomes (such as the reputation ranking in Deliveroo's Frank algorithm) <ref>Zappalà (2023), pp. 625, 636.</ref>.
* '''Limitations of Individual GDPR Protections''': Article 22 GDPR focuses primarily on individual data protection, which proves insufficient to address the collective power imbalances inherent in workplace algorithmic management <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 629.</ref>.
* '''Regulatory Regression under the Decreto Lavoro''': Adding the phrase "fully automated" in the 2023 amendment allows employers to potentially evade transparency duties by maintaining nominal or symbolic human intervention ("token human involvement") <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 643.</ref>.
* '''Trade Union Enforcement''': Trade unions (such as Filcams-CGIL) successfully leveraged Article 1-bis before the Labour Court of Palermo (2023) to force digital delivery platforms to disclose their algorithmic parameters and weighting metrics <ref>Zappalà (2023), pp. 646, 647.</ref>.

== Related Entities & Focus Status ==
* '''[[Loredana Zappalà]]''': Lead Author; Associate Professor of Labour Law at the University of Catania <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 623.</ref>.
* '''[[Consiglio di Stato]]''': Italian Supreme Administrative Court <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 630.</ref>.
* '''[[Filcams-CGIL]]''': Italian Trade Union active in enforcement litigation against platform algorithms <ref>Zappalà (2023), pp. 646, 647.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Zappalà (2023), pp. 623–652.</ref>
* '''Geovanny Widya Berlianty P''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Zappalà (2023), pp. 623–652.</ref>

Il '''Quadro Politico di Diritto del Lavoro sulla Trasparenza e Comprensibilità dei Sistemi Decisionali Automatizzati''' (''Transparency and Comprehensibility of Working Conditions and Automated Decisions: Is It Possible to Open the Black Box?'') è un quadro di analisi del diritto del lavoro digitale formulato da Loredana Zappalà. Esamina i limiti della trasparenza e della comprensibilità nella gestione algoritmica (''algorithmic management''), valuta il recepimento della Direttiva (UE) 2019/1152 nell'ordinamento italiano (''Decreto Trasparenza'' / D.Lgs. 104/2022 in combinato disposto con il ''Decreto Lavoro'' / D.L. 48/2023), confronta tali novità con l'Articolo 22 del GDPR e la proposta di Direttiva UE sul lavoro tramite piattaforma, ed evidenzia il ruolo della contrattazione collettiva e dei sindacati nell'apertura della "scatola nera" (''black box'') delle decisioni automatizzate nei luoghi di lavoro <ref>Zappalà, L. (2023). Transparency and Comprehensibility of Working Conditions and Automated Decisions: Is It Possible to Open the Black Box?. ''The Italian Law Journal'', 9(2), 623–652.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Scritto da [[Loredana Zappalà]] (Professoressa Associata di Diritto del Lavoro presso l'Università degli Studi di Catania), questo studio valuta l'impatto dei sistemi decisionali automatizzati e della gestione algoritmica sui diritti e sulla dignità dei lavoratori <ref>Zappalà (2023), pp. 623, 625.</ref>.

L'analisi evidenzia che la trasparenza algoritmica non deve ridursi a una mera informativa formale, ma deve garantire la "conoscibilità" e la "comprensibilità"—ossia la traduzione delle formule matematiche complesse in regole giuridiche ed operative accessibili <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 630.</ref>. Sebbene l'Italia abbia introdotto l'Articolo 1-bis nel D.Lgs. 152/1997 tramite il ''Decreto Trasparenza'' per imporre ai datori di lavoro l'obbligo di ostensione della logica algoritmica, tale tutela è stata ridimensionata dal ''Decreto Lavoro'' del 2023, che ha limitato l'obbligo ai soli sistemi "integralmente" automatizzati <ref>Zappalà (2023), pp. 639, 643.</ref>. L'autrice sostiene che la contrattazione collettiva e la co-determinazione sindacale rimangono gli strumenti fondamentali per negoziare i parametri algoritmici e prevenire discriminazioni automatizzate <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 651.</ref>.

== Base Giuridica ==
* '''Diritto dell'Unione Europea''':
** ''Direttiva (UE) 2019/1152'' (Relativa a condizioni di lavoro trasparenti e prevedibili) <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 634.</ref>.
** ''Regolamento Generale sulla Protezione dei Dati'' (GDPR / Regolamento UE 2016/679): Articoli 13, 14, 15 e Articolo 22 (processo decisionale automatizzato relativo alle persone fisiche e diritto ad una spiegazione) <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 629.</ref>.
** ''Proposta di Direttiva UE sul Lavoro tramite Piattaforma Digitale'' (COM(2021) 762 final): Articoli 6, 7 e 8 (monitoraggio e riesame umano dei sistemi automatizzati) <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 635.</ref>.
** ''Proposta di Regolamento sull'Intelligenza Artificiale dell'UE'' (EU AI Act - COM(2021) 206 final) <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 635.</ref>.
* '''Legislazione del Lavoro Italiana''':
** ''Decreto Legislativo 27 giugno 2022, n. 104'' (''Decreto Trasparenza''): Ha introdotto l'Articolo 1-bis nel D.Lgs. 152/1997, stabilendo obblighi di informazione sui sistemi decisionali e di monitoraggio automatizzati <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 639.</ref>.
** ''Decreto-Legge 4 maggio 2023, n. 48'' (''Decreto Lavoro''), convertito in ''Legge 85/2023'': Ha ristretto l'ambito applicativo dell'Articolo 1-bis ai soli sistemi "integralmente automatizzati" <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 643.</ref>.
** ''Statuto dei Lavoratori'' (Legge 20 maggio 1970, n. 300): Articolo 4 (impianti audiovisivi e altri strumenti di controllo) e Articolo 8 (divieto di indagini sulle opinioni e fatti non rilevanti) <ref>Zappalà (2023), pp. 644, 650.</ref>.
* '''Giurisprudenza Principale''':
** ''Consiglio di Stato'': Sentenza 13 dicembre 2019, n. 8472 (Caso sul trasferimento dei docenti: principi di conoscibilità, comprensibilità dell'algoritmo e Human-in-the-Loop) <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 630.</ref>.
** ''Tribunale di Bologna'': Sentenza 31 dicembre 2020 (Caso dell'algoritmo Frank - Deliveroo Italia) <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 636.</ref>.
** ''Garante per la Protezione dei Dati Personali'': Provvedimento 10 giugno 2021, n. 234 (Foodinho) e Provvedimento Deliveroo <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 638.</ref>.
** ''Corte d'Appello di Amsterdam'' (''Gerechtshof Amsterdam''): Sentenze 4 aprile 2023 (Casi sulla trasparenza algoritmica di Uber e Ola Cabs) <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 637.</ref>.
** ''Tribunale di Palermo'': Sentenze 31 marzo 2023 (Filcams-CGIL c. Uber Eats) e 20 giugno 2023 (Filcams-CGIL c. Foodinho/Glovo) <ref>Zappalà (2023), pp. 646, 647.</ref>.
** ''Tribunale di Torino'': Sentenza 5 agosto 2023 <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 648.</ref>.

== Analisi Politica e Attuazione ==
* '''L'Opacità della "Scatola Nera"''': La complessità dei modelli algoritmici e dell'apprendimento automatico genera opacità nella valutazione dei lavoratori e nell'assegnazione dei compiti, comportando il rischio di esiti discriminatori (come il punteggio di affidabilità nell'algoritmo Frank di Deliveroo) <ref>Zappalà (2023), pp. 625, 636.</ref>.
* '''Limiti della Tutela Individuale del GDPR''': L'Articolo 22 del GDPR si concentra prevalentemente sulla protezione dei dati individuali, rivelandosi insufficiente a riequilibrare le asimmetrie di potere collettive nella gestione algoritmica del lavoro <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 629.</ref>.
* '''Ridimensionamento Normativo del Decreto Lavoro''': L'inserimento dell'avverbio "integralmente" nella riforma del 2023 rischia di consentire ai datori di lavoro di eludere gli obblighi di trasparenza introducendo un intervento umano meramente formale o simbolico (''token human involvement'') <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 643.</ref>.
* '''Azione Sindacale e Applicazione Giudiziale''': Le organizzazioni sindacali (come la Filcams-CGIL) hanno utilizzato con successo l'Articolo 1-bis dinanzi al Tribunale di Palermo (2023) per imporre alle piattaforme digitali di consegna cibo l'ostensione dei parametri e dei fattori di ponderazione degli algoritmi <ref>Zappalà (2023), pp. 646, 647.</ref>.

== Entità Correlate e Stato degli Individui ==
* '''[[Loredana Zappalà]]''': Autrice principale; Professoressa Associata di Diritto del Lavoro presso l'Università degli Studi di Catania <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 623.</ref>.
* '''[[Consiglio di Stato]]''': Consiglio di Stato della Repubblica Italiana <ref>Zappalà (2023), p. 630.</ref>.
* '''[[Filcams-CGIL]]''': Organizzazione sindacale italiana attiva nel contenzioso sulla trasparenza algoritmica <ref>Zappalà (2023), pp. 646, 647.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Non trovato nelle fonti disponibili.]]'' <ref>Zappalà (2023), pp. 623–652.</ref>

| legal_basis = Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001; Regulation (EC) No 45/2001; CFR Art. 8, 42; Legge 241/1990 (Italy)
| date = 2010 (IJPL Publication); November 8, 2007 (CFI Judgment T-194/04); October 15, 2009 (AG Sharpston Opinion)

}}

The '''Policy Framework on the Convergence of National Administrative Procedures, EU Law Codification, and the Balancing of Document Access vs. Data Protection Rights''' (''Kerangka Kebijakan Konvergensi Prosedur Administrasi Nasional, Kodifikasi Hukum UE, dan Penyeimbangan Hak Akses Dokumen vs Perlindungan Data'') is a comparative administrative law policy and analysis framework developed by Jacques Ziller. It examines the convergence of national administrative law (such as amendments to Italian *Legge 241/1990*), the challenges of codifying administrative procedures at the European Union level, and the conflict (collision/clash) between the right to access documents (*Regulation No. 1049/2001 / Art. 42 CFR*) and the right to personal data protection (*Regulation No. 45/2001 / Directive 95/46 / Art. 8 CFR*), as tested in the landmark case ''Commission v Bavarian Lager'' (Case C-28/08 P / T-194/04) <ref>Ziller, J. (2010). The Convergence of National Administrative Procedures: Comments on the European Perspective. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 02(01), 290–295.</ref>.

== Summary ==
Authored by [[Jacques Ziller]], Professor of European Law at the [[Università degli Studi di Pavia]], this article analyzes the dynamics of national administrative law convergence and codification challenges at the European Union level <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 290, 292.</ref>. Ziller reviews the clash between transparency rights (*access to documents*) and privacy rights (*data protection*) in the landmark ''Bavarian Lager'' case <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 291, 293.</ref>. The study criticizes the flawed use of comparative law by the European Commission during the recast procedure of *Regulation No. 1049/2001*, and underscores the vital role of independent authorities like the *European Ombudsman* and the *EDPS* as extra-judicial mechanisms protecting citizens' rights <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 291, 294, 295.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
This framework and jurisprudence are rooted in supranational EU and national legal instruments:
* '''[[Regulation (EC) No 1049/2001]]''': Governs public access to European Parliament, Council, and Commission documents <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 291, 292.</ref>.
* '''[[Regulation (EC) No 45/2001]] & [[Directive 95/46/EC]]''': Regulates the protection of personal data processed by EU institutions and bodies <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 291, 292.</ref>.
* '''[[Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union]] (CFR)''':
** *Article 8*: Right to the protection of personal data <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 292.</ref>.
** *Article 42*: Right of access to documents of EU institutions <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 292.</ref>.
* '''[[Legge 7 agosto 1990 n. 241]] (Italy)''': Italian Administrative Procedure Act reformed in 2005 by incorporating principles from German and French law <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 290.</ref>.
* '''[[Swedish Freedom of the Press Act 1776]]''': Historical Swedish public information disclosure legislation <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 291.</ref>.
* '''Key Jurisprudence''': Case *Commission v Bavarian Lager* (Case C-28/08 P; Court of First Instance Judgment T-194/04; Advocate General Eleanor Sharpston Opinion, October 15, 2009) <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 290, 291, 293.</ref>.

== Background & Legal Convergence ==
Administrative law development in Europe is no longer strictly bound to the traditional Napoleonic system <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 290.</ref>. Modern French administrative tradition was heavily influenced by liberal thinkers Benjamin Constant, Alexis de Tocqueville, and Vivien de Goubert <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 290.</ref>. In recent developments, member states like Italy reformed *Legge 241/1990* by translating norms from the German Code of Administrative Procedure (*Verwaltungsverfahrensgesetz*) and *Conseil d'État* case law <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 290.</ref>.

== Policy Problems & Objectives ==
=== Problems Addressed ===
* '''Collision of Rights''': Clash between public transparency (*Regulation 1049/2001*) and privacy (*Regulation 45/2001*).
* '''Misuse of Comparative Law''': The European Commission's attempt to restrict document access to "final/completed documents" modeled on the Swedish Press Act 1776 ignored Sweden's unique structure of 240 independent agencies, which would drastically curtail openness if applied to the EU.
* '''Bureaucracy vs. Transparency''': Tendency of public bodies to over-rely on data protection exemptions to avoid administrative burden rather than applying overriding public interest tests.

=== Objectives ===
* Map the challenges of codifying general administrative procedure law at the EU level <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 292, 293.</ref>.
* Resolve collisions between transparency and personal data protection <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 293, 294.</ref>.
* Develop operational *balancing of interests* mechanisms outside judicial bodies <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 294, 295.</ref>.

== Key Provisions & The Bavarian Lager Case ==
* '''Clash of Rights''': The *Bavarian Lager* case highlighted the direct contradiction between *Regulation No. 1049/2001* and *Regulation No. 45/2001* <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 291, 292.</ref>.
* '''Two Resolution Methods''':
# *Strict Categorisation (AG Sharpston)*: Constructing theoretical categories of situations, deemed unworkable in practical circumstances <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 293, 294.</ref>.
# *Balancing of Interests (CFI)*: Weighing public transparency interests against individual privacy protection on a case-by-case basis <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 294.</ref>.

== Role of Independent Bodies ==
Public bureaucracies tend to misuse privacy exemptions to deny documents and save administrative resources <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 294.</ref>. The *Bavarian Lager* case proved the vital necessity of specialized independent authorities—the [[European Ombudsman]] and the [[European Data Protection Supervisor]] (EDPS)—to enforce citizens' rights prior to or as an alternative to judicial litigation <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 294, 295.</ref>.

== Relationship with Focus Entities ==
* '''[[Jacques Ziller]]''': Lead Author and Professor of European Law at the University of Pavia <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 290.</ref>.
* '''[[European Ombudsman]]''': Independent Supervisor for EU Document Access <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 292, 294, 295.</ref>.
* '''[[European Data Protection Supervisor]] (EDPS)''': Independent EU Personal Data Protection Authority <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 294, 295.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 290–295.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Not found in available sources.]]'' <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 290–295.</ref>

Il '''Quadro Politico sulla Convergenza delle Procedure Amministrative Nazionali, Codificazione del Diritto UE e Bilanciamento tra Accesso ai Documenti e Protezione dei Dati''' (''Kerangka Kebijakan Konvergensi Prosedur Administrasi Nasional, Kodifikasi Hukum UE, dan Penyeimbangan Hak Akses Dokumen vs Perlindungan Data'') è un quadro di analisi e politica del diritto amministrativo comparato sviluppato da Jacques Ziller. Esso esamina il fenomeno della convergenza del diritto amministrativo nazionale (come le riforme della *Legge 241/1990* in Italia), le sfide della codificazione dei procedimenti amministrativi a livello dell'Unione Europea, nonché il conflitto (collisione/contrasto) tra il diritto di accesso ai documenti (*Regolamento n. 1049/2001 / Art. 42 CDFUE*) e il diritto alla protezione dei dati personali (*Regolamento n. 45/2001 / Direttiva 95/46 / Art. 8 CDFUE*), come testato nella causa di riferimento ''Commissione v. Bavarian Lager'' (Causa C-28/08 P / T-194/04) <ref>Ziller, J. (2010). The Convergence of National Administrative Procedures: Comments on the European Perspective. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 02(01), 290–295.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Scritto da [[Jacques Ziller]], Professore di Diritto Europeo presso l'[[Università degli Studi di Pavia]], l'articolo analizza le dinamiche di convergenza del diritto amministrativo nazionale e le sfide di codificazione a livello UE <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 290, 292.</ref>. Ziller esamina il contrasto tra i diritti di trasparenza (*accesso ai documenti*) e i diritti alla riservatezza (*protezione dei dati*) nel famoso caso ''Bavarian Lager'' <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 291, 293.</ref>. Lo studio critica l'uso improprio del diritto comparato da parte della Commissione Europea nella procedura di rifusione del *Regolamento n. 1049/2001* e sottolinea il ruolo cruciale di autorità indipendenti come il *Mediazione Europeo* (Ombudsman) e il *GAEDP* (EDPS) quali meccanismi extra-giudiziali a tutela dei diritti dei cittadini <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 291, 294, 295.</ref>.

== Base Giuridica ==
Questo quadro e la relativa giurisprudenza si fondono su strumenti giuridici sovranazionali dell'UE e nazionali:
* '''[[Regolamento (CE) n. 1049/2001]]''': Disciplina l'accesso del pubblico ai documenti del Parlamento europeo, del Consiglio e della Commissione <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 291, 292.</ref>.
* '''[[Regolamento (CE) n. 45/2001]] & [[Direttiva 95/46/CE]]''': Disciplinano la tutela delle persone fisiche con riguardo al trattamento dei dati personali da parte delle istituzioni e degli organismi comunitari <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 291, 292.</ref>.
* '''[[Carta dei diritti fondamentali dell'Unione europea]] (CDFUE)''':
** *Articolo 8*: Protezione dei dati di carattere personale <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 292.</ref>.
** *Articolo 42*: Diritto di accesso ai documenti delle istituzioni dell'UE <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 292.</ref>.
* '''[[Legge 7 agosto 1990 n. 241]] (Italia)''': Legge sul procedimento amministrativo italiano, riformata nel 2005 recependo principi del diritto tedesco e francese <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 290.</ref>.
* '''[[Legge svedese sulla libertà di stampa 1776]]''': Storica legislazione svedese sull'accesso all'informazione pubblica <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 291.</ref>.
* '''Giurisprudenza Chiave''': Causa *Commissione v. Bavarian Lager* (Causa C-28/08 P; Sentenza del Tribunale di primo grado T-194/04; Conclusioni dell'Avvocato Generale Eleanor Sharpston del 15 ottobre 2009) <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 290, 291, 293.</ref>.

== Contestualizzazione e Convergenza Giuridica ==
L'evoluzione del diritto amministrativo in Europa non è più rigidamente legata al sistema napoleonico tradizionale <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 290.</ref>. La tradizione amministrativa francese moderna è stata fortemente influenzata da pensatori liberali come Benjamin Constant, Alexis de Tocqueville e Vivien de Goubert <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 290.</ref>. Recentemente, stati membri come l'Italia hanno riformato la *Legge 241/1990* mutuando norme dal codice di procedura amministrativa tedesco (*Verwaltungsverfahrensgesetz*) e dalla giurisprudenza del *Conseil d'État* <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 290.</ref>.

== Problemi Politici ed Obiettivi ==
=== Problemi Affrontati ===
* '''Collisione dei Diritti''': Contrasto tra trasparenza pubblica (*Regolamento 1049/2001*) e privacy (*Regolamento 45/2001*).
* '''Uso Errato del Diritto Comparato''': Il tentativo della Commissione Europea di limitare l'accesso ai soli "documenti definitivi/completati" prendendo a modello la legge svedese del 1776 ha ignorato la struttura svedese articolata in 240 agenzie indipendenti, rischiando di restringere drasticamente la trasparenza nell'UE.
* '''Inerzia Burocratica''': La tendenza delle pubbliche amministrazioni ad abusare delle eccezioni sulla privacy per risparmiare risorse amministrative anziché applicare la verifica dell'interesse pubblico prevalente.

=== Obiettivi ===
* Mappare le sfide della codificazione della procedura amministrativa generale a livello UE <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 292, 293.</ref>.
* Risolvere il conflitto tra trasparenza e protezione dei dati personali <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 293, 294.</ref>.
* Sviluppare meccanismi operativi di *bilanciamento degli interessi* al di fuori degli organi giurisdizionali <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 294, 295.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Chiave e il Caso Bavarian Lager ==
* '''Scontro tra Diritti''': Il caso *Bavarian Lager* ha evidenziato la diretta contraddizione tra il *Regolamento n. 1049/2001* e il *Regolamento n. 45/2001* <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 291, 292.</ref>.
* '''Due Metodi di Risoluzione''':
# *Categorizzazione Rigida (AG Sharpston)*: Costruzione teorica di categorie di situazioni, giudicata poco pratica nel concreto <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 293, 294.</ref>.
# *Bilanciamento degli Interessi (CFI)*: Ponderazione caso per caso tra l'interesse pubblico alla trasparenza e la tutela della riservatezza individuale <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 294.</ref>.

== Ruolo degli Organi Indipendenti ==
Le burocrazie pubbliche tendono ad abusare delle eccezioni di riservatezza per negare i documenti e risparmiare tempo <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 294.</ref>. Il caso *Bavarian Lager* ha dimostrato la necessità di autorità indipendenti specializzate—il [[Mediazione Europeo]] e il [[Garante Europeo della Protezione dei Dati]] (EDPS)—per tutelare i diritti dei cittadini prima o in alternativa al ricorso giudiziario <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 294, 295.</ref>.

== Relazioni con le Entità di Riferimento ==
* '''[[Jacques Ziller]]''': Autore principale e Professore di Diritto Europeo presso l'Università di Pavia <ref>Ziller (2010), p. 290.</ref>.
* '''[[Mediazione Europeo]]''': Autorità Indipendente per l'Accesso ai Documenti UE <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 292, 294, 295.</ref>.
* '''[[Garante Europeo della Protezione dei Dati]] (EDPS)''': Autorità Indipendente per la Protezione dei Dati Personali nell'UE <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 294, 295.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Non presente nelle fonti disponibili.]]'' <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 290–295.</ref>
* '''[[Geovanny Widya Berlianty P]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Non presente nelle fonti disponibili.]]'' <ref>Ziller (2010), pp. 290–295.</ref>

'''Greek Constitutionalism Framework: The First Revolutionary Constitutions''' (''Two Centuries of Greek Constitutionalism: The First Revolutionary Constitutions'') is a constitutional law and historical analysis framework formulated by Georgios Th. Zois. It examines the foundations of modern Greek constitutionalism, the formation of democratic ideals within the Greek national and constitutional identity, evaluates the first three Revolutionary Constitutions (Epidaurus 1822, Astros 1823, and Troezen 1827), and maps the evolution of popular sovereignty and human rights protections under the influence of the European Enlightenment, the American Revolution (1776), and the French Revolution (1789) <ref>Zois, G.Th. (2021). Two Centuries of Greek Constitutionalism: The First Revolutionary Constitutions. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 13(2), 223–231.</ref>.

== Overview ==
Authored by [[Georgios Th. Zois]] (PhD Candidate in Public Law at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens), this paper analyzes the emergence of the Greek constitutional tradition during the 1821 War of Independence <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 223, 224.</ref>. Greek constitutionalism grew out of the European and Modern Greek Enlightenment (spearheaded by Rigas Feraios through his 1797 work *New Political Constitution*) <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 224, 225.</ref>. During the revolution, three National Assemblies enacted three pioneering constitutions: 
# ''The Epidaurus Constitution (1822)'', declaring independence and establishing provisional government structures <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 225–227.</ref>;
# ''The Astros Constitution (1823)'', strengthening parliament, abolishing slavery, and guaranteeing freedom of the press <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 227, 228.</ref>;
# ''The Troezen Constitution (1827)'', explicitly proclaiming popular sovereignty and a strict separation of powers <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 228, 229.</ref>.

== Legal Basis ==
* '''The First Three Revolutionary Constitutions of Greece''':
** ''Provisional Constitution of Greece / Epidaurus Constitution (January 1, 1822)'': Drafted by a 12-member committee with contributions from Italian revolutionary Vincenzo Gallina and Alexandros Mavrokordatos <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 225, 226.</ref>.
** ''Constitution of Astros (April 1823)'': Enacted by the Second National Assembly at Astros <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 227, 228.</ref>.
** ''Political Constitution of Greece / Troezen Constitution (May 1, 1827)'': Enacted by the Third National Assembly at Troezen <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 228, 229.</ref>.
* '''Early Constitutional Works & International Treaties''':
** ''New Political Constitution of Rigas Feraios (1797)'' <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 224, 225.</ref>.
** ''London Protocol (February 3, 1830)'' <ref>Zois (2021), p. 230.</ref>.
* '''Subsequent Greek Constitutions''': Constitutions of 1864, 1911, 1927 (Second Hellenic Republic), 1952, and 1975.

== Background & Policy Context ==
Prior to the 1821 War of Independence, liberal and democratic concepts spread across Greek society via the Modern Greek Enlightenment <ref>Zois (2021), p. 224.</ref>. The Declaration of Independence on January 15, 1822, highlighted the urgent necessity of organizing the Greek nation under a written constitution to replace regional provisional bodies (Peloponnesian Senate, Western & Eastern Continental Greece) and present a unified political state to European powers (Great Britain, France, Russia) <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 225, 226.</ref>.

== Policy Objectives ==
# Establish an independent, internationally recognized Greek national state <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 225, 226, 230.</ref>.
# Prevent arbitrary rule by limiting state power and enforcing the separation of powers <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 223, 228, 229.</ref>.
# Guarantee basic human rights, equal rights under the law, freedom of the press, and the total abolition of slavery and torture <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 227–229.</ref>.

== Scope & Key Provisions ==
1. '''Epidaurus Constitution (1822)''': Composed of 110 paragraphs, guaranteed equality before the law, outlawed torture, protected property, and divided authority between an Executive Body (5 members) and a Legislative Body <ref>Zois (2021), p. 227.</ref>. It received praise from philosopher Jeremy Bentham in 1823 <ref>Zois (2021), p. 227.</ref>.
2. '''Astros Constitution (1823)''': Abolished slavery entirely on Greek soil, guaranteed press freedom, and reduced executive veto power from absolute to suspensive <ref>Zois (2021), p. 228.</ref>.
3. '''Troezen Constitution (1827)''': The most democratic constitution of its time; explicitly declared that sovereignty lies with the people (*Article 5*), instituted a single executive under Governor Ioannis Kapodistrias (7-year term), and mandated a strict separation of powers (*Article 36*) <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 228, 229.</ref>.

== Implementation & Policy Gaps ==
* '''Implementation Hurdles''': The operational implementation of these constitutions was severely hindered by ongoing warfare against Ottoman forces and internal civil strife in 1824 <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 228–230.</ref>. In January 1828, Governor Kapodistrias suspended the 1827 Constitution due to national emergency conditions <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 229, 230.</ref>.
* '''Institutional Paralysis''': The 1822 Epidaurus model caused gridlock due to co-equal powers between the legislative branch and the collective executive body <ref>Zois (2021), p. 227.</ref>.
* '''Foreign Monarchy Intervention''': The 1830 London Protocol imposed an absolute monarchy under King Otto of Bavaria (1832–1844), temporarily interrupting democratic constitutional development <ref>Zois (2021), p. 230.</ref>.

== Impact & Legacy ==
Despite short operational lifespans, the core pillars of popular sovereignty and fundamental civil rights established in these revolutionary documents served as enduring doctrinal foundations for all subsequent Greek Constitutions (1864, 1911, 1927, 1952, and 1975) <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 229, 230.</ref>.

* '''[[Ioannis Kapodistrias]]''': First Governor of Greece, elected by the Third National Assembly at Troezen in 1827 <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 228–230.</ref>.

'''Quadro Politico del Costituzionalismo Greco: Le Prime Costituzioni Rivoluzionarie''' (''Two Centuries of Greek Constitutionalism: The First Revolutionary Constitutions'') è un quadro di analisi storico-giuridica e di diritto costituzionale formulato da Georgios Th. Zois per esaminare i fondamenti del costituzionalismo moderno in Grecia e la formazione dell'idealismo democratico nell'identità nazionale e costituzionale greca; valutare le prime tre Costituzioni Rivoluzionarie (Epidauro 1822, Astro 1823 e Trezene 1827); e mappare l'evoluzione del principio di sovranità popolare e la tutela dei diritti umani sotto l'influenza dell'Illuminismo europeo, della Rivoluzione Americana (1776) e della Rivoluzione Francese (1789) <ref>Zois, G.Th. (2021). Two Centuries of Greek Constitutionalism: The First Revolutionary Constitutions. ''Italian Journal of Public Law'', 13(2), 223–231.</ref>.

== Sintesi ==
Scritto da [[Georgios Th. Zois]] (dottorando in Diritto Pubblico presso l'Università Nazionale e Capodistriana di Atene), l'articolo analizza la nascita della tradizione costituzionale greca durante la Guerra d'Indipendenza del 1821 <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 223, 224.</ref>. Il costituzionalismo greco si è sviluppato dall'Illuminismo europeo e dal Neogreco Illuminismo (promosso da Rigas Feraios attraverso l'opera *Nuova Costituzione Politica* del 1797) <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 224, 225.</ref>. Durante il periodo rivoluzionario, tre Assemblee Nazionali hanno approvato tre costituzioni pioniere:
# ''La Costituzione di Epidauro (1822)'', che proclamò l'indipendenza e istituì una struttura di governo provvisorio <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 225–227.</ref>;
# ''La Costituzione di Astro (1823)'', che rafforzò il parlamento, abolì la schiavitù e garantì la libertà di stampa <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 227, 228.</ref>;
# ''La Costituzione di Trezene (1827)'', che proclamò esplicitamente la sovranità popolare e la separazione dei poteri <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 228, 229.</ref>.

== Base Giuridica ==
* '''Le Prime Tre Costituzioni Rivoluzionarie della Grecia''':
** ''Costituzione Provvisoria della Grecia / Costituzione di Epidauro (1 gennaio 1822)'': Redatta da un comitato di 12 membri con il contributo del rivoluzionario italiano Vincenzo Gallina e di Alexandros Mavrokordatos <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 225, 226.</ref>.
** ''Costituzione di Astro (aprile 1823)'': Approvata dalla Seconda Assemblea Nazionale ad Astro <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 227, 228.</ref>.
** ''Costituzione Politica della Grecia / Costituzione di Trezene (1 maggio 1827)'': Approvata dalla Terza Assemblea Nazionale a Trezene <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 228, 229.</ref>.
* '''Opere Costituzionali Primarie e Trattati Internazionali''':
** ''Nuova Costituzione Politica di Rigas Feraios (1797)'' <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 224, 225.</ref>.
** ''Protocollo di Londra (3 febbraio 1830)'' <ref>Zois (2021), p. 230.</ref>.
* '''Costituzioni Greche Successive''': Costituzioni del 1864, 1911, 1927 (Seconda Repubblica Ellenica), 1952 e 1975.

== Contesto e Obiettivi ==
Prima della Guerra d'Indipendenza del 1821, le idee liberali e democratiche si diffusero nella società greca grazie all'Illuminismo Neogreco <ref>Zois (2021), p. 224.</ref>. La Dichiarazione d'Indipendenza del 15 gennaio 1822 sottolineò la necessità urgente di organizzare la nazione greca sotto una costituzione scritta per sostituire i governi regionali provvisori e presentare uno Stato unificato alle grandi potenze europee (Regno Unito, Francia, Russia) <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 225, 226.</ref>.

I principali obiettivi politici includevano:
1. Fondare uno Stato nazionale greco indipendente e riconosciuto a livello internazionale <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 225, 226, 230.</ref>.
2. Prevenire l'autoritarismo limitando il potere statale e applicando la separazione dei poteri <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 223, 228, 229.</ref>.
3. Garantire i diritti umani fondamentali, l'uguaglianza davanti alla legge, la libertà di stampa e l'abolizione totale della schiavitù e della tortura <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 227–229.</ref>.

== Disposizioni Principali e Ambito ==
1. '''Costituzione di Epidauro (1822)''': Composta da 110 paragrafi, garantiva l'uguaglianza dei cittadini di fronte alla legge, proibiva la tortura, tutelava la proprietà e divideva il potere tra un Organo Esecutivo (5 membri) e un Organo Legislativo <ref>Zois (2021), p. 227.</ref>. Fu elogiata dal filosofo Jeremy Bentham nel 1823 <ref>Zois (2021), p. 227.</ref>.
2. '''Costituzione di Astro (1823)''': Abolì completamente la schiavitù sul suolo greco, garantì la libertà di stampa e ridusse il veto esecutivo da assoluto a sospensivo <ref>Zois (2021), p. 228.</ref>.
3. '''Costituzione di Trezene (1827)''': La costituzione più democratica dell'epoca; proclamò esplicitamente che la sovranità risiede nel popolo (*Articolo 5*), istituì un esecutivo monocratico sotto il Governatore Ioannis Kapodistrias (mandato di 7 anni) e impose una rigorosa separazione dei poteri (*Articolo 36*) <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 228, 229.</ref>.

== Attuazione e Criticità Politiche ==
* '''Ostacoli all'Attuazione''': L'applicazione pratica di queste costituzioni fu fortemente ostacolata dal conflitto continuo contro l'Impero Ottomano e dalle guerre civili interne del 1824 <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 228–230.</ref>. Nel gennaio 1828, il Governatore Kapodistrias sospese la Costituzione del 1827 a causa dell'emergenza nazionale <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 229, 230.</ref>.
* '''Paralisi Istituzionale''': La Costituzione del 1822 creò una situazione di stallo a causa della parità di potere tra il parlamento e l'esecutivo collettivo <ref>Zois (2021), p. 227.</ref>.
* '''Intervento Monarchico Straniero''': Il Protocollo di Londra del 1830 impose una monarchia assoluta sotto Re Ottone di Baviera (1832–1844), interrompendo temporaneamente lo sviluppo costituzionale democratico <ref>Zois (2021), p. 230.</ref>.

== Grafico della Conoscenza ed Entità Correlate ==
* '''[[Georgios Th. Zois]]''': Autore principale / Dottorando in Diritto Pubblico presso l'NKUA <ref>Zois (2021), p. 223.</ref>.
* '''[[National and Kapodistrian University of Athens|Università Nazionale e Capodistriana di Atene]]''': Istituzione accademica dell'autore <ref>Zois (2021), p. 223.</ref>.
* '''[[Ioannis Kapodistrias]]''': Primo Governatore della Grecia, eletto dalla Terza Assemblea Nazionale a Trezene nel 1827 <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 228–230.</ref>.
* '''[[Cecep Mustafa]]''': ''[[ENTITY IDENTITY UNCERTAIN|Non trovato nelle fonti disponibili.]]'' <ref>Zois (2021), pp. 223–231.</ref>

title: Juvenile Diversion Indicator
wikitext:
{{Knowledge|id=RENSTRA-INDICATOR-1.10-DICTIONARY|type=Indicator Definition|domain=Juvenile Justice|jurisdiction=Indonesia|source=Renstra Mahkamah Agung 2025–2029|evidence=E3 — Official Primary Source|ai_readiness=5|status=VERIFIED}}

= Juvenile Diversion Performance Indicator =
The indicator measures successful resolution of juvenile cases through diversion.

== Eligibility ==
The Renstra identifies eligible cases as those carrying a maximum imprisonment threat below seven years and which are not repeat offences.

== Successful Diversion ==
Success requires:

* a determination that diversion was successful; and
* a judicial determination terminating examination of the case.

== Formula ==
<nowiki><math> \frac{\text{Juvenile cases successfully resolved through diversion}} {\text{Juvenile cases completing diversion}}\times100\% </math></nowiki>

= Knowledge Management =
'''Knowledge management''' concerns the processes, systems, people, technologies, and governance mechanisms used to create, capture, organize, preserve, discover, share, and reuse knowledge.

== Judicial Knowledge Management ==
In judicial environments, knowledge management may connect:

* Laws
* Decisions
* Procedures
* Policies
* Research
* Training
* Institutional experience
* Data
* Technology

== Knowledge Lifecycle ==
'''CREATE''' → '''CAPTURE''' → '''CLASSIFY''' → '''STORE''' → '''CONNECT''' → '''RETRIEVE''' → '''REUSE''' → '''UPDATE''' → '''ARCHIVE'''

== Knowledge Repository ==
A repository may contain:

* Documents
* Structured pages
* Metadata
* Datasets
* Multimedia
* References
* Learning materials

== Wiki as Knowledge Infrastructure ==
A MediaWiki-based repository can provide:

* Version history
* Internal links
* Categories
* Templates
* Structured metadata
* Search
* Collaborative editing
* Knowledge navigation

A wiki is a tool; its value depends on governance, content quality, structure, and maintenance.

== Knowledge Graph ==
Knowledge management becomes more powerful when entities and relationships are explicitly represented.

Example:

Court → decides → Case

Case → applies → Law

Law → protects → Right

AI System → affects → Judicial Process

== AI and Knowledge Management ==
AI can assist with:

* Classification
* Summarization
* Metadata
* Search
* Translation
* Relationship discovery
* Duplicate detection
* Updating

Human verification remains essential.

== Knowledge Governance ==
Governance should address:

* Ownership
* Access
* Editorial standards
* Versioning
* Verification
* Security
* Retention
* Archiving

KNOWLEDGE]], [[Supreme Court of Indonesia (Mahkamah Agung RI)]], [[Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy (Pustrajak)]], [[Direktori Putusan]], [[SIPP]], == Core Definition == The **Landmark Decisions** repository (*Putusan Landmark*) is the specialized jurisprudential sub-hub within the Judicial Knowledge Hub that collects, analyzes, and indexes pivotal Supreme Court and Constitutional Court rulings that establish binding legal precedents, resolve major statutory ambiguities, or fundamentally transform national legal doctrine. * **Simple Definition:** The curated collection of the most important, game-changing court rulings in Indonesian history that set binding rules for all future judges to follow. * **Legal / Technical Definition:** The institutional repository implementing semantic vector indexing and jurimetric metadata tagging across landmark verdicts (*Putusan Mahkamah Agung* and *Putusan Mahkamah Konstitusi*), extracting their core *ratio decidendi* while enforcing Tier 1 epistemic verification and data anonymization (*anonimisasi putusan*). * **Plain-Language Explanation: '''It acts as the "hall of fame" for judicial rulings, making it instantly clear how past supreme court decisions shaped modern Indonesian law and how lower courts must rule on similar cases today.''' == Why It Matters == * **Establishes Binding Precedents (*Jurisprudensi*):** Provides lower-court judges with clear, authoritative interpretations of complex statutes to ensure consistent rulings nationwide. * **Resolves Statutory Ambiguities:** Clarifies conflicting or vague provisions in parliamentary statutes, bridging the gap between legislative text and real-world justice. * **Drives Legal Evolution:** Documents how judicial interpretation adapts existing codes to modern realities, such as digital transactions, cybercrime (*UU ITE*), and human rights protection. * **Powers Advanced Legal Research:** Equips researchers, policy analysts (*Hakim Yustisial*), and advocates with structured *ratio decidendi* summaries for academic drafting and litigation. == Key Principles == ; Principle of Binding Precedential Authority (Asas Kekuatan Mengikat Preseden / Jurisprudensi) * **Meaning:** Landmark rulings delivered by the Supreme Court establish authoritative guidance that appellate and district courts must follow unless distinct factual or legal exceptions justify departure. * **Why It Matters:** Essential for maintaining legal certainty (*kepastian hukum*) and preventing chaotic, contradictory rulings across regional courts. * **Legal Basis / Source:** Law No. 48 of 2009 on Judicial Power; Supreme Court Chamber Guidelines. * **Related Concepts:** *Stare decisis*, jurisprudence, binding precedent. ; Principle of Ratio Decidendi Extraction (Asas Ekstraksi Ratio Decidendi) * **Meaning:** Curation of landmark decisions must focus strictly on the core legal reasoning (*ratio decidendi*) rather than incidental remarks (*obiter dicta*), ensuring future courts apply the true legal principle established by the ruling. * **Why It Matters:** Prevents misapplication of court verdicts to factual scenarios not contemplated by the original bench. * **Legal Basis / Source:** Master Philosophical & Methodological Standard; Pustrajak Curation Guidelines. * **Related Concepts:** Ratio decidendi, legal reasoning, judicial holding. ; Principle of Epistemic Integrity and Verification (Asas Integritas Epistemik Putusan) * **Meaning:** Summaries and metadata attached to landmark decisions must undergo rigorous Tier 1 source verification against official court archives before publication in the hub. * **Why It Matters:** Protects legal researchers and automated RAG AI tools from relying on misquoted or unverified case summaries. * **Legal Basis / Source:** Master Epistemic & Quality Control Standard. * **Related Concepts:** Source verification, anti-fabrication safeguards, verified jurisprudence. == Legal / == Important Decisions & Jurisprudential Milestones == * Decision: Supreme Court Landmark Ruling on Electronic Evidence Admissibility * *Issuing Body:* Mahkamah Agung RI (Criminal Chamber Plenary) * *Case Reference:* Landmark Precedent on UU ITE Electronic Records * *Legal Principle:* Electronic documents and digital logs presented with cryptographic hash verification constitute legally valid primary evidence under Article 5 of the UU ITE. * *Why It Matters:* Set the binding national precedent for cybercrime prosecution and digital forensics. * *Official Source:* Supreme Court Jurisprudence Reports. == Key Legislation & Standards == * Instrument: Law No. 48 of 2009 on Judicial Power. * *Jurisdiction:* Indonesia. * *Status:* In force. * *Relevant Provisions:* Mandates that courts examine cases based on living law and uphold supreme jurisprudence. * Instrument: Supreme Court Regulation on Direktori Putusan and Judgment Publication. == Timeline == {| class="wikitable Knowledge Hub RAG Suite |Enabled semantic AI querying across all indexed landmark decisions. |- |'''2045-08-18''' |Golden Indonesia Centenary Target |Full digital indexing of a century of supreme jurisprudence for the nation's centenary. |} == Debates & Controversies == * Debate: Strict Precedent Adherence (*Stare Decisis*) vs. Judicial Adaptability (*Hukum Progresif*) * *Position A (Strict Precedent):* Lower courts must follow Supreme Court landmark decisions rigidly to ensure national legal predictability and equality. * *Position B (Progressive Adaptation):* Rigid adherence to aging precedents can trap the law in outdated paradigms; judges must retain flexibility to deliver substantive justice (*hukum progresif*). * *Evidence:* Judicial debates surrounding landmark rulings on changing social and economic conditions. * *Current Status:* Harmonized through established doctrine: landmark precedents bind lower courts unless distinguished by fundamentally novel factual or statutory circumstances. == Rule-of-Law Connection == * *Legal Certainty:* Landmark decisions eliminate conflicting interpretations across thousands of district courts, reinforcing predictable contract and criminal enforcement. * *Transparency:* Open public access to binding precedents allows citizens and businesses to understand legal boundaries clearly. == AI & Future of Law == * *RAG AI Landmark Retrieval:* Allowing judges and lawyers to query the Landmark Decisions sub-hub using natural language to retrieve precise *ratio decidendi* instantly. * *Automated Precedent Mapping:* AI knowledge graphs mapping how newer landmark rulings modify, affirm, or overrule older supreme court precedents over time. == Common Misconceptions == * *Myth:* Every single verdict issued by a district court automatically becomes a "landmark decision." * *Reality:* Only pivotal rulings from the Supreme Court or Constitutional Court that establish novel legal principles or unify conflicting interpretations are curated as landmark decisions. * *Source:* Pustrajak Precedent Curation Standards. * *Myth:* Landmark decisions carry the exact same formal legislative weight as parliamentary statutes. * *Reality:* While highly authoritative and practically binding under judicial practice (*jurisprudensi tetap*), judicial precedents operate below statutory law in the formal norm hierarchy (Law No. 12/2011). * *Source:* Normative Hierarchy Doctrine. == Practical Example == * *Scenario:* A commercial judge in Surabaya is presiding over a complex cross-border e-commerce contract dispute involving digital signatures and electronic breach of contract notices. * *Question:* How does the judge utilize the Landmark Decisions repository? * *Applicable Principle:* Binding Precedential Authority & Ratio Decidendi (Landmark Decisions Hub). * *Analysis:* 1. The judge navigates to the Judicial Knowledge Hub -> Landmark Decisions sub-hub. 2. Searches for recent Supreme Court landmark rulings concerning electronic signatures and UU ITE contract validity. 3. Extracts the core *ratio decidendi* from the supreme precedent and applies the legal reasoning to resolve the Surabaya commercial dispute consistently. * *Limitation:* Precedents provide authoritative guidance, but the judge must carefully verify that the factual matrix of the current case matches the cited landmark ruling. == Key Terms == {| class="wikitable" style="width:100%;" !Term !Definition !Related Term |- |'''Ratio Decidendi''' |The crucial legal reasoning and principle upon which a landmark judicial decision is founded. |Precedent, Landmark Decisions |- |'''Jurisprudensi Tetap''' |Established supreme court jurisprudence that lower courts consistently follow as binding authority. |Precedent, Stare Decisis |- |'''Direktori Putusan''' |The official national open-data portal indexing raw court judgments prior to landmark curation. |Open Data, SIPP |- |'''Obiter Dicta''' |Incidental remarks or judicial observations made in a judgment that do not form part of the binding ratio decidendi. |Legal Reasoning, Precedent |} == Related Wiki Pages == * [[JUDICIAL KNOWLEDGE]] * [[Supreme Court of Indonesia (Mahkamah Agung RI)]] * [[Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy (Pustrajak)]] * [[Direktori Putusan]] * [[SIPP]] * == Knowledge Relationships == * '''Landmark Decisions''' → *is a sub-hub of* → [[JUDICIAL KNOWLEDGE]] * '''Landmark Decisions''' → *curated by* → [[Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy (Pustrajak)]] & [[Supreme Court of Indonesia (Mahkamah Agung RI)]] * '''Landmark Decisions''' → *derived from* → [[Direktori Putusan]] & [[SIPP]] * '''Landmark Decisions''' → *align with* → [[Master Epistemic & Quality Control Standard]] & [[Master Philosophical & Methodological Standard]] * '''Landmark Decisions''' → *uphold principles of* → [[Law No. 48/2009 (Judicial Power)]] & [[1945 Constitution of Indonesia (Article 24)]] == Sources == === Tier 1 — Official / Primary Sources === # {{CanonicalID|WIKI-LEGISLATION-UU-ITE-1-2024}} == Knowledge Metadata == * '''Title:''' Law No. 1 of 2024 (Second Amendment to UU ITE): Electronic Evidence, Cybercrime Regulation, and Digital Space Governance * '''Canonical Topic:''' Law No. 1 of 2024 Amending UU ITE (Electronic Information and Transactions) * '''Topic Type:''' Law / Statute / Master Cyber Law Instrument * '''Jurisdiction:''' Indonesia * '''Legal Domain:''' Cyber Law, Criminal Law, Electronic Evidence, Information Technology, Administrative Law * '''Status:''' Stable / Active Master Cyber Statute * '''Last Reviewed:''' 2026-08-27 * '''Next Review Recommended:''' 2027-08-27 * '''Primary Sources:''' Law No. 1 of 2024 (Second Amendment to Law No. 11 of 2008 on Electronic Information and Transactions), Law No. 11 of 2008, Law No. 19 of 2016, Criminal Procedure Code (KUHAP), State Gazette of the Republic of Indonesia. * '''Related Wiki Pages:''' [[Judicial Knowledge Hub]], [[Cybercrime & Digital Forensics in courts]], [[ISO/IEC 27037]], [[Master System Design Blueprint]], [[Supreme Court of Indonesia (Mahkamah Agung RI)]] == Core Definition == ** Law No. 1 of 2024** (formally enacting the second amendment to **Law No. 11 of 2008 on Electronic Information and Transactions** / **UU ITE**) is the primary national statutory framework governing electronic commerce, digital transactions, cybercrime definitions, online content moderation, and the legal admissibility of electronic evidence across Indonesian courts. * **Simple Definition:** The updated national cyber law that sets the rules for online behavior, regulates digital contracts, criminalizes cyber offenses like hacking and defamation, and ensures electronic files can be used as legal evidence in court. * **Legal / Technical Definition:** The master statutory instrument establishing the legal validity of electronic records and digital signatures (matching UNCITRAL model laws), defining prohibited cyber acts (such as illegal access, data tampering, and restructured defamation provisions), and empowering state authorities with electronic system oversight and child protection mandates. * **Plain-Language Explanation: '''It acts as the core legal foundation of Indonesia's digital space, balancing internet freedom and commercial growth with criminal accountability for cybercrime and the protection of electronic evidence.''' == Why It Matters == * **Validates Electronic Evidence in Courts:** Explicitly establishes that electronic information, electronic documents, and computer printouts constitute an extended, legally binding form of evidence (*alat bukti*) under Indonesian procedural law. * **Restructures Contentious Cybercrimes:** Refines controversial provisions from the original 2008 statute—such as defamation (Article 27A) and hate speech—to reduce potential over-criminalization and protect free expression. * **Strengthens Child Online Protection:** Introduces dedicated mandates requiring electronic system operators to enforce robust safety features and protections for minors utilizing digital platforms. * **Regulates Electronic Certification and Signatures:** Provides clear legal recognition for digital certificates and electronic signatures, securing e-commerce and digital banking transactions nationwide. == Key Principles == ; Principle of Legal Certainty in Digital Spaces (Asas Kepastian Hukum Ruang Digital) * **Meaning:** Electronic transactions, digital communications, and cyber operations must be governed by transparent, predictable legal rules to protect users and foster economic trust. * **Why It Matters:** Essential for securing national e-commerce and preventing fraudulent online practices. * **Legal Basis / Source:** Law No. 1/2024 Art. 3; UNCITRAL Model Law Framework. * **Related Concepts:** E-commerce security, digital legal certainty, electronic contracts. ; Principle of Electronic Evidence Admissibility (Asas Validitas Alat Bukti Elektronik) * **Meaning:** Computer records, logs, and digital files processed through compliant electronic systems possess equivalent legal weight to traditional physical documents in judicial proceedings. * **Why It Matters:** Enables courts to prosecute modern cybercriminals using native digital artifacts. * **Legal Basis / Source:** Law No. 1/2024 Art. 5; Criminal Procedure Code (KUHAP). * **Related Concepts:** Electronic document, cryptographic integrity, digital forensics. ; Principle of Proportionality in Cyber Enforcement (Asas Proporsionalitas Penegakan Hukum Siber) * **Meaning:** Restrictions on digital speech and enforcement of cyber offenses must be applied proportionally, safeguarding individual reputations while upholding public order. * **Why It Matters:** Prevents the statute from being misused to stifle legitimate criticism or public debate. * **Legal Basis / Source:** Law No. 1/2024 Explanatory Memorandum; Constitutional Court Jurisprudence. * **Related Concepts:** Defamation balance, freedom of expression, state moderation. == Legal / Institutional Framework == 
1945 Constitution of the Republic of Indonesia (Freedom of Expression & Due Process)
       ↓
Law No. 11 of 2008 on Electronic Information and Transactions (Original UU ITE)
       ↓
Law No. 19 of 2016 (First Amendment)
       ↓
Law No. 1 of 2024 (Second Amendment / Current UU ITE Consolidated Framework):
- Recognition of Electronic Evidence & Signatures (Articles 5 & 6)
- Restructured Prohibited Acts (Defamation under Art. 27A, Hacking under Arts. 30–32)
- Child Protection & Electronic System Operator Obligations (Article 16 & 17)
       ↓
Adjudication & Execution across Courts via SIPP, ISO/IEC 27037 Forensics, & Direktori Putusan
== Indonesia Section == * **Evolutionary Context:** Enacted initially as **Law No. 11 of 2008**, amended by **Law No. 19 of 2016**, and comprehensively revised via **Law No. 1 of 2024**, the statute represents Indonesia’s primary legislative response to rapid digital transformation. * **Key Structural Changes Introduced in Law No. 1/2024:** 1. *Refined Defamation Clauses:* Separated and clarified defamation provisions (relocated to Article 27A), establishing them explicitly as complaint-based offenses (*delik aduan*) requiring direct victim reports. 2. *Expanded Evidentiary Scope:* Clarified that electronic documents, system printouts, and digital logs are valid extensions of evidence under Indonesian procedural codes. 3. *Platform Accountability:* Imposed clearer administrative and operational guidelines for Electronic System Operators (*Penyelenggara Sistem Elektronik / PSE*). * **Nomenclature:** Undang-Undang Nomor 1 Tahun 2024 tentang Perubahan Kedua atas UU Nomor 11 Tahun 2008 tentang Informasi dan Transaksi Elektronik — *Law No. 1 of 2024 (Second Amendment to UU ITE)*. == Comparative Perspective == | Jurisdiction | Master Cyber Law Statute | Electronic Evidence Recognition | Defamation & Speech Regulation | Cross-Border Jurisdiction | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Indonesia** | **Law No. 1 of 2024 (UU ITE Amendment)** | Explicitly recognized as valid legal evidence under Article 5. | Regulated via restructured criminal provisions (Art. 27A) as complaint-based offenses. | Extraterritorial reach over acts causing legal effect within Indonesia. | | **United States** | Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA) & Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA). | Self-authenticating electronic records under Federal Rules of Evidence (FRE 902). | Handled primarily through civil defamation tort law rather than federal criminal statutes. | Broad extraterritorial enforcement for federal cyber offenses affecting US infrastructure. | | **Singapore** | Computer Misuse Act (CMA) & Electronic Transactions Act (ETA). | Fully recognized electronic records and advanced digital signatures. | Strict criminal defamation and online falsehood laws (e.g., POFMA). | Extraterritorial jurisdiction over offenses impacting Singapore's national security or economy. | | **European Union** | Budapest Convention on Cybercrime & eIDAS Regulation. | Standardized across member states under eIDAS digital trust services. | Balanced under EU fundamental rights and national penal codes. | Harmonized cross-border investigative cooperation via e-CODEX. == Important Decisions & Regulatory Milestones == * Decision: Constitutional Court Reviews on UU ITE Defamation and Hate Speech Provisions * *Issuing Body:* Constitutional Court of Indonesia (Mahkamah Konstitusi) * *Case Reference:* Landmark Judicial Review Decisions on Articles 27 and 28 UU ITE * *Legal Principle:* To prevent arbitrary criminalization of free speech, defamation charges under the UU ITE must be treated strictly as complaints requiring personal victim standing, and provisions must not criminalize objective public criticism. * *Why It Matters:* Prompted legislative revisions culminating in Law No. 1/2024 to curb misuse of ambiguous clauses. * *Official Source:* Constitutional Court Reports. == Key Legislation & Standards == * Instrument: Law No. 1 of 2024 concerning the Second Amendment to Law No. 11 of 2008 on Information and Electronic Transactions (UU ITE). * *Jurisdiction:* Indonesia. * *Status:* In force. * *Relevant Provisions:* Articles 1 through 54 (Electronic evidence validity, prohibited cyber acts, data protection operators, and criminal penalties). * *Official Source:* State Gazette of the Republic of Indonesia. == Timeline == {| class="wikitable sortable" style="width:100%;" !Date !Milestone / Legislative Event !Significance |- |'''2008-04-21''' |Enactment of Law No. 11 of 2008 (Original UU ITE) |Established Indonesia's first comprehensive legal framework for electronic transactions and cybercrime. |- |'''2016-10-27''' |Enactment of Law No. 19 of 2016 (First Amendment) |Adjusted criminal penalties for defamation and added provisions regarding the right to be forgotten. |- |'''2024-01-02''' |Promulgation of Law No. 1 of 2024 (Second Amendment) |Restructured penalty thresholds, clarified defamation rules (Art. 27A), and reinforced electronic evidence standards. |- |'''2026-08-01''' |Integration into Master Knowledge Architecture |Standardized UU ITE citations across Pustrajak research repositories and Judicial Knowledge Hub nodes. |} == Debates & Controversies == * Debate: Protection of Individual Reputation vs. Freedom of Expression Online * *Position A (Pro-Strict Regulation):* Cyber defamation laws are vital to protect citizens from malicious online bullying, character assassination, and harassment on social media. * *Position B (Pro-Free Speech Reform):* Ambiguous cyber defamation clauses have historically been weaponized as "rubber articles" (*pasal karet*) to silence investigative journalists, activists, and political critics. * *Evidence:* High-profile criminal prosecutions under earlier versions of the UU ITE. * *Current Status:* Partially addressed in Law No. 1/2024 by introducing explicit exceptions for public interest disclosures and making defamation a complaint-based offense, though civil society groups continue monitoring implementation. == Rule-of-Law Connection == * *Legal Certainty:* Provides clear statutory definitions for cyber offenses, enabling prosecutors and judges to penalize digital fraud and hacking consistently. * *Evidentiary Modernization:* Formally anchors digital forensic science into national procedural law, allowing courts to process modern electronic evidence. * *Balancing Rights:* Seeks equilibrium between punishing malicious cyber actors and protecting citizens' constitutional right to communicate freely. == AI & Future of Law == * *AI-Generated Defamation and Deepfakes:* Utilizing Law No. 1/2024 provisions to prosecute malicious actors who deploy generative AI to create and distribute deepfake pornography or fraudulent impersonations online. * *Automated Content Filtering Oversight:* Balancing state electronic system oversight powers with judicial review to ensure AI content moderation remains transparent and proportionate. == Common Misconceptions == * *Myth:* Law No. 1 of 2024 completely decriminalized online defamation in Indonesia. * *Reality:* Online defamation was not abolished; rather, it was restructured (relocated to Article 27A) with reduced maximum prison sentences and a requirement that it must be prosecuted as a personal complaint (*delik aduan*). * *Source:* Law No. 1 of 2024 Article 27A. * *Myth:* Digital screenshots of text messages are automatically accepted by courts as conclusive proof under UU ITE without verification. * *Reality:* While Article 5 recognizes electronic documents as valid evidence, courts still require expert forensic verification and chain-of-custody proof to ensure screenshots or files have not been fabricated. * *Source:* Cybercrime Adjudication Benchbooks; ISO/IEC 27037. == Practical Example == * *Scenario:* A business owner discovers a competitor is running an automated botnet attack that hacks into their e-commerce server database, stealing customer records and altering pricing files. * *Question:* How do prosecutors apply Law No. 1 of 2024 to prosecute the offense? * *Applicable Principle:* Illegal Access and Data Interference (Law No. 1/2024 Arts. 30 & 32). * *Analysis:* 1. Law enforcement cyber units seize server logs and deploy ISO/IEC 27037 forensic write-blockers to extract digital evidence. 2. Prosecutors file charges under Article 30 (illegal system intrusion) and Article 32 (unauthorized alteration or transmission of electronic documents) of Law No. 1/2024. 3. The court admits the forensic server logs as valid electronic evidence under Article 5, resulting in a criminal conviction. * *Limitation:* Prosecution requires identifying the physical or digital perpetrators behind proxy servers, which often demands international mutual legal assistance (MLA). == Key Terms == {| class="wikitable" style="width:100%;" !Term !Definition !Related Term |- |'''UU Negara Republik Indonesia Tahun 2009 Nomor 157''), Law No. 14/1985 on the Supreme Court, Law No. 24/2003 on the Constitutional Court. * '''Related Wiki Pages:''' [[Judicial Knowledge Hub]], [[Supreme Court of Indonesia (Mahkamah Agung RI)]], [[Master Institutional Architecture]], [[Strategic Governance Framework]], [[Master Jurisprudential & Legal Theory Framework]], [[Center for Legal and Judicial Policy Strategy (Pustrajak)]] == Core Definition == ** Law No. 48 of 2009 on Judicial Power** (*Undang-Undang Nomor 48 Tahun 2009 tentang Kekuasaan Kehakiman*) is the primary national statutory enactment that operationalizes Chapter IX of the 1945 Constitution, defining the organization, independence, guarantees, and foundational principles governing all state judicial power in Indonesia. * **Simple Definition:** The primary national law passed by parliament that guarantees court independence, defines how the court system is organized, and sets the core ethical and procedural rules that all judges must follow. * **Legal / Technical Definition:** The master statutory instrument regulating the separation of judicial authority between the Supreme Court and the Constitutional Court, establishing the four specialized judicial branches (*Empat Lingkungan Peradilan*), prohibiting external interference, mandating reasoned judgments (Article 50), and enforcing the judicial duty to explore unwritten living law (Article 5). * **Plain-Language Explanation:** It acts as the legal cornerstone of the entire justice system, ensuring that judges are completely independent, free from political pressure, and bound solely by the law, justice, and the constitution when resolving disputes. == Why It Matters == * **Guarantees Absolute Judicial Independence:** Codifies constitutional safeguards ensuring that judges render verdicts free from pressure, influence, or intervention by executive or legislative branches. * **Establishes the Four Judicial Jurisdictions:** Formally structures the specialized court branches (General, Religious, State Administrative, and Military Courts) under the Supreme Court. * **Mandates Substantive Justice and Living Law:** Directs judges not to act as mere mechanical mouthpieces of statutes, but to actively explore unwritten customary norms and community justice values (*hukum yang hidup*). * **Enforces Strict Adjudication Accountability:** Requires every court decision to contain comprehensive legal reasoning and factual evaluations (Article 50), protecting litigants against arbitrary rulings. == Key Principles == ; Principle of Independent Judicial Authority (Asas Kekuasaan Kehakiman yang Merdeka) * **Meaning:** Judicial power is an independent power possessed by state courts to administer justice to uphold law and justice, completely free from interference by other state organs. * **Why It Matters:** Absolute prerequisite for the separation of powers and the protection of civil liberties against state overreach. * **Legal Basis / Source:** 1945 Constitution Art. 24(1); Law No. 48/2009 Arts. 1 & 3. * **Related Concepts:** Judicial independence, separation of powers, anti-interference. ; Principle of Simple, Fast, and Low-Cost Justice (Asas Peradilan Sederhana, Cepat, dan Biaya Ringan) * **Meaning:** Courts must administer justice efficiently, avoiding bureaucratic delays and financial barriers that prevent ordinary citizens from accessing legal remedies. * **Why It Matters:** Combats procedural backlogs and ensures timely, economically viable access to justice. * **Legal Basis / Source:** Law No. 48/2009 Art. 2(4); Access to justice. * **Related Concepts:** Procedural economy, small claims, e-Court efficiency. ; Principle of Duty to Explore Living Law and Prohibit Non Liquet (Asas Kewajiban Menggali Hukum dan Larangan Non Liquet) * **Meaning:** Judges are prohibited from refusing to examine or decide a case on the grounds that the written law is unclear or absent (*non liquet*); instead, they have a statutory duty to explore unwritten customary norms and community values. * **Why It Matters:** Prevents legal vacuums and ensures justice is delivered even in novel or complex disputes. * **Legal Basis / Source:** Law No. 48/2009 Art. 5(1) & (2). * **Related Concepts:** Rechtsvinding, living law (*hukum yang hidup*), judicial gap-filling. == Legal / Institutional Framework ==

== Indonesia Section == * **Enactment & Reform Background:** Enacted on October 29, 2009, Law No. 48/2009 replaced earlier post-reform judicial power statutes (Law No. 4/2004 and Law No. 14/1970), consolidating the One-Roof administrative system (*Satu Atap*) and reinforcing the dual apex court model. * **Core Statutory Mandates for Judges:** 1. *Article 5(1):* Judges must explore, follow, and understand legal values and a sense of justice living in society (*hukum yang hidup dalam masyarakat*). 2. *Article 5(2):* Prohibition of *non liquet* — courts cannot refuse to try a case due to unclear or missing statutory law. 3. *Article 50(1):* Every court decision must be accompanied by the legal reasons and considerations (*pertimbangan hukum*) upon which the ruling is based. * **Nomenclature:** Undang-Undang Nomor 48 Tahun 2009 tentang Kekuasaan Kehakiman — *Law No. 48 of 2009 on Judicial Power*; Asas Kekuasaan Kehakiman — *Principles of Judicial Power*. == Comparative Perspective == {| class="wikitable sortable" style="width:100%;" !Jurisdiction !Master Judicial Power Statute !Constitutional Independence Guarantee !Judicial Gap-Filling Rule !Judge Reasoning Standard |- |'''Indonesia''' |**Law No. 48 of 2009 on Judicial Power** |Guaranteed under 1945 Constitution Art. 24 and Law 48/2009 Arts. 1 & 3. |Explicit statutory duty under Art. 5(1) to explore living law; == Important Decisions & Jurisprudential Milestones == * Decision: Constitutional Court Rulings on Judicial Independence and Ethics * *Issuing Body:* Constitutional Court of Indonesia (Mahkamah Konstitusi) * *Case Reference:* Landmark Constitutional Review Cases on Judicial Authority and Disciplinary Boundaries * *Legal Principle:* Provisions of Law No. 48/2009 must be interpreted to ensure that oversight bodies never infringe upon the core independence of judges in deciding active legal disputes. * *Why It Matters:* Reaffirmed the constitutional limits of administrative and ethical supervision over judicial decision-making. * *Official Source:* Constitutional Court Reports. == Key Legislation & Standards == * Instrument: Law on Judicial Power * *Number / Year:* Law No. 48 of 2009 * *Jurisdiction:* Indonesia * *Status:* In force * *Relevant Provisions:* Articles 1–123 (Independence of judiciary, organization of courts, trial principles, judicial ethics, and transitional provisions). * *Official Source:* State Gazette of the Republic of Indonesia. == Timeline == {| class="wikitable sortable" style="width:100%;" !Date !Milestone / Legislative Event !Significance |-
